answers.question: Find the smallest element in an array (keep a variable `min`, update it when you find something smaller).
answers.shortTitle: Find the smallest element in an array

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the smallest element is a linear scan where you seed a `min` variable with the first element and then iterate, replacing `min` whenever you find a value smaller than the current `min`. It is O(n) time and O(1) space, the mirror image of finding the maximum.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya runs a shop with current account CUR3001 and wants to know her smallest single sale of the day so she can decide a minimum order value. She points at her first sale and says "smallest so far." She reads each later sale, and every time a sale is smaller than the one her finger is on, she moves to that smaller one. At the end her finger rests on the smallest sale.
s1_definition.oneliner: Assume the first element is the smallest, then walk the array once and downgrade `min` whenever something smaller appears.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the smallest element is a linear scan where you seed a `min` variable with the first element and then iterate, replacing `min` whenever you find a value smaller than the current `min`. It is O(n) time and O(1) space, the mirror image of finding the maximum.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya runs a shop with current account CUR3001 and wants to know her smallest single sale of the day so she can decide a minimum order value. She points at her first sale and says "smallest so far." She reads each later sale, and every time a sale is smaller than the one her finger is on, she moves to that smaller one. At the end her finger rests on the smallest sale.

**One line to remember:** Assume the first element is the smallest, then walk the array once and downgrade `min` whenever something smaller appears.

sections.s2_technical:
The algorithm keeps one variable, `min`, that remembers the smallest value seen so far. You seed it with the first element rather than a huge constant like `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, because seeding with a real element is always correct and avoids guessing an upper bound — important in banking where amounts can be very large.

The loop runs from index 1 to the end. For each element you ask whether it is smaller than `min` using `compareTo`, where a result less than zero means the current element is smaller. For example `current.compareTo(min) < 0` means "this sale beats the record for smallest," so you set `min = current`.

Because we deal with money, amounts are `BigDecimal`. A `BigDecimal` of `100.00` and `100.0` are equal in value but have different scale; `compareTo` correctly treats them as equal, which is exactly what we want for comparisons. A senior nuance is again the empty array: there is no smallest of nothing, so we throw `IllegalArgumentException`.

Time complexity is O(n) and space is O(1). Just like finding the maximum, you cannot skip any element, because a skipped element might have been the smallest.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Priya wants to set a minimum order value for her shop and asks National Bank of India's merchant dashboard: "What was my smallest sale today?" The system holds today's sale amounts on CUR3001 and must find the single smallest one. This is exactly how the find-smallest algorithm works — we keep a running smallest and downgrade it as we scan.

Problem 2 — If there were no sales today, the list is empty and there is no smallest sale. Returning zero would wrongly suggest a zero-rupee sale happened, so we guard the empty case and throw a clear exception.

The code has an `Account` class holding the sale amounts, and a `SalesAnalyzer` class with a `findSmallestSale` method. The demo loads Priya's sales and logs the smallest.

Step 5 — Compare `640.00` with `min`. Not smaller than `250.75`, so `min` stays `250.75`.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the smallest element in an array is the mirror image of finding the largest, and I solve it with a single linear pass using constant extra space. I seed a minimum variable with the first element, then I iterate through the remaining elements, and whenever I find a value smaller than my current minimum I downgrade the minimum to that value. When the loop finishes, the minimum variable holds the smallest element. It is linear time because I visit each element once and constant space because I hold only one tracking variable.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to power a merchant dashboard feature for Priya, who runs a shop on a current account. She wanted to know her smallest sale of the day to decide a minimum order value, so I scan the list of today's sale amounts and return the smallest. Every amount is a BigDecimal, and I compare using the compareTo method where a negative result means the current value is smaller, because BigDecimal does not support the plain less-than operator.

I always seed the minimum with the first real element rather than a giant constant like Integer dot MAX underscore VALUE, because seeding with an actual element is guaranteed correct and I never have to guess an upper bound. I also guard the empty list: if the merchant had no sales today, there is no smallest sale, so I throw an IllegalArgumentException instead of returning a misleading zero. That guard keeps the feature honest in a real financial system.

answers.question: Count how many times a given number appears in an array (loop + counter).
answers.shortTitle: Count how many times a given number appears in an array

s1_definition.profdef: Counting occurrences is a linear scan where you walk the array and increment a counter each time an element equals the target value. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space. The only subtlety for money is comparing with `compareTo` (value equality) rather than `equals` (which also checks scale).
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh wants to know how many times exactly Rs.5000 was debited from his account SAV2001 this month, perhaps a recurring subscription. He reads each transaction in his passbook, and every time the amount is exactly Rs.5000 he makes a tally mark. At the end, the number of tally marks is the count.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk the array once with a counter, and add one to the counter every time an element matches the target.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Counting occurrences is a linear scan where you walk the array and increment a counter each time an element equals the target value. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space. The only subtlety for money is comparing with `compareTo` (value equality) rather than `equals` (which also checks scale).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh wants to know how many times exactly Rs.5000 was debited from his account SAV2001 this month, perhaps a recurring subscription. He reads each transaction in his passbook, and every time the amount is exactly Rs.5000 he makes a tally mark. At the end, the number of tally marks is the count.

**One line to remember:** Walk the array once with a counter, and add one to the counter every time an element matches the target.

sections.s2_technical:
You start a counter at zero. You loop through every element and compare it with the target. If they match, you increment the counter. There is no early exit, because the same value can appear multiple times anywhere in the array, so you must check every element.

For money, comparison must use `compareTo` returning zero, not `equals`. The reason is that `new BigDecimal("5000")` and `new BigDecimal("5000.00")` are the same amount but are NOT equal under `equals` because their scale differs. Using `target.compareTo(current) == 0` treats both as the same amount, which is what a bank customer expects. For plain `int` arrays you would simply use `==`.

Time complexity is O(n) because you examine every element. Space is O(1) because you keep only the counter. A senior nuance is deciding what "equal" means for your domain — for currency it is value equality, so `compareTo` is the correct tool.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India offers Rajesh a feature: "How many times was exactly Rs.5000 debited this month?" so he can spot recurring charges. The system holds his transaction amounts and must count how many equal the target. This is exactly how the count-occurrences algorithm works — loop and tally matches.

Problem 2 — The amounts might be stored with different scales, such as `5000` and `5000.00`, but the customer means the same amount. This is exactly why we compare with compareTo and value equality, not with equals, so scale differences do not cause us to miss a match.

The code has an `Account` holding amounts and a `TransactionCounter` class with a `countOccurrences` method. The demo counts how many times Rs.5000 appears.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Counting how many times a value appears in an array is a straightforward linear scan with a counter. I start a counter at zero, loop through every element, and increment the counter each time the element matches the target. There is no early exit because the target can appear anywhere, even multiple times, so I must inspect every element. The time complexity is linear and the space complexity is constant.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to build a recurring charge detector. Rajesh wanted to know how many times exactly five thousand rupees was debited this month so he could spot a subscription he forgot about. I loop through his transaction amounts and tally each one that equals five thousand.

The important nuance here is how I compare money. I compare BigDecimal values using the compareTo method and check for a result of zero, rather than using the equals method. The reason is that five thousand written as plain five thousand and five thousand written with two decimal places are the same amount of money, but the equals method considers them different because their scale differs. By using compareTo I treat them as equal in value, which is exactly what the customer means, so a scale difference in how the amount was stored never causes me to miss a genuine match.

answers.question: Check if a given number exists in an array (linear search — loop through and compare each element).
answers.shortTitle: Check if a given number exists in an array

s1_definition.profdef: Linear search walks the array from start to end comparing each element with the target. The moment a match is found it returns true (early exit); if the loop ends without a match it returns false. It runs in O(n) worst case and O(1) space, and it works on unsorted data, unlike binary search.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya wants to confirm whether a specific cheque of Rs.9800 was ever cleared on her account CUR3001. She reads cleared cheques one by one. The instant she sees Rs.9800 she says "yes, found it" and stops reading. If she reaches the end of the list without seeing it, she concludes it was never cleared.
s1_definition.oneliner: Scan the array and return true at the first match; return false only after checking every element.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Linear search walks the array from start to end comparing each element with the target. The moment a match is found it returns true (early exit); if the loop ends without a match it returns false. It runs in O(n) worst case and O(1) space, and it works on unsorted data, unlike binary search.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya wants to confirm whether a specific cheque of Rs.9800 was ever cleared on her account CUR3001. She reads cleared cheques one by one. The instant she sees Rs.9800 she says "yes, found it" and stops reading. If she reaches the end of the list without seeing it, she concludes it was never cleared.

**One line to remember:** Scan the array and return true at the first match; return false only after checking every element.

sections.s2_technical:
Linear search is the simplest search. You loop over each element and compare it with the target. The key efficiency feature is the early return: as soon as you find a match you stop, because you only need to know whether it exists, not how many times. If no element matches, you return false after the loop.

For money, comparison uses `compareTo` returning zero for value equality, so `target.compareTo(current) == 0` correctly matches `9800` and `9800.00`. For primitive `int` arrays you would use `==`.

The best case is O(1) when the target is the first element. The worst case is O(n) when the target is last or absent. Average case is O(n/2), which is still O(n). Space is O(1). Linear search is the right choice when the array is unsorted; if it were sorted you could use binary search for O(log n), but sorting first only pays off if you search many times.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Priya disputes a charge and National Bank of India needs to verify: "Was a Rs.9800 cheque ever cleared on CUR3001?" The system holds her cleared cheque amounts and must answer yes or no. This is exactly how linear search works — scan and return true on the first match.

Problem 2 — The dispute system only needs a yes or no, not a count, so we should stop at the first match to save work on long lists. This is exactly why linear search uses an early return instead of scanning the whole list.

The code has an `Account` holding amounts and a `ChequeVerifier` class with a `contains` method. The demo checks whether Rs.9800 exists.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Checking whether a value exists in an array is a linear search. I loop through the elements comparing each with the target, and the moment I find a match I return true and stop, which is the early exit that makes this efficient when the element is near the front. If the loop finishes without any match, I return false. The worst case is linear time when the target is at the end or absent, and the space is constant.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used linear search in the dispute resolution flow. When Priya disputed a charge, the system needed to confirm whether a specific cheque amount had ever cleared on her account. The dispute flow only needs a yes or no answer, not a count, so I stop at the first match rather than scanning the entire history, which matters when an account has thousands of cleared cheques.

For money I compare BigDecimal values with the compareTo method and check for zero, so an amount stored as nine thousand eight hundred matches one stored as nine thousand eight hundred point zero zero, because they are the same value even though their scale differs. I also note that linear search is the correct choice here because the cheque history is unsorted. If the data were sorted I could use binary search for logarithmic time, but sorting first only pays off when I expect to search the same data many times.

answers.question: Reverse an array (swap first with last, second with second-last, using two pointers).
answers.shortTitle: Reverse an array

s1_definition.profdef: Reversing an array in place uses the two-pointer technique. One pointer starts at the left end and one at the right end; you swap the two elements, then move the left pointer right and the right pointer left, stopping when they meet in the middle. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space because you only swap, never allocate a second array.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh has a printed statement where transactions are listed oldest first, but he wants newest first. He puts one finger on the top line and one on the bottom line, swaps those two lines, then moves both fingers inward by one and swaps again. He keeps going until his fingers meet in the middle. Now the whole statement is reversed without needing a second sheet of paper.
s1_definition.oneliner: Swap the two ends and move inward with two pointers until they meet, reversing the array in place.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reversing an array in place uses the two-pointer technique. One pointer starts at the left end and one at the right end; you swap the two elements, then move the left pointer right and the right pointer left, stopping when they meet in the middle. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space because you only swap, never allocate a second array.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh has a printed statement where transactions are listed oldest first, but he wants newest first. He puts one finger on the top line and one on the bottom line, swaps those two lines, then moves both fingers inward by one and swaps again. He keeps going until his fingers meet in the middle. Now the whole statement is reversed without needing a second sheet of paper.

**One line to remember:** Swap the two ends and move inward with two pointers until they meet, reversing the array in place.

sections.s2_technical:
The two-pointer approach uses `left` starting at index 0 and `right` starting at the last index. In each step you swap `array[left]` and `array[right]`, then do `left++` and `right--`. You continue while `left < right`. When they meet or cross, every element has been placed in its mirrored position.

In-place reversal is important because it uses O(1) extra space. You only need one temporary variable to hold a value during the swap. The alternative of building a new reversed array uses O(n) extra space, which is wasteful for large statements.

The loop runs n/2 times because each iteration fixes two elements, so the time is O(n). A single middle element in an odd-length array stays in place and needs no swap, which the `left < right` condition handles automatically. This works for any element type — here we reverse `BigDecimal` transaction amounts.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India stores Rajesh's transactions oldest first in the database, but the mobile app must display newest first so he sees recent activity at the top. The system must reverse the list of amounts. This is exactly how the two-pointer reversal works — swap the ends and move inward.

Problem 2 — The app runs on phones with limited memory, so we should reverse in place rather than allocating a second array. This is exactly why we use the in-place two-pointer swap, which needs only one temporary variable.

The code has an `Account` holding amounts in an array, and a `StatementReverser` class with a `reverseInPlace` method. The demo reverses Rajesh's amounts and logs before and after.

Input: amounts `[1000, 2000, 3000, 4000]`, with `left=0` and `right=3`.

Step 1 — Swap index 0 and index 3. Array becomes `[4000, 2000, 3000, 1000]`. Move `left` to 1, `right` to 2.

Step 2 — `left=1 < right=2`, so swap index 1 and index 2. Array becomes `[4000, 3000, 2000, 1000]`. Move `left` to 2, `right` to 1.

Step 3 — Now `left=2` is not less than `right=1`, so the loop stops. The array is fully reversed.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] After (newest first):  [4000.00, 3000.00, 2000.00, 1000.00]
```

```text
    │ left >= right → stop
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reversing an array is a textbook two-pointer problem that I solve in place. I put one pointer at the left end and one at the right end, swap the two elements they point at, then move the left pointer one step right and the right pointer one step left. I keep going while the left pointer is still before the right pointer. When they meet in the middle, the whole array is reversed. The loop runs about half the length of the array, so it is linear time, and because I only use a single temporary variable for the swap, it is constant extra space.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this when displaying statements. The database stores Rajesh's transactions oldest first, but the mobile app needs to show the newest transactions at the top. Rather than issuing a second expensive sorted query or building a whole new array, I reverse the list in place inside the service layer.

The in-place aspect is the part I emphasise in an interview, because the naive solution is to create a brand new array and copy elements into it backwards, which doubles the memory. On a phone displaying a long statement that extra memory matters, so the two-pointer swap that needs only one temporary variable is the professional choice. An odd-length array handles itself automatically, because when the two pointers land on the same middle element the condition stops the loop and that single element correctly stays in place.

answers.question: Find the average of all elements in an array (sum / length).
answers.shortTitle: Find the average of all elements in an array

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the average is a two-part linear operation: sum every element in one pass, then divide the sum by the number of elements. For money you accumulate into a `BigDecimal` sum and divide with an explicit scale and `RoundingMode` to avoid non-terminating decimal errors. It is O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh wants to know his average monthly spending at National Bank of India. He adds up all twelve monthly spend figures into one running total, then divides that total by twelve. The result is his typical monthly spend, which he uses for budgeting.
s1_definition.oneliner: Add everything into a running sum, then divide by the count, rounding explicitly because it is money.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the average is a two-part linear operation: sum every element in one pass, then divide the sum by the number of elements. For money you accumulate into a `BigDecimal` sum and divide with an explicit scale and `RoundingMode` to avoid non-terminating decimal errors. It is O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh wants to know his average monthly spending at National Bank of India. He adds up all twelve monthly spend figures into one running total, then divides that total by twelve. The result is his typical monthly spend, which he uses for budgeting.

**One line to remember:** Add everything into a running sum, then divide by the count, rounding explicitly because it is money.

sections.s2_technical:
You keep a `BigDecimal` running sum initialised to `BigDecimal.ZERO`. You loop once over the elements, adding each with `sum = sum.add(current)`. After the loop you divide by the count.

Division is where money needs care. `BigDecimal.divide` without a rounding specification throws an `ArithmeticException` if the result is a non-terminating decimal, for example ten divided by three. So you always call the overload that takes a scale and a `RoundingMode`, for example `sum.divide(new BigDecimal(count), 2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP)` which gives two decimal places rounded half up, the standard for rupees and paise.

You must guard the empty case because dividing by zero is undefined; averaging nothing has no meaning, so throw `IllegalArgumentException`. Time is O(n) for the single summation pass and space is O(1) for the sum accumulator. A senior nuance is choosing the rounding mode deliberately: HALF_UP is the common banking choice for display, while HALF_EVEN (banker's rounding) reduces cumulative bias in large aggregations.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India offers Rajesh a budgeting insight: "Your average monthly spend." The system holds his monthly spend figures and must compute their average. This is exactly how the average algorithm works — sum then divide.

Problem 2 — Spending figures rarely divide evenly, so the average often has many decimal places. Showing a customer a number with ten decimal places looks broken, and an unrounded BigDecimal division would even crash. This is exactly why we divide with an explicit scale of two and HALF_UP rounding.

The code has an `Account` holding monthly spends and a `SpendAnalyzer` class with a `findAverage` method. The demo computes and logs Rajesh's average spend.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the average of an array is a two-step linear operation. First I sum every element in a single pass, and then I divide the sum by the number of elements. The summation is linear time and I keep only one accumulator, so the extra space is constant.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to give Rajesh a budgeting insight showing his average monthly spend. I accumulate his monthly spend figures into a running total and divide by the number of months.

The part I always stress for a financial system is the division. Every amount is a BigDecimal, and BigDecimal division without a rounding instruction throws an ArithmeticException whenever the result does not terminate, such as a total that does not divide evenly by the count. So I always use the divide overload that takes an explicit scale and a rounding mode, specifically two decimal places with HALF_UP rounding, which is the standard for displaying rupees and paise. I also guard the empty case, because the average of no data is undefined and dividing by zero would crash, so I throw an IllegalArgumentException with a clear message instead. For very large aggregations I would consider banker's rounding, HALF_EVEN, to avoid a cumulative upward bias, but for customer-facing display HALF_UP is the expected behaviour.

answers.question: Copy one array into another array.
answers.shortTitle: Copy one array into another array

s1_definition.profdef: Copying an array creates a new array of the same length and places each source element into the corresponding position of the destination. In Java you can loop manually, or use `System.arraycopy`, `Arrays.copyOf`, or `clone()`. For arrays of objects these produce a shallow copy: the references are duplicated but the objects themselves are shared. It is O(n) time and O(n) space for the new array.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India wants to archive Rajesh's current transaction list before running a risky recalculation. A clerk photocopies the whole list onto a fresh sheet so the original is safe. If the recalculation goes wrong, the archived copy is untouched and can be restored.
s1_definition.oneliner: Make a fresh array of the same size and place each element into it; for objects this copies references, not the objects themselves.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Copying an array creates a new array of the same length and places each source element into the corresponding position of the destination. In Java you can loop manually, or use `System.arraycopy`, `Arrays.copyOf`, or `clone()`. For arrays of objects these produce a shallow copy: the references are duplicated but the objects themselves are shared. It is O(n) time and O(n) space for the new array.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India wants to archive Rajesh's current transaction list before running a risky recalculation. A clerk photocopies the whole list onto a fresh sheet so the original is safe. If the recalculation goes wrong, the archived copy is untouched and can be restored.

**One line to remember:** Make a fresh array of the same size and place each element into it; for objects this copies references, not the objects themselves.

sections.s2_technical:
The clearest way to copy is a manual loop: create `BigDecimal[] dest = new BigDecimal[src.length]` and then `for (int i = 0; i < src.length; i++) dest[i] = src[i];`. This gives you full control and is easy to read.

Java also provides faster built-ins. `System.arraycopy(src, 0, dest, 0, src.length)` is a native method that is usually the fastest. `Arrays.copyOf(src, src.length)` allocates and copies in one call. `src.clone()` also produces a new array with the same contents. All of these produce a shallow copy for object arrays, meaning `dest[i]` points at the same `BigDecimal` object as `src[i]`.

For `BigDecimal` the shallow copy is perfectly safe because `BigDecimal` is immutable: you cannot change the number inside it, you can only create a new one. So even though the copy shares references, nobody can mutate a shared amount. If the elements were mutable objects, like a mutable `Account`, you would need a deep copy, cloning each element, to keep the archive truly independent. Time is O(n) and space is O(n) for the destination.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Before National Bank of India applies an interest recalculation to Rajesh's transaction amounts, it wants a backup of the original list so it can roll back if the recalculation produces wrong figures. The system must copy the array into a separate archive array. This is exactly how array copying works — allocate a new array and place each element in.

Problem 2 — The amounts are BigDecimal, which is immutable, so a shallow copy is safe and cheap. This is exactly why we can use a simple copy here without worrying that a change to the archive would leak back into the original, because nobody can mutate a BigDecimal in place.

The code has an `ArchiveService` class with a `backup` method showing a manual loop, and it also demonstrates `Arrays.copyOf`. The demo backs up Rajesh's amounts, modifies the original, and shows the archive is unaffected.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Copying an array means creating a brand new array of the same length and placing each source element into the matching position of the destination. In Java I can do this with a simple loop, or with the built-in helpers like System dot arraycopy, Arrays dot copyOf, or the clone method. All of them run in linear time and allocate a destination of the same size, so the space is linear too.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used array copying to take a backup before a risky interest recalculation. Before the batch job overwrites Rajesh's transaction amounts, I copy the original list into an archive array, so if the recalculation produces wrong figures I can roll back to the archived copy.

The subtle point I always raise is shallow versus deep copy. For an array of objects, these copy operations duplicate the references, not the objects themselves, so both arrays point at the same underlying objects. In my case the elements are BigDecimal, which is immutable, so a shallow copy is completely safe: nobody can change the number inside a BigDecimal, they can only replace a slot with a new BigDecimal, and replacing a slot in one array does not affect the other. If the elements had been mutable objects, I would need a deep copy that clones each element, otherwise a change through one array would be visible through the other, which would defeat the whole purpose of an archive.

answers.question: Print even and odd numbers separately from an array (check `num % 2 == 0`).
answers.shortTitle: Print even and odd numbers separately from an array

s1_definition.profdef: Separating even and odd numbers is a linear pass where you test each integer with the modulo operator. If `num % 2 == 0` the number is even, otherwise it is odd, and you route it into the matching collection. It is O(n) time, and O(n) space to hold the two result lists.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India assigns each account a numeric branch-batch id. For a maintenance window they process even-numbered batches on one server and odd-numbered batches on another to split the load. A clerk reads each batch id and drops it into the "even" tray or the "odd" tray.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each number, if dividing by two leaves no remainder it is even, otherwise odd — route it accordingly.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Separating even and odd numbers is a linear pass where you test each integer with the modulo operator. If `num % 2 == 0` the number is even, otherwise it is odd, and you route it into the matching collection. It is O(n) time, and O(n) space to hold the two result lists.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India assigns each account a numeric branch-batch id. For a maintenance window they process even-numbered batches on one server and odd-numbered batches on another to split the load. A clerk reads each batch id and drops it into the "even" tray or the "odd" tray.

**One line to remember:** For each number, if dividing by two leaves no remainder it is even, otherwise odd — route it accordingly.

sections.s2_technical:
The modulo operator `%` gives the remainder of integer division. `num % 2` is `0` for even numbers and `1` for positive odd numbers. So the test `num % 2 == 0` cleanly classifies each value. You loop once over the array, apply the test, and add each number to either the evens list or the odds list.

A nuance is negative numbers: in Java, `-3 % 2` is `-1`, not `1`, because the result takes the sign of the dividend. So the robust odd test is `num % 2 != 0` rather than `num % 2 == 1`, which would wrongly classify negative odds. In our banking batch ids the numbers are positive, but writing `!= 0` is the safe habit.

Time is O(n) for the single pass. Space is O(n) to store the two lists, which together hold all n elements. If you only needed to print and not store, you could print inside the loop and use O(1) extra space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a nightly batch and wants to split work across two servers by batch id: even ids go to server A, odd ids to server B. The system must separate a list of batch ids into evens and odds. This is exactly how the even-odd split works — test each with modulo and route it.

Problem 2 — Some cancelled batches carry negative sentinel ids, and we must still classify them correctly. This is exactly why we test odd as remainder not equal to zero rather than remainder equal to one, because in Java a negative odd number gives a remainder of minus one.

The code has a `BatchSplitter` class with a `split` method returning a holder of two lists. The demo splits a list of batch ids and logs both lists.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Separating even and odd numbers is a single linear pass where I test each integer with the modulo operator. If a number divided by two leaves no remainder it is even, otherwise it is odd, and I route it into the appropriate collection. The pass is linear time, and I use linear space to hold the two result lists.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to split nightly batch work across two servers. Each batch carries a numeric id, and I send even-numbered batches to one server and odd-numbered batches to another to balance the load.

The nuance I always mention is negative numbers. In Java the modulo operator keeps the sign of the dividend, so a negative odd number like minus five gives a remainder of minus one, not plus one. If I tested for odd by checking whether the remainder equals one, I would wrongly classify every negative odd number. So the robust test is to check whether the remainder is not equal to zero, which correctly identifies odd numbers regardless of sign. In our batch ids a cancelled batch can carry a negative sentinel id, so handling that correctly matters in production.

answers.question: What is a String in Java — a sequence of characters, immutable (cannot be changed after creation).
answers.shortTitle: What is a String in Java

s1_definition.profdef: A `String` in Java is an object that represents a sequence of characters. Its defining property is immutability: once a String object is created, its contents can never change. Every operation that appears to modify a String, such as `concat` or `toUpperCase`, actually returns a brand new String and leaves the original untouched. String literals are interned in the String pool so identical literals share one object.
s1_definition.analogy: A String is like a printed cheque at National Bank of India. Once the cheque is printed with "Rajesh Kumar" and an amount, you cannot erase and rewrite it. If you need a different amount, you print a new cheque. The old cheque still exists exactly as printed. That is why a String never changes — any "change" produces a new String, like printing a fresh cheque.
s1_definition.oneliner: A String is an immutable sequence of characters — you never change it, you only create a new one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A `String` in Java is an object that represents a sequence of characters. Its defining property is immutability: once a String object is created, its contents can never change. Every operation that appears to modify a String, such as `concat` or `toUpperCase`, actually returns a brand new String and leaves the original untouched. String literals are interned in the String pool so identical literals share one object.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A String is like a printed cheque at National Bank of India. Once the cheque is printed with "Rajesh Kumar" and an amount, you cannot erase and rewrite it. If you need a different amount, you print a new cheque. The old cheque still exists exactly as printed. That is why a String never changes — any "change" produces a new String, like printing a fresh cheque.

**One line to remember:** A String is an immutable sequence of characters — you never change it, you only create a new one.

sections.s2_technical:
Internally a modern Java String wraps a byte array holding the characters plus an encoding flag, and it is declared `final` so the class cannot be subclassed and the backing data cannot be reassigned. Because the contents never change, Strings are safe to share freely across threads without any synchronisation, and they are safe to use as keys in a HashMap because their hash code never changes after creation.

Immutability is why String operations return new objects. For example `String masked = accountId.substring(0, 2) + "XXXX";` builds a new String; `accountId` itself is unchanged. Similarly `name.toUpperCase()` returns a new uppercase String and leaves `name` alone. If you ignore the returned value, nothing appears to happen, which is the classic beginner bug: writing `name.trim();` on its own line does nothing useful because you discarded the new String.

Java maintains a String pool. String literals like `"SAV2001"` written in code are interned, so two identical literals refer to the same object, and `==` between them is true. But Strings created with `new String("SAV2001")` are distinct objects, so you must always compare String contents with `.equals()`, never with `==`. When you build a String in a loop, repeated concatenation creates many throwaway objects, so you use a mutable `StringBuilder` instead for efficiency, then call `toString()` once at the end.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A String in Java is an object representing a sequence of characters, and its single most important property is immutability. Once a String is created, its contents can never change. Every method that looks like it modifies a String, such as substring, concat, or toUpperCase, actually returns a brand new String and leaves the original completely untouched. The String class is declared final, so it cannot be subclassed, and its backing data cannot be reassigned.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, this property is what makes PII masking safe. When I mask Rajesh's account id to show only the first two characters, the masking produces a new String, and the real account id stored in memory and the database is never altered, which is important for auditing. I rely on the same property to share Strings freely across threads without synchronisation, and to use Strings as HashMap keys, because an immutable object has a hash code that never changes after creation.

The practical consequence I always highlight is comparison. Because a String literal written in code is interned in the String pool while a String created with the new keyword is a separate object, two Strings can hold the same characters but be different objects in memory. So I always compare String contents with the equals method, never with the double-equals operator, because double-equals compares object identity and would silently fail when a value read from a web form does not happen to be the same pooled object as the stored value. I also use a StringBuilder when I build a String in a loop, because repeated concatenation of immutable Strings creates many throwaway objects.

answers.question: Reverse a string (convert to char array, swap from both ends, or use StringBuilder.reverse()).
answers.shortTitle: Reverse a string

s1_definition.profdef: Reversing a string produces a new string with the characters in opposite order. Because String is immutable you cannot reverse it in place; you either convert to a `char[]` and swap with two pointers, or you use `new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString()`. Both are O(n) time and O(n) space, since a new sequence of characters must be created.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India generates a reversed reference code from a transaction id for a simple checksum. Rajesh's id "TXN123" becomes "321NXT". A clerk writes the characters out backwards onto a new slip, because the original id slip cannot be rewritten.
s1_definition.oneliner: Build a new string with the characters flipped — swap from both ends of a char array, or use StringBuilder.reverse().
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reversing a string produces a new string with the characters in opposite order. Because String is immutable you cannot reverse it in place; you either convert to a `char[]` and swap with two pointers, or you use `new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString()`. Both are O(n) time and O(n) space, since a new sequence of characters must be created.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India generates a reversed reference code from a transaction id for a simple checksum. Rajesh's id "TXN123" becomes "321NXT". A clerk writes the characters out backwards onto a new slip, because the original id slip cannot be rewritten.

**One line to remember:** Build a new string with the characters flipped — swap from both ends of a char array, or use StringBuilder.reverse().

sections.s2_technical:
The simplest professional approach is `new StringBuilder(original).reverse().toString()`. StringBuilder is a mutable character buffer, so its `reverse` method flips the characters in place inside the builder, and then `toString` produces the final String. This is concise and correct.

The manual approach shows you understand the mechanics. You call `original.toCharArray()` to get a mutable `char[]`, then use two pointers: `left` at index 0 and `right` at the last index. You swap `chars[left]` and `chars[right]`, move inward, and continue while `left < right`. Finally `new String(chars)` builds the reversed String. This mirrors the array-reversal two-pointer technique.

Both are O(n) time and O(n) space, because the original String is immutable so a new character sequence must be allocated. A senior nuance is Unicode: a single visible character can be composed of a surrogate pair of two chars, and naive char-by-char reversal can corrupt such characters. StringBuilder.reverse handles surrogate pairs correctly, which is one reason to prefer it in production.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India derives a short reversed reference from a transaction id for a lightweight verification code printed on Rajesh's receipt. The system takes the id and produces its reverse. This is exactly how string reversal works — flip the characters into a new string.

Problem 2 — Because a String cannot be changed in place, we cannot just rearrange the original; we must build a new string. This is exactly why we convert to a char array or use StringBuilder, both of which create a fresh character sequence.

The code has a `ReferenceGenerator` class with two methods: `reverseManual` using a char array and two pointers, and `reverseBuiltIn` using StringBuilder. The demo reverses a transaction id with both.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reversing a string produces a new string with the characters in the opposite order. Because a String in Java is immutable, I cannot reverse it in place, so I must create a new sequence of characters. The clean production approach is to wrap the string in a StringBuilder, call its reverse method, and convert back to a String. The manual approach, which shows I understand the mechanics, is to convert the string to a character array and use two pointers, one from each end, swapping and moving inward until they meet, then build a new string from the array. Both approaches are linear time and linear space because a new character sequence has to be allocated.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used string reversal to generate a lightweight verification reference from a transaction id, printed on the customer's receipt. Rajesh's transaction id becomes its reverse as a simple checksum-style code.

The nuance I raise in an interview is Unicode correctness. A single visible character can be made of a surrogate pair of two underlying char values, and a naive character-by-character reversal can split and corrupt that pair. The StringBuilder reverse method is aware of surrogate pairs and keeps them intact, which is why I prefer it in production over hand-rolled reversal when the input might contain characters beyond the basic range.

answers.question: Check if a string is a palindrome (same forwards and backwards, e.g., "madam") — compare first and last characters moving inward.
answers.shortTitle: Check if a string is a palindrome

s1_definition.profdef: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. The efficient check uses two pointers, one at each end, comparing the characters they point at and moving inward; if any pair differs it is not a palindrome. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, which beats the simpler approach of reversing the whole string and comparing.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India lets Rajesh choose a short memorable code, and the UI flags codes that read the same both ways as "symmetric" for fun. A clerk checks a code by comparing the first and last letters, then the second and second-last, moving toward the middle. If every pair matches, it is a palindrome.
s1_definition.oneliner: Compare the outermost characters and move inward; if every mirrored pair matches it is a palindrome.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. The efficient check uses two pointers, one at each end, comparing the characters they point at and moving inward; if any pair differs it is not a palindrome. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, which beats the simpler approach of reversing the whole string and comparing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India lets Rajesh choose a short memorable code, and the UI flags codes that read the same both ways as "symmetric" for fun. A clerk checks a code by comparing the first and last letters, then the second and second-last, moving toward the middle. If every pair matches, it is a palindrome.

**One line to remember:** Compare the outermost characters and move inward; if every mirrored pair matches it is a palindrome.

sections.s2_technical:
The two-pointer method puts `left` at index 0 and `right` at the last index. You compare `chars at left` with `chars at right`. If they differ, you return false immediately, because a single mismatch rules out a palindrome. If they match, you move `left` forward and `right` backward and repeat while `left < right`. If the loop completes without a mismatch, the string is a palindrome.

This is better than the naive method of reversing the string and calling equals, because the two-pointer approach exits early on the first mismatch and uses only constant extra space, whereas reversing allocates a whole new string. The early exit matters for long inputs that fail near the start.

A practical nuance is normalisation. Real palindrome checks often ignore case and non-letter characters, so "Madam" or "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" count as palindromes. You handle this by lowercasing and stripping non-alphanumeric characters before the two-pointer scan. Time stays O(n) and space is O(1) for the scan itself, though normalisation into a cleaned string costs O(n) space.

Problem 1 — National Bank of India's app lets Rajesh pick a short reference code and shows a playful "symmetric code" badge when the code reads the same both ways. The system must check whether a code is a palindrome. This is exactly how the palindrome check works — compare mirrored characters moving inward.

Problem 2 — Customers type codes with mixed case and spaces, but "Madam" and "madam" should both count. This is exactly why we normalise to lowercase and strip non-letter characters before comparing.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A palindrome is a string that reads the same forwards and backwards, and the efficient way to check one is the two-pointer technique. I place one pointer at the start and one at the end, compare the two characters, and if they differ I return false immediately. If they match, I move both pointers inward and repeat until they meet in the middle. If I never find a mismatch, the string is a palindrome. This runs in linear time with constant extra space.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this in a small user-facing feature where the app shows a playful symmetric-code badge when a customer picks a reference code that reads the same both ways. Before I run the two-pointer scan I normalise the input by lowercasing it and stripping out anything that is not a letter or digit, so that a code typed as Madam with a capital M, or one with spaces, is still recognised correctly.

I specifically prefer the two-pointer method over the simpler approach of reversing the whole string and comparing it with the original. The two-pointer method exits on the very first mismatched pair, which is much faster when the string fails the test early, and it uses only constant extra space, whereas reversing allocates an entire new string. That early-exit plus constant-space combination is the reason interviewers like to see the two-pointer solution rather than the reverse-and-compare shortcut.

answers.question: Count vowels and consonants in a string (loop through each character, check if a/e/i/o/u).
answers.shortTitle: Count vowels and consonants in a string

s1_definition.profdef: Counting vowels and consonants is a single linear pass where you examine each character, classify it as a vowel if it is one of a, e, i, o, u, as a consonant if it is any other letter, and ignore anything that is not a letter such as digits and spaces. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space because you keep just two counters.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India wants a quick readability metric on Rajesh's chosen account nickname. A clerk reads each letter of the nickname and makes a tally in the "vowel" column for a, e, i, o, u and in the "consonant" column for the rest, skipping any numbers or spaces.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk the string once, tally vowels and consonants, and skip anything that is not a letter.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Counting vowels and consonants is a single linear pass where you examine each character, classify it as a vowel if it is one of a, e, i, o, u, as a consonant if it is any other letter, and ignore anything that is not a letter such as digits and spaces. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space because you keep just two counters.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India wants a quick readability metric on Rajesh's chosen account nickname. A clerk reads each letter of the nickname and makes a tally in the "vowel" column for a, e, i, o, u and in the "consonant" column for the rest, skipping any numbers or spaces.

**One line to remember:** Walk the string once, tally vowels and consonants, and skip anything that is not a letter.

sections.s2_technical:
You keep two integer counters, both starting at zero. You loop over each character, usually after lowercasing so you only test five vowel letters instead of ten. For each character you first check it is a letter with `Character.isLetter(c)`; if it is not a letter, you skip it so digits and punctuation do not inflate either count. If it is a letter, you test whether it is a vowel, and if so increment the vowel counter, otherwise increment the consonant counter.

A clean way to test vowels is a helper such as `"aeiou".indexOf(c) >= 0`, which returns a non-negative index when the character is found. Lowercasing first means you do not need to list both cases. Only counting characters that pass the isLetter check is the detail that separates correct code from naive code, because a nickname like "SAV 2001" contains a space and digits that are neither vowel nor consonant.

Time is O(n) for the single pass and space is O(1) for the two counters. This generalises easily: you could extend it to count digits or whitespace with more counters, but the core pattern of classify-and-tally stays the same.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Counting vowels and consonants is a single linear pass with two counters. I lowercase the string so I only have to test five vowel letters, then I loop through each character. For each character I first check whether it is a letter at all, and if it is not a letter I skip it, so digits, spaces, and punctuation do not pollute the counts. If it is a letter I test whether it is one of a, e, i, o, u, incrementing the vowel counter if so and the consonant counter otherwise. The whole thing is linear time and constant space.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this in a small analytics panel that shows how many vowels and consonants a customer's account nickname contains. Rajesh can set a nickname, and the panel breaks down its letters.

The detail I emphasise is the isLetter guard. Nicknames frequently contain digits and spaces, like Rajesh followed by a number, and a naive implementation that only checks for vowels and treats everything else as a consonant would wrongly count the digits and the space as consonants. By checking that the character is a letter first and skipping it otherwise, the counts stay accurate, which is the difference between a toy solution and one I would ship.

answers.question: Check if two strings are anagrams (same letters in different order, e.g., "listen" and "silent") — sort both and compare, or use character frequency count.
answers.shortTitle: Check if two strings are anagrams

s1_definition.profdef: Two strings are anagrams if they contain exactly the same characters with the same frequencies, just in a different order. The optimal check builds a frequency count of characters, incrementing for the first string and decrementing for the second; if all counts end at zero they are anagrams. This is O(n) time and O(1) space for a fixed alphabet. The simpler alternative sorts both strings and compares, which is O(n log n).
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India wants to detect duplicate payee names entered with letters shuffled, a trick sometimes used in fraud. "Rajesh" and "Hersja" use the same letters rearranged. A clerk tallies each letter of the first name, then crosses one off for each letter of the second name; if every tally cancels to zero, the names use identical letters.
s1_definition.oneliner: Anagrams have identical character frequencies — count up for one string, count down for the other, and check everything cancels to zero.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Two strings are anagrams if they contain exactly the same characters with the same frequencies, just in a different order. The optimal check builds a frequency count of characters, incrementing for the first string and decrementing for the second; if all counts end at zero they are anagrams. This is O(n) time and O(1) space for a fixed alphabet. The simpler alternative sorts both strings and compares, which is O(n log n).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India wants to detect duplicate payee names entered with letters shuffled, a trick sometimes used in fraud. "Rajesh" and "Hersja" use the same letters rearranged. A clerk tallies each letter of the first name, then crosses one off for each letter of the second name; if every tally cancels to zero, the names use identical letters.

**One line to remember:** Anagrams have identical character frequencies — count up for one string, count down for the other, and check everything cancels to zero.

sections.s2_technical:
The frequency-count method is the efficient one. You first check the lengths: if they differ, they cannot be anagrams, so return false immediately. Otherwise you keep a count per character. You loop over the first string incrementing the count for each character, and over the second string decrementing. If any count goes negative or ends non-zero, the strings are not anagrams. In practice you can use an `int[26]` for lowercase letters or a `HashMap<Character,Integer>` for arbitrary characters.

The sort-and-compare method is simpler to write: convert both to char arrays, sort them, and compare. If the sorted sequences are equal, the strings are anagrams. This is correct and easy to reason about, but it costs O(n log n) because of the sort, versus O(n) for the frequency count.

Normalisation matters: usually you lowercase and ignore spaces so "Listen" and "Silent" count as anagrams. The frequency approach uses O(1) space when the alphabet is fixed at 26 letters, because the counter array size does not grow with input length. A senior nuance is that for Unicode text beyond ASCII you would use a HashMap keyed by code point rather than a fixed 26-slot array.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a fraud check: a fraudster sometimes re-enters an existing payee name with the letters shuffled to slip past an exact-match filter. The system must detect when two names are anagrams of each other. This is exactly how the anagram check works — compare character frequencies.

Problem 2 — Names come in mixed case and may contain spaces, but "Priya Sharma" and "Ayirp Amrahs" should still be flagged. This is exactly why we lowercase and strip spaces before counting characters.

The code has a `FraudNameChecker` class with an `areAnagrams` method using the frequency-count approach. The demo checks a few name pairs.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: `"Rajesh"` and `"Hersja"`.

Step 1 — Normalise both to lowercase without spaces: `"rajesh"` and `"hersja"`. Lengths are both 6, so we proceed.

Step 2 — Count up over `"rajesh"`: r=1, a=1, j=1, e=1, s=1, h=1.

Step 3 — Count down over `"hersja"`: h goes to 0, e goes to 0, r goes to 0, s goes to 0, j goes to 0, a goes to 0. No count ever goes negative.

Step 4 — Since lengths matched and nothing went negative, every count is zero, so return true.

Step 5 — For `"Rajesh"` versus `"Priya"`, the lengths differ (6 versus 5), so it returns false at the quick-reject step.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] 'Priya Sharma' vs 'Ayirp Amrahs' anagram? true
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] 'Rajesh' vs 'Hersja' anagram? true
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] 'Rajesh' vs 'Priya' anagram? false
```

```text
    │ length 6 == 6 ✓
    │ count up:   {r:1,a:1,j:1,e:1,s:1,h:1}
    │ count down: h→0 e→0 r→0 s→0 j→0 a→0  (never negative)

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Two strings are anagrams when they contain exactly the same characters with the same frequencies, only in a different order. The optimal way I check this is a frequency count. I first compare lengths, because strings of different length can never be anagrams, which is a cheap early reject. Then I build a count of characters, adding one for each character of the first string and subtracting one for each character of the second string. If any count goes negative or ends non-zero, they are not anagrams; if everything cancels to zero, they are. This is linear time, and constant space when the alphabet is fixed.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used anagram detection in a fraud check. A fraudster sometimes re-enters an existing payee name with the letters shuffled to slip past an exact-match filter, so I compare a new payee name against known names to see if one is an anagram of another and flag it for manual review. Before comparing I normalise the names by lowercasing them and removing spaces, so a name like Priya Sharma matches its shuffled form regardless of case or spacing.

I always mention the alternative of sorting both strings and comparing them, which is simpler to write but costs order n log n because of the sort, compared with linear time for the frequency count. For a fraud service that checks every incoming payment against many stored names, the linear frequency approach is the better choice. For text beyond basic ASCII I would key the counts by code point in a HashMap rather than using a fixed array of twenty-six slots.

answers.question: Find the first non-repeating character in a string (use a LinkedHashMap to count frequency, then find first with count 1).
answers.shortTitle: Find the first non-repeating character in a string

s1_definition.profdef: The first non-repeating character is the earliest character in the string that appears exactly once. The standard solution makes two passes with a `LinkedHashMap`: the first pass counts the frequency of each character, and because LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order, the second pass finds the first entry whose count is one. It is O(n) time and O(k) space where k is the number of distinct characters.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India generates coupon codes and needs to pick the first unique letter as a sub-key. In "SAVER" every letter is unique, so "S" wins, but in "SETTLES" the letter that appears only once and comes first is the answer. A clerk tallies every letter, then reads the code again from the start and picks the first letter whose tally is exactly one.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count every character's frequency, then scan in original order and return the first one with a count of exactly one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The first non-repeating character is the earliest character in the string that appears exactly once. The standard solution makes two passes with a `LinkedHashMap`: the first pass counts the frequency of each character, and because LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order, the second pass finds the first entry whose count is one. It is O(n) time and O(k) space where k is the number of distinct characters.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India generates coupon codes and needs to pick the first unique letter as a sub-key. In "SAVER" every letter is unique, so "S" wins, but in "SETTLES" the letter that appears only once and comes first is the answer. A clerk tallies every letter, then reads the code again from the start and picks the first letter whose tally is exactly one.

**One line to remember:** Count every character's frequency, then scan in original order and return the first one with a count of exactly one.

sections.s2_technical:
The reason a `LinkedHashMap` is chosen over a plain `HashMap` is ordering. A plain HashMap does not remember the order in which keys were inserted, so you could not reliably find the first unique character from the map alone. A LinkedHashMap keeps keys in insertion order, so iterating it yields characters in the order they first appeared, which is exactly what first means here.

The first pass iterates the string and does `freq.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum)`, which inserts the character with count 1 the first time and adds 1 on later appearances. The second pass iterates the LinkedHashMap's entries in insertion order and returns the key of the first entry whose value is 1. If no entry has a count of 1, there is no non-repeating character, and you return a sentinel such as a special value or an Optional.

An alternative second pass is to iterate the original string again and look up each character's count in the map, returning the first whose count is 1; this works with a plain HashMap too, because the string itself provides the order. Both are O(n) time. The LinkedHashMap approach is elegant because the order lives in the map. Space is O(k) for the distinct characters, bounded by the alphabet size.
sections.s3_banking:

The system must find the first non-repeating character. This is exactly how the first-unique algorithm works — count then scan.

Problem 2 — Some codes have no unique letter at all, like "AABB", and the system must handle that gracefully instead of crashing. This is exactly why we return a clear sentinel when no character has a count of one.

The code has a `CouponKeyService` class with a `firstUnique` method using a LinkedHashMap. The demo processes several codes.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: code `"SETTLES"`.

Step 1 — Pass one counts characters into the LinkedHashMap in insertion order: S appears at positions 0 and 6 so S is 2, E appears at 1 and 5 so E is 2, T appears at 2 and 3 so T is 2, L appears once so L is 1. The map order is S, E, T, L.

Step 2 — Pass two iterates the map in that order. S has count 2, skip. E has count 2, skip. T has count 2, skip. L has count 1, so return L.

Step 3 — For `"SAVER"` every character is unique, so the first entry S has count 1 and is returned. For `"AABB"` both A and B have count 2, so no entry has count 1 and the method returns null, logged as NONE.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Code 'SETTLES' first unique char = L
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Code 'SAVER' first unique char = S
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Code 'AABB' first unique char = NONE
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the first non-repeating character means finding the earliest character in the string that appears exactly once. I solve it with two passes over a LinkedHashMap. In the first pass I count the frequency of every character, and in the second pass I iterate the map and return the first character whose count is one. The whole thing is linear time, and the space is proportional to the number of distinct characters, which is bounded by the alphabet.

The reason I specifically choose a LinkedHashMap rather than a plain HashMap is ordering. A plain HashMap does not remember the order in which I inserted the keys, so I could not reliably determine which unique character came first. A LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order, so when I iterate it the characters come out in the order they first appeared in the string, which is exactly what the word first means in this problem.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used this to derive a sub-key for promotional coupon codes. From a generated code I pick the first letter that appears only once, which reduces collisions in a secondary index. I also handle the case where no character is unique, such as a code where every letter repeats, by returning a clear sentinel instead of crashing, so the calling code can fall back to another key-generation strategy gracefully.

answers.question: What is a linked list — a chain of nodes, each node holds data + a pointer to the next node; unlike array, nodes are NOT stored side by side in memory.
answers.shortTitle: What is a linked list

s1_definition.profdef: A linked list is a linear data structure made of nodes, where each node stores a piece of data and a reference to the next node. The list is accessed through a head reference to the first node, and the last node points to null. Unlike an array, the nodes are not stored in contiguous memory; they can live anywhere on the heap and are connected only by their next references.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps a chain of pending transactions for Rajesh. Each transaction slip has the transaction details plus an arrow pointing to the next slip. The slips are scattered in different drawers, but each one tells you where the next one is. You start from the first slip (the head) and follow the arrows until you reach a slip whose arrow points to nothing, which is the end.
s1_definition.oneliner: A linked list is a chain of nodes where each node holds data and a pointer to the next, connected by references rather than by sitting side by side in memory.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A linked list is a linear data structure made of nodes, where each node stores a piece of data and a reference to the next node. The list is accessed through a head reference to the first node, and the last node points to null. Unlike an array, the nodes are not stored in contiguous memory; they can live anywhere on the heap and are connected only by their next references.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps a chain of pending transactions for Rajesh. Each transaction slip has the transaction details plus an arrow pointing to the next slip. The slips are scattered in different drawers, but each one tells you where the next one is. You start from the first slip (the head) and follow the arrows until you reach a slip whose arrow points to nothing, which is the end.

**One line to remember:** A linked list is a chain of nodes where each node holds data and a pointer to the next, connected by references rather than by sitting side by side in memory.

sections.s2_technical:
A node is a small object with two parts: the data it carries, and a `next` reference to the following node. The list itself usually holds only a `head` reference, which points to the first node. To reach any node you start at the head and follow next references one by one. The final node's next is null, which signals the end.

The defining contrast with an array is memory layout. An array stores its elements in one continuous block, so element `i` is found instantly by computing an address offset, giving O(1) random access. A linked list stores nodes anywhere on the heap, so to reach the fifth node you must walk through the first four, giving O(n) access. The trade-off is that inserting or deleting at the front of a linked list is O(1) because you just re-point a reference, whereas inserting at the front of an array is O(n) because every element must shift.

In Java you rarely write your own linked list for application code because `java.util.LinkedList` exists, but understanding the structure matters for interviews and for problems like reversing a list or detecting a cycle. A singly linked list has one next pointer per node; a doubly linked list adds a previous pointer so you can walk backwards, which is how `java.util.LinkedList` is actually implemented. A senior nuance is that linked lists have poor cache locality because nodes are scattered, so for pure iteration an ArrayList is usually faster in practice despite the same big-O.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India processes Rajesh's pending transactions in the order they arrived, and new transactions are frequently added. A linked list models this chain of pending slips, where each slip points to the next. This is exactly what a linked list is — a chain of nodes connected by next references.

Problem 2 — We need to add a new pending transaction quickly at the front of the chain without shifting everything. This is exactly why a linked list is useful: inserting at the head is a constant-time pointer change.

The code has a `TransactionNode` class holding an amount and a next reference, and a `PendingTransactions` class with `addFront` and `printAll`. The demo builds a small chain and walks it.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three addFront calls with 1000, 2000, then 3000.

Step 1 — addFront(1000): a new node with 1000 is created, its next is null (head was null), and head now points to it. Chain: 1000.

Step 2 — addFront(2000): a new node with 2000 is created, its next points to the 1000 node, and head moves to the 2000 node. Chain: 2000 then 1000.

Step 3 — addFront(3000): a new node with 3000 is created, its next points to the 2000 node, and head moves to the 3000 node. Chain: 3000 then 2000 then 1000.

Step 4 — printAll starts at head (3000) and follows next references, printing 3000, then 2000, then 1000, then reaching null and stopping. Because we always inserted at the front, the newest is first.

```
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO] Pending transactions (head to tail):
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO]   Rs.3000.00
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO]   Rs.2000.00
2026-10-26 18:58:41 [INFO]   Rs.1000.00
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A linked list is a linear data structure made of nodes, where each node holds a piece of data and a reference to the next node. The list is reached through a head reference to the first node, and the very last node points to null to mark the end. The defining characteristic, compared with an array, is that the nodes are not stored side by side in memory; they can sit anywhere on the heap and are connected only by their next references, so I follow the chain by starting at the head and hopping from one node to the next.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, I used a linked chain to model Rajesh's pending transactions, where each pending slip points to the next one. New transactions arrive constantly, and I add them at the front of the chain, which is a constant-time operation because I simply create a new node, point it at the current head, and move the head to the new node. Nothing else has to shift.

The trade-off I always explain is access versus modification. Reaching the fifth node means walking through the first four, so random access is linear time, whereas an array gives constant-time access by index. In exchange, inserting or deleting at the front of a linked list is constant time, while doing the same in an array forces every later element to shift. I also mention that linked lists have poor cache locality because the nodes are scattered in memory, so for pure iteration an ArrayList is often faster in practice even though the big-O looks similar, and that Java's own LinkedList is actually a doubly linked list with a previous pointer as well so it can be traversed in both directions.

answers.question: What is the difference between array and linked list — array has fast access by index O(1) but slow insert/delete; linked list has slow access O(n) but fast insert/delete at head O(1).
answers.shortTitle: What is the difference between array and linked list

s1_definition.profdef: An array stores elements in one contiguous block of memory, giving O(1) random access by index but O(n) insertion or deletion in the middle because elements must shift. A linked list stores elements as scattered nodes connected by references, giving O(n) access because you must traverse, but O(1) insertion or deletion at a known position such as the head. Arrays have better cache locality; linked lists avoid costly resizing and shifting.
s1_definition.analogy: An array is like a row of numbered lockers at National Bank of India bolted side by side; Rajesh can jump straight to locker five instantly, but to squeeze a new locker into the middle every later locker must be unbolted and moved. A linked list is like a treasure hunt where each clue points to the next hiding spot; adding a new clue at the start is trivial, but to reach the fifth clue you must follow the first four.
s1_definition.oneliner: Array gives fast index access but slow middle insert; linked list gives slow access but fast head insert.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An array stores elements in one contiguous block of memory, giving O(1) random access by index but O(n) insertion or deletion in the middle because elements must shift. A linked list stores elements as scattered nodes connected by references, giving O(n) access because you must traverse, but O(1) insertion or deletion at a known position such as the head. Arrays have better cache locality; linked lists avoid costly resizing and shifting.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** An array is like a row of numbered lockers at National Bank of India bolted side by side; Rajesh can jump straight to locker five instantly, but to squeeze a new locker into the middle every later locker must be unbolted and moved. A linked list is like a treasure hunt where each clue points to the next hiding spot; adding a new clue at the start is trivial, but to reach the fifth clue you must follow the first four.

**One line to remember:** Array gives fast index access but slow middle insert; linked list gives slow access but fast head insert.

sections.s2_technical:
Access is the first difference. An array element at index `i` is found by computing a memory offset from the base address, which is a single arithmetic step, so access is O(1). A linked list has no such offset; to reach the node at position `i` you start at the head and follow `i` next references, so access is O(n).

Insertion and deletion is the second difference. Inserting into the middle of an array requires shifting every element after the insertion point to make room, which is O(n), and the same for deletion. Inserting at the head of a linked list is O(1) because you only re-point one reference; even inserting in the middle is O(1) once you already hold a reference to the preceding node, though finding that node is O(n).

Memory is the third difference. An array is a single contiguous block, so it has excellent cache locality: when the CPU loads one element it pulls neighbouring elements into cache, making iteration fast. A linked list scatters nodes across the heap, so iteration suffers cache misses, and each node also carries the overhead of a reference field. However, a fixed array must be resized by allocating a bigger array and copying when it fills, whereas a linked list grows one node at a time with no copying. In Java, `ArrayList` is backed by an array and `LinkedList` is a doubly linked list; for most workloads ArrayList wins in practice because of cache locality, and you reach for LinkedList mainly when you do many insertions and removals at the ends.

Problem 1 — National Bank of India needs to look up Rajesh's transaction at a specific position in a statement instantly, which favours an array. This is exactly where array O(1) index access shines.

Problem 2 — The bank also maintains a queue of newly arriving transactions where new items are constantly added at the front, which favours a linked list. This is exactly where linked-list O(1) head insertion shines.

The code has an `ArrayBackedStatement` using a BigDecimal array for fast positional access, and a `LinkedPendingQueue` using nodes for fast head insertion. The demo times both operations conceptually and logs the results so the difference is visible.
