answers.question: Find the second-largest element without sorting (track top two in one pass).
answers.shortTitle: Find the Second-Largest Element Without Sorting

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the second-largest element without sorting is a single-pass algorithm that maintains two trackers, the largest seen so far and the second-largest seen so far. For each element you first check if it beats the largest, in which case the old largest becomes the second-largest and the element becomes the new largest; otherwise you check if it is between the two and update the second-largest. This runs in linear time with constant extra space, far cheaper than sorting, which is N log N.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to know the two highest transactions on Priya's account this month, specifically the runner-up, because the top transaction is often a known salary credit and the second-highest is the one the risk team actually scrutinises. Instead of ranking every transaction, a clerk walks the list once holding a gold medal and a silver medal. When a bigger amount appears, the current gold holder is demoted to silver and the newcomer takes gold. By the end, the silver medal shows the second-largest.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a gold and a silver tracker; a new champion pushes gold down to silver, otherwise it may just claim silver.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the second-largest element without sorting is a single-pass algorithm that maintains two trackers, the largest seen so far and the second-largest seen so far. For each element you first check if it beats the largest, in which case the old largest becomes the second-largest and the element becomes the new largest; otherwise you check if it is between the two and update the second-largest. This runs in linear time with constant extra space, far cheaper than sorting, which is N log N.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to know the two highest transactions on Priya's account this month, specifically the runner-up, because the top transaction is often a known salary credit and the second-highest is the one the risk team actually scrutinises. Instead of ranking every transaction, a clerk walks the list once holding a gold medal and a silver medal. When a bigger amount appears, the current gold holder is demoted to silver and the newcomer takes gold. By the end, the silver medal shows the second-largest.

**One line to remember:** Keep a gold and a silver tracker; a new champion pushes gold down to silver, otherwise it may just claim silver.

sections.s2_technical:
You maintain two variables, largest and secondLargest, both conceptually starting at negative infinity, which in Java you represent with the smallest possible value for the type or, more safely, with a sentinel and a found flag. For each element you apply an ordered check. First, if the element is greater than largest, then the current largest is no longer the top, so you move largest into secondLargest and then set largest to the element. Otherwise, if the element is greater than secondLargest but strictly less than largest, you set secondLargest to the element.

The order of those two checks is critical. You must update secondLargest from the old largest before you overwrite largest, otherwise you lose the value that should become the runner-up. Getting that ordering wrong is the most common bug in this problem.

A key design decision is how to treat duplicates. If the largest value appears twice, is the second-largest the same value or the next distinct value? The requirement decides. For a strict distinct second-largest you add the condition that the element must be strictly less than largest to be a secondLargest candidate, which skips duplicates of the maximum. For a positional second-largest you allow equality. In banking I usually want the distinct second-highest amount, so I use the strict version.

A senior point is edge cases. An array with fewer than two elements has no second-largest, so I guard that and signal it clearly rather than returning a meaningless sentinel. An array where every element is identical also has no distinct second-largest under the strict definition, which I handle explicitly. Being precise about these cases is what separates a robust solution from one that passes only the happy path.

Another senior point is the data type and comparison. For money I use BigDecimal and compareTo for the reasons described earlier, and I avoid initialising the trackers with a magic minimum constant; instead I seed from the first two elements after sorting just those two, or I carry a found flag, which keeps the logic correct for negative amounts.

A small finance-domain example: `BigDecimal largest = a, secondLargest = b-or-less; for each x: if (x.compareTo(largest) > 0) { secondLargest = largest; largest = x; } else if (x.compareTo(largest) < 0 && x.compareTo(secondLargest) > 0) { secondLargest = x; }` yields the distinct runner-up in one pass.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India risk team monitors Priya's current account and wants the second-highest transaction of the month. The highest is usually a predictable large credit like a property rental settlement, so it is the runner-up that signals an unusual pattern worth reviewing. Finding the second-largest in a single pass, without sorting the whole month, is exactly this top-two tracking.

This is exactly how the second-largest scan works in Java — we hold a gold and a silver tracker and demote gold to silver whenever a bigger amount arrives.

Problem 2 — The month may contain duplicate large amounts, for example two identical rent credits, and the risk team wants the second-largest distinct amount, not a repeat of the maximum. So the code must use the strict version that skips duplicates of the largest, and it must handle a month with fewer than two distinct amounts by reporting that there is no runner-up.

What the code will do: a `RunnerUpService` class with `secondLargest(BigDecimal[] amounts)` that tracks the top two distinct values in one pass and guards the too-few-elements and all-equal cases. The demo scans Priya's monthly amounts including a duplicate and logs the distinct runner-up.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Priya's amounts are `250000`, `48000`, `250000`, `120000`, and `9000`.

Step 1: We guard the length; five elements is enough. Both largest and secondLargest start as null.

Step 2: First element `250000`. largest is null, so we demote null into secondLargest and set largest to `250000`. Now largest is `250000`, secondLargest is null.

Step 3: Element `48000`. It is not greater than `250000`. It is strictly less than largest and secondLargest is null, so secondLargest becomes `48000`.

Step 4: Element `250000` again. It is not greater than largest, because it equals it. The strict less-than check fails because it is not strictly below largest, so it is skipped. This is how duplicates of the maximum are ignored.

Step 5: Element `120000`. It is not greater than largest. It is strictly less than `250000` and greater than the current secondLargest `48000`, so secondLargest becomes `120000`.

Step 6: Element `9000`. It is not greater than largest and not greater than secondLargest `120000`, so nothing changes. The loop ends with largest `250000` and secondLargest `120000`. The distinct runner-up is `120000`, correctly skipping the duplicated maximum.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T15:50:00Z INFO Second-largest (distinct) = Rs.120000
2026-10-26T15:50:00Z INFO Risk review: second-highest distinct = Rs.120000
```

    │ 48000  → silver=48000
    │ 250000 → ==gold → SKIP (duplicate of max)
    │ 120000 → <gold, >silver → silver=120000
    │ 9000   → no change
    ▼
  gold=250000, silver=120000
    │
    ▼
  Output: distinct runner-up Rs.120000 (max duplicate ignored)
```

  3.     → gold=250000, skip duplicate, silver=120000
  4.     → Optional.of(120000)
  5.   → log distinct runner-up
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the second-largest element without sorting is a single pass that tracks the top two values. I keep a largest and a second-largest, and for each element I apply an ordered check: if the element beats the largest, I first move the current largest down into the second-largest and then make the element the new largest; otherwise, if it sits strictly between the two, I update the second-largest. One pass gives the answer in linear time, which is cheaper than sorting.

The detail that trips most people up is the ordering inside the first branch. I must copy the old largest into the second-largest before I overwrite the largest, otherwise I lose the value that should become the runner-up. I also decide deliberately how to treat duplicates: for a distinct second-largest I require the candidate to be strictly less than the largest, which skips repeats of the maximum, and that is usually what the business wants.

I handle the edge cases explicitly. An array with fewer than two elements has no runner-up, and an array where everything equals the maximum has no distinct runner-up, so I return an Optional that is empty rather than a misleading sentinel. For money I use BigDecimal with compareTo and avoid magic minimum constants so negative amounts work correctly.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the risk team's monthly scan of Priya's account, where the highest transaction is usually a predictable large credit like a rental settlement, so it is the second-highest distinct amount that actually gets scrutinised. The month often contains duplicate large amounts, so the strict distinct version correctly ignores the repeated maximum and reports the real runner-up. Explaining the ordering rule, the duplicate policy, and the Optional for the empty cases shows the interviewer that I handle the tricky parts, not just the obvious scan.

answers.question: Reverse an array in-place (two-pointer swap from ends).
answers.shortTitle: Reverse an Array In-Place

s1_definition.profdef: Reversing an array in-place swaps elements from the two ends moving inward, using one pointer at the start and one at the end that step toward each other and exchange their elements until they meet. It mutates the original array, uses only constant extra space, and runs in linear time because it performs about half the array length in swaps. No new array is allocated, which is the point of the in-place requirement.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose the National Bank of India has Rajesh's transaction history listed oldest-first, but the mobile app must show newest-first. Rather than copying into a second list, two clerks start at opposite ends of the same list, swap the two entries they are holding, then each take one step toward the middle and swap again, continuing until they meet in the centre. The single list ends up reversed with no second list needed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Put one pointer at each end, swap, step both inward, and stop when they meet.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reversing an array in-place swaps elements from the two ends moving inward, using one pointer at the start and one at the end that step toward each other and exchange their elements until they meet. It mutates the original array, uses only constant extra space, and runs in linear time because it performs about half the array length in swaps. No new array is allocated, which is the point of the in-place requirement.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose the National Bank of India has Rajesh's transaction history listed oldest-first, but the mobile app must show newest-first. Rather than copying into a second list, two clerks start at opposite ends of the same list, swap the two entries they are holding, then each take one step toward the middle and swap again, continuing until they meet in the centre. The single list ends up reversed with no second list needed.

**One line to remember:** Put one pointer at each end, swap, step both inward, and stop when they meet.

sections.s2_technical:
The two-pointer technique uses a left index starting at zero and a right index starting at the last position, which is the length minus one. While left is less than right, you swap the elements at left and right, then increment left and decrement right. When left is no longer less than right, the pointers have met or crossed, and the array is fully reversed.

The loop runs about half the length of the array, performing one swap each time, so it does roughly length over two swaps, which is linear time overall. It uses only a single temporary for the swap, so the extra space is constant, which satisfies the in-place requirement.

A subtle point is the stopping condition. You loop while left is strictly less than right. If the array has an odd length, the exact middle element stays in place and does not need swapping with itself, and the strict less-than condition naturally handles that because left and right meet exactly at the middle and the loop stops. If you wrote less-than-or-equal instead, you would swap the middle element with itself, which is harmless but wasteful, and if you continued past the middle you would reverse it back, so the strict condition is important.

A senior point is mutation versus a fresh copy. In-place reversal changes the caller's array, which is efficient but has a side effect that can surprise callers who still hold a reference. In production I document that the method mutates its argument, and when I need the original preserved I offer a separate method that returns a reversed copy. Choosing mutation or copy is a deliberate API decision, not an accident.

Another senior point is the standard library. For objects you can wrap the array as a list and call the library reverse, and streams can reverse too, but those allocate or box. For primitive arrays and for a true constant-space in-place reversal, the explicit two-pointer loop is the right tool, and it is exactly what interviewers want to see because it demonstrates pointer control.

A small finance-domain example: `int left = 0, right = txns.length - 1; while (left < right) { String t = txns[left]; txns[left] = txns[right]; txns[right] = t; left++; right--; }` reverses a transaction-id array in place so newest appears first.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores Rajesh's transaction references in an array in chronological order, oldest first, because that is how they are appended as they occur. The mobile app's activity screen must display them newest first. Reversing the array in place gives the newest-first order without allocating a second array, which matters on memory-constrained mobile backends serving many users. Reversing in place with two pointers is exactly this operation.

This is exactly how in-place reversal works in Java — two pointers start at the ends and swap inward until they meet.

Problem 2 — Some callers still need the original chronological array for audit, so mutating the shared array would corrupt their view. The service must offer a non-mutating variant that returns a reversed copy, leaving the original intact, so the audit path and the display path do not interfere.

What the code will do: an `ActivityService` class with `reverseInPlace(String[] txns)` that mutates the array using two pointers, and `reversedCopy(String[] txns)` that returns a new reversed array without touching the original. The demo reverses Rajesh's transaction references for display and shows the audit copy is untouched.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the chronological array is `TXN-001, TXN-002, TXN-003, TXN-004, TXN-005`.

Step 1: `reversedCopy` first makes a copy of the array so the original is safe. Then it calls `reverseInPlace` on the copy. left starts at `0` and right starts at `4`.

Step 2: left `0` is less than right `4`, so we swap positions zero and four. The copy becomes `TXN-005, TXN-002, TXN-003, TXN-004, TXN-001`. Then left becomes `1` and right becomes `3`.

Step 3: left `1` is less than right `3`, so we swap positions one and three. The copy becomes `TXN-005, TXN-004, TXN-003, TXN-002, TXN-001`. Then left becomes `2` and right becomes `2`.

Step 4: left `2` is not less than right `2`, so the loop stops. The middle element `TXN-003` was never swapped because it sits exactly in the centre of an odd-length array, which the strict less-than condition handles.

Step 5: `reversedCopy` returns the reversed copy as the display order, newest first. The original chronological array is still in its original order, so the audit path sees an untouched list. This is the whole reason for the copy variant.

Step 6: The demo then calls `reverseInPlace` directly on the original, which mutates it to newest-first as well, demonstrating the deliberate difference between mutating and non-mutating variants.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T16:00:00Z INFO Display (newest first): [TXN-005, TXN-004, TXN-003, TXN-002, TXN-001]
2026-10-26T16:00:00Z INFO Audit (unchanged original): [TXN-001, TXN-002, TXN-003, TXN-004, TXN-005]
2026-10-26T16:00:00Z INFO After in-place reverse: [TXN-005, TXN-004, TXN-003, TXN-002, TXN-001]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [TXN-001, TXN-002, TXN-003, TXN-004, TXN-005]
    │
    ▼
  reversedCopy → copy, then two-pointer reverse the copy
    │ left=0,right=4 → swap → [005,002,003,004,001]
    │ left=1,right=3 → swap → [005,004,003,002,001]
    │ left=2,right=2 → stop (middle stays)
    ▼
  copy = [005,004,003,002,001]   original UNCHANGED
    │

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reversing an array in place uses the two-pointer technique. I put one index at the start and one at the end, and while the left index is less than the right I swap the two elements, then step the left index forward and the right index backward. When they meet, the array is reversed. It does about half the length in swaps, so it is linear time, and it uses a single temporary, so the extra space is constant, which is exactly what in-place means.

The detail I always get right is the stopping condition: I loop while left is strictly less than right. For an odd-length array the middle element sits exactly where the pointers meet and never needs swapping with itself, and the strict condition handles that cleanly. Using less-than-or-equal would either swap the middle with itself wastefully or, if I over-ran, reverse elements back.

The API decision I highlight is mutation versus copy. In-place reversal changes the caller's array, which is efficient but a side effect that can surprise code still holding the reference, so I document the mutation and provide a separate method that returns a reversed copy when the original must be preserved.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to present Rajesh's transaction references newest first on the mobile activity screen, where the stored order is oldest first. I use the non-mutating copy variant for display so the audit path still sees the original chronological array, and I expose the in-place variant for the memory-constrained path where mutation is acceptable. Explaining the two-pointer loop, the odd-length stopping condition, and the mutation-versus-copy choice shows the interviewer I understand pointer control and the API consequences of mutating shared data.

answers.question: Check if an array is sorted (compare adjacent elements).
answers.shortTitle: Check if an Array Is Sorted

s1_definition.profdef: Checking whether an array is sorted is a single-pass scan that compares each element with its immediate neighbour. For ascending order you verify that every element is less than or equal to the one after it; the moment you find a pair where the earlier element is greater than the later one, the array is not sorted and you return false. If the scan reaches the end without a violation, the array is sorted. It runs in linear time with constant space and fails fast.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India produces a daily settlement file where transactions must already be ordered by timestamp before the next system ingests them. To verify the file is in order, a clerk walks down the rows comparing each row's time with the next row's time. The instant a later row has an earlier time, the file is out of order and the clerk stops and flags it. If every adjacent pair is in order all the way down, the file passes.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk adjacent pairs; if any earlier element is greater than the next, it is not sorted; otherwise it is.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Checking whether an array is sorted is a single-pass scan that compares each element with its immediate neighbour. For ascending order you verify that every element is less than or equal to the one after it; the moment you find a pair where the earlier element is greater than the later one, the array is not sorted and you return false. If the scan reaches the end without a violation, the array is sorted. It runs in linear time with constant space and fails fast.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India produces a daily settlement file where transactions must already be ordered by timestamp before the next system ingests them. To verify the file is in order, a clerk walks down the rows comparing each row's time with the next row's time. The instant a later row has an earlier time, the file is out of order and the clerk stops and flags it. If every adjacent pair is in order all the way down, the file passes.

**One line to remember:** Walk adjacent pairs; if any earlier element is greater than the next, it is not sorted; otherwise it is.

sections.s2_technical:
The algorithm loops from the first element to the second-to-last, and at each position i it compares the element at i with the element at i plus one. For ascending order the rule is that the element at i must be less than or equal to the element at i plus one. If you ever find the element at i strictly greater than the element at i plus one, the order is broken, so you return false immediately. Reaching the end with no violation means the array is sorted, so you return true.

Empty arrays and single-element arrays are trivially sorted, because there are no adjacent pairs to violate the order, so the loop simply does not execute and you return true. Handling those cases naturally is one reason the adjacent-pair formulation is clean.

A design decision is strict versus non-strict ordering. Using less-than-or-equal allows equal neighbours, which treats an array with duplicates as sorted; using strictly-less-than would reject duplicates and check for a strictly increasing sequence. For most banking checks, such as timestamps that can tie, non-strict ascending is what you want, but for a strictly increasing sequence of unique identifiers you would use the strict comparison. I pick the comparison to match the requirement.

A senior point is generality. Rather than hard-coding ascending, I accept a Comparator so the same method checks ascending, descending, or any custom order, and for money I use BigDecimal with compareTo for the usual precision reasons. Passing a comparator makes the check reusable across sort orders without duplicating the loop.

Another senior point is why fail-fast matters. On a large settlement file that is usually in order, the common case still requires a full scan, but when a file is corrupt near the top, failing fast at the first violation avoids scanning millions of remaining rows, which is a real latency saving in a batch pipeline.

A small finance-domain example: `for (int i = 0; i < times.length - 1; i++) { if (times[i].compareTo(times[i + 1]) > 0) return false; } return true;` confirms a timestamp array is in non-descending order.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India receives a daily settlement file whose rows must be sorted by transaction timestamp before a downstream reconciliation engine ingests it, because that engine assumes order and would produce wrong results on an unsorted file. Before ingestion the pipeline must verify the file is sorted and reject it early if not. Checking sortedness by comparing adjacent timestamps is exactly this verification.

This is exactly how the sorted check works in Java — we compare each timestamp with the next and fail fast on the first out-of-order pair.

Problem 2 — Some files legitimately contain multiple transactions with the same timestamp, so the check must treat equal neighbours as still sorted, meaning non-strict ascending, and the same utility must be reusable to check a descending order for a different report. This calls for a comparator-driven check rather than a hard-coded direction.

What the code will do: an `OrderCheckService` with `isSorted(BigDecimal[] values, Comparator<BigDecimal> cmp)` that scans adjacent pairs and fails fast, plus convenience methods for ascending and descending. The demo checks a sorted timestamp array, an unsorted one, and a descending report.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the good timestamp array is `1001, 1001, 1050, 1099` and the corrupt one is `1001, 1200, 1150, 1300`.

Step 1: `isAscending(goodTimes)` calls `isSorted` with natural order. The array has four elements, so we scan pairs from index zero.

Step 2: Index zero compares `1001` with `1001`. They are equal, so compareTo returns zero, which is not greater than zero, so no violation; equal neighbours are allowed under non-strict ascending.

Step 3: Index one compares `1001` with `1050`; in order. Index two compares `1050` with `1099`; in order. The loop ends with no violation, so the good file returns true.

Step 4: `isAscending(badTimes)` scans the corrupt array. Index zero compares `1001` with `1200`; in order.

Step 5: Index one compares `1200` with `1150`. Here the earlier element is greater than the later one, so compareTo returns a positive number, which is greater than zero. This is a violation, so we log the index and return false immediately, without checking index two. That is the fail-fast behaviour that saves work on a large corrupt file.

Step 6: `isDescending(descReport)` checks `99000, 50000, 9000` with a reverse-order comparator. Each adjacent pair is decreasing, so no violation occurs and it returns true, showing the same loop serves any order via the comparator.

Final output:

2026-10-26T16:10:00Z WARNING Out of order at index 1: 1200 then 1150
2026-10-26T16:10:00Z INFO Corrupt file sorted ascending? false
2026-10-26T16:10:00Z INFO Array is sorted for the given order
2026-10-26T16:10:00Z INFO Report sorted descending? true
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Checking whether an array is sorted is a single pass over adjacent pairs. For ascending order I compare each element with the next and require the earlier one to be less than or equal to the later one, and the moment I find a pair where the earlier element is greater, I return false immediately. If I reach the end with no violation, the array is sorted. It is linear time, constant space, and fails fast.

Empty and single-element arrays are trivially sorted because there are no pairs to violate, so the loop simply does not run. I also decide strict versus non-strict ordering deliberately: less-than-or-equal allows equal neighbours, which is right when duplicates are legitimate, such as timestamps that can tie, while strictly-less-than enforces a strictly increasing sequence.

To make it reusable I accept a Comparator so the same loop checks ascending, descending, or any custom order, and for money I compare BigDecimal with compareTo for precision. Fail-fast matters in practice: on a large file that is corrupt near the top, returning at the first violation avoids scanning millions of remaining rows.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this as an order gate in the settlement ingestion pipeline, because the downstream reconciliation engine assumes the file is sorted by timestamp and would produce wrong results otherwise. Files can legitimately contain tied timestamps, so I use non-strict ascending, and the comparator-driven design lets me reuse the same check for a descending report. Explaining the fail-fast behaviour, the duplicate policy, and the comparator abstraction shows the interviewer that I write reusable, efficient validation rather than a one-off loop.

answers.question: Remove duplicates from a sorted array in-place (slow=insert position, fast=scan).
answers.shortTitle: Remove Duplicates from a Sorted Array In-Place

s1_definition.profdef: Removing duplicates from a sorted array in-place uses two pointers: a slow pointer marking the last position of a unique run, and a fast pointer scanning ahead. Because the array is sorted, duplicates sit next to each other, so whenever the fast pointer finds a value different from the one at the slow pointer, you advance the slow pointer and copy the new value there. The count of unique elements is the slow pointer plus one, achieved in linear time with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a sorted list of the distinct account identifiers that touched a settlement run, but the raw list repeats each identifier once per transaction. The bank wants each identifier only once. A clerk keeps a finger on the last unique identifier written and runs another finger down the list; every time the scanning finger lands on a new identifier different from the last unique one, the clerk writes it just after the kept position. The front of the list ends up holding each identifier exactly once.
s1_definition.oneliner: Slow pointer holds the last unique value; when fast finds a new value, bump slow and copy it there.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Removing duplicates from a sorted array in-place uses two pointers: a slow pointer marking the last position of a unique run, and a fast pointer scanning ahead. Because the array is sorted, duplicates sit next to each other, so whenever the fast pointer finds a value different from the one at the slow pointer, you advance the slow pointer and copy the new value there. The count of unique elements is the slow pointer plus one, achieved in linear time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a sorted list of the distinct account identifiers that touched a settlement run, but the raw list repeats each identifier once per transaction. The bank wants each identifier only once. A clerk keeps a finger on the last unique identifier written and runs another finger down the list; every time the scanning finger lands on a new identifier different from the last unique one, the clerk writes it just after the kept position. The front of the list ends up holding each identifier exactly once.

**One line to remember:** Slow pointer holds the last unique value; when fast finds a new value, bump slow and copy it there.

sections.s2_technical:
The precondition is that the array is already sorted, which is what makes this cheap, because equal values are guaranteed to be adjacent, so a single linear scan is enough to collapse runs of duplicates. If the array were not sorted you could not do this in one pass without extra structures.

You start the slow pointer at index zero, treating the first element as already unique. The fast pointer scans from index one to the end. For each fast position, you compare the element there with the element at the slow pointer. If they are equal, it is a duplicate, so you do nothing and let fast move on. If they differ, you have found the next unique value, so you increment slow and copy the fast element into the slow position.

When the scan finishes, the first slow-plus-one positions of the array contain the unique values in order, and the count of uniques is slow plus one. The elements beyond that prefix are leftover and considered logically removed; in Java you typically return the new length and treat the array prefix as the valid data, since Java arrays cannot be resized. If you need an exactly-sized result, you copy the prefix into a new array of that length.

A senior point is that this only removes duplicates; it does not shrink the backing array, because arrays are fixed size. So the honest contract is that the method returns the new logical length, and the caller must respect that length and ignore the tail. Documenting this clearly avoids callers reading stale data in the tail.

Another senior point is comparison correctness. For objects, including BigDecimal, you compare with compareTo or equals appropriately rather than the equality operator, which compares references. For BigDecimal specifically, two values like one point zero and one point zero zero are equal numerically but not by equals because of scale, so if numeric equality is intended I use compareTo equal to zero to detect duplicates, which is a subtle but important choice in finance.

A small finance-domain example: `int slow = 0; for (int fast = 1; fast < ids.length; fast++) { if (ids[fast].compareTo(ids[slow]) != 0) { slow++; ids[slow] = ids[fast]; } } int uniqueCount = slow + 1;` collapses a sorted identifier array to its distinct prefix.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India produces a sorted list of the account identifiers that participated in a settlement run, but because an account can appear in many transactions the list repeats identifiers. A downstream notification service must message each distinct account exactly once, so the pipeline must collapse the sorted list to unique identifiers without allocating a large second list, since the run can be huge. Removing duplicates in place with the slow-fast two pointers is exactly this.

This is exactly how in-place duplicate removal works in Java — the slow pointer keeps the last unique value and the fast pointer copies forward each new distinct value.

Problem 2 — Identifiers are stored as BigDecimal numeric codes, and numerically equal codes with different trailing scale must be treated as the same account. So the duplicate test must use compareTo equal to zero rather than equals, and the method must return the unique count so the caller knows how much of the prefix is valid without reading the stale tail.

What the code will do: a `DedupeService` with `removeDuplicates(BigDecimal[] sortedIds)` using the two-pointer technique and compareTo, returning the unique count. The demo collapses a sorted settlement identifier list and logs the distinct prefix and count.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the sorted identifiers are `2001, 2001.00, 3001, 3001, 3001, 4005`.

Step 1: The array is non-empty, so we proceed. slow starts at index zero, holding `2001`, treated as the first unique.

Step 2: fast is at index one, holding `2001.00`. compareTo between `2001.00` and `2001` returns zero because they are numerically equal despite the scale difference, so this is a duplicate and we skip it. This is why we use compareTo instead of equals.

Step 3: fast is at index two, holding `3001`. compareTo with the slow value `2001` is non-zero, so it is a new unique. We increment slow to one and copy `3001` into position one. The prefix is now `2001, 3001`.

Step 4: fast is at index three, holding `3001`. compareTo with the slow value `3001` is zero, a duplicate, so we skip. fast at index four is also `3001`, again a duplicate, skipped. The three copies of `3001` collapse to one.

Step 5: fast is at index five, holding `4005`. compareTo with the slow value `3001` is non-zero, so it is unique. We increment slow to two and copy `4005` into position two. The prefix is now `2001, 3001, 4005`.

Step 6: The scan ends. slow is two, so the unique count is slow plus one, which is three. The first three positions hold the distinct accounts, and the caller uses only that prefix, ignoring the stale tail. The notification service will message each of the three accounts once.

2026-10-26T16:20:00Z INFO Distinct accounts to notify (3): [2001, 3001, 4005]

    ▼
  prefix [2001, 3001, 4005], uniqueCount = slow+1 = 3
    │  (tail positions 3..5 are stale, ignored)
    ▼

  4.   → notify each of 3 distinct accounts

Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place uses two pointers. A slow pointer marks the last position of a unique value, and a fast pointer scans ahead. At the end, the unique count is the slow pointer plus one, and it is all done in one linear pass with constant extra space.

The honest contract I always state is that Java arrays cannot shrink, so the method does not truly delete anything; it compacts the distinct values into the front prefix and returns the new logical length, and the caller must use only that prefix and ignore the stale tail. Making that contract explicit stops callers from reading leftover data.

The finance-specific subtlety is the equality test. For BigDecimal, equals also considers scale, so one thousand and one thousand point zero zero are not equal by equals even though they are numerically the same. When I mean numeric equality I test compareTo equal to zero, which correctly collapses the same account written with different scale.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to collapse a sorted list of account identifiers from a settlement run so the notification service messages each distinct account exactly once, without allocating a huge second list on a large run. Identifiers are numeric BigDecimal codes, so I dedupe by compareTo to treat scale-different values as the same account, and I return the unique count so the caller knows how much of the prefix is valid. answers.question: Move all zeros to the end while preserving order (two-pointer swap).
answers.shortTitle: Move All Zeros to the End While Preserving Order

s1_definition.profdef: Moving all zeros to the end while preserving the relative order of the non-zero elements is a two-pointer, in-place algorithm. A write pointer tracks where the next non-zero value should go, and a scan pointer walks the whole array; every time the scan pointer finds a non-zero value it is placed at the write position and the write pointer advances. After the scan, all positions from the write pointer to the end are filled with zeros. It is linear time and constant space, and the non-zero elements keep their original order, which is what makes it a stable partition.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a row of settlement slots for Rajesh's day, where some slots carry a real amount and some are empty, shown as zero. The bank wants all the real amounts compacted to the front in the same order they occurred, with the empty slots pushed to the back. A clerk keeps a finger on the next front slot to fill and runs another finger across every slot; each real amount found is slid forward to the kept position, and whatever is left at the back becomes empty.
s1_definition.oneliner: Write pointer collects non-zeros in order at the front; fill the rest with zeros at the end.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Moving all zeros to the end while preserving the relative order of the non-zero elements is a two-pointer, in-place algorithm. A write pointer tracks where the next non-zero value should go, and a scan pointer walks the whole array; every time the scan pointer finds a non-zero value it is placed at the write position and the write pointer advances. After the scan, all positions from the write pointer to the end are filled with zeros. It is linear time and constant space, and the non-zero elements keep their original order, which is what makes it a stable partition.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a row of settlement slots for Rajesh's day, where some slots carry a real amount and some are empty, shown as zero. The bank wants all the real amounts compacted to the front in the same order they occurred, with the empty slots pushed to the back. A clerk keeps a finger on the next front slot to fill and runs another finger across every slot; each real amount found is slid forward to the kept position, and whatever is left at the back becomes empty.

**One line to remember:** Write pointer collects non-zeros in order at the front; fill the rest with zeros at the end.

sections.s2_technical:
The classic two-pass version is the easiest to reason about. In the first pass you keep a write index starting at zero and scan the array; each time you see a non-zero value you store it at the write index and increment the write index. After this pass, the first write-index positions hold all the non-zero values in their original relative order. In the second step you fill every position from the write index to the end with zero. Both passes are linear, so the whole thing is linear time.

There is a one-pass swap variant. You keep the write index and scan; when you find a non-zero value you swap it with the value at the write index and advance the write index. This moves zeros rightward as you go. It does more writes than the fill version when there are many zeros because of the swaps, but it is a single pass and is common in interviews. I usually mention both and note that the fill version does fewer writes when zeros are frequent.

A critical requirement is stability: the non-zero values must keep their original order. Both the write-and-fill and the swap approaches preserve order because they process elements left to right and never reorder two non-zeros relative to each other. If you instead swapped from both ends you would be faster at moving zeros but you would scramble the order of the non-zeros, which violates the requirement.

A senior point is minimising writes. If the array is mostly non-zero, you want to avoid writing a value back onto itself. A small optimisation skips the store when the write index already equals the scan index, which avoids redundant self-writes and slightly reduces memory traffic on large arrays. For a banking batch over millions of slots this is a measurable saving.

Another senior point is generality. The same pattern is a stable partition around any predicate, not just zero. By replacing the non-zero test with any condition, you push all elements failing the predicate to the end while keeping the passing ones in order, which is a reusable building block. For money I use BigDecimal and test compareTo against zero rather than the equality operator.

A small finance-domain example: `int write = 0; for (int scan = 0; scan < a.length; scan++) { if (a[scan].signum() != 0) { a[write++] = a[scan]; } } while (write < a.length) { a[write++] = BigDecimal.ZERO; }` compacts non-zero amounts to the front and zeros to the back.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes Rajesh's daily settlement slots, where many slots are empty placeholders holding zero and the rest hold real transaction amounts. A reporting module must present the real amounts compacted to the front in the exact order they occurred, with the empty slots pushed to the back, and it must do this in place to avoid allocating a second array for a very large day. Moving zeros to the end while preserving order is exactly this stable compaction.

This is exactly how move-zeros works in Java — a write pointer gathers the non-zero amounts in order and the tail is filled with zeros.

Problem 2 — The order of the real amounts is audit-significant, so the compaction must be stable: two real amounts must never swap their relative positions. This rules out the faster two-ends swap and requires the left-to-right write approach, and amounts are BigDecimal so the zero test uses signum rather than equals.

What the code will do: a `SlotCompactor` with `moveZerosToEnd(BigDecimal[] slots)` using the write-and-fill two-pointer approach with signum, preserving order. The demo compacts Rajesh's day of settlement slots and logs the result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the slots are `5000, 0, 12000, 0, 0, 800`.

Step 1: write starts at zero. scan at index zero finds `5000`, which is non-zero. write equals scan, so no redundant copy; write advances to one.

Step 2: scan at index one finds `0`. It is zero, so nothing happens and write stays at one.

Step 3: scan at index two finds `12000`, non-zero. write is one and scan is two, so we copy `12000` into position one. The array front is now `5000, 12000`. write advances to two.

Step 4: scan at indices three and four both find `0`, so nothing happens and write stays at two. scan at index five finds `800`, non-zero, so we copy `800` into position two. The front is now `5000, 12000, 800`. write advances to three.

Step 5: The scan ends. All non-zero amounts have been written to the front in their original order, preserving the audit-significant sequence. write is three, meaning three real amounts.

Step 6: We fill the tail from position three to the end with zero, giving `5000, 12000, 800, 0, 0, 0`. The compaction is stable and done entirely in place with no second array.

Final output:

2026-10-26T16:30:00Z INFO Compacted slots: [5000, 12000, 800, 0, 0, 0]
2026-10-26T16:30:00Z INFO After (non-zeros front, order kept): [5000, 12000, 800, 0, 0, 0]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Moving all zeros to the end while preserving order is a two-pointer in-place algorithm. I keep a write pointer for the next front position and scan the whole array; every non-zero value I find I place at the write position and advance the write pointer, then after the scan I fill everything from the write pointer to the end with zeros. It is linear time and constant space.

The requirement I never lose sight of is stability: the non-zero values must keep their original relative order. Both the write-and-fill version and the one-pass swap version preserve order because they process left to right and never reorder two non-zeros. A faster two-ends approach would move zeros quicker but scramble the non-zeros, which breaks the requirement, so I avoid it when order matters.

I also mention a small optimisation: skip the store when the write index already equals the scan index, which avoids pointless self-writes on a mostly-non-zero array and reduces memory traffic on large inputs. And I note that this is really a stable partition around a predicate, so replacing the non-zero test with any condition reuses the same code; for money I test BigDecimal with signum rather than equals.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to compact Rajesh's daily settlement slots, pushing the empty zero slots to the back while keeping the real amounts in the exact order they occurred, because that order is audit-significant. It runs in place to avoid allocating a second array for a huge day, and the zero test uses signum because amounts are BigDecimal. Explaining the stability requirement, the two approaches, and the self-write optimisation shows the interviewer that I understand in-place partitioning and respect the ordering constraint that the business actually depends on.

answers.question: Rotate an array by K positions (reverse whole → reverse first K → reverse rest).
answers.shortTitle: Rotate an Array by K Positions

s1_definition.profdef: Rotating an array to the right by K positions moves each element K places to the right, with the elements that fall off the end wrapping to the front. The elegant in-place technique is the triple reversal: first reverse the entire array, then reverse the first K elements, then reverse the remaining elements. This runs in linear time with constant extra space, after first reducing K modulo the length so that rotations larger than the array are handled correctly.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India keeps a rolling window of the last few days of Rajesh's balances, and at day-end it must shift the window so the newest days appear first, wrapping the oldest around. Imagine the days written on a strip of paper. The clerk flips the whole strip over, which reverses everything, then flips just the first part back, then flips the rest back. After these three flips the strip shows the days rotated into the new arrangement, all done on the one strip without copying to a new one.
s1_definition.oneliner: Reduce K by the length, then reverse the whole array, reverse the first K, and reverse the rest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Rotating an array to the right by K positions moves each element K places to the right, with the elements that fall off the end wrapping to the front. The elegant in-place technique is the triple reversal: first reverse the entire array, then reverse the first K elements, then reverse the remaining elements. This runs in linear time with constant extra space, after first reducing K modulo the length so that rotations larger than the array are handled correctly.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India keeps a rolling window of the last few days of Rajesh's balances, and at day-end it must shift the window so the newest days appear first, wrapping the oldest around. Imagine the days written on a strip of paper. The clerk flips the whole strip over, which reverses everything, then flips just the first part back, then flips the rest back. After these three flips the strip shows the days rotated into the new arrangement, all done on the one strip without copying to a new one.

**One line to remember:** Reduce K by the length, then reverse the whole array, reverse the first K, and reverse the rest.

sections.s2_technical:
The first essential step is to reduce K modulo the array length. If the array has length n and K is larger than n, rotating by K is the same as rotating by K modulo n, because every full n rotations return to the start. If you skip this, indices go out of range. You also handle a negative K if left rotation is allowed by converting it to the equivalent right rotation, and you treat an empty or single-element array as needing no rotation.

The triple-reversal works because reversing the whole array puts the last K elements at the front but in reverse order, and puts the first n minus K elements at the back also in reverse order. Reversing the first K elements fixes the order of the block that should lead, and reversing the remaining elements fixes the order of the trailing block. The net effect is a correct right rotation by K.

Walk through a small example to make it concrete. Take one, two, three, four, five and rotate right by two. Reverse the whole array to get five, four, three, two, one. Reverse the first two to get four, five, three, two, one. Reverse the rest to get four, five, one, two, three, which is the original rotated right by two. Each reversal is the two-pointer swap from the ends.

A senior point is comparing approaches. A naive approach copies elements into a new array at shifted positions, which is simple but uses linear extra space. Another approach rotates one step at a time K times, which is quadratic and far too slow for large K. The triple reversal is linear time and constant space, which is why it is the preferred in-place solution. There is also a juggling or cyclic-replacement algorithm that achieves the same bounds; I usually prefer triple reversal because it is the easiest to get right and to explain.

Another senior point is direction clarity. Right rotation and left rotation differ only by how you split K, and mixing them up is a common bug. I always state explicitly which direction the method rotates and document it, and I test both a small K and a K larger than the length to prove the modulo reduction works.

A small finance-domain example: `k = k % n; reverse(a, 0, n - 1); reverse(a, 0, k - 1); reverse(a, k, n - 1);` right-rotates the balance window by k in place.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India maintains a fixed-size rolling window of Rajesh's recent daily closing balances for a trend chart. At day-end the window must be rotated so the display aligns with a new reference day, effectively shifting elements by a chosen offset with wrap-around. Doing this in place avoids allocating a new window array every day for every customer, which matters at scale. Rotating the array by K with the triple reversal is exactly this.

This is exactly how array rotation works in Java — reduce K, then three reversals rearrange the window in place.

Problem 2 — The chosen offset can sometimes exceed the window length, for example when a configuration mistake sets a large shift, so the code must reduce K modulo the length to stay correct and in range rather than throwing an index error. This shows the importance of the modulo step and of handling the trivial empty and single-element cases.

What the code will do: a `WindowRotator` with `rotateRight(BigDecimal[] window, int k)` that reduces K, then performs three in-place reversals via a private reverse helper. The demo rotates Rajesh's balance window by a normal K and by a K larger than the length.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the balance window is `100, 200, 300, 400, 500` and we rotate right by `2`.

Step 1: n is five. We normalise k as two modulo five, which stays two. It is not zero, so we rotate.

Step 2: We reverse the whole window from index zero to four, turning `100, 200, 300, 400, 500` into `500, 400, 300, 200, 100`. The last two elements are now at the front but in reversed order.

Step 3: We reverse the first k, which is indices zero to one, turning `500, 400` into `400, 500`. The window is now `400, 500, 300, 200, 100`. The leading block is now in correct order.

Step 4: We reverse the rest, indices two to four, turning `300, 200, 100` into `100, 200, 300`. The window becomes `400, 500, 100, 200, 300`, which is the original rotated right by two.

Step 5: The demo then rotates by seven. We normalise seven modulo five to two, so this is the same as another right rotation by two. Without the modulo step, k of seven would run reversals with out-of-range indices.

Step 6: The three reversals run again on the already-rotated window, producing `200, 300, 400, 500, 100`. Everything happened in place on the single window array, using only a temporary inside the reverse helper.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T16:40:00Z INFO Before: [100, 200, 300, 400, 500]
2026-10-26T16:40:00Z INFO Rotated right by 2: [400, 500, 100, 200, 300]
2026-10-26T16:40:00Z INFO After rotateRight(2): [400, 500, 100, 200, 300]
2026-10-26T16:40:00Z INFO Rotated right by 2: [200, 300, 400, 500, 100]
2026-10-26T16:40:00Z INFO After rotateRight(7): [200, 300, 400, 500, 100]
```

    │ reverse all      → [500,400,300,200,100]
    │ reverse first 2  → [400,500,300,200,100]
    │ reverse rest     → [400,500,100,200,300]
    ▼
  rotated right by 2
    │
    ├─ k=7 → 7 % 5 = 2 → same triple reversal again
    ▼
  Output: [200,300,400,500,100] (oversized k handled by modulo)
```

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: WindowRotator only rotates windows                        │
  │  O: add rotateLeft by adjusting k split, reverse reused       │
  │  D: callers depend on rotateRight signature, not the trick    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐

  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + rotateRight(window, k): void       │  O(n)/O(1)
  │  - reverse(window, from, to): void    │  two-pointer helper
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      rotateRight contract:
        Pre:  window may be null/short (no-op)
        Post: right-rotated by k; k normalised mod n (handles k>=n,<0)

  ── State Diagram: Rotation Steps ─────────────────────────

  [k = k%n] ──k==0?──→ [NO-OP]
      │ else
      ▼
  [reverse all] → [reverse 0..k-1] → [reverse k..n-1] → [DONE]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. WindowDemo.main()
  2.   → rotateRight(window, 2)
  3.     → reverse all, first 2, rest → [400,500,100,200,300]
  4.   → rotateRight(window, 7) → 7%5=2 → [200,300,400,500,100]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Rotating an array right by K moves each element K places to the right with wrap-around, and the elegant in-place way is the triple reversal: reverse the whole array, then reverse the first K elements, then reverse the rest. It runs in linear time and constant space.

The first thing I always do is reduce K modulo the length, because rotating by more than the length is the same as rotating by K modulo the length, and skipping that step sends indices out of range. I also normalise a negative K into the equivalent right rotation and treat empty or single-element arrays as no-ops.

I can explain why the triple reversal works: reversing the whole array brings the last K elements to the front but in reverse, so reversing the first K fixes their order and reversing the remaining elements fixes the trailing block. Compared with the alternatives, copying into a new array uses linear extra space and rotating one step at a time K times is quadratic, so the triple reversal is the best in-place choice, and it is easier to get right than the cyclic juggling algorithm.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to rotate Rajesh's rolling window of recent daily closing balances at day-end so the trend chart aligns with a new reference day, doing it in place so we do not allocate a fresh window array per customer per day. A misconfigured offset can exceed the window length, so the modulo normalisation keeps it correct and in range. Explaining the modulo step, why the three reversals produce the rotation, and the comparison with the slower alternatives shows the interviewer that I know the efficient in-place solution and its edge cases.

answers.question: Find the missing number in 1..N (sum formula or XOR trick).
answers.shortTitle: Find the Missing Number in 1..N

s1_definition.profdef: Given an array that should contain the numbers one through N but is missing exactly one, finding the missing number can be done in linear time and constant space. The sum method computes the expected total of one through N using the formula N times N plus one over two, then subtracts the actual sum of the array, and the difference is the missing number. The exclusive-or method XORs all the indices-values together with the full range so that every present number cancels, leaving only the missing one.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India issues cheque serial numbers one through N for Rajesh's cheque book, and when the processed cheques come back exactly one serial is missing. Rather than ticking off each serial on a list, the clerk knows what the total of all serials should add up to, adds up the serials that actually came back, and the gap between the two totals is precisely the missing serial number. One quick subtraction reveals it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Expected sum minus actual sum gives the missing number, or XOR everything so present numbers cancel and only the missing one remains.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Given an array that should contain the numbers one through N but is missing exactly one, finding the missing number can be done in linear time and constant space. The sum method computes the expected total of one through N using the formula N times N plus one over two, then subtracts the actual sum of the array, and the difference is the missing number. The exclusive-or method XORs all the indices-values together with the full range so that every present number cancels, leaving only the missing one.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India issues cheque serial numbers one through N for Rajesh's cheque book, and when the processed cheques come back exactly one serial is missing. Rather than ticking off each serial on a list, the clerk knows what the total of all serials should add up to, adds up the serials that actually came back, and the gap between the two totals is precisely the missing serial number. One quick subtraction reveals it.

**One line to remember:** Expected sum minus actual sum gives the missing number, or XOR everything so present numbers cancel and only the missing one remains.

sections.s2_technical:
The sum method relies on a known closed-form total. The numbers one through N add up to N times N plus one, all divided by two. You compute that expected total, then loop once over the array adding up the actual values, and the missing number is the expected total minus the actual total. It is a single pass plus a constant-time formula, so linear time and constant space.

The one real danger with the sum method is overflow. For large N the expected total can exceed the int range, so I compute it in a long. Using long for the running sum and the formula keeps the arithmetic correct even when N is in the millions, which is a realistic size for serial numbers.

The exclusive-or method avoids overflow entirely because XOR is a bit operation. You XOR together all the numbers from one through N, and also XOR in every element of the array. Every number that is present appears an even number of times across those two groups and cancels to zero, because a value XOR itself is zero, so what remains is the single missing number that appeared only once in the full range. It is also a single pass and constant space, and it never overflows, which is why some engineers prefer it.

A senior point is handling the two common framings. Sometimes the range is zero through N with one missing, and sometimes it is one through N; the formula and the XOR range must match the framing exactly, off by one errors here are the classic bug. I always confirm the inclusive bounds before coding.

Another senior point is what to do if more than one number could be missing or if there are duplicates. The single-missing assumption is what makes these tricks work; if two numbers were missing, the sum would only tell you their combined total, not each one, and you would need a different technique such as a presence set or solving a small system with sum and sum-of-squares. I state this assumption explicitly so the solution is honest about its scope.

A small finance-domain example using the sum method: `long n = serials.length + 1; long expected = n * (n + 1) / 2; long actual = 0; for (int s : serials) actual += s; long missing = expected - actual;` reveals the one missing cheque serial.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India issues Rajesh a cheque book with serial numbers one through N, and at reconciliation the processed cheques come back as an array that contains every serial except one, because one cheque is still outstanding. The bank must identify the single missing serial quickly, even for a large book, without building a big lookup structure. Finding the missing number by the sum difference is exactly this.

This is exactly how the missing-number trick works in Java — expected total minus actual total reveals the gap.

Problem 2 — Serial numbers can be large, so the expected total can overflow a 32-bit integer, and the reconciliation must stay exact. The code must compute the sum in a long to avoid overflow, and it should also offer the XOR variant, which cannot overflow at all, as a robust alternative. This shows awareness of the overflow pitfall and a safe alternative.

What the code will do: a `ReconciliationService` with `missingBySum(int[] serials)` using the long-safe sum formula and `missingByXor(int[] serials)` using the exclusive-or cancellation. The demo finds the missing cheque serial both ways and confirms they agree.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the processed serials are `1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8`, with serial five outstanding.

Step 1: `missingBySum` computes N as the array length seven plus one, which is eight. The expected total of one through eight is eight times nine over two, which is thirty-six, computed in a long.

Step 2: We loop over the array adding the actual values: one plus two plus three plus four plus six plus seven plus eight, which is thirty-one.

Step 3: The missing number is the expected thirty-six minus the actual thirty-one, which is five. That is the outstanding cheque serial, found with one pass and one formula.

Step 4: `missingByXor` computes N as eight. It XORs the full range one through eight into an accumulator, then XORs each present serial into the same accumulator.

Step 5: Every serial that is present appears once in the range loop and once in the array loop, so it is XORed twice and cancels to zero. Serial five appears only in the range loop, so it does not cancel.

Step 6: The accumulator is left holding five, which the method returns. The demo compares the two results; they agree, so it logs that serial five is outstanding. If they disagreed, that would indicate corrupt input, which the severe log would flag.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T16:50:00Z INFO missingBySum: expected=36 actual=31 missing=5
2026-10-26T16:50:00Z INFO missingByXor: missing=5
2026-10-26T16:50:00Z INFO Missing cheque serial (sum) = 5
2026-10-26T16:50:00Z INFO Missing cheque serial (xor) = 5
2026-10-26T16:50:00Z INFO Both methods agree: serial 5 is outstanding
```

```
  Input: processed [1,2,3,4,6,7,8], N=8
    │
    ├─ SUM method
    │   expected = 8×9/2 = 36 (long)
    │   actual   = 1+2+3+4+6+7+8 = 31
    │   missing  = 36 - 31 = 5
    │
    ├─ XOR method
    │   acc = (1^2^...^8) ^ (1^2^3^4^6^7^8)
    │   present cancel in pairs → acc = 5
    ▼
  Both = 5 → serial 5 outstanding (methods cross-check)
```
sections.s5c_hld:

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the single missing number in one through N can be done in linear time and constant space two ways. The sum method computes the expected total of one through N with the closed-form formula N times N plus one over two, subtracts the actual sum of the array, and the difference is the missing number. The exclusive-or method XORs the whole range and all the elements together so every present number cancels in pairs and only the missing one survives.

The pitfall I always guard against in the sum method is overflow: for large N the expected total exceeds the int range, so I compute it in a long. The XOR method sidesteps overflow entirely because it is a bit operation, which is why I often offer it as the robust alternative, and in a reconciliation context I run both and cross-check that they agree, flagging corrupt input if they do not.

I am explicit about the assumptions. These tricks work because exactly one number is missing; if two were missing the sum would only give their combined total and I would need a different approach, such as a presence set or solving with both the sum and the sum of squares. I also confirm the inclusive bounds, zero-to-N versus one-to-N, because an off-by-one there is the classic bug.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to find the single outstanding cheque serial during reconciliation, where Rajesh's cheque book is serial numbers one through N and all but one come back processed. Serials can be large, so I accumulate in a long for the sum method and offer the overflow-free XOR method as a cross-check. Explaining the two methods, the overflow fix, and the single-missing assumption shows the interviewer that I know the elegant tricks and the real constraints that make one safer than the other.

answers.question: Contains Duplicate — check using HashSet in O(n).
answers.shortTitle: Contains Duplicate — Check Using a HashSet in O(n)

s1_definition.profdef: The contains-duplicate problem asks whether any value appears more than once in a collection. The efficient solution scans the collection once, adding each element to a HashSet; the HashSet's add method returns false when the element is already present, so the first time add returns false you have found a duplicate and return true. This runs in average linear time because HashSet operations are average constant time, using linear extra space for the set.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India processes a batch of transaction identifiers and must be sure none was submitted twice, because a duplicate identifier means a transaction could be applied twice and Rajesh could be charged twice. A clerk keeps a box of identifiers already seen and drops each new identifier in; the moment an identifier is already in the box, the clerk shouts "duplicate" and stops. Checking the box is near-instant, so the whole batch is cleared in one quick pass.
s1_definition.oneliner: Add each element to a HashSet; the first time add returns false you have a duplicate.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The contains-duplicate problem asks whether any value appears more than once in a collection. The efficient solution scans the collection once, adding each element to a HashSet; the HashSet's add method returns false when the element is already present, so the first time add returns false you have found a duplicate and return true. This runs in average linear time because HashSet operations are average constant time, using linear extra space for the set.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India processes a batch of transaction identifiers and must be sure none was submitted twice, because a duplicate identifier means a transaction could be applied twice and Rajesh could be charged twice. A clerk keeps a box of identifiers already seen and drops each new identifier in; the moment an identifier is already in the box, the clerk shouts "duplicate" and stops. Checking the box is near-instant, so the whole batch is cleared in one quick pass.

**One line to remember:** Add each element to a HashSet; the first time add returns false you have a duplicate.

sections.s2_technical:
A HashSet stores unique elements and offers average constant-time add and contains, because it hashes each element to a bucket. The neat part is that add returns a boolean: true if the element was newly added and false if it was already present. So you do not even need a separate contains call; you loop over the collection, call add on each element, and if add ever returns false you immediately return true for contains-duplicate. If the loop finishes with every add returning true, there were no duplicates and you return false.

This is average linear time. Each add is average constant time, and you do one per element, so the total is linear in the number of elements. The trade-off is linear extra space for the set, which is the classic time-for-space exchange: you spend memory to avoid the N log N cost of sorting or the quadratic cost of comparing every pair.

A senior point is the alternatives and when they win. If you are allowed to mutate and sort the input, sorting first then scanning adjacent equal elements finds duplicates in N log N time with no extra set, which is better when memory is tight. The brute-force double loop comparing every pair is quadratic and only acceptable for tiny inputs. The HashSet approach is the right default when you want the fastest average time and can afford the memory.

Another senior point is correctness of equality and hashing. The HashSet relies on the elements implementing equals and hashCode consistently. For your own identifier class you must override both, and they must agree, otherwise the set may treat equal identifiers as different and miss duplicates. For BigDecimal there is a famous trap: BigDecimal equals also considers scale, so one and one point zero are not equal and hash differently, which means a HashSet would not treat them as duplicates even though they are numerically equal. If numeric duplication is what matters, I normalise the scale first or key on the stripped value.

A third point is early exit. Returning the moment the first duplicate is found avoids scanning the rest, which on a large batch with an early duplicate saves real time. I also size the HashSet with an expected capacity when I know the input size, to avoid rehashing as it grows.

A small finance-domain example: `Set<String> seen = new HashSet<>(ids.length * 2); for (String id : ids) { if (!seen.add(id)) return true; } return false;` returns true as soon as a repeated transaction id appears.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India receives a batch of transaction identifiers to apply to accounts, and applying the same identifier twice would double-charge a customer like Rajesh. Before processing, the batch must be checked for any repeated identifier, and because batches are large the check must be fast and must stop at the first duplicate. Detecting a duplicate with a HashSet in one pass is exactly this guard.

This is exactly how contains-duplicate works in Java — we add each identifier to a set and the first time add returns false we have found a repeat.

Problem 2 — Some identifiers are numeric amounts stored as BigDecimal where numerically equal values could carry different scale, so a naive HashSet of BigDecimal would miss numeric duplicates. The check must normalise the scale so that numerically equal values are treated as duplicates, demonstrating awareness of the BigDecimal equals-and-hashCode trap.

What the code will do: a `DuplicateGuard` with `hasDuplicate(String[] ids)` using a pre-sized HashSet and early exit, plus `hasNumericDuplicate(BigDecimal[] amounts)` that strips trailing zeros so numeric equality is honoured. The demo checks a clean batch, a batch with a repeated id, and numerically equal amounts.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the duplicate batch is `TXN-001, TXN-002, TXN-001`.

Step 1: `hasDuplicate` checks the length; three elements is enough. We create a HashSet pre-sized to twice the length to avoid rehashing as it fills.

Step 2: We add `TXN-001`. The set was empty, so add returns true, meaning it was newly inserted, no duplicate yet.

Step 3: We add `TXN-002`. It was not present, so add returns true again. The set now holds two identifiers.

Step 4: We add `TXN-001` again. It is already in the set, so add returns false. That false is our signal: we log the duplicate and return true immediately, without looking at any further elements. This early exit is what saves time on large batches.

Step 5: For the clean batch, every add returns true, the loop completes, and the method returns false, meaning no duplicates.

Step 6: For the numeric check, we add the stripped form of `100`, which is a canonical value, then we add the stripped form of `100.00`, which strips to the same canonical value, so add returns false and we report a numeric duplicate. Without stripping, BigDecimal equals would treat them as different because of scale and we would miss the duplicate.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T17:00:00Z INFO No duplicate identifiers in batch
2026-10-26T17:00:00Z INFO Clean batch has duplicate? false
2026-10-26T17:00:00Z WARNING Duplicate transaction id detected: TXN-001
2026-10-26T17:00:00Z INFO Dup batch has duplicate? true
2026-10-26T17:00:00Z WARNING Numeric duplicate amount detected: 100.00
2026-10-26T17:00:00Z INFO Numerically equal amounts duplicate? true
```

```
  Input: [TXN-001, TXN-002, TXN-001]
    │
    ▼

    │ add TXN-001 → true (new)
    │ add TXN-002 → true (new)
    │ add TXN-001 → false (present) → DUPLICATE → early exit
    ▼ true
  Numeric path: [100, 100.00]
    │ stripTrailingZeros → both canonical → add false → duplicate
    ▼ true
  Output: duplicate batch rejected before processing
```

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: DuplicateGuard only detects duplicates                    │
  │  O: numeric variant added without touching the string one     │
  │  D: callers depend on boolean result, not the set internals   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │             DuplicateGuard            │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + hasDuplicate(ids: String[]):bool   │  O(n) avg, early exit
  │  + hasNumericDuplicate(amts):bool     │  stripTrailingZeros key
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      hasDuplicate contract:
        Pre:  ids may be null/short (false)
        Post: true at first repeat; relies on equals/hashCode
      BigDecimal trap: equals considers scale → normalise first

  ── State Diagram: Add Result ─────────────────────────────

  [add(x)==true] ──→ [new, continue]
  [add(x)==false]──→ [DUPLICATE: return true]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. DuplicateDemo.main()
  2.   → hasDuplicate([TXN-001,TXN-002,TXN-001]) → true at 3rd
  3.   → hasDuplicate(clean) → false
  4.   → hasNumericDuplicate([100,100.00]) → true
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The contains-duplicate problem asks whether any value appears more than once, and the fast solution is a single pass with a HashSet. I add each element to the set, and because HashSet's add returns false when the element is already present, the first time add returns false I have found a duplicate and return true. If every add succeeds, there are no duplicates. It is average linear time because HashSet operations are average constant time, at the cost of linear extra memory for the set.

I always weigh the trade-off. The HashSet approach spends memory to get the fastest average time, which is the right default. If memory is tight and I may mutate the input, sorting first and scanning adjacent equal elements finds duplicates in N log N with no extra set, and the brute-force double loop is quadratic and only fine for tiny inputs.

The correctness point I stress is equality and hashing. HashSet depends on equals and hashCode being consistent, so for my own identifier types I override both. For BigDecimal there is a famous trap: equals also considers scale, so one hundred and one hundred point zero zero are not equal and hash differently, which means a plain HashSet would miss that numeric duplicate. When numeric equality is what matters I normalise the scale first, for example by stripping trailing zeros, before putting values in the set.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to guard a batch of transaction identifiers before applying them, because a repeated identifier could double-charge a customer like Rajesh. The guard pre-sizes the set, exits at the first duplicate, and for numeric amounts normalises scale so numerically equal values are caught. Explaining the add-returns-false trick, the memory trade-off, and the BigDecimal equals trap shows the interviewer that I know the efficient solution and the subtle correctness issues that bite in real financial data.
