answers.question: Longest Palindromic Substring — expand-around-center O(n²) or Manacher's O(n).
answers.shortTitle: Longest Palindromic Substring — Expand Around Center O(n²)

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Palindromic Substring problem finds the longest contiguous substring that reads the same forward and backward. The expand-around-center solution treats every position, and every gap between positions, as a potential palindrome center and expands outward while the mirrored characters match, keeping the longest span found. It runs in quadratic time with constant extra space, while Manacher's algorithm achieves linear time with more complex bookkeeping.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India scans a reference string and wants the longest stretch that is symmetric like a mirror. The idea is to stand at every possible center, both on a character and between two characters, and push outward one step at a time as long as the characters on the left and right keep matching. Whichever center produces the widest mirror wins. It is like dropping a pin at each spot and seeing how far the symmetry extends.
s1_definition.oneliner: Try every character and every gap as a center, expand while both sides match, and keep the longest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Palindromic Substring problem finds the longest contiguous substring that reads the same forward and backward. The expand-around-center solution treats every position, and every gap between positions, as a potential palindrome center and expands outward while the mirrored characters match, keeping the longest span found. It runs in quadratic time with constant extra space, while Manacher's algorithm achieves linear time with more complex bookkeeping.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India scans a reference string and wants the longest stretch that is symmetric like a mirror. The idea is to stand at every possible center, both on a character and between two characters, and push outward one step at a time as long as the characters on the left and right keep matching. Whichever center produces the widest mirror wins. It is like dropping a pin at each spot and seeing how far the symmetry extends.

**One line to remember:** Try every character and every gap as a center, expand while both sides match, and keep the longest.

sections.s2_technical:
A palindrome is defined by a center and symmetric expansion. There are two kinds of centers: an odd-length palindrome has a single character at its center, and an even-length palindrome has its center between two characters. So for a string of length n there are 2n minus one possible centers, one at each character and one in each gap between adjacent characters.

The expand-around-center method loops over every index and treats it both as an odd center, with left and right both starting at that index, and as an even center, with left at that index and right at the next index. For each center you expand: while the left index is in bounds, the right index is in bounds, and the characters at left and right are equal, you move left one step back and right one step forward. When the expansion stops, the palindrome spans from just inside the final left to just inside the final right, and you compute its length. You track the overall longest span, remembering its start and end to return the substring at the end.

The time is quadratic because there are a linear number of centers and each expansion can take linear time in the worst case, such as a string of all identical characters. The space is constant because you only track indices and the best span, never building extra structures. This quadratic approach is the one most interviewers expect you to code correctly, with Manacher's linear algorithm as a known follow-up rather than the default.

A senior point is handling both center parities in one pass with a small helper. The helper takes a left and right starting index and returns the length of the palindrome centered there after expanding. You call it once with left equal to right for odd centers and once with right equal to left plus one for even centers, take the larger, and if it beats the best, update the start and end using arithmetic on the center and the returned length. Getting the start and end arithmetic exactly right, especially the even case, is where bugs hide.

Another senior point is Manacher's algorithm, which reaches linear time by transforming the string with separators and reusing previously computed palindrome radii via a mirror property around the current rightmost palindrome boundary. I mention that it exists and is linear, but I note it is rarely required to code live and is error-prone, so I lead with expand-around-center and offer Manacher's as the optimization if pressed.

A small finance-domain example: `for(int i=0;i<n;i++){ int a=expand(s,i,i); int b=expand(s,i,i+1); int len=Math.max(a,b); if(len>best){ start=i-(len-1)/2; end=i+len/2; } }` finds the longest mirrored span.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India examines reference strings for the longest symmetric segment, a mirror-like run, as part of a pattern-detection utility that flags unusual structured identifiers. The strings are moderate in length, so the quadratic expand-around-center approach is acceptable and simplest to get right. Finding the longest palindromic substring is exactly this.

This is exactly how expand-around-center works in Java — trying every character and every gap as a center and expanding while both sides match.

Problem 2 — Palindromes can be odd length, centered on a character, or even length, centered between two characters, and both must be checked, and an empty or single-character string is trivially its own answer. This shows the two-parity centers and the trivial edge cases.

What the code will do: a `PalindromeFinder` with `longestPalindrome(String s)` using expand-around-center over both parities, tracking the best span. The demo finds the longest palindromic substring in several reference strings.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the reference string `babad`.

Step 1: at index zero, character `b`, the odd expansion starts with left and right both zero. The characters match trivially, then left goes to minus one which is out of bounds, so expansion stops with length one. The even expansion with left zero and right one compares `b` and `a`, which differ, so length zero. The best length so far is one, span is just `b`.

Step 2: at index one, character `a`, the odd expansion compares outward: left zero `b` and right two `b` match, so it expands to the substring `bab` of length three, then left minus one stops it. The even expansion compares `a` and `b`, differ, length zero. Three beats one, so we update the span: start is index one minus one which is zero, end is index one plus one which is two, giving `bab`.

Step 3: at index two, character `b`, the odd expansion compares left one `a` and right three `a`, match, expanding to `aba` of length three, then left zero `b` and right four `d` differ, stopping. Length three ties the best but does not exceed it, so the span stays `bab`.

Step 4: at indices three and four the expansions produce lengths of at most one, not beating three. The loop ends with the span `bab`, which we return. Depending on tie handling, `aba` is an equally valid answer; this implementation keeps the first longest found.

Step 5: for `cbbd` the even center between the two `b` characters at indices one and two expands to `bb` of length two, which beats the odd single-character palindromes, so the answer is `bb`. For a single character `a` the odd expansion gives length one and the answer is `a`.

2026-10-26T21:20:00Z INFO Result = bb
2026-10-26T21:20:00Z INFO Longest palindrome = 'a'
2026-10-26T21:20:00Z INFO Result = a
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Palindromic Substring finds the longest contiguous substring that reads the same both ways, and I solve it with expand-around-center in quadratic time and constant space. The insight is that every palindrome has a center, and there are two kinds: an odd-length palindrome centered on a single character and an even-length one centered between two characters, giving two times n minus one possible centers for a string of length n.

For each index I expand twice, once as an odd center with left and right both at the index, and once as an even center with right one past left, pushing outward while the characters on both sides match and stay in bounds. A small helper returns the palindrome length for a given center, and I use the center and that length to compute the start and end of the span, keeping the longest. Getting the start and end arithmetic right, especially for the even case, is where most bugs appear, so I derive it carefully.

I always mention Manacher's algorithm as the linear-time follow-up. It transforms the string with separators and reuses previously computed palindrome radii through a mirror property around the current rightmost palindrome, reaching linear time, but it is intricate and error-prone to write live, so I lead with expand-around-center and offer Manacher's only if asked for better than quadratic. I also handle the trivial cases where an empty or single-character string is its own answer.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used expand-around-center in a pattern-detection utility that flags reference strings containing an unusually long symmetric segment, checking both odd and even centers over moderate-length identifiers. Explaining the two center parities, the expansion helper, the span arithmetic, and knowing when Manacher's would be warranted shows the interviewer that I can implement the expected solution correctly while being aware of the optimal one.

answers.question: Palindromic Substrings — count all (expand-around-center).
answers.shortTitle: Palindromic Substrings — Count All (Expand Around Center)

s1_definition.profdef: The Palindromic Substrings problem counts how many contiguous substrings of a string are palindromes, counting different positions separately even when the text is identical. The expand-around-center solution treats every character and every gap as a center and counts one palindrome for each successful expansion step outward while the mirrored characters match. It runs in quadratic time with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to count every symmetric segment inside a reference string, where the same segment at different places counts each time. Standing at every possible center, both on a character and between two characters, each time you push outward and the two sides still match, that is one more palindrome to tally. You add up all these successful expansions across all centers.
s1_definition.oneliner: For every center, each outward step where both sides match is one more palindrome; sum them all.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Palindromic Substrings problem counts how many contiguous substrings of a string are palindromes, counting different positions separately even when the text is identical. The expand-around-center solution treats every character and every gap as a center and counts one palindrome for each successful expansion step outward while the mirrored characters match. It runs in quadratic time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to count every symmetric segment inside a reference string, where the same segment at different places counts each time. Standing at every possible center, both on a character and between two characters, each time you push outward and the two sides still match, that is one more palindrome to tally. You add up all these successful expansions across all centers.

**One line to remember:** For every center, each outward step where both sides match is one more palindrome; sum them all.

sections.s2_technical:
This is the counting cousin of the longest-palindrome problem, and it uses the same expand-around-center machinery. The difference is that instead of tracking the single longest span, you count how many palindromes each center yields. Every center yields at least one palindrome, the single character or, for even centers, requires the two adjacent characters to match to count even the smallest one.

For each of the two times n minus one centers, you expand outward. Each time the left and right characters are equal and both in bounds, you increment a running count, because the substring from left to right is itself a palindrome, then you move left back and right forward to check the next larger palindrome sharing that center. The moment the characters differ or you go out of bounds, you stop expanding this center and move to the next. The total count accumulates every palindrome centered anywhere.

The reason this counts correctly without double counting is that each palindrome has a unique center and a unique radius, so it is produced by exactly one center at exactly one expansion step. An odd-length palindrome comes from a character center, an even-length one from a gap center, and the expansion radius pins down its exact span. So summing one per successful expansion over all centers counts each distinct palindromic substring exactly once by position.

A senior point is the shared helper design. A single helper takes a left and right start, expands while the characters match, and returns the number of palindromes found from that center, which is simply the number of successful expansion steps. You call it with left equal to right for odd centers and left, right equal to i and i plus one for even centers, and sum the two returns across all i. This mirrors the longest-palindrome helper but returns a count instead of a length, which keeps the code clean and reuses the same reasoning.

Another senior point is the quadratic bound and the linear alternative. The worst case, a string of all identical characters, has a quadratic number of palindromic substrings, so even just enumerating them is quadratic and no algorithm can count them faster than producing them if it listed them; but counting only, Manacher's algorithm computes the per-center radii in linear time and sums them, giving linear total time for the count. I lead with expand-around-center for clarity and mention Manacher's as the linear option.

A small finance-domain example: `int count=0; for(int i=0;i<n;i++){ count+=expand(s,i,i); count+=expand(s,i,i+1); }` where expand returns the number of matching outward steps, totals all palindromic substrings.

Problem 2 — Single characters always count as palindromes, so a length-n string has at least n of them, and an empty string has zero, both of which the same code must produce. This shows the baseline single-character count and the empty-input edge case.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the reference string `aaa`.

Step 1: at index zero, the odd center expands: left and right both zero, `a` equals itself, count one for the single `a`, then left goes out of bounds and stops. The even center with left zero and right one compares `a` and `a`, match, count one for the substring `aa` spanning indices zero and one, then left out of bounds stops. So index zero contributed two palindromes.

Step 2: at index one, the odd center expands: `a` at one alone, count one, then left zero `a` and right two `a` match, count one for `aaa`, then out of bounds stops. So the odd center at index one contributed two, the single `a` and the full `aaa`.

Step 3: at index one, the even center with left one and right two compares `a` and `a`, match, count one for the substring `aa` spanning indices one and two, then left zero `a` and right three out of bounds stops. So index one contributed three total.

Step 4: at index two, the odd center gives the single `a`, count one, then out of bounds. The even center with left two and right three is out of bounds immediately, count zero. So index two contributed one.

Step 5: summing the contributions, index zero gave two, index one gave three, index two gave one, totaling six palindromic substrings: three single characters, two `aa` segments at different positions, and one `aaa`. For `abc`, each character is a palindrome but no two adjacent characters match, so the count is three.

2026-10-26T21:30:00Z INFO Count = 3
2026-10-26T21:30:00Z INFO Palindromic substrings = 6
2026-10-26T21:30:00Z INFO Count = 6

Palindromic Substrings counts how many contiguous substrings of a string are palindromes, counting different positions separately, and I solve it with the same expand-around-center machinery as the longest-palindrome problem, in quadratic time and constant space. The difference is that instead of tracking the single longest span, I count one palindrome for every successful outward expansion step at every center.

For each of the two times n minus one centers, I expand outward while the mirrored characters match, incrementing the count each time they do, because the substring from the current left to right is itself a palindrome. A single helper returns the number of matching expansion steps from a given center, and I call it once for the odd center on each character and once for the even center in each gap, summing the results.

The reason this counts each palindrome exactly once, with no double counting, is that every palindromic substring has a unique center and a unique radius, so it is produced by exactly one center at exactly one expansion step. I also know the complexity floor: a string of all identical characters has a quadratic number of palindromic substrings, and while listing them is inherently quadratic, counting only can be done in linear time with Manacher's per-center radii, which I offer as the optimization while leading with the clearer expand-around-center.

answers.question: Minimum Window Substring — sliding window with frequency map.
answers.shortTitle: Minimum Window Substring — Sliding Window With Frequency Map

s1_definition.profdef: The Minimum Window Substring problem finds the shortest contiguous substring of a source string that contains all characters of a target string, including duplicates. The sliding-window solution expands the right edge until the window covers all required characters, then contracts the left edge as far as possible while still covering them, recording the smallest valid window. It runs in linear time using a frequency map of required characters and a satisfied-count.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India scans a long string of transaction codes and must find the shortest stretch that contains a required set of codes, each the right number of times, perhaps to locate the tightest segment covering a mandatory checklist. You grow a window on the right until it contains everything required, then you tighten it from the left as much as possible while it still satisfies the checklist, and you keep the tightest satisfying window found.
s1_definition.oneliner: Expand right until the window has everything needed, then shrink left while it still does, tracking the smallest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Minimum Window Substring problem finds the shortest contiguous substring of a source string that contains all characters of a target string, including duplicates. The sliding-window solution expands the right edge until the window covers all required characters, then contracts the left edge as far as possible while still covering them, recording the smallest valid window. It runs in linear time using a frequency map of required characters and a satisfied-count.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India scans a long string of transaction codes and must find the shortest stretch that contains a required set of codes, each the right number of times, perhaps to locate the tightest segment covering a mandatory checklist. You grow a window on the right until it contains everything required, then you tighten it from the left as much as possible while it still satisfies the checklist, and you keep the tightest satisfying window found.

**One line to remember:** Expand right until the window has everything needed, then shrink left while it still does, tracking the smallest.

sections.s2_technical:
You need two ideas: a way to know what the target requires, and a way to know when the current window satisfies it. The target's requirements are a frequency map, how many of each character are needed. The window tracks how many of those requirements are currently met. A compact way is to keep a counter of how many distinct required characters are fully satisfied in the window, and compare it to the number of distinct required characters.

You keep a need map from character to required count, and a have map or a window count. You move the right index forward, and for each character you add it to the window; if it is a required character and the window's count for it just reached the needed count, you increment a formed counter. When formed equals the number of distinct required characters, the window is valid, meaning it contains all requirements. At that point you try to shrink: while the window is still valid, you record its length if it is the smallest so far, then remove the character at the left index, advance left, and if removing a required character drops its window count below the needed count, you decrement formed, which ends the shrink.

The reason this is linear is the same amortized argument as other sliding windows: the right index moves forward across the whole string once, and the left index also only moves forward, never backward, so each character is added once and removed at most once. The formed counter lets you test validity in constant time per step instead of rescanning the window.

A senior point is handling duplicate requirements correctly. If the target needs two of a character, the formed counter must only increment when the window's count reaches exactly the needed two, not on the first occurrence, and must only decrement when shrinking drops it below two. Using the equality check at the exact threshold, rather than a mere presence check, is what makes duplicates work. Many buggy versions use a set and silently fail when the target has repeats.

Another senior point is the result tracking and the no-answer case. You record the best window as a start index and a length, updating only when a strictly smaller valid window appears, and if no valid window is ever formed you return an empty string. For an open character set you use HashMaps; for a fixed small alphabet arrays are faster. In banking I note the target may be larger than any window, so the empty result must be clean.

A small finance-domain example: `need` built from the target, `formed` counting satisfied requirements, expanding right and contracting left while `formed == required`, recording the minimal start and length, returns the tightest covering segment.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has a long log of single-character transaction codes and must find the shortest contiguous stretch that contains a mandatory set of codes with required multiplicities, for example the tightest window that includes at least one debit, two credits, and one transfer, to locate the most compact compliant segment. The log is long, so the search must be linear. Finding the minimum window substring is exactly this.

This is exactly how Minimum Window Substring works in Java — expanding the right edge until the window covers all required codes, then contracting the left edge while it still does.

Problem 2 — The target may require duplicates, such as two credits, so the satisfaction check must respect counts, not mere presence, and the required set may never fit, in which case the result is empty. This shows the duplicate-count handling and the no-answer edge case.

What the code will do: a `MinWindowFinder` with `minWindow(String source, String target)` using a sliding window with a need map and a formed counter. The demo finds the tightest covering window for a code log and target.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the source code log `ADOBECODEBANC` and the target `ABC`, requiring one A, one B, and one C.

Step 1: the need map is A one, B one, C one, so required is three. We expand right, adding each character to the window. By the time the right edge reaches the first `C` at index five, the window `ADOBEC` contains one A, one B, and one C, so formed reaches three and the window is valid.

Step 2: now we contract from the left while valid. The window `ADOBEC` has length six. We remove `A` at index zero; the window's A count drops below the needed one, so formed drops to two and the shrink stops, with left now at one. The best window so far is `ADOBEC` length six.

Step 3: we keep expanding right. As more characters arrive, the window regains the missing A when a later A appears, formed returns to three, and we contract again, each time recording a smaller valid window if found. Through the middle of the string the tightest valid windows get shorter as the required characters cluster.

Step 4: near the end, the right edge reaches the final `C` in the tail `BANC`. At that point the window can be contracted down to exactly `BANC`, which contains one B, one A, and one C, a length of four, which is smaller than any previous valid window, so the best becomes `BANC`.

Step 5: the scan finishes with the best window `BANC` of length four, returned as the answer. For the target `CC` on `DCCTC`, the tightest window covering two C characters is the adjacent `CC`. For the target `ABC` on `DD`, no window ever forms all three, so formed never reaches three and the result is the empty string.

2026-10-26T21:40:00Z INFO Minimum window = 'CC'
2026-10-26T21:40:00Z INFO Window = 'CC'

2026-10-26T21:40:00Z INFO Window = ''

sections.s6_takeaway:
Minimum Window Substring finds the shortest contiguous substring of a source that contains all characters of a target, including duplicates, and I solve it with an expand-and-contract sliding window in linear time. I build a need map of how many of each character the target requires, and I track how many distinct requirements the current window fully satisfies with a formed counter. I expand the right edge until formed equals the number of distinct required characters, meaning the window covers everything, then I contract the left edge as far as possible while it stays valid, recording the smallest valid window.

The amortized-linear argument is the same as other sliding windows: the right index sweeps the string once and the left index only moves forward, so each character is added once and removed at most once, and the formed counter lets me check validity in constant time instead of rescanning the window each step.

The detail that separates a correct solution from a common buggy one is duplicate requirements. If the target needs two of a character, I increment formed only when the window's count reaches exactly the needed two, and decrement it only when contracting drops it below two, using an exact-threshold equality check rather than a mere presence test. A version that uses a set instead of counts silently fails whenever the target has repeats. I also track the best window as a start and length, returning an empty string cleanly when no valid window ever forms.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on long transaction-code logs to locate the tightest contiguous segment containing a mandatory set of codes with required multiplicities, such as the most compact stretch covering a compliance checklist. Explaining the need map and formed counter, the amortized-linear sweep, and especially the exact-count handling of duplicates shows the interviewer that I understand the hardest sliding-window problem rather than a simplified presence-only version.

answers.question: Valid Parentheses — stack matching pairs.
answers.shortTitle: Valid Parentheses — Stack Matching Pairs

s1_definition.profdef: The Valid Parentheses problem checks whether a string of brackets, round, square, and curly, is correctly balanced and properly nested. The stack solution pushes each opening bracket and, on each closing bracket, verifies the top of the stack is the matching opener and pops it, rejecting on any mismatch or empty stack, and finally requires the stack to be empty. It runs in linear time with stack space proportional to the nesting depth.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India validates nested grouping markers in a formula string used for fee calculations, where every opening bracket must be closed by the right kind in the right order. Imagine a stack of plates. Each time you see an opening bracket you put a plate on top. Each time you see a closing bracket, the plate on top must be its exact partner, and you remove it. If the top is the wrong kind, or there is no plate, the string is invalid, and at the end the stack must be empty.
s1_definition.oneliner: Push openers, and on each closer the stack top must be its exact match; the stack must end empty.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Valid Parentheses problem checks whether a string of brackets, round, square, and curly, is correctly balanced and properly nested. The stack solution pushes each opening bracket and, on each closing bracket, verifies the top of the stack is the matching opener and pops it, rejecting on any mismatch or empty stack, and finally requires the stack to be empty. It runs in linear time with stack space proportional to the nesting depth.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India validates nested grouping markers in a formula string used for fee calculations, where every opening bracket must be closed by the right kind in the right order. Imagine a stack of plates. Each time you see an opening bracket you put a plate on top. Each time you see a closing bracket, the plate on top must be its exact partner, and you remove it. If the top is the wrong kind, or there is no plate, the string is invalid, and at the end the stack must be empty.

**One line to remember:** Push openers, and on each closer the stack top must be its exact match; the stack must end empty.

sections.s2_technical:
Balanced brackets follow a last-opened-first-closed discipline, which is exactly what a stack models. You scan the string character by character. When you see an opening bracket, one of round, square, or curly, you push it onto the stack. When you see a closing bracket, you must check that the stack is not empty and that its top element is the corresponding opening bracket; if so, you pop the top, otherwise the string is invalid and you return false immediately.

The two failure conditions on a closer are both important. If the stack is empty when you meet a closer, there is no opener to match, so it is invalid, like closing a bracket that was never opened. If the stack top is a different kind of opener, the nesting is crossed, like opening a round bracket then trying to close it with a curly one, which is also invalid. Only when the top is the exact matching opener do you pop and continue.

After the whole string is scanned, you require the stack to be empty. A non-empty stack means some opening brackets were never closed, so the string is unbalanced even though no mismatch occurred during the scan. This final emptiness check is as essential as the per-closer checks; forgetting it would wrongly accept a string like a single opening bracket.

A senior point is using a map from each closing bracket to its expected opening bracket, which makes the matching logic clean and easy to extend to more bracket types. On a closing bracket you look up its expected opener and compare it to the popped or peeked top. This avoids a tangle of if-else comparisons and keeps the code readable and correct.

Another senior point is the early-exit efficiency and the odd-length shortcut. You return false the instant a mismatch or an empty-stack-on-closer occurs, so invalid strings often fail fast. A quick optimization is that a string of odd length can never be balanced, so you can reject it in constant time up front. For memory, the stack grows to at most the maximum nesting depth, which for deeply nested fee formulas is worth noting.

A small finance-domain example: `Deque<Character> st=new ArrayDeque<>(); for(char c:s.toCharArray()){ if(isOpen(c)) st.push(c); else { if(st.isEmpty() || st.pop()!=match.get(c)) return false; } } return st.isEmpty();` validates a bracketed formula.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores fee-calculation formulas as strings with nested grouping brackets, round for precedence, square and curly for structured sections, and a validator must confirm every bracket is balanced and correctly nested before the formula is parsed, so a malformed formula is rejected early. The validation runs on every formula edit so it must be linear. Checking valid parentheses with a stack is exactly this.

This is exactly how Valid Parentheses works in Java — pushing openers and matching each closer against the stack top.

Problem 2 — A formula might close a bracket that was never opened, or leave an opener unclosed, or cross bracket types, and all three must be rejected. This shows the empty-stack-on-closer, the non-empty-at-end, and the crossed-type failure conditions.

What the code will do: a `BracketValidator` with `isValid(String formula)` using a stack and a closer-to-opener map with the final emptiness check. The demo validates several bracketed formulas.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the fee formula `{[(1+2)*3]}`.

Step 1: we scan left to right with an empty stack. The first character is `{`, an opener, so we push it; the stack is `{`. The next is `[`, an opener, push; the stack is `{ [`. The next is `(`, an opener, push; the stack is `{ [ (`.

Step 2: the characters `1`, `+`, `2` are not brackets, so they are ignored. The next is `)`, a closer; its expected opener is `(`, and the stack top is `(`, so they match, we pop, and the stack becomes `{ [`.

Step 3: the characters `*`, `3` are ignored. The next is `]`, a closer; its expected opener is `[`, and the stack top is `[`, so they match, we pop, and the stack becomes `{`.

Step 4: the final character is `}`, a closer; its expected opener is `{`, and the stack top is `{`, so they match, we pop, and the stack becomes empty. The scan ends, the stack is empty, so the formula is valid.

Step 5: for `([)]`, after pushing `(` and `[`, the closer `)` expects `(` but the stack top is `[`, a crossed mismatch, so we return false immediately. For `((`, both openers are pushed and never closed, so at the end the stack is non-empty and the result is false.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T21:50:00Z INFO '{[(1+2)*3]}' is VALID
2026-10-26T21:50:00Z INFO Result = true
2026-10-26T21:50:00Z INFO '([)]' is INVALID
2026-10-26T21:50:00Z INFO Result = false
2026-10-26T21:50:00Z INFO '((' is INVALID
2026-10-26T21:50:00Z INFO Result = false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: "{[(1+2)*3]}"
    │ scan chars; push openers; match closers to stack top
    ▼
  '{' push → [{] ; '[' push → [{,[] ; '(' push → [{,[,(]
  ')' top '(' match → pop → [{,[]
  ']' top '[' match → pop → [{]
  '}' top '{' match → pop → []
    │ stack empty at end?
    ▼
  valid = true   ("([)]" crossed → false ; "((" leftover → false)
    ▼
  Output: balanced yes/no
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Valid Parentheses checks whether a string of round, square, and curly brackets is balanced and properly nested, and I solve it with a stack in linear time, because balanced brackets follow a last-opened-first-closed discipline that a stack models exactly. I scan the string, push every opening bracket, and on every closing bracket I verify the stack is non-empty and its top is the exact matching opener, popping on a match and returning false immediately on any mismatch or empty stack.

Both closer failure conditions matter. An empty stack on a closer means closing a bracket that was never opened, and a wrong-kind top means the nesting is crossed, like opening a round bracket and closing it with a curly one. Only an exact-match top is popped and allowed to continue. Equally essential is the final check that the stack is empty, because leftover openers mean some brackets were never closed, which would otherwise be wrongly accepted.

I keep the matching clean with a map from each closing bracket to its expected opener, which reads clearly and extends easily to more bracket types, and I return false the instant a problem is found so invalid strings fail fast. I also note the constant-time odd-length shortcut, since a string of odd length can never balance, and that the stack grows only to the maximum nesting depth.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to validate fee-calculation formulas with nested grouping brackets before parsing them, rejecting malformed formulas early on every edit, including the crossed-type and unclosed-opener cases. Explaining the stack discipline, the two closer failure conditions, the final emptiness check, and the closer-to-opener map shows the interviewer that I understand why the stack is the right tool and have covered every failure mode.

answers.question: Longest Valid Parentheses — stack tracking indices.
answers.shortTitle: Longest Valid Parentheses — Stack Tracking Indices

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Valid Parentheses problem finds the length of the longest contiguous substring of round brackets that is correctly balanced. The stack-of-indices solution pushes the index of each opening bracket and a base marker, and on each closing bracket pops and computes the length of the valid run from the current index back to the new stack top, tracking the maximum. It runs in linear time with stack space proportional to the input.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a string of grouping markers and wants the longest unbroken stretch that is perfectly balanced, ignoring any broken parts. Think of keeping a stack of positions. When you open a bracket you note its position. When you close one, you pair it off and measure how long the balanced run now extends, from here back to the last unmatched position. The widest such measured run is the answer.
s1_definition.oneliner: Push indices with a base marker, and on each close pop and measure the run back to the new top, tracking the max.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Valid Parentheses problem finds the length of the longest contiguous substring of round brackets that is correctly balanced. The stack-of-indices solution pushes the index of each opening bracket and a base marker, and on each closing bracket pops and computes the length of the valid run from the current index back to the new stack top, tracking the maximum. It runs in linear time with stack space proportional to the input.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a string of grouping markers and wants the longest unbroken stretch that is perfectly balanced, ignoring any broken parts. Think of keeping a stack of positions. When you open a bracket you note its position. When you close one, you pair it off and measure how long the balanced run now extends, from here back to the last unmatched position. The widest such measured run is the answer.

**One line to remember:** Push indices with a base marker, and on each close pop and measure the run back to the new top, tracking the max.

sections.s2_technical:
Unlike the simple validity check, here you need the length of the longest balanced run, which requires tracking positions, not just counts. The elegant method keeps a stack of indices with a sentinel base. You initialize the stack with minus one, which acts as a base marker just before the string, representing the last position that was not part of a valid substring.

You scan the string. For an opening bracket at index i, you push i onto the stack. For a closing bracket, you pop the top. Then there are two cases. If the stack is now empty, this closing bracket has no matching opener and itself becomes a new base, so you push its index as the new base marker. If the stack is not empty, the current valid run extends from just after the new top to the current index, so its length is the current index minus the new stack top, and you update the maximum with that length.

The base marker is the clever part. The value on the bottom of the stack is always the index of the most recent position that broke validity, either a minus one at the start or an unmatched closing bracket. By measuring the current index minus this base, you capture the full length of the valid substring ending at the current position, including runs that span multiple pairs like several adjacent or nested groups. This is why the stack holds indices rather than bracket characters.

A senior point is why popping before measuring is correct. When you meet a closing bracket, popping removes the matching opener's index, and the new top is the boundary of the enclosing valid run. The subtraction then spans everything from that boundary to now, which correctly includes inner completed pairs. If you measured before popping, you would miscount by one pair. Getting this order right is where subtle off-by-one bugs appear.

Another senior point is the alternative two-pass counter method, which scans left to right counting opens and closes and resets when they cross, then scans right to left symmetrically, using constant space instead of a stack. Both are linear; the stack method is the most common to explain, and I mention the two-pass counter as a constant-space variant. There is also a dynamic-programming formulation, which I note exists.

A small finance-domain example: `Deque<Integer> st=new ArrayDeque<>(); st.push(-1); int best=0; for(int i=0;i<s.length();i++){ if(s.charAt(i)=='(') st.push(i); else { st.pop(); if(st.isEmpty()) st.push(i); else best=Math.max(best, i-st.peek()); } }` finds the longest balanced run length.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes grouping-marker strings from partially corrupted formula fragments and wants the length of the longest contiguous balanced stretch, to recover the largest intact grouped section for salvage parsing. The fragments can be long, so the scan must be linear. Finding the longest valid parentheses run is exactly this.

This is exactly how Longest Valid Parentheses works in Java — a stack of indices with a base marker that measures each valid run back to the last unmatched position.

Problem 2 — A fragment may start with stray closing brackets or contain broken sections between valid ones, and the base marker must reset correctly at each break so runs are measured accurately, and an empty fragment gives zero. This shows the base-marker reset logic and the empty-input edge case.

What the code will do: a `LongestValidFinder` with `longestValid(String markers)` using a stack of indices with a minus-one base and pop-then-measure. The demo finds the longest balanced run in several marker strings.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the marker string `)()())`.

Step 1: the stack starts with the base marker minus one and best is zero. Index zero is `)`, a closer; we pop the minus one, the stack is now empty, so this unmatched closer becomes a new base and we push index zero. The stack is now `0`.

Step 2: index one is `(`, an opener; we push index one. The stack is `0, 1`. Index two is `)`, a closer; we pop index one, the stack top is now index zero, not empty, so the run length is the current index two minus the top zero, which is two, and best becomes two.

Step 3: index three is `(`, an opener; we push index three. The stack is `0, 3`. Index four is `)`, a closer; we pop index three, the stack top is now index zero, so the run length is index four minus zero, which is four, and best becomes four. This correctly spans the balanced run `()()` from index one through four, including both pairs.

Step 4: index five is `)`, a closer; we pop index zero, the stack becomes empty, so this unmatched closer becomes a new base and we push index five. The stack is `5`. No run is measured here because the stack was empty after popping.

Step 5: the scan ends with best four, the length of the longest balanced run `()()`. The base marker at index zero let the measurement at index four span both pairs correctly, and the resets at the stray closers kept broken sections from inflating the count. For `(()` the best is the inner `()` of length two, and an empty string gives zero.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T22:00:00Z INFO Longest valid run = 2
2026-10-26T22:00:00Z INFO Run = 2
2026-10-26T22:00:00Z INFO Longest valid run = 4
2026-10-26T22:00:00Z INFO Run = 4
2026-10-26T22:00:00Z INFO Longest valid run = 0
2026-10-26T22:00:00Z INFO Run = 0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: ")()())"  stack=[-1] best=0
    │ scan indices; push '(' index; on ')' pop then measure or rebase
    ▼
  i0 ')' pop -1 → empty → push 0        stack=[0]
  i1 '(' push 1                         stack=[0,1]
  i2 ')' pop 1 → top 0 → len 2-0=2 best=2
  i3 '(' push 3                         stack=[0,3]
  i4 ')' pop 3 → top 0 → len 4-0=4 best=4
  i5 ')' pop 0 → empty → push 5         stack=[5]
    ▼
  best = 4  ("(()" → 2 ; "" → 0)
    ▼
  Output: longest balanced run length
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Longest Valid Finder ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Stack of INDICES with a base marker (-1 or unmatched closer) │
  │  Pop-then-measure: length = i - new stack top                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: finder only computes the longest valid run                │
  │  O: swap to two-pass counter (O(1) space), no caller change   │
  │  D: callers depend on the int length, not the stack           │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           LongestValidFinder          │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + longestValid(markers): int          │  O(n)/O(n)
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      longestValid contract:
        Pre:  markers non-null (else IllegalArgumentException)
        Post: length of longest balanced contiguous run
        Base marker tracks last invalid position; pop before measure

  ── State Diagram: Scan ───────────────────────────────────

  ['('] ──push i──→ [continue]
  [')'] ──pop; empty? push i (rebase) : best=max(best, i-top)──→
      │ end
      ▼
  [return best]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. LongestValidDemo.main()
  2.   → longestValid(")()())")
  3.     → push indices, pop+measure on closers
  4.     → best grows to 4
  5.     → return 4
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Valid Parentheses finds the length of the longest contiguous balanced substring of round brackets, and unlike a simple validity check it needs positions, so I use a stack of indices in linear time. I seed the stack with a minus-one base marker representing the last position that broke validity. For an opening bracket I push its index, and for a closing bracket I pop, then if the stack is empty this closer is unmatched and becomes a new base that I push, otherwise the current valid run length is the current index minus the new stack top, which I use to update the maximum.

The base marker is the heart of the method. The bottom of the stack always holds the index of the most recent position that broke validity, either the initial minus one or an unmatched closing bracket, so subtracting it from the current index captures the full length of the valid substring ending here, including runs that span several adjacent or nested pairs. That is why the stack stores indices rather than bracket characters.

The subtle correctness point is popping before measuring. When I meet a closer, popping removes the matching opener's index and the new top becomes the boundary of the enclosing valid run, so the subtraction spans every inner completed pair. Measuring before popping would miscount by one pair, which is a classic off-by-one bug here. I also know the constant-space two-pass counter variant, scanning left to right and right to left resetting when opens and closes cross, which I offer when memory is tight.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on grouping-marker strings from partially corrupted formula fragments to recover the longest intact balanced section for salvage parsing, with the base marker resetting correctly at each broken section. Explaining the index stack, the base-marker semantics, the pop-then-measure order, and the constant-space alternative shows the interviewer that I understand why this is harder than plain validity and how the index arithmetic stays correct.

answers.question: Valid Parenthesis String with `*` wildcard — greedy min/max open-count range.
answers.shortTitle: Valid Parenthesis String With `*` Wildcard — Greedy Min/Max Open-Count Range

s1_definition.profdef: This problem checks whether a string of round brackets and asterisk wildcards can be made valid, where each asterisk may be an opening bracket, a closing bracket, or an empty string. The greedy solution tracks a range of possible open-bracket counts, a low and a high, updating both as it scans, clamping the low at zero and rejecting if the high ever goes negative, and accepting if zero lies within the final range. It runs in linear time with constant space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has grouping strings where some markers are flexible placeholders that could act as an opener, a closer, or nothing. The validator keeps track of the smallest and largest number of still-open brackets that are possible so far. A flexible placeholder widens this range, a real opener raises both ends, and a real closer lowers both. If it is ever impossible to have any open brackets, even at the optimistic high end, the string fails; if at the end zero open brackets is achievable, it can be made valid.
s1_definition.oneliner: Track a low and high of possible open counts; clamp low at zero, fail if high goes negative, accept if zero is in range at the end.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem checks whether a string of round brackets and asterisk wildcards can be made valid, where each asterisk may be an opening bracket, a closing bracket, or an empty string. The greedy solution tracks a range of possible open-bracket counts, a low and a high, updating both as it scans, clamping the low at zero and rejecting if the high ever goes negative, and accepting if zero lies within the final range. It runs in linear time with constant space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has grouping strings where some markers are flexible placeholders that could act as an opener, a closer, or nothing. The validator keeps track of the smallest and largest number of still-open brackets that are possible so far. A flexible placeholder widens this range, a real opener raises both ends, and a real closer lowers both. If it is ever impossible to have any open brackets, even at the optimistic high end, the string fails; if at the end zero open brackets is achievable, it can be made valid.

**One line to remember:** Track a low and high of possible open counts; clamp low at zero, fail if high goes negative, accept if zero is in range at the end.

sections.s2_technical:
The asterisk makes a naive stack insufficient because each wildcard has three interpretations, and trying all combinations is exponential. The greedy insight is to track the range of possible counts of currently open brackets rather than a single count. You keep two numbers: low, the minimum possible open count, and high, the maximum possible open count, both starting at zero.

As you scan each character you update the range. For an opening bracket, both low and high increase by one, because it definitely adds an open bracket. For a closing bracket, both low and high decrease by one, because it definitely removes one. For an asterisk, the range widens: low decreases by one, since the asterisk could be a closing bracket reducing open count, and high increases by one, since it could be an opening bracket increasing it. The asterisk could also be empty, which is a value between, already covered by the range.

Two guards keep the range meaningful. If high ever becomes negative, it means even the most optimistic interpretation has more closers than openers at this point, which can never be valid, so you return false immediately. If low becomes negative, you clamp it to zero, because you can never have fewer than zero open brackets; a surplus of potential closers simply means some asterisks are treated as empty rather than as closers. Forgetting to clamp low would let it drift negative and wrongly reject valid strings.

A senior point is why checking low equals zero at the end is the acceptance test, not low at most zero. After clamping, low is the minimum achievable open count. The string can be made valid only if it is possible to end with exactly zero open brackets, and because high is at least low and the range is continuous, zero is achievable exactly when low has reached zero by the end. If low is still positive at the end, every interpretation leaves unmatched openers, so it fails.

Another senior point is that this greedy range method replaces a two-stack or dynamic-programming approach with constant space and a single pass, which is both simpler and faster. The alternative uses two stacks, one for opener indices and one for asterisk indices, matching greedily; it is correct but more code. For banking validation of flexible grouping strings the range method is my default.

A small finance-domain example: `int lo=0,hi=0; for(char c:s.toCharArray()){ if(c=='('){lo++;hi++;} else if(c==')'){lo--;hi--;} else {lo--;hi++;} if(hi<0) return false; if(lo<0) lo=0; } return lo==0;` validates a wildcard grouping string.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India accepts flexible grouping strings in a template system where an asterisk placeholder can stand for an opening bracket, a closing bracket, or nothing, and a validator must decide whether the template can be filled to form a balanced grouping. The templates are long, so validation must be linear. Checking a valid parenthesis string with wildcards is exactly this.

This is exactly how the wildcard validity check works in Java — tracking the range of possible open-bracket counts with a greedy low and high.

Problem 2 — A template may have more potential closers than openers at some point, which must fail only if even the optimistic interpretation is impossible, and leftover mandatory openers at the end must fail. This shows the high-goes-negative rejection, the low-clamp, and the end-low-equals-zero acceptance.

What the code will do: a `WildcardValidator` with `canBeValid(String template)` using the greedy min/max open-count range. The demo validates several wildcard templates.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the template `(*)`.

Step 1: low and high both start at zero. The first character is `(`, a real opener, so low becomes one and high becomes one. High is not negative and low is not negative, so no guard triggers.

Step 2: the next character is `*`, a wildcard. Low decreases by one to zero, since the asterisk could be a closer, and high increases by one to two, since it could be an opener. The range of possible open counts is now zero to two. Neither guard triggers.

Step 3: the next character is `)`, a real closer, so low decreases to minus one and high decreases to one. High is still non-negative. But low is now negative, so we clamp it to zero. The range is now zero to one.

Step 4: the scan ends. We check whether low equals zero, and it does, meaning it is possible to end with exactly zero open brackets, for example by treating the asterisk as empty so the string is just `()`. So the template can be made valid and we return true.

Step 5: for `(*))`, the extra closer is absorbed by treating the asterisk as an opener, and low still reaches zero at the end, so it is valid. For `)(`, the very first character is a closer, so low and high both go to minus one; high being negative triggers the immediate rejection, correctly identifying that no interpretation can fix a string starting with an unmatched closer.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T22:10:00Z INFO '(*)' CAN be valid
2026-10-26T22:10:00Z INFO Result = true
2026-10-26T22:10:00Z INFO '(*))' CAN be valid
2026-10-26T22:10:00Z INFO Result = true
2026-10-26T22:10:00Z INFO ')(' CANNOT be valid
2026-10-26T22:10:00Z INFO Result = false
```

```

    │ '(' low++,high++ ; ')' low--,high-- ; '*' low--,high++
    ▼
  '(' → low1 high1
  '*' → low0 high2
  ')' → low-1→clamp0  high1
    │ high<0 ever? no ; end low==0?
    ▼
  low==0 → true   (")(" → high<0 at i0 → false)
    ▼
  Output: can-be-valid yes/no
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Valid Parenthesis String with a wildcard checks whether a string of round brackets and asterisks can be made valid, where each asterisk may be an opener, a closer, or empty. A naive stack fails because each wildcard has three interpretations, so instead of a single open count I track a range, a low and a high of the possible number of currently open brackets, in a single linear pass with constant space.

As I scan, an opener raises both low and high by one, a closer lowers both by one, and an asterisk widens the range, lowering low because it could be a closer and raising high because it could be an opener, with the empty interpretation covered in between. Two guards keep the range meaningful: if high ever goes negative, even the most optimistic interpretation has too many closers, so I reject immediately, and if low goes negative I clamp it to zero, because you can never have fewer than zero open brackets and extra potential closers just become empty asterisks.

The acceptance test is that low equals zero at the end. After clamping, low is the minimum achievable open count, and since the range is continuous up to high, ending with exactly zero open brackets is possible precisely when low has reached zero; if low is still positive, every interpretation leaves unmatched openers. I always explain why clamping low is essential, because without it the count drifts negative and wrongly rejects valid strings, which is the most common bug.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to validate flexible grouping templates where an asterisk placeholder can stand for an opener, a closer, or nothing, deciding whether a template can be filled to form a balanced grouping, in one linear pass. Explaining the low-high range, the three-way asterisk update, the high-negative rejection, the low-clamp, and the end-low-equals-zero acceptance shows the interviewer that I can reason about an ambiguous input with a clean greedy invariant instead of brute force.

answers.question: Check if two strings are rotations of each other (`s1+s1` contains `s2`).
answers.shortTitle: Check If Two Strings Are Rotations of Each Other — s1+s1 Contains s2

s1_definition.profdef: Two strings are rotations of each other if one can be obtained by moving some prefix of the other to its end. The elegant check concatenates the first string with itself, forming a doubled string that contains every possible rotation as a substring, and tests whether the second string is a substring of that doubled string, after confirming the lengths are equal. It runs in linear time with the right substring search, or using the built-in contains in practice.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India compares two circular reference codes to decide if one is just the other spun around to start at a different point, like reading the same ring of letters from a different position. The trick is to write the first code twice in a row. Every way of spinning the first code to a new starting point appears somewhere inside that doubled code. So if the second code appears anywhere inside the doubled first code, and they are the same length, one is a rotation of the other.
s1_definition.oneliner: If lengths match and the second string is a substring of the first concatenated with itself, they are rotations.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Two strings are rotations of each other if one can be obtained by moving some prefix of the other to its end. The elegant check concatenates the first string with itself, forming a doubled string that contains every possible rotation as a substring, and tests whether the second string is a substring of that doubled string, after confirming the lengths are equal. It runs in linear time with the right substring search, or using the built-in contains in practice.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India compares two circular reference codes to decide if one is just the other spun around to start at a different point, like reading the same ring of letters from a different position. The trick is to write the first code twice in a row. Every way of spinning the first code to a new starting point appears somewhere inside that doubled code. So if the second code appears anywhere inside the doubled first code, and they are the same length, one is a rotation of the other.

**One line to remember:** If lengths match and the second string is a substring of the first concatenated with itself, they are rotations.

sections.s2_technical:
A rotation moves a prefix of a string to the back. For example, rotating `abcde` by two positions gives `cdeab`. The key observation is that every rotation of a string appears as a contiguous substring of that string concatenated with itself. If you write `abcde` twice you get `abcdeabcde`, and inside it you can find `bcdea`, `cdeab`, `deabc`, and `eabcd`, which are exactly all the non-trivial rotations, plus the original.

So the algorithm is: first check that the two strings have the same length, because strings of different lengths can never be rotations. If the lengths differ you return false immediately, which also guards against a shorter string accidentally being found inside the doubled longer one. Then you build the doubled string by concatenating the first string with itself, and you test whether the second string occurs as a substring of that doubled string. If it does, they are rotations; if not, they are not.

The length check is not optional. Without it, a short string like `ab` would be found inside the doubling of a longer string that happens to contain it, falsely reporting a rotation. Requiring equal lengths ensures that a found substring is a genuine full rotation, not a coincidental fragment. This is the single most common mistake in this problem.

A senior point is the complexity of the substring search. Using a naive substring scan, the contains check can be quadratic in the worst case. To guarantee linear time you use a linear-time string matching algorithm such as Knuth-Morris-Pratt to search for the second string inside the doubled first string, which runs in time proportional to the combined length. In an interview I state that the built-in contains is convenient but that for a strict linear guarantee I would use KMP, which shows I know the underlying cost.

Another senior point is the empty-string and identical-string cases. Two empty strings are trivially rotations of each other, and any string is a rotation of itself with a zero-position rotation, both of which the length check and the substring check handle naturally since a string is always a substring of its own doubling. For money-adjacent identifiers I treat the characters as plain text, and I note that case sensitivity should be defined up front if the codes might differ only in case.

A small finance-domain example: `if(s1.length()!=s2.length()) return false; return (s1+s1).contains(s2);` decides whether two circular reference codes are rotations, with KMP substituted for contains when linear time is required.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India uses circular reference codes where the same code may be recorded starting at a different position by different systems, and a reconciliation feature must decide whether two codes are rotations of one another, meaning they represent the same underlying circular identifier. The reconciliation runs over many pairs so it should be efficient. Checking whether two strings are rotations by the doubled-string trick is exactly this.

This is exactly how the rotation check works in Java — concatenating the first code with itself and testing whether the second code is a substring.

Problem 2 — Codes of different lengths can never be rotations and must be rejected instantly, and identical or empty codes must be accepted as trivial rotations. This shows the mandatory length guard and the trivial-case handling.

What the code will do: a `RotationChecker` with `areRotations(String a, String b)` using the length check and the doubled-string substring test. The demo compares several pairs of reference codes.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the two reference codes `ABCDE` and `CDEAB`.

Step 1: we compare lengths. Both codes have five characters, so the length check passes and we proceed. If they had differed in length we would have returned false right here.

Step 2: we build the doubled string by concatenating the first code with itself, giving `ABCDEABCDE`. This doubled string contains every rotation of `ABCDE` as a contiguous slice, including `BCDEA`, `CDEAB`, `DEABC`, and `EABCD`, as well as the original.

Step 3: we test whether the second code `CDEAB` appears as a substring of `ABCDEABCDE`. Scanning the doubled string, `CDEAB` begins at position two and runs through position six, so it is present. Therefore `CDEAB` is a rotation of `ABCDE` and we return true.

Step 4: for the pair `ABCDE` and `ABCED`, the lengths match, so we build `ABCDEABCDE` and search for `ABCED`. No slice of the doubled string equals `ABCED` because the letter order within it does not appear in any rotation, so the substring test fails and we return false.

Step 5: for `AB` and `ABC`, the lengths are two and three, which differ, so the length guard returns false immediately without building a doubled string, correctly preventing the shorter string from being coincidentally matched inside a longer doubling.

2026-10-26T22:20:00Z INFO 'ABCDE' / 'ABCED' → not rotations
2026-10-26T22:20:00Z INFO Result = false
2026-10-26T22:20:00Z INFO 'AB' / 'ABC' → different length, not rotations
2026-10-26T22:20:00Z INFO Result = false
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Checking whether two strings are rotations of each other asks if one can be formed by moving a prefix of the other to its end, and the elegant solution uses the observation that every rotation of a string appears as a contiguous substring of that string concatenated with itself. So I first confirm the two strings have equal length, then build the first string doubled and test whether the second string is a substring of it; if so, they are rotations.

The length check is mandatory, not a formality. Without it a short string could be found inside the doubling of a longer one and falsely reported as a rotation, so requiring equal lengths guarantees that any substring match is a genuine full rotation rather than a coincidental fragment. That omission is the single most common mistake on this problem.

On complexity, the built-in contains is convenient but can be quadratic in the worst case, so for a strict linear-time guarantee I search for the second string inside the doubled first string with the Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm, which runs in time proportional to the combined length. I also note that empty strings and identical strings are trivially rotations, handled naturally because a string is always a substring of its own doubling, and that case sensitivity should be defined up front if codes might differ only in case.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a reconciliation feature for circular reference codes, where different systems may record the same code starting at a different position, to decide whether two codes represent the same underlying circular identifier. Explaining the doubled-string insight, the mandatory length guard, and the KMP upgrade for strict linear time shows the interviewer that I know both the clever trick and the hidden cost behind the one-liner.

answers.question: Explain the Two Pointers technique — opposite-end vs same-direction vs fast/slow variants.
answers.shortTitle: Explain the Two Pointers Technique — Opposite-End vs Same-Direction vs Fast/Slow

s1_definition.profdef: The two pointers technique uses two index variables that walk through a data structure, usually a sorted array or a linked list, to solve a problem in linear time and constant extra space. The three common variants are opposite-end pointers that start at both ends and move toward each other, same-direction pointers where a slow pointer and a fast pointer both move forward at different rules, and fast/slow pointers where one pointer moves twice as fast as the other to detect cycles or find a midpoint.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh is checking a long printed ledger of transactions at the National Bank of India. Instead of scanning every pair of rows, he places one finger at the top and one finger at the bottom and moves them toward each other, or he keeps one finger on the last "good" row while another finger scans ahead looking for the next valid entry. Two fingers, one pass, no photocopying the whole ledger.
s1_definition.oneliner: Two pointers turns an O(n squared) nested-loop scan into a single O(n) sweep using two moving indexes instead of one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The two pointers technique uses two index variables that walk through a data structure, usually a sorted array or a linked list, to solve a problem in linear time and constant extra space. The three common variants are opposite-end pointers that start at both ends and move toward each other, same-direction pointers where a slow pointer and a fast pointer both move forward at different rules, and fast/slow pointers where one pointer moves twice as fast as the other to detect cycles or find a midpoint.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh is checking a long printed ledger of transactions at the National Bank of India. Instead of scanning every pair of rows, he places one finger at the top and one finger at the bottom and moves them toward each other, or he keeps one finger on the last "good" row while another finger scans ahead looking for the next valid entry. Two fingers, one pass, no photocopying the whole ledger.

**One line to remember:** Two pointers turns an O(n squared) nested-loop scan into a single O(n) sweep using two moving indexes instead of one.

sections.s2_technical:
The opposite-end variant works on sorted data. You keep a `left` index at the start and a `right` index at the end, and based on a comparison you move one of them inward. For example, to find a pair of account balances summing to a target you compare the sum of the two ends: if the sum is too small you move `left` up to increase it, if too large you move `right` down. In code: `while (left < right) { int sum = a[left] + a[right]; if (sum == target) return ...; else if (sum < target) left++; else right--; }`. Each element is visited once, so it is O(n).

The same-direction variant uses a slow `write` pointer and a fast `read` pointer moving the same way. The fast pointer scans every element, and the slow pointer only advances when a condition is met, which is how in-place compaction works. For example, removing zero balances: `if (a[read] != 0) { a[write] = a[read]; write++; }`. The slow pointer marks the boundary of the processed region.

The fast/slow variant moves one pointer one step and the other two steps. In a linked list this finds the middle (`slow` lands at the midpoint when `fast` reaches the end) and detects cycles (if there is a loop, `fast` eventually laps `slow` and they meet). For example: `while (fast != null && fast.next != null) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; }`.

A senior-level nuance is knowing the precondition for each variant. Opposite-end almost always requires sorted input, same-direction requires that you only ever need to keep elements you have already seen, and fast/slow requires a sequence you can advance deterministically. Picking the wrong variant, such as opposite-end on unsorted data, silently produces wrong answers.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps a sorted list of settlement amounts for the day, and the reconciliation team must find two settlements that together equal a disputed amount. Scanning every pair is slow when there are millions of rows. This is exactly how opposite-end two pointers works — because the list is sorted, moving the low or high finger based on the current sum finds the pair in one pass.

Problem 2 — After a batch run, the ledger array has many cancelled entries marked as zero, and we must compact the real entries to the front without allocating a second array. This is exactly how same-direction two pointers works — a slow write pointer builds the clean list while a fast read pointer scans everything.

Problem 3 — The audit team receives a linked list of transaction nodes and must find the middle transaction for a quick sanity check without counting the length twice. This is exactly how fast/slow two pointers works — the fast pointer reaches the end just as the slow pointer reaches the middle.

The code below has one demo class that shows all three variants on banking data: a sorted-amount pair finder, an in-place ledger compactor, and a middle-node finder on a transaction linked list.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: sorted amounts [100, 250, 400, 650, 900] with target 650; ledger [500, 0, 300, 0, 0, 900]; transaction list T1 to T5.

Step 1: For the opposite-end search, `left` points at 100 and `right` at 900. The sum is 1000, larger than 650, so `right` moves down to 650. The data array does not change; only the indexes move.

Step 2: Now sum is 100 plus 650 which is 750, still too large, so `right` moves to 400. Sum becomes 100 plus 400 equals 500, too small, so `left` moves to 250. Sum is 250 plus 400 equals 650, a match, and we return the pair.

Step 3: For compaction, the `write` pointer starts at 0. The `read` pointer scans each entry. When it sees 500 (non-zero) it copies it to position 0 and `write` becomes 1. It skips the zero. It copies 300 to position 1 and `write` becomes 2. It skips two zeros, copies 900 to position 2, `write` becomes 3.

Step 4: The first three slots now hold 500, 300, 900, and `write` equals 3 tells us how many real entries survived. The tail of the array still holds stale values but we ignore them.

Step 5: For the middle finder, slow and fast both start at T1. Fast jumps to T3 while slow moves to T2. Fast jumps to T5 while slow moves to T3. Fast's next is null so we stop; slow at T3 is the middle.

```

2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Compacted ledger kept 3 entries: [500, 300, 900]
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Fast/slow middle transaction: T3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The two pointers technique uses two index variables that traverse a data structure together to reduce a quadratic brute-force solution to a single linear pass with constant extra space. There are three variants I reach for. The opposite-end variant starts one pointer at the beginning and one at the end of a sorted collection and moves them inward based on a comparison, which is ideal for problems like finding a pair that sums to a target. The same-direction variant uses a slow write pointer and a fast read pointer moving the same way, which is perfect for in-place work like removing or compacting elements. The fast and slow variant advances one pointer twice as fast as the other, which detects cycles and finds the midpoint of a linked list.

The most important thing I keep in mind is the precondition for each variant. Opposite-end almost always assumes the data is sorted, because the decision to move the left or right pointer only makes sense when the values are ordered. If I apply it to unsorted data it will quietly give wrong answers, so I either confirm the input is sorted or sort it first and account for that cost.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used all three in the reconciliation service. I used opposite-end pointers on the day's sorted settlement amounts to find two settlements matching a disputed figure, same-direction pointers to compact a ledger array by dropping cancelled zero entries in place without a second array, and fast and slow pointers to jump to the middle transaction of a linked list for a quick audit sample without counting the length twice.

The reason this matters in banking is scale and memory. When a reconciliation batch has millions of rows, turning a nested comparison into one sweep is the difference between a job finishing in seconds and timing out, and doing it in place avoids doubling memory on a server that is already under load. Explaining the three variants, their preconditions, and a real use for each shows the interviewer that I understand not just the trick but when each form is correct.
