answers.question: Two Sum on sorted array — left+right pointer, O(1) space.
answers.shortTitle: Two Sum on a Sorted Array — Left and Right Pointers, O(1) Space

s1_definition.profdef: Two Sum on a sorted array finds two elements whose values add up to a given target using opposite-end two pointers. A `left` pointer starts at the smallest value and a `right` pointer at the largest; based on whether their sum is below or above the target you move one pointer inward. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, improving on the hash-map version which needs O(n) memory.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh has a sorted list of past deposit amounts and wants to know which two deposits together equal a disputed figure. He puts one finger on the smallest deposit and one on the largest. If their total is too small he slides the low finger up to a bigger deposit; if too big he slides the high finger down. He finds the pair without scribbling a side list of everything he has seen.
s1_definition.oneliner: On sorted data, two opposite-end pointers find a target pair in one linear pass with zero extra memory.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Two Sum on a sorted array finds two elements whose values add up to a given target using opposite-end two pointers. A `left` pointer starts at the smallest value and a `right` pointer at the largest; based on whether their sum is below or above the target you move one pointer inward. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, improving on the hash-map version which needs O(n) memory.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh has a sorted list of past deposit amounts and wants to know which two deposits together equal a disputed figure. He puts one finger on the smallest deposit and one on the largest. If their total is too small he slides the low finger up to a bigger deposit; if too big he slides the high finger down. He finds the pair without scribbling a side list of everything he has seen.

**One line to remember:** On sorted data, two opposite-end pointers find a target pair in one linear pass with zero extra memory.

sections.s2_technical:
The method keeps two indexes, `left` at index 0 and `right` at the last index. The loop condition is `while (left < right)`. Inside, you compute `sum = a[left] + a[right]`. Three cases follow. If `sum == target` you found the answer and return the indexes or the values. If `sum < target` the only way to increase the sum is to move `left` up to a larger value, so `left++`. If `sum > target` you must decrease the sum, so `right--`.

Why does moving a single pointer never miss a valid pair? Because the array is sorted, when `sum < target` the value at `left` is too small even when paired with the largest remaining value at `right`, so `left` can never be part of the answer and is safely discarded. The symmetric argument holds when `sum > target`. This is the key correctness insight interviewers probe.

A code snippet for banking amounts: `int[] twoSum(int[] amounts, int target) { int l = 0, r = amounts.length - 1; while (l < r) { int s = amounts[l] + amounts[r]; if (s == target) return new int[]{l, r}; if (s < target) l++; else r--; } return new int[]{-1, -1}; }`. Each iteration moves at least one pointer, and they never cross back, so total work is linear.

A senior nuance is the precondition: the array must be sorted, and many interviewers hand you the classic LeetCode variant where indexes are one-based. If the input is unsorted and you cannot change ordering, the hash-map approach is correct instead because sorting would destroy original indexes unless you keep a mapping. Also watch for integer overflow on very large amounts, for which you would use `long` or `BigDecimal` in real money code.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India reconciliation desk sees a disputed charge and suspects it is the sum of two legitimate debits that were double-counted. The debits are already stored sorted by amount. They must find whether two of them add up to the disputed amount. This is exactly how sorted Two Sum works — opposite-end pointers close in on the pair without extra memory.

Problem 2 — Because real money cannot use int, the service works in paise-as-long internally and reports BigDecimal rupees so there is no rounding error. The pointer logic is identical; only the number type is wider.

The code shows a `ReconciliationService` with a `findMatchingPair` method using long paise, a small demo on Rajesh's sorted debit list, and a success and a failure case.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: sorted debits in paise [10000, 25000, 40000, 65000, 90000], target 65000 paise (650 rupees).

Step 1: `left` is index 0 (10000) and `right` is index 4 (90000). The sum is 100000, bigger than 65000, so `right` drops to index 3 (65000). The array is untouched; only `right` changed.

Step 2: Sum is 10000 plus 65000 equals 75000, still bigger, so `right` drops to index 2 (40000). Sum is 10000 plus 40000 equals 50000, now smaller than 65000, so `left` rises to index 1 (25000).

Step 3: Sum is 25000 plus 40000 equals 65000, which matches, so we return indexes [1, 2]. Converting back to rupees gives 250.00 plus 400.00 equals 650.00.

Step 4: For the second call with target 1 paise, the smallest possible sum is 10000 plus 25000 which is already far above 1, so `right` keeps dropping until `left` meets `right` and the loop ends with no match, returning [-1, -1].

```

2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Pair indexes for 650.00: [1, 2] = 250.00 + 400.00
2026-10-26 21:00:03 WARNING No pair sums to target 1 paise
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Pair indexes for 0.01: [-1, -1]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Two Sum on a sorted array finds two values that add up to a target using opposite-end two pointers, giving linear time and constant extra space. I place a left pointer on the smallest value and a right pointer on the largest. If their sum is less than the target I move the left pointer up to a larger value, if the sum is greater than the target I move the right pointer down to a smaller value, and if the sum equals the target I return the pair. Each pointer only moves inward and they never cross back, so the whole array is scanned once.

The correctness argument is the part interviewers want to hear. Because the array is sorted, when the current sum is too small the smallest value can never contribute to a valid pair even alongside the largest remaining value, so I can safely discard it by advancing the left pointer, and the mirror image holds when the sum is too large. That reasoning is why moving one pointer at a time never skips the answer.

The trade-off against the hash-map version is memory. The hash-map approach works on unsorted data in linear time but needs linear extra space to remember what it has seen, while the sorted two-pointer approach needs no extra space but requires the input to already be sorted. I pick based on whether the data is sorted and whether memory is tight.

In my banking work at the National Bank of India I used this in the reconciliation service to decide whether a disputed charge was the sum of two legitimate debits that had been double-counted, working in long paise internally to avoid overflow and reporting BigDecimal rupees so there was never a rounding error. answers.question: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array — slow/fast pointer.
answers.shortTitle: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array — Slow/Fast Pointer In Place

s1_definition.profdef: Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place uses same-direction two pointers. A slow pointer marks the position where the next unique value belongs, and a fast pointer scans every element. When the fast pointer finds a value different from the last kept one, it is copied to the slow position and the slow pointer advances. The method returns the count of unique elements and runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh has a sorted printout of account numbers where some appear more than once because of repeated statement imports. He keeps one finger on the slot where the next fresh number should go and scans ahead with another finger. Each time he sees a number different from the last kept one, he writes it into the fresh slot and moves on. He compacts the list without a second sheet of paper.
s1_definition.oneliner: A slow write pointer plus a fast scan pointer compacts a sorted array to its unique values in one pass with no extra memory.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place uses same-direction two pointers. A slow pointer marks the position where the next unique value belongs, and a fast pointer scans every element. When the fast pointer finds a value different from the last kept one, it is copied to the slow position and the slow pointer advances. The method returns the count of unique elements and runs in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh has a sorted printout of account numbers where some appear more than once because of repeated statement imports. He keeps one finger on the slot where the next fresh number should go and scans ahead with another finger. Each time he sees a number different from the last kept one, he writes it into the fresh slot and moves on. He compacts the list without a second sheet of paper.

**One line to remember:** A slow write pointer plus a fast scan pointer compacts a sorted array to its unique values in one pass with no extra memory.

sections.s2_technical:
Because the array is sorted, every group of duplicates is contiguous, so you only ever compare the current element with the last one you decided to keep. The slow pointer `k` starts at index 0 (the first element is always unique). The fast pointer `i` starts at index 1 and scans forward. The rule is: if `a[i] != a[k]`, then this is a new unique value, so advance `k` and copy `a[k] = a[i]`.

A code snippet: `int removeDuplicates(int[] a) { if (a.length == 0) return 0; int k = 0; for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) { if (a[i] != a[k]) { k++; a[k] = a[i]; } } return k + 1; }`. The returned value `k + 1` is the number of unique elements, and the first `k + 1` slots hold them in order. Everything after that is considered garbage.

Why compare against `a[k]` and not `a[i-1]`? In the classic "keep one copy" version both work because the kept region is a prefix of the unique values. But if the variant allows at most two copies, you compare against `a[k-1]` to check the count, which is why anchoring on the slow pointer region is the cleaner mental model that generalizes.

A senior nuance is that this only works because the input is sorted; on unsorted data duplicates are not adjacent and you would need a set, costing O(n) memory. Also the method does not shrink the array (Java arrays are fixed length); it returns the logical length, and callers must respect that boundary. In real services you often copy the prefix into a right-sized structure before returning.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India imports daily transaction IDs from several branches into one sorted file, and because of retries the same ID sometimes appears multiple times. Before posting to the ledger the service must keep exactly one copy of each ID. This is exactly how remove-duplicates-in-place works — a slow write pointer keeps the first copy of each ID while a fast pointer skips repeats.

Problem 2 — Memory is tight during the nightly batch, so we cannot allocate a second array the size of millions of IDs. The in-place approach reuses the same array and just reports how many unique IDs remain.

The code shows a `LedgerDeduplicator` with `dedupe`, a demo on a sorted list of transaction IDs with repeats, and the compacted result.

Input: sorted transaction IDs [1001, 1001, 1002, 1003, 1003, 1003, 1004].

Step 1: The slow pointer `k` is 0, pointing at 1001. The fast pointer `i` starts at 1, also 1001. Since they are equal, this is a duplicate, so nothing is written and only `i` advances.

Step 2: `i` is now 2 (1002), different from `a[k]` which is 1001. So `k` advances to 1 and we copy 1002 into slot 1. The array now begins 1001, 1002.

Step 3: `i` is 3 (1003), different from `a[k]` which is 1002, so `k` advances to 2 and 1003 is copied to slot 2. For `i` at 4 and 5, the value is still 1003 equal to `a[k]`, so they are skipped.

Step 4: `i` is 6 (1004), different from 1003, so `k` advances to 3 and 1004 is copied to slot 3. The scan ends.

Step 5: The method returns `k + 1` which is 4. The first four slots hold the unique IDs 1001, 1002, 1003, 1004 in order, and the rest of the array is ignored.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place is a same-direction two-pointer problem. I keep a slow pointer that marks the slot where the next unique value should be written, and a fast pointer that scans every element. The first element is always unique so the slow pointer starts there, and whenever the fast pointer finds a value different from the one at the slow pointer, I advance the slow pointer and copy the new value into that slot. At the end the slow pointer plus one gives the count of unique values, and they sit compacted at the front of the array.

The reason this works is that the array is sorted, so all copies of a value are next to each other, which means I only need to compare the current element against the last value I decided to keep rather than against everything before it. On unsorted data this breaks because duplicates are scattered, and I would instead need a hash set at the cost of linear extra memory.

A practical detail I always mention is that Java arrays cannot shrink, so the method does not physically remove anything; it returns the logical length and the caller must treat only that prefix as valid. In production I usually copy that prefix into a right-sized collection before handing it on.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the nightly ledger batch. Branch imports were merged into one sorted file of transaction IDs, and because of import retries the same ID could appear several times, so before posting to the ledger I deduplicated in place to keep exactly one copy of each ID. Doing it in place mattered because the batch handled millions of IDs and a second array would have doubled memory on an already loaded server. Explaining the slow-and-fast movement, the sorted precondition, and the fixed-length caveat shows the interviewer I understand the algorithm and its real constraints.

answers.question: Move Zeroes — two-pointer compaction.
answers.shortTitle: Move Zeroes — Two-Pointer Compaction Keeping Order

s1_definition.profdef: Move Zeroes rearranges an array so that all zero values move to the end while the relative order of the non-zero values is preserved, done in place. It uses a same-direction two-pointer compaction: a slow pointer marks where the next non-zero value goes, and a fast pointer scans every element, placing each non-zero at the slow position. After the scan, the remaining tail is filled with zeros. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya has a list of this month's charges where cancelled charges show as zero. She wants all the real charges pushed to the front in the same order they happened, with the zeros swept to the back. She keeps one finger on the next clean slot and scans with another; every real charge gets written forward, then the leftover slots at the end become zeros.
s1_definition.oneliner: Write every non-zero to the front with a slow pointer, then pad the rest with zeros — order preserved, no extra array.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Move Zeroes rearranges an array so that all zero values move to the end while the relative order of the non-zero values is preserved, done in place. It uses a same-direction two-pointer compaction: a slow pointer marks where the next non-zero value goes, and a fast pointer scans every element, placing each non-zero at the slow position. After the scan, the remaining tail is filled with zeros. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya has a list of this month's charges where cancelled charges show as zero. She wants all the real charges pushed to the front in the same order they happened, with the zeros swept to the back. She keeps one finger on the next clean slot and scans with another; every real charge gets written forward, then the leftover slots at the end become zeros.

**One line to remember:** Write every non-zero to the front with a slow pointer, then pad the rest with zeros — order preserved, no extra array.

sections.s2_technical:
The clean approach has two phases but a single pass does most of the work. Phase one: a slow pointer `insert` starts at 0, and a fast pointer `i` scans the whole array. Whenever `a[i] != 0`, you write `a[insert] = a[i]` and advance `insert`. After this phase the first `insert` slots hold all non-zero values in their original order. Phase two: fill indexes from `insert` to the end with 0.

A code snippet: `void moveZeroes(int[] a) { int insert = 0; for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { if (a[i] != 0) { a[insert++] = a[i]; } } while (insert < a.length) { a[insert++] = 0; } }`. The relative order of non-zeros is preserved because we copy them in the order we encounter them.

An alternative single-phase swap version avoids the fill loop: whenever `a[i] != 0`, swap `a[i]` with `a[insert]` and advance `insert`. This keeps zeros and non-zeros moving in one go and writes fewer times when zeros are rare. Both are O(n); the swap version minimizes writes, which can matter on write-expensive media.

A senior nuance is "stability," meaning the non-zero order must not change, which the copy and swap approaches both guarantee because they move elements left only into already-processed slots. A common mistake is sorting or using a partition that reverses order; that fails the ordering requirement. Also note the problem says in place, so allocating a second array is a disqualifying answer even though it is trivially correct.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India shows Priya's monthly statement, but cancelled line items appear as zero amounts scattered through the list. The UI wants all real charges grouped at the top in the exact order they occurred, with the empty placeholders at the bottom. This is exactly how Move Zeroes works — non-zeros are compacted forward preserving order, zeros pushed to the tail.

Problem 2 — The statement array is large and shared, so we must not allocate a copy; we rearrange the same array in place.

The code shows a `StatementCompactor` with `moveZeroes`, a demo on Priya's charge array with scattered zeros, and the compacted output.

    Pre:  a non-null
    Post: non-zeros first in original order, zeros at end
    Space: O(1), stable ordering guaranteed

  ── State Diagram: per fast step ──────────────────────────

  [SCAN] ─a[i]==0→ [SCAN] (skip)
     │ ─a[i]!=0→ [WRITE] (a[insert++]=a[i]) → [SCAN]
     ▼
  [i==n] → [PAD] (fill zeros) → [DONE]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. main() → compactor.moveZeroes(charges)
  2.   → phase 1 pulls non-zeros forward
  3.   → phase 2 pads zeros
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Move Zeroes rearranges an array so every zero ends up at the back while the non-zero values keep their original order, and it must be done in place. I treat it as a same-direction two-pointer compaction. A slow pointer marks the next slot for a non-zero value, and a fast pointer scans the whole array; each time the fast pointer sees a non-zero, I copy it to the slow slot and advance the slow pointer. After that single pass, the front holds all the non-zeros in order, and I fill the remaining tail with zeros.

The property interviewers test is stability, meaning the non-zero order must not change. The copy approach preserves it naturally because I write non-zeros in the exact order I meet them, only ever moving them left into slots I have already processed. If I instead sorted or used an order-breaking partition, I would get the zeros in place but fail the ordering requirement. There is also a swap variant that moves zeros and non-zeros in a single phase and minimizes the number of writes when zeros are rare, which is worth mentioning.

The in-place constraint is the whole point of the problem. Allocating a second array and filtering is trivially correct but disqualifying, so I always stay within the original array using only two index variables.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the statement service. Priya's monthly statement had cancelled line items showing as zero amounts scattered through the list, and the UI wanted the real charges grouped at the top in the exact order they occurred with the empty placeholders at the bottom. I compacted the shared statement array in place to avoid copying a large structure. Explaining the slow-and-fast compaction, the stability guarantee, the swap alternative, and the in-place constraint shows the interviewer I know both the algorithm and why each rule exists.

answers.question: Valid Palindrome — left/right skipping non-alphanumeric.
answers.shortTitle: Valid Palindrome — Left/Right Pointers Skipping Non-Alphanumeric

s1_definition.profdef: The Valid Palindrome check decides whether a string reads the same forward and backward after ignoring non-alphanumeric characters and treating letters case-insensitively. It uses opposite-end two pointers: a `left` pointer from the start and a `right` pointer from the end, each skipping characters that are not letters or digits, comparing the lowercased characters. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India issues reference codes that are supposed to be symmetric for a validity check, but they contain dashes and spaces for readability. To verify, Rajesh reads from both ends toward the middle, skipping any dash or space, and checks that each matching pair of real characters is the same letter or digit regardless of case.
s1_definition.oneliner: Two pointers close in from both ends, skip punctuation, compare lowercased characters, and declare a palindrome if they meet without a mismatch.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Valid Palindrome check decides whether a string reads the same forward and backward after ignoring non-alphanumeric characters and treating letters case-insensitively. It uses opposite-end two pointers: a `left` pointer from the start and a `right` pointer from the end, each skipping characters that are not letters or digits, comparing the lowercased characters. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India issues reference codes that are supposed to be symmetric for a validity check, but they contain dashes and spaces for readability. To verify, Rajesh reads from both ends toward the middle, skipping any dash or space, and checks that each matching pair of real characters is the same letter or digit regardless of case.

**One line to remember:** Two pointers close in from both ends, skip punctuation, compare lowercased characters, and declare a palindrome if they meet without a mismatch.

sections.s2_technical:
You set `left = 0` and `right = s.length() - 1`. The loop runs while `left < right`. Inside, you first advance `left` past any character where `Character.isLetterOrDigit` is false, and similarly retreat `right` past non-alphanumeric characters. The method `Character.isLetterOrDigit(c)` returns true for letters and digits and false for punctuation and spaces, for example `Character.isLetterOrDigit('-')` is false so that position is skipped.

Once both pointers rest on alphanumeric characters, you compare them case-insensitively with `Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(left)) != Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(right))`; if they differ it is not a palindrome and you return false. If they match, you move both inward and continue.

A code snippet: `boolean isPalindrome(String s) { int l = 0, r = s.length() - 1; while (l < r) { while (l < r && !Character.isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(l))) l++; while (l < r && !Character.isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(r))) r--; if (Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(l)) != Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(r))) return false; l++; r--; } return true; }`. Each character is examined at most once, so it is linear.

A senior nuance is guarding the inner skip loops with `l < r` so the pointers cannot cross while skipping, which prevents reading past the middle on strings that are all punctuation. An empty string or a string of only punctuation is considered a valid palindrome because the pointers meet immediately. Avoid the tempting but wasteful approach of stripping and reversing the string, which allocates extra memory and is O(n) space rather than the O(1) two-pointer version.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India prints customer reference codes with dashes and spaces so humans can read them, but an internal rule says the alphanumeric core must be a palindrome as a quick checksum. The service must validate a code ignoring formatting and case. This is exactly how Valid Palindrome works — two pointers skip the separators and compare the real characters from both ends.

Problem 2 — Codes can be empty or all separators in edge records, and the validator must treat those as trivially valid rather than crashing.

The code shows a `RefCodeValidator` with `isValidPalindrome`, a demo on a formatted code that is a palindrome and one that is not.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the code "A1b2-2b1A". The alphanumeric core is A, 1, b, 2, 2, b, 1, A.

Step 1: `left` is at index 0 on 'A' and `right` is at the last index on 'A'. Both are alphanumeric. Lowercasing both gives 'a' and 'a', equal, so both move inward.

Step 2: `left` is on '1' and `right` is on '1'. Equal, move inward. `left` is on 'b' and `right` is on 'b'. Equal, move inward.

Step 3: `left` is now on '2' and `right` on '2' but there is a dash in the middle. The skip loops advance past the dash so both pointers land on the two '2' characters. They are equal; moving inward makes `left` cross `right` and the loop ends. Result is true.

Step 4: For "SAV-2001-CUR", `left` starts on 'S' and `right` on 'R'. After lowercasing, 's' and 'r' differ immediately, so the method returns false without scanning further.

Step 5: For the empty string, `left` is 0 and `right` is -1, so the loop body never runs and the method returns true, treating empty as a trivial palindrome.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Valid Palindrome checks whether a string reads the same forward and backward once I ignore everything that is not a letter or digit and treat letters case-insensitively. I solve it with opposite-end two pointers, one starting at the front and one at the back. Before each comparison I advance the left pointer past any non-alphanumeric character and retreat the right pointer the same way, then I compare the two characters after lowercasing them. If any pair differs it is not a palindrome, and if the pointers meet in the middle without a mismatch it is.

The subtle correctness point is guarding the inner skip loops with the same left-less-than-right condition as the outer loop, so the pointers can never cross each other while skipping punctuation. That guard is what makes strings that are entirely punctuation, or empty strings, come out as valid palindromes rather than causing an out-of-bounds read, because the pointers simply meet immediately.

I deliberately avoid the naive approach of stripping the string down to alphanumerics, reversing it, and comparing, because that allocates extra memory and is linear space, whereas the two-pointer method is constant space and examines each character only once.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to validate printed customer reference codes. The codes carried dashes and spaces for human readability, but an internal checksum rule required the alphanumeric core to be a palindrome, so the validator walked in from both ends skipping the separators and comparing the real characters without regard to case. I made sure empty or all-separator codes in edge records were treated as trivially valid rather than crashing. Explaining the skip-and-compare logic, the bounded skip loops, and the choice to avoid extra allocation shows the interviewer I understand both the algorithm and the defensive details that matter in production.

answers.question: Container With Most Water — opposite-end, move shorter side.
answers.shortTitle: Container With Most Water — Opposite-End, Move the Shorter Side

s1_definition.profdef: Container With Most Water takes an array of heights representing vertical lines and finds two lines that, with the x-axis, form a container holding the most water. The area between two lines is the smaller of the two heights multiplied by the distance between them. Opposite-end two pointers start at both ends and repeatedly move the pointer at the shorter line inward, tracking the maximum area, in O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of each bar as the balance on a day, and we want the widest, deepest "reserve pool" we can form between two days. The water level is capped by the shorter of the two day-balances, and the width is the number of days between them. Rajesh starts with the first and last day, keeps whichever is taller, and moves the shorter day inward hoping to find a taller wall that holds more.
s1_definition.oneliner: Water is limited by the shorter wall, so moving the shorter pointer inward is the only move that can possibly increase the area.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Container With Most Water takes an array of heights representing vertical lines and finds two lines that, with the x-axis, form a container holding the most water. The area between two lines is the smaller of the two heights multiplied by the distance between them. Opposite-end two pointers start at both ends and repeatedly move the pointer at the shorter line inward, tracking the maximum area, in O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of each bar as the balance on a day, and we want the widest, deepest "reserve pool" we can form between two days. The water level is capped by the shorter of the two day-balances, and the width is the number of days between them. Rajesh starts with the first and last day, keeps whichever is taller, and moves the shorter day inward hoping to find a taller wall that holds more.

**One line to remember:** Water is limited by the shorter wall, so moving the shorter pointer inward is the only move that can possibly increase the area.

sections.s2_technical:
Set `left = 0` and `right = n - 1`. The area for the current pair is `Math.min(h[left], h[right]) * (right - left)`. You record the maximum area seen so far, then move inward. The key decision: move the pointer at the shorter line. If `h[left] < h[right]` move `left++`, else move `right--`.

Why move the shorter side? The area is bounded by the shorter line. If you move the taller line inward, the width shrinks and the height is still capped by the unchanged shorter line, so the area cannot increase. Moving the shorter line is the only move that gives a chance at a taller limiting wall that could overcome the lost width. This greedy argument is the core of the solution.

A code snippet on day balances: `int maxArea(int[] h) { int l = 0, r = h.length - 1, best = 0; while (l < r) { int area = Math.min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l); best = Math.max(best, area); if (h[l] < h[r]) l++; else r--; } return best; }`. Each step moves one pointer, they never cross back, so it is linear.

A senior nuance is why the greedy does not miss a better pair: when we discard the shorter line, every pair that still includes that shorter line as the limiting wall would have had width no larger than the current one, so none of them can beat what we already considered; discarding it loses nothing. When the two heights are equal, moving either side is fine because both would be limited identically. The brute-force alternative compares every pair in O(n squared), which the two-pointer approach reduces to O(n).
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India treasury models a liquidity window as two days, where the usable reserve between them is capped by the lower end-of-day balance times the number of days in the window. The treasury wants the window that maximizes this product. This is exactly how Container With Most Water works — the limiting height is the smaller balance and the width is the day gap.

Problem 2 — There can be thousands of days, so an all-pairs scan is too slow for an interactive dashboard, which is why the linear two-pointer approach matters.

The code shows a `LiquidityWindowAnalyzer` with `maxReserve`, a demo on a series of daily balances, and the best window's reserve value.

Input: balances [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7], indexes 0 to 8.

Step 1: `left` at index 0 (height 1), `right` at index 8 (height 7). The limiting height is 1, width is 8, area is 8. Best is 8. Since the left wall is shorter, move `left` to index 1.

Step 2: `left` at index 1 (height 8), `right` at index 8 (height 7). Limiting height 7, width 7, area 49. Best is now 49. The right wall is shorter, so move `right` to index 7.

Step 3: `left` 8, `right` index 7 (height 3). Height 3, width 6, area 18, not better. Move `right` to index 6 (height 8). Height 8, width 5, area 40, not better. Move `right` (equal heights, move right) to index 5 (height 4). Area is 4 times 4 equals 16.

Step 4: Continuing, every remaining pair yields an area below 49 because the width keeps shrinking faster than the height can grow. The best stays 49.

Step 5: The loop ends when the pointers meet, and the method returns 49 as the maximum reserve window value.

```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Container With Most Water asks me to pick two vertical lines from an array of heights so that the container they form with the ground holds the most water, where the water volume is the shorter of the two heights multiplied by the horizontal distance between them. I solve it with opposite-end two pointers starting at the first and last lines. At each step I compute the current area, update my running maximum, and then move the pointer sitting on the shorter line inward.

The reason I always move the shorter side is the heart of the solution. The area is capped by the shorter line, so if I moved the taller line inward the width would shrink while the height stayed limited by the same short line, and the area could never improve. Moving the shorter line is the only move that gives a chance at a taller limiting wall that might more than make up for the lost width. When the two heights are equal, moving either side is fine because both are limited the same way.

The subtle guarantee is that discarding the shorter line never loses a better answer, because any other pair that still used that short line as its limit would have had a width no larger than the one I just evaluated, so it could not beat what I already recorded. That is why the greedy pass is correct and I do not need the brute-force comparison of every pair, which would be quadratic.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this shape of problem in the treasury dashboard to find the liquidity window between two days whose usable reserve, capped by the lower end-of-day balance and scaled by the number of days, was largest. With thousands of days an all-pairs scan was far too slow for an interactive dashboard, so the linear two-pointer approach made it responsive. Explaining the area formula, the move-the-shorter-wall rule, and why discarding the shorter line is safe shows the interviewer I understand the greedy reasoning rather than just the code.

answers.question: 3Sum — sort + two-pointer for remaining pair.
answers.shortTitle: 3Sum — Sort Then Two-Pointer for the Remaining Pair

s1_definition.profdef: The 3Sum problem finds all unique triplets in an array that sum to zero (or a target). The efficient approach sorts the array, then fixes one element and uses opposite-end two pointers on the remaining subarray to find pairs that complete the triplet. Duplicate triplets are skipped by advancing past repeated values. It runs in O(n squared) time and O(1) extra space beyond the sort.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to find every set of three adjustments that net to zero so they cancel out. Rajesh sorts the adjustments, then fixes the first one and uses two fingers from the ends of the rest to find a matching pair that brings the total to zero, skipping repeats so he never reports the same trio twice.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort first, fix one element, then run opposite-end two pointers on the rest — skipping duplicates — to collect all triplets in O(n squared).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The 3Sum problem finds all unique triplets in an array that sum to zero (or a target). The efficient approach sorts the array, then fixes one element and uses opposite-end two pointers on the remaining subarray to find pairs that complete the triplet. Duplicate triplets are skipped by advancing past repeated values. It runs in O(n squared) time and O(1) extra space beyond the sort.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to find every set of three adjustments that net to zero so they cancel out. Rajesh sorts the adjustments, then fixes the first one and uses two fingers from the ends of the rest to find a matching pair that brings the total to zero, skipping repeats so he never reports the same trio twice.

**One line to remember:** Sort first, fix one element, then run opposite-end two pointers on the rest — skipping duplicates — to collect all triplets in O(n squared).

sections.s2_technical:
First sort the array; this enables both the two-pointer pair search and easy duplicate skipping. Then loop with an index `i` from 0 to n-3, fixing `a[i]` as the first element of the triplet. If `a[i]` is greater than the target and all values are non-negative after sorting you can break early, a common optimization.

For each fixed `i`, set `left = i + 1` and `right = n - 1`. Compute `sum = a[i] + a[left] + a[right]`. If the sum equals the target, record the triplet, then move both pointers inward while skipping duplicates: `while (left < right && a[left] == a[left+1]) left++;` and similarly for `right`. If the sum is less than the target move `left` up; if greater move `right` down.

A code snippet: `for (int i = 0; i < n - 2; i++) { if (i > 0 && a[i] == a[i-1]) continue; int l = i+1, r = n-1; while (l < r) { int s = a[i]+a[l]+a[r]; if (s == 0) { result.add(List.of(a[i],a[l],a[r])); while (l<r && a[l]==a[l+1]) l++; while (l<r && a[r]==a[r-1]) r--; l++; r--; } else if (s < 0) l++; else r--; } }`. The `continue` on `i` skips duplicate first elements.

A senior nuance is the three places duplicates must be skipped: the fixed element `i`, the left pointer after a match, and the right pointer after a match. Missing any produces duplicate triplets. The overall complexity is O(n squared) because the sort is O(n log n) and the fixed-element loop with the inner two-pointer scan is O(n squared), which dominates. This is a classic example of reducing a naive O(n cubed) triple loop to O(n squared) using sorting plus two pointers.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a month-end netting process where ledger adjustments can be positive or negative, and the risk team wants every unique group of three adjustments that cancel to zero so they can be closed together. This is exactly how 3Sum works — sort the adjustments and find all zero-summing triplets.

Problem 2 — The same cancelling trio must never be reported twice even if duplicate adjustment amounts exist, which is why duplicate skipping is essential.

The code shows a `NettingService` with `findZeroTriplets`, a demo on a list of signed adjustments, and the unique triplets found.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: adjustments [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2, 2]. After sorting it is already [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2, 2].

Step 1: `i` is 0 fixing -4. `left` at -1 (index 1), `right` at 2 (index 6). Sum is -4 minus 1 plus 2 equals -3, less than zero, so `left` moves up. It keeps moving because the sum stays negative until `left` passes `right`, so -4 yields no triplet.

Step 2: `i` is 1 fixing -1. `left` at index 2 (-1), `right` at index 6 (2). Sum is -1 minus 1 plus 2 equals 0, a match, so we record [-1, -1, 2]. We then skip the duplicate 2 at `right` and move both inward.

Step 3: Now `left` at index 3 (0), `right` at index 4 (1). Sum is -1 plus 0 plus 1 equals 0, another match, so we record [-1, 0, 1]. Pointers move inward and cross, ending this fixed element.

Step 4: `i` is 2 fixing -1 again, but since it equals the previous `a[i-1]` it is skipped to avoid duplicate triplets. `i` is 3 fixing 0; `left` and `right` search but no zero-sum pair is found.

Step 5: `i` is 4 fixing 1, which is greater than 0, so the early break stops the loop. The result is the two unique triplets [-1, -1, 2] and [-1, 0, 1].

sections.s6_takeaway:
The 3Sum problem asks me to find every unique triplet in an array that sums to zero, and the efficient approach combines sorting with two pointers. I first sort the array, which lets me both run an opposite-end pointer search and skip duplicates cleanly. Then I fix each element as the first member of the triplet, and for the remaining part of the array I place a left pointer just after the fixed element and a right pointer at the end, moving them inward based on whether the current three-way sum is below, above, or equal to zero.

The detail that separates a correct answer from a buggy one is duplicate handling in three distinct places. I skip a fixed element if it equals the previous fixed element, and after recording a matching triplet I advance the left pointer past any repeated value and retreat the right pointer past any repeated value before moving both inward. Missing any of these three skips produces the same triplet more than once, which is the most common mistake on this problem.

On complexity, sorting is order n log n, and the fixed-element loop wrapping the linear two-pointer scan is order n squared, which dominates, so the whole thing is quadratic with constant extra space beyond the sort. That is a big improvement over the naive triple loop which is cubic.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the month-end netting service. Ledger adjustments could be positive or negative, and the risk team wanted every unique group of three adjustments that cancelled to zero so they could be closed together, and because duplicate adjustment amounts were common the duplicate-skipping logic ensured no cancelling trio was ever reported twice. Explaining the sort, the fix-one-plus-two-pointer structure, and especially the three duplicate-skip points shows the interviewer I understand both the algorithm and the correctness pitfalls.

answers.question: Trapping Rain Water — two-pointer with left-max/right-max.
answers.shortTitle: Trapping Rain Water — Two-Pointer With Left-Max and Right-Max

s1_definition.profdef: Trapping Rain Water computes how much water is held between bars of varying heights after rain. The two-pointer solution tracks the running maximum height seen from the left and from the right, and at each step processes the side with the smaller boundary, adding the trapped water above the current bar. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, improving on the prefix-array version that uses O(n) space.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture daily reserve levels as bars; dips between higher peaks can hold "trapped liquidity." Rajesh walks inward from both ends, always stepping on the side whose tallest wall so far is shorter, because that side's trapped amount is fully determined, and he adds up the water each dip holds.
s1_definition.oneliner: Process the side with the smaller boundary wall; the water above a bar equals that side's running max minus the bar's own height.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Trapping Rain Water computes how much water is held between bars of varying heights after rain. The two-pointer solution tracks the running maximum height seen from the left and from the right, and at each step processes the side with the smaller boundary, adding the trapped water above the current bar. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, improving on the prefix-array version that uses O(n) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture daily reserve levels as bars; dips between higher peaks can hold "trapped liquidity." Rajesh walks inward from both ends, always stepping on the side whose tallest wall so far is shorter, because that side's trapped amount is fully determined, and he adds up the water each dip holds.

**One line to remember:** Process the side with the smaller boundary wall; the water above a bar equals that side's running max minus the bar's own height.

sections.s2_technical:
Use `left = 0`, `right = n - 1`, and two running maxima `leftMax` and `rightMax` both starting at 0. The loop runs while `left < right`. The decision: if `h[left] < h[right]`, the left boundary is the limiting wall for the left bar, so you process left; otherwise process right.

When processing left: if `h[left] >= leftMax`, update `leftMax = h[left]` (no water, this bar is a new wall); else add `leftMax - h[left]` to the total (this bar is below the left wall, so it traps that much). Then `left++`. The symmetric logic applies on the right using `rightMax` and `right--`.

A code snippet on reserve bars: `int trap(int[] h) { int l=0, r=h.length-1, lm=0, rm=0, total=0; while (l<r) { if (h[l] < h[r]) { if (h[l]>=lm) lm=h[l]; else total+=lm-h[l]; l++; } else { if (h[r]>=rm) rm=h[r]; else total+=rm-h[r]; r--; } } return total; }`. Each bar is handled once, so it is linear.

The key insight interviewers probe: why is it safe to use only the near-side max? When `h[left] < h[right]`, we know there exists some wall on the right at least as tall as `h[right]`, which is at least as tall as `h[left]`, so the water over the left bar is bounded solely by `leftMax`; the right side can only be taller and never reduces it. That guarantee is what lets us commit to the left bar's water immediately. A senior nuance is that this halves the memory of the two-prefix-array method while keeping the same linear time, which matters for very wide inputs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India treasury visualizes daily reserve levels as a skyline and wants to quantify total "trapped liquidity," the reserve that is held in dips between higher balance peaks and cannot be drawn down without breaching a wall. This is exactly how Trapping Rain Water works — each dip below the surrounding peaks holds water.

Problem 2 — The series can be very long, so the two-pointer constant-space method is preferred over building two large prefix-max arrays.

The code shows a `TrappedLiquidityAnalyzer` with `trap`, a demo on a reserve skyline, and the total trapped amount.

Input: skyline [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1].

Step 1: `left` at index 0 (0), `right` at index 11 (1). Since `h[left]` 0 is less than `h[right]` 1, process left. `h[left]` 0 is at least `leftMax` 0, so `leftMax` becomes 0, no water. Move `left` to 1.

Step 2: `h[left]` 1 versus `h[right]` 1, not strictly less, so process right. `h[right]` 1 is at least `rightMax` 0, so `rightMax` becomes 1, no water. Move `right` to 10 (2). Now process left side as `h[left]` 1 is less than 2; it updates `leftMax` to 1.

Step 3: Continuing, index 2 has height 0 with `leftMax` 1, so it traps 1 unit. Index 4 has height 1 with `leftMax` 2 (after index 3 set it), trapping 1 unit, and index 5 height 0 traps 2 units, index 6 height 1 traps 1 unit.

Step 4: On the right side, as the pointer moves left from index 10, bars below the running right max contribute their trapped amounts similarly. The running maxima ensure each bar's water is counted exactly once.

Step 5: Summing all trapped contributions yields 6 units of trapped liquidity, which the method returns.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Trapping Rain Water computes how much water collects in the dips between bars of different heights, and the two-pointer version does it in linear time with constant extra space. I keep a left pointer and a right pointer along with the running maximum height seen from each side. At every step I process whichever side currently has the smaller boundary wall, and for the bar there I either raise that side's running maximum if the bar is a new wall, or I add the difference between that running maximum and the bar's height as trapped water.

The insight that makes this correct is why the near-side maximum alone is enough. When the left bar is shorter than the right bar, I already know the right side has some wall at least as tall as the right bar, which is at least as tall as the left bar, so the water over the left bar is limited purely by the left running maximum and the right can only make it taller, never shallower. That certainty lets me commit the left bar's water immediately and move on, and the mirror logic holds when the right side is the limiter.

Compared with the alternative that precomputes a left-max array and a right-max array, the two-pointer method gives the same linear time but uses constant memory instead of two extra arrays, which matters when the series is very wide.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the treasury dashboard to quantify trapped liquidity, the reserve held in dips between higher balance peaks that could not be drawn down without breaching a wall. The daily series was long, so the constant-space two-pointer method was preferable to building two large prefix-max arrays. Explaining the process-the-smaller-side rule, the near-side-max correctness argument, and the memory advantage shows the interviewer I understand the reasoning behind this classic hard problem rather than just memorizing the loop.

answers.question: Sort Colors (Dutch National Flag) — three pointers for 0s, 1s, 2s.
answers.shortTitle: Sort Colors (Dutch National Flag) — Three Pointers for 0s, 1s, 2s

s1_definition.profdef: The Dutch National Flag algorithm sorts an array containing only three distinct values (0, 1, 2) in a single pass using three pointers: `low` marks the boundary of the 0 region, `high` marks the boundary of the 2 region, and `mid` scans the array. It partitions the array into zeros, ones, and twos in O(n) time and O(1) extra space without a general sort.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India classifies each pending request as low, medium, or high risk, coded 0, 1, 2. Instead of running a full sort, Rajesh sweeps once: anything low he swaps to the front, anything high he swaps to the back, and medium stays where it is, so the pile ends up grouped low then medium then high in one pass.
s1_definition.oneliner: Three pointers partition a 0/1/2 array in one pass — swap 0s to the front, 2s to the back, leave 1s in the middle.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Dutch National Flag algorithm sorts an array containing only three distinct values (0, 1, 2) in a single pass using three pointers: `low` marks the boundary of the 0 region, `high` marks the boundary of the 2 region, and `mid` scans the array. It partitions the array into zeros, ones, and twos in O(n) time and O(1) extra space without a general sort.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India classifies each pending request as low, medium, or high risk, coded 0, 1, 2. Instead of running a full sort, Rajesh sweeps once: anything low he swaps to the front, anything high he swaps to the back, and medium stays where it is, so the pile ends up grouped low then medium then high in one pass.

**One line to remember:** Three pointers partition a 0/1/2 array in one pass — swap 0s to the front, 2s to the back, leave 1s in the middle.

sections.s2_technical:
Initialize `low = 0`, `mid = 0`, `high = n - 1`. The loop runs while `mid <= high`. There are three cases based on `a[mid]`.

If `a[mid] == 0`, swap `a[low]` and `a[mid]`, then increment both `low` and `mid`, because the value coming from `low` is already processed (it can only be a 1 that we have seen). If `a[mid] == 1`, it is in its correct middle region, so just increment `mid`. If `a[mid] == 2`, swap `a[mid]` and `a[high]`, then decrement `high` only, and crucially do not increment `mid`, because the value swapped in from `high` is unexamined and must be checked next.

A code snippet classifying risk codes: `void sort012(int[] a) { int low=0, mid=0, high=a.length-1; while (mid<=high) { if (a[mid]==0) { swap(a,low++,mid++); } else if (a[mid]==1) { mid++; } else { swap(a,mid,high--); } } }`. The invariant is that everything before `low` is 0, everything between `low` and `mid` is 1, and everything after `high` is 2; the unknown region is between `mid` and `high`.

The nuance interviewers test is why `mid` does not advance after a 2-swap: the element brought from the high end has not been classified yet, so advancing `mid` would skip examining it and could leave a 0 stranded in the middle. The algorithm is a single linear pass, unlike counting sort which is also O(n) but needs two passes or extra counts; the Dutch flag is an elegant in-place one-pass partition and is the canonical answer when exactly three categories exist.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India fraud queue tags each pending transaction with a risk tier: 0 low, 1 medium, 2 high. The review tool must group them low-to-high so reviewers clear the safe ones quickly and escalate the risky ones, and it must do this in one pass on a large live queue. This is exactly how the Dutch National Flag algorithm works — three pointers partition the three tiers in a single sweep.

Problem 2 — The queue array is large and shared, so we sort in place without a second array or a general comparison sort.

The code shows a `RiskQueueSorter` with `sortByTier`, a demo on a mixed risk-tier array, and the grouped result.

Input: risk tiers [2, 0, 1, 2, 1, 0, 0, 2, 1].

Step 1: `low` 0, `mid` 0, `high` 8. `a[mid]` is 2, so swap `a[0]` and `a[8]` giving [1,0,1,2,1,0,0,2,2], decrement `high` to 7, `mid` stays 0 to re-examine the new value.

Step 2: `a[mid]` is now 1, so just advance `mid` to 1. `a[1]` is 0, so swap `a[low]` and `a[mid]` (both make 0 go front), increment `low` to 1 and `mid` to 2. The front now holds a 0.

Step 3: Scanning continues: 1s advance `mid`, 0s swap to the growing front region, and 2s swap to the shrinking back region without moving `mid`. Each 2-swap pulls an unexamined value into `mid` which is then classified on the next iteration.

Step 4: The unknown window between `mid` and `high` keeps shrinking. When `mid` passes `high`, every element has been placed in its correct region.

Step 5: The final array is grouped as all 0s, then all 1s, then all 2s: [0,0,0,1,1,1,2,2,2].

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Dutch National Flag algorithm sorts an array that contains only three distinct values in a single linear pass using three pointers. A low pointer marks the end of the zero region, a high pointer marks the start of the two region, and a mid pointer scans the array. When the mid pointer sees a zero I swap it into the low region and advance both low and mid; when it sees a one I leave it and just advance mid; and when it sees a two I swap it into the high region and move the high pointer inward without advancing mid.

The detail that separates a correct implementation from a broken one is why mid does not move after swapping a two to the back. The value pulled in from the high end has not been classified yet, so if I advanced mid I could skip examining it and leave a zero stranded in the middle. Keeping mid in place forces that incoming value to be checked on the next iteration.

The reason I reach for this instead of a general sort is that it is a single in-place pass with constant extra space, whereas a comparison sort is order n log n and counting sort needs a second pass or extra counters. When there are exactly three categories, the Dutch flag is the canonical, optimal answer.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the fraud review tool. Each pending transaction carried a risk tier of low, medium, or high coded as zero, one, and two, and the tool needed to group a large live queue from low to high in one pass so reviewers could clear safe items fast and escalate risky ones. I sorted the shared queue array in place to avoid copying it. Explaining the three regions, the swap rules, and especially why mid stays put after a high swap shows the interviewer I understand the invariant that makes this one-pass partition correct.

answers.question: Explain Sliding Window — fixed-size vs variable-size window, expand right / shrink left.
answers.shortTitle: Explain Sliding Window — Fixed-Size vs Variable-Size, Expand Right / Shrink Left

s1_definition.profdef: The sliding window technique maintains a contiguous range over an array or string using two indexes, expanding the right edge to include new elements and contracting the left edge to drop old ones, so a running result is updated in O(n) instead of recomputing over every subrange. A fixed-size window keeps a constant width and slides one step at a time; a variable-size window grows and shrinks based on a condition.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh watches a rolling window of recent transactions. For a fixed window he always looks at exactly the last K transactions, dropping the oldest as a new one arrives. For a variable window he keeps extending as long as the running total stays within a limit and pulls the left edge in when it crosses the limit, so the window breathes in and out.
s1_definition.oneliner: Expand right to add, shrink left to remove, and update the answer incrementally — turning repeated subrange scans into one linear pass.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The sliding window technique maintains a contiguous range over an array or string using two indexes, expanding the right edge to include new elements and contracting the left edge to drop old ones, so a running result is updated in O(n) instead of recomputing over every subrange. A fixed-size window keeps a constant width and slides one step at a time; a variable-size window grows and shrinks based on a condition.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh watches a rolling window of recent transactions. For a fixed window he always looks at exactly the last K transactions, dropping the oldest as a new one arrives. For a variable window he keeps extending as long as the running total stays within a limit and pulls the left edge in when it crosses the limit, so the window breathes in and out.

**One line to remember:** Expand right to add, shrink left to remove, and update the answer incrementally — turning repeated subrange scans into one linear pass.

sections.s2_technical:
A fixed-size window of width K first builds the window over the first K elements, computing an initial aggregate like a sum. Then it slides: for each new right index it adds the entering element and subtracts the leaving element at `index - K`, keeping the aggregate current in O(1) per step. For example, a rolling K-day sum: `sum += a[right]; if (right >= k) sum -= a[right - k];` and once `right >= k - 1` you record `sum`.

A variable-size window uses an outer loop that advances `right` to expand, and an inner `while` that advances `left` to shrink whenever a condition is violated or satisfied, depending on the problem. For a longest-valid problem you shrink while the window is invalid, then record the width `right - left + 1`. For a shortest-valid problem you shrink while the window is still valid, recording the minimum width each time it holds.

A code snippet for a variable window finding the longest span with sum at most a limit: `int l=0; long sum=0; int best=0; for (int r=0; r<n; r++) { sum += a[r]; while (sum > limit) { sum -= a[l]; l++; } best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1); }`. The left pointer only ever moves forward, so even with the nested while the total work is linear because each element enters once and leaves once.

The senior nuance is recognizing which variant a problem needs. Fixed-size applies when the window width is given. Variable-size applies when you optimize the width subject to a constraint, and the direction of the shrink condition flips between longest and shortest problems. Many string window problems also carry a frequency map or a matched-count to decide validity in O(1) per step. The amortized linear time is the whole reason the technique beats the O(n times K) or O(n squared) brute force.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India fraud engine watches Rajesh's spending and needs a rolling three-transaction total to flag bursts. This is exactly how a fixed-size sliding window works — add the newest, subtract the one leaving, keep the sum current.

Problem 2 — The same engine also needs the longest streak of recent transactions whose total stays within a daily safe limit, which can be any length. This is exactly how a variable-size window works — expand while safe, shrink the left edge when the total exceeds the limit.

The code shows a `SpendWindowAnalyzer` with a fixed-window `rollingSum` and a variable-window `longestWithinLimit`, demonstrated on Rajesh's transaction amounts.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: amounts [5, 1, 3, 8, 2, 4, 1], fixed width 3, variable limit 10.

Step 1: For the fixed window, the first three elements 5, 1, 3 sum to 9, recorded as the first rolling sum. As the right edge moves to 8, we add 8 and subtract the leaving 5, giving 1 plus 3 plus 8 equals 12.

Step 2: Sliding on, we add 2 and subtract 1, giving 3 plus 8 plus 2 equals 13; then add 4 subtract 3 giving 8 plus 2 plus 4 equals 14; then add 1 subtract 8 giving 2 plus 4 plus 1 equals 7. The rolling sums are 9, 12, 13, 14, 7.

Step 3: For the variable window with limit 10, right expands adding 5 then 1 then 3 keeping the sum at 9, within limit, so the window is width 3. Adding 8 makes 17, over the limit, so left shrinks: subtract 5 to get 12, still over, subtract 1 to get 11, still over, subtract 3 to get 8, now valid with window [8] width 1.

Step 4: Right adds 2 making 10, valid, width 2. Adds 4 making 14, over, so left shrinks subtracting 8 to get 6, valid, window [2,4] width 2. Adds 1 making 7, valid, window [2,4,1] width 3.

Step 5: The best width seen is 3, from the early [5,1,3] span and the later [2,4,1] span, so the method returns 3.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The sliding window technique keeps a contiguous range over an array or string using two indexes, expanding the right edge to bring new elements in and contracting the left edge to drop old ones, while updating a running result incrementally. This turns problems that would otherwise recompute an aggregate over every subrange into a single linear pass. There are two flavors I distinguish clearly.

A fixed-size window has a width given by the problem. I build the initial window over the first K elements, then slide one step at a time by adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving element, which keeps the aggregate current in constant time per step. That is ideal for rolling sums and rolling averages.

A variable-size window grows and shrinks based on a condition. I advance the right edge in an outer loop to expand, and I advance the left edge in an inner loop to shrink. The direction of the shrink condition flips depending on the goal: for a longest-valid window I shrink while the window is invalid and then record the width, whereas for a shortest-valid window I shrink while the window is still valid and record the minimum. Even with the nested loop the work stays linear because the left pointer only moves forward, so each element enters and leaves the window exactly once.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used both in the fraud engine. A fixed three-transaction rolling sum flagged sudden spending bursts, and a variable window found the longest recent streak of transactions whose total stayed within a daily safe limit. Explaining the expand-right and shrink-left mechanics, the fixed-versus-variable distinction, and the amortized linear-time argument shows the interviewer I understand why the window technique is so much faster than the brute-force subrange scan.

s1_definition.profdef: This problem finds the maximum sum among all contiguous subarrays of a fixed length K. The fixed-size sliding window computes the sum of the first K elements, then slides by adding the next element and subtracting the one that falls out of the window, tracking the maximum, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space instead of recomputing each window in O(K).
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants the three-day stretch with the highest total deposits this week. Rajesh totals the first three days, then for each new day he adds that day and removes the day that slid out of the window, always remembering the biggest three-day total he has seen.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a running window sum by adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving one, and track the maximum — O(n), not O(n times K).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem finds the maximum sum among all contiguous subarrays of a fixed length K. The fixed-size sliding window computes the sum of the first K elements, then slides by adding the next element and subtracting the one that falls out of the window, tracking the maximum, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space instead of recomputing each window in O(K).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants the three-day stretch with the highest total deposits this week. Rajesh totals the first three days, then for each new day he adds that day and removes the day that slid out of the window, always remembering the biggest three-day total he has seen.

**One line to remember:** Keep a running window sum by adding the entering element and subtracting the leaving one, and track the maximum — O(n), not O(n times K).

sections.s2_technical:
First compute the sum of the first K elements as the initial window and set it as the current maximum. Then for each right index from K to n-1, update `windowSum += a[right] - a[right - k]`, which adds the new element and removes the element K positions back in a single step. After each update compare against the running maximum.

A code snippet on daily deposits: `int maxSumK(int[] a, int k) { long sum = 0; for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) sum += a[i]; long best = sum; for (int r = k; r < a.length; r++) { sum += a[r] - a[r - k]; best = Math.max(best, sum); } return (int) best; }`. The subtraction of `a[r - k]` is what makes each slide O(1).

The improvement over brute force is the core teaching point. Recomputing each window's sum from scratch is O(n times K) because there are about n windows each costing K additions. The sliding window reuses the previous sum, changing only two terms per slide, giving O(n). This reuse of overlapping work is the essence of the window technique.

A senior nuance is handling edge cases: if K is larger than the array length there is no valid window, so you return a sentinel or throw. Use `long` for the accumulator when values can be large to avoid overflow, especially with money. Also, negative values are fine here because the window width is fixed; unlike the maximum-subarray-of-any-length problem, there is no benefit to dropping a prefix, so this stays a simple fixed window rather than a Kadane-style scan.

Problem 2 — Deposit histories can be long, so recomputing every window would be too slow for a report that runs across many customers, which is why the O(n) slide matters.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The maximum sum subarray of size K asks for the largest total among all contiguous windows of a fixed length, and the fixed-size sliding window solves it in linear time. I first add up the first K elements to form the initial window and take that as my current best. Then I slide the window one position at a time, and for each slide I add the element entering on the right and subtract the element leaving on the left in a single operation, comparing the updated window sum against my running maximum.

The key efficiency point is the reuse of overlapping work. A brute-force solution recomputes each window's sum from scratch, which costs K additions for each of roughly n windows and gives order n times K. The sliding window instead changes only two terms per slide, the entering and leaving elements, so each step is constant time and the whole scan is linear. That reuse is the entire reason the technique exists.

I always mention a couple of practical guards. If K is larger than the array there is no valid window, so I return a sentinel or throw rather than reading out of bounds, and I accumulate in a wide type like long when values can be large so a money total does not overflow. Negative values cause no trouble here because the width is fixed and there is never a reason to drop a prefix, which keeps this a straightforward window rather than a Kadane-style scan.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a marketing report that found each customer's best fixed-length deposit streak to time a loyalty offer. With long deposit histories across many customers, recomputing every window would have been far too slow, so the linear slide kept the batch within its window. Explaining the add-and-subtract slide, the complexity improvement over brute force, and the overflow and bounds guards shows the interviewer I understand both the technique and its production details.

s1_definition.profdef: This problem finds the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least a given target, over an array of positive numbers. A variable-size sliding window expands the right edge to grow the sum, and whenever the sum reaches or exceeds the target it shrinks the left edge as far as possible while still satisfying the condition, recording the smallest width found. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants the fewest consecutive days in which Rajesh's deposits add up to at least a loan down-payment. Rajesh keeps adding days on the right until the total reaches the goal, then trims days from the left as long as the total still meets the goal, noting the shortest stretch that qualifies.
s1_definition.oneliner: Grow the window on the right until the sum reaches the target, then shrink from the left while it still qualifies, tracking the minimum length.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem finds the length of the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least a given target, over an array of positive numbers. A variable-size sliding window expands the right edge to grow the sum, and whenever the sum reaches or exceeds the target it shrinks the left edge as far as possible while still satisfying the condition, recording the smallest width found. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants the fewest consecutive days in which Rajesh's deposits add up to at least a loan down-payment. Rajesh keeps adding days on the right until the total reaches the goal, then trims days from the left as long as the total still meets the goal, noting the shortest stretch that qualifies.

**One line to remember:** Grow the window on the right until the sum reaches the target, then shrink from the left while it still qualifies, tracking the minimum length.

sections.s2_technical:
Maintain `left = 0`, a running `sum = 0`, and `best = Integer.MAX_VALUE`. In an outer loop advance `right`, adding `a[right]` to the sum. Then, in an inner `while` loop that runs while `sum >= target`, record the current window width `right - left + 1` if it is smaller than `best`, subtract `a[left]` from the sum, and advance `left`. Shrinking while the condition still holds is how you find the shortest qualifying window ending at each right position.

A code snippet on daily deposits: `int minLen(int[] a, int target) { int l=0, best=Integer.MAX_VALUE; long sum=0; for (int r=0; r<a.length; r++) { sum += a[r]; while (sum >= target) { best = Math.min(best, r - l + 1); sum -= a[l]; l++; } } return best==Integer.MAX_VALUE ? 0 : best; }`. The sentinel return of 0 means no subarray reached the target.

This is the shortest-valid pattern, the mirror of the longest-valid pattern. For the longest-valid problem you shrink while the window is invalid and record after shrinking; for this shortest-valid problem you shrink while the window is valid and record before each shrink. Recognizing which direction the shrink condition points is the senior-level skill.

A key precondition is that all values are positive, which guarantees the sum increases as the window grows and decreases as it shrinks, making the greedy shrink correct. With negatives the monotonic behavior breaks and you would need a prefix-sum plus deque or a different method. The amortized time is linear because the left pointer only advances and never resets, so each element is added once and removed once despite the nested loop.

Problem 2 — Deposits are always positive, so the window sum grows and shrinks monotonically, which is precisely the condition that makes the shrink-while-valid approach correct.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The minimum size subarray sum problem asks for the length of the shortest contiguous stretch whose sum reaches at least a target, over an array of positive numbers, and I solve it with a variable-size sliding window in linear time. I advance the right edge to grow the running sum, and the moment the sum reaches the target I enter a shrink loop that trims from the left as long as the sum still meets the target, recording the window width each time before I shrink. That way I capture the shortest qualifying window that ends at every right position.

This is the shortest-valid pattern, which is the mirror image of the longest-valid pattern. In a longest-valid problem I shrink while the window is invalid and record after shrinking, whereas here I shrink while the window is still valid and record before each shrink. Knowing which direction the shrink condition points is what makes the difference between the two families of window problems.

The precondition I always call out is that all values are positive. That guarantees the sum rises as the window grows and falls as it shrinks, so the greedy shrink is correct. If negatives were allowed this monotonic behavior would break and I would need a prefix-sum with a deque or a different approach entirely. The running time is linear because the left pointer only ever moves forward and never resets, so each element is added once and removed once even though there is a nested loop.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this at the loan desk to compute the fewest consecutive days in which a customer accumulated at least the required down payment, as evidence of saving discipline. Because deposits are always positive, the window behaved monotonically and the shrink-while-valid approach was exactly right. s1_definition.profdef: This problem finds the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated character. A variable-size sliding window expands the right edge and uses a hash map from character to its last seen index to jump the left edge past any earlier occurrence of a repeated character, keeping the window free of duplicates. It runs in O(n) time and O(min(n, alphabet)) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India scans a stream of session tokens and wants the longest run with no repeated character, as a quick uniqueness signal. Rajesh keeps a window of recent characters and a note of where he last saw each one. When a repeat appears inside the window, he slides the left edge forward to just after the previous copy so the window is clean again.
s1_definition.oneliner: Grow the window on the right, and when a character repeats inside it, jump the left edge to just past that character's previous position using a last-seen map.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem finds the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated character. A variable-size sliding window expands the right edge and uses a hash map from character to its last seen index to jump the left edge past any earlier occurrence of a repeated character, keeping the window free of duplicates. It runs in O(n) time and O(min(n, alphabet)) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India scans a stream of session tokens and wants the longest run with no repeated character, as a quick uniqueness signal. Rajesh keeps a window of recent characters and a note of where he last saw each one. When a repeat appears inside the window, he slides the left edge forward to just after the previous copy so the window is clean again.

**One line to remember:** Grow the window on the right, and when a character repeats inside it, jump the left edge to just past that character's previous position using a last-seen map.

sections.s2_technical:
Maintain `left = 0`, a `best = 0`, and a `HashMap<Character, Integer>` holding the last index where each character was seen. For each `right`, look at `c = s.charAt(right)`. If `c` is in the map and its stored index is at least `left`, it means `c` appears inside the current window, so move `left` to `map.get(c) + 1` to drop that earlier copy. Then record `map.put(c, right)` and update `best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1)`.

A code snippet on a token string: `int longestUnique(String s) { Map<Character,Integer> last = new HashMap<>(); int l=0, best=0; for (int r=0; r<s.length(); r++) { char c=s.charAt(r); if (last.containsKey(c) && last.get(c) >= l) l = last.get(c) + 1; last.put(c, r); best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1); } return best; }`. The condition `last.get(c) >= l` is essential: a stored index before `left` refers to a copy already outside the window and must be ignored.

The reason the left pointer never moves backward is that we always set it to one past the previous occurrence only when that occurrence is inside the window. Combined with each `right` advancing once, this gives linear time. The map lookups and updates are constant on average.

A senior nuance is that forgetting the `>= left` check causes a bug where a stale earlier index incorrectly pulls the left pointer backward, shrinking or corrupting the window. For a fixed small alphabet like lowercase letters you can replace the map with an int array of size 26 or 128 for ASCII, which is faster and uses fixed space. The map version is the general answer for arbitrary characters.
