sections.s6_takeaway:
The longest substring without repeating characters is a variable-size sliding window problem backed by a map that remembers where each character was last seen. I advance the right edge one character at a time, and whenever the current character has a previous occurrence that lies inside the current window, I jump the left edge to one position past that previous occurrence so the window becomes duplicate-free again. After each step I update the best length from the current window width.

The detail that makes or breaks this solution is checking that the stored previous index is at least the current left pointer before I jump. A character might have been seen earlier but already fallen outside the window, and if I blindly moved the left pointer to that stale index I would pull it backward and corrupt the window. The at-least-left guard ensures the left pointer only ever moves forward, which both keeps correctness and guarantees linear time because each index is visited once on the right and the left pointer never resets.

For arbitrary characters I use a hash map keyed by character, but when the alphabet is small and fixed, such as lowercase letters or ASCII, I can replace the map with a small integer array for speed and fixed memory. The algorithm is otherwise identical.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the security service to measure the longest run of distinct characters in session token strings as a cheap entropy heuristic that flagged suspiciously weak tokens. Because tokens used arbitrary characters, the general hash-map version fit best. Explaining the window expansion, the last-seen map, and especially the at-least-left guard that keeps the pointer from moving backward shows the interviewer I understand the correctness subtlety that trips up most candidates.

answers.question: Longest Repeating Character Replacement — window where `size - maxFreq ≤ K`.
answers.shortTitle: Longest Repeating Character Replacement — Window Where size − maxFreq ≤ K

s1_definition.profdef: This problem finds the longest substring you can make of a single repeated character if you are allowed to replace at most K characters. A variable-size sliding window tracks the frequency of each character inside it and the count of the most frequent one; the window is valid when its size minus that maximum frequency is at most K, meaning the non-dominant characters that must be replaced do not exceed K. It runs in O(n) time.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a string of status codes and wants the longest stretch it could turn into one uniform code by correcting at most K entries. Rajesh grows a window and notes which status appears most. If the number of entries that are not the majority exceeds K, he shrinks from the left, because those are the ones he would have to correct.
s1_definition.oneliner: A window is valid when the number of characters to replace — its size minus the most frequent character's count — is at most K.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem finds the longest substring you can make of a single repeated character if you are allowed to replace at most K characters. A variable-size sliding window tracks the frequency of each character inside it and the count of the most frequent one; the window is valid when its size minus that maximum frequency is at most K, meaning the non-dominant characters that must be replaced do not exceed K. It runs in O(n) time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a string of status codes and wants the longest stretch it could turn into one uniform code by correcting at most K entries. Rajesh grows a window and notes which status appears most. If the number of entries that are not the majority exceeds K, he shrinks from the left, because those are the ones he would have to correct.

**One line to remember:** A window is valid when the number of characters to replace — its size minus the most frequent character's count — is at most K.

sections.s2_technical:
Keep a frequency array `count` of size 26 (for uppercase letters), `left = 0`, `maxFreq = 0`, and `best = 0`. For each `right`, increment the frequency of `s.charAt(right)` and update `maxFreq` to the larger of itself and that character's new count. The window is invalid when `(right - left + 1) - maxFreq > K`, meaning more than K characters differ from the dominant one. When invalid, decrement the frequency of `s.charAt(left)` and advance `left` by one.

A code snippet on status codes: `int longestRepl(String s, int k) { int[] cnt = new int[26]; int l=0, maxF=0, best=0; for (int r=0; r<s.length(); r++) { cnt[s.charAt(r)-'A']++; maxF = Math.max(maxF, cnt[s.charAt(r)-'A']); if ((r - l + 1) - maxF > k) { cnt[s.charAt(l)-'A']--; l++; } best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1); } return best; }`. Note the window shrinks by at most one per step, so it never contracts more than it grows.

A subtle and famous point is that `maxFreq` is never decreased even when characters leave the window. This looks like a bug but is intentional: `best` only grows when we find a window with a larger valid size, and a stale, slightly-too-high `maxFreq` can only make the window appear valid for sizes we already achieved, never produce a larger wrong answer. Because the window length only ever moves up or stays, the final answer remains correct, and avoiding the recomputation of the true max keeps it linear.

A senior nuance is why the single-step shrink works: since the window grew by one this step, shrinking by at most one keeps the length monotonic, and the invariant `size - maxFreq <= k` is restored or maintained. Attempting to recompute the true maximum frequency on every shrink would add an O(26) or O(n) factor and is unnecessary. This trick of a non-decreasing `maxFreq` is the interview highlight.

This is exactly how longest-repeating-character-replacement works — the window is valid when the entries needing correction do not exceed K.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Repeating Character Replacement asks for the longest substring I can turn into a single repeated character when I am allowed to replace at most K characters, and I solve it with a variable-size sliding window plus a frequency count. As I extend the right edge I increase the count of the incoming character and track the highest frequency of any single character in the window. The window is valid exactly when its size minus that highest frequency is at most K, because that difference is the number of non-dominant characters I would have to replace.

The famous subtlety is that I never decrease the tracked maximum frequency even when characters leave the window. That looks wrong, but it is deliberate and safe. The best length only ever increases, and a slightly stale maximum frequency can only let the window appear valid for sizes I have already reached, never fabricate a larger wrong answer. Because the window length is monotonic, the final result stays correct, and skipping the recomputation of the true maximum is what keeps the algorithm linear.

That monotonic behavior is also why shrinking by a single step is enough. Since the window grew by one this iteration, trimming at most one from the left keeps the length from ever decreasing while restoring the validity condition, so I never need an inner loop or an O(26) recount on each shrink.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the compliance service. Daily account status codes were stored as a string, and the team wanted the longest stretch that could be made uniform by correcting at most K mis-tagged entries, as a measure of data cleanliness. Because status codes were a small fixed set of uppercase letters, a 26-length frequency array was ideal. Explaining the validity condition, the deliberately non-decreasing maximum frequency, and the single-step shrink shows the interviewer I understand the clever invariant that makes this problem linear rather than quadratic.

answers.question: Find All Anagrams in a String — fixed-size window with frequency comparison.
answers.shortTitle: Find All Anagrams in a String — Fixed-Size Window With Frequency Comparison

s1_definition.profdef: This problem returns the start indexes of every substring of a text that is an anagram of a given pattern. A fixed-size sliding window the length of the pattern slides across the text, maintaining a character-frequency count that is compared against the pattern's frequency; a match means the window is an anagram. Using a matched-count optimization it runs in O(n) time and O(alphabet) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India looks for every place in a transaction-reference string where a window of characters is a rearrangement of a known suspicious code. Rajesh slides a fixed-width window the size of the code and keeps a tally of letters inside it; whenever the tally matches the code's tally, that starting spot is an anagram hit.
s1_definition.oneliner: Slide a window the size of the pattern and compare character counts; equal counts mean the window is an anagram.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem returns the start indexes of every substring of a text that is an anagram of a given pattern. A fixed-size sliding window the length of the pattern slides across the text, maintaining a character-frequency count that is compared against the pattern's frequency; a match means the window is an anagram. Using a matched-count optimization it runs in O(n) time and O(alphabet) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India looks for every place in a transaction-reference string where a window of characters is a rearrangement of a known suspicious code. Rajesh slides a fixed-width window the size of the code and keeps a tally of letters inside it; whenever the tally matches the code's tally, that starting spot is an anagram hit.

**One line to remember:** Slide a window the size of the pattern and compare character counts; equal counts mean the window is an anagram.

sections.s2_technical:
Build a frequency array `need` of size 26 for the pattern. Slide a window of width equal to the pattern length over the text, keeping a `window` frequency array. For each new right index add its character to `window`, and once the window exceeds the pattern length, remove the leftmost character. Whenever the window width equals the pattern length, compare the two arrays; if equal, record the start index.

A faster variant uses a single `matches` counter instead of comparing 26 cells each step. It counts how many of the 26 letters currently have equal frequency in the window and the pattern, updating `matches` incrementally as characters enter and leave, and reports a hit when `matches == 26`. A code snippet of the simpler array-compare version: `for (int r=0; r<text.length(); r++) { window[text.charAt(r)-'a']++; if (r >= pLen) window[text.charAt(r-pLen)-'a']--; if (r >= pLen-1 && Arrays.equals(window, need)) result.add(r - pLen + 1); }`.

The two methods trade clarity for speed. Comparing arrays each step is O(26) per position, which is O(26n) overall, still linear in n with a constant factor. The matched-count version removes that constant factor and is the senior-level answer, but both are acceptable and the array-compare version is easier to get right under pressure.

A senior nuance is the off-by-one on when to start comparing: you only compare once the window has reached the full pattern width, which is at right index pattern-length minus one and every index after. Also remember to shrink the window by removing the character that falls off the left as the window advances, otherwise the window grows unbounded and the counts drift.

This is exactly how find-all-anagrams works — a fixed window compared by character frequency.

Problem 2 — The reference string is long, so an O(n) sliding comparison is required rather than checking every substring independently.

Input: text "cbaebabacd", pattern "abc" of length 3. The need array has a 1, b 1, c 1.

Step 1: Right 0 'c', window c 1. Right 1 'b', window b 1 c 1. Right 2 'a', window a 1 b 1 c 1; width is now 3 so we compare, and it equals need, so start index 0 is recorded (the substring "cba").

Step 2: Right 3 'e', window adds e, and since right is at least pLen we drop the leftmost 'c' at index 0. Window is a 1 b 1 e 1, not equal to need. No hit.

Step 3: Right 4 'b', add b (b now 2) and drop 'b' at index 1 (b back to 1). Window a 1 b 1 e 1, still has e, no match. Right 5 'a', add a (a 2) drop 'a' at index 2 (a back to 1). Window a 1 b 1 e... wait e dropped later; net window over indexes 3-5 is "eba" which has e, no match.

Step 4: Right 6 'b', add b, drop 'e' at index 3. Window over indexes 4-6 is "bab" with a 1 b 2, not equal. Right 7 'a', add a, drop 'b' at index 4. Window indexes 5-7 "aba" a 2 b 1, not equal.

Step 5: Right 8 'c', add c, drop 'a' at index 5. Window indexes 6-8 "bac" a 1 b 1 c 1 equals need, record start index 6. Right 9 'd' breaks the match. Final hits are indexes 0 and 6.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Find All Anagrams in a String returns the starting index of every window in a text that is a rearrangement of a given pattern, and I solve it with a fixed-size sliding window the length of the pattern. I build a character-frequency count for the pattern, then slide a same-width window across the text, adding the character entering on the right and removing the character leaving on the left. Whenever the window reaches the pattern's width, I compare the window's frequency count against the pattern's; if they are equal the window is an anagram and I record its starting index.

There are two ways to do the comparison. The straightforward way compares the two frequency arrays at each position, which costs a constant factor of twenty-six per step and is still linear in the length of the text. The faster way maintains a single matched-letter counter that updates incrementally as characters enter and leave, reporting a hit when all twenty-six letters match, which removes that constant factor. Both are acceptable, and I usually reach for the array comparison first because it is easier to get right under pressure and mention the matched-count optimization as the improvement.

The details that catch people out are the off-by-one on when to start comparing, which is only once the window has grown to the full pattern width, and remembering to drop the character that slides off the left edge as the window advances, otherwise the counts drift and every later comparison is wrong.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the fraud service. The team had a known suspicious character pattern and needed every position in a long transaction-reference string where a same-length window was a permutation of it, since fraud rings sometimes reorder a code. The reference strings were long, so the linear sliding comparison was essential rather than checking each substring independently. Explaining the window slide, the frequency comparison, the matched-count optimization, and the off-by-one and shrink details shows the interviewer I understand both the algorithm and the pitfalls.

answers.question: Fruit Into Baskets / Longest with At Most K Distinct — variable window + char count.
answers.shortTitle: Fruit Into Baskets / Longest With At Most K Distinct — Variable Window + Char Count

s1_definition.profdef: This problem finds the longest contiguous subarray containing at most K distinct values; the Fruit Into Baskets variant is the special case where K equals two. A variable-size sliding window grows the right edge and, whenever the number of distinct values in the window exceeds K, shrinks the left edge while decrementing counts until the distinct count is back within K. It runs in O(n) time and O(K) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants the longest run of consecutive transactions that touches at most K different merchant categories, as a loyalty-pattern signal. Rajesh grows a window and keeps a tally of how many distinct categories it holds; when a new category pushes the count past K, he shrinks from the left, removing categories until only K remain.
s1_definition.oneliner: Expand the window and track distinct counts in a map; when distinct exceeds K, shrink from the left until it is at most K again.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem finds the longest contiguous subarray containing at most K distinct values; the Fruit Into Baskets variant is the special case where K equals two. A variable-size sliding window grows the right edge and, whenever the number of distinct values in the window exceeds K, shrinks the left edge while decrementing counts until the distinct count is back within K. It runs in O(n) time and O(K) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants the longest run of consecutive transactions that touches at most K different merchant categories, as a loyalty-pattern signal. Rajesh grows a window and keeps a tally of how many distinct categories it holds; when a new category pushes the count past K, he shrinks from the left, removing categories until only K remain.

**One line to remember:** Expand the window and track distinct counts in a map; when distinct exceeds K, shrink from the left until it is at most K again.

sections.s2_technical:
Keep a `HashMap<T, Integer>` counting occurrences of each value in the window, `left = 0`, and `best = 0`. For each `right`, increment the count of the entering value. Then, while the map has more than K keys, decrement the count of the value at `left`; if that count reaches zero remove the key from the map, and advance `left`. After the window is valid, update `best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1)`.

A code snippet on merchant categories: `int longestAtMostK(int[] cat, int k) { Map<Integer,Integer> cnt = new HashMap<>(); int l=0, best=0; for (int r=0; r<cat.length; r++) { cnt.merge(cat[r], 1, Integer::sum); while (cnt.size() > k) { int lv = cat[l]; cnt.merge(lv, -1, Integer::sum); if (cnt.get(lv) == 0) cnt.remove(lv); l++; } best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1); } return best; }`. The map size is exactly the number of distinct values in the window, which is the quantity we constrain.

Removing a key when its count hits zero is essential, because the map's size is how we measure distinctness; leaving a zero-count key would overstate the distinct count and shrink the window incorrectly. The Fruit Into Baskets problem is literally this with K equal to two, framed as two baskets each holding one fruit type.

The amortized time is linear because the left pointer only advances and each element enters and leaves the window once. A senior nuance is that the inner while shrinks only as much as needed to restore the at-most-K invariant, never more, which preserves the longest valid window ending at the current right. Using `merge` keeps the count updates concise and correct.

Problem 2 — Categories are arbitrary integer codes, so a hash map counts occurrences, and removing zero-count keys keeps the distinct measure accurate.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The longest subarray with at most K distinct values, of which Fruit Into Baskets is the K-equals-two special case, is a variable-size sliding window problem backed by a count map. I grow the window on the right and increment the count of each entering value. Whenever the number of distinct values in the window, which is exactly the size of the map, exceeds K, I shrink from the left by decrementing the count of the leaving value and advancing the left pointer. After the window is valid again I update the best length.

The one detail I always emphasize is removing a key from the map when its count drops to zero. The map's size is how I measure distinctness, so if I left a zero-count key in place the size would overstate the number of distinct values and I would shrink the window more than necessary, producing a wrong answer. Removing the key keeps the distinct measure exact.

The inner shrink loop is careful to trim only as much as needed to restore the at-most-K condition and no more, which preserves the longest valid window ending at the current right position. The running time is linear because the left pointer only ever advances, so each element enters and leaves the window exactly once despite the nested loop.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the analytics service to find the longest run of consecutive card transactions that stayed within at most K distinct merchant categories, as a signal of concentrated spending for a targeted reward. Categories were arbitrary integer codes, so a hash map counted occurrences, and the zero-count key removal kept the distinct count accurate. Explaining the expand-and-shrink mechanics, the map size as the distinct measure, and the critical zero-count key removal shows the interviewer I understand why this window stays correct and linear.

answers.question: Minimum Window Substring — expand/shrink with frequency map + matched count.
answers.shortTitle: Minimum Window Substring — Expand/Shrink With Frequency Map + Matched Count

s1_definition.profdef: Minimum Window Substring finds the shortest substring of a text that contains all characters of a pattern including their required multiplicities. A variable-size sliding window expands the right edge until the window satisfies all requirements, then shrinks the left edge as far as possible while still satisfying them, recording the smallest valid window. A need map plus a matched counter make each step constant, giving O(n) time.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India must find the shortest slice of a long log that contains every required event code at least as many times as specified. Rajesh extends the slice to the right until it covers all required codes, then trims the left as much as possible while still covering them, remembering the tightest slice.
s1_definition.oneliner: Expand until the window has everything required, then shrink from the left while it still does, tracking the minimum window.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Minimum Window Substring finds the shortest substring of a text that contains all characters of a pattern including their required multiplicities. A variable-size sliding window expands the right edge until the window satisfies all requirements, then shrinks the left edge as far as possible while still satisfying them, recording the smallest valid window. A need map plus a matched counter make each step constant, giving O(n) time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India must find the shortest slice of a long log that contains every required event code at least as many times as specified. Rajesh extends the slice to the right until it covers all required codes, then trims the left as much as possible while still covering them, remembering the tightest slice.

**One line to remember:** Expand until the window has everything required, then shrink from the left while it still does, tracking the minimum window.

sections.s2_technical:
Build a `need` map of required character counts from the pattern, and track `required = need.size()` distinct characters that must be fully satisfied. Use a `window` map, a `formed` counter of how many distinct characters currently meet their required count, `left = 0`, and best bounds. For each `right`, add the character to `window`; if its window count equals its need count, increment `formed`.

While `formed == required`, the window is valid: record it if smaller than the best seen, then shrink by removing the character at `left` from `window`; if that drops its window count below its need count, decrement `formed`, and advance `left`. A code snippet: `while (formed == required) { if (r - l + 1 < bestLen) { bestLen = r - l + 1; bestStart = l; } char lc = s.charAt(l); window.merge(lc, -1, Integer::sum); if (need.containsKey(lc) && window.get(lc) < need.get(lc)) formed--; l++; }`.

The matched-count idea is what keeps it linear. Instead of re-scanning the window each step to check coverage, `formed` tells you in O(1) whether all requirements are met, updated only when a character crosses its required threshold entering or leaving. This mirrors the matched-count trick in the anagram problem but handles multiplicities and a subset rather than an exact permutation.

A senior nuance is tracking `formed` against the number of distinct required characters, not the total pattern length, and only decrementing `formed` when a character's window count falls strictly below its need. Characters not in `need` are still added to the window map but never affect `formed`, so extra characters are allowed as long as all required ones are present. Returning the best start and length at the end reconstructs the substring.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India incident team has a long event-code log and a set of required codes with minimum counts that together indicate a specific failure pattern, and they want the shortest contiguous log slice that contains them all so they can zoom into the root cause. This is exactly how minimum-window-substring works — the tightest window covering all requirements.

Problem 2 — Logs are huge, so a matched-count window that runs in a single linear pass is required rather than checking every slice.

The code shows an `IncidentLogAnalyzer` with `minCoveringWindow`, a demo on an event-code string and a required pattern, and the shortest covering slice.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Minimum Window Substring finds the shortest slice of a text that contains every character of a pattern with its required multiplicity, and I solve it with a variable-size sliding window that expands then shrinks. I build a need map of required counts and track how many distinct required characters are fully satisfied with a counter I call formed. I grow the right edge, adding each character to a window map, and when a character's window count reaches its required count I increment formed. Once formed equals the number of distinct required characters, the window is valid, so I record it if it is the smallest so far and then shrink from the left as long as it stays valid.

The matched-count counter is what keeps this linear. Rather than re-scanning the whole window each step to check whether it still covers everything, formed answers that in constant time and only changes when a character crosses its required threshold on the way in or out. It is the same idea as the matched-count trick in the anagram problem, extended to handle multiplicities and the fact that I need a superset rather than an exact permutation.

The subtle points I emphasize are that formed is compared against the number of distinct required characters, not the total pattern length, that I only decrement formed when a character's count falls strictly below its requirement, and that characters not in the need map are still added to the window but never affect formed, which is how extra characters are tolerated.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the incident service. We had a long event-code log and a set of required codes with minimum counts that together signalled a specific failure, and the team wanted the shortest contiguous log slice containing them all so they could zoom straight to the root cause. Because the logs were huge, the single-pass matched-count window was essential. answers.question: Sliding Window Maximum — monotonic deque maintaining decreasing order.
answers.shortTitle: Sliding Window Maximum — Monotonic Deque Maintaining Decreasing Order

s1_definition.profdef: Sliding Window Maximum returns the maximum of every contiguous window of size K as the window slides across an array. A monotonic deque of indices, kept in decreasing order of their values, gives the current window maximum at the front in O(1); each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the whole computation is O(n) time and O(K) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India tracks a rolling K-minute peak of transaction rates. Rajesh keeps a short queue of candidate peak times, always ordered so the biggest is at the front. When a new, larger rate arrives it knocks out every smaller candidate behind it, and when a candidate falls out of the time window it is removed from the front.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a deque of indices with decreasing values; the front is always the window maximum, and each index enters and leaves at most once.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sliding Window Maximum returns the maximum of every contiguous window of size K as the window slides across an array. A monotonic deque of indices, kept in decreasing order of their values, gives the current window maximum at the front in O(1); each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the whole computation is O(n) time and O(K) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India tracks a rolling K-minute peak of transaction rates. Rajesh keeps a short queue of candidate peak times, always ordered so the biggest is at the front. When a new, larger rate arrives it knocks out every smaller candidate behind it, and when a candidate falls out of the time window it is removed from the front.

**One line to remember:** Keep a deque of indices with decreasing values; the front is always the window maximum, and each index enters and leaves at most once.

sections.s2_technical:
Use an `ArrayDeque<Integer>` holding array indices, maintained so the values at those indices are strictly decreasing from front to back. For each new index `r`: first, pop from the back while the value at the back index is less than or equal to `a[r]`, because those can never be the maximum while `a[r]` is in the window. Then push `r` to the back. Next, remove the front index if it has slid out of the window, meaning `front <= r - k`. Finally, once `r >= k - 1`, the value at the front index is the maximum of the current window.

A code snippet on transaction rates: `int[] maxWindow(int[] a, int k) { Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>(); int[] out = new int[a.length - k + 1]; for (int r=0; r<a.length; r++) { while (!dq.isEmpty() && a[dq.peekLast()] <= a[r]) dq.pollLast(); dq.offerLast(r); if (dq.peekFirst() <= r - k) dq.pollFirst(); if (r >= k - 1) out[r - k + 1] = a[dq.peekFirst()]; } return out; }`.

Why store indices and not values? Because the eviction from the front depends on position, so you must know where each candidate sits to tell when it leaves the window. The decreasing-order invariant guarantees the front is the maximum: anything smaller that arrived earlier was already popped when a larger value came in, so only genuine candidates remain, newest-and-smaller toward the back.

The linear time is the key result. Although there is an inner while loop, each index is added to the deque exactly once and removed at most once, so the total number of deque operations across the whole scan is bounded by two times n. A senior nuance is using `<=` rather than `<` on the back-pop so equal values do not linger uselessly, and remembering the front-eviction check uses the index, which is why storing indices rather than values is mandatory.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India operations dashboard shows the rolling peak transaction rate over every K-minute window to spot load spikes. This is exactly how sliding-window-maximum works — the maximum of each sliding window.

Problem 2 — The rate series streams continuously and is long, so recomputing each window's max naively would be too slow, and the monotonic deque gives each window's max in amortized constant time.

The code shows a `PeakRateAnalyzer` with `rollingMax`, a demo on a rate series with window size 3, and the array of window maxima.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Sliding Window Maximum returns the maximum of every window of size K as it slides across an array, and the efficient solution is a monotonic deque of indices kept in decreasing order of their values. For each new index I first pop from the back of the deque every index whose value is less than or equal to the new value, because those can never be the maximum while the larger new value is in the window, then I push the new index. I evict the front index if it has slid out of the window, and once the window is full the value at the front index is the maximum.

The reason I store indices rather than values is that evicting the front depends on position. I need to know where each candidate sits so I can tell exactly when it leaves the window, and that is impossible if I only kept values. The decreasing-order invariant is what makes the front always the maximum, because any smaller earlier value was already popped when a larger value arrived, so only real candidates remain with the newest and smallest toward the back.

The headline property is linear time. Even though there is an inner while loop, each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total deque work across the whole array is bounded by twice the length. I also use less-than-or-equal on the back pop rather than strict less-than so equal values do not linger uselessly.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the operations dashboard to show the rolling peak transaction rate over every K-minute window and spot load spikes. Because the rate series streamed continuously and was long, recomputing each window's maximum naively would have been too slow, and the monotonic deque gave each window's maximum in amortized constant time. Explaining the decreasing-deque invariant, why indices are stored, and the amortized linear analysis shows the interviewer I understand the data-structure insight behind this hard problem.

answers.question: Max Consecutive Ones III — sliding window allowing at most K zero flips.
answers.shortTitle: Max Consecutive Ones III — Sliding Window Allowing At Most K Zero Flips

s1_definition.profdef: Max Consecutive Ones III finds the longest run of consecutive 1s obtainable in a binary array if you may flip at most K zeros to ones. A variable-size sliding window grows the right edge, counting zeros inside the window; when the zero count exceeds K the left edge shrinks until at most K zeros remain, and the largest window seen is the answer. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a daily uptime string where 1 means a service was up and 0 means down, and it may excuse at most K down-days as maintenance. Rajesh finds the longest stretch of "up" days he can claim if he is allowed to recolor at most K down-days as up, growing a window and shrinking it whenever it contains too many excused downs.
s1_definition.oneliner: Slide a window counting zeros; keep it valid while zeros are at most K, and the widest such window is the answer.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Max Consecutive Ones III finds the longest run of consecutive 1s obtainable in a binary array if you may flip at most K zeros to ones. A variable-size sliding window grows the right edge, counting zeros inside the window; when the zero count exceeds K the left edge shrinks until at most K zeros remain, and the largest window seen is the answer. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a daily uptime string where 1 means a service was up and 0 means down, and it may excuse at most K down-days as maintenance. Rajesh finds the longest stretch of "up" days he can claim if he is allowed to recolor at most K down-days as up, growing a window and shrinking it whenever it contains too many excused downs.

**One line to remember:** Slide a window counting zeros; keep it valid while zeros are at most K, and the widest such window is the answer.

sections.s2_technical:
Maintain `left = 0`, a `zeros` counter, and `best = 0`. For each `right`, if `a[right] == 0` increment `zeros`. Then, while `zeros > k`, if `a[left] == 0` decrement `zeros`, and advance `left`. After restoring validity, update `best = Math.max(best, right - left + 1)`. The window width always represents a run of 1s achievable by flipping at most K of its zeros.

A code snippet on the uptime array: `int longestOnes(int[] a, int k) { int l=0, zeros=0, best=0; for (int r=0; r<a.length; r++) { if (a[r]==0) zeros++; while (zeros > k) { if (a[l]==0) zeros--; l++; } best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1); } return best; }`. There is no need to physically flip anything; counting the zeros inside the window is enough because any window with at most K zeros can be turned into all ones by flipping them.

A slight variation keeps the left pointer moving without a nested loop by only advancing it one step when the zero budget is exceeded, which makes the window non-shrinking and returns the final window width. Both are linear; the explicit shrink version is clearer for explaining the invariant.

A senior nuance is that this is the general form of several problems: setting K to zero gives the plain longest run of ones, and the same window structure solves "longest substring with at most K of some character replaced." The invariant is simply that the window never contains more zeros than the flip budget, and because each pointer only moves forward it is linear despite the inner loop.

```
  │            UptimeAnalyzer           │
  │ ────────────────────────────────── │
  │ + longestAvailability(a, k): int   │  O(n) O(1)
  └────────────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for longestAvailability:
    Pre:  a is 0/1, k >= 0
    Post: longest window with at most k zeros
    Invariant: zeros in window never exceeds k

  ── State Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────

  [GROW] add right (zeros++ if 0) → [CHECK]
  [CHECK] ─zeros<=k→ update best → [GROW]
          ─zeros>k→ shrink (zeros-- if a[left]==0) → [CHECK]
     ▼
  [right==n] → [DONE]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. main() → analyzer.longestAvailability(uptime, 2)
  2.   → window counts zeros, shrinks over budget
  3.   → return 7
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Max Consecutive Ones III asks for the longest run of ones I can achieve in a binary array if I may flip at most K zeros, and it is a clean variable-size sliding window. I grow the right edge and count the zeros inside the window. As long as the zero count is within the flip budget the window is valid, and whenever a new zero pushes the count above K, I shrink from the left until the window contains at most K zeros again. The widest window I ever hold is the answer.

The insight that makes this simple is that I never actually flip anything. Any window containing at most K zeros can be turned into an unbroken run of ones by flipping exactly those zeros, so counting them is all I need, and the window width directly equals the achievable run length. That reframing turns a flipping problem into a plain zero-counting window.

This structure is more general than it looks. Setting the budget to zero gives the ordinary longest run of ones, and the exact same window solves the longest substring with at most K of some character replaced. The invariant is just that the window never holds more zeros than the budget, and because both pointers only move forward the algorithm is linear even with the inner shrink loop.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the service-level team's reporting. Daily uptime was recorded as a binary string, and the SLA rules allowed excusing up to K down-days as planned maintenance when computing the longest continuous availability stretch, so the flip budget mapped directly onto excused outages. With a long uptime history the linear window was essential rather than testing every stretch. Explaining the zero-counting window, the no-actual-flip insight, and the generality of the pattern shows the interviewer I understand the problem beyond memorizing the loop.

answers.question: Find the middle element of a linked list (slow/fast pointer).
answers.shortTitle: Find the Middle Element of a Linked List — Slow/Fast Pointer

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the middle of a singly linked list uses the fast and slow pointer technique. A slow pointer advances one node at a time while a fast pointer advances two; when the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer is at the middle. It finds the midpoint in a single pass, O(n) time and O(1) space, without first counting the length.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India stores a chain of transaction nodes and wants the middle transaction for a quick spot-check. Rajesh walks two fingers: one steps on every node, the other skips every other node. When the fast finger runs off the end, the slow finger is sitting right in the middle.
s1_definition.oneliner: Move one pointer by one and another by two; when the fast one finishes, the slow one is at the middle.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the middle of a singly linked list uses the fast and slow pointer technique. A slow pointer advances one node at a time while a fast pointer advances two; when the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer is at the middle. It finds the midpoint in a single pass, O(n) time and O(1) space, without first counting the length.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India stores a chain of transaction nodes and wants the middle transaction for a quick spot-check. Rajesh walks two fingers: one steps on every node, the other skips every other node. When the fast finger runs off the end, the slow finger is sitting right in the middle.

**One line to remember:** Move one pointer by one and another by two; when the fast one finishes, the slow one is at the middle.

sections.s2_technical:
Start both `slow` and `fast` at the head. Loop while `fast != null && fast.next != null`, moving `slow = slow.next` and `fast = fast.next.next` each iteration. When the loop ends, `slow` points at the middle node. For an odd-length list the slow pointer lands exactly on the single middle; for an even-length list this formulation lands on the second of the two middle nodes.

A code snippet on a transaction list: `Node middle(Node head) { Node slow = head, fast = head; while (fast != null && fast.next != null) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; } return slow; }`. The two conditions in the while guard against a null-pointer exception: `fast != null` covers even lengths where fast steps onto null, and `fast.next != null` covers odd lengths where fast stops on the last node.

If you need the first of the two middles on an even list, start fast at `head.next` instead, or equivalently loop while `fast.next != null && fast.next.next != null`. This small change is a common interview follow-up, so knowing both variants is valuable.

The advantage over the naive two-pass method, which counts the length then walks half of it, is that this is a single pass and never needs the total length. A senior nuance is that this same slow-fast skeleton underlies cycle detection and finding a cycle's start, so recognizing the pattern connects several linked-list problems. The guard order in the while condition matters: `fast != null` must be checked before `fast.next` to avoid dereferencing null.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps the day's transactions as a singly linked list and the audit tool needs the middle transaction as a quick sampling point without scanning twice. This is exactly how the slow/fast middle finder works — one pass lands the slow pointer at the center.

Problem 2 — The list length is unknown at call time and counting it first would be a wasted extra pass over a potentially long chain, so the single-pass approach is preferred.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the middle of a singly linked list is the classic fast-and-slow pointer problem. I start both a slow pointer and a fast pointer at the head, then advance the slow pointer one node and the fast pointer two nodes on each iteration. When the fast pointer runs off the end of the list, the slow pointer is sitting at the middle, and I have done it in a single pass without ever counting the list's length.

The guard in the loop condition is the detail I always get right. I check that the fast pointer is not null and that its next is not null before moving, and the order matters because I must confirm the fast pointer itself is non-null before I dereference its next. The first condition handles even-length lists where the fast pointer steps onto null, and the second handles odd-length lists where the fast pointer stops on the last node.

With this formulation the slow pointer lands on the single middle of an odd-length list and on the second of the two middles of an even-length list. If an interviewer asks for the first of the two middles instead, I either start the fast pointer one node ahead or loop on the fast pointer's next and next-next, which is a common follow-up worth knowing. The advantage over the naive approach of counting the length and then walking halfway is that this is a single pass that never needs the total count.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the audit tool. The day's transactions were held as a singly linked list and the tool needed the middle transaction as a quick sampling point without scanning the chain twice, and since the length was unknown at call time the single-pass slow-and-fast approach avoided a wasted counting pass over a long list. Explaining the one-and-two stepping, the null-safety guard order, and the odd-versus-even landing shows the interviewer I understand the technique that also underlies cycle detection.

answers.question: Detect a cycle in a linked list (Floyd's slow/fast pointer).
answers.shortTitle: Detect a Cycle in a Linked List — Floyd's Slow/Fast Pointer

s1_definition.profdef: Floyd's cycle detection, also called the tortoise and hare, determines whether a linked list contains a cycle. A slow pointer moves one node per step and a fast pointer moves two; if there is a cycle the fast pointer eventually laps the slow pointer and they meet, and if the fast pointer reaches null the list is acyclic. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India links transaction nodes, and a corrupted import could accidentally point a node back into the chain, forming an endless loop that would hang a traversal. Rajesh sends two fingers around the chain, one slow and one fast; if the chain loops, the fast finger keeps circling and eventually catches the slow one, proving there is a loop.
s1_definition.oneliner: Move slow by one and fast by two; if they ever meet there is a cycle, and if fast hits null there is none.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Floyd's cycle detection, also called the tortoise and hare, determines whether a linked list contains a cycle. A slow pointer moves one node per step and a fast pointer moves two; if there is a cycle the fast pointer eventually laps the slow pointer and they meet, and if the fast pointer reaches null the list is acyclic. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India links transaction nodes, and a corrupted import could accidentally point a node back into the chain, forming an endless loop that would hang a traversal. Rajesh sends two fingers around the chain, one slow and one fast; if the chain loops, the fast finger keeps circling and eventually catches the slow one, proving there is a loop.

**One line to remember:** Move slow by one and fast by two; if they ever meet there is a cycle, and if fast hits null there is none.

sections.s2_technical:
Start both `slow` and `fast` at the head. Loop while `fast != null && fast.next != null`, moving `slow = slow.next` and `fast = fast.next.next`. After each move, if `slow == fast` (same node reference) a cycle exists and you return true. If the loop exits because fast became null, the list ends, so there is no cycle and you return false.

A code snippet on a transaction list: `boolean hasCycle(Node head) { Node slow = head, fast = head; while (fast != null && fast.next != null) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; if (slow == fast) return true; } return false; }`. The comparison is reference equality because we are detecting a structural loop, not comparing values.

Why are they guaranteed to meet if a cycle exists? Once both pointers are inside the loop, the fast pointer gains one node of ground on the slow pointer every step, so the gap between them shrinks by one each iteration until it becomes zero; they cannot jump past each other because the gap changes by exactly one. In an acyclic list the fast pointer simply walks off the end and the guard stops the loop.

A senior nuance is that this uses constant memory, unlike the alternative of storing visited nodes in a hash set which is also O(n) time but O(n) space. The reference comparison is essential; comparing node values could falsely report a cycle on a list with duplicate values. This detection is also the first half of finding the cycle's starting node, which builds directly on the meeting point.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India builds transaction chains from imported data, and a bad import can create a loop where a later node points back to an earlier one, which would cause any traversal to run forever. Before processing, the service must detect such a loop. This is exactly how Floyd's cycle detection works — slow and fast meet if and only if there is a loop.

Problem 2 — Memory is constrained in the import path, so the constant-space pointer method is preferred over a visited-set.

The code shows a `ChainIntegrityChecker` with `hasCycle`, a demo on a clean chain and a deliberately corrupted looping chain.

Step 3: Slow moves to T3, fast jumps from T3 to T4 then to T4's next which is T2, so fast is at T2. Different, continue.

Step 4: Slow moves to T4, fast jumps from T2 to T3 then to T4, so fast is at T4. Now slow equals fast at T4, so a cycle is detected and the method returns true.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Floyd's cycle detection, the tortoise and hare, decides whether a linked list has a loop using two pointers and no extra memory. I start a slow pointer and a fast pointer at the head, advance the slow one by a single node and the fast one by two nodes each step, and check whether they ever point at the same node. If they meet there is a cycle, and if the fast pointer reaches the end of the list there is none.

The reason the meeting is guaranteed when a cycle exists is a clean argument I always give. Once both pointers are inside the loop, the fast pointer closes the gap to the slow pointer by exactly one node every step, so the distance between them shrinks by one each iteration until it reaches zero. Because the gap changes by exactly one, the fast pointer cannot leap over the slow pointer without landing on it, so a meeting is inevitable. In an acyclic list the fast pointer just walks off the end and the guard stops the loop.

Two details matter. The comparison is reference equality on the nodes, not value equality, because I am detecting a structural loop and a list with duplicate values would otherwise produce a false positive. And the approach uses constant memory, which is its advantage over the alternative of storing every visited node in a hash set, which costs linear extra space.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the chain integrity checker. Transaction chains were built from imported data, and a bad import could point a later node back to an earlier one, creating a loop that would make any traversal run forever, so before processing I detected such loops with the tortoise and hare. Because memory was constrained in the import path, the constant-space method was preferred over a visited set. Explaining the one-and-two stepping, the shrinking-gap argument, and the reference-equality and memory points shows the interviewer I understand why Floyd's algorithm is correct and efficient.

answers.question: Linked List Cycle II — find the start of the cycle.
answers.shortTitle: Linked List Cycle II — Find the Start of the Cycle

s1_definition.profdef: Linked List Cycle II finds the node where a cycle begins, or reports none. It first uses Floyd's tortoise and hare to find a meeting point inside the loop, then resets one pointer to the head and advances both pointers one step at a time; the node where they meet again is the cycle's entry point. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India not only wants to know a transaction chain loops, but exactly which node the loop re-enters, so it can snip the bad link. Rajesh first catches the two fingers inside the loop, then moves one finger back to the start and walks both one step at a time; the spot where they meet again is where the loop begins.
s1_definition.oneliner: After the tortoise and hare meet, move one pointer to the head and step both by one; their next meeting is the cycle's start.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Linked List Cycle II finds the node where a cycle begins, or reports none. It first uses Floyd's tortoise and hare to find a meeting point inside the loop, then resets one pointer to the head and advances both pointers one step at a time; the node where they meet again is the cycle's entry point. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India not only wants to know a transaction chain loops, but exactly which node the loop re-enters, so it can snip the bad link. Rajesh first catches the two fingers inside the loop, then moves one finger back to the start and walks both one step at a time; the spot where they meet again is where the loop begins.

**One line to remember:** After the tortoise and hare meet, move one pointer to the head and step both by one; their next meeting is the cycle's start.

sections.s2_technical:
Phase one is ordinary Floyd detection: advance slow by one and fast by two until they meet, or return null if fast reaches the end. Phase two: set one pointer back to the head, keep the other at the meeting point, and advance both by one node per step. The node where they meet is the start of the cycle.

A code snippet: `Node detectCycleStart(Node head) { Node slow = head, fast = head; while (fast != null && fast.next != null) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; if (slow == fast) { Node p = head; while (p != slow) { p = p.next; slow = slow.next; } return p; } } return null; }`. The second loop advances both by one until they coincide at the entry node.

The math behind phase two is the senior-level explanation. Let the distance from the head to the cycle start be `a`, and let the slow pointer have traveled `a + b` to the meeting point where `b` is the distance from the cycle start to the meeting point. Because fast travels twice as far, `2(a + b) = a + b + n*L` for some whole number of loops `L`, which simplifies to `a = n*L - b`. That means the distance from the head to the cycle start equals the distance from the meeting point onward to the cycle start (modulo full loops), so stepping both pointers one at a time from the head and the meeting point lands them together exactly at the entry.

A senior nuance is that this elegant equality is why no counting or extra storage is needed; it falls out of the two-to-one speed ratio. The alternative hash-set method also finds the start but uses linear extra space. Handling the no-cycle case by returning null when fast falls off the end is essential.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India detected that an imported transaction chain loops, and now the repair tool must find the exact node where the loop re-enters so it can break that single bad link and restore a proper list. This is exactly how Cycle II works — it pinpoints the cycle's start node.

Problem 2 — The repair runs in the same memory-constrained import path, so the constant-space two-phase pointer method is used rather than a visited-set.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Linked List Cycle II finds the exact node where a cycle begins, and it builds on Floyd's tortoise and hare in two phases. In phase one I advance a slow pointer by one and a fast pointer by two until they meet inside the loop, or I return null if the fast pointer reaches the end. In phase two I move one pointer back to the head, keep the other at the meeting point, and advance both by a single node at a time; the node where they meet again is the start of the cycle.

The reason phase two works is a short piece of algebra I can walk through. If the distance from the head to the cycle start is a, and the slow pointer has traveled a plus b to reach the meeting point where b is the distance from the cycle start to the meeting point, then because the fast pointer traveled twice as far, two times a plus b equals a plus b plus some whole number of loop lengths. That simplifies to a equals a whole number of loop lengths minus b, which means the distance from the head to the entry equals the distance from the meeting point around to the entry. So stepping both pointers one at a time from those two places lands them together precisely at the cycle start.

That equality is exactly why no counting and no extra storage are needed; it falls straight out of the two-to-one speed ratio. The hash-set alternative also finds the start but uses linear extra space, and I always handle the acyclic case by returning null when the fast pointer runs off the end.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the chain repair tool. After detecting that an imported transaction chain looped, the tool needed the exact re-entry node so it could break that single bad link and restore a proper list, and because the repair ran in the same memory-constrained import path the constant-space two-phase method was ideal. Explaining the two phases, the distance equality that justifies the second phase, and the no-extra-memory property shows the interviewer I understand the mathematics behind this elegant algorithm.

answers.question: Happy Number — detect cycle in digit-sum sequence using fast/slow.
answers.shortTitle: Happy Number — Detect a Cycle in the Digit-Square Sequence With Fast/Slow

s1_definition.profdef: A happy number is one that eventually reaches 1 when you repeatedly replace it with the sum of the squares of its digits; if instead the process loops forever without reaching 1, the number is unhappy. Treating the sequence of transformed values as a virtual linked list, Floyd's fast and slow pointers detect whether it cycles: if the fast pointer reaches 1 the number is happy, and if slow and fast meet elsewhere there is a cycle and it is unhappy. It runs in O(log n) style iterations with O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India validates a customer PIN rule where repeatedly squaring and summing digits should collapse to 1. Rajesh runs the transformation twice as fast with one pointer and once with another; if the fast one lands on 1 the PIN satisfies the rule, but if the two ever meet on the same non-one value, the sequence is stuck in a loop and the PIN fails.
s1_definition.oneliner: Square-and-sum the digits repeatedly; using fast and slow, reaching 1 means happy, meeting elsewhere means an unhappy cycle.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A happy number is one that eventually reaches 1 when you repeatedly replace it with the sum of the squares of its digits; if instead the process loops forever without reaching 1, the number is unhappy. Treating the sequence of transformed values as a virtual linked list, Floyd's fast and slow pointers detect whether it cycles: if the fast pointer reaches 1 the number is happy, and if slow and fast meet elsewhere there is a cycle and it is unhappy. It runs in O(log n) style iterations with O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India validates a customer PIN rule where repeatedly squaring and summing digits should collapse to 1. Rajesh runs the transformation twice as fast with one pointer and once with another; if the fast one lands on 1 the PIN satisfies the rule, but if the two ever meet on the same non-one value, the sequence is stuck in a loop and the PIN fails.

**One line to remember:** Square-and-sum the digits repeatedly; using fast and slow, reaching 1 means happy, meeting elsewhere means an unhappy cycle.

sections.s2_technical:
The transformation `next(n)` sums the squares of the decimal digits: for each digit `d`, add `d*d`, using `n % 10` to get the last digit and `n / 10` to drop it. For example `next(19)` is 1 squared plus 9 squared equals 82. The sequence of repeated `next` values behaves like a linked list where each value points to its successor, and an unhappy number produces a cycle that never includes 1.

Apply Floyd: `slow = next(slow)` once and `fast = next(next(fast))` twice per iteration, looping until `fast == 1` or `slow == fast`. A code snippet: `boolean isHappy(int n) { int slow = n, fast = next(n); while (fast != 1 && slow != fast) { slow = next(slow); fast = next(next(fast)); } return fast == 1; }` with `int next(int x) { int s = 0; while (x > 0) { int d = x % 10; s += d * d; x /= 10; } return s; }`.

Using fast and slow instead of a hash set of seen values keeps the space constant. Both approaches are correct: the set records every value until a repeat or 1 appears, while Floyd needs only two running values. Because the digit-square sum of any number quickly falls into a bounded range (for typical inputs the values stay small), the number of iterations is small.

A senior nuance is why this maps to cycle detection at all: the `next` function is deterministic, so from any starting value the trajectory is a fixed path that either terminates at 1 (which maps to itself since `next(1)` is 1) or enters a repeating loop. That determinism is exactly the linked-list-successor property Floyd requires. The known unhappy cycle famously passes through 4, so an alternative is to check for 4, but Floyd is the general cycle-based answer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India enforces a playful PIN-strength rule: a candidate numeric code is accepted only if its digit-square-sum sequence collapses to 1, otherwise it is rejected as looping. This is exactly how the Happy Number check works — detect whether the deterministic sequence reaches 1 or cycles.

Problem 2 — The check must use constant memory because it runs inline during code validation, so Floyd's fast/slow is used rather than storing a set of seen values.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the happy code 19 and the unhappy code 20.

Step 1: For 19, slow starts at 19 and fast starts at next(19) which is 1 squared plus 9 squared equals 82. They differ and fast is not 1, so continue.

Step 2: slow becomes next(19) equals 82; fast becomes next(next(82)). next(82) is 64 plus 4 equals 68, and next(68) is 36 plus 64 equals 100. So fast is 100. Different, continue.

Step 3: slow becomes next(82) equals 68; fast becomes next(next(100)). next(100) is 1, and next(1) is 1, so fast is 1. The loop condition fast not equal to 1 fails, so the loop stops.

Step 4: Since fast equals 1, the method returns true: 19 is happy and the code is accepted.

Step 5: For 20, the sequence enters the well-known cycle that passes through 4, 16, 37, 58, 89, 145, 42, 20 and never reaches 1. The fast pointer eventually meets the slow pointer on a value in that loop, so the loop ends with fast not equal to 1 and the method returns false, rejecting the code.

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Code 19 accepted? true
2026-10-26 21:00:03 WARNING Code 20 loops (unhappy)
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Code 20 accepted? false
```

```
    ▼
  slow==fast in loop, fast≠1 → happy=false
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A happy number is one that reaches 1 when I repeatedly replace it with the sum of the squares of its digits, and an unhappy number instead falls into an endless loop. The clever framing is that the sequence of transformed values behaves exactly like a linked list, because the transformation is deterministic so each value points to a single successor, which means I can detect a loop with Floyd's fast and slow pointers. I advance the slow value by one transformation and the fast value by two each iteration, stopping when the fast value becomes 1, which means happy, or when the two values meet somewhere else, which means an unhappy cycle.

The transformation itself just walks the digits with modulo ten and integer division, squaring each digit and summing. The number 1 maps to itself, which is the terminating fixed point, and any unhappy number eventually enters a repeating loop that never contains 1.

The reason I prefer fast and slow over a hash set of seen values is constant memory. The set approach is equally correct and records every value until it sees a repeat or reaches 1, but Floyd needs only two running values. Because the digit-square sum quickly collapses into a small bounded range, the number of iterations is small regardless.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a playful PIN-strength rule in the security service, where a candidate numeric code was accepted only if its digit-square-sum sequence collapsed to 1 and rejected if it looped. Because the check ran inline during code validation, the constant-space fast and slow approach fit better than storing a set of seen values. Explaining the deterministic-successor insight that makes it a cycle problem, the fast-and-slow mechanics, and the memory advantage shows the interviewer I can recognize a hidden linked-list structure in a numeric problem.

answers.question: Find the Duplicate Number — Floyd's on index→value mapping.
answers.shortTitle: Find the Duplicate Number — Floyd's on Index-to-Value Mapping

s1_definition.profdef: Given an array of n+1 integers where every value is between 1 and n, exactly one value is duplicated, and the task is to find it without modifying the array and using constant extra space. Treating each value as a pointer to the next index forms a linked list with a cycle whose entry is the duplicate, so Floyd's two-phase cycle detection finds it in O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a list of branch codes where one code was accidentally entered twice, and the array is read-only. Rajesh treats each slot's value as an arrow pointing to another slot; because the duplicate makes two arrows land on the same slot, the arrows form a loop, and the slot where the loop begins is the repeated code.
s1_definition.oneliner: Follow values as next-index pointers; the duplicate creates a cycle, and Floyd's algorithm finds the cycle's entry, which is the duplicate.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Given an array of n+1 integers where every value is between 1 and n, exactly one value is duplicated, and the task is to find it without modifying the array and using constant extra space. Treating each value as a pointer to the next index forms a linked list with a cycle whose entry is the duplicate, so Floyd's two-phase cycle detection finds it in O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a list of branch codes where one code was accidentally entered twice, and the array is read-only. Rajesh treats each slot's value as an arrow pointing to another slot; because the duplicate makes two arrows land on the same slot, the arrows form a loop, and the slot where the loop begins is the repeated code.

**One line to remember:** Follow values as next-index pointers; the duplicate creates a cycle, and Floyd's algorithm finds the cycle's entry, which is the duplicate.

sections.s2_technical:
Define the successor of position `i` as `a[i]`, so moving from index `i` goes to index `a[i]`. Since every value is in the range 1 to n and there are n+1 slots, this mapping always stays within bounds and, because one value repeats, two different indices point to the same next index, which forms a cycle. The entry node of that cycle is the duplicated value.

Phase one runs Floyd starting from index 0: `slow = a[slow]` once and `fast = a[a[fast]]` twice until they meet. Phase two resets one pointer to 0 and advances both by one step (`slow = a[slow]`, `finder = a[finder]`) until they meet; the meeting index is the duplicate. A code snippet: `int findDup(int[] a) { int slow = a[0], fast = a[a[0]]; while (slow != fast) { slow = a[slow]; fast = a[a[fast]]; } int f = 0; while (f != slow) { f = a[f]; slow = a[slow]; } return f; }`.

The reason the cycle entry equals the duplicate is the same algebra as Linked List Cycle II: the distance equality from the two-to-one speed ratio makes the second phase converge exactly at the loop entry, and here that entry is the value two indices point into, which is the repeated number. The array is never modified and only two integer pointers are used.

A senior nuance is why obvious alternatives are rejected: sorting modifies the array or needs a copy, a hash set uses linear space, and the clever negation trick mutates the input. The Floyd mapping is the unique approach that satisfies both the read-only and constant-space constraints. It requires that values are in 1 to n so that no value equals an index you start outside of; starting slow at `a[0]` avoids the self-loop at index 0.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India loads a read-only array of branch routing codes in which exactly one code was duplicated by a data-entry error, and the validation service must identify the repeated code without altering the array and without extra memory. This is exactly how Find the Duplicate works — the duplicate is the cycle entry in the index-to-value mapping.

Problem 2 — The array is shared and immutable in this path, so sorting, a hash set, or the negation trick are all disallowed, leaving Floyd's mapping as the correct method.

The code shows a `RoutingCodeValidator` with `findDuplicate`, a demo on a routing-code array with one repeat, and the duplicate value.

Step 3: Phase two begins. finder starts at 0 while slow stays at 2. Both advance one step. finder becomes a[0] equals 1; slow becomes a[2] equals 4. Different.

Step 5: The convergence value 3 is the duplicate, exactly the code that was entered twice. The array was never modified and only integer pointers were used. The method returns 3.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Find the Duplicate Number gives me an array of n plus one integers whose values all lie between 1 and n, with exactly one value repeated, and asks me to find that value without modifying the array and in constant space. The key trick is to treat each value as a pointer to the next index, so moving from a position goes to the position named by its value. Because there are more slots than distinct values and one value repeats, two different positions point to the same next index, which forms a cycle, and the entry node of that cycle is the duplicated value.

That reframing lets me use Floyd's two-phase cycle detection. In phase one I advance a slow pointer by one hop and a fast pointer by two hops through this value-as-index mapping until they meet. In phase two I reset one pointer to the start and advance both by a single hop until they meet again, and the position where they converge is the duplicate. The correctness is the same distance equality as Linked List Cycle II, falling out of the two-to-one speed ratio.

The reason I reach for this specific method is the pair of constraints. Sorting would modify the array or need a copy, a hash set would use linear extra memory, and the negation trick mutates the input, so all three are disallowed when the array must stay read-only and memory must be constant. Floyd's mapping is the one approach that satisfies both, and starting the slow pointer at the first value rather than at index zero avoids the self-loop at position zero.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the routing-code validation service. A read-only array of branch routing codes had exactly one code duplicated by a data-entry error, and the service had to identify it without altering the shared array and without extra memory, which ruled out sorting, a hash set, and in-place marking. Explaining the value-as-pointer reframing, the two-phase Floyd detection, and why the constraints force this method shows the interviewer I can see a hidden cycle-detection problem inside an array question.

answers.question: Reverse a linked list — iterative (prev/curr/next) and recursive.
answers.shortTitle: Reverse a Linked List — Iterative (prev/curr/next) and Recursive

s1_definition.profdef: Reversing a singly linked list makes the last node the new head and flips every next pointer to point backward. The iterative method walks the list with three references, previous, current, and next, rewiring each node's link as it goes, in O(n) time and O(1) space. The recursive method reverses the rest of the list first and then fixes the current node's link, in O(n) time and O(n) stack space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India stores a chain of transactions oldest-to-newest and wants to display it newest-to-oldest. Rajesh walks the chain and flips each arrow to point to the node he just came from, keeping a note of the previous node, the current node, and the next node so he never loses the rest of the chain while flipping.
s1_definition.oneliner: Flip each next pointer to the previous node, tracking previous, current, and next so the remaining list is never lost.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reversing a singly linked list makes the last node the new head and flips every next pointer to point backward. The iterative method walks the list with three references, previous, current, and next, rewiring each node's link as it goes, in O(n) time and O(1) space. The recursive method reverses the rest of the list first and then fixes the current node's link, in O(n) time and O(n) stack space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India stores a chain of transactions oldest-to-newest and wants to display it newest-to-oldest. Rajesh walks the chain and flips each arrow to point to the node he just came from, keeping a note of the previous node, the current node, and the next node so he never loses the rest of the chain while flipping.

**One line to remember:** Flip each next pointer to the previous node, tracking previous, current, and next so the remaining list is never lost.

sections.s2_technical:
The iterative approach uses three references. Start `prev = null` and `curr = head`. In a loop while `curr != null`: save `next = curr.next`, set `curr.next = prev` to flip the link, then advance `prev = curr` and `curr = next`. When the loop ends, `prev` is the new head. Saving `next` before flipping is essential, because once `curr.next` is overwritten the rest of the list would be unreachable otherwise.

A code snippet on a transaction list: `Node reverse(Node head) { Node prev = null, curr = head; while (curr != null) { Node next = curr.next; curr.next = prev; prev = curr; curr = next; } return prev; }`. Each node is visited once and only pointers change, so it is linear time and constant space.

The recursive approach reverses from the tail. If the list is empty or a single node, return it. Otherwise recurse on `head.next` to reverse the remainder, which returns the new head; then set `head.next.next = head` to make the next node point back to the current one, and set `head.next = null` to terminate. A code snippet: `Node reverseRec(Node head) { if (head == null || head.next == null) return head; Node newHead = reverseRec(head.next); head.next.next = head; head.next = null; return newHead; }`.

The two differ in space. The iterative version uses constant extra memory, while the recursive version uses stack frames proportional to the list length, which can overflow on very long lists. A senior nuance is that the recursive rewiring line `head.next.next = head` is the crux: after the rest is reversed, the original successor of the current node must point back to it. Interviewers often ask for both, and the iterative one is preferred in production precisely because it avoids deep recursion on large lists.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps a customer's transaction chain in chronological order but the statement view must show newest first, so the service reverses the linked list. This is exactly how linked-list reversal works — every next pointer is flipped so traversal runs the other way.

Problem 2 — Statements can be long, so the production path uses the iterative constant-space reversal to avoid deep recursion, while the recursive version is kept for clarity and small lists.

Input: the transaction list T1, T2, T3, T4.

Step 1: Iterative. prev is null, curr is T1. Save next as T2, flip T1's next to null, advance prev to T1 and curr to T2. The reversed part so far is just T1 pointing to null.

Step 2: Save next as T3, flip T2's next to T1, advance prev to T2 and curr to T3. The reversed part is T2 pointing to T1.

Step 3: Save next as T4, flip T3's next to T2, advance prev to T3 and curr to T4. Then save next as null, flip T4's next to T3, advance prev to T4 and curr to null. The loop ends and prev is T4, the new head. The list reads T4, T3, T2, T1.

Step 4: Recursive on a fresh T1 to T4. The calls descend until the base case returns T4 as the new head. Unwinding, T3's successor T4 is made to point back to T3, then T3's forward link is nulled; similarly T2 and T1 are rewired on the way back up.

Step 5: Both methods produce the same reversed chain T4 to T1, shown as the newest-first statement order.

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Recursive reversed: T4 -> T3 -> T2 -> T1
```
