sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Search II asks for every dictionary word that can be traced through adjacent cells of a grid, each cell used at most once per word. The naive approach runs a separate grid search for each word, which repeats enormous amounts of work. My efficient solution builds one Trie from all the words so their shared prefixes are tested together, then sweeps the grid a single time with a depth-first backtracking search that walks a Trie pointer in lock-step with the grid path.

Before stepping into a cell, I check whether its character is a child of the current Trie node, and if not I abandon the path immediately. This pruning is the whole reason the single-Trie approach wins: any prefix that no dictionary word shares is cut off at once. When the Trie pointer reaches a node whose stored word field is set, I collect that word and clear the field so the same word is not reported twice. I mark the cell visited before recursing into its four neighbors and restore it on the way back so other paths can reuse it, which is the backtracking.

The details interviewers look for are sharing one Trie across all words rather than one per word, storing the full word string on the terminal node for constant-time collection, and the correct mark-and-restore to enforce the use-each-cell-once rule per path. The worst-case cost is the number of cells times four to the power of the longest word length, but pruning makes the practical cost far smaller.

In my project at National Bank of India, I applied this to a fraud-pattern grid where flagged activity is encoded as a character matrix and compliance keeps a watchlist of coded patterns. Building one Trie from the whole watchlist let me find every embedded pattern in a single sweep, and the prefix pruning meant dead starting cells were discarded instantly rather than driving a full search per watchlist entry.

answers.question: Given a dictionary of root words and a sentence, replace every word in the sentence that has a root in the dictionary as a prefix with the shortest such root. Return the resulting sentence.
answers.shortTitle: Replace Words — Trie for shortest prefix (root) replacement

s1_definition.profdef: Replace Words inserts every root into a Trie, then for each word in the sentence walks the Trie character by character and replaces the word with the first root encountered, which is the shortest matching prefix. If no root prefixes the word, the word is left unchanged.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the bank normalizing long product names to their shortest official code. You keep a directory of official short codes, and whenever a customer types a long product name, you walk the name letter by letter against the directory and the moment you complete an official code you stop and swap the long name for that short code. If you never complete any official code, you keep the name as-is.
s1_definition.oneliner: Insert roots into a Trie, then for each sentence word walk the Trie and replace it with the first (shortest) root hit, else leave it unchanged.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Replace Words inserts every root into a Trie, then for each word in the sentence walks the Trie character by character and replaces the word with the first root encountered, which is the shortest matching prefix. If no root prefixes the word, the word is left unchanged.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the bank normalizing long product names to their shortest official code. You keep a directory of official short codes, and whenever a customer types a long product name, you walk the name letter by letter against the directory and the moment you complete an official code you stop and swap the long name for that short code. If you never complete any official code, you keep the name as-is.

**One line to remember:** Insert roots into a Trie, then for each sentence word walk the Trie and replace it with the first (shortest) root hit, else leave it unchanged.

sections.s2_technical:
Insert every root into a Trie with an end-of-word flag so that reaching a flagged node means a complete root has been matched. For example: mark `node.isWord = true;` at the end of each root insert.

For each word in the sentence, walk the Trie from the root following the word's characters. The moment the walk reaches a node whose end-of-word flag is set, stop and use the prefix walked so far as the replacement, because the first flagged node encountered is necessarily the shortest root that prefixes the word. For example: `if (node.isWord) return prefixSoFar;`.

If the walk falls off the Trie, meaning a character has no child, or reaches the end of the word without ever hitting a flagged node, the original word is kept unchanged. The replacement is applied per word and the words are rejoined with spaces.

The time cost is the total number of characters across all sentence words, since each character is examined at most once during its word's walk, plus the cost of building the Trie from the roots. A senior nuance is that stopping at the first flagged node guarantees the shortest root without sorting roots by length, and that a word is only replaced when a full root is matched, not merely when characters happen to line up.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Replace Words asks me to swap each word of a sentence for the shortest dictionary root that prefixes it, leaving words with no matching root untouched. My solution inserts every root into a Trie with an end-of-word flag, then processes each sentence word by walking the Trie character by character.

The key insight is that the first flagged node I encounter while walking is automatically the shortest root, because flagged nodes appear in increasing prefix length along a path. So the moment the walk reaches an end-of-word node, I stop and return the prefix walked so far as the replacement, without needing to sort roots by length or examine the rest of the word. If the walk falls off the Trie because a character has no child, or if it reaches the end of the word without hitting any flagged node, I keep the original word.

What interviewers check is that I stop at the first root rather than the longest, that I only replace on a genuine end-of-word match rather than on partial character alignment, and that the overall cost is linear in the total characters of the sentence plus the Trie build. This is cleaner and faster than comparing each word against every root.

In my project at National Bank of India, I used this to normalize free-text product descriptions to their shortest official root code before feeding analytics. Each descriptive word was walked against a Trie of official roots and collapsed to the first root it completed, so savings became sav and loanaccount became loan, while words with no official root, like current, passed through unchanged. Stopping at the first root kept normalization fast even over long descriptions and a large root dictionary.

answers.question: Given an unsorted array of integers and a value K, return the Kth largest element (by value, not the Kth distinct element).
answers.shortTitle: Kth Largest Element in an Array — min-heap of size K or QuickSelect

s1_definition.profdef: Two efficient techniques solve this. A min-heap of size K keeps only the K largest elements seen so far, so its smallest element, the heap root, is the Kth largest overall after one pass. QuickSelect partitions the array around a pivot like quicksort but recurses into only the side containing the target rank, giving average linear time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine finding the tenth-largest deposit of the day. The heap approach keeps a shortlist of exactly the ten biggest deposits seen so far; whenever a bigger deposit arrives, it bumps out the smallest on the shortlist, and at the end the smallest on that shortlist is the tenth-largest. QuickSelect instead picks a sample deposit, splits the rest into bigger and smaller piles, and keeps narrowing to the pile that must contain the rank you want.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a size-K min-heap whose root is the Kth largest (O(n log K)), or use QuickSelect to partition toward the target rank in average O(n).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Two efficient techniques solve this. A min-heap of size K keeps only the K largest elements seen so far, so its smallest element, the heap root, is the Kth largest overall after one pass. QuickSelect partitions the array around a pivot like quicksort but recurses into only the side containing the target rank, giving average linear time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine finding the tenth-largest deposit of the day. The heap approach keeps a shortlist of exactly the ten biggest deposits seen so far; whenever a bigger deposit arrives, it bumps out the smallest on the shortlist, and at the end the smallest on that shortlist is the tenth-largest. QuickSelect instead picks a sample deposit, splits the rest into bigger and smaller piles, and keeps narrowing to the pile that must contain the rank you want.

**One line to remember:** Keep a size-K min-heap whose root is the Kth largest (O(n log K)), or use QuickSelect to partition toward the target rank in average O(n).

sections.s2_technical:
The min-heap approach pushes each element and, whenever the heap size exceeds K, removes the smallest. This keeps exactly the K largest elements, so the root is the Kth largest. For example: `heap.offer(x); if (heap.size() > K) heap.poll();` then `return heap.peek();`. The time is n log K and the extra space is K.

QuickSelect treats the problem as finding the element at index n minus K in sorted order. It chooses a pivot, partitions the array so smaller elements go left and larger go right, and checks where the pivot landed. For example: `int p = partition(a, lo, hi);` then compare `p` with the target index.

If the pivot index equals the target, that element is the answer. If the target is to the left, recurse left; otherwise recurse right. Because only one side is explored, the average cost is linear, though a bad pivot sequence can degrade to quadratic, which randomized pivoting mitigates. For example: swap a random index into the pivot position before partitioning.

A senior nuance is the trade-off: the heap is simple, stable in worst case at n log K, and ideal for streaming because it processes elements one at a time, while QuickSelect is faster on average at linear time but mutates the array and has a quadratic worst case unless the pivot is randomized. The choice depends on whether data arrives as a stream and whether in-place mutation is acceptable.

Problem 2 — Amounts arrive continuously during the day, so a streaming-friendly method that holds only K values is preferred over sorting everything. This is exactly why the size-K min-heap is used here, with QuickSelect noted as the in-memory alternative.

The input amounts are 5000, 12000, 800, 25000, 3000, 17500, 9000 with K equal to three.

Step 1: The heap method pushes 5000, 12000, 800, filling a heap of size three with those values.

Step 2: It pushes 25000, size becomes four, so it removes the smallest which is 800, leaving 5000, 12000, 25000.

Step 3: It pushes 3000, removes the new smallest 3000, so the heap still holds 5000, 12000, 25000.

Step 4: It pushes 17500, removes 5000, leaving 12000, 17500, 25000. It pushes 9000, removes 9000, leaving 12000, 17500, 25000. The root is 12000, the third largest.

Step 5: QuickSelect targets index seven minus three equals four in ascending order. Sorted, the array is 800, 3000, 5000, 9000, 12000, 17500, 25000, and index four is 12000.

Step 6: QuickSelect partitions around random pivots, recursing only into the side holding index four, and returns 12000 without fully sorting. Both methods agree on 12000.

Finding the Kth largest element has two strong solutions, and I pick between them based on context. The size-K min-heap keeps only the K largest elements seen so far: I push each element and, whenever the heap grows past K, I remove the smallest. After one pass the heap root is the Kth largest, because exactly the K biggest values remain and the root is the smallest of those. This runs in n log K time with K extra space and is ideal when data arrives as a stream, since it consumes elements one at a time.

QuickSelect is the in-memory alternative and is faster on average. I reframe the question as finding the element at index n minus K in ascending sorted order, then partition the array around a pivot like quicksort but recurse into only the side that contains that target index. Because I discard one side each step, the average cost is linear. The catch is a bad pivot sequence can degrade to quadratic, so I randomize the pivot to make that practically impossible.

The trade-off is what interviewers want: the heap is simple, worst-case n log K, streaming-friendly, and leaves the input untouched; QuickSelect is average linear but mutates the array and needs randomization to avoid the quadratic worst case. Stating that trade-off clearly is the senior signal.

In my project at National Bank of India, the risk desk set a daily alert threshold from the Kth largest transaction amount. Because amounts streamed in all day, I used the size-K min-heap so the system held only K values at any moment and produced the threshold in a single pass, keeping QuickSelect as the option for batch recomputation over a finished day's data held fully in memory.

Then either you keep a shortlist of the three highest tallies, swapping out the smallest whenever a higher one appears, or you drop each type into a bucket labelled by its count and read the buckets from the high-count end until you have three.
s1_definition.oneliner: Tally frequencies in a HashMap, then take the top K with a size-K min-heap (O(n log K)) or with frequency-indexed bucket sort (O(n)).

**Professional definition:** Count each element's frequency in a HashMap, then select the top K either with a size-K min-heap ordered by frequency, giving n log K time, or with bucket sort where buckets are indexed by frequency, giving linear time. The bucket approach exploits that frequencies range only from one to n.

Then either you keep a shortlist of the three highest tallies, swapping out the smallest whenever a higher one appears, or you drop each type into a bucket labelled by its count and read the buckets from the high-count end until you have three.

sections.s2_technical:
First build a frequency map from element to its count in one pass. For example: `freq.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum);`. This costs linear time and holds one entry per distinct element.

The heap approach maintains a min-heap of size K ordered by frequency. It offers each distinct element and, when the heap exceeds K, removes the least frequent, so the K most frequent remain. For example: `heap.offer(entry); if (heap.size() > K) heap.poll();` with a comparator on count. This costs n log K.

The bucket approach creates an array of buckets indexed from zero to n, placing each element into the bucket equal to its frequency, then scans buckets from the highest index downward collecting elements until K are gathered. For example: `buckets[freq.get(x)].add(x);` then iterate from the top. Because a frequency can be at most n, the bucket array is bounded and the whole method is linear.

A senior nuance is choosing bucket sort when K is large or linear time matters, since it beats the heap's log factor, while the heap is preferable when K is small relative to the number of distinct elements or when memory for n buckets is undesirable. Both begin with the same frequency map; they differ only in the selection step.

The input is ten transaction types and K equal to two.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Top K Frequent Elements always starts with one linear pass to build a frequency map from each element to its count. The only decision is how to select the K highest counts from that map, and I know two methods.

The min-heap method keeps a heap of size K ordered by frequency: I offer each distinct element and, when the heap exceeds K, I remove the least frequent, so the K most frequent survive. This costs n log K and is best when K is small compared to the number of distinct elements. The bucket-sort method exploits the fact that a frequency can be at most n, so I create n plus one buckets indexed by frequency, drop each element into the bucket matching its count, and scan from the highest-count bucket downward collecting elements until I have K. That is linear time, with no log factor, which is why I prefer it when K is large or latency matters.

The insight interviewers reward is recognizing that frequencies are bounded by n, which is exactly what makes bucket sort linear and lets it beat the heap. Both share the identical first step and differ only in selection, so I describe the trade-off rather than treating one as universally correct.

In my project at National Bank of India, the operations dashboard displayed the K most frequent transaction types for the day. Because daily volume was large and the dashboard had to refresh quickly, I used bucket sort for linear selection, keeping the min-heap as the fallback when K was tiny relative to the handful of distinct types, so the tiles updated without a sorting bottleneck.

answers.question: Given K sorted linked lists, merge them into one sorted linked list and return its head.
answers.shortTitle: Merge K Sorted Lists — min-heap of K heads

s1_definition.profdef: Merge K Sorted Lists uses a min-heap holding the current head node of each list. Repeatedly extract the smallest head, append it to the output, and push that node's successor. Because the heap always surfaces the global minimum among the fronts, the output is produced in sorted order in n log K time, where n is the total node count.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine K sorted queues of pending settlements, each already ordered by time. To merge them into one master-ordered stream, you look only at the front of each queue, pick the earliest, move it to the master list, and advance that queue by one. A small priority board of K fronts tells you instantly which queue currently has the earliest item.
s1_definition.oneliner: Put the K list heads in a min-heap; repeatedly pop the smallest, append it, and push its next, giving a sorted merge in O(n log K).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Merge K Sorted Lists uses a min-heap holding the current head node of each list. Repeatedly extract the smallest head, append it to the output, and push that node's successor. Because the heap always surfaces the global minimum among the fronts, the output is produced in sorted order in n log K time, where n is the total node count.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine K sorted queues of pending settlements, each already ordered by time. To merge them into one master-ordered stream, you look only at the front of each queue, pick the earliest, move it to the master list, and advance that queue by one. A small priority board of K fronts tells you instantly which queue currently has the earliest item.

**One line to remember:** Put the K list heads in a min-heap; repeatedly pop the smallest, append it, and push its next, giving a sorted merge in O(n log K).

sections.s2_technical:
Seed a min-heap with the head of every non-empty list, ordered by node value. For example: `for (ListNode l : lists) if (l != null) heap.offer(l);`. The heap size never exceeds K.

Repeatedly poll the smallest node, append it to the tail of the result list, and if that node has a successor, push the successor into the heap. For example: `ListNode n = heap.poll(); tail.next = n; tail = n; if (n.next != null) heap.offer(n.next);`.

Continue until the heap is empty, at which point every node has been appended exactly once in nondecreasing order. A dummy head node simplifies appending by avoiding a special case for the first element. The total work is one heap push and pop per node, each costing log K, so the overall time is n log K and the extra space is K for the heap.

A senior nuance is that this beats the alternative of concatenating all lists and sorting, which is n log n, because the merge exploits the fact that each list is already sorted and only ever compares K fronts. An equally good alternative is pairwise divide-and-conquer merging, also n log K, which avoids a heap but uses recursion; the heap version is often clearer and naturally streaming.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, settlement events arrive from K regional systems, each stream already sorted by timestamp. The clearing engine must merge them into one globally time-ordered stream. This is exactly how Merge K Sorted Lists works — it merges pre-sorted streams by always taking the earliest front.

Problem 2 — The streams are long and must be merged without first sorting everything together. This is exactly why the min-heap of K heads is used, keeping only K fronts in memory at a time.

The mini-project builds a `SettlementMerger` with a `ListNode` and the heap merge, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo over three sorted streams.

The input is three sorted streams: A with 100, 400, 700; B with 200, 500, 800; C with 150, 300, 900.

Step 1: The heap is seeded with the three heads 100, 200, 150. The smallest is 100 from A, which is appended and A advances to 400, pushed into the heap.

Step 4: The heap holds 400, 500, 300. The smallest is 300 from C, appended, C advances to 900.

Step 5: Continuing, the merge emits 400 from A, then 500 from B, then 700 from A, then 800 from B, then 900 from C, each time taking the earliest front and advancing that stream.

Step 6: When all streams are exhausted and the heap empties, the merged order is 100, 150, 200, 300, 400, 500, 700, 800, 900, globally sorted.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Merge K Sorted Lists asks me to combine K already-sorted lists into one sorted list. The naive idea of concatenating everything and sorting ignores that each list is already ordered and costs n log n. My efficient solution uses a min-heap holding the current head of each list, which lets me always find the global minimum among just the K fronts.

I seed the heap with every non-empty list head, then repeatedly poll the smallest node, append it to the output tail, and push that node's successor if it exists. Because the heap always surfaces the earliest front across all lists, the output comes out in sorted order. Each node is pushed and popped exactly once, each operation costing log K, so the total is n log K time with K extra space, and a dummy head node removes the special case for appending the first element.

The reason this beats sort-everything is that it compares only K fronts at a time rather than reordering all n elements, exploiting the per-list sorted property. I mention the equally efficient pairwise divide-and-conquer merge as an alternative with the same n log K bound, choosing the heap version because it is clear and naturally streaming.

In my project at National Bank of India, settlement events arrived from several regional systems, each stream already sorted by timestamp, and the clearing engine had to merge them into one globally time-ordered stream. The min-heap of K heads merged the long streams while holding only K fronts in memory, producing the master order in a single pass without ever sorting the combined volume from scratch.

answers.question: Design a data structure that supports adding integers from a stream and returning the median of all values added so far, in logarithmic add time and constant median time.
answers.shortTitle: Find Median from Data Stream — two heaps (max-heap lower + min-heap upper)

s1_definition.profdef: Two balanced heaps split the stream in half: a max-heap holds the lower half so its top is the largest of the small values, and a min-heap holds the upper half so its top is the smallest of the large values. The heaps are kept balanced in size, so the median is either the max-heap top (odd count) or the average of both tops (even count).
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine tracking the median transaction amount as amounts stream in all day. You keep two piles: a low pile ordered so the biggest low value sits on top, and a high pile ordered so the smallest high value sits on top. You keep the piles nearly equal in height, so the median is right at the boundary — either the top of the bigger pile or the average of the two tops.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, balanced in size; the median is the larger heap's top or the average of both tops.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Two balanced heaps split the stream in half: a max-heap holds the lower half so its top is the largest of the small values, and a min-heap holds the upper half so its top is the smallest of the large values. The heaps are kept balanced in size, so the median is either the max-heap top (odd count) or the average of both tops (even count).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine tracking the median transaction amount as amounts stream in all day. You keep two piles: a low pile ordered so the biggest low value sits on top, and a high pile ordered so the smallest high value sits on top. You keep the piles nearly equal in height, so the median is right at the boundary — either the top of the bigger pile or the average of the two tops.

**One line to remember:** Keep a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, balanced in size; the median is the larger heap's top or the average of both tops.

sections.s2_technical:
Maintain a max-heap called low and a min-heap called high. On each add, push to low first, then move low's top to high to ensure every element in low is no larger than every element in high. For example: `low.offer(x); high.offer(low.poll());`.

Rebalance so the heaps differ in size by at most one, keeping low at least as large as high. If high grows larger than low, move high's top back to low. For example: `if (high.size() > low.size()) low.offer(high.poll());`. This ordering and balancing are the invariants that place the median at the boundary.

To read the median, if the total count is odd then low holds one extra element and its top is the median; if even, the median is the average of low's top and high's top. For example: `return low.size() > high.size() ? low.peek() : (low.peek() + high.peek()) / 2.0;`.

Each add does a constant number of heap operations, each log n, so add is log n and median read is constant. A senior nuance is the push-then-shift pattern that guarantees correct partitioning without comparing against both tops manually, and choosing which heap holds the extra element consistently so the odd-count median is unambiguous. Integer overflow in the average should be handled with care for large values.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a monitoring service reports the running median transaction amount as amounts stream in, to detect drift from normal behavior. The system must add amounts and query the median efficiently at any time. This is exactly how Find Median from Data Stream works — two heaps maintain the median incrementally.

Problem 2 — Sorting the whole history on every query would be far too slow for a live stream. This is exactly why two balanced heaps are used, giving logarithmic add and constant median.

The mini-project builds a `RunningMedian` service over the two heaps, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo that streams amounts and prints the median after each.

sections.s5_journey:
The input stream is 5000, 3000, 8000, 1000, 10000.

Step 1: Add 5000. It goes into low then shifts to high, then rebalances back into low. Low holds 5000, high empty. Count one is odd, median is 5000.

Step 2: Add 3000. Pushed to low then its top 5000 shifts to high, leaving low with 3000 and high with 5000. Count two is even, median is the average of 3000 and 5000, which is 4000.

Step 3: Add 8000. Pushed to low, low's top shifts to high, then rebalance returns the smaller to low. Low holds 5000, high holds 8000, and low has the extra, so median is 5000.

Step 4: Add 1000. After the push-shift-rebalance, low holds 1000 and 3000 wait — low holds the lower two and high the upper two, count four is even, median is the average of the two boundary tops, which is 4000.

Step 5: Add 10000. Count five is odd, the heaps settle with low holding the extra element and its top being 5000, so the median is 5000.

Step 6: Throughout, each add did only a few heap operations and the median was read from the tops in constant time.

```text
         top = largest low      |   top = smallest high
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Find Median from Data Stream asks for the running median with fast adds and instant median reads, which rules out re-sorting the history each query. My solution keeps two heaps that split the data at the median: a max-heap for the lower half, so its top is the largest small value, and a min-heap for the upper half, so its top is the smallest large value.

On each add I push the new value into the low heap, then move low's top into the high heap, which guarantees every element in low is no larger than every element in high. Then I rebalance so the two heaps differ in size by at most one, keeping low at least as large, by moving high's top back if high ever grows bigger. These invariants place the median exactly at the boundary: with an odd count low holds the extra element and its top is the median, and with an even count the median is the average of the two tops.

The detail interviewers listen for is the push-then-shift pattern, which partitions correctly without manually comparing against both tops, plus consistently choosing which heap carries the extra element so the odd-count median is unambiguous, and being careful with overflow when averaging large values. Each add is a constant number of log n heap operations and the median read is constant.

In my project at National Bank of India, a monitoring service reported the running median transaction amount as amounts streamed in all day, to catch drift from normal behavior. The two-heap structure let every amount be absorbed in logarithmic time and the median be read instantly on each tick, so the monitor stayed real-time instead of re-sorting the growing history on every query.

answers.question: Design a class that is initialized with a value K and an initial list of numbers, and supports an add operation that inserts a new number and returns the Kth largest element among all numbers seen so far.
answers.shortTitle: Kth Largest in a Stream — maintain a min-heap of size K

s1_definition.profdef: Kth Largest in a Stream keeps a min-heap of size K holding the K largest values seen so far. On add, push the new value and, if the heap exceeds K, remove the smallest; the heap root is then always the Kth largest. Each add costs log K and the query is the root in constant time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine always knowing the fifth-largest donation received so far as donations keep arriving. You keep a shortlist of exactly the five biggest. When a new donation comes, you add it to the shortlist and, if the list grew to six, you drop the smallest. The smallest on that shortlist of five is always the fifth-largest overall.
s1_definition.oneliner: A size-K min-heap holds the K largest so far; each add pushes then trims to K, and the root is the Kth largest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kth Largest in a Stream keeps a min-heap of size K holding the K largest values seen so far. On add, push the new value and, if the heap exceeds K, remove the smallest; the heap root is then always the Kth largest. Each add costs log K and the query is the root in constant time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine always knowing the fifth-largest donation received so far as donations keep arriving. You keep a shortlist of exactly the five biggest. When a new donation comes, you add it to the shortlist and, if the list grew to six, you drop the smallest. The smallest on that shortlist of five is always the fifth-largest overall.

**One line to remember:** A size-K min-heap holds the K largest so far; each add pushes then trims to K, and the root is the Kth largest.

sections.s2_technical:
The constructor builds a min-heap and feeds the initial numbers through the same add logic so the heap ends holding at most the K largest. For example: `for (int n : nums) add(n);`.

The add operation pushes the new value, then if the heap size exceeds K it removes the smallest element, keeping exactly the K largest values. For example: `heap.offer(val); if (heap.size() > K) heap.poll();`. After this the root is the smallest of the K largest, which is the Kth largest overall.

Returning the answer is simply reading the heap root, a constant-time peek. For example: `return heap.peek();`. The heap never holds more than K elements, so memory is bounded by K regardless of how many values stream in.

Each add is a single push and possibly a single poll, each log K, so the per-add cost is log K, far cheaper than re-sorting. A senior nuance is that when fewer than K values have been seen, the heap simply holds all of them and its root is still the correct answer for the current count, and that this structure is the canonical way to answer a repeated Kth-largest query on a growing stream without unbounded memory.

The input seeds K equal to three with amounts 4000, 5000, 8000, 2000, then adds 3000, 10000, 1000.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kth Largest in a Stream asks me to return the Kth largest value among everything seen so far, repeatedly, as new values arrive. The clean solution is a min-heap capped at size K that always holds exactly the K largest values seen. Its root, the smallest of those K, is by definition the Kth largest overall.

The add operation pushes the new value and, if the heap then exceeds K, removes the smallest, trimming back to the K largest. After that, I read the root in constant time to answer the query. The constructor simply feeds the initial numbers through the same add logic, so the heap settles into holding the K largest from the start, and when fewer than K values have been seen the heap holds all of them and the root is still the correct current answer.

The property interviewers want me to articulate is that the heap never grows beyond K, so memory is bounded no matter how long the stream runs, and each add is just one push and at most one poll at log K cost. This is the canonical way to answer a repeated Kth-largest query on an unbounded stream without storing the whole history.

In my project at National Bank of India, a fraud dashboard showed the Kth largest transaction amount as a live high-value watermark that updated with every incoming transaction. The size-K min-heap let the dashboard respond to each new amount in logarithmic time while holding only K values, so the watermark stayed current without the memory growing as the day's transaction stream lengthened.

answers.question: Given an array of points on a plane and a value K, return the K points closest to the origin, where distance is Euclidean (the square root of x squared plus y squared).
answers.shortTitle: K Closest Points to Origin — max-heap of size K by distance

s1_definition.profdef: K Closest Points keeps a max-heap of size K ordered by squared distance from the origin. Each point is offered, and when the heap exceeds K the farthest point, at the heap top, is removed, leaving the K closest. Squared distance is compared directly to avoid costly square roots.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of finding the five bank branches nearest to a customer's location. You keep a shortlist of five, but ordered so the farthest of the five sits on top. When you consider a new branch, you add it and, if the shortlist grew to six, you drop the current farthest. The five that remain are the nearest.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use a size-K max-heap keyed on squared distance; offer each point and evict the farthest when size exceeds K, leaving the K closest in O(n log K).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** K Closest Points keeps a max-heap of size K ordered by squared distance from the origin. Each point is offered, and when the heap exceeds K the farthest point, at the heap top, is removed, leaving the K closest. Squared distance is compared directly to avoid costly square roots.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of finding the five bank branches nearest to a customer's location. You keep a shortlist of five, but ordered so the farthest of the five sits on top. When you consider a new branch, you add it and, if the shortlist grew to six, you drop the current farthest. The five that remain are the nearest.

**One line to remember:** Use a size-K max-heap keyed on squared distance; offer each point and evict the farthest when size exceeds K, leaving the K closest in O(n log K).

sections.s2_technical:
Use a max-heap whose ordering compares squared distance, largest on top, so the point farthest from the origin is the first to be evicted. Comparing squared distance avoids the square root, which is monotonic and therefore order-preserving. For example: `long d = (long) x * x + (long) y * y;`.

Offer each point into the heap; whenever the heap grows beyond K, poll the top, which removes the current farthest. For example: `heap.offer(p); if (heap.size() > K) heap.poll();`. This keeps exactly the K closest points at all times.

After all points are processed, the heap contains the answer, which can be drained into an array. For example: `while (!heap.isEmpty()) result.add(heap.poll());`. The time is n log K and the extra space is K, since the heap never exceeds K entries.

A senior nuance is that a max-heap of size K is used rather than a min-heap of all n points because capping at K bounds memory and cost, and that comparing squared distances rather than true Euclidean distances both avoids floating-point and is safe because squaring preserves ordering for nonnegative distances. QuickSelect on squared distance is an alternative giving average linear time when all points fit in memory.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, the mobile app shows the K nearest ATMs to the customer's current coordinates. The system must return the K closest points by distance. This is exactly how K Closest Points works — a size-K heap keyed on distance.

Problem 2 — The ATM network is large, so holding all distances sorted is wasteful when only K are needed. This is exactly why a size-K max-heap is used, bounding memory at K.

The mini-project builds an `AtmLocator` service using the max-heap on squared distance, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo over several ATM coordinates.

sections.s5_journey:
The input ATMs are at (1,3), (-2,2), (5,8), (0,1), (3,3) with K equal to two.

Step 1: Compute squared distances: (1,3) is ten, (-2,2) is eight, (5,8) is eighty-nine, (0,1) is one, (3,3) is eighteen.

Step 2: Offer (1,3) and (-2,2), filling the heap of size two with squared distances ten and eight, the top being ten which is the farther.

Step 3: Offer (5,8) with distance eighty-nine, size three, so poll the farthest, which is eighty-nine itself, leaving ten and eight.

Step 4: Offer (0,1) with distance one, size three, poll the farthest which is ten, leaving eight and one.

Step 5: Offer (3,3) with distance eighteen, size three, poll the farthest which is eighteen, leaving eight and one.

Step 6: The heap now holds (-2,2) at eight and (0,1) at one, the two closest. Draining gives those two points as the answer.

```text
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: locator computes nearest; distance isolated in sq()   │
  │  O: QuickSelect alternative swappable behind same API     │

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   AtmLocator                          │
  │  + kClosest(points, k): int[][]       │ O(n log K)
  │  - sq(p): long                        │ squared distance
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Max-heap evicts farthest; squaring preserves distance ordering.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
K Closest Points to Origin asks for the K points nearest the origin. My efficient solution keeps a max-heap of size K ordered by distance, with the farthest point on top. I offer each point, and when the heap exceeds K I poll the top, which removes the current farthest, so the heap always holds exactly the K closest points seen so far. When all points are processed, the heap is the answer.

A deliberate detail is comparing squared distances rather than true Euclidean distances. Squaring is monotonic for nonnegative values, so it preserves ordering, and it avoids both the cost and the floating-point imprecision of square roots. I also use a long for the squared sum to avoid overflow on large coordinates. The whole thing is n log K time and K extra space, because the heap never grows beyond K.

The choice interviewers probe is why a size-K max-heap rather than a min-heap over all points or a full sort: capping the heap at K bounds both memory and per-element cost, which matters when n is large and K is small. I mention QuickSelect on squared distance as an average-linear alternative when all points fit in memory.

In my project at National Bank of India, the mobile app showed the K nearest ATMs to the customer's coordinates. Treating the customer as the origin, I used the size-K max-heap keyed on squared distance so the service scanned the large ATM network once, held only K candidates in memory, and returned the nearest ATMs quickly without sorting the entire network or paying for square roots.

answers.question: Given a list of tasks represented by characters and a cooldown value N, where the same task must be separated by at least N intervals, return the minimum number of intervals needed to finish all tasks (idle intervals count).
answers.shortTitle: Task Scheduler — most-frequent-first with cooldown

s1_definition.profdef: Task Scheduler computes the minimum schedule length using a formula driven by the most frequent task. The busiest task forces a skeleton of slots separated by the cooldown, and the answer is the maximum of that skeleton length and the total number of tasks. A greedy heap simulation is the alternative that reproduces the same count.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a batch processor that must run jobs but cannot run the same job type twice within N minutes, needing an idle gap otherwise. The job type that appears most often sets the rhythm: you lay out those copies with mandatory gaps between them, fill the gaps with other job types, and if there are more jobs than gaps you simply pack them in. The schedule length is whichever is larger: the gapped skeleton or the raw job count.
s1_definition.oneliner: The answer is the maximum of total tasks and the skeleton length driven by the most frequent task, which is (maxCount − 1) × (N + 1) + (number of tasks tied at maxCount).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Task Scheduler computes the minimum schedule length using a formula driven by the most frequent task. The busiest task forces a skeleton of slots separated by the cooldown, and the answer is the maximum of that skeleton length and the total number of tasks. A greedy heap simulation is the alternative that reproduces the same count.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a batch processor that must run jobs but cannot run the same job type twice within N minutes, needing an idle gap otherwise. The job type that appears most often sets the rhythm: you lay out those copies with mandatory gaps between them, fill the gaps with other job types, and if there are more jobs than gaps you simply pack them in. The schedule length is whichever is larger: the gapped skeleton or the raw job count.

**One line to remember:** The answer is the maximum of total tasks and the skeleton length driven by the most frequent task, which is (maxCount − 1) × (N + 1) + (number of tasks tied at maxCount).

sections.s2_technical:
Count the frequency of each task and find the maximum frequency, plus how many distinct tasks share that maximum. For example: `int maxCount = ...; int maxFreqTasks = ...;` from the frequency table.

The most frequent task must appear maxCount times, each separated by N cooldown slots, forming maxCount minus one full blocks of size N plus one, then a final group holding every task tied at the maximum. The skeleton length is therefore the product of maxCount minus one and N plus one, plus the number of tasks tied at the maximum. For example: `int skeleton = (maxCount - 1) * (n + 1) + maxFreqTasks;`.

The answer is the larger of this skeleton and the total number of tasks, because if there are so many distinct tasks that the gaps are all filled, no idle time is needed and the schedule is simply the task count. For example: `return Math.max(skeleton, tasks.length);`.

This is constant time after counting, since it depends only on frequencies, not on simulating each interval. A senior nuance is understanding why the maximum with total tasks is correct: the skeleton bounds the length from below when one task dominates, while a dense, varied workload fills every idle slot so the raw count dominates; a max-heap simulation that always runs the currently most frequent available task yields the identical number and is useful to explain the greedy intuition.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a batch engine runs job types but must space repeats of the same type by a cooldown to avoid resource contention. The system must compute the minimum number of intervals, including idles, to finish a day's jobs. This is exactly how Task Scheduler works.

Problem 2 — The schedule length must be computed instantly from job counts rather than by stepping through every interval. This is exactly why the frequency formula is used, with the heap simulation as an explanatory alternative.

The mini-project builds a `BatchScheduler` service implementing the formula, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo over a day's job list.

sections.s5_journey:
The input jobs are A, A, A, B, B, C with cooldown two.

Step 1: Count frequencies: A appears three times, B twice, C once. The maximum count is three, held by A, and one task is tied at the maximum.

Step 2: A must run three times with at least two slots between repeats, forming two full blocks of size three, which is cooldown two plus one.

Step 3: The skeleton is two blocks times three slots each, plus one final A, giving six plus one equals seven — wait, the formula is maxCount minus one which is two, times cooldown plus one which is three, equals six, plus tiedAtMax which is one, equals seven.

Step 4: A valid layout is A B C, A B idle, A, where the gaps after each A are filled by B and C, and one idle slot remains because only B and C are available to fill two gap slots per block.

Step 5: The total number of jobs is six, which is less than the skeleton seven, so the answer is the maximum, seven.

Step 6: Counting the layout A B C A B idle A gives seven intervals, matching the formula.


```text
  freq: A:3  B:2  C:1   maxCount=3  tiedAtMax=1

  skeleton driven by busiest (A):
    [A _ _][A _ _][A]  blocks of size (cooldown+1)=3
     A B C  A B .  A      fill gaps with B,C; one idle
  skeleton = (3-1)*(2+1)+1 = 7
  answer = max(skeleton=7, totalJobs=6) = 7
```

```text
  ═══ LLD — Task Scheduler ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Frequency-driven closed-form formula (no simulation)     │
  │  Alternative: greedy max-heap running most-frequent first │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: scheduler only computes interval count                │
  │  O: cooldown is a parameter; logic unchanged              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   BatchScheduler                      │
  │  + leastIntervals(jobs, cd): int      │ O(n) count, O(1) formula
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  intervals = max( (maxCount-1)*(cd+1)+tiedAtMax , totalJobs )
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Task Scheduler asks for the minimum number of intervals, including idles, to run all tasks when identical tasks must be separated by a cooldown. The elegant solution is a closed-form formula driven by the most frequent task, avoiding any interval-by-interval simulation. I count frequencies, find the maximum count, and count how many tasks are tied at that maximum.

The busiest task must appear its full count of times, each separated by cooldown slots, which forms a skeleton of maxCount minus one blocks, each of size cooldown plus one, followed by a final group containing every task tied at the maximum. So the skeleton length is maxCount minus one, times cooldown plus one, plus the number tied at the maximum. The answer is the larger of this skeleton and the total number of tasks, because a dense, varied workload fills all the idle gaps and then the raw task count dominates, while a single dominating task leaves gaps and the skeleton dominates.

What interviewers check is that I can justify the maximum with total tasks rather than treating the skeleton as always correct, and that I understand the greedy intuition: a max-heap that always runs the currently most frequent available task produces the identical count, which is the simulation view of the same idea.

In my project at National Bank of India, a batch engine ran job types that could not repeat within a cooldown to avoid resource contention, and I needed the minimum number of intervals to plan capacity for the day. The frequency formula gave the schedule length instantly from the job counts, so capacity planning did not require stepping through every interval, and the most-frequent job correctly set the rhythm of the schedule.

answers.question: Given a two-dimensional grid of '1's (land) and '0's (water), count the number of islands, where an island is formed by connecting adjacent land cells horizontally or vertically and is surrounded by water.
answers.shortTitle: Number of Islands — DFS/BFS grid traversal

s1_definition.profdef: Number of Islands scans every cell, and whenever it finds an unvisited land cell it increments the island count and launches a flood fill, by depth-first or breadth-first search, that marks the entire connected land component as visited. Each cell is visited once, giving linear time in the grid size.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a map of branch locations where land cells are branches and water cells are gaps, and connected branches form a regional cluster. You sweep the map, and each time you hit a branch you have not yet counted, you add one cluster and then walk outward marking every branch connected to it so you do not count the same cluster twice.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sweep the grid; on each unvisited land cell, count one island and flood-fill its whole connected component as visited, in O(rows × cols).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Number of Islands scans every cell, and whenever it finds an unvisited land cell it increments the island count and launches a flood fill, by depth-first or breadth-first search, that marks the entire connected land component as visited. Each cell is visited once, giving linear time in the grid size.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a map of branch locations where land cells are branches and water cells are gaps, and connected branches form a regional cluster. You sweep the map, and each time you hit a branch you have not yet counted, you add one cluster and then walk outward marking every branch connected to it so you do not count the same cluster twice.

**One line to remember:** Sweep the grid; on each unvisited land cell, count one island and flood-fill its whole connected component as visited, in O(rows × cols).

sections.s2_technical:
Iterate over every cell. When a cell is land and not yet visited, increment the island counter and start a flood fill from it. For example: `if (grid[r][c] == '1') { count++; dfs(grid, r, c); }`.

The flood fill marks the current land cell as visited, commonly by overwriting it with water, then recurses or enqueues its four orthogonal neighbors that are still land. For example: `grid[r][c] = '0'; dfs(up); dfs(down); dfs(left); dfs(right);`. This consumes the whole connected component so it is never counted again.

Bounds checks guard each neighbor so the search never steps outside the grid, and the water check stops it at the component boundary. For example: `if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= rows || c >= cols || grid[r][c] == '0') return;`.

Each cell is touched at most a constant number of times, so the total time is proportional to the number of cells, with recursion depth or queue size bounded by the grid in the worst case. A senior nuance is choosing BFS over DFS when the grid is very large to avoid stack overflow from deep recursion, and noting that overwriting visited land in place saves an extra visited matrix but mutates the input, which may require copying if the caller needs the grid preserved.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a coverage map marks cells where the bank has a presence, and connected cells form service clusters. The system must count how many distinct clusters exist. This is exactly how Number of Islands works — each connected land component is one cluster.

Problem 2 — The map is large and the count must come from a single linear sweep, not repeated scans. This is exactly why flood fill marks each component once as it is counted.

The input is a four-by-five grid with three separate land clusters.

Step 1: The sweep reaches cell zero-zero, a land cell. The count becomes one and a flood fill starts there.

Step 2: The flood marks zero-zero, then zero-one and one-zero, which are connected land, overwriting them to water so they are not recounted. That first cluster is consumed.

Step 3: The sweep continues and reaches zero-four, a separate land cell. The count becomes two and a flood marks zero-four and one-four.

Step 4: The sweep reaches two-two, a land cell. The count becomes three and a flood marks two-two, three-two, and three-three as one cluster.

Step 5: Every remaining cell is water or already overwritten, so no further islands are counted.

Step 6: The sweep finishes having counted three clusters, each flooded exactly once.

```text
    0 0 1 1 0

  A found → flood → B found → flood → C found → flood
```

```text
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: counter only counts; flood isolated in helper         │
  │  O: swap DFS↔BFS without changing count loop              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   CoverageClusterCounter              │
  │  + countClusters(grid): int           │ O(rows·cols)
  │  - flood(grid, r, c): void            │ marks one component
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Each cell visited once; flood consumes a whole component.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Number of Islands asks me to count connected components of land in a grid, where cells connect horizontally and vertically. My approach sweeps every cell, and whenever I find a land cell that has not been visited, I increment the island count and launch a flood fill that marks the entire connected component as visited so it is never counted again.

The flood fill is a depth-first or breadth-first search that marks the current land cell, typically by overwriting it with water, then explores its four orthogonal neighbors that are still land, with bounds and water checks stopping it at the grid edge and the component boundary. Because each cell is touched a constant number of times, the total time is linear in the number of cells.

The senior points are choosing BFS over recursive DFS when the grid is huge to avoid a stack overflow from deep recursion, and recognizing that overwriting visited land in place avoids a separate visited matrix but mutates the input, so I copy the grid first if the caller needs it preserved. These trade-offs show I understand the cost beyond the happy path.

In my project at National Bank of India, a coverage map marked cells where the bank had a presence, and connected cells formed service clusters. Counting the clusters was exactly this problem: I swept the map once and flood-filled each cluster as I counted it, so even a large coverage grid produced the cluster count in a single linear pass without recounting any component.

answers.question: Given a reference to a node in a connected undirected graph, return a deep copy of the entire graph, where each node contains a value and a list of its neighbors.
answers.shortTitle: Clone Graph — BFS/DFS with HashMap old→new

s1_definition.profdef: Clone Graph performs a traversal, depth-first or breadth-first, keeping a HashMap from each original node to its clone. When visiting a node, it creates the clone once, records it in the map, then wires each neighbor by cloning neighbors on demand and linking, using the map to avoid re-cloning and to terminate on cycles.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of duplicating a network of interlinked accounts, where each account points to the accounts it is linked with. You copy each account exactly once and keep a ledger mapping each original to its copy. As you follow links, you look up the ledger: if a copy already exists you link to it, otherwise you make the copy first, which prevents infinite loops when accounts link back to each other.
s1_definition.oneliner: Traverse the graph keeping a HashMap from original to clone; create each clone once and wire neighbors through the map to handle cycles and shared nodes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Clone Graph performs a traversal, depth-first or breadth-first, keeping a HashMap from each original node to its clone. When visiting a node, it creates the clone once, records it in the map, then wires each neighbor by cloning neighbors on demand and linking, using the map to avoid re-cloning and to terminate on cycles.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of duplicating a network of interlinked accounts, where each account points to the accounts it is linked with. You copy each account exactly once and keep a ledger mapping each original to its copy. As you follow links, you look up the ledger: if a copy already exists you link to it, otherwise you make the copy first, which prevents infinite loops when accounts link back to each other.

**One line to remember:** Traverse the graph keeping a HashMap from original to clone; create each clone once and wire neighbors through the map to handle cycles and shared nodes.

sections.s2_technical:
Keep a map from original node to its clone, which serves both as the visited set and the lookup for already-created clones. For example: `Map<Node, Node> clones = new HashMap<>();`.

When a node is first seen, create its clone and store the mapping before processing neighbors, so that a neighbor pointing back to this node finds the clone already present and does not recurse infinitely. For example: `Node copy = new Node(node.val); clones.put(node, copy);`.

For each neighbor of the original, get or create its clone through the map, then add that clone to the current clone's neighbor list. For example: `for (Node nb : node.neighbors) copy.neighbors.add(cloneOf(nb));` where cloneOf consults the map first. This wires the copied graph with the same structure.

The time is linear in nodes plus edges, since each node and edge is processed once, and the space is linear for the map and the clone graph. A senior nuance is that the clone must be inserted into the map before its neighbors are expanded, otherwise cycles cause infinite recursion, and that either DFS with recursion or BFS with a queue works, both relying on the map as the single source of truth for what has already been cloned.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a linked-account graph must be deep-copied into a sandbox for what-if analysis without touching the live graph. The system must produce an independent copy preserving all links, including cycles. This is exactly how Clone Graph works.

Problem 2 — Accounts can link back to each other forming cycles, so the copy must avoid infinite loops and shared references. This is exactly why the original-to-clone map is used.

The mini-project builds an `AccountGraphCloner` using DFS plus a map, a `Node` class, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo over a small cyclic account graph.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a triangle graph with nodes 1, 2, 3 all linked to each other, starting at node 1.

Step 1: Visiting node 1, the map has no clone, so a clone of 1 is created and stored in the map before any neighbor work.

Step 2: Expanding node 1's neighbors, the first is node 2. The map has no clone of 2, so a clone of 2 is created and stored, then its neighbors are expanded.

Step 3: Node 2's neighbors include node 1, which is already in the map, so the existing clone of 1 is returned and linked, avoiding infinite recursion.

Step 4: Node 2's other neighbor is node 3. A clone of 3 is created and stored, and its neighbors are expanded.

Step 5: Node 3's neighbors are node 2 and node 1, both already cloned, so their existing clones are linked from the map.

Step 6: Recursion unwinds, every original node has exactly one distinct clone, and the triangle structure including the cycle is reproduced in the copy.


```text
        neighbor 1 in map → reuse 1' (cycle handled)
        visit 3 → make 3' (map: 3→3')
          neighbors 2,1 in map → reuse 2',1'
  result: 1'—2'—3'—1' identical structure, all distinct objects
```

```text
  │   AccountGraphCloner                  │
  │  + clone(start): Node                 │ O(V+E)
  │  - dfs(node, clones): Node            │ memoized recursion
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  Map doubles as visited set + clone lookup → cycles terminate.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Clone Graph asks for a deep copy of a connected undirected graph given a starting node. My solution traverses the graph, depth-first or breadth-first, keeping a HashMap from each original node to its clone. That map serves double duty: it is both the visited set and the lookup for clones I have already created.

The crucial ordering is that when I first see a node, I create its clone and put it in the map before I expand its neighbors. If I expanded neighbors first, a neighbor pointing back to this node would find no clone yet and recurse forever, so inserting the clone early is exactly what makes cycles terminate. Then for each neighbor I get or create its clone through the map and add it to the current clone's neighbor list, wiring the copy with the same structure as the original.

The cost is linear in nodes plus edges because each is processed once, with linear space for the map and the copy. What interviewers check is that I insert the clone into the map before recursing and that I use the map as the single source of truth for what is already cloned, which is what distinguishes a correct cycle-safe clone from one that loops or duplicates nodes.

In my project at National Bank of India, I deep-copied a linked-account graph into a sandbox for what-if analysis without touching the live graph. Because accounts could link back to one another forming cycles, the original-to-clone map was essential: it let me copy each account exactly once and reproduce every link, including the cycles, giving analysts an independent graph to experiment on safely.

answers.question: Given a grid of cell heights, water can flow from a cell to a neighbor of equal or lower height. The Pacific borders the top and left edges, the Atlantic the bottom and right. Return all cells from which water can reach both oceans.
answers.shortTitle: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow — multi-source BFS/DFS from both oceans

s1_definition.profdef: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow reverses the flow and runs a multi-source traversal from each ocean's border cells inward, moving only to neighbors of equal or greater height. Cells reachable from the Pacific border and cells reachable from the Atlantic border are each marked, and the answer is the intersection of the two reachable sets.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a terrain of account-balance heights where funds drain downhill to two settlement pools, one touching the top-left edges and one the bottom-right edges. Instead of asking from every cell whether it drains to both pools, you start at each pool's edge and climb uphill marking every cell that could drain into it. Cells marked by both climbs are the ones that reach both pools.
s1_definition.oneliner: Reverse the flow: BFS/DFS inward from each ocean's border going uphill, mark each ocean's reachable set, and return the cells in both sets.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Pacific Atlantic Water Flow reverses the flow and runs a multi-source traversal from each ocean's border cells inward, moving only to neighbors of equal or greater height. Cells reachable from the Pacific border and cells reachable from the Atlantic border are each marked, and the answer is the intersection of the two reachable sets.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a terrain of account-balance heights where funds drain downhill to two settlement pools, one touching the top-left edges and one the bottom-right edges. Instead of asking from every cell whether it drains to both pools, you start at each pool's edge and climb uphill marking every cell that could drain into it. Cells marked by both climbs are the ones that reach both pools.

**One line to remember:** Reverse the flow: BFS/DFS inward from each ocean's border going uphill, mark each ocean's reachable set, and return the cells in both sets.

sections.s2_technical:
Create two boolean matrices, one for cells that can reach the Pacific and one for the Atlantic. Seed the Pacific search from the top row and left column, and the Atlantic search from the bottom row and right column. For example: start DFS from every border cell of each ocean.

Each search moves from a cell to a neighbor only if the neighbor's height is equal or greater, because this is the reverse of water flowing downhill. For example: `if (grid[nr][nc] >= grid[r][c] && !visited[nr][nc]) dfs(nr, nc);`. Marking a cell means water from that cell could reach the ocean whose border seeded the search.

After both searches, scan every cell and collect those marked reachable in both matrices, which are the cells draining to both oceans. For example: `if (pacific[r][c] && atlantic[r][c]) result.add(...);`.

The time is linear in the number of cells because each cell is visited at most a constant number of times per ocean, and the space is linear for the two matrices. A senior nuance is the key reversal of direction: searching outward from every cell to both oceans would be far more expensive, whereas seeding from the borders and climbing uphill computes both reachable sets in two linear sweeps, and the equal-or-greater comparison correctly models the reversed downhill flow.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a settlement-terrain model assigns each cell a height, and liquidity drains to two pools bordered by opposite edges. The system must find cells that can feed both pools. This is exactly how Pacific Atlantic Water Flow works — the intersection of two border-seeded reachable sets.

Problem 2 — Checking every cell's drainage to both pools independently would be wasteful, so the flow is reversed and seeded from the borders. This is exactly why multi-source traversal from each edge is used.

The mini-project builds a `LiquidityFlowAnalyzer` using DFS from both borders, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo over a height grid.

The input is a five-by-five height grid, with the Pacific on the top and left and the Atlantic on the bottom and right.

Step 1: The Pacific search seeds from every top-row and left-column cell and climbs uphill, marking each cell from which water could reach the Pacific.

Step 2: The Atlantic search seeds from every bottom-row and right-column cell and climbs uphill, marking cells that could reach the Atlantic.

Step 4: A cell high on a ridge near the center gets marked by both searches because water from it can run down toward both edges.

Step 5: After both searches, the analyzer scans every cell and collects those marked in both matrices.

Step 6: The result is the set of cells draining to both pools, computed in two linear sweeps rather than per-cell outward searches.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Pacific Atlantic Water Flow asks which cells can drain to both oceans, where water flows to equal-or-lower neighbors and the two oceans border opposite edges. The naive idea runs a search from every cell to test whether it reaches both oceans, which is extremely expensive. My efficient solution reverses the flow: I start from each ocean's border cells and climb uphill, moving only to neighbors of equal or greater height, which is exactly the reverse of water running downhill.

I keep two boolean matrices, one per ocean. I seed the Pacific search from the top row and left column, and the Atlantic search from the bottom row and right column, marking every cell each search can reach. A marked cell means water from that cell could reach that ocean. After both searches, I scan the grid and collect the cells marked in both matrices, which are the ones draining to both oceans.

The insight interviewers are testing is the reversal of direction, because it turns a per-cell outward search into just two linear border-seeded sweeps, and the equal-or-greater comparison correctly models the reversed downhill flow. The whole thing is linear in the number of cells with linear extra space for the two matrices.

In my project at National Bank of India, a settlement-terrain model gave each cell a height and liquidity drained to two pools bordered by opposite edges. Finding cells that could feed both pools was this exact problem, and seeding the search from each pool's border and climbing uphill let me compute both reachable sets in two linear passes and return their intersection, instead of testing drainage from every cell independently.

answers.question: Given a grid where each cell is empty, a fresh orange, or a rotten orange, every minute any fresh orange adjacent to a rotten one becomes rotten. Return the minimum minutes until no fresh orange remains, or negative one if impossible.
answers.shortTitle: Rotting Oranges — multi-source BFS

s1_definition.profdef: Rotting Oranges is a multi-source breadth-first search where all initially rotten cells form the starting frontier at time zero. Each BFS level represents one minute, spreading rot to adjacent fresh cells. The number of levels is the answer, and if any fresh cell is never reached, the result is negative one.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a fraud contagion spreading across linked accounts, where some accounts start flagged and each minute the flag spreads to directly linked clean accounts. You start the clock with all initially flagged accounts together and advance one minute per wave. The number of waves until every reachable account is flagged is the time; if some account can never be reached, the spread can never finish.
s1_definition.oneliner: Seed a BFS with all rotten cells at once, process level by level counting minutes, and return the last minute or negative one if fresh cells remain unreachable.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Rotting Oranges is a multi-source breadth-first search where all initially rotten cells form the starting frontier at time zero. Each BFS level represents one minute, spreading rot to adjacent fresh cells. The number of levels is the answer, and if any fresh cell is never reached, the result is negative one.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a fraud contagion spreading across linked accounts, where some accounts start flagged and each minute the flag spreads to directly linked clean accounts. You start the clock with all initially flagged accounts together and advance one minute per wave. The number of waves until every reachable account is flagged is the time; if some account can never be reached, the spread can never finish.

**One line to remember:** Seed a BFS with all rotten cells at once, process level by level counting minutes, and return the last minute or negative one if fresh cells remain unreachable.

sections.s2_technical:
Enqueue every initially rotten cell into a queue and count the fresh cells. For example: `if (grid[r][c] == 2) queue.add(cell); else if (grid[r][c] == 1) fresh++;`. All rotten cells sharing time zero is what makes this multi-source.

Process the queue in levels, where each level is all cells that became rotten in the previous minute. For each cell, rot its fresh orthogonal neighbors, decrement the fresh count, and enqueue them for the next level. For example: process `size = queue.size()` cells, then increment the minute counter if anything rotted.

Continue until the queue is empty. If the fresh count reached zero, the number of elapsed levels is the answer; otherwise some fresh orange was unreachable and the answer is negative one. For example: `return fresh == 0 ? minutes : -1;`.

The time is linear in the number of cells since each is enqueued once, and the space is bounded by the grid for the queue. A senior nuance is that multi-source BFS naturally computes the time for the last orange to rot because all sources advance in lockstep, which a single-source BFS repeated per source could not do efficiently, and that the fresh counter is the clean way to detect the impossible case rather than rescanning the grid.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a fraud-contagion model marks some accounts as compromised and spreads the flag to directly linked accounts each tick. The system must find the minimum ticks until every reachable account is flagged. This is exactly how Rotting Oranges works — multi-source spread measured in levels.

Problem 2 — Some accounts may be unreachable from any compromised source, which must be detected rather than looped on forever. This is exactly why the fresh counter and the negative-one result are used.

The mini-project builds a `ContagionSimulator` using multi-source BFS, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo over a contagion grid.

Step 6: The queue drains with fresh equal to zero, so every reachable account was compromised in four minutes, which is the answer.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Rotting Oranges asks for the minimum minutes until rot spreads from all initially rotten cells to every fresh cell, or negative one if some fresh cell can never be reached. The right tool is a multi-source breadth-first search, where every initially rotten cell is placed in the queue at time zero so they all spread in lockstep.

I count the fresh cells up front, then process the queue level by level, where each level represents one minute. For each rotten cell I rot its fresh orthogonal neighbors, decrement the fresh count, and enqueue the newly rotten cells for the next minute. When the queue empties, if the fresh count is zero the number of elapsed levels is the answer, and if any fresh cell remains it was unreachable, so I return negative one.

The insight interviewers want is why multi-source is correct: because all sources advance together, the level count directly gives the time for the last orange to rot, which repeated single-source searches could not do cleanly. The fresh counter is the elegant way to detect the impossible case without rescanning the grid, and the whole algorithm is linear in the number of cells.

In my project at National Bank of India, a fraud-contagion model started with some compromised accounts and spread the compromise flag to directly linked accounts each tick. Computing the minimum ticks to flag every reachable account was exactly this problem, and seeding the BFS with all compromised accounts at once gave the spread time directly, while the fresh counter flagged accounts that no source could ever reach.
