answers.question: Given accounts where each is a name followed by emails, merge accounts that share any email. Return merged accounts with the name and sorted unique emails.
answers.shortTitle: Accounts Merge — union emails that belong to the same person

s1_definition.profdef: Assign each distinct email an integer id, union all emails within the same account row, then group emails by their Union-Find root. Each root becomes one merged account; attach the owner name (recorded per email) and output the emails sorted. Two accounts merge transitively whenever they share at least one email.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India sometimes has the same customer registered under multiple profiles that share an email. If profile A and profile B share one email, they are the same person; and if B and C share another, then A, B, and C are all one person. You link shared emails, then gather every email that ends up under the same head into one clean profile.
s1_definition.oneliner: Union emails that appear together, then group by root — each root is one merged person with sorted emails.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Assign each distinct email an integer id, union all emails within the same account row, then group emails by their Union-Find root. Each root becomes one merged account; attach the owner name (recorded per email) and output the emails sorted. Two accounts merge transitively whenever they share at least one email.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India sometimes has the same customer registered under multiple profiles that share an email. If profile A and profile B share one email, they are the same person; and if B and C share another, then A, B, and C are all one person. You link shared emails, then gather every email that ends up under the same head into one clean profile.

**One line to remember:** Union emails that appear together, then group by root — each root is one merged person with sorted emails.

sections.s2_technical:
Give each first-seen email a unique id and remember which name owns it. For example: `emailToId.putIfAbsent(email, emailToId.size());` and `emailToName.put(email, name);`.

Within each account, union the first email's id with every other email's id, so all emails of one row share a root. For example: `union(id(firstEmail), id(otherEmail));`.

Group emails by their root into lists, sort each list, and prepend the owning name. For example: `root -> [name, sortedEmail1, sortedEmail2, ...]`. The time is dominated by sorting the emails, roughly n log n in the number of emails, with the unions being near-constant.

A senior nuance is that emails, not names, are the identity key, because two different people can share a name but never a verified email, so unioning on names would be incorrect.

Accounts Merge is a Union-Find problem where the identity key is the email, not the name. I give every distinct email a unique integer id and record which name owns each email. Using the email as the merge key was critical, because two different customers can share a name but never a verified email, so unioning on names would have wrongly fused distinct people.

answers.question: Given an n×n adjacency matrix where isConnected[i][j] = 1 means city i and city j are directly connected, return the number of provinces (connected groups of cities).
answers.shortTitle: Number of Provinces — count friend circles via Union-Find

s1_definition.profdef: Treat the symmetric adjacency matrix as an undirected graph over n cities. Start the province count at n and union every pair (i, j) where isConnected[i][j] equals one; each successful union decrements the count. The remaining count is the number of connected components, i.e., provinces.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India groups its regional hubs into provinces based on who shares a direct data line. If hub i and hub j share a line they are in the same province, and provinces grow transitively. Count the hubs, merge every directly connected pair, and whatever separate groups remain are the provinces.
s1_definition.oneliner: Start at n, union every connected pair in the matrix, and the leftover count is the number of provinces.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Treat the symmetric adjacency matrix as an undirected graph over n cities. Start the province count at n and union every pair (i, j) where isConnected[i][j] equals one; each successful union decrements the count. The remaining count is the number of connected components, i.e., provinces.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India groups its regional hubs into provinces based on who shares a direct data line. If hub i and hub j share a line they are in the same province, and provinces grow transitively. Count the hubs, merge every directly connected pair, and whatever separate groups remain are the provinces.

**One line to remember:** Start at n, union every connected pair in the matrix, and the leftover count is the number of provinces.

sections.s2_technical:
Initialize Union-Find over n cities with the count set to n. Scan the upper triangle of the matrix to avoid redundant work, since it is symmetric. For example: `for (int i=0;i<n;i++) for (int j=i+1;j<n;j++) if (m[i][j]==1 && union(i,j)) count--;`.

Each one in the matrix that links two cities in different sets reduces the count; a one between already-connected cities changes nothing. The diagonal is always one (a city is connected to itself) and is simply skipped by starting j at i+1.

The time is n squared because the whole matrix is scanned, with near-constant union cost per edge, and the space is the parent and rank arrays. A senior nuance is that if the input were an edge list rather than a dense matrix, the time would drop to the number of edges, so the n-squared cost here is a property of the dense input representation, not of Union-Find.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, regional data hubs are connected by direct lines described in a connectivity matrix, and the network team needs to know how many independent provinces exist so each province gets one failover plan. This is exactly how counting provinces works.

Problem 2 — A direct line between two hubs already in the same province does not create a new province. This is exactly why a union only decrements the count on a real merge.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Number of Provinces is Union-Find applied to a symmetric adjacency matrix. I start a province counter at n, because each of the n cities begins in its own group, and then I scan the matrix unioning every pair of cities marked as directly connected. I scan only the upper triangle since the matrix is symmetric, and I skip the diagonal because a city is trivially connected to itself. Every union that merges two previously separate groups decrements the counter by one.

When the scan completes, the counter holds the number of connected components, which is the number of provinces. The cost is n squared because the dense matrix must be fully scanned, with each edge costing only the near-constant Union-Find operation; if the input were an edge list instead, it would drop to the number of edges.

In my project at National Bank of India, regional data hubs were described by a connectivity matrix and the network team needed the number of independent provinces so each province could get its own failover plan. Union-Find gave a clean count, and because a direct line between two hubs already in the same province never created a spurious new group, the number of failover plans we provisioned stayed exactly right.

answers.question: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible subsets (the power set) using backtracking.
answers.shortTitle: Subsets — include or exclude each element

s1_definition.profdef: The power set is generated by a depth-first backtracking that, at each index, records the current partial subset and then recurses on remaining elements. Each element is either taken or skipped, producing 2^n subsets. Adding the current path to the result at every node of the recursion tree (not only at leaves) yields all subsets including the empty set.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India offers n optional add-on services. A customer can pick any combination — none, some, or all. Listing every possible package is listing the power set: for each add-on you branch into "include it" and "leave it out," and every point along the way is a valid package.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each element choose include or exclude; record the path at every step to get all 2^n subsets.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The power set is generated by a depth-first backtracking that, at each index, records the current partial subset and then recurses on remaining elements. Each element is either taken or skipped, producing 2^n subsets. Adding the current path to the result at every node of the recursion tree (not only at leaves) yields all subsets including the empty set.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India offers n optional add-on services. A customer can pick any combination — none, some, or all. Listing every possible package is listing the power set: for each add-on you branch into "include it" and "leave it out," and every point along the way is a valid package.

**One line to remember:** For each element choose include or exclude; record the path at every step to get all 2^n subsets.

sections.s2_technical:
Use a recursive helper carrying a start index and the current path. At entry, record a copy of the path into the result; then loop from start to the end, add an element, recurse with the next index, and remove it (backtrack). For example: `result.add(new ArrayList<>(path)); for (int i=start;i<nums.length;i++){ path.add(nums[i]); backtrack(i+1); path.remove(path.size()-1); }`.

Recording at every entry (including the first, empty path) captures the empty subset and all sizes. Using `i+1` as the next start prevents reusing earlier elements and avoids permutations of the same subset.

The time is O(n · 2^n) because there are 2^n subsets and copying each costs up to n, and the recursion depth is n. A senior nuance is that an equivalent bitmask enumeration over 0..2^n-1 produces the same subsets iteratively, which some interviewers prefer for its lack of recursion.

Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a premium account bundles optional add-on services, and the product team wants to enumerate every possible add-on package to price them. This is exactly how generating subsets works.

Problem 2 — Every combination, including the empty package and the full package, is valid and must appear exactly once. This is exactly why the path is recorded at every recursion node and the start index advances.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Subsets, or the power set, is the foundational backtracking problem. I use a recursive helper that carries a start index and the current partial subset, and the single most important detail is that I record a copy of the path at every node of the recursion, not only at the leaves, which is what captures the empty set and every intermediate size. Inside the loop I take an element, recurse with the next index, and then remove it to backtrack, exploring the include-and-exclude choice for each element.

Advancing the start index by one on each recursive call is what prevents reusing earlier elements and stops me from generating permutations of the same subset. The whole thing is O(n times 2 to the n), because there are 2 to the n subsets and copying each costs up to n.

In my project at National Bank of India, the product team needed to enumerate every possible package of optional account add-ons in order to price each combination, and this backtracking generated the complete catalog of packages exactly once each. When an interviewer prefers an iterative approach, I mention that a bitmask enumeration over zero to 2-to-the-n-minus-one produces the identical set without recursion.

answers.question: Given an array that may contain duplicates, return all unique subsets using backtracking.
answers.shortTitle: Subsets II (with duplicates) — sort then skip duplicates

s1_definition.profdef: Sort the array so equal values are adjacent, then run the standard subsets backtracking with one extra guard: within a single recursion level, skip an element if it equals the previous element already considered at that level (i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]). This suppresses duplicate subsets while still allowing a repeated value to be used deeper in the path.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India has add-on vouchers where some are identical. Two identical vouchers should not produce two different-looking-but-equal packages. By lining up identical vouchers and, at each decision point, using an identical voucher only once as the "first" choice, you avoid listing the same package twice.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort, then at each level skip a value equal to its predecessor to drop duplicate subsets.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sort the array so equal values are adjacent, then run the standard subsets backtracking with one extra guard: within a single recursion level, skip an element if it equals the previous element already considered at that level (i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1]). This suppresses duplicate subsets while still allowing a repeated value to be used deeper in the path.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India has add-on vouchers where some are identical. Two identical vouchers should not produce two different-looking-but-equal packages. By lining up identical vouchers and, at each decision point, using an identical voucher only once as the "first" choice, you avoid listing the same package twice.

**One line to remember:** Sort, then at each level skip a value equal to its predecessor to drop duplicate subsets.

sections.s2_technical:
Sort first so duplicates sit together. In the loop, record the path at entry as usual, but skip when the current index is beyond the level's start and equals the previous value. For example: `if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) continue;`.

The condition `i > start` is crucial: it allows the first occurrence at a level to be chosen (and recursed, where the duplicate can legitimately extend the path) but blocks a second identical choice at the same level, which would create a duplicate subset.

The time remains O(n · 2^n) in the worst case of all-distinct elements, less when duplicates prune branches. A senior nuance is that the same skip pattern reappears in Combination Sum II and Permutations II, so recognizing it as the general "skip same-level duplicates" idiom saves re-deriving it each time.

Subsets II extends the power-set backtracking to inputs that contain duplicates, where the goal is every distinct subset with no repeats in the output. The two essential moves are sorting the array first so equal values are adjacent, and then adding a guard inside the loop that skips an element when its index is beyond the current level's start and it equals the previous element. The worst-case cost is still O(n times 2 to the n).

answers.question: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible orderings (permutations) using backtracking.
answers.shortTitle: Permutations — backtracking with a used[] array

s1_definition.profdef: Build each permutation by choosing an unused element at every position via depth-first backtracking. A boolean used[] array marks elements already placed in the current path; when the path length equals n, record it as a complete permutation, then undo the choice to explore alternatives. This produces all n! orderings.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India must try every order in which n settlement batches could run when order affects outcome. At each slot you pick a batch not yet used, fill all slots, record that full ordering, then unpick to try a different arrangement.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fill positions one by one with unused elements; when full, record the ordering and backtrack — n! results.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Build each permutation by choosing an unused element at every position via depth-first backtracking. A boolean used[] array marks elements already placed in the current path; when the path length equals n, record it as a complete permutation, then undo the choice to explore alternatives. This produces all n! orderings.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India must try every order in which n settlement batches could run when order affects outcome. At each slot you pick a batch not yet used, fill all slots, record that full ordering, then unpick to try a different arrangement.

**One line to remember:** Fill positions one by one with unused elements; when full, record the ordering and backtrack — n! results.

sections.s2_technical:
Carry a path list and a used[] boolean array. When the path size equals n, record a copy. Otherwise loop over all indices, skip used ones, choose an element (mark used, append), recurse, then undo. For example: `if (used[i]) continue; used[i]=true; path.add(nums[i]); backtrack(); path.remove(last); used[i]=false;`.

Unlike subsets, there is no start index, because every position can draw from any unused element, which is what generates orderings rather than combinations.

The time is O(n · n!) because there are n! permutations, each of length n to copy. A senior nuance is the swap-based in-place variant that avoids the used[] array by swapping elements into position, trading clarity for a small constant-factor space saving.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Permutations is the backtracking problem for generating every ordering of distinct elements. I carry the current partial ordering plus a boolean used array, and whenever the path reaches length n I record a copy as a complete permutation. Otherwise I loop over every index, skip the ones already used, choose an unused element by marking it and appending it, recurse, and then undo both actions to explore the remaining arrangements.

The key structural difference from subsets is that there is no start index: every position is free to draw from any element not yet placed, which is precisely what produces orderings rather than combinations. The cost is O(n times n factorial), since there are n factorial permutations and copying each costs n.

In my project at National Bank of India, a simulation had to evaluate every possible run order of a small set of distinct end-of-day settlement batches to assess order-dependent risk, and this backtracking enumerated them cleanly with each batch used exactly once per ordering. If space is at a premium I mention the in-place swap variant that drops the used array by swapping elements directly into position.

answers.question: Given an array that may contain duplicate integers, return all unique permutations.
answers.shortTitle: Permutations II (with duplicates) — sort then skip same-level duplicates

s1_definition.profdef: Sort the array, then run permutation backtracking with a used[] array and an extra guard: skip nums[i] if it equals nums[i-1] and the previous equal element has not been used at this branch (used[i-1] is false). This canonical ordering ensures each group of identical values is placed left-to-right, generating each distinct permutation exactly once.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India schedules batches where some are interchangeable (same type). Swapping two identical batches does not create a genuinely different schedule. By insisting identical batches are always placed in their fixed left-to-right order, you count each truly distinct schedule once.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort, then skip a duplicate value whose equal predecessor is unused at this branch to avoid repeated permutations.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sort the array, then run permutation backtracking with a used[] array and an extra guard: skip nums[i] if it equals nums[i-1] and the previous equal element has not been used at this branch (used[i-1] is false). This canonical ordering ensures each group of identical values is placed left-to-right, generating each distinct permutation exactly once.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India schedules batches where some are interchangeable (same type). Swapping two identical batches does not create a genuinely different schedule. By insisting identical batches are always placed in their fixed left-to-right order, you count each truly distinct schedule once.

**One line to remember:** Sort, then skip a duplicate value whose equal predecessor is unused at this branch to avoid repeated permutations.

sections.s2_technical:
After sorting, inside the loop skip used elements as before, and additionally skip when the current equals the previous and the previous is not currently used. For example: `if (used[i] || (i>0 && nums[i]==nums[i-1] && !used[i-1])) continue;`.

The `!used[i-1]` test enforces that among equal values, an earlier copy must be placed before a later copy, which removes the mirror-image duplicates. If instead you wrote `used[i-1]`, you would keep duplicates and drop valid ones, so the condition direction matters.

The worst-case time is O(n · n!) when all elements are distinct, with duplicates pruning branches. A senior nuance is that the same canonical-order trick (fix the order within equal groups) is the general recipe for de-duplicating any permutation/combination enumeration.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Permutations II generates every unique ordering when the input contains duplicate values. I sort first so equal values are adjacent, then run the standard permutation backtracking with the used array, and I add one guard: I skip the current element if it equals the previous element and that previous equal element is not currently used in this branch. If I flipped it to require the predecessor to be used, I would keep duplicates and drop valid permutations. answers.question: Given distinct candidates and a target, return all unique combinations that sum to target. Each candidate may be used an unlimited number of times.
answers.shortTitle: Combination Sum — reusable candidates, keep index to dedup

s1_definition.profdef: Depth-first backtracking that, at each step, either reuses the current candidate (recurse with the same index, allowing repeats) or advances to the next candidate. Passing the current index (not index+1) when reusing permits unlimited repetition while the non-decreasing index order prevents permutations of the same combination. A branch is recorded when the remaining target hits zero and pruned when it goes negative.
s1_definition.analogy: A customer at National Bank of India wants to reach an exact savings target using fixed-denomination recurring deposits, and the same denomination can be used many times. You try adding a denomination, keep trying the same one as long as the target is not exceeded, and whenever you hit the target exactly you record that plan.
s1_definition.oneliner: Recurse with the same index to allow reuse; stop at zero, prune below zero, advance index to avoid reordered duplicates.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Depth-first backtracking that, at each step, either reuses the current candidate (recurse with the same index, allowing repeats) or advances to the next candidate. Passing the current index (not index+1) when reusing permits unlimited repetition while the non-decreasing index order prevents permutations of the same combination. A branch is recorded when the remaining target hits zero and pruned when it goes negative.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A customer at National Bank of India wants to reach an exact savings target using fixed-denomination recurring deposits, and the same denomination can be used many times. You try adding a denomination, keep trying the same one as long as the target is not exceeded, and whenever you hit the target exactly you record that plan.

**One line to remember:** Recurse with the same index to allow reuse; stop at zero, prune below zero, advance index to avoid reordered duplicates.

sections.s2_technical:
Carry a start index, the remaining target, and the current path. If remaining is zero, record a copy; if negative, return. Otherwise loop from start, subtract the candidate, recurse with the same index to allow reuse, then backtrack. For example: `path.add(cand[i]); backtrack(i, remain - cand[i]); path.remove(last);`.

Passing `i` rather than `i+1` is what permits the same candidate to repeat; keeping the loop starting at `start` prevents going backward, which is what stops reordered duplicates like [2,3] and [3,2].

Sorting candidates lets you break early when a candidate exceeds the remaining target. The time is exponential in the worst case, bounded by the number of combinations times their length. A senior nuance is that pruning with a sorted array (`if (cand[i] > remain) break;`) dramatically cuts the search on realistic inputs.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Combination Sum asks for every combination of candidates that sums to a target, where each candidate can be used any number of times. I solve it with backtracking that carries a start index and the remaining target. When the remaining target reaches zero I record the current path, and if it ever goes negative I abandon the branch. The crucial detail is that when I recurse after choosing a candidate I pass the same index rather than the next one, which is what allows a candidate to be reused as many times as needed.

Keeping the loop anchored at the start index, so it never goes backward, is what guarantees each combination appears in non-decreasing order and therefore only once, rather than as several reordered duplicates. Sorting the candidates lets me break out of the loop as soon as a candidate exceeds the remaining target, which prunes the search sharply.

In my project at National Bank of India, an advisor tool listed every recurring-deposit plan built from fixed denomination slabs that reached a customer's exact savings goal, with slabs reusable without limit. This backtracking produced all valid plans, and the sorted-break pruning kept it responsive even for larger goals.

answers.shortTitle: Combination Sum II — each number used once, skip duplicates

s1_definition.profdef: Sort the candidates, then backtrack advancing the start index by one each step so no element is reused, with a same-level duplicate skip (i > start and cand[i] == cand[i-1]) to avoid duplicate combinations. Record when the remaining target is zero and prune on overshoot.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India issues one-time cashback coupons, some of identical value, and a customer can use each coupon only once. To list every distinct set of coupons that reaches a target, you consume each coupon at most once and avoid listing the same-valued coupon twice at the same choice point.
s1_definition.oneliner: Advance index by one (use-once) and skip same-level duplicates to get unique combinations from a multiset.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sort the candidates, then backtrack advancing the start index by one each step so no element is reused, with a same-level duplicate skip (i > start and cand[i] == cand[i-1]) to avoid duplicate combinations. Record when the remaining target is zero and prune on overshoot.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India issues one-time cashback coupons, some of identical value, and a customer can use each coupon only once. To list every distinct set of coupons that reaches a target, you consume each coupon at most once and avoid listing the same-valued coupon twice at the same choice point.

**One line to remember:** Advance index by one (use-once) and skip same-level duplicates to get unique combinations from a multiset.

sections.s2_technical:
Sort so duplicates are adjacent. In the loop, skip a same-level duplicate, subtract the candidate, and recurse with `i+1` so the element is not reused. For example: `if (i>start && cand[i]==cand[i-1]) continue; path.add(cand[i]); backtrack(i+1, remain-cand[i]);`.

Advancing to `i+1` enforces use-once, distinguishing this from Combination Sum where the same index was reused. The duplicate skip ensures that identical values at the same level produce the combination only once.

Sorting also enables the `cand[i] > remain` break for pruning. The time is exponential in the worst case, well pruned on realistic inputs. A senior nuance is that the use-once rule plus the duplicate skip together handle the classic coin-collection-from-a-multiset problem cleanly, which is why this template is worth memorizing.

answers.question: Given a string of digits 2–9, return all letter combinations the number could spell, based on the classic phone keypad mapping.
answers.shortTitle: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number

s1_definition.profdef: Map each digit to its keypad letters and backtrack across the digit positions: at depth d, append each letter of digit d and recurse to depth d+1, recording a combination when the path length equals the number of digits. The result size is the product of the per-digit letter counts.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India lets customers create a vanity reference by typing digits that map to letters on a keypad, like old phone spelling. For each digit you try each of its letters, moving to the next digit, until you've spelled a full word-length combination.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each digit append each of its letters and recurse to the next digit; record when all digits are consumed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Map each digit to its keypad letters and backtrack across the digit positions: at depth d, append each letter of digit d and recurse to depth d+1, recording a combination when the path length equals the number of digits. The result size is the product of the per-digit letter counts.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India lets customers create a vanity reference by typing digits that map to letters on a keypad, like old phone spelling. For each digit you try each of its letters, moving to the next digit, until you've spelled a full word-length combination.

**One line to remember:** For each digit append each of its letters and recurse to the next digit; record when all digits are consumed.

sections.s2_technical:
Store a digit-to-letters map (2 maps to "abc", and so on). Backtrack with an index into the digit string and a StringBuilder path. When the index equals the string length, record the path; otherwise loop over the current digit's letters, append one, recurse with index+1, and remove it. For example: `for (char c : map.get(digit)) { sb.append(c); backtrack(index+1); sb.deleteCharAt(sb.length()-1); }`.

An empty input must return an empty list, not a list containing an empty string, so guard that case. The time is O(4^n · n) in the worst case, since digits seven and nine have four letters each.

A senior nuance is that an iterative queue-based expansion produces the same result without recursion, which can be cleaner when the digit count is large and stack depth is a concern.

answers.question: Given n pairs of parentheses, generate all combinations of well-formed (balanced) parentheses.
answers.shortTitle: Generate Parentheses — track open and close counts

s1_definition.profdef: Backtrack building the string character by character, maintaining counts of open and close parentheses used. Append an open parenthesis while open < n, and append a close parenthesis while close < open; record the string when its length reaches 2n. These two invariants guarantee only valid sequences are ever built, so no validity check is needed at the end.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of opening and closing nested approval brackets in National Bank of India's workflow. You may open a new bracket as long as you have brackets left to open, and you may only close one if there is an open bracket waiting. Follow those two rules and every sequence you build is automatically balanced.
s1_definition.oneliner: Open while open < n, close while close < open, record at length 2n — never generate an invalid string.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Backtrack building the string character by character, maintaining counts of open and close parentheses used. Append an open parenthesis while open < n, and append a close parenthesis while close < open; record the string when its length reaches 2n. These two invariants guarantee only valid sequences are ever built, so no validity check is needed at the end.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of opening and closing nested approval brackets in National Bank of India's workflow. You may open a new bracket as long as you have brackets left to open, and you may only close one if there is an open bracket waiting. Follow those two rules and every sequence you build is automatically balanced.

**One line to remember:** Open while open < n, close while close < open, record at length 2n — never generate an invalid string.

sections.s2_technical:
Carry open and close counts and a StringBuilder. When length is 2n, record the result. Otherwise, if open < n, append '(' and recurse with open+1; if close < open, append ')' and recurse with close+1; undo each append. For example: `if (open < n) { sb.append('('); backtrack(open+1, close); sb.deleteCharAt(last); }`.

The invariant `close < open` is what forbids closing more than has been opened, keeping every prefix valid. Because invalid prefixes are never created, the algorithm visits only the Catalan-number many valid strings.

The count of results is the n-th Catalan number, and the time is proportional to that count times the string length. A senior nuance is that this "build only valid states" approach is far more efficient than generating all 2^(2n) strings and filtering, which is a common naive mistake.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, an approval-rule builder composes nested approval brackets, and the tool must enumerate every well-formed nesting of n bracket pairs for a template picker. This is exactly how Generate Parentheses works.

Problem 2 — A bracket can only be closed if one is currently open, and all brackets must eventually close. This is exactly why the open-and-close count invariants guarantee balanced output.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Generate Parentheses is a backtracking problem where the elegance comes from never building an invalid string in the first place. I track two counts, how many open parentheses and how many close parentheses I have placed, and I build the string character by character. I may append an open parenthesis as long as the open count is below n, and I may append a close parenthesis only when the close count is strictly less than the open count. When the string reaches length two n it is guaranteed balanced, so I record it with no further validation.

The invariant that close must stay below open is what forbids closing a bracket that was never opened, keeping every prefix valid. Because I only ever visit valid states, I generate exactly the n-th Catalan number of strings, which is dramatically better than producing all two-to-the-two-n strings and filtering.

In my project at National Bank of India, an approval-rule builder let designers compose nested approval brackets, and the tool enumerated every well-formed nesting of n pairs for a template picker. This count-invariant backtracking produced only balanced templates, which is both faster and simpler than generate-then-filter.

answers.question: Given a string, partition it so that every substring of the partition is a palindrome, and return all possible palindrome partitionings.
answers.shortTitle: Palindrome Partitioning — backtrack with palindrome check at each cut

s1_definition.profdef: Backtrack over cut positions: at a start index, try every end index, and if the substring start..end is a palindrome, add it to the path and recurse from end+1. When start reaches the string length, the path is a complete valid partition. The palindrome test at each cut prunes branches that can never lead to a valid partition.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India must split a reference string into symmetric blocks for a checksum scheme. At each point you try cutting off a leading block; you keep it only if it reads the same forwards and backwards, then continue splitting the rest. Every way of splitting into all-symmetric blocks is a valid answer.
s1_definition.oneliner: Try every prefix cut, keep only palindromic prefixes, recurse on the remainder until the whole string is consumed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Backtrack over cut positions: at a start index, try every end index, and if the substring start..end is a palindrome, add it to the path and recurse from end+1. When start reaches the string length, the path is a complete valid partition. The palindrome test at each cut prunes branches that can never lead to a valid partition.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India must split a reference string into symmetric blocks for a checksum scheme. At each point you try cutting off a leading block; you keep it only if it reads the same forwards and backwards, then continue splitting the rest. Every way of splitting into all-symmetric blocks is a valid answer.

**One line to remember:** Try every prefix cut, keep only palindromic prefixes, recurse on the remainder until the whole string is consumed.

sections.s2_technical:
Carry a start index and a path of substrings. When start equals the length, record a copy of the path. Otherwise loop end from start to the end; if substring start..end is a palindrome, add it, recurse from end+1, and remove it. For example: `if (isPalindrome(s,start,end)) { path.add(s.substring(start,end+1)); backtrack(end+1); path.remove(last); }`.

The palindrome check uses two pointers moving inward. For better performance you can precompute a boolean DP table isPal[i][j] so each check is O(1), making the overall cost dominated by the number of partitions.

The worst-case time is O(n · 2^n) because a string of all identical characters has 2^(n-1) partitions, each of length up to n. A senior nuance is that the DP precomputation turns repeated palindrome checks from O(n) each into O(1), which matters on adversarial inputs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a legacy reference code must be split into symmetric segments for a validation scheme, and the tool needs every valid segmentation. This is exactly how palindrome partitioning works.

Problem 2 — A segment is only acceptable if it is a palindrome, and the segments together must cover the whole code. This is exactly why each prefix is palindrome-checked before recursing on the remainder.

Step 3: Back at start zero, the prefix "aa" is a palindrome, so recurse on "b".

Step 4: "b" is a palindrome, giving the partition [aa, b].

```text
  │  - isPalindrome(s,lo,hi): boolean     │
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Palindrome Partitioning asks for every way to split a string so that each piece is a palindrome. I solve it with backtracking over cut positions: from a start index I try every possible end index, and if the substring from start to end is a palindrome I add it to the current path and recurse from the position just after it. When the start index reaches the end of the string, the path holds a complete valid partition and I record a copy.

The palindrome check at each cut is what prunes the search, because a non-palindromic prefix can never belong to a valid partition and that branch is abandoned immediately. For adversarial inputs like a run of identical characters I precompute a boolean table of which substrings are palindromes, turning each check into constant time; the worst-case number of partitions is still exponential.

In my project at National Bank of India, a legacy reference code had to be split into symmetric segments for a validation scheme, and the tool enumerated every valid segmentation. The backtracking produced them in order, and the precomputed palindrome table kept it fast on the pathological all-same-character references.

answers.question: Given a 2D board of characters and a word, return true if the word exists in the grid by connecting horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, where each cell is used at most once.
answers.shortTitle: Word Search — DFS on a grid with visited marking

s1_definition.profdef: For each cell matching the first letter, run a depth-first search that matches successive letters by moving to the four orthogonal neighbors, marking the current cell visited to prevent reuse within the path, and unmarking it on backtrack. Return true as soon as the full word is matched; otherwise continue from other start cells.
s1_definition.analogy: On a grid of stamped characters at National Bank of India, you trace a security phrase by stepping up, down, left, or right onto the next matching character, never stepping on the same cell twice in one trace. If you can spell the whole phrase, it exists on the grid.
s1_definition.oneliner: DFS from each matching start, mark cells visited along the path, unmark on backtrack, succeed when the word is fully matched.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** For each cell matching the first letter, run a depth-first search that matches successive letters by moving to the four orthogonal neighbors, marking the current cell visited to prevent reuse within the path, and unmarking it on backtrack. Return true as soon as the full word is matched; otherwise continue from other start cells.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** On a grid of stamped characters at National Bank of India, you trace a security phrase by stepping up, down, left, or right onto the next matching character, never stepping on the same cell twice in one trace. If you can spell the whole phrase, it exists on the grid.

**One line to remember:** DFS from each matching start, mark cells visited along the path, unmark on backtrack, succeed when the word is fully matched.

sections.s2_technical:
For each cell, call a DFS carrying the index of the next character to match. If the index equals the word length, return true. If out of bounds, mismatched, or already visited, return false. Otherwise mark the cell (for instance temporarily overwrite it), try the four directions, then restore it. For example: `char tmp = board[r][c]; board[r][c] = '#'; boolean found = dfs(...up) || ...; board[r][c] = tmp;`.

Temporarily overwriting the cell is a common trick to mark visited without a separate array, restored on backtrack so other search paths can use it. Short-circuiting with `||` returns as soon as any direction succeeds.

The time is O(rows · cols · 4^L) in the worst case where L is the word length, because each start can branch four ways per letter. A senior nuance is pruning start cells by an early frequency check: if the board lacks enough of any letter in the word, fail fast.

Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a grid of stamped characters encodes security phrases, and a verifier must confirm whether a given phrase can be traced through adjacent cells. This is exactly how Word Search works.

Problem 2 — A single trace may not reuse a cell, though different traces may reuse it. This is exactly why cells are marked visited along the current path and restored on backtrack.

The input is a three-by-three grid and the phrase NBIEY.

Step 1: DFS starts at (0,0) matching N, marks it, and moves right to (0,1) matching B.

Step 2: From B it moves right to (0,2) matching I, then down to (1,2) matching E, then down to (2,2) matching Y.

Step 3: The index now equals the phrase length, so the trace returns true and each visited cell is restored on the way back.

Step 4: For NBZ, no neighbor of B matches Z, so all branches fail and the verifier returns false.

```text
  start cells matching word[0]='N' → (0,0)
    (0,0)N → (0,1)B → (0,2)I → (1,2)E → (2,2)Y → idx==len → TRUE
    mark '#' on enter, restore on exit (path-local visited)
  NBZ: B has no 'Z' neighbor → FALSE
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Search is grid backtracking. I scan the board for cells matching the first letter and launch a depth-first search from each, carrying the index of the next letter I need to match. The search succeeds when that index reaches the word length, and it fails when I step off the board, hit a mismatch, or revisit a cell already on the current path. For each matching cell I mark it visited, try all four orthogonal directions, and then restore it on the way back so other search paths can still use it.

A neat trick is to mark the cell by temporarily overwriting its character with a sentinel and restoring it on backtrack, which avoids a separate visited array. The short-circuit or across the four directions returns as soon as any one succeeds. The worst case is the board size times four to the word length.

In my project at National Bank of India, a grid of stamped characters encoded security phrases and a verifier confirmed whether a given phrase could be traced through adjacent cells without reusing a cell. The DFS-with-restore pattern handled it directly, and I added a quick letter-frequency pre-check so phrases requiring letters the board lacked failed fast.

answers.question: Place n queens on an n×n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other, and return all distinct solutions (or the count).
answers.shortTitle: N-Queens — place queens row by row, check conflicts

s1_definition.profdef: Backtrack one row at a time, trying each column in the current row and placing a queen only where no existing queen shares the column or either diagonal. Track occupied columns and both diagonal families (row−col and row+col) in sets for O(1) conflict checks. When all n rows are filled, record the board configuration.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine placing n non-conflicting audit checkpoints on an n-by-n schedule grid where no two checkpoints may share a column or a diagonal time-slot. You fill one row at a time, placing a checkpoint only in a safe column, and backtrack whenever a row has no safe spot.
s1_definition.oneliner: One queen per row; a column is safe if its column and both diagonals are free; backtrack when a row is stuck.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Backtrack one row at a time, trying each column in the current row and placing a queen only where no existing queen shares the column or either diagonal. Track occupied columns and both diagonal families (row−col and row+col) in sets for O(1) conflict checks. When all n rows are filled, record the board configuration.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine placing n non-conflicting audit checkpoints on an n-by-n schedule grid where no two checkpoints may share a column or a diagonal time-slot. You fill one row at a time, placing a checkpoint only in a safe column, and backtrack whenever a row has no safe spot.

**One line to remember:** One queen per row; a column is safe if its column and both diagonals are free; backtrack when a row is stuck.

sections.s2_technical:
Recurse by row. For each column in the row, check three sets: used columns, the "down-right" diagonal keyed by row−col, and the "down-left" diagonal keyed by row+col. If all are free, place the queen (add keys), recurse to the next row, then remove the keys. For example: `if (!cols.contains(c) && !diag1.contains(r-c) && !diag2.contains(r+c)) { place; backtrack(r+1); unplace; }`.

Using row−col and row+col as diagonal identifiers gives constant-time conflict checks, which is far faster than scanning the board each time. When the row index reaches n, a full valid placement exists and is recorded.

The time is bounded by the branching of columns per row with heavy pruning, far below n to the n in practice. A senior nuance is that the two diagonal invariants (difference constant and sum constant) are the key insight that makes the conflict test O(1).

sections.s6_takeaway:
N-Queens is the classic constraint-satisfaction backtracking problem. I place one queen per row and, for each row, try every column, placing a queen only where it does not conflict with any already-placed queen. The key to making the conflict test fast is tracking three sets: the occupied columns, one diagonal family keyed by row minus column, and the other keyed by row plus column. Those two diagonal identities are the insight that turns each conflict check into a constant-time set lookup instead of a board scan.

When I place a queen I add its column and both diagonal keys, recurse to the next row, and on backtrack I remove exactly those keys. Reaching row n means all queens are placed without conflict, so I record the configuration. The pruning from the three sets keeps the real search far below the naive n-to-the-n bound.

In my project at National Bank of India, compliance needed to place n audit checkpoints on an n-by-n scheduling grid so that no two conflicted by column or diagonal time-slot, and it wanted every valid arrangement. The row-by-row backtracking with constant-time conflict sets produced all placements efficiently, which is exactly the N-Queens template applied to a scheduling constraint.

answers.question: Write a program to solve a 9×9 Sudoku board by filling empty cells so that every row, column, and 3×3 box contains the digits 1–9 exactly once.
answers.shortTitle: Sudoku Solver — row, column, and box constraint checking

s1_definition.profdef: Backtracking over empty cells: find the next empty cell, try digits 1–9, place a digit only if it is absent from its row, column, and 3×3 box, then recurse. If the recursion fails, undo and try the next digit; if no digit works, return false to trigger backtracking higher up. The board is solved when no empty cell remains.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a 9-by-9 reconciliation grid at National Bank of India where each row, column, and sub-block must contain each code exactly once. You fill the first blank with a candidate that does not already appear in its row, column, or block, move on, and if you get stuck you erase and try a different candidate.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fill each empty cell with a digit valid in its row, column, and box; recurse; undo on dead ends until the grid is complete.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Backtracking over empty cells: find the next empty cell, try digits 1–9, place a digit only if it is absent from its row, column, and 3×3 box, then recurse. If the recursion fails, undo and try the next digit; if no digit works, return false to trigger backtracking higher up. The board is solved when no empty cell remains.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a 9-by-9 reconciliation grid at National Bank of India where each row, column, and sub-block must contain each code exactly once. You fill the first blank with a candidate that does not already appear in its row, column, or block, move on, and if you get stuck you erase and try a different candidate.

**One line to remember:** Fill each empty cell with a digit valid in its row, column, and box; recurse; undo on dead ends until the grid is complete.

sections.s2_technical:
Scan for an empty cell (a dot). For each digit one to nine, check validity against the same row, column, and the 3×3 box whose top-left is `(r/3)*3, (c/3)*3`. If valid, place it and recurse; if the recursion returns true the board is solved, otherwise reset the cell to empty and try the next digit. For example: `if (isValid(board,r,c,d)) { board[r][c]=d; if (solve(board)) return true; board[r][c]='.'; }`.

Returning true all the way up on the first complete fill stops the search, since Sudoku asks for one solution. The box index arithmetic maps any cell to its 3×3 region for the uniqueness check.

The worst-case time is exponential, but real puzzles are solved quickly because the row/column/box checks prune most branches immediately. A senior nuance is the minimum-remaining-value heuristic (fill the most constrained cell first), which dramatically speeds up hard puzzles.

Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a 9-by-9 reconciliation grid must be completed so each row, column, and sub-block holds each code exactly once, and the tool must fill the blanks automatically. This is exactly how a Sudoku solver works.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Sudoku solver is backtracking over the empty cells of the grid. I find the next empty cell, try the digits one through nine in it, and place a digit only when it does not already appear in that cell's row, its column, or its three-by-three box. After placing a valid digit I recurse; if the recursion eventually fills the whole grid I propagate true all the way up and stop, and if it gets stuck I reset the cell to empty and try the next digit. When a cell has no valid digit at all I return false, which triggers backtracking in the caller.

The box-index arithmetic, taking row over three times three and column over three times three, maps any cell to its region for the uniqueness check. Real puzzles solve quickly because the three-way validity check prunes most candidates immediately, even though the worst case is exponential.

In my project at National Bank of India, a nine-by-nine reconciliation grid had to be completed so each row, column, and sub-block contained each code exactly once, and the tool filled the blanks automatically. This constraint backtracking solved it reliably, and for the hardest grids I applied the minimum-remaining-value heuristic, always filling the most constrained cell first, which cut the search time sharply.

answers.question: How do you recognize that a problem should be solved with dynamic programming? Explain overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure, and the difference between memoization and tabulation.
answers.shortTitle: How to Identify a DP Problem — overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure

s1_definition.profdef: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has optimal substructure (an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions of subproblems) and overlapping subproblems (the same subproblems recur). You then cache subproblem answers. Memoization is top-down recursion that stores results on first computation; tabulation is bottom-up iteration that fills a table in dependency order. Both convert exponential recursion into polynomial time.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, computing a daily settlement total depends on smaller totals you already computed, and those smaller totals get asked for again and again. Instead of recomputing them, you write each answer in a ledger the first time and read it back later. DP is just "solve each piece once, store it, reuse it."
s1_definition.oneliner: If subproblems repeat and the best overall answer is built from best sub-answers, cache them — that's dynamic programming.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Dynamic programming applies when a problem has optimal substructure (an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions of subproblems) and overlapping subproblems (the same subproblems recur). You then cache subproblem answers. Memoization is top-down recursion that stores results on first computation; tabulation is bottom-up iteration that fills a table in dependency order. Both convert exponential recursion into polynomial time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, computing a daily settlement total depends on smaller totals you already computed, and those smaller totals get asked for again and again. Instead of recomputing them, you write each answer in a ledger the first time and read it back later. DP is just "solve each piece once, store it, reuse it."

**One line to remember:** If subproblems repeat and the best overall answer is built from best sub-answers, cache them — that's dynamic programming.

sections.s2_technical:
Optimal substructure means the final answer can be expressed as a combination of answers to smaller instances; for example, the cheapest way to make an amount uses the cheapest way to make a smaller amount plus one coin. Overlapping subproblems means a naive recursion revisits identical states, like Fibonacci recomputing fib(3) many times.

Memoization keeps the natural recursion but adds a cache checked at entry. For example: `if (memo.containsKey(n)) return memo.get(n); int r = solve(n-1)+solve(n-2); memo.put(n, r); return r;`.

Tabulation removes recursion and fills an array from base cases upward in an order where every dependency is already computed. For example: `dp[0]=0; dp[1]=1; for (i=2..n) dp[i]=dp[i-1]+dp[i-2];`.

Both are the same complexity; tabulation avoids recursion-stack overhead and enables space optimization by keeping only the last few states. A senior nuance is that many 2D tabulations compress to 1D (or two rows) once you notice each row depends only on the previous one.

Problem 2 — The projection's best answer is composed of best sub-answers, so caching is valid. This is exactly optimal substructure, and the demo contrasts memoization and tabulation on the same recurrence.

sections.s6_takeaway:
I identify a dynamic programming problem by checking for two properties. The first is optimal substructure, meaning the best overall answer can be assembled from the best answers to smaller subproblems; the second is overlapping subproblems, meaning a naive recursion would solve the same subproblem many times. When both hold, caching subproblem answers turns an exponential recursion into a polynomial algorithm.

There are two styles. Memoization is top-down: I keep the natural recursion but add a cache that I check on entry and populate on first computation, so each state is solved once. Tabulation is bottom-up: I fill a table starting from the base cases in an order where every dependency is already computed, which avoids recursion-stack overhead and often lets me shrink the table to just the last few states, giving constant space.

In my project at National Bank of India, an interest projection recomputed the same intermediate subtotals repeatedly, which was the tell-tale sign of overlapping subproblems, and because the projection was built from smaller projections it had optimal substructure. I implemented it both top-down with a cache and bottom-up with two rolling variables, and the bottom-up version ran in linear time with constant memory.

answers.question: You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. In how many distinct ways can you reach the top of n stairs?
answers.shortTitle: Climbing Stairs — dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]

s1_definition.profdef: The number of ways to reach step i equals the ways to reach step i−1 (then take a single step) plus the ways to reach step i−2 (then take a double step), so dp[i] = dp[i−1] + dp[i−2] with base cases dp[0]=1 and dp[1]=1. This is the Fibonacci recurrence, solvable bottom-up in linear time and constant space.
s1_definition.analogy: A customer at National Bank of India climbs a rewards tier ladder one or two tiers at a time. The ways to reach a given tier is the ways to reach the tier just below (then step one) plus the ways to reach two tiers below (then step two). Add those and you have the count for every tier.
s1_definition.oneliner: Ways to reach step i = ways to i−1 plus ways to i−2 — it's Fibonacci.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The number of ways to reach step i equals the ways to reach step i−1 (then take a single step) plus the ways to reach step i−2 (then take a double step), so dp[i] = dp[i−1] + dp[i−2] with base cases dp[0]=1 and dp[1]=1. This is the Fibonacci recurrence, solvable bottom-up in linear time and constant space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A customer at National Bank of India climbs a rewards tier ladder one or two tiers at a time. The ways to reach a given tier is the ways to reach the tier just below (then step one) plus the ways to reach two tiers below (then step two). Add those and you have the count for every tier.

**One line to remember:** Ways to reach step i = ways to i−1 plus ways to i−2 — it's Fibonacci.

sections.s2_technical:
The last move into step i is either a single step from i−1 or a double step from i−2, and those two groups of paths are disjoint and cover all possibilities, so you add them. For example: `dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2];`.

Base cases: there is one way to stand at the ground (do nothing) and one way to reach the first step. Iterating upward keeps only the last two values, since dp[i] depends on just the previous two. For example: `cur = prev1 + prev2; prev2 = prev1; prev1 = cur;`.

The time is O(n) and the space is O(1) with the rolling variables. A senior nuance is that a generalized "climb up to k steps" variant sums the previous k values, which is the k-step Fibonacci and still linear.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Climbing Stairs is the gateway dynamic programming problem, and it is just Fibonacci in disguise. The number of distinct ways to reach step i is the number of ways to reach step i minus one, from which you take a single step, plus the number of ways to reach step i minus two, from which you take a double step. Those two sets of paths are disjoint and together cover every possibility, so I add them, giving the recurrence dp of i equals dp of i minus one plus dp of i minus two.

The base cases are one way to be at the ground and one way to reach the first step. Because each value depends only on the previous two, I keep two rolling variables instead of a full array, which gives linear time and constant space.

In my project at National Bank of India, a loyalty ladder let members advance one or two tiers per action, and marketing wanted the count of distinct progression paths to a target tier. This rolling Fibonacci computation answered it instantly, and I noted that a generalized up-to-k-steps variant simply sums the previous k counts and remains linear.

answers.question: Given an array of non-negative house values, find the maximum amount you can rob without robbing two adjacent houses.
answers.shortTitle: House Robber — cannot rob adjacent houses

s1_definition.profdef: At each house i the best achievable total is the larger of skipping it (carry forward the best up to i−1) or robbing it (its value plus the best up to i−2), giving dp[i] = max(dp[i−1], nums[i] + dp[i−2]). Rolling two variables yields the maximum in linear time and constant space. The adjacency constraint is encoded by reaching back two positions when robbing.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India selecting non-adjacent time slots to run high-value promotions, since two back-to-back slots conflict. At each slot you either skip it and keep your running best, or take it and add it to your best from two slots ago. You keep whichever is larger.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each house take the max of skip (best so far) or rob (value plus best from two back).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** At each house i the best achievable total is the larger of skipping it (carry forward the best up to i−1) or robbing it (its value plus the best up to i−2), giving dp[i] = max(dp[i−1], nums[i] + dp[i−2]). Rolling two variables yields the maximum in linear time and constant space. The adjacency constraint is encoded by reaching back two positions when robbing.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of National Bank of India selecting non-adjacent time slots to run high-value promotions, since two back-to-back slots conflict. At each slot you either skip it and keep your running best, or take it and add it to your best from two slots ago. You keep whichever is larger.

**One line to remember:** For each house take the max of skip (best so far) or rob (value plus best from two back).

sections.s2_technical:
Maintain two running bests: the best including up to the previous house and up to the house before that. At each house compute the new best as the larger of carrying the previous best forward or robbing the current house plus the best two houses back. For example: `cur = Math.max(prev1, nums[i] + prev2); prev2 = prev1; prev1 = cur;`.

Robbing the current house forbids the immediately previous one, which is why you add to prev2 (two houses back) rather than prev1. Skipping simply inherits prev1.

The time is O(n) and the space is O(1). A senior nuance is House Robber II, where the houses form a circle so the first and last are adjacent; you solve it by running the linear version twice, once excluding the first house and once excluding the last, and taking the max.

House Robber is a one-dimensional decision DP. answers.question: Given an array of daily prices, find the maximum profit from a single buy and a single later sell. If no profit is possible, return 0.
answers.shortTitle: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock — track min price and max profit

s1_definition.profdef: Scan prices once, maintaining the minimum price seen so far and the maximum profit achievable by selling on the current day (current price minus the running minimum). Update both each day; the answer is the maximum profit, defaulting to zero when prices only fall. This is a single-pass O(n) greedy/DP hybrid using O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: A trader at National Bank of India wants to buy a share on one day and sell it on a later day for the biggest gain. As you walk through the days, you remember the cheapest price so far and ask, "if I sell today, how much do I make?" You keep the best such answer.
s1_definition.oneliner: Track the lowest price so far and the best sell-today profit; the maximum of those profits is the answer.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Scan prices once, maintaining the minimum price seen so far and the maximum profit achievable by selling on the current day (current price minus the running minimum). Update both each day; the answer is the maximum profit, defaulting to zero when prices only fall. This is a single-pass O(n) greedy/DP hybrid using O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A trader at National Bank of India wants to buy a share on one day and sell it on a later day for the biggest gain. As you walk through the days, you remember the cheapest price so far and ask, "if I sell today, how much do I make?" You keep the best such answer.

**One line to remember:** Track the lowest price so far and the best sell-today profit; the maximum of those profits is the answer.

sections.s2_technical:
Initialize the minimum price to the first day and max profit to zero. Each day, update the minimum if the price is lower, else compute the profit of selling today and update the max profit. For example: `minPrice = Math.min(minPrice, p); maxProfit = Math.max(maxProfit, p - minPrice);`.

Because you only ever sell after buying at the running minimum, every candidate respects the buy-before-sell order. If prices only decline, max profit stays zero, correctly signaling no profitable trade.

The time is O(n) and the space is O(1). A senior nuance is that the multi-transaction variant (Stock II) sums every positive day-to-day difference, and the with-cooldown variant becomes a small state machine, so recognizing which variant you face dictates the technique.

Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock for a single transaction is a clean single-pass algorithm. I walk through the prices maintaining two things: the lowest price seen so far, which is the best day to have bought, and the best profit I could lock in by selling on the current day, which is the current price minus that running minimum. Each day I either lower the minimum or update the maximum profit, and the answer is that maximum, defaulting to zero when the market only declines.

Because I always compute the sell profit against a minimum that occurred earlier in the scan, every candidate respects the buy-before-sell ordering automatically, so I never need to compare all pairs of days. It runs in linear time and constant space.

In my project at National Bank of India's trading desk, a strategy identified the maximum single-trade gain over a price history, and this running-minimum approach computed it in one pass over the live feed. I always clarify which variant is in play, because the multi-transaction version just sums every positive day-to-day move and the cooldown version becomes a small state machine, so naming the variant determines the right technique.

answers.question: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return that sum. Explain Kadane's algorithm.
answers.shortTitle: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's Algorithm) — running sum reset at negatives

s1_definition.profdef: Kadane's algorithm scans once, maintaining the best subarray sum ending at the current index as current = max(num, current + num), and the global answer as the max over all current values. Restarting with num alone whenever the running sum would hurt (current + num < num) captures the optimal ending-here sum, so the global maximum emerges in O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: Scanning daily net cash flows at National Bank of India, you track the best streak ending today: either extend yesterday's streak by today's amount, or start fresh today if the past streak is dragging you down. The best streak ever seen is your answer.
s1_definition.oneliner: current = max(num, current + num); answer = max(answer, current) — extend or restart each step.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kadane's algorithm scans once, maintaining the best subarray sum ending at the current index as current = max(num, current + num), and the global answer as the max over all current values. Restarting with num alone whenever the running sum would hurt (current + num < num) captures the optimal ending-here sum, so the global maximum emerges in O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Scanning daily net cash flows at National Bank of India, you track the best streak ending today: either extend yesterday's streak by today's amount, or start fresh today if the past streak is dragging you down. The best streak ever seen is your answer.

**One line to remember:** current = max(num, current + num); answer = max(answer, current) — extend or restart each step.

sections.s2_technical:
Initialize both current and answer to the first element. For each subsequent number, set current to the larger of the number alone or current plus the number, then update answer. For example: `current = Math.max(num, current + num); best = Math.max(best, current);`.

Choosing the number alone effectively discards a negative prefix, because any prefix that made the running sum worse than starting fresh can never be part of an optimal subarray ending here. Initializing to the first element (not zero) handles all-negative arrays correctly, returning the largest single element.

The time is O(n) and the space is O(1). A senior nuance is that tracking the start and end indices alongside the sums recovers the actual subarray, and that a divide-and-conquer solution exists in O(n log n) but Kadane's linear scan is strictly better.

Maximum Subarray is solved by Kadane's algorithm in a single linear pass. I keep two values: the best subarray sum ending exactly at the current position, and the best sum seen anywhere so far. At each element I set the ending-here sum to the larger of the element alone or the previous ending-here sum plus the element, which is the decision to either start a fresh subarray or extend the existing one. Then I update the global best.

Restarting with the element alone is what discards a harmful negative prefix, because any prefix that dragged the running sum below starting fresh can never be part of an optimal subarray ending at this position. Initializing both values to the first element, rather than zero, is the detail that makes all-negative arrays return the largest single element correctly.

answers.question: Given coin denominations and a target amount, return the fewest number of coins needed to make that amount, or -1 if it cannot be made.
answers.shortTitle: Coin Change — minimum coins to make an amount

s1_definition.profdef: Bottom-up DP where dp[a] is the minimum coins to make amount a, initialized to a sentinel (amount+1) and dp[0]=0. For each amount from 1 to target and each coin that fits, dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a−coin]+1). The answer is dp[target], or −1 if it remains the sentinel, computed in O(amount · coins) time.
s1_definition.analogy: A teller at National Bank of India must hand out an exact amount using the fewest notes from available denominations. For each amount, the best (fewest notes) is one more than the best for the amount left after removing one note, tried across every denomination that fits. You build the table upward to the target.
s1_definition.oneliner: dp[a] = min over coins of dp[a−coin] + 1; sentinel means unreachable, so return -1.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Bottom-up DP where dp[a] is the minimum coins to make amount a, initialized to a sentinel (amount+1) and dp[0]=0. For each amount from 1 to target and each coin that fits, dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a−coin]+1). The answer is dp[target], or −1 if it remains the sentinel, computed in O(amount · coins) time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A teller at National Bank of India must hand out an exact amount using the fewest notes from available denominations. For each amount, the best (fewest notes) is one more than the best for the amount left after removing one note, tried across every denomination that fits. You build the table upward to the target.

**One line to remember:** dp[a] = min over coins of dp[a−coin] + 1; sentinel means unreachable, so return -1.

sections.s2_technical:
Create dp of size amount+1, fill with a sentinel larger than any real answer, and set dp[0] to zero because zero amount needs zero coins. For each amount a, try every coin that does not exceed a and relax the minimum. For example: `if (coin <= a) dp[a] = Math.min(dp[a], dp[a - coin] + 1);`.

Iterating amounts outward guarantees dp[a−coin] is already final when used, which is why this is unbounded (coins reusable): the inner coin loop may use the same denomination repeatedly across increasing amounts. At the end, if dp[target] is still the sentinel the target is unreachable, so return −1.

The time is O(amount · number of coins) and the space is O(amount). A senior nuance is that this is the minimization variant of the unbounded knapsack, and greedy (always take the largest coin) fails for arbitrary denominations, which is exactly why DP is required rather than greedy.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Coin Change for the minimum number of coins is a bottom-up dynamic programming problem. I define dp of a as the fewest coins to make amount a, initialize every entry to a sentinel larger than any possible answer, and set dp of zero to zero because no coins are needed for a zero amount. Then for each amount from one up to the target I try every coin that fits and relax the value to the minimum of its current value and one plus dp of the amount remaining after that coin.

Iterating the amounts outward guarantees that the subproblem dp of amount-minus-coin is already final when I use it, and because the inner loop can pick the same denomination at every larger amount, coins are effectively unlimited. If dp of the target is still the sentinel at the end, the amount is unreachable and I return minus one.

In my project at National Bank of India, an ATM had to dispense an exact amount using the fewest notes from its available denominations, and some amounts were impossible with the loaded cassettes. I used this DP rather than a greedy largest-note-first rule, because greedy fails for arbitrary denomination sets, whereas the bottom-up relaxation always finds the true minimum or correctly reports that the amount cannot be dispensed.

answers.question: Given coin denominations and a target amount, return the total number of distinct combinations that make up that amount (order does not matter). Coins may be reused.
answers.shortTitle: Coin Change II — number of ways to make an amount

s1_definition.profdef: Unbounded-knapsack counting DP where dp[a] is the number of combinations that sum to amount a. We iterate coins in the OUTER loop and amounts in the INNER loop so each combination is counted once regardless of order, using dp[a] += dp[a−coin]. Base case dp[0]=1, time O(amount · coins), space O(amount).
s1_definition.analogy: A teller at National Bank of India wants to know how many different note combinations add up to a requested amount. For each denomination she adds in turn, she extends every smaller total by that note. Putting the coin loop outside stops her from counting "5 then 1" and "1 then 5" as two different ways.
s1_definition.oneliner: Coins outside, amounts inside, dp[a] += dp[a−coin], dp[0]=1 counts combinations not permutations.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Unbounded-knapsack counting DP where dp[a] is the number of combinations that sum to amount a. We iterate coins in the OUTER loop and amounts in the INNER loop so each combination is counted once regardless of order, using dp[a] += dp[a−coin]. Base case dp[0]=1, time O(amount · coins), space O(amount).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A teller at National Bank of India wants to know how many different note combinations add up to a requested amount. For each denomination she adds in turn, she extends every smaller total by that note. Putting the coin loop outside stops her from counting "5 then 1" and "1 then 5" as two different ways.

**One line to remember:** Coins outside, amounts inside, dp[a] += dp[a−coin], dp[0]=1 counts combinations not permutations.

sections.s2_technical:
Create dp of size amount+1, set dp[0] to one because there is exactly one way to make zero (take nothing), and leave the rest zero. Then loop over each coin on the outside and, for each coin, sweep amounts from the coin value up to target adding dp[a−coin]. For example: `for (int coin : coins) for (int a = coin; a <= amount; a++) dp[a] += dp[a - coin];`.

The order matters deeply. If amounts were outside and coins inside, you would count ordered sequences (permutations) and overcount. Coin-outer means each denomination is fully considered before moving on, so combinations are counted exactly once.

The time is O(amount · number of coins) and space is O(amount). A senior nuance is that this is the counting twin of the minimization Coin Change, and the loop order is the single most common bug: swapping the loops silently changes the answer from combinations to permutations.

The input denominations are one, two, five with target five.

Step 1: dp[0] is one and every other entry starts at zero.

Step 2: After processing coin one, every amount has exactly one combination (all ones), so dp[5] is one.

Step 3: After processing coin two, dp[5] grows to count combinations using twos, reaching three.

Step 4: After processing coin five, dp[5] gains the single-five combination, reaching four.

Step 5: The final answers are four ways for five and zero ways for three using only twos.

```text
2026-10-27T01:20:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — ATM Combination Planner (Coin Change II)
2026-10-27T01:20:00Z [INFO] Amount 5 has 4 combinations
2026-10-27T01:20:00Z [INFO] 5 with {1,2,5} → 4
2026-10-27T01:20:00Z [INFO] Amount 3 has 0 combinations
2026-10-27T01:20:00Z [INFO] 3 with {2} → 0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  dp[0]=1, rest=0
    for coin in {1,2,5}:        ← coin OUTER = combinations
      for a=coin..5: dp[a] += dp[a-coin]
  after coin1: dp[5]=1 ; after coin2: dp[5]=3 ; after coin5: dp[5]=4
```
