sections.s6_takeaway:
Coin Change II is a counting dynamic programming problem on the unbounded knapsack. I define dp of a as the number of distinct combinations that sum to amount a, I set dp of zero to one because there is exactly one way to make nothing, and I leave the rest at zero. Then for each coin I sweep amounts from the coin value up to the target and add dp of the amount minus the coin.

The single most important detail is the loop order. The coin loop must be on the outside and the amount loop on the inside, because that counts each combination exactly once. If I reversed them I would count ordered sequences, so five then one and one then five would be treated as two different ways, which overcounts.

In my project at National Bank of India, a cash-planning tool needed to report how many distinct note combinations could satisfy a withdrawal so the ATM team could gauge flexibility. I used this counting DP with the coin loop outside, and I always call out the loop order in interviews because swapping it is the classic silent bug that turns combinations into permutations.

answers.question: Given two strings, return the length of their longest common subsequence — characters that appear in both in the same relative order but not necessarily contiguously.
answers.shortTitle: Longest Common Subsequence — 2D DP on two strings

s1_definition.profdef: Classic 2D DP where dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i characters of string A and first j of string B. If the characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]+1; otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]). Time O(m·n), space O(m·n) or O(min(m,n)) with a rolling row.
s1_definition.analogy: Two branches of National Bank of India each keep a transaction-code log. The compliance team wants the longest shared ordered pattern. When the current codes match, the shared pattern grows by one; when they differ, the best is whichever side we drop a character from.
s1_definition.oneliner: Match ⇒ diagonal+1; mismatch ⇒ max of top and left.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Classic 2D DP where dp[i][j] is the LCS length of the first i characters of string A and first j of string B. If the characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]+1; otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]). Time O(m·n), space O(m·n) or O(min(m,n)) with a rolling row.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Two branches of National Bank of India each keep a transaction-code log. The compliance team wants the longest shared ordered pattern. When the current codes match, the shared pattern grows by one; when they differ, the best is whichever side we drop a character from.

**One line to remember:** Match ⇒ diagonal+1; mismatch ⇒ max of top and left.

sections.s2_technical:
Build a table of size (m+1) by (n+1) with a zero border, where dp[i][j] answers the subproblem for prefixes of length i and j. When A.charAt(i−1) equals B.charAt(j−1) the characters can join the subsequence, so dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]+1. For example: `if (a.charAt(i-1)==b.charAt(j-1)) dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1]+1;`.

When they differ we cannot extend, so we take the better of ignoring the last character of A or of B: `else dp[i][j]=Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);`. The answer sits in dp[m][n].

Time and space are both O(m·n), reducible to O(min(m,n)) because each row needs only the previous row. A senior nuance is that LCS underlies file-diff tools and edit-distance variants, and reconstructing the actual subsequence requires backtracking through the table from dp[m][n].

Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, compliance compares two accounts' ordered transaction-code logs to find the longest shared ordered pattern that might indicate coordinated activity. This is exactly how Longest Common Subsequence works.

Problem 2 — Shared codes need not be adjacent, only in the same order, so a contiguous match test is wrong. This is exactly why the DP allows skipping characters on either side.

sections.s5_journey:
The input strings are abcde and ace.

Step 1: The table starts with a zero top row and zero left column representing empty prefixes.

Step 2: The letter a matches a, giving dp of one at that cell by taking the diagonal plus one.

Step 3: The letter c matches c and the letter e matches e, each extending the best diagonal, building toward three.

Step 4: Mismatched cells copy the larger of the top or left neighbor, carrying the best found so far.

Step 5: The bottom-right cell holds three, and abc versus def finds no shared letters so it holds zero.

```text
2026-10-27T01:30:00Z [INFO] abcde vs ace → 3
2026-10-27T01:30:00Z [INFO] LCS(abc,def) = 0
2026-10-27T01:30:00Z [INFO] abc vs def → 0
```

```text
  d    0  1  2  2
  e    0  1  2  3   ← dp[m][n] = 3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Common Subsequence is the textbook two-dimensional dynamic programming problem. I define dp of i and j as the length of the longest common subsequence of the first i characters of the first string and the first j characters of the second. I keep a zero border for empty prefixes, and I fill the table row by row.

The transition has two cases. When the current characters match, they can join the subsequence, so the answer is one plus the diagonal cell. When they differ I cannot extend, so I take the larger of dropping the last character of either string, which is the maximum of the top and the left cell. The answer is the bottom-right cell, and I can reconstruct the actual subsequence by walking back through the table.

In my project at National Bank of India, compliance compared two accounts' ordered transaction-code logs to find the longest shared ordered pattern that might indicate coordinated activity. Because shared codes do not have to be adjacent, only in the same order, I used this subsequence DP rather than a contiguous-match test, and the same table structure is what powers file-diff tools and edit distance.

answers.question: Given an array of integers, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. Aim for O(n log n).
answers.shortTitle: Longest Increasing Subsequence — O(n log n) patience sort

s1_definition.profdef: Patience-sorting DP that maintains a tails array where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each number, binary-search the first tail that is greater than or equal to it and replace it (or append if larger than all). The tails length is the LIS length, computed in O(n log n) time, O(n) space.
s1_definition.analogy: A portfolio analyst at National Bank of India scans a daily price stream and tracks the longest run of rising prices, not necessarily consecutive. She keeps a shelf of candidate runs ordered by their smallest ending value and slots each new price into the tightest fit, which keeps every run as extendable as possible.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep smallest tails; binary-search the slot; tails length is the LIS.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Patience-sorting DP that maintains a tails array where tails[k] is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each number, binary-search the first tail that is greater than or equal to it and replace it (or append if larger than all). The tails length is the LIS length, computed in O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A portfolio analyst at National Bank of India scans a daily price stream and tracks the longest run of rising prices, not necessarily consecutive. She keeps a shelf of candidate runs ordered by their smallest ending value and slots each new price into the tightest fit, which keeps every run as extendable as possible.

**One line to remember:** Keep smallest tails; binary-search the slot; tails length is the LIS.

sections.s2_technical:
Maintain a list called tails. For each number x, binary-search for the leftmost tail that is greater than or equal to x. If none exists, x extends the longest run so append it; otherwise replace that tail with x because a smaller tail keeps future extension easier. For example: `int pos = lowerBound(tails, x); if (pos==tails.size()) tails.add(x); else tails.set(pos, x);`.

The tails array is always sorted, which is exactly why binary search is valid. Note that tails is not the actual subsequence, only a device whose length equals the LIS length; reconstructing the real subsequence needs extra parent pointers.

The time is O(n log n) because each of the n numbers does one binary search, and space is O(n). A senior nuance is that using lower bound gives strictly increasing, while upper bound gives non-decreasing, so the bound choice encodes the strictness requirement.

Problem 2 — A quadratic scan is too slow on long price histories, so an n-log-n method is required. This is exactly why the patience-sorting tails array with binary search is used.

sections.s5_journey:
The input prices are ten, nine, two, five, three, seven, one hundred one, eighteen.

Step 1: Ten starts the tails as a single run ending at ten.

Step 2: Nine replaces ten because a smaller tail is better, then two replaces nine for the same reason.

Step 3: Five appends to make a run of length two, three replaces five to tighten it, seven appends for length three.

Step 4: One hundred one appends for length four, then eighteen replaces one hundred one to keep the length-four run as low as possible.

Step 5: The tails array ends with length four, which is the answer corresponding to two, three, seven, eighteen.

```text
2026-10-27T01:40:00Z [INFO] prices → LIS = 4
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Longest Increasing Subsequence in n-log-n time uses patience sorting. I keep a tails array where the entry at index k is the smallest possible tail value of an increasing subsequence of length k plus one. For each number I binary-search the first tail that is greater than or equal to it; if there is none I append the number because it extends the longest run, otherwise I replace that tail with the number because a smaller tail keeps future extension easier.

The tails array stays sorted at all times, which is what makes the binary search valid, and the final length of tails equals the length of the longest increasing subsequence. It is important to understand that tails is not the actual subsequence, only a length device; rebuilding the real subsequence needs parent pointers. Using the lower bound gives a strictly increasing result, while the upper bound would allow equal values.

In my project at National Bank of India, the portfolio desk needed the longest stretch of rising closing prices to judge momentum, and those rising days did not have to be consecutive. The naive quadratic approach was too slow on long histories, so I used this patience-sorting method with binary search to get the answer in n-log-n time.

answers.question: Given two strings, return the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, or replacements needed to turn the first string into the second.
answers.shortTitle: Edit Distance — minimum insert, delete, replace (Levenshtein)

s1_definition.profdef: 2D DP (Levenshtein) where dp[i][j] is the edit distance between the first i characters of A and first j of B. If characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]; otherwise dp[i][j] = 1 + min(delete dp[i−1][j], insert dp[i][j−1], replace dp[i−1][j−1]). Borders are dp[i][0]=i and dp[0][j]=j. Time and space O(m·n).
s1_definition.analogy: The data-quality team at National Bank of India must fix a mistyped account holder name into the official spelling using the fewest single-letter edits. If the current letters agree, no edit is needed there; if they differ, pick the cheapest of deleting, inserting, or replacing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Match ⇒ diagonal; mismatch ⇒ 1 + min(delete, insert, replace).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** 2D DP (Levenshtein) where dp[i][j] is the edit distance between the first i characters of A and first j of B. If characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]; otherwise dp[i][j] = 1 + min(delete dp[i−1][j], insert dp[i][j−1], replace dp[i−1][j−1]). Borders are dp[i][0]=i and dp[0][j]=j. Time and space O(m·n).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The data-quality team at National Bank of India must fix a mistyped account holder name into the official spelling using the fewest single-letter edits. If the current letters agree, no edit is needed there; if they differ, pick the cheapest of deleting, inserting, or replacing.

**One line to remember:** Match ⇒ diagonal; mismatch ⇒ 1 + min(delete, insert, replace).

sections.s2_technical:
Build a table of size (m+1) by (n+1). The first column dp[i][0] is i because turning an i-length prefix into an empty string needs i deletions, and the first row dp[0][j] is j because building a j-length string from empty needs j insertions. These borders are the base cases.

When A.charAt(i−1) equals B.charAt(j−1) no operation is needed, so dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]. For example: `if (a.charAt(i-1)==b.charAt(j-1)) dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1];`. Otherwise take one plus the cheapest neighbor: delete from A is dp[i−1][j], insert into A is dp[i][j−1], and replace is dp[i−1][j−1]: `else dp[i][j]=1+Math.min(dp[i-1][j-1], Math.min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]));`.

The answer is dp[m][n], time and space O(m·n), reducible to two rows. A senior nuance is that edit distance powers spell-checkers and fuzzy name matching in KYC, and weighting the three operations differently produces generalized variants.

Problem 2 — A plain equality check only says same or different, not how close, which cannot drive a fuzzy-match threshold. This is exactly why the minimum-operations DP is used.

The input strings are horse and ros.

Step 1: The borders are filled, so dp of i and zero is i and dp of zero and j is j, representing pure deletions or insertions.

Step 2: Comparing h to r is a mismatch, taking one plus the cheapest neighbor.

Step 3: The run toward turning horse into ros accumulates a replace of h with r, a delete of a letter, and a replace of e with s.

Step 4: Matching letters like o and o copy the diagonal with no added cost.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Edit Distance, also called Levenshtein distance, is a two-dimensional dynamic programming problem. I define dp of i and j as the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, or replacements to turn the first i characters of one string into the first j characters of the other. The borders are the base cases: turning a prefix into empty costs one deletion per character, and building a prefix from empty costs one insertion per character.

For the body, when the current characters match I copy the diagonal cell because no edit is needed there. When they differ I take one plus the cheapest of three neighbors: the cell above is a deletion, the cell to the left is an insertion, and the diagonal is a replacement. The answer is the bottom-right cell, and I can shrink the space to two rows because each row only needs the one before it.

In my project at National Bank of India, KYC records sometimes had a mistyped holder name, and we needed to know how far it was from the official spelling to tell a likely typo from a genuinely different person. A plain equality check only says same or different, so I used this minimum-operations DP to drive a fuzzy-match threshold, which is the same idea behind spell-checkers.

answers.question: Given item weights and values and a knapsack capacity, maximize total value where each item may be taken at most once (0 or 1).
answers.shortTitle: 0/1 Knapsack — maximize value under a weight capacity

s1_definition.profdef: Bounded-knapsack DP where dp[c] is the best value achievable with capacity c. We process each item once and sweep capacities DOWNWARD (from capacity to the item weight) so each item is used at most once: dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c−weight]+value). Time O(items · capacity), space O(capacity).
s1_definition.analogy: A treasury officer at National Bank of India must load a secure cash van that holds a limited total weight, choosing among sealed cassettes each with a weight and a value. Each cassette can be loaded at most once. For every capacity she asks whether adding this cassette beats leaving it out.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each item once ⇒ sweep capacity DOWNWARD; dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c−w]+v).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Bounded-knapsack DP where dp[c] is the best value achievable with capacity c. We process each item once and sweep capacities DOWNWARD (from capacity to the item weight) so each item is used at most once: dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c−weight]+value). Time O(items · capacity), space O(capacity).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A treasury officer at National Bank of India must load a secure cash van that holds a limited total weight, choosing among sealed cassettes each with a weight and a value. Each cassette can be loaded at most once. For every capacity she asks whether adding this cassette beats leaving it out.

**One line to remember:** Each item once ⇒ sweep capacity DOWNWARD; dp[c] = max(dp[c], dp[c−w]+v).

sections.s2_technical:
Create a one-dimensional dp of size capacity+1 initialized to zero. For each item, iterate capacity from the full capacity down to the item's weight, relaxing dp[c] with dp[c−weight]+value. For example: `for (int c = capacity; c >= w[i]; c--) dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], dp[c - w[i]] + v[i]);`.

The downward sweep is the crucial 0/1 detail. Going downward means dp[c−weight] still refers to a state that has not yet included the current item, so each item is counted at most once. Sweeping upward would let the same item be reused, which is the unbounded knapsack instead.

The time is O(items · capacity) and space is O(capacity) after the one-dimensional reduction from the natural two-dimensional table. A senior nuance is that knapsack capacity is pseudo-polynomial (polynomial in the numeric capacity, not its bit length), which is why huge capacities need different techniques.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a cash van has a strict weight limit, and the treasury must choose which sealed cassettes to load to maximize the transported value. Each cassette is unique and loaded at most once. This is exactly how 0/1 Knapsack works.

Problem 2 — Loading the same cassette twice is physically impossible, so reuse must be forbidden. This is exactly why capacities are swept downward.

sections.s5_journey:
The input weights are one, three, four, five with values one, four, five, seven and capacity seven.

Step 1: dp starts all zero, meaning no value loaded at any capacity.

Step 2: Processing the weight-one item downward sets dp of capacities one through seven to one.

Step 3: Processing the weight-three value-four item lifts mid capacities, for example dp of four becomes five by combining weights one and three.

Step 4: Processing the weight-four value-five and weight-five value-seven items relaxes further, and dp of seven reaches nine by combining weights three and four.

Step 5: The final answer at capacity seven is nine.

```text
2026-10-27T02:00:00Z [INFO] National Bank of India — Treasury Van Loader (0/1 Knapsack)
2026-10-27T02:00:00Z [INFO] Best value for capacity 7 = 9
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The zero-one knapsack is a bounded dynamic programming problem. I define dp of c as the best total value I can achieve with a remaining capacity of c, starting from all zeros. I process each item once, and for each item I sweep the capacity from the full capacity down to the item's weight, relaxing dp of c with dp of c minus the weight plus the value.

The direction of the sweep is the whole trick. Sweeping downward guarantees that dp of c minus the weight still refers to a state that has not yet included the current item, so every item is used at most once, which is the zero-one rule. If I swept upward instead, the same item could be reused, and that would be the unbounded knapsack.

In my project at National Bank of India, a cash van had a strict weight limit and the treasury had to pick which sealed cassettes to load to maximize the transported value, where each cassette could be loaded only once. I used this one-dimensional knapsack with a downward capacity sweep, and I always mention that the complexity is pseudo-polynomial in the capacity, which matters when the capacity is very large.

answers.question: Given an array of positive integers, determine whether it can be split into two subsets with equal sums.
answers.shortTitle: Partition Equal Subset Sum — subset-sum DP

s1_definition.profdef: Reduces to subset-sum: the array can be split equally if and only if the total is even and some subset sums to total/2. Use a boolean dp[s] meaning "sum s is reachable," initialize dp[0]=true, and for each number sweep s DOWNWARD updating dp[s] |= dp[s−num]. Time O(n · target), space O(target).
s1_definition.analogy: An auditor at National Bank of India wants to divide a set of transaction amounts into two piles of exactly equal total. If the grand total is odd this is impossible. Otherwise she checks whether some combination reaches half the total, because that half automatically leaves the other half behind.
s1_definition.oneliner: Total even and a subset hits total/2; boolean dp swept downward.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reduces to subset-sum: the array can be split equally if and only if the total is even and some subset sums to total/2. Use a boolean dp[s] meaning "sum s is reachable," initialize dp[0]=true, and for each number sweep s DOWNWARD updating dp[s] |= dp[s−num]. Time O(n · target), space O(target).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** An auditor at National Bank of India wants to divide a set of transaction amounts into two piles of exactly equal total. If the grand total is odd this is impossible. Otherwise she checks whether some combination reaches half the total, because that half automatically leaves the other half behind.

**One line to remember:** Total even and a subset hits total/2; boolean dp swept downward.

sections.s2_technical:
First compute the total. If it is odd, return false immediately because two equal integer piles are impossible. Otherwise set target to total/2 and create a boolean dp of size target+1 with dp[0]=true, since a sum of zero is always reachable by taking nothing.

For each number, sweep s from target down to the number and set dp[s] to dp[s] OR dp[s−num]. For example: `for (int s = target; s >= num; s--) dp[s] = dp[s] || dp[s - num];`. The downward sweep is the same 0/1 trick as knapsack, ensuring each number is used at most once. The answer is dp[target].

The time is O(n · target) and space is O(target). A senior nuance is that this is exactly the 0/1 knapsack feasibility variant with weights equal to values, and if an actual partition is needed you backtrack through a two-dimensional table or keep parent flags.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Partition Equal Subset Sum reduces cleanly to a subset-sum feasibility problem. The array can be split into two equal halves if and only if the total is even and some subset sums to exactly half the total, because that subset automatically leaves the other half behind. So I first check parity: if the total is odd I return false immediately.

For the feasibility test I use a boolean dynamic programming array where dp of s means the sum s is reachable. I initialize dp of zero to true because taking nothing reaches zero, and for each number I sweep the sums from the target down to the number, setting dp of s to itself or dp of s minus the number. The downward sweep is the same zero-one trick as the knapsack, so each number is used at most once, and the answer is dp of the target.

In my project at National Bank of India, an auditor needed to split a batch of settlement amounts into two equal halves for a two-way reconciliation. I recognized this as the zero-one knapsack feasibility variant where the weight equals the value, reduced it to reaching half the total, and solved it with a one-dimensional boolean table.

answers.question: Given a string and a dictionary of words, determine whether the string can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words.
answers.shortTitle: Word Break — can a string be segmented into dictionary words

s1_definition.profdef: 1D DP where dp[i] means "the prefix of length i can be segmented." dp[0]=true, and dp[i] is true if some j<i has dp[j]=true and the substring from j to i is in the dictionary. Time O(n² · L) with substring/lookup cost, space O(n).
s1_definition.analogy: A payments parser at National Bank of India receives a concatenated instruction string with no separators and must check whether it splits cleanly into known command words. A position is reachable if an earlier reachable position is followed by a valid word ending here.
s1_definition.oneliner: dp[i] true if some dp[j] true and substring(j,i) is a dictionary word.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** 1D DP where dp[i] means "the prefix of length i can be segmented." dp[0]=true, and dp[i] is true if some j<i has dp[j]=true and the substring from j to i is in the dictionary. Time O(n² · L) with substring/lookup cost, space O(n).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A payments parser at National Bank of India receives a concatenated instruction string with no separators and must check whether it splits cleanly into known command words. A position is reachable if an earlier reachable position is followed by a valid word ending here.

**One line to remember:** dp[i] true if some dp[j] true and substring(j,i) is a dictionary word.

sections.s2_technical:
Put the dictionary into a HashSet for constant-time lookups. Create a boolean dp of size n+1 with dp[0]=true, meaning the empty prefix is trivially segmentable. For each end position i from 1 to n, try every start j from 0 to i−1: if dp[j] is true and the substring from j to i is a dictionary word, mark dp[i] true and stop the inner loop. For example: `if (dp[j] && dict.contains(s.substring(j, i))) { dp[i] = true; break; }`.

The reasoning is that a prefix is segmentable exactly when it ends with a valid word whose starting point is itself a segmentable prefix. The answer is dp[n].

The time is O(n²) substring attempts, each costing up to O(L) for the substring and lookup, and space is O(n). A senior nuance is that the related "Word Break II" that returns all sentences can blow up exponentially, so it needs memoized backtracking rather than simple DP.
sections.s3_banking:

Problem 2 — A greedy left-to-right longest-word match can fail because an early wrong cut blocks a valid later split. This is exactly why DP that remembers every reachable boundary is needed.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Break is a one-dimensional dynamic programming problem over the positions of the string. I define dp of i as whether the prefix of length i can be segmented into dictionary words. I put the dictionary into a hash set for constant-time lookups, and I set dp of zero to true because the empty prefix is trivially segmentable.

For each end position I look back at every start position and ask two things: is that start itself a segmentable boundary, and is the substring between the start and the end a dictionary word. If both hold, the end position is segmentable. The intuition is that a prefix is segmentable exactly when it ends in a valid word whose starting point is also segmentable, and the answer is dp of the full length.

In my project at National Bank of India, a legacy channel sent payment instructions as one concatenated string of command words with no separators, and the parser had to verify a clean split before executing. A greedy longest-word match could fail because an early wrong cut blocks a valid later split, so I used this DP that remembers every reachable boundary, and I note that the variant returning all sentences needs memoized backtracking because the output can be exponential.

answers.question: A message of digits is encoded where 1 maps to A through 26 maps to Z. Given a digit string, count how many ways it can be decoded.
answers.shortTitle: Decode Ways — count decodings of a digit string

s1_definition.profdef: 1D DP like Fibonacci with validity guards, where dp[i] is the number of decodings of the first i digits. dp[i] adds dp[i−1] if the single digit is 1 through 9, and adds dp[i−2] if the two-digit number is 10 through 26. Base dp[0]=1. Time O(n), space O(1) with rolling variables.
s1_definition.analogy: A back-office clerk at National Bank of India decodes a numeric reference where each letter was stored as a number. At each position she can read one digit as a letter if it is not zero, or combine it with the previous digit if together they form ten to twenty-six, summing both ways.
s1_definition.oneliner: dp[i] = (single valid ? dp[i−1] : 0) + (pair valid ? dp[i−2] : 0).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** 1D DP like Fibonacci with validity guards, where dp[i] is the number of decodings of the first i digits. dp[i] adds dp[i−1] if the single digit is 1 through 9, and adds dp[i−2] if the two-digit number is 10 through 26. Base dp[0]=1. Time O(n), space O(1) with rolling variables.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A back-office clerk at National Bank of India decodes a numeric reference where each letter was stored as a number. At each position she can read one digit as a letter if it is not zero, or combine it with the previous digit if together they form ten to twenty-six, summing both ways.

**One line to remember:** dp[i] = (single valid ? dp[i−1] : 0) + (pair valid ? dp[i−2] : 0).

sections.s2_technical:
Create dp of size n+1 with dp[0]=1 (one way to decode the empty string) and dp[1] equal to one if the first digit is not zero, otherwise zero. For each position i from 2 to n, add dp[i−1] when the current single digit is between 1 and 9, and add dp[i−2] when the two-digit number formed with the previous digit is between 10 and 26. For example: `if (s.charAt(i-1) != '0') dp[i] += dp[i-1]; int two = Integer.parseInt(s.substring(i-2, i)); if (two >= 10 && two <= 26) dp[i] += dp[i-2];`.

The two validity guards are everything. A leading zero cannot stand alone, and a pair above 26 or below 10 (like 09) is invalid. The answer is dp[n].

The time is O(n) and space is O(1) if you keep only the last two values. A senior nuance is that strings containing a zero that cannot pair (like 30) decode to zero ways, so careful zero handling is the main source of bugs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, archived references stored letters as numbers, and a clerk must count how many distinct letter strings a numeric reference could represent to flag ambiguous ones for manual review. This is exactly how Decode Ways works.

Problem 2 — Zeros and pairs above twenty-six make some readings invalid, so naive counting is wrong. This is exactly why the two validity guards gate each addition.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Decode Ways is a one-dimensional dynamic programming problem shaped like Fibonacci but with validity guards. I define dp of i as the number of ways to decode the first i digits. The base cases are dp of zero equal to one for the empty string and dp of one equal to one when the first digit is not zero.

For each later position I make two guarded additions. If the current single digit is between one and nine it can stand alone as a letter, so I add dp of the previous position. If the two-digit number formed with the digit before it is between ten and twenty-six it forms a valid letter, so I add dp of the position two back. The two guards are the whole problem, because a leading zero cannot stand alone and a pair like oh-nine or thirty is invalid.

In my project at National Bank of India, archived references stored letters as numbers, and a clerk had to count how many distinct letter strings a numeric reference could represent so ambiguous ones went to manual review. I used this linear DP with constant space by keeping only the last two counts, and I was careful with zeros because mishandling them is the classic source of wrong answers.

answers.question: A robot starts at the top-left of an m by n grid and may move only right or down. Count how many distinct paths reach the bottom-right.
answers.shortTitle: Unique Paths — count grid paths moving right or down

s1_definition.profdef: Grid DP where dp[i][j] is the number of paths to cell (i,j). The first row and first column are all 1 (only one way along an edge), and dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + dp[i][j−1]. Time O(m·n), space O(n) with a rolling row; closed form is the binomial C(m+n−2, m−1).
s1_definition.analogy: A courier at National Bank of India routes a sealed document across a grid of branch offices, only ever moving east or south. The number of ways to reach any office is the ways to reach the office to its west plus the ways to reach the office to its north.
s1_definition.oneliner: dp[i][j] = paths from above + paths from the left; edges are all 1.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Grid DP where dp[i][j] is the number of paths to cell (i,j). The first row and first column are all 1 (only one way along an edge), and dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + dp[i][j−1]. Time O(m·n), space O(n) with a rolling row; closed form is the binomial C(m+n−2, m−1).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A courier at National Bank of India routes a sealed document across a grid of branch offices, only ever moving east or south. The number of ways to reach any office is the ways to reach the office to its west plus the ways to reach the office to its north.

**One line to remember:** dp[i][j] = paths from above + paths from the left; edges are all 1.

sections.s2_technical:
Create a dp grid of size m by n. Fill the entire first row and first column with one, because along the top edge the robot can only keep moving right and along the left edge only down, so there is exactly one path to each edge cell. These are the base cases.

For every interior cell, the robot arrives either from directly above or directly to the left, so dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + dp[i][j−1]. For example: `dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1];`. The answer is the bottom-right cell dp[m−1][n−1].

The time and space are O(m·n), and the space reduces to O(n) by keeping a single rolling row. A senior nuance is that there is a closed-form combinatorial answer, the binomial coefficient of m+n−2 choose m−1, because every path is a fixed arrangement of right and down moves.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Unique Paths is a grid dynamic programming problem. I define dp of i and j as the number of distinct paths from the top-left to cell i, j, given that the robot moves only right or down. The base cases are the whole first row and first column, which are all ones because along an edge there is exactly one straight path.

For every interior cell the robot arrives either from directly above or directly from the left, so the number of paths to it is the sum of the paths to those two neighbors. The answer is the bottom-right cell. I can reduce the memory to a single rolling row because each row depends only on the one above it, and there is even a closed-form answer as a binomial coefficient, since every path is just a fixed arrangement of right and down moves.

In my project at National Bank of India, a document courier moved across a grid of branch offices going only east or south, and operations wanted the count of distinct routes for capacity planning. Enumerating routes explicitly is exponential, so I used this grid DP that simply sums the two incoming directions, which is linear in the number of cells.

**One line to remember:** dp[i][j] = cost + min(from above, from left).

sections.s2_technical:
Create a dp grid of the same size. The top-left cell equals its own cost. The first row is a running sum because the only way along the top is to keep moving right, and the first column is a running sum because the only way down the left is to keep moving down. These are the base cases.

For each interior cell, add the cell's own cost to the cheaper of the cell above and the cell to the left: `dp[i][j] = grid[i][j] + Math.min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);`. The answer is the bottom-right cell dp[m−1][n−1].

The time and space are O(m·n), and space reduces to O(n) with a rolling row, or you can overwrite the input grid in place for O(1) extra space. A senior nuance is that because all costs are non-negative this simple DP suffices, but if negative costs or arbitrary moves were allowed you would need a shortest-path algorithm like Dijkstra instead.

answers.question: Given an array where each element is the maximum jump length from that position, determine whether you can reach the last index starting from the first.
answers.shortTitle: Jump Game — can you reach the last index (greedy reachability)

s1_definition.profdef: Greedy reachability: track the farthest index reachable so far. Iterate left to right; if the current index exceeds the farthest reach, return false; otherwise extend reach to max(reach, i + nums[i]). Reachable if reach eventually covers the last index. Time O(n), space O(1).
s1_definition.analogy: A settlement pipeline at National Bank of India has stages, and each stage lists how many stages ahead it can skip to. An operator walks forward tracking the farthest stage currently reachable; if he ever stands beyond that frontier he is stuck, otherwise he can finish.
s1_definition.oneliner: Track farthest reach; if i > reach you are stuck; else extend reach.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Greedy reachability: track the farthest index reachable so far. Iterate left to right; if the current index exceeds the farthest reach, return false; otherwise extend reach to max(reach, i + nums[i]). Reachable if reach eventually covers the last index. Time O(n), space O(1).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A settlement pipeline at National Bank of India has stages, and each stage lists how many stages ahead it can skip to. An operator walks forward tracking the farthest stage currently reachable; if he ever stands beyond that frontier he is stuck, otherwise he can finish.

**One line to remember:** Track farthest reach; if i > reach you are stuck; else extend reach.

sections.s2_technical:
Keep a single variable reach starting at zero, the farthest index you can get to. Walk i from zero to the last index. At each step, if i is greater than reach you can never have arrived here, so return false. Otherwise update reach to the maximum of its current value and i plus nums[i]. For example: `if (i > reach) return false; reach = Math.max(reach, i + nums[i]);`.

The greedy works because reachability is monotone: if you can reach index i you can reach any index up to reach, so you only ever need the single farthest frontier, not which exact path got there. If the loop finishes without getting stuck, the last index is reachable.

The time is O(n) and space is O(1). A senior nuance is that this is far cheaper than the equivalent O(n²) DP where dp[i] marks reachability from each prior jumpable index; the greedy frontier collapses that whole table into one number.
sections.s3_banking:

Problem 2 — Trying every jump combination is exponential and needless. This is exactly why a single greedy reachability frontier is enough.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Jump Game is a greedy reachability problem. I keep a single variable for the farthest index I can reach so far and walk the array left to right. At each index, if the index is already beyond my farthest reach then I could never have arrived there and I return false; otherwise I extend the reach to the maximum of its current value and the index plus the jump available there.

The greedy is correct because reachability is monotone: if I can reach some index I can reach everything up to my current frontier, so I never need to know which exact path got me there, only the single farthest point. If the walk completes without getting stranded, the last index is reachable.

In my project at National Bank of India, a settlement pipeline had stages where each stage declared how many stages ahead it could skip, and operations needed to know if the final stage was reachable from the start. Rather than trying every jump combination, which is exponential, I used this constant-space greedy frontier, and I point out in interviews that it collapses the equivalent quadratic reachability DP into one number.

answers.question: Given an array where each element is the maximum jump length, return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the last index (assume the end is always reachable).
answers.shortTitle: Jump Game II — minimum jumps to reach the end (greedy BFS layers)

s1_definition.profdef: Greedy layered BFS: treat each jump as expanding a range. Maintain the current jump's far boundary and the farthest reachable overall; when the index reaches the current boundary, increment the jump count and move the boundary to the farthest. Time O(n), space O(1).
s1_definition.analogy: A courier at National Bank of India wants the fewest hops across stages. Within one hop he can land anywhere in a window; he scouts the whole window to find the farthest he could then reach, and only counts a new hop when he steps off the edge of the current window.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count a jump when i hits the current window end; extend the window to farthest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Greedy layered BFS: treat each jump as expanding a range. Maintain the current jump's far boundary and the farthest reachable overall; when the index reaches the current boundary, increment the jump count and move the boundary to the farthest. Time O(n), space O(1).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A courier at National Bank of India wants the fewest hops across stages. Within one hop he can land anywhere in a window; he scouts the whole window to find the farthest he could then reach, and only counts a new hop when he steps off the edge of the current window.

**One line to remember:** Count a jump when i hits the current window end; extend the window to farthest.

sections.s2_technical:
Keep three values: jumps counted, the current window's end boundary, and the farthest reachable. Walk i from zero to the second-to-last index (you never need to jump from the last index). At each step extend farthest to max(farthest, i + nums[i]). When i equals the current boundary, you have exhausted the current jump's range, so increment jumps and set the boundary to farthest. For example: `farthest = Math.max(farthest, i + nums[i]); if (i == end) { jumps++; end = farthest; }`.

This is breadth-first search expressed greedily: each jump is one BFS layer, and the boundary marks where the current layer ends. Because you always extend to the farthest reachable within a layer before incrementing, the count is minimal.

The time is O(n) and space is O(1). A senior nuance is why you iterate only to n−2: reaching or passing the last index inside the final window already counts the jump, so iterating to n−1 would overcount by one.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Jump Game II asks for the minimum number of jumps, and I solve it with a greedy layered breadth-first search expressed in constant space. I keep three things: the jump count, the far boundary of the current jump's window, and the farthest index reachable overall. As I walk the array I always extend the farthest reachable using the current index plus its jump.

The key moment is when the index reaches the current window's boundary. That means I have scouted the entire range of the current jump, so I increment the jump count and move the window boundary out to the farthest I found. Each window is one breadth-first layer, and because I always expand to the farthest reachable before counting a new jump, the count is minimal. I iterate only to the second-to-last index, because reaching the end inside the final window already counts that jump and going one further would overcount.

In my project at National Bank of India, a courier crossed settlement stages and had to use the fewest hops because each hop carried a fixed handling cost. Reaching the end is not the same as reaching it cheaply, so I used this greedy window expansion that gives the minimum number of hops in linear time.

answers.question: Given a string, return the longest contiguous substring that reads the same forwards and backwards.
answers.shortTitle: Longest Palindromic Substring — expand around center

s1_definition.profdef: Expand-around-center technique: every palindrome has a center, either a single character (odd length) or a gap between two characters (even length). For each of the 2n−1 centers, expand outward while the characters match and track the longest span. Time O(n²), space O(1).
s1_definition.analogy: A reference-code checker at National Bank of India looks for the longest mirror-symmetric stretch inside a code. It stands at each possible middle point and grows outward in both directions as long as the two sides keep matching, remembering the widest mirror it finds.
s1_definition.oneliner: Try every center, expand while both sides match, keep the longest span.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Expand-around-center technique: every palindrome has a center, either a single character (odd length) or a gap between two characters (even length). For each of the 2n−1 centers, expand outward while the characters match and track the longest span. Time O(n²), space O(1).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A reference-code checker at National Bank of India looks for the longest mirror-symmetric stretch inside a code. It stands at each possible middle point and grows outward in both directions as long as the two sides keep matching, remembering the widest mirror it finds.

**One line to remember:** Try every center, expand while both sides match, keep the longest span.

sections.s2_technical:
There are 2n−1 possible centers: n single-character centers for odd-length palindromes and n−1 between-character centers for even-length palindromes. For each center, expand with two pointers moving outward while they stay in bounds and the characters are equal, then record the span if it beats the best. For example: `while (l >= 0 && r < s.length() && s.charAt(l) == s.charAt(r)) { l--; r++; }`.

After the loop, the valid palindrome is from l+1 to r−1 because the loop overshoots by one on each side. You call the expansion once with the center as (i, i) for odd length and once as (i, i+1) for even length, and keep the maximum.

The time is O(n²) because each of the roughly 2n centers can expand up to O(n), and space is O(1). A senior nuance is that Manacher's algorithm solves this in O(n) by reusing mirror information, but expand-around-center is the expected interview answer for its simplicity and constant space.

Longest Palindromic Substring is best solved with the expand-around-center technique. The key insight is that every palindrome has a center, which is either a single character for odd-length palindromes or the gap between two characters for even-length palindromes, so there are about two times n minus one centers to try.

For each center I expand two pointers outward as long as they stay in bounds and the characters on both sides match, then I record the span if it beats the longest found so far. Because the expansion overshoots by one on each side when it stops, the actual palindrome length is the right pointer minus the left pointer minus one. I run the expansion once treating the center as a single character and once as a gap between two characters, and keep the maximum.

In my project at National Bank of India, a validator scanned reference codes for the longest mirror-symmetric stretch, because some legacy codes embedded palindromic checksums. answers.question: Given a string, return the length of the longest subsequence that reads the same forwards and backwards (characters need not be contiguous).
answers.shortTitle: Longest Palindromic Subsequence — interval DP

s1_definition.profdef: Interval DP where dp[i][j] is the longest palindromic subsequence length within the substring from i to j. If the ends match, dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j−1]+2; otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j−1]). Equivalent to the LCS of the string with its reverse. Time O(n²), space O(n²).
s1_definition.analogy: A pattern analyst at National Bank of India wants the longest mirror-symmetric pattern inside a code where she may skip characters. If the two ends of a window are the same symbol, they wrap a smaller mirror and add two; if not, she drops whichever end helps more.
s1_definition.oneliner: Ends match ⇒ inner+2; else max of dropping either end.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Interval DP where dp[i][j] is the longest palindromic subsequence length within the substring from i to j. If the ends match, dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j−1]+2; otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j−1]). Equivalent to the LCS of the string with its reverse. Time O(n²), space O(n²).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A pattern analyst at National Bank of India wants the longest mirror-symmetric pattern inside a code where she may skip characters. If the two ends of a window are the same symbol, they wrap a smaller mirror and add two; if not, she drops whichever end helps more.

**One line to remember:** Ends match ⇒ inner+2; else max of dropping either end.

sections.s2_technical:
Use a table dp[i][j] over intervals, filled by increasing interval length. Every single character is a palindrome of length one, so dp[i][i] = 1 is the base case. For a window from i to j, if the end characters are equal they contribute two around the best inner palindrome, so dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j−1]+2. For example: `if (s.charAt(i)==s.charAt(j)) dp[i][j]=dp[i+1][j-1]+2;`.

If the ends differ, drop one end and take the better of the two shorter windows: `else dp[i][j]=Math.max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]);`. Because dp[i][j] depends on smaller intervals, iterate i from the end backward and j forward, or iterate by length. The answer is dp[0][n−1].

The time and space are O(n²). A senior nuance is that this exactly equals the longest common subsequence of the string with its reverse, which is a clean alternative derivation, and the subsequence version is harder than the substring version because non-contiguity forbids the simple center expansion.

Problem 2 — Because characters may be skipped, center expansion does not apply and an interval DP is required. This is exactly why dp over substrings by growing length is used.

sections.s5_journey:
The input string is bbbab.

Step 1: Every single character cell starts at one as the base case.

Step 2: Adjacent equal pairs like the two b characters give length two by wrapping an empty inner window and adding two.

Step 3: Larger windows with matching ends add two to their inner best, so stretches of b characters accumulate.

Step 4: The full window from index zero to four has ends b and b that match, adding two around the inner best.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Palindromic Subsequence is an interval dynamic programming problem. I define dp of i and j as the length of the longest palindromic subsequence inside the substring from index i to index j. The base case is that every single character is a palindrome of length one, and I fill the table by growing interval length so that smaller intervals are ready before larger ones.

The transition has two cases. If the two end characters of the window are equal, they wrap around the best inner palindrome and add two to it. If they differ, I drop one end and take the better of the two shorter windows, which is the maximum of excluding the left end or the right end. The answer is the cell covering the whole string.

In my project at National Bank of India, a pattern analyst searched codes for the longest mirror-symmetric pattern while allowing skipped characters, to detect deliberately embedded symmetric markers. Because characters may be skipped, the simple center-expansion trick does not apply, so I used this interval DP, and I like to point out that it is exactly the longest common subsequence of the string with its own reverse.

answers.question: Given an integer array, find the contiguous subarray with the largest product and return that product.
answers.shortTitle: Maximum Product Subarray — track max and min together

s1_definition.profdef: Linear DP that tracks both the running maximum and running minimum product ending at each index, because a negative number swaps them. At each element: newMax = max(x, x·max, x·min), newMin = min(x, x·max, x·min). Track the global maximum. Time O(n), space O(1).
s1_definition.analogy: A returns analyst at National Bank of India multiplies consecutive daily growth factors to find the best stretch. A single loss factor (a negative) can flip the biggest gain into the biggest loss and vice versa, so she keeps both the best and worst running product at every day.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep running max AND min; a negative swaps them; answer is the global max.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Linear DP that tracks both the running maximum and running minimum product ending at each index, because a negative number swaps them. At each element: newMax = max(x, x·max, x·min), newMin = min(x, x·max, x·min). Track the global maximum. Time O(n), space O(1).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A returns analyst at National Bank of India multiplies consecutive daily growth factors to find the best stretch. A single loss factor (a negative) can flip the biggest gain into the biggest loss and vice versa, so she keeps both the best and worst running product at every day.

**One line to remember:** Keep running max AND min; a negative swaps them; answer is the global max.

sections.s2_technical:
Unlike maximum sum, product has a twist: multiplying by a negative turns a large positive into a large negative and a large negative into a large positive. So you must carry both the maximum and the minimum product ending at the current index. Initialize both and the answer to the first element.

At each next element x, compute candidates x, x times the previous max, and x times the previous min, then set the new max to the largest and the new min to the smallest. For example: `int cand1 = x*max, cand2 = x*min; max = Math.max(x, Math.max(cand1, cand2)); min = Math.min(x, Math.min(cand1, cand2));`. Update the global answer with the new max. Note you must compute the new max from the OLD max and min, so capture them before overwriting.

The time is O(n) and space is O(1). A senior nuance is that zeros naturally reset both running products because x itself becomes a candidate, so the subarray effectively restarts after a zero without any special casing.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a returns analyst multiplies consecutive daily growth factors to find the most profitable contiguous stretch of trading days. This is exactly how Maximum Product Subarray works.

Problem 2 — A single negative growth factor can flip the sign of the running product, so tracking only the maximum misses the case where a future negative turns a current minimum into the new maximum. This is exactly why both the running max and min are carried.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Maximum Product Subarray is a linear dynamic programming problem with a twist compared to the maximum sum version. The twist is that multiplying by a negative number flips a large positive product into a large negative one and vice versa, so I cannot track only the running maximum. I carry both the running maximum product and the running minimum product ending at the current index.

At each element I compute three candidates: the element alone, the element times the previous maximum, and the element times the previous minimum. The new maximum is the largest of these and the new minimum is the smallest, and I always compute them from the old values before overwriting. I update a global answer with each new maximum. Zeros need no special handling because the element itself is a candidate, which naturally restarts the subarray.

In my project at National Bank of India, a returns analyst multiplied consecutive daily growth factors to find the most profitable contiguous stretch of trading days. Because one negative factor could flip the running product, I tracked both the best and the worst running product so a later negative could turn the worst into the best, and it runs in linear time with constant space.

answers.question: Given two strings, return the length of the longest substring (contiguous) that appears in both.
answers.shortTitle: Longest Common Substring — contiguous match 2D DP

s1_definition.profdef: 2D DP where dp[i][j] is the length of the common substring ending exactly at A[i−1] and B[j−1]. If they match, dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]+1; if not, dp[i][j] = 0 (the run breaks). Track the global maximum cell. Time O(m·n), space O(m·n) or O(n) rolling.
s1_definition.analogy: A log-forensics tool at National Bank of India compares two server logs to find the longest identical contiguous block, maybe a replayed request. When the current characters match the shared run grows by one; the instant they differ the run resets to zero.
s1_definition.oneliner: Match ⇒ diagonal+1; mismatch ⇒ 0; answer is the biggest cell, not the corner.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** 2D DP where dp[i][j] is the length of the common substring ending exactly at A[i−1] and B[j−1]. If they match, dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]+1; if not, dp[i][j] = 0 (the run breaks). Track the global maximum cell. Time O(m·n), space O(m·n) or O(n) rolling.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A log-forensics tool at National Bank of India compares two server logs to find the longest identical contiguous block, maybe a replayed request. When the current characters match the shared run grows by one; the instant they differ the run resets to zero.

**One line to remember:** Match ⇒ diagonal+1; mismatch ⇒ 0; answer is the biggest cell, not the corner.

sections.s2_technical:
This looks like Longest Common Subsequence but differs crucially because a substring must be contiguous. So dp[i][j] means the length of the common run ending exactly at those two positions, not the best up to here. When the characters match, extend the diagonal: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]+1. For example: `if (a.charAt(i-1)==b.charAt(j-1)) dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1]+1;`.

When they differ the run is broken, so dp[i][j] resets to zero rather than inheriting a neighbor. Because the answer is not necessarily at the bottom-right corner, you track a running maximum over all cells as you fill them.

The time and space are O(m·n), reducible to O(n) with a rolling row. A senior nuance is that the only structural differences from LCS are the reset to zero on mismatch and taking the global maximum instead of the corner, which is a common interview trap when people conflate substring with subsequence.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a forensics tool compares two server request logs to find the longest identical contiguous block, which may indicate a replayed or duplicated request. This is exactly how Longest Common Substring works.

Problem 2 — A replay must be a contiguous identical run, so skipping characters as in subsequence matching would give false positives. This is exactly why the run resets to zero on any mismatch.

Longest Common Substring looks almost identical to Longest Common Subsequence but differs in two important ways because a substring must be contiguous. I define dp of i and j as the length of the common run that ends exactly at those two positions, not the best up to here. When the current characters match, I extend the diagonal by one, building a contiguous run.

The two differences from the subsequence version are the heart of the problem. First, when the characters differ, the run is broken, so the cell resets to zero rather than inheriting from a neighbor. Second, because the longest run can end anywhere, the answer is the global maximum over all cells, not the bottom-right corner. Conflating these with the subsequence version is a classic trap.

In my project at National Bank of India, a forensics tool compared two server request logs to find the longest identical contiguous block that might indicate a replayed request. answers.question: Given an array of non-negative integers and a target, assign a plus or minus sign to each number so the signed sum equals the target, and count the number of ways.
answers.shortTitle: Target Sum — assign + and - signs to reach a target

s1_definition.profdef: Transform into subset-sum counting. If P is the subset assigned plus and N the subset assigned minus, then P−N=target and P+N=total, so P=(total+target)/2. Count subsets summing to that value with dp[s] += dp[s−num]. Valid only if total+target is non-negative and even. Time O(n · P), space O(P).
s1_definition.analogy: An adjustment clerk at National Bank of India must mark each pending amount as a credit or a debit so the net equals a required figure, and wants to know how many sign assignments work. This equals choosing which amounts become credits, so it reduces to counting subsets that hit a fixed total.
s1_definition.oneliner: P=(total+target)/2; count subsets summing to P; dp[s] += dp[s−num].
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Transform into subset-sum counting. If P is the subset assigned plus and N the subset assigned minus, then P−N=target and P+N=total, so P=(total+target)/2. Count subsets summing to that value with dp[s] += dp[s−num]. Valid only if total+target is non-negative and even. Time O(n · P), space O(P).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** An adjustment clerk at National Bank of India must mark each pending amount as a credit or a debit so the net equals a required figure, and wants to know how many sign assignments work. This equals choosing which amounts become credits, so it reduces to counting subsets that hit a fixed total.

**One line to remember:** P=(total+target)/2; count subsets summing to P; dp[s] += dp[s−num].

sections.s2_technical:
Let the positive subset sum be P and the negative subset sum be N. Then P minus N is the target and P plus N is the total, so adding the two equations gives P equals (total plus target) divided by two. If total plus target is negative or odd, no assignment works, so return zero.

Now the problem is: how many subsets sum to P. Use a one-dimensional counting dp where dp[s] is the number of subsets summing to s, with dp[0]=1, sweeping s downward for each number: `for (int s = P; s >= num; s--) dp[s] += dp[s - num];`. The downward sweep keeps each number used once. The answer is dp[P].

The time is O(n · P) and space is O(P). A senior nuance is handling the edge where a number is zero: a zero can be assigned either sign without changing the sum, which the subset-count naturally accounts for since dp[0] already includes the empty choice and zeros simply double counts through the standard recurrence.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, an adjustment clerk marks each pending amount as a credit or a debit so the net adjustment equals a required figure, and wants the number of valid sign assignments. This is exactly how Target Sum works.

Problem 2 — Enumerating all two-to-the-n sign combinations is infeasible for many amounts. This is exactly why the problem is reduced to a subset-sum count.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Target Sum asks how many ways I can assign a plus or minus sign to each number so the signed sum equals a target, and the elegant move is to transform it into a subset-sum count. If I call the plus-signed subset P and the minus-signed subset N, then P minus N is the target and P plus N is the total. Adding those equations gives P equal to the total plus the target, all divided by two.

So I first check feasibility: if the total plus the target is negative or odd, then P would be fractional or impossible and the answer is zero. Otherwise the question becomes how many subsets sum to P, which I count with a one-dimensional counting dynamic programming array. I set dp of zero to one and for each number sweep sums downward adding dp of the sum minus the number, so each number is used once. The answer is dp of P.

In my project at National Bank of India, an adjustment clerk marked each pending amount as a credit or a debit so the net adjustment equaled a required figure and wanted the number of valid assignments. Enumerating two-to-the-n combinations was infeasible, so I reduced it to this subset-sum count that runs in time proportional to the number of amounts times the target subset sum.

answers.question: Given strings s1, s2, and s3, determine whether s3 is formed by interleaving s1 and s2, preserving the left-to-right order of each.
answers.shortTitle: Interleaving String — can two strings interleave to form a third

s1_definition.profdef: 2D DP where dp[i][j] is true if the first i characters of s1 and first j of s2 can interleave to form the first i+j characters of s3. dp[i][j] holds if the last char came from s1 (dp[i−1][j] and s1[i−1]==s3[i+j−1]) or from s2 (dp[i][j−1] and s2[j−1]==s3[i+j−1]). Time O(m·n), space O(n).
s1_definition.analogy: A merge auditor at National Bank of India checks whether a combined transaction stream was produced by interleaving two source streams without reordering either. At each merged position she asks whether the next character could have come from stream one or from stream two, keeping each stream's internal order.
s1_definition.oneliner: dp[i][j] = (fromS1 and match) OR (fromS2 and match); length must equal m+n.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** 2D DP where dp[i][j] is true if the first i characters of s1 and first j of s2 can interleave to form the first i+j characters of s3. dp[i][j] holds if the last char came from s1 (dp[i−1][j] and s1[i−1]==s3[i+j−1]) or from s2 (dp[i][j−1] and s2[j−1]==s3[i+j−1]). Time O(m·n), space O(n).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A merge auditor at National Bank of India checks whether a combined transaction stream was produced by interleaving two source streams without reordering either. At each merged position she asks whether the next character could have come from stream one or from stream two, keeping each stream's internal order.

**One line to remember:** dp[i][j] = (fromS1 and match) OR (fromS2 and match); length must equal m+n.

sections.s2_technical:
First, if the length of s3 is not the sum of the lengths of s1 and s2, return false immediately. Otherwise build a boolean table dp of size (m+1) by (n+1), where dp[i][j] says whether the first i of s1 and first j of s2 can interleave into the first i+j of s3. The base case dp[0][0] is true.

Each merged character at position i+j−1 of s3 must come from either s1 or s2. It came from s1 if dp[i−1][j] is true and s1 at i−1 equals s3 at i+j−1; it came from s2 if dp[i][j−1] is true and s2 at j−1 equals s3 at i+j−1. For example: `dp[i][j] = (i>0 && dp[i-1][j] && s1.charAt(i-1)==s3.charAt(i+j-1)) || (j>0 && dp[i][j-1] && s2.charAt(j-1)==s3.charAt(i+j-1));`. The answer is dp[m][n].

The time is O(m·n) and space reduces to O(n) with a rolling row. A senior nuance is that a naive recursive interleaving check branches exponentially, so the whole point of the DP is to collapse the overlapping subproblems defined purely by the pair of prefix lengths.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a merge auditor verifies that a combined event stream was produced by interleaving two source feeds without reordering either feed. This is exactly how Interleaving String works.

Problem 2 — A greedy character-by-character match fails because at a position both feeds may offer the same next character and only one choice leads to a full valid interleave. This is exactly why the DP explores both origins at every cell.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Interleaving String is a two-dimensional dynamic programming problem. First I do a quick guard: if the length of the third string is not the sum of the lengths of the first two, it cannot be an interleaving, so I return false immediately. Otherwise I define dp of i and j as whether the first i characters of the first string and the first j of the second can interleave to form the first i plus j characters of the third.

For each cell the current merged character must have come from exactly one of the two sources. It came from the first string if the cell above was reachable and the first string's character matches, or it came from the second string if the cell to the left was reachable and the second string's character matches. The base case is the empty-empty cell being true, and the answer is the bottom-right cell.

In my project at National Bank of India, a merge auditor verified that a combined event stream was produced by interleaving two source feeds without reordering either. A greedy match fails when both feeds offer the same next character and only one choice completes a valid interleave, so I used this DP keyed on the pair of prefix lengths, which collapses the exponential recursion into a quadratic table.

answers.question: Given strings s and t, count the number of distinct subsequences of s that equal t.
answers.shortTitle: Distinct Subsequences — count occurrences of t as a subsequence of s

s1_definition.profdef: 2D counting DP where dp[i][j] is the number of ways the first i characters of s form the first j characters of t. If s[i−1]==t[j−1], dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] (use it) + dp[i−1][j] (skip it); otherwise dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j]. Base dp[i][0]=1. Time O(m·n), space O(n).
s1_definition.analogy: A pattern-counter at National Bank of India counts how many times a short approval code appears as an ordered (not necessarily contiguous) subsequence inside a long audit log. At each log character that matches the next needed code character, she either uses it or skips it, adding both counts.
s1_definition.oneliner: Match ⇒ use+skip (diagonal+above); mismatch ⇒ skip only (above). dp[i][0]=1.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** 2D counting DP where dp[i][j] is the number of ways the first i characters of s form the first j characters of t. If s[i−1]==t[j−1], dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] (use it) + dp[i−1][j] (skip it); otherwise dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j]. Base dp[i][0]=1. Time O(m·n), space O(n).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A pattern-counter at National Bank of India counts how many times a short approval code appears as an ordered (not necessarily contiguous) subsequence inside a long audit log. At each log character that matches the next needed code character, she either uses it or skips it, adding both counts.

**One line to remember:** Match ⇒ use+skip (diagonal+above); mismatch ⇒ skip only (above). dp[i][0]=1.

sections.s2_technical:
Build a table dp of size (m+1) by (n+1). The first column dp[i][0] is one, because the empty target t is always matchable exactly once by taking no characters. The first row (except the corner) is zero, because a non-empty target cannot be formed from an empty s.

When s at i−1 equals t at j−1, the current s character may be used to match the current t character, contributing dp[i−1][j−1], or skipped, contributing dp[i−1][j], so dp[i][j] is their sum. For example: `if (s.charAt(i-1)==t.charAt(j-1)) dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1]+dp[i-1][j]; else dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j];`. When they differ, the s character cannot help, so we only carry the skip count. The answer is dp[m][n].

The time is O(m·n), space reduces to O(n) by iterating j from high to low on a single row. A senior nuance is that counts can grow very large (they commonly overflow int on big inputs), so production code uses long or modular arithmetic.

Problem 2 — Each matching log character offers a choice to use or skip it, and all choices must be counted. This is exactly why the match case sums the use and skip subproblems.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Distinct Subsequences is a two-dimensional counting dynamic programming problem. I define dp of i and j as the number of ways the first i characters of the source string can form the first j characters of the target. The base case is the entire first column being one, because the empty target is always matched exactly once by taking no characters.

The transition depends on whether the current source character matches the current target character. When they match I have a choice: use the source character to satisfy the target character, which contributes the diagonal cell, or skip the source character, which contributes the cell above, so I add both. When they differ the source character cannot help, so I carry only the skip count from the cell above. The answer is the bottom-right cell.

In my project at National Bank of India, an audit tool counted how many times a short approval code appeared as an ordered subsequence within a long transaction log, to gauge how many potential approval chains existed. Because each matching character offered a use-or-skip choice, I summed those two subproblems, and I used long types because these counts can easily overflow a thirty-two-bit integer on large logs.

answers.question: Implement regular expression matching where '.' matches any single character and '*' matches zero or more of the preceding element, over the entire input string.
answers.shortTitle: Regular Expression Matching — '.' and '*' with DP

s1_definition.profdef: 2D DP where dp[i][j] means the first i chars of text match the first j chars of pattern. A '*' gives two options: zero occurrences (dp[i][j−2]) or one-more occurrence when the preceding pattern char matches the current text char (dp[i−1][j]). A normal char or '.' requires a single-char match plus dp[i−1][j−1]. Time O(m·n), space O(m·n).
s1_definition.analogy: A reference-format validator at National Bank of India checks whether an account reference matches a pattern with wildcards. A dot matches any one character, and a star means the thing before it can repeat any number of times including zero, so at a star the validator tries both using none and using one more.
s1_definition.oneliner: '*' = skip two (zero) OR consume one text char if prev matches; '.'/char = single match + diagonal.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** 2D DP where dp[i][j] means the first i chars of text match the first j chars of pattern. A '*' gives two options: zero occurrences (dp[i][j−2]) or one-more occurrence when the preceding pattern char matches the current text char (dp[i−1][j]). A normal char or '.' requires a single-char match plus dp[i−1][j−1]. Time O(m·n), space O(m·n).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A reference-format validator at National Bank of India checks whether an account reference matches a pattern with wildcards. A dot matches any one character, and a star means the thing before it can repeat any number of times including zero, so at a star the validator tries both using none and using one more.

**One line to remember:** '*' = skip two (zero) OR consume one text char if prev matches; '.'/char = single match + diagonal.

sections.s2_technical:
Build dp of size (m+1) by (n+1) where m is the text length and n the pattern length. dp[0][0] is true. The first row needs special handling: a pattern like a* or a*b* can match an empty text, so dp[0][j] is true when the pattern char at j−1 is a star and dp[0][j−2] is true.

For the body, if the pattern char is a normal char or a dot, it must match the single current text char, so dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] AND (pattern matches text). For example: `boolean single = p.charAt(j-1)=='.' || p.charAt(j-1)==s.charAt(i-1);`. If the pattern char is a star, there are two cases: zero occurrences of the preceding element, giving dp[i][j−2], OR one more occurrence when the preceding pattern element matches the current text char, giving dp[i−1][j]. Combine with OR.

The time and space are O(m·n). A senior nuance is that the star case is the whole difficulty: it looks back two positions for the zero case and consumes one text character for the many case, and forgetting the zero case or the preceding-char match guard are the two classic bugs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a validator checks whether an account reference matches a wildcard pattern where a dot stands for any character and a star allows the previous element to repeat. This is exactly how Regular Expression Matching works.

Problem 2 — The star must allow zero or many repetitions, so a simple left-to-right scan cannot decide without backtracking. This is exactly why the DP encodes both the zero-occurrence and the one-more-occurrence branches.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Regular Expression Matching with dot and star is a two-dimensional dynamic programming problem. I define dp of i and j as whether the first i characters of the text match the first j characters of the pattern. The empty-empty cell is true, and I handle the first row specially so that patterns like a-star or a-star-b-star can match an empty text by letting each star take zero occurrences.

The body has two cases. If the pattern character is a normal character or a dot, it must match the single current text character, so the cell is true only if the diagonal is true and the single character matches. If the pattern character is a star, there are two possibilities combined with an OR: the star takes zero occurrences of the element before it, which looks back two positions, or the star takes one more occurrence when the preceding element matches the current text character, which consumes one text character and stays on the same pattern position.

In my project at National Bank of India, a validator checked whether an account reference matched a wildcard pattern where a dot stood for any character and a star allowed the previous element to repeat. The star is the whole difficulty because it must allow both zero and many repetitions, so I encoded both branches in the DP rather than trying a single left-to-right scan that cannot backtrack correctly.
