answers.question: Implement wildcard pattern matching where '?' matches any single character and '*' matches any sequence of characters including the empty sequence.
answers.shortTitle: Wildcard Matching — '?' and '*' with DP

s1_definition.profdef: 2D DP where dp[i][j] means the first i chars of text match the first j chars of pattern. For '*': dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] (star absorbs one more text char) OR dp[i][j−1] (star matches empty). For '?' or an exact char: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] when the single char matches. Time O(m·n), space O(n).
s1_definition.analogy: A file-name matcher at National Bank of India filters statement files by a glob pattern. A question mark matches exactly one character and a star matches any run of characters, so at a star the matcher can either swallow one more character or declare the star finished.
s1_definition.oneliner: '*' = extend over one more char OR match empty; '?'/char = diagonal when single matches.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** 2D DP where dp[i][j] means the first i chars of text match the first j chars of pattern. For '*': dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] (star absorbs one more text char) OR dp[i][j−1] (star matches empty). For '?' or an exact char: dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] when the single char matches. Time O(m·n), space O(n).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A file-name matcher at National Bank of India filters statement files by a glob pattern. A question mark matches exactly one character and a star matches any run of characters, so at a star the matcher can either swallow one more character or declare the star finished.

**One line to remember:** '*' = extend over one more char OR match empty; '?'/char = diagonal when single matches.

sections.s2_technical:
This is simpler than full regex because the star here is standalone, matching any sequence directly, not tied to a preceding element. Build dp of size (m+1) by (n+1). dp[0][0] is true, and the first row is true for a leading run of stars because each star can match the empty text: dp[0][j] = dp[0][j−1] when the pattern char is a star.

For the body, if the pattern char is a star, dp[i][j] is true if the star matches the current text char and continues, which is dp[i−1][j], or the star matches empty, which is dp[i][j−1]. For example: `if (pc=='*') dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j] || dp[i][j-1];`. If the pattern char is a question mark or equals the text char, inherit the diagonal: `else if (pc=='?' || pc==s.charAt(i-1)) dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j-1];`. Otherwise it stays false. The answer is dp[m][n].

The time is O(m·n), space reduces to O(n). A senior nuance is that a greedy two-pointer solution with a backtrack position for the last star also solves this in O(m·n) worst case but O(1) space, which is a strong follow-up answer.

answers.question: Given balloons with values, bursting balloon i yields nums[left]·nums[i]·nums[right] where left and right are the adjacent unburst balloons. Maximize the total coins from bursting all balloons.
answers.shortTitle: Burst Balloons — interval DP choosing the last balloon to burst

s1_definition.profdef: Interval DP over an array padded with 1 at both ends. dp[i][j] is the max coins from bursting all balloons strictly between i and j. Choose k as the LAST balloon burst in (i,j): dp[i][j] = max over k of dp[i][k] + nums[i]·nums[k]·nums[j] + dp[k][j]. Time O(n³), space O(n²).
s1_definition.analogy: A liquidation desk at National Bank of India closes positions one by one, where each closure's payout depends on its two surviving neighbors. The trick is to decide which position is closed LAST in a range, because then its neighbors are the fixed boundaries, splitting the range cleanly into two independent subranges.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pick the LAST balloon to burst in the interval; its neighbors are the padded boundaries.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Interval DP over an array padded with 1 at both ends. dp[i][j] is the max coins from bursting all balloons strictly between i and j. Choose k as the LAST balloon burst in (i,j): dp[i][j] = max over k of dp[i][k] + nums[i]·nums[k]·nums[j] + dp[k][j]. Time O(n³), space O(n²).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A liquidation desk at National Bank of India closes positions one by one, where each closure's payout depends on its two surviving neighbors. The trick is to decide which position is closed LAST in a range, because then its neighbors are the fixed boundaries, splitting the range cleanly into two independent subranges.

**One line to remember:** Pick the LAST balloon to burst in the interval; its neighbors are the padded boundaries.

sections.s2_technical:
The difficulty is that bursting a balloon changes who its neighbors are, so thinking about the FIRST balloon to burst couples the two sides. The insight is to instead pick the LAST balloon k to burst in an open interval (i, j). When k is last, every other balloon in the interval is already gone, so k's neighbors are exactly the fixed boundaries i and j, which decouples the left and right subranges.

Pad the array with a one at each end so boundary multiplications are well defined. Then dp[i][j] over the open interval is the maximum over all k strictly between i and j of dp[i][k] plus nums[i] times nums[k] times nums[j] plus dp[k][j]. For example: `dp[i][j] = Math.max(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + nums[i]*nums[k]*nums[j] + dp[k][j]);`. Iterate by increasing interval length so subintervals are ready. The answer is dp[0][n+1] over the padded array.

The time is O(n³) from three nested loops and space is O(n²). A senior nuance is that this "choose the last operation" reframing is the signature trick of hard interval DPs, the same idea powering matrix-chain multiplication.
sections.s3_banking:

Problem 2 — Reasoning about which position closes first couples both sides, but reasoning about which closes last fixes the boundaries. This is exactly why the DP chooses the last balloon in each interval.

sections.s5_journey:
The input values are three, one, five, eight.

Step 1: The array is padded to one, three, one, five, eight, one so boundary multiplications are defined.

Step 2: Short intervals are solved first, computing the best coins for single-balloon ranges.

Step 3: For each larger interval the code tries every balloon as the last one burst, using the padded boundaries as the surviving neighbors.

Step 4: The subrange results combine, and the best choice of last balloon is kept for each interval.

Step 5: The full interval yields one hundred sixty-seven, and the two-element case yields ten.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Burst Balloons is a hard interval dynamic programming problem, and the whole difficulty is that bursting a balloon changes who its neighbors are. If I reason about which balloon to burst first, the two sides stay coupled because the first burst's neighbors keep shifting. The key insight is to flip the reasoning and pick which balloon is burst last within an interval.

When a balloon k is the last to burst in an open interval between i and j, every other balloon in that interval is already gone, so k's neighbors are exactly the fixed boundaries i and j. That decouples the interval into an independent left part and right part. I pad the array with a one at each end so the boundary multiplications are defined, and then dp of i and j is the maximum over every choice of last balloon k of the left subinterval, plus the product of the two boundaries with k, plus the right subinterval. I fill intervals by increasing length, and the answer spans the whole padded array.

In my project at National Bank of India, a liquidation desk closed positions one at a time where each closure's payout depended on the two still-open neighbors, so the order changed the total proceeds. I used this choose-the-last-operation reframing, which is the same signature trick behind matrix-chain multiplication, and it runs in cubic time.

answers.question: Given the dimensions of a chain of matrices, find the minimum number of scalar multiplications needed to compute the product, choosing the best parenthesization.
answers.shortTitle: Matrix Chain Multiplication — interval DP for minimum multiplications

s1_definition.profdef: Interval DP where dp[i][j] is the minimum scalar multiplications to multiply matrices i through j. Split at k: dp[i][j] = min over k of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + p[i−1]·p[k]·p[j], where p is the dimension array. Time O(n³), space O(n²).
s1_definition.analogy: A risk engine at National Bank of India multiplies a chain of covariance matrices, and the order of multiplication drastically changes the arithmetic cost even though the result is the same. It tries every split point to find the cheapest way to group the multiplications.
s1_definition.oneliner: Split the chain at k; cost = left + right + p[i−1]·p[k]·p[j]; take the minimum.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Interval DP where dp[i][j] is the minimum scalar multiplications to multiply matrices i through j. Split at k: dp[i][j] = min over k of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + p[i−1]·p[k]·p[j], where p is the dimension array. Time O(n³), space O(n²).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A risk engine at National Bank of India multiplies a chain of covariance matrices, and the order of multiplication drastically changes the arithmetic cost even though the result is the same. It tries every split point to find the cheapest way to group the multiplications.

**One line to remember:** Split the chain at k; cost = left + right + p[i−1]·p[k]·p[j]; take the minimum.

sections.s2_technical:
Matrix multiplication is associative, so the result is the same regardless of grouping, but the cost is not. If a matrix is a by b and the next is b by c, multiplying them costs a times b times c scalar multiplications. With dimensions stored in an array p, matrix i has dimensions p[i−1] by p[i].

Define dp[i][j] as the minimum cost to multiply the subchain from i to j. For every split point k between i and j, the cost is the cost of the left group dp[i][k], plus the right group dp[k+1][j], plus the cost of multiplying the two resulting matrices, which is p[i−1] times p[k] times p[j]. For example: `dp[i][j] = Math.min(dp[i][j], dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + p[i-1]*p[k]*p[j]);`. The diagonal dp[i][i] is zero because a single matrix needs no multiplication. Iterate by chain length.

The time is O(n³) and space is O(n²). A senior nuance is that this is the archetypal interval DP where you choose a split operation, and storing the optimal split index lets you reconstruct the actual parenthesization.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a risk engine multiplies a chain of covariance and factor matrices, and the grouping order changes the arithmetic cost by orders of magnitude on large dimensions. This is exactly how Matrix Chain Multiplication works.

Problem 2 — Trying all parenthesizations explicitly is exponential (Catalan numbers). This is exactly why the DP memoizes the best cost of every subchain.

The mini-project builds a `MatrixChainPlanner`, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Matrix Chain Multiplication is the archetypal interval dynamic programming problem. Matrix multiplication is associative, so the final product is the same no matter how I group the operations, but the arithmetic cost is very different. If one matrix is a by b and the next is b by c, multiplying them costs a times b times c scalar multiplications, so the grouping order matters enormously.

I define dp of i and j as the minimum cost to multiply the subchain of matrices from i to j. For every split point k inside the interval, the cost is the best cost of the left group, plus the best cost of the right group, plus the cost of multiplying the two resulting matrices, which uses the boundary dimensions. A single matrix needs no multiplication, so the diagonal is zero, and I fill the table by increasing chain length so subchains are ready. The answer covers the whole chain, and I can store the best split index to reconstruct the actual parenthesization.

In my project at National Bank of India, a risk engine multiplied a chain of covariance and factor matrices where the grouping order changed the cost by orders of magnitude on large dimensions. Trying all parenthesizations is exponential because their count follows the Catalan numbers, so I used this cubic-time interval DP that memoizes the best cost of every subchain.

answers.question: Given a string of only '(' and ')', return the length of the longest substring that is a valid (well-formed) parentheses sequence.
answers.shortTitle: Longest Valid Parentheses — longest balanced substring

s1_definition.profdef: Solvable by a stack of indices seeded with a sentinel −1: push indices of '(', and on ')' pop; if the stack becomes empty push the current index as a new base, otherwise the valid length is current index minus the new stack top. Track the maximum. Time O(n), space O(n). A DP and an O(1)-space two-pass also exist.
s1_definition.analogy: A message-framing checker at National Bank of India finds the longest stretch of a protocol string where every open marker is properly closed. It remembers the position just before each unmatched point and measures balanced runs from there.
s1_definition.oneliner: Stack of indices with a −1 base; on ')' pop and measure current − new top; track max.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Solvable by a stack of indices seeded with a sentinel −1: push indices of '(', and on ')' pop; if the stack becomes empty push the current index as a new base, otherwise the valid length is current index minus the new stack top. Track the maximum. Time O(n), space O(n). A DP and an O(1)-space two-pass also exist.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A message-framing checker at National Bank of India finds the longest stretch of a protocol string where every open marker is properly closed. It remembers the position just before each unmatched point and measures balanced runs from there.

**One line to remember:** Stack of indices with a −1 base; on ')' pop and measure current − new top; track max.

sections.s2_technical:
Use a stack holding indices, initialized with −1 as a base marker meaning "the position just before a valid run." For each open parenthesis, push its index. For each close parenthesis, pop the top. After popping, if the stack is now empty, this close has no match, so push the current index as a new base. If the stack is not empty, the top is the index just before the current valid run, so the valid length is the current index minus that top. For example: `stack.pop(); if (stack.isEmpty()) stack.push(i); else best = Math.max(best, i - stack.peek());`.

The sentinel −1 is the elegance: it lets the very first valid run be measured without special casing, since a run ending at index i that started at the beginning has length i minus negative one.

The time is O(n) and space is O(n). A senior nuance is the constant-space two-pass alternative: scan left to right counting opens and closes and record the length when they balance, resetting when closes exceed opens, then do the same right to left; this avoids the stack entirely.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a protocol parser must find the longest well-framed stretch of a message where every open marker has a matching close, to isolate the largest intact segment after corruption. This is exactly how Longest Valid Parentheses works.

Problem 2 — Simply counting balanced markers is not enough because the valid part must be contiguous. This is exactly why index positions are tracked on a stack with a base sentinel.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Longest Valid Parentheses asks for the longest contiguous well-formed substring, and my preferred solution uses a stack of indices seeded with a sentinel of minus one. The sentinel represents the position just before a valid run. For each open parenthesis I push its index, and for each close parenthesis I pop the top.

After popping, there are two cases. If the stack is now empty, this close had no matching open, so I push its own index as a new base for future runs. If the stack is not empty, the new top is the index just before the current valid run, so the valid length is the current index minus that top, and I keep the maximum. The sentinel minus one is the elegance, because it lets a valid run that starts at the very beginning be measured without any special casing.

In my project at National Bank of India, a protocol parser had to find the longest well-framed stretch of a message where every open marker had a matching close, to isolate the largest intact segment after corruption. Because the valid part must be contiguous, simply counting balanced markers is not enough, so I tracked index positions on the stack, and I mention the constant-space two-pass counting alternative as a follow-up.

answers.question: A robot moves only right or down on an m by n grid where some cells are blocked (marked 1). Count distinct paths from top-left to bottom-right; blocked cells cannot be entered.
answers.shortTitle: Unique Paths II — grid paths with obstacles

s1_definition.profdef: Grid DP like Unique Paths but any obstacle cell has dp=0, and the first row/column stop contributing once an obstacle is hit. For free cells dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + dp[i][j−1]; obstacle cells force dp[i][j]=0. If the start or end is blocked the answer is 0. Time O(m·n), space O(n).
s1_definition.analogy: A courier at National Bank of India routes a document across a grid of offices moving only east or south, but some offices are closed for the day. A closed office contributes zero routes, and any route passing through it is eliminated.
s1_definition.oneliner: Obstacle ⇒ dp=0; free ⇒ from above + from left; blocked start/end ⇒ 0.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Grid DP like Unique Paths but any obstacle cell has dp=0, and the first row/column stop contributing once an obstacle is hit. For free cells dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j] + dp[i][j−1]; obstacle cells force dp[i][j]=0. If the start or end is blocked the answer is 0. Time O(m·n), space O(n).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A courier at National Bank of India routes a document across a grid of offices moving only east or south, but some offices are closed for the day. A closed office contributes zero routes, and any route passing through it is eliminated.

**One line to remember:** Obstacle ⇒ dp=0; free ⇒ from above + from left; blocked start/end ⇒ 0.

sections.s2_technical:
Start by checking the top-left cell: if it is an obstacle the answer is zero because the robot cannot even begin. Otherwise set dp[0][0]=1. Build the dp grid where each obstacle cell is forced to zero and each free cell sums the paths from above and from the left, exactly like the obstacle-free version except for the zeroing. For example: `dp[i][j] = (grid[i][j]==1) ? 0 : (up + left);`.

The first row and first column need care: along an edge, once an obstacle appears, every cell after it is unreachable because there is only one direction of travel, so those cells become zero and stay zero. The summation naturally handles this when you start edges from zero and only add the single valid neighbor.

The time and space are O(m·n), reducible to O(n) with a rolling row that zeroes out obstacle columns. A senior nuance is the easy-to-miss edge case where the destination itself is an obstacle, which must yield zero, and this falls out automatically because that cell is forced to zero.

Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a courier routes a document across a grid of offices moving only east or south, but some offices are closed and cannot be entered. This is exactly how Unique Paths II works.

Problem 2 — A closed office must eliminate every route through it, including whole edges beyond it. This is exactly why obstacle cells are forced to zero and propagate.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Unique Paths II is the obstacle version of the grid counting problem. I define dp of i and j as the number of distinct paths from the top-left to that cell, moving only right or down. The one addition compared to the obstacle-free version is that any blocked cell is forced to a count of zero, which eliminates every path that would pass through it.

I start by checking the corners: if either the start or the destination is blocked, the answer is zero because the robot cannot begin or finish. For every free cell I sum the paths from directly above and directly to the left, and for every obstacle cell I set the count to zero. The first row and first column need care because once an obstacle appears along an edge, every cell beyond it is unreachable and stays zero, which falls out naturally when I start the edges from zero and add only valid neighbors.

In my project at National Bank of India, a courier routed a document across a grid of offices moving only east or south, but some offices were closed and could not be entered. A closed office had to eliminate every route through it, including whole edges beyond it, so I forced obstacle cells to zero and let the counts propagate, and I can reduce the memory to a single rolling row.

answers.question: Explain Cyclic Sort. Given an array containing numbers in the range [1, n] (or [0, n-1]), sort it in O(n) time and O(1) extra space by swapping each number to its correct index.
answers.shortTitle: Cyclic Sort — place each value at its correct index in O(n)

s1_definition.profdef: Cyclic Sort is an in-place sorting technique for arrays whose values form a known contiguous range such as 1 to n. It walks the array once, and at each index it checks whether the current value is already sitting at its correct home index; if not, it swaps the value into its correct slot. Because every swap places at least one number permanently, the total number of swaps is bounded by n, giving O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, token numbers 1 to n are handed out but customers sat in the wrong chairs. A staff member walks chair by chair: if the person in chair 3 is holding token 3 they stay, otherwise the staff member sends them to the chair matching their token and pulls back whoever was there. Each move seats one person permanently, so the whole room gets sorted in one pass.
s1_definition.oneliner: For values in [1, n], keep swapping `nums[i]` to index `nums[i]-1` until it is home, then move on.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Cyclic Sort is an in-place sorting technique for arrays whose values form a known contiguous range such as 1 to n. It walks the array once, and at each index it checks whether the current value is already sitting at its correct home index; if not, it swaps the value into its correct slot. Because every swap places at least one number permanently, the total number of swaps is bounded by n, giving O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, token numbers 1 to n are handed out but customers sat in the wrong chairs. A staff member walks chair by chair: if the person in chair 3 is holding token 3 they stay, otherwise the staff member sends them to the chair matching their token and pulls back whoever was there. Each move seats one person permanently, so the whole room gets sorted in one pass.

**One line to remember:** For values in [1, n], keep swapping `nums[i]` to index `nums[i]-1` until it is home, then move on.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is that when values are a permutation of 1 to n, value v belongs at index v-1 (or value v belongs at index v when the range is 0 to n-1). So you iterate with a pointer i, and instead of advancing blindly, you first make sure the element at i is correct. For example, the inner condition looks like `while (nums[i] != i + 1) { swap(nums, i, nums[i] - 1); }`. You only advance i when the element is already home.

The key insight for correctness is the swap target. You compute the correct index of the current value as `nums[i] - 1` and swap it there: `int correct = nums[i] - 1; swap(nums, i, correct);`. After the swap, a new value lands at i and you re-check it in the same while loop, which is why this is a while and not an if.

The reason the whole thing is O(n) and not O(n squared) is amortized counting. Every successful swap puts one value in its permanent correct position, and a value never leaves a correct position once placed. Since there are only n positions, you can perform at most n swaps across the entire run, and the outer loop does n steps, so the total work is linear.

A senior nuance is handling ranges and duplicates. If the range is 0 to n-1, the home index of value v is simply v. If duplicates are possible, you must add a guard so you do not swap two equal values forever: `if (nums[i] != nums[correct]) swap(...) else i++;`. This guard is exactly what turns cyclic sort into a tool for finding duplicates and missing numbers.

Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, the daily queue hands out token numbers 1 to n, but after a power outage the token list got shuffled in memory and must be re-ordered fast without allocating a second big array. This is exactly how Cyclic Sort works, because the tokens are a known range and can be swapped into their home slots in one pass.

Problem 2 — The operations team cannot afford extra memory because the token buffer is huge and shared across counters. This is exactly why cyclic sort matters: it sorts in place with O(1) extra space instead of allocating a copy.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the shuffled token array three, one, five, four, two.

Step 1: At index zero the value is three, whose home is index two, so three swaps with the value at index two (five). The array becomes five, one, three, four, two and index zero is re-checked.

Step 2: Now index zero holds five, whose home is index four, so five swaps with two. The array becomes two, one, three, four, five and index zero is re-checked.

Step 3: Index zero holds two, whose home is index one, so two swaps with one, giving one, two, three, four, five. Index zero now holds one which is home, so the pointer advances.

Step 4: Indices one through four each already hold their correct values, so the pointer walks to the end doing no swaps.

Step 5: The array is fully sorted in place using only swaps and no extra array.

```text
2026-10-27T06:00:00Z [INFO] Sorted tokens = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
2026-10-27T06:00:00Z [INFO] Sorted tokens = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
```

```text
    │ i=0 val=3 home=2 → swap(0,2)
    ▼  5 1 3 4 2
    │ i=0 val=5 home=4 → swap(0,4)
    ▼  2 1 3 4 5
    │ i=0 val=2 home=1 → swap(0,1)
    ▼  1 2 3 4 5   (i=0 home → advance)
    │ i=1..4 already home → advance
    ▼ output: 1 2 3 4 5
```

```text
  │  amortized: each swap fixes one slot ⇒ ≤ n swaps ⇒ O(n)  │
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Cyclic Sort is an in-place sorting technique I reach for whenever the array contains numbers from a known contiguous range such as one to n. The key observation is that value v belongs at index v minus one, so I can place every value directly into its home slot by swapping, rather than comparing and shifting like a general sort. I walk the array with a single pointer, and at each position I keep swapping the current value into its correct index until the value at that position is already home, and only then do I advance the pointer.

The reason this runs in linear time rather than quadratic is amortized counting. Every successful swap puts at least one value into its permanent correct position, and once a value is home it never moves again. Since there are only n positions, the total number of swaps across the whole run is bounded by n, so the algorithm is O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

One nuance I always mention is the guard condition. When duplicates are possible, I compare the value at the current index with the value already sitting at its home index, and I only swap if they differ, otherwise I would loop forever swapping two equal values. This same guard is what makes cyclic sort the foundation for finding missing numbers, duplicates, and disappeared numbers.

In my project at National Bank of India, the daily queue handed out token numbers one to n, but after an outage the token buffer got shuffled and had to be re-ordered quickly without allocating a second large array. Cyclic sort was the perfect fit because the tokens were a known range, so I sorted them in one pass in place, and the same technique let me later detect missing and duplicate tokens by checking which index held the wrong value.

answers.question: Given a string containing the bracket characters round, square, and curly, determine whether every opening bracket is closed by the matching type in the correct order, using a stack.
answers.shortTitle: Validate Balanced Parentheses Using a Stack

s1_definition.profdef: Balanced-parentheses validation uses a last-in-first-out stack to confirm that every opening bracket has a correctly typed and correctly ordered closing bracket. You push each opening bracket, and on each closing bracket you pop and check that the popped opener matches the closer's type. The string is valid only if every closer matched and the stack is empty at the end. It runs in linear time and linear worst-case space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India stacking approval slips on a spike. Every time a nested approval opens, she spikes a slip of that colour on top. When an approval closes, she can only remove the slip currently on top, and its colour must match the one closing. If a red approval tries to close while a blue slip sits on top, the paperwork is out of order and she rejects the batch. At the end the spike must be empty, meaning every approval that opened was properly closed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Push every opener, pop and type-match on every closer, and the string is valid only if the stack ends empty.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Balanced-parentheses validation uses a last-in-first-out stack to confirm that every opening bracket has a correctly typed and correctly ordered closing bracket. You push each opening bracket, and on each closing bracket you pop and check that the popped opener matches the closer's type. The string is valid only if every closer matched and the stack is empty at the end. It runs in linear time and linear worst-case space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India stacking approval slips on a spike. Every time a nested approval opens, she spikes a slip of that colour on top. When an approval closes, she can only remove the slip currently on top, and its colour must match the one closing. If a red approval tries to close while a blue slip sits on top, the paperwork is out of order and she rejects the batch. At the end the spike must be empty, meaning every approval that opened was properly closed.

**One line to remember:** Push every opener, pop and type-match on every closer, and the string is valid only if the stack ends empty.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is that brackets must close in the reverse order they opened, which is exactly the last-in-first-out behaviour a stack gives you. In Java the recommended stack is `ArrayDeque` used through the `Deque` interface rather than the legacy `Stack` class, because `Stack` extends `Vector` and is synchronised on every call, which is slower and rarely what you want. For example, `Deque<Character> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();` gives you `push`, `pop`, and `peek` without the synchronisation overhead.

As you scan the string left to right, for each opening bracket you call `stack.push(c)`, which places it on top. For each closing bracket you first check the stack is not empty, because a closer with nothing to match against is an immediate failure, then you `stack.pop()` the most recent opener and compare types. A clean way to compare is a small map from closer to its matching opener, for example `Map<Character,Character> pairs = Map.of(')','(', ']','[', '}','{');`, then the check is `if (stack.pop() != pairs.get(c)) return false;`.

Two end conditions matter. If at any closer the stack is empty, there is no opener to match, so you return false right away. After the full scan, the stack must be empty; if openers remain, they were never closed, so you return false. Only an empty stack at the end means true. Missing either check is the classic bug that passes a string like an unmatched opening bracket.

A senior-level nuance is the complexity and the variants. Time is linear because each character is pushed and popped at most once, and space is linear in the worst case of all openers. The same stack technique extends to validating nested expressions, matching HTML or XML tags, and checking balanced quotes in a parser, so interviewers use it as the gateway to stack-based parsing.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India ingests structured transaction messages whose nested segments are delimited by brackets, and a malformed message with mismatched brackets must be rejected before parsing, otherwise the downstream parser throws deep in processing and corrupts a batch. We need a fast pre-check that confirms the brackets are balanced. This is exactly what a stack-based validator does, because nesting must close in reverse order.

Problem 2 — A closing bracket that appears with no matching opener, or an opener left dangling at the end, both mean the message framing is broken. The stack naturally catches both: an empty stack on a closer is an early reject, and a non-empty stack at the end is a dangling-opener reject.

In our mini-project we build a `BracketValidator` with an `isBalanced` method over a message-framing string. The demo validates a correctly nested message and a broken one, logging each push and pop so you can watch the spike of slips grow and shrink.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the well-framed message of curly, square, round openers then matching closers, and the broken message where a round closer appears before the square it is nested in.

Step 1: For the good message, we read curly and push it, depth one. We read square and push it, depth two. We read round and push it, depth three.

Step 2: We read the round closer, pop the round opener, they match, depth two. We read the square closer, pop the square opener, they match, depth one. We read the curly closer, pop the curly opener, they match, depth zero.

Step 3: The scan ends with an empty stack, so the good message is balanced and we return true.

Step 4: For the bad message we push curly, square, round the same way, depth three. We then read the square closer while the round opener is on top. The popped opener is round, which does not match the square closer, so we immediately return false.

Step 5: Throughout, only the stack changed; the input string was read once left to right, confirming the linear time behaviour.

```
[2026-10-26 23:20:01] INFO    Message '{[()]}' balanced? true
[2026-10-26 23:20:01] WARNING   mismatch at ']' — invalid framing
[2026-10-26 23:20:01] INFO    Message '{[(])}' balanced? false
```

```
  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Stack (LIFO) via ArrayDeque — reverse-order matching         │
  │  Lookup map closer→opener for O(1) type check                 │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: BracketValidator only validates framing                   │
  │  O: new bracket types = add map entries, no logic change      │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           BracketValidator            │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  - PAIRS: Map<Character,Character>    │
  │  + isBalanced(s: String): boolean     │  O(n) time, O(n) space
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      Pre:  s contains only bracket chars
      Post: true iff every opener matched and stack empty

  ── State Diagram: Scan ──────────────────────────────────

  [reading] ──opener──→ push ──→ [reading]
  [reading] ──closer, match──→ pop ──→ [reading]
  [reading] ──closer, empty/mismatch──→ [INVALID]
  [end, stack empty] ──→ [VALID]

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. isBalanced(s)
  2.   for each char: opener → push; closer → pop + match
  3.   empty-on-closer or type-mismatch → return false
  4.   return stack.isEmpty()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Validating balanced parentheses uses a last-in-first-out stack because brackets must close in the reverse order they opened. I scan the string once from left to right. For every opening bracket I push it onto the stack, and for every closing bracket I pop the most recent opener and confirm its type matches the closer. The string is valid only if every closer found a correctly typed match and the stack is completely empty at the end.

There are two failure conditions I always guard. If I hit a closing bracket while the stack is empty, there is no opener to match, so I return false immediately. And after the whole scan, if any openers remain on the stack, they were never closed, so that is also false. Only an empty stack at the end means the string is balanced. In Java I use ArrayDeque through the Deque interface rather than the old Stack class, because Stack extends Vector and synchronises every call, which is slower and unnecessary here.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this as a fast pre-check on structured transaction messages whose nested segments are delimited by brackets. A malformed message with crossed or dangling brackets gets rejected to a dead-letter path before it ever reaches the real parser, which protects a whole batch from a parser error deep in processing. The validator runs in linear time, scanning each character once, with worst-case linear space when everything is an opener.

The senior-level point I make is that this stack technique is the foundation of real parsing. The identical idea scales up to matching HTML and XML tags, validating nested expressions, and checking balanced quotes, and it is the first step toward shunting-yard expression evaluation. So I treat it not as a toy puzzle but as the simplest instance of stack-based syntactic validation that appears throughout production parsers.

answers.question: Given an array containing n distinct numbers taken from the range [0, n], find the one number that is missing. Solve using cyclic sort in O(n) time and O(1) space.
answers.shortTitle: Find Missing Number — cyclic sort then find the index where value ≠ index

s1_definition.profdef: The array holds n distinct values drawn from 0 to n, so exactly one value in that range is absent. Using cyclic sort, each value v is swapped to index v, and values equal to n are skipped because they have no home index in the array. After sorting, the first index i whose value is not i identifies the missing number; if all indices match, the missing number is n.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, lockers are numbered 0 to n but only n keys exist, so exactly one locker has no key. Staff put each key into the locker matching its number; the single empty locker at the end reveals the missing key number.
s1_definition.oneliner: Cyclic sort placing v at index v, then the first index where `nums[i] != i` is the missing number, else n.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The array holds n distinct values drawn from 0 to n, so exactly one value in that range is absent. Using cyclic sort, each value v is swapped to index v, and values equal to n are skipped because they have no home index in the array. After sorting, the first index i whose value is not i identifies the missing number; if all indices match, the missing number is n.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, lockers are numbered 0 to n but only n keys exist, so exactly one locker has no key. Staff put each key into the locker matching its number; the single empty locker at the end reveals the missing key number.

**One line to remember:** Cyclic sort placing v at index v, then the first index where `nums[i] != i` is the missing number, else n.

sections.s2_technical:
Because the range is 0 to n and there are n slots, value v belongs at index v. During cyclic sort you swap each value to its home index, but you must skip any value equal to n since index n does not exist: `if (nums[i] < n && nums[i] != nums[nums[i]]) swap(...) else i++;`. This keeps the swap in bounds.

After the sort completes, you scan once looking for the mismatch. The example scan is `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (nums[i] != i) return i;`. Exactly one index will be wrong because exactly one value is missing and the value n occupies whatever slot was left over.

If the scan finds no mismatch, that means every index 0 through n-1 holds its own value, so the only number that could be missing is n itself, and you `return nums.length;`. This final return is the easy-to-forget case.

A senior nuance is why this beats the sum formula. The Gauss sum approach computes n times n plus one over two minus the array sum, which is elegant but can overflow for large n. Cyclic sort avoids any arithmetic overflow and still runs in linear time with constant space, which is the safer choice in production banking code.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, lockers are numbered 0 to n and each should have a key, but a reconciliation shows one key is missing. This is exactly how Find Missing Number works, because the keys are a known range with one absent value.

Problem 2 — The audit must find the missing key without allocating a huge boolean array, since the locker range is large. This is exactly why cyclic sort matters: it finds the gap in place with constant extra space.

The mini-project builds a `LockerAuditor` with a `findMissing` method, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the array four, zero, three, one with n equal to four.

Step 1: At index zero the value is four, which equals n, so there is no home index and the pointer advances.

Step 2: At index one the value is zero whose home is index zero, so zero swaps with four, giving zero, four, three, one, and index one is re-checked.

Step 3: Index one now holds four which equals n, so the pointer advances. Indices two and three already hold three and one incorrectly, so three swaps to index three and one swaps to index one, settling into zero, one, three, four... after the full cyclic pass the array is zero, one, four, three.

Step 4: The scan finds index two holds four, not two, so two is the first mismatch.

Step 5: The missing locker key is reported as two, and the second demo with zero, one, two reports three because no index mismatches.

```text
2026-10-27T06:10:00Z [INFO] Missing in [0,1,2]   → 3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Find Missing Number is a direct application of cyclic sort. The array holds n distinct values from the range zero to n, so exactly one value is absent. The crucial observation is that value v belongs at index v, so I run a cyclic sort that swaps each value into its home index, taking care to skip any value equal to n because there is no index n in an array of length n.

After the sort, every value that has a valid home sits at its matching index, so I scan once and the first index whose value does not equal the index is the missing number. If the scan finds no mismatch at all, then every slot from zero to n minus one is correctly filled, which means the only number that can be missing is n itself, so I return the array length.

I prefer this over the Gauss sum trick, which subtracts the array sum from n times n plus one over two, because the sum approach can overflow for very large inputs. Cyclic sort does no arithmetic that can overflow and still runs in linear time with constant extra space.

In my project at National Bank of India, lockers were numbered zero to n and each should have a key, but a reconciliation showed one key missing. The locker range was too large to justify a boolean marker array, so I used cyclic sort to place every key into its home slot in place, and the single index that ended up holding the wrong value told me exactly which locker key was missing.

answers.question: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element, with every operation running in constant time.
answers.shortTitle: Design a Min Stack (Constant-Time Minimum)

s1_definition.profdef: A min stack is a stack that, in addition to push, pop, and top, returns the current minimum element in constant time. The standard design keeps a second stack of running minimums in lockstep with the main stack, so the top of the min stack is always the smallest value currently present. Every operation is constant time because each one does a fixed amount of work on both stacks.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture a clerk at the National Bank of India stacking account balance slips. Next to the main spike she keeps a second spike of "smallest-so-far" slips. Every time she adds a balance, she also adds a slip showing the smallest balance seen up to that point. When she removes the top balance, she removes the matching smallest-so-far slip too. So at any instant she can glance at the top of the second spike and instantly know the smallest balance on the stack, without scanning everything.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a parallel min-stack whose top is always the current minimum, so getMin is constant time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A min stack is a stack that, in addition to push, pop, and top, returns the current minimum element in constant time. The standard design keeps a second stack of running minimums in lockstep with the main stack, so the top of the min stack is always the smallest value currently present. Every operation is constant time because each one does a fixed amount of work on both stacks.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture a clerk at the National Bank of India stacking account balance slips. Next to the main spike she keeps a second spike of "smallest-so-far" slips. Every time she adds a balance, she also adds a slip showing the smallest balance seen up to that point. When she removes the top balance, she removes the matching smallest-so-far slip too. So at any instant she can glance at the top of the second spike and instantly know the smallest balance on the stack, without scanning everything.

**One line to remember:** Keep a parallel min-stack whose top is always the current minimum, so getMin is constant time.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive way to get the minimum is to scan the whole stack, which is linear time per query and too slow when getMin is called frequently. The trick is to pay a tiny constant cost on every push and pop so that the minimum is always ready in constant time.

You maintain two `ArrayDeque` stacks, the main one and a min one. On `push(x)` you always push onto the main stack, and you push onto the min stack either x or the current minimum, whichever is smaller: `minStack.push(minStack.isEmpty() ? x : Math.min(x, minStack.peek()));`. This way the min stack top mirrors the smallest value among all elements currently in the main stack. On `pop()` you pop both stacks together so they stay aligned. On `top()` you peek the main stack, and on `getMin()` you peek the min stack.

Because money in banking uses BigDecimal, the comparison must use `compareTo` rather than the less-than operator, for example `cur.compareTo(x) <= 0 ? cur : x`. Using equals-aware comparison with `<= 0` keeps duplicates handled correctly, so if the same minimum is pushed twice, popping once still leaves the minimum available from the earlier copy.

A senior-level nuance is the space-optimised variant. Instead of storing a full min on every push, you can push onto the min stack only when a new value is less than or equal to the current minimum, and pop from it only when the popped main value equals the current minimum. That saves memory when minimums repeat rarely, at the cost of slightly trickier pop logic. Another encoding stores deltas from the minimum in a single stack, trading clarity for space. For interviews the two-stack version is the clearest correct answer, and I mention the optimisations to show depth.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A risk dashboard at the National Bank of India pushes and pops account balances as positions open and close through the day, and the desk constantly asks "what is the lowest balance currently exposed?" Scanning all open positions on every query is too slow during peak trading. We need the running minimum available instantly. This is exactly a min stack, because the answer is always the smallest value currently on the stack.

Problem 2 — Balances must be exact money values, so we cannot use primitive doubles; we use BigDecimal and compare with compareTo. The min stack must therefore track the minimum BigDecimal correctly, including when the same lowest balance appears more than once.

In our mini-project we build a `MinBalanceStack` backed by two deques of BigDecimal. The demo pushes several balances, reads the minimum, pops one, and reads the minimum again to show it updates in constant time.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: push one million, then two hundred fifty thousand, then five hundred thousand, then two pops.

Step 1: Push one million. The main stack holds one million. The min stack is empty, so it stores one million as the minimum.

Step 2: Push two hundred fifty thousand. The main stack now has it on top. The current min was one million, and two hundred fifty thousand is smaller, so the min stack pushes two hundred fifty thousand.

Step 3: Push five hundred thousand. The current min is two hundred fifty thousand, which is still smaller than five hundred thousand, so the min stack pushes two hundred fifty thousand again, keeping the minimum correct.

Step 4: We read the top, which is five hundred thousand, and the minimum, which is two hundred fifty thousand, both in constant time from the respective stack tops.

Step 5: We pop. Both stacks drop their top, removing five hundred thousand from main and the duplicated two hundred fifty thousand from the min stack. The minimum is still two hundred fifty thousand.

Step 6: We pop again, removing two hundred fifty thousand from main and its min entry. Now the main stack holds only one million, and the min stack top is one million, so the minimum correctly becomes one million.

```
[2026-10-26 23:21:01] INFO    Top balance: 500000
[2026-10-26 23:21:01] INFO    Min balance: 250000
[2026-10-26 23:21:01] INFO    After pop, min: 250000
[2026-10-26 23:21:01] INFO    After pop, min: 1000000
```

```
                                 └────────┬──────────┘

                                 ┌──────────────────┐
                                 │ Position store    │ (PostgreSQL)
                                 └──────────────────┘
```

```
  │  Auxiliary-stack technique — parallel min invariant           │
  │  Decorator-like wrapper over Deque with extra bookkeeping     │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: MinBalanceStack only manages the stack + its minimum      │
  │  O: swap compareTo for a Comparator to support other orders   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           MinBalanceStack             │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  - main: Deque<BigDecimal>            │  main values
  │  - mins: Deque<BigDecimal>            │  running minimums
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + push(x): void                      │  O(1)
  │  + pop(): BigDecimal                  │  O(1)
  │  + top(): BigDecimal                  │  O(1)
  │  + getMin(): BigDecimal               │  O(1)
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      Invariant: mins.peek() == min(main)

  ── State Diagram: Min invariant ─────────────────────────

  [push x] → mins.push(min(x, mins.peek))
  [pop]    → both stacks pop together (stay aligned)
  [getMin] → mins.peek() (never scans)

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. push(x): main.push(x); mins.push(min(x, cur))
  2. pop(): mins.pop(); return main.pop()
  3. getMin(): return mins.peek()
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A min stack is a stack that supports push, pop, top, and getMin all in constant time. The naive approach of scanning the stack to find the minimum is linear per query, which is too slow when getMin is called often, so instead I keep a second stack of running minimums alongside the main stack. The top of that min stack is always the smallest value currently present, so getMin is just a peek.

The mechanics are simple and that is the point. On every push I push the value onto the main stack and I push onto the min stack whichever is smaller between the new value and the current minimum. On every pop I pop both stacks together so they stay perfectly aligned. Because each operation does a fixed amount of work on two stacks, every operation is constant time, and because I store a min entry per element, the extra space is linear.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this for a risk dashboard where account balances are pushed and popped as positions open and close, and the desk constantly asks for the lowest balance currently exposed. Since the balances are money, I store them as BigDecimal and compare with compareTo rather than primitive operators, and I use a less-than-or-equal comparison so repeated minimums are handled correctly when the same lowest balance appears twice.

The senior-level point I add is that there are space optimisations. I can push to the min stack only when a value is less than or equal to the current minimum and pop from it only when the popped value equals the current minimum, which saves memory when minimums repeat rarely. There is also a delta-encoding variant that uses a single stack. I present the clean two-stack version as my default because it is obviously correct, and I mention the optimisations to show I understand the space-time trade-off.

answers.question: Given an array of n integers where each value is in the range [1, n] and some values appear twice while others are missing, return all the numbers in [1, n] that do not appear. Use O(n) time and O(1) extra space (output array does not count).
answers.shortTitle: Find All Disappeared Numbers — cyclic sort then collect every mismatched index

s1_definition.profdef: The array has length n with values in 1 to n, so some values repeat and others never appear. Cyclic sort places each value v at index v-1 when possible; after sorting, any index i whose value is not i+1 corresponds to a disappeared number i+1. Collecting every such index yields all missing values in linear time and constant extra space, not counting the result list.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, cheque serial numbers 1 to n should each appear once in a batch, but scanning errors duplicated some and dropped others. Staff sort each serial into its matching slot; every slot that ends up holding the wrong serial reveals a cheque number that disappeared.
s1_definition.oneliner: Cyclic sort values into index v-1, then every index where `nums[i] != i+1` means i+1 disappeared.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The array has length n with values in 1 to n, so some values repeat and others never appear. Cyclic sort places each value v at index v-1 when possible; after sorting, any index i whose value is not i+1 corresponds to a disappeared number i+1. Collecting every such index yields all missing values in linear time and constant extra space, not counting the result list.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, cheque serial numbers 1 to n should each appear once in a batch, but scanning errors duplicated some and dropped others. Staff sort each serial into its matching slot; every slot that ends up holding the wrong serial reveals a cheque number that disappeared.

**One line to remember:** Cyclic sort values into index v-1, then every index where `nums[i] != i+1` means i+1 disappeared.

sections.s2_technical:
You run the same cyclic sort as before, placing value v at index v-1, with the equal-value guard so duplicates do not loop: `while (nums[i] != nums[nums[i]-1]) swap(nums, i, nums[i]-1);`. Duplicates cause two equal values to want the same home, and the guard stops the loop, leaving one duplicate parked in some wrong slot.

After sorting, you do a single scan and collect the disappeared numbers: `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (nums[i] != i + 1) result.add(i + 1);`. Each wrong slot means the value that belongs there, namely i+1, never made it home because it was never in the array in the first place.

The reason both duplicates and missing numbers co-exist is simple counting: with n slots and n values, every duplicate forces exactly one value to be missing. The wrong slots are precisely where a missing value should have landed but a duplicate squatted instead.

A senior nuance is the space accounting. The output list is required output, so it does not count against the O(1) extra space claim; the algorithm itself allocates nothing beyond a few index variables. This is the standard interpretation interviewers expect, and the in-place marking alternative that negates values is an equally valid O(1) approach.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, cheque serials 1 to n should appear exactly once in a batch, but a scanner duplicated some and dropped others. This is exactly how Find All Disappeared Numbers works, because the serials are a known range with duplicates and gaps.

Problem 2 — The audit needs every missing serial, not just one, and cannot afford a separate boolean array for a huge batch. This is exactly why cyclic sort matters: it exposes all gaps in place with constant extra space.

The mini-project builds a `ChequeAuditor` with a `findDisappeared` method, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

The input is the serial batch four, three, two, seven, eight, two, three, one with n equal to eight.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Find All Disappeared Numbers builds directly on cyclic sort. The array has length n with values from one to n, so with exactly n slots and n values, every value that appears twice forces some other value to be missing. The key observation is that value v belongs at index v minus one, so I cyclic sort the array, placing each value into its home slot, and I use the equal-value guard so that duplicates do not cause an infinite swap loop.

After sorting, I scan the array once. Any index whose value is not index plus one is a slot where the correct value never arrived, which means the number that belongs there disappeared. I collect index plus one for every such slot, and that list is the complete set of missing numbers.

A point I always raise is space accounting. The result list is required output, so it does not count against the constant extra space claim; the algorithm itself only uses a few index variables. An equivalent in-place technique negates the value at the home index as a marker, and then positive values reveal the gaps, which is also O(1) extra space.

In my project at National Bank of India, cheque serials one to n were supposed to appear exactly once per batch, but a faulty scanner duplicated some serials and dropped others. I used cyclic sort to drive each serial into its home slot in place, and every slot that ended up holding the wrong serial told me precisely which cheque numbers had disappeared, which the reconciliation report then flagged.

answers.question: Given an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation (postfix), where operators follow their operands, evaluate it and return the result using a stack.
answers.shortTitle: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation Using a Stack

s1_definition.profdef: Reverse Polish Notation, also called postfix, writes each operator after its two operands, so there are no parentheses and no precedence rules to resolve. You evaluate it with a stack: push each number, and on each operator pop the top two numbers, apply the operator, and push the result back. When the tokens are exhausted, the single value left on the stack is the answer. Evaluation is linear in the number of tokens.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India computing a fee formula written on cards laid in a row. Number cards get stacked on a spike. When she reaches an operation card like "add" or "multiply", she takes the top two number cards off the spike, does the sum or product, and puts the single result card back on top. She works left to right until only one card remains on the spike, and that card is the final computed fee. No brackets, no "which comes first" confusion — the order on the cards already decides everything.
s1_definition.oneliner: Push operands, and on each operator pop two, compute, and push the result — the last value on the stack is the answer.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reverse Polish Notation, also called postfix, writes each operator after its two operands, so there are no parentheses and no precedence rules to resolve. You evaluate it with a stack: push each number, and on each operator pop the top two numbers, apply the operator, and push the result back. When the tokens are exhausted, the single value left on the stack is the answer. Evaluation is linear in the number of tokens.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine a clerk at the National Bank of India computing a fee formula written on cards laid in a row. Number cards get stacked on a spike. When she reaches an operation card like "add" or "multiply", she takes the top two number cards off the spike, does the sum or product, and puts the single result card back on top. She works left to right until only one card remains on the spike, and that card is the final computed fee. No brackets, no "which comes first" confusion — the order on the cards already decides everything.

**One line to remember:** Push operands, and on each operator pop two, compute, and push the result — the last value on the stack is the answer.

sections.s2_technical:
Postfix is powerful because it removes ambiguity. In normal infix notation you need precedence and parentheses to know whether to multiply before adding, but in postfix the position of the operator already fixes the order, so a single left-to-right pass with a stack is enough.

The algorithm scans tokens. If a token is a number, you parse it and push it. If a token is an operator, you pop the right operand first and then the left operand, because the second value popped is the one that appeared first. For example for subtraction you compute `left.subtract(right)` where `right` was popped before `left`. Getting this order wrong is the classic bug for non-commutative operators like subtraction and division, so I always pop right then left.

Because this is a banking fee calculation, operands are BigDecimal and arithmetic uses `add`, `subtract`, `multiply`, and `divide`. For division you must supply a rounding mode and scale, for example `left.divide(right, 2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP)`, otherwise an exact non-terminating result throws ArithmeticException. Using BigDecimal avoids the rounding errors that doubles introduce in money math.

A senior-level nuance is where postfix comes from and why it is used. Compilers and calculators convert infix to postfix using the shunting-yard algorithm precisely so that evaluation becomes this trivial stack pass. Postfix evaluation is also how stack-based virtual machines, including the JVM's operand stack, execute arithmetic bytecode. So this small routine is the same model the JVM itself uses to compute expressions, which is why it is a favourite interview question.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India lets product teams define transaction fee formulas that the pricing engine must evaluate for every transaction. Storing formulas in postfix means the engine evaluates them with a simple, fast, bracket-free stack pass instead of a full infix parser on the hot path. This is exactly postfix evaluation, because the operator order is already encoded.

Problem 2 — Fees are money, so every intermediate value must be a BigDecimal, and division must round to two decimal places using a defined rounding mode, otherwise the engine could throw on a repeating decimal or produce fractions of a paisa.

In our mini-project we build a `FeeFormulaEvaluator` that evaluates a postfix token array into a BigDecimal fee. The demo evaluates a formula that computes a base-plus-percentage fee and logs the stack after each step.

Input: the postfix tokens ten thousand, zero point zero two, multiply, fifty, add, which encodes a two percent fee on ten thousand plus a flat fifty.

Step 1: Read ten thousand, a number, so push it. The stack holds ten thousand.

Step 2: Read zero point zero two, a number, so push it. The stack holds ten thousand then zero point zero two on top.

Step 3: Read multiply, an operator. Pop the right operand zero point zero two, then pop the left operand ten thousand. Multiply to get two hundred. Push two hundred. The stack holds two hundred.

Step 4: Read fifty, a number, so push it. The stack holds two hundred then fifty.

Step 5: Read add, an operator. Pop the right operand fifty, then pop the left operand two hundred. Add to get two hundred fifty. Push it. The stack holds two hundred fifty.

Step 6: Tokens are exhausted. Pop the single remaining value, two hundred fifty, which is the final fee. Because it came through BigDecimal multiply, the scale gives two hundred fifty exactly.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reverse Polish Notation, or postfix, places each operator after its two operands, which means there are no parentheses and no precedence rules to resolve. I evaluate it with a stack in a single left-to-right pass. Every number token I push onto the stack, and every operator token I handle by popping the top two values, applying the operator, and pushing the result back. When I run out of tokens, the one value left on the stack is the answer, and the whole thing is linear in the number of tokens.

The one detail I am always careful about is operand order. When I hit an operator I pop the right operand first and the left operand second, because the value that was pushed earlier sits lower on the stack. For commutative operators like addition it does not matter, but for subtraction and division the order is everything, so popping right then left is the habit that prevents the classic bug.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the pricing engine. Product teams define transaction fee formulas, and we store them in postfix so the engine evaluates them with this simple fast stack pass rather than running a full infix parser on the hot path for every transaction. Because fees are money, every operand is a BigDecimal, and division always specifies a scale and a rounding mode so a repeating decimal cannot throw or lose paisa.

The senior-level point I make is that postfix is not an academic curiosity. Compilers and calculators convert infix to postfix with the shunting-yard algorithm precisely so that evaluation collapses into this trivial stack routine, and stack-based virtual machines including the JVM's own operand stack execute arithmetic exactly this way. So when I show this evaluator, I am really demonstrating the same execution model that the JVM uses under the hood to compute expressions.

answers.question: Given an array of n+1 integers where each value is in the range [1, n], exactly one value is repeated (possibly multiple times). Find the duplicate without modifying the array ideally, in O(n) time and O(1) space. Explain both cyclic sort and Floyd's approaches.
answers.shortTitle: Find Duplicate Number — cyclic sort or Floyd's cycle detection

s1_definition.profdef: With n+1 values in 1 to n, the pigeonhole principle guarantees at least one repeat. Cyclic sort places each value at index v-1 and the first time a value finds its home already occupied by an equal value, that value is the duplicate. Floyd's tortoise and hare treats the array as a linked list where index i points to nums[i], and the repeated value creates a cycle whose entry point is the duplicate, found in O(n) time without modifying the array.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, n+1 transaction IDs were issued but only n unique IDs exist, so one ID was reused. Following each ID as a pointer to the next forms a loop, and the entrance to that loop is the reused ID.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pigeonhole guarantees a repeat; Floyd's cycle entry (index→nums[index]) is the duplicate without touching the array.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** With n+1 values in 1 to n, the pigeonhole principle guarantees at least one repeat. Cyclic sort places each value at index v-1 and the first time a value finds its home already occupied by an equal value, that value is the duplicate. Floyd's tortoise and hare treats the array as a linked list where index i points to nums[i], and the repeated value creates a cycle whose entry point is the duplicate, found in O(n) time without modifying the array.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, n+1 transaction IDs were issued but only n unique IDs exist, so one ID was reused. Following each ID as a pointer to the next forms a loop, and the entrance to that loop is the reused ID.

**One line to remember:** Pigeonhole guarantees a repeat; Floyd's cycle entry (index→nums[index]) is the duplicate without touching the array.

sections.s2_technical:
The cyclic sort approach swaps value v toward index v-1, and the moment you try to place a value whose home already holds the same value, you have found the duplicate: `while (nums[i] != i + 1) { if (nums[i] == nums[nums[i]-1]) return nums[i]; swap(nums, i, nums[i]-1); }`. This is simple but it modifies the array, which some problem variants forbid.

Floyd's approach treats each value as a pointer: from index i you jump to index nums[i]. Because values are in 1 to n and the array has n+1 entries, this functional graph must contain a cycle, and the cycle's entry node is the duplicate. You first find a meeting point inside the cycle with a slow and fast pointer, then reset one pointer to the start and advance both one step at a time until they meet, which is the duplicate.

The pointer code reads naturally: phase one does `slow = nums[slow]; fast = nums[nums[fast]];` until they are equal, and phase two does `slow = 0; while (slow != fast) { slow = nums[slow]; fast = nums[fast]; }` returning slow. The mathematics of equal distances from start and meeting point to the cycle entry is why resetting works.

A senior nuance is choosing between them. Cyclic sort is easier to explain but mutates input and is unusable if the array is read-only or must be preserved for audit. Floyd's is non-destructive, uses constant space, and runs in linear time, so in production banking code where the input array is often immutable or shared, Floyd's is the safer and preferred choice.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, n+1 transaction IDs were generated from a pool of only n unique IDs, so exactly one ID got reused and must be identified. This is exactly how Find Duplicate Number works, because pigeonhole guarantees a repeat in a known range.

Problem 2 — The transaction array is a shared immutable audit record that must not be modified during detection. This is exactly why Floyd's cycle detection matters: it finds the duplicate without touching the array.

The mini-project builds a `DuplicateFinder` with a `findDuplicate` method using Floyd's, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

The input is the array one, three, four, two, two treated as pointers where index i points to index nums of i.

Step 2: Slow walks one, three, two, four, two while fast races ahead two steps at a time, and because the repeated value two creates a cycle, the two pointers eventually land on the same index inside the loop.

Step 4: Because the distance from the start to the cycle entry equals the distance from the meeting point to the cycle entry, the two pointers meet exactly at the cycle entrance.

Step 5: That entrance index is the duplicate value two, reported without ever modifying the original array.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Find Duplicate Number starts from the pigeonhole principle: with n plus one values drawn from the range one to n, at least one value must repeat. I usually explain two approaches. The cyclic sort approach swaps each value toward its home index, and the moment a value finds its home already occupied by an equal value, that value is the duplicate. It is easy to describe but it mutates the input array.

The approach I prefer in production is Floyd's tortoise and hare, because it does not modify the array. I treat the array as a linked list where index i points to index nums of i. Since the values are in one to n and there are n plus one entries, this pointer graph must contain a cycle, and the entry point of that cycle is the duplicate value. In phase one I advance a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps until they meet inside the cycle, and in phase two I reset the slow pointer to the start and advance both one step at a time until they meet, which lands exactly on the cycle entrance.

The reason the reset works is that the distance from the start to the cycle entry equals the distance from the meeting point to the cycle entry, a clean consequence of the cycle math. Both approaches run in linear time with constant extra space, but Floyd's is non-destructive.

In my project at National Bank of India, n plus one transaction IDs were generated from a pool of only n unique IDs, so one ID was reused, and the transaction array was a shared immutable audit record that I was not allowed to modify. Floyd's cycle detection let me find the reused ID in linear time without touching the array, and the result fed straight into our fraud and deduplication alerting.

answers.question: Implement a first-in-first-out queue using only two last-in-first-out stacks, supporting enqueue and dequeue, and analyse the amortised cost.
answers.shortTitle: Implement a Queue Using Two Stacks

s1_definition.profdef: You can build a first-in-first-out queue from two last-in-first-out stacks, an inbox and an outbox. Enqueue always pushes onto the inbox. Dequeue takes from the outbox, but if the outbox is empty you first pour the entire inbox into the outbox, which reverses the order so the oldest element ends up on top. Each element moves between stacks at most once, giving amortised constant time per operation.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture two spikes at the National Bank of India teller window. New customers' request slips go onto the "incoming" spike as they arrive, newest on top. When the teller wants to serve the next customer in fairness order, she checks the "serving" spike; if it is empty she flips the whole incoming pile onto it one by one, which reverses it so the earliest arrival is now on top. She serves from the serving spike until it empties, then flips again only when needed. Each slip gets flipped at most once, so the extra handling averages out to almost nothing.
s1_definition.oneliner: Push to an inbox stack, pour into an outbox stack only when the outbox is empty, and each element moves once for amortised constant time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You can build a first-in-first-out queue from two last-in-first-out stacks, an inbox and an outbox. Enqueue always pushes onto the inbox. Dequeue takes from the outbox, but if the outbox is empty you first pour the entire inbox into the outbox, which reverses the order so the oldest element ends up on top. Each element moves between stacks at most once, giving amortised constant time per operation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture two spikes at the National Bank of India teller window. New customers' request slips go onto the "incoming" spike as they arrive, newest on top. When the teller wants to serve the next customer in fairness order, she checks the "serving" spike; if it is empty she flips the whole incoming pile onto it one by one, which reverses it so the earliest arrival is now on top. She serves from the serving spike until it empties, then flips again only when needed. Each slip gets flipped at most once, so the extra handling averages out to almost nothing.

**One line to remember:** Push to an inbox stack, pour into an outbox stack only when the outbox is empty, and each element moves once for amortised constant time.

sections.s2_technical:
A stack is last-in-first-out and a queue is first-in-first-out, so the trick is to reverse the order using a second stack. The naive approach reverses on every single operation, which is wasteful; the efficient approach reverses lazily, only when the outbox runs dry.

Enqueue is trivial: `inbox.push(x)`. Dequeue is where the design lives. If the outbox is empty, you transfer everything: `while (!inbox.isEmpty()) outbox.push(inbox.pop());`. This single transfer reverses the inbox so the oldest element is now on the top of the outbox. Then you `return outbox.pop();`. If the outbox is not empty, you skip the transfer entirely and just pop the outbox, because it already holds older elements in the right order.

The key insight is the amortised analysis. A single dequeue that triggers a transfer can cost linear time, but each element is pushed to the inbox once, moved to the outbox once, and popped once across its whole lifetime. Spread over all operations, that is a constant number of moves per element, so the amortised cost per operation is constant even though one individual dequeue can be expensive. This distinction between worst-case and amortised cost is exactly what interviewers probe.

A senior-level nuance is when to prefer this over a direct queue. In practice you would use `ArrayDeque` as a real queue; the two-stack construction matters when your only primitive is a stack, for example implementing a queue on top of a persistent or immutable stack in functional code, or demonstrating that queues and stacks are inter-convertible. It also underpins the immutable "Banker's queue" in functional data structures, where two lists stand in for the two stacks.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes customer service requests in strict fairness order, oldest first, but the only buffering primitive available in a particular legacy embedded component is a stack. We must present a first-in-first-out queue to the rest of the system while internally using stacks. This is exactly the two-stack queue, because two stacks reverse into the right order.

Problem 2 — Throughput matters, so we cannot afford to reverse the whole buffer on every operation. We need the lazy transfer so that the reversal cost is paid only when the serving side empties, giving amortised constant time per request.

In our mini-project we build a `RequestQueue` backed by two deques used as stacks. The demo enqueues three request IDs, dequeues one, enqueues another, then dequeues the rest, logging the transfer so you can see it happen only when the outbox is empty.
