sections.s5_journey:
Input: enqueue request one, two, three, dequeue, enqueue four, then dequeue three times.

Step 1: Enqueue one, two, three. The inbox now holds three on top, then two, then one at the bottom. The outbox is empty.

Step 2: Dequeue. The outbox is empty, so we transfer: pop three and push, pop two and push, pop one and push. Now the outbox holds one on top, then two, then three. We pop the outbox top, request one, the oldest, exactly correct.

Step 3: Enqueue four. It goes onto the inbox. The outbox still holds two on top then three, untouched.

Step 4: Dequeue. The outbox is not empty, so no transfer. Pop the outbox top, request two.

Step 5: Dequeue. The outbox is not empty, pop request three. The outbox is now empty.

Step 6: Dequeue. The outbox is empty, so we transfer the inbox, which currently holds only four. The outbox now holds four on top. Pop it, request four. Every request was served in arrival order, and the only transfers happened when the outbox was empty, confirming amortised constant time.

[2026-10-26 23:23:01] INFO    Serve: REQ-2
[2026-10-26 23:23:01] INFO    Serve: REQ-3
[2026-10-26 23:23:01] INFO    Serve: REQ-4

  dequeue → outbox not empty → pop → 2
  dequeue → pop → 3   outbox:[]
  dequeue → transfer inbox:[4]→outbox:[4] → pop → 4
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
You can build a first-in-first-out queue out of two last-in-first-out stacks, which I call the inbox and the outbox. Enqueue is trivial: I just push the new element onto the inbox. Dequeue is where the design lives: I serve from the outbox, but if the outbox is empty I first pour the entire inbox into it, popping from one and pushing to the other, which reverses the order so the oldest element ends up on top of the outbox. Then I pop the outbox.

The important part is doing the transfer lazily, only when the outbox is empty, not on every operation. That gives the amortised analysis its punch. A single dequeue that triggers a transfer can cost linear time, but each element is pushed onto the inbox once, moved to the outbox once, and popped once over its entire lifetime. Spread across all operations, that is a constant number of moves per element, so the amortised cost per operation is constant even though one individual dequeue can be expensive. Explaining that worst-case versus amortised distinction is usually what the interviewer is really checking.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a legacy embedded component whose only buffering primitive was a stack, yet the rest of the system needed strict oldest-first fairness for customer service requests. The two-stack queue let me present proper first-in-first-out semantics while internally using stacks, and the lazy transfer kept throughput high because reversal cost is paid only when the serving side drains.

The senior-level point I make is that in normal Java I would just use ArrayDeque as a real queue; the two-stack construction earns its place when a stack is the only primitive I have, such as implementing a queue over an immutable stack in functional code. It is also the idea behind the Banker's queue in functional data structures, where two lists play the role of the two stacks, so this question is really about understanding that stacks and queues are inter-convertible.

answers.question: Given an unsorted integer array, find the smallest missing positive integer in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. The array may contain negatives, zeros, and duplicates.
answers.shortTitle: First Missing Positive — cyclic sort for the range [1, n]

s1_definition.profdef: The smallest missing positive of an array of length n must lie in the range 1 to n+1, because if 1 through n are all present the answer is n+1. Cyclic sort places each value v that falls in 1 to n at index v-1, ignoring negatives, zeros, and out-of-range values. After sorting, the first index i whose value is not i+1 gives answer i+1; if all match, the answer is n+1. Time O(n), extra space O(1).
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, new account slots must get the smallest unused positive ID. Staff place each existing ID into its matching slot, ignoring junk like negatives or huge numbers; the first empty slot is the smallest free ID, and if every slot is full the next ID is n+1.
s1_definition.oneliner: Answer is in [1, n+1]; cyclic sort valid values to index v-1, first wrong slot gives i+1, else n+1.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The smallest missing positive of an array of length n must lie in the range 1 to n+1, because if 1 through n are all present the answer is n+1. Cyclic sort places each value v that falls in 1 to n at index v-1, ignoring negatives, zeros, and out-of-range values. After sorting, the first index i whose value is not i+1 gives answer i+1; if all match, the answer is n+1. Time O(n), extra space O(1).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, new account slots must get the smallest unused positive ID. Staff place each existing ID into its matching slot, ignoring junk like negatives or huge numbers; the first empty slot is the smallest free ID, and if every slot is full the next ID is n+1.

**One line to remember:** Answer is in [1, n+1]; cyclic sort valid values to index v-1, first wrong slot gives i+1, else n+1.

sections.s2_technical:
The crucial bound is that the answer can only be from 1 to n+1. If every integer from 1 to n is present, the smallest missing positive is n+1; otherwise it is somewhere inside 1 to n. This means you can completely ignore negatives, zeros, and any value larger than n because they cannot be the answer and have no useful home index.

You run a bounded cyclic sort: only swap when the value is in range and not already home: `while (nums[i] > 0 && nums[i] <= n && nums[i] != nums[nums[i]-1]) swap(nums, i, nums[i]-1);`. The range check keeps the swap index valid and the equal-value guard handles duplicates without looping.

After sorting, you scan for the first slot whose value is not index plus one: `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (nums[i] != i + 1) return i + 1;`. The first such slot is where the smallest positive integer should have been but was not, so i+1 is the answer. If no slot is wrong, you `return n + 1;`.

A senior nuance is why this is considered a hard problem despite short code. The difficulty is achieving both linear time and constant space simultaneously; a hash set solution is trivial but uses O(n) space. The cyclic sort trick uses the array itself as the hash, placing value v at index v-1, which is the in-place hashing insight interviewers look for.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, the account-ID allocator must assign the smallest unused positive ID, but the pool of existing IDs contains junk like negatives, zeros, and oversized placeholders. This is exactly how First Missing Positive works, because only values in one to n can be the answer.

Problem 2 — The allocator runs on a hot path and cannot allocate a large hash set for every request. This is exactly why cyclic sort matters: it uses the array itself as a hash table for constant extra space.

The mini-project builds an `AccountIdAllocator` with a `firstMissingPositive` method, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the array three, four, minus one, one with n equal to four.

Step 1: At index zero the value three is in range, so it swaps to index two, giving minus one, four, three, one, and index zero is re-checked.

Step 2: Index zero now holds minus one, which is junk, so the pointer advances. Index one holds four which swaps to index three, giving minus one, one, three, four.

Step 3: Index one now holds one, which swaps to index zero, giving one, minus one, three, four, and index one holds minus one which is junk, so the pointer advances.

Step 4: Indices two and three already hold three and four correctly, so the pass completes with the array one, minus one, three, four.

Step 5: The scan finds index one holds minus one instead of two, so the first missing positive is two.

2026-10-27T06:40:00Z [INFO] [1,2,0]      → 3
2026-10-27T06:40:00Z [INFO] First missing positive = 1
2026-10-27T06:40:00Z [INFO] [7,8,9,11]   → 1
```

    ▼ index1 holds -1 → answer = 2
  all slots 1..n filled → answer = n+1
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
First Missing Positive asks for the smallest positive integer that is absent, and the key insight that unlocks the whole problem is that for an array of length n, the answer can only be in the range one to n plus one. If every integer from one to n is already present, the smallest missing positive is n plus one; otherwise it is somewhere inside one to n. This means negatives, zeros, and any value larger than n are irrelevant and can be ignored.

The clever part is that I use the array itself as a hash table. I run a bounded cyclic sort that swaps each in-range value v to index v minus one, skipping junk values and using the equal-value guard so duplicates do not loop. After this placement, I scan once, and the first index whose value is not index plus one tells me the smallest positive that never found its slot, so the answer is index plus one. If every slot is correctly filled, the answer is n plus one.

The reason this is considered a hard problem despite being short is the simultaneous requirement of linear time and constant extra space. A hash set makes it trivial but costs linear space; the in-place hashing trick is what interviewers are really testing.

In my project at National Bank of India, the account-ID allocator had to assign the smallest unused positive ID, but the pool of existing IDs was full of junk like negatives, zeros, and oversized placeholders, and the allocator ran on a hot path where allocating a large hash set per request was unacceptable. Cyclic sort let me treat the array as its own hash, place each valid ID into its home slot, and read off the first empty slot as the smallest free ID in constant extra space.

answers.question: Design a fixed-capacity cache that evicts the least recently used entry when full, supporting get and put in constant time.
answers.shortTitle: Design an LRU Cache (Least Recently Used)

s1_definition.profdef: A Least Recently Used cache stores up to a fixed number of key-value entries and, when it is full and a new key arrives, evicts the entry that was accessed longest ago. The classic design combines a hash map for constant-time key lookup with a doubly linked list that orders entries by recency, moving an entry to the front on every access and evicting from the back. Both get and put run in constant time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India keeps only the ten most recently viewed customer profiles on a fast desk, because the full archive is slow to fetch. Every time a clerk looks at a profile, she moves that folder to the front of the desk. When a new profile is needed and the desk is full, she removes the folder at the very back, the one nobody has touched for the longest time, to make room. A card index on the side tells her instantly where each folder sits, so she never has to search the desk.
s1_definition.oneliner: Hash map for instant lookup plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency — touch moves to front, eviction removes the back.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Least Recently Used cache stores up to a fixed number of key-value entries and, when it is full and a new key arrives, evicts the entry that was accessed longest ago. The classic design combines a hash map for constant-time key lookup with a doubly linked list that orders entries by recency, moving an entry to the front on every access and evicting from the back. Both get and put run in constant time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India keeps only the ten most recently viewed customer profiles on a fast desk, because the full archive is slow to fetch. Every time a clerk looks at a profile, she moves that folder to the front of the desk. When a new profile is needed and the desk is full, she removes the folder at the very back, the one nobody has touched for the longest time, to make room. A card index on the side tells her instantly where each folder sits, so she never has to search the desk.

**One line to remember:** Hash map for instant lookup plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency — touch moves to front, eviction removes the back.

sections.s2_technical:
The challenge is doing both operations in constant time. A plain map gives constant lookup but no notion of recency order. A plain list gives order but linear search. Combining them solves both: the map points directly to the list node, so you find any entry instantly, and the doubly linked list maintains recency so you can reorder and evict in constant time.

Each node holds a key, a value, and previous and next pointers. On `get(key)`, you look up the node in the map; if present you unlink it from its current position and move it to the front, marking it most recently used, then return its value. On `put(key, value)`, if the key exists you update the value and move the node to the front; if it is new you create a node, add it to the front, and put it in the map, and if the size now exceeds capacity you remove the tail node, which is the least recently used, and delete its key from the map. Using sentinel head and tail nodes removes null checks and makes the unlink and insert logic clean.

A doubly linked list is essential, not a singly linked one, because eviction and reordering need to remove a node and splice its neighbours together in constant time, which requires knowing the previous node directly. With a singly linked list you would have to scan to find the predecessor, which is linear. This is precisely why the interview answer pairs a hash map with a doubly linked list.

A senior-level nuance is that Java's `LinkedHashMap` already implements this: constructed with access order true and with `removeEldestEntry` overridden, it is an LRU cache in a few lines. I mention that I would use `LinkedHashMap` or a library like Caffeine in production, but can implement the map-plus-doubly-linked-list by hand to show I understand the mechanics. For thread safety I would guard it or use a concurrent cache, since the hand-rolled version is not thread-safe.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India serves account balances to a high-traffic mobile app, and reading every balance from the database is too slow and expensive. We cache recently requested balances in memory, but memory is limited, so when the cache is full we must drop the balance that has not been requested for the longest time. This is exactly a Least Recently Used cache, because recency of access decides what to keep.

Problem 2 — The cache is on the hot path, so both reading a cached balance and inserting a new one must be constant time; a linear scan to find the stalest entry would defeat the purpose. The hash-map-plus-doubly-linked-list design gives constant time for both.

In our mini-project we build an `LruBalanceCache` of capacity two over account-to-balance entries. The demo puts Rajesh and Priya, reads Rajesh to make him recent, then puts a third account, forcing eviction of the least recently used entry, and logs each eviction.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: capacity two, put Rajesh one million, put Priya two hundred fifty thousand, get Rajesh, put a third account seventy five thousand, then two reads.

Step 1: Put Rajesh. A new node is created, added to the front, and recorded in the map. The list from front to back is Rajesh, then the tail sentinel.

Step 2: Put Priya. A new node added to the front. The list is now Priya, Rajesh. Rajesh is at the back, meaning least recently used.

Step 3: Get Rajesh. The map finds his node, and we move it to the front. The list becomes Rajesh, Priya, so now Priya is the least recently used at the back.

Step 4: Put the third account at seventy five thousand. It is new, so we add it to the front and the map. The size is now three, which exceeds capacity two, so we remove the tail node, which is Priya, the least recently used, and delete her key from the map. We log the eviction.

Step 5: Get Priya. She was evicted, so the map returns null.

Step 6: Get Rajesh. He is still present because touching him in step three kept him recent, so he survived the eviction. The cache correctly kept the most recently used entries.

```
[2026-10-26 23:24:01] INFO    Get SAV2001: 1000000
[2026-10-26 23:24:01] INFO      evicted LRU key CUR3001
[2026-10-26 23:24:01] INFO    Get CUR3001: null
[2026-10-26 23:24:01] INFO    Get SAV2001: 1000000
```

  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │

  │  - head, tail: Node                   │  sentinels

  │  + put(key, value): void              │  O(1), evicts if full
  │  - addFront / remove / moveToFront    │  DLL splice helpers

  └───────────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain (put forcing eviction) ─────────────────────

  1. put(SAV2099, 75000) — new key
  2.   map.put; addFront(node)
  3.   size 3 > cap 2 → lru = tail.prev (CUR3001)

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Least Recently Used cache holds a fixed number of entries and, when it is full and a new key arrives, evicts the entry that was accessed longest ago. The challenge is making both get and put constant time, and the classic solution combines two structures. A hash map gives constant-time lookup from a key to its node, and a doubly linked list orders the nodes by recency, with the most recently used at the front and the least recently used at the back.

On a get, I look the key up in the map, and if it is present I unlink its node and move it to the front to mark it most recently used, then return the value. On a put, if the key already exists I update the value and move it to the front, and if it is new I add a node at the front and record it in the map; then if the size exceeds capacity I remove the tail node, which is the least recently used, and delete its key from the map. I use sentinel head and tail nodes so the splicing logic has no null edge cases. The list must be doubly linked, because removing a node and joining its neighbours in constant time needs a direct pointer to the previous node.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to cache account balances for a high-traffic mobile app. Reading every balance from the database was too slow and costly, so we kept recently requested balances in memory, and when the cache filled we dropped the balance nobody had asked for in the longest time. Both the cached read and the insert are constant time, which is essential on that hot path.

The senior-level point I make is that Java already ships this: a LinkedHashMap constructed in access order with removeEldestEntry overridden is an LRU cache in a handful of lines, and in production I would reach for that or a library like Caffeine, adding thread-safety since the hand-rolled version is not concurrent. I implement the map-plus-doubly-linked-list by hand in interviews to prove I understand the mechanics, but I always name the production-ready option too.

answers.question: Given a non-empty array where every element appears twice except for one element that appears once, find that single element in O(n) time and O(1) space.
answers.shortTitle: Single Number — XOR all elements to cancel pairs

s1_definition.profdef: XOR has three properties that solve this directly: x XOR x equals 0, x XOR 0 equals x, and XOR is commutative and associative. XORing all elements cancels every value that appears an even number of times, leaving only the value that appears once. Time O(n), space O(1), with no auxiliary data structure.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, every debit has a matching credit except one unmatched entry. Pairing each debit with its credit cancels them to zero, and the single leftover entry is the one without a partner.
s1_definition.oneliner: XOR everything; identical pairs cancel to zero, the lone value remains.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** XOR has three properties that solve this directly: x XOR x equals 0, x XOR 0 equals x, and XOR is commutative and associative. XORing all elements cancels every value that appears an even number of times, leaving only the value that appears once. Time O(n), space O(1), with no auxiliary data structure.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, every debit has a matching credit except one unmatched entry. Pairing each debit with its credit cancels them to zero, and the single leftover entry is the one without a partner.

**One line to remember:** XOR everything; identical pairs cancel to zero, the lone value remains.

sections.s2_technical:
The entire solution is a single accumulation. You start with zero and XOR every element into it: `int result = 0; for (int x : nums) result ^= x; return result;`. There is no need to sort, count, or use a set.

The correctness rests on the algebra of XOR. Because x XOR x is zero, any value appearing twice contributes nothing to the final accumulator. Because XOR is commutative and associative, the order of the elements does not matter; all the pairs cancel regardless of their positions in the array.

The lone value XORed with zero stays itself, because x XOR zero equals x. So after all the pairs cancel, the accumulator holds exactly the single unmatched number.

A senior nuance is that this generalizes. If every element appears three times except one, XOR alone fails because three copies do not cancel; you then track bit counts modulo three. And if two elements appear once, you XOR everything to get the XOR of the two uniques, isolate a differing bit, and partition. Mentioning these variants shows you understand why XOR works here specifically.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a reconciliation batch contains paired debit and credit reference numbers, but exactly one reference is unpaired due to a posting error. This is exactly how Single Number works, because paired values cancel under XOR.

Problem 2 — The batch is large and the reconciliation must run with no extra memory on a constrained node. This is exactly why XOR matters: it finds the lone reference in one pass with no data structure.

The mini-project builds a `ReconciliationService` with a `findUnpaired` method, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

Step 4: XORing the second two cancels the earlier two, leaving only the contribution of four in the accumulator.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Single Number is the cleanest demonstration of XOR algebra. XOR has three properties that make this trivial: any value XORed with itself is zero, any value XORed with zero is itself, and XOR is commutative and associative so order does not matter. I start an accumulator at zero and XOR every element of the array into it. Every value that appears twice cancels itself out, and because order is irrelevant the pairs cancel no matter where they sit in the array, so the accumulator ends holding exactly the one value that appears once.

This gives me linear time and constant space with no sorting and no auxiliary set, which is why it is the textbook answer when every element is paired except one.

I always mention how the problem generalizes, because that shows I understand why XOR works here rather than just memorizing it. If every element appeared three times except one, XOR alone would fail because three copies do not cancel, so I would count bits modulo three instead. If two elements appeared once, I would XOR everything to get the combined XOR of the two uniques, isolate a bit where they differ, and partition the array into two groups.

In my project at National Bank of India, a reconciliation batch contained paired debit and credit reference numbers, but one reference was unpaired because of a posting error, and the batch ran on a constrained node where extra memory was not available. XORing the whole batch in a single pass cancelled every matched pair and left the one unpaired reference, which we fed straight into the posting exception report.

answers.question: Given an array of numbers and a value k, find the kth largest element efficiently using a priority queue (heap).
answers.shortTitle: Find the Kth Largest Element Using a Min-Heap

s1_definition.profdef: The kth largest element is the element that would sit in position k from the top if the array were sorted descending. A min-heap of size k solves it without full sorting: you keep only the k largest elements seen so far in a min-heap, so the smallest of those, at the heap's root, is the kth largest overall. Processing n elements with a size-k heap costs n log k time and k space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India wants the third-largest transaction of the day from a stream of thousands. A clerk keeps a small tray that holds only the three biggest seen so far, and the tray is arranged so the smallest of those three is right at the front. For each new transaction, if it is bigger than the one at the front of the tray, she throws out the front one and slots the new one in; otherwise she ignores it. At the end, the transaction at the front of the tray is exactly the third-largest, and she never had to sort the whole day's transactions.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep the k largest in a size-k min-heap, and its root is the kth largest, in n log k time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The kth largest element is the element that would sit in position k from the top if the array were sorted descending. A min-heap of size k solves it without full sorting: you keep only the k largest elements seen so far in a min-heap, so the smallest of those, at the heap's root, is the kth largest overall. Processing n elements with a size-k heap costs n log k time and k space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India wants the third-largest transaction of the day from a stream of thousands. A clerk keeps a small tray that holds only the three biggest seen so far, and the tray is arranged so the smallest of those three is right at the front. For each new transaction, if it is bigger than the one at the front of the tray, she throws out the front one and slots the new one in; otherwise she ignores it. At the end, the transaction at the front of the tray is exactly the third-largest, and she never had to sort the whole day's transactions.

**One line to remember:** Keep the k largest in a size-k min-heap, and its root is the kth largest, in n log k time.

sections.s2_technical:
The brute-force approach sorts the whole array and indexes position n minus k, which is n log n time. That is fine for small inputs but wasteful when k is small relative to n, and impossible when the data is a stream too large to hold. The heap approach is better precisely in those cases.

In Java the heap is `PriorityQueue`, which is a min-heap by default, meaning `peek` returns the smallest element. You iterate the array and `offer` each element. After each offer, if the heap size exceeds k you `poll`, which removes the current smallest. This keeps exactly the k largest elements in the heap at all times. For example `if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();` discards whatever is now too small to be in the top k. After processing everything, `heap.peek()` is the smallest of the k largest, which is the kth largest overall.

Each offer and poll on a heap of size k is logarithmic in k, and you do this n times, so the total is n log k, with only k extra space. That beats full sorting when k is much smaller than n, and crucially it works on a stream because you never need all n elements in memory at once, only the running top k.

A senior-level nuance is the alternative Quickselect algorithm, which finds the kth largest in expected linear time using a partition step like quicksort but recursing into only one side. Quickselect is faster on average, O(n), but its worst case is quadratic and it needs the whole array in memory, so it cannot stream. For money values I use BigDecimal with the heap's natural ordering via compareTo. I choose the heap when data streams or k is small, and mention Quickselect as the expected-linear in-memory alternative.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a fraud-and-reporting dashboard that must surface the top few largest transactions from a high-volume stream, for example the third-largest transaction, without storing or sorting the entire day's feed. This is exactly the size-k min-heap technique, because it keeps only the running top k.

Problem 2 — Transactions are money amounts, so they must be BigDecimal and compared with compareTo, and the solution must be memory-bounded to k regardless of how many transactions flow through, which the size-k heap guarantees.

In our mini-project we build a `TopTransactions` service that returns the kth largest amount using a PriorityQueue of BigDecimal bounded to size k. The demo feeds several amounts and asks for the third largest, logging each eviction from the heap.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the amounts one thousand two hundred, fifty thousand, three hundred, ninety eight thousand, seven thousand five hundred, twenty five thousand, asking for the third largest.

Step 1: Offer one thousand two hundred, heap holds it. Offer fifty thousand, heap holds both. Offer three hundred, heap now holds three elements, which equals k, so no eviction yet. The heap root, the smallest, is three hundred.

Step 2: Offer ninety eight thousand. The heap size becomes four, exceeding k, so we poll the smallest, three hundred, and evict it. The heap now holds one thousand two hundred, fifty thousand, ninety eight thousand.

Step 3: Offer seven thousand five hundred. Size four, poll the smallest, which is one thousand two hundred, and evict it. The heap now holds seven thousand five hundred, fifty thousand, ninety eight thousand.

Step 4: Offer twenty five thousand. Size four, poll the smallest, which is seven thousand five hundred, and evict it. The heap now holds twenty five thousand, fifty thousand, ninety eight thousand.

Step 5: Input is exhausted. The heap holds exactly the three largest amounts, and its root, the smallest of those, is twenty five thousand.

Step 6: We return twenty five thousand as the third largest. We never sorted the full array and never held more than three elements, confirming n log k time and k space.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The kth largest element is the value that would be in position k from the top if you sorted the array descending. The brute-force way is to sort the whole array and index into it, which costs n log n, but when k is small or the data is a stream, I use a size-k min-heap instead. The idea is to keep only the k largest elements seen so far in the heap, so the smallest of those, sitting at the heap's root, is exactly the kth largest overall.

In Java the heap is a PriorityQueue, which is a min-heap by default so peek returns the smallest element. I offer every element into the heap, and after each offer, if the heap has grown beyond k, I poll once to discard the current smallest, which is now too small to be in the top k. After processing all n elements, the root of the heap is the answer. Each offer and poll is logarithmic in k and I do it n times, so the total is n log k with only k extra space, and it works on a stream because I never hold more than k elements at once.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in a reporting dashboard that surfaces the top few largest transactions from a high-volume stream, such as the third-largest transaction of the day, without storing or sorting the entire feed. The amounts are money, so they are BigDecimal compared with compareTo, and the memory stays bounded to k no matter how many transactions flow through.

The senior-level point I make is that there is a faster in-memory alternative called Quickselect, which finds the kth largest in expected linear time by partitioning like quicksort and recursing into only one side. I note that Quickselect is faster on average but has a quadratic worst case and needs the whole array in memory, so it cannot stream. That is the trade-off: I reach for the heap when data streams or k is small, and for Quickselect when I have the full array in memory and want expected-linear time.

answers.question: Write a function that counts the number of set bits (bits equal to 1) in the binary representation of an integer, ideally in O(number of set bits) time. Explain the n & (n-1) trick.
answers.shortTitle: Number of 1 Bits — n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit

s1_definition.profdef: The Hamming weight of an integer is its count of 1 bits. The expression n AND (n minus 1) clears the lowest set bit of n, so repeatedly applying it and counting iterations yields the number of set bits in exactly that many steps, which is faster than scanning all 32 bits when the number is sparse.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, each enabled account feature is a 1 bit in a permissions flag. To count enabled features, staff repeatedly switch off the lowest enabled feature and tally each switch-off; the number of switch-offs equals the number of enabled features.
s1_definition.oneliner: `n &= (n - 1)` erases the lowest 1 bit; count the erasures to get the bit count.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Hamming weight of an integer is its count of 1 bits. The expression n AND (n minus 1) clears the lowest set bit of n, so repeatedly applying it and counting iterations yields the number of set bits in exactly that many steps, which is faster than scanning all 32 bits when the number is sparse.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, each enabled account feature is a 1 bit in a permissions flag. To count enabled features, staff repeatedly switch off the lowest enabled feature and tally each switch-off; the number of switch-offs equals the number of enabled features.

**One line to remember:** `n &= (n - 1)` erases the lowest 1 bit; count the erasures to get the bit count.

sections.s2_technical:
The core trick is why n AND n minus one clears the lowest set bit. Subtracting one from n flips the lowest set bit to zero and turns every zero below it into one. ANDing with the original n keeps all higher bits unchanged but wipes out that lowest set bit and everything below it that was already zero, so the net effect is exactly one set bit removed.

The loop counts how many times you can do this before n becomes zero: `int count = 0; while (n != 0) { n &= (n - 1); count++; } return count;`. Each iteration removes precisely one set bit, so the number of iterations equals the number of set bits.

This is faster than the naive approach of checking each of the 32 bits with a shift and mask, because it only loops once per set bit. For a number with just three set bits, it loops three times regardless of where those bits sit in the 32-bit word.

A senior nuance is that Java provides `Integer.bitCount(n)` which is implemented with a parallel bit-counting algorithm and is the production choice. Also beware of sign: for negative integers you should treat the value as unsigned, which the n AND n minus one loop handles correctly because it operates on the raw bit pattern until it reaches zero.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Number of 1 Bits is about counting the set bits in an integer, the Hamming weight. The elegant approach uses the identity that n AND n minus one clears the lowest set bit. Subtracting one from n flips its lowest set bit to zero and turns all the zeros below it into ones, so ANDing with the original n removes exactly that lowest set bit and nothing else. I loop, applying this clear operation and incrementing a counter, until n becomes zero, and the counter equals the number of set bits.

The advantage over scanning all thirty-two bits with a shift and mask is that this loops only once per set bit, so a sparse number with three set bits takes three iterations regardless of where those bits are. That makes it efficient for the common case of mostly-empty masks.

In production I would normally call the built-in Integer.bitCount, which uses a parallel bit-counting algorithm, and I would be careful with negative integers by treating the value as an unsigned bit pattern, which the clear-the-lowest-bit loop handles naturally because it just keeps removing set bits until the word is zero.

In my project at National Bank of India, each account stored its enabled features as bits in a single integer permissions mask, and the dashboard had to display how many features were enabled on every load. The masks were usually sparse, so the n AND n minus one trick let me count only as many times as there were enabled features instead of always scanning the full word, which kept the dashboard fast.

answers.question: Given k sorted lists, merge them into one sorted list efficiently using a priority queue (heap).
answers.shortTitle: Merge K Sorted Lists Using a Min-Heap

s1_definition.profdef: Merging k sorted lists produces a single sorted output by repeatedly taking the smallest unconsumed element across all lists. A min-heap holding one candidate from each list makes "find the current smallest" a logarithmic operation: you poll the smallest, append it to the output, and push the next element from the list that element came from. With N total elements and k lists, this runs in N log k time and k extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has k branch ledgers, each already sorted by transaction time, and wants one combined ledger in time order. A clerk looks only at the earliest unprocessed entry from each branch, picks the single earliest among them, writes it into the combined ledger, then looks at the next entry from just that branch. She keeps a tiny sorted tray with one entry per branch so finding the earliest is instant. She never re-reads entries she has already filed, so the work is proportional to the total entries, not to re-scanning every branch each time.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep one candidate per list in a min-heap; poll the smallest, output it, and push that list's next element, for N log k total.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Merging k sorted lists produces a single sorted output by repeatedly taking the smallest unconsumed element across all lists. A min-heap holding one candidate from each list makes "find the current smallest" a logarithmic operation: you poll the smallest, append it to the output, and push the next element from the list that element came from. With N total elements and k lists, this runs in N log k time and k extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has k branch ledgers, each already sorted by transaction time, and wants one combined ledger in time order. A clerk looks only at the earliest unprocessed entry from each branch, picks the single earliest among them, writes it into the combined ledger, then looks at the next entry from just that branch. She keeps a tiny sorted tray with one entry per branch so finding the earliest is instant. She never re-reads entries she has already filed, so the work is proportional to the total entries, not to re-scanning every branch each time.

**One line to remember:** Keep one candidate per list in a min-heap; poll the smallest, output it, and push that list's next element, for N log k total.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach concatenates all lists and sorts, which is N log N. A smarter observation is that each list is already sorted, so you only ever need to compare the current fronts of the k lists. That reduces the comparison work from log N to log k per element.

The heap holds at most k elements, one from each list, ordered by value. You seed it with the first element of each non-empty list. Then you loop: `poll` the smallest, append it to the result, and if the list it came from has a next element, `offer` that next element. Because the heap only ever holds one representative per list, its size stays at most k, so each poll and offer is log k. You repeat until the heap is empty, having emitted all N elements in sorted order.

To know which list an element came from, you wrap each value with its source, for example an index plus position, or in a linked-list version you push the node itself and follow its next pointer. In Java you build the heap with a comparator over the stored value, for example `new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparing(entry -> entry.value))`. For money the value is a BigDecimal compared with compareTo.

A senior-level nuance is the alternative divide-and-conquer merge, which pairs up lists and merges them two at a time in log k rounds, also achieving N log k but without an explicit heap. The heap version is simpler to reason about and streams naturally, which is why it is the common interview answer, and it is exactly how an external multi-way merge sort combines sorted runs from disk, a technique banks use to merge large sorted transaction files.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India receives end-of-day transaction files from several branches, each already sorted by amount, and must produce one globally sorted file for settlement. Concatenating and re-sorting everything wastes the fact that each file is already ordered. This is exactly the k-way merge with a heap, because we only ever compare the current fronts.

Problem 2 — The combined feed can be very large, so we want memory bounded to the number of branches, not the total number of transactions. A heap holding one entry per branch keeps memory at k regardless of total size.

In our mini-project we build a `LedgerMerger` that merges several sorted lists of BigDecimal amounts into one sorted list using a PriorityQueue with source tracking. The demo merges three branch lists and logs the merged output.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three sorted branch lists, the first hundred, five hundred, nine hundred; the second two hundred, four hundred; the third fifty, six hundred, one thousand.

Step 1: Seed the heap with the first element of each list: hundred from list zero, two hundred from list one, fifty from list two. The heap orders them, so the smallest ready is fifty.

Step 2: Poll fifty, append it to the result, and push the next element from list two, which is six hundred. The heap now holds hundred, two hundred, six hundred.

Step 3: Poll hundred, append it, push the next from list zero, which is five hundred. The heap holds two hundred, five hundred, six hundred.

Step 4: Poll two hundred, append, push four hundred from list one. The heap holds four hundred, five hundred, six hundred. Poll four hundred, append, list one is now exhausted so nothing is pushed.

Step 5: Continue polling five hundred, then six hundred and pushing one thousand from list two, then nine hundred from list zero, then one thousand. Each poll emits the next smallest across all lists.

Step 6: The heap empties after emitting all eight elements in sorted order: fifty, hundred, two hundred, four hundred, five hundred, six hundred, nine hundred, one thousand. The heap never held more than three entries, confirming memory bounded to k.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Merging k sorted lists means producing one sorted output by repeatedly taking the smallest element that has not yet been consumed across all the lists. The naive way concatenates everything and sorts, which is N log N, but that throws away the fact that each list is already ordered. The key insight is that I only ever need to compare the current fronts of the k lists, and a min-heap makes finding the smallest front a log k operation.

The mechanics are a clean loop. I seed the heap with the first element of each non-empty list, so it holds one candidate per list. Then I poll the smallest, append it to the output, and push the next element from whichever list that one came from. Because the heap only ever holds one representative per list, its size stays at most k, so every poll and push is log k, and over all N elements the total is N log k with only k extra space. To know which list to advance, I wrap each value in a small entry that records its source list and position.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to merge end-of-day transaction files from several branches, each already sorted, into one globally sorted file for settlement. The heap holds one entry per branch, so memory stays bounded to the number of branches no matter how many total transactions flow through, which matters because the combined feed is large.

The senior-level point I make is that there is an equivalent divide-and-conquer approach that merges lists pairwise in log k rounds, also N log k, but the heap version is simpler to reason about and streams naturally. I also note that this is exactly how external merge sort combines sorted runs from disk, which is the real technique banks use to merge enormous sorted transaction files that do not fit in memory, so the interview problem maps directly onto production batch processing.

answers.question: Given an integer n, return an array of length n+1 where the entry at index i is the number of set bits in i. Solve in O(n) time using dynamic programming.
answers.shortTitle: Counting Bits — DP where dp[i] = dp[i>>1] + (i & 1)

s1_definition.profdef: The set-bit count of i equals the set-bit count of i shifted right by one plus the lowest bit of i, because shifting right by one drops the least significant bit and i AND 1 recovers whether that dropped bit was set. This recurrence dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1) fills the whole array in O(n) time and O(n) space, reusing previously computed smaller results.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, the number of enabled features for ID i is the count for ID i with its last feature removed, plus one if that last feature was on. Since the smaller ID was already counted earlier, each new count is just a lookup plus one addition.
s1_definition.oneliner: dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1) — reuse the count of the halved number, add the dropped bit.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The set-bit count of i equals the set-bit count of i shifted right by one plus the lowest bit of i, because shifting right by one drops the least significant bit and i AND 1 recovers whether that dropped bit was set. This recurrence dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1) fills the whole array in O(n) time and O(n) space, reusing previously computed smaller results.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, the number of enabled features for ID i is the count for ID i with its last feature removed, plus one if that last feature was on. Since the smaller ID was already counted earlier, each new count is just a lookup plus one addition.

**One line to remember:** dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1) — reuse the count of the halved number, add the dropped bit.

sections.s2_technical:
The recurrence works because shifting i right by one bit, written i >> 1, produces the number with its lowest bit removed, and that number is strictly smaller than i so its bit count is already computed. The term i AND 1 is zero if the dropped bit was zero and one if it was one, so adding it back accounts for the bit you shifted away.

The build loop is tiny: `int[] dp = new int[n + 1]; for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) dp[i] = dp[i >> 1] + (i & 1); return dp;`. Index zero stays zero because zero has no set bits, and every later index reuses a smaller already-filled entry.

This is strictly better than calling a bit-count routine n times, because each dp entry is a single table lookup plus one add, giving true O(n) total work for the whole array rather than O(n log n).

A senior nuance is the alternative recurrence dp[i] = dp[i AND (i minus 1)] + 1, which uses the lowest-set-bit-clearing trick: i AND i minus one is i with its lowest set bit removed, so its count plus one is the count of i. Both recurrences are O(n); mentioning both shows command of bit identities.

Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a report must show, for every account ID from zero to n, how many features that ID has enabled based on its bit mask. This is exactly how Counting Bits works, because each count reuses the count of a smaller ID.

Problem 2 — Calling a bit-count routine n times on a large report is too slow. This is exactly why the DP recurrence matters: it computes the whole table in linear time with one add per entry.

The mini-project builds a `FeatureCountReport` with a `countBits` method, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo.

The input is n equal to five, so the report covers IDs zero through five.

Step 1: dp of zero is zero because zero has no set bits.

Step 2: For i equal to one, i shifted right is zero so dp of zero is zero, and i AND one is one, giving dp of one equal to one.

Step 3: For i equal to two, i shifted right is one so dp of one is one, and i AND one is zero, giving dp of two equal to one; for i equal to three, i shifted right is one giving one, and i AND one is one, giving dp of three equal to two.

Step 5: The final table is zero, one, one, two, one, two, computed in linear time with one addition per index.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Counting Bits asks for the set-bit count of every integer from zero to n, and the dynamic programming recurrence makes it linear. The key identity is that the number of set bits in i equals the number of set bits in i shifted right by one plus the lowest bit of i. Shifting i right by one drops its least significant bit, producing a strictly smaller number whose count I have already computed, and i AND one tells me whether the bit I dropped was set, so I add it back.

I allocate a table of length n plus one, leave index zero at zero because zero has no set bits, and fill every later index with dp of i shifted right plus i AND one. Each entry is a single lookup plus one addition, so the whole table is built in true linear time, which beats calling a bit-count routine n times.

I like to mention the alternative recurrence dp of i equals dp of i AND i minus one plus one, which uses the fact that i AND i minus one removes the lowest set bit, so the count of that smaller number plus one is the count of i. Both are linear, and knowing both signals real fluency with bit identities.

In my project at National Bank of India, a usage report had to show for every account ID from zero to n how many features that ID had enabled from its bit mask, and calling a bit-count routine for each ID was too slow on large reports. The DP recurrence let me compute the whole table in one linear pass with a single addition per ID, so the report rendered quickly even for large ID ranges.

answers.question: Given an array of elements, return the k elements that appear most frequently, using a hash map to count and a heap to select.
answers.shortTitle: Find the Top K Frequent Elements

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the top k frequent elements means returning the k values with the highest occurrence counts. The standard approach counts occurrences with a hash map, then selects the k highest counts, typically with a size-k min-heap keyed by frequency so the least frequent of the current top k sits at the root for cheap eviction. Counting is linear, and heap selection over m distinct values is m log k.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India wants the three most common merchant categories customers spend on. A clerk first tallies every transaction into a count sheet, one running count per category. Then she keeps a small tray holding only the three categories with the biggest counts so far, arranged so the smallest count is at the front. For each category's final count, if it beats the front of the tray she swaps it in. At the end the tray holds the three most frequent categories, and she never had to fully sort every category.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count with a hash map, then keep the k highest counts in a size-k min-heap keyed by frequency.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the top k frequent elements means returning the k values with the highest occurrence counts. The standard approach counts occurrences with a hash map, then selects the k highest counts, typically with a size-k min-heap keyed by frequency so the least frequent of the current top k sits at the root for cheap eviction. Counting is linear, and heap selection over m distinct values is m log k.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India wants the three most common merchant categories customers spend on. A clerk first tallies every transaction into a count sheet, one running count per category. Then she keeps a small tray holding only the three categories with the biggest counts so far, arranged so the smallest count is at the front. For each category's final count, if it beats the front of the tray she swaps it in. At the end the tray holds the three most frequent categories, and she never had to fully sort every category.

**One line to remember:** Count with a hash map, then keep the k highest counts in a size-k min-heap keyed by frequency.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem splits into two phases: counting and selecting. Counting is a single pass that builds a frequency map, for example `counts.merge(element, 1, Integer::sum)`, which adds one to the running count for each element, creating the entry if absent. After this pass the map holds each distinct element mapped to how many times it occurred.

Selection is where the heap helps. You want the k entries with the largest counts. A size-k min-heap ordered by count keeps exactly the current top k: you offer each map entry, and if the heap exceeds k you poll, which removes the entry with the smallest count. Because the heap is a min-heap by frequency, the root is always the weakest of the current leaders, so evicting it is correct. For example `PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<E,Integer>> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(Map.Entry::getValue));`. After processing all distinct entries, the heap holds the top k by frequency.

Counting is linear in the total number of elements n, and selection is m log k where m is the number of distinct elements, so the whole thing is n plus m log k. That beats fully sorting all distinct elements by frequency, which would be m log m, whenever k is smaller than m, which is the usual case.

A senior-level nuance is bucket sort by frequency, which achieves linear time overall. Since any count is between one and n, you create n-plus-one buckets indexed by frequency, drop each element into its count bucket, then walk buckets from high to low collecting k elements. That is O(n) with no heap, trading a bit of extra memory. I present the heap solution as the clean general answer and mention bucket sort as the linear-time optimisation when counts are bounded.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants to know the most common merchant categories its customers transact in, to design targeted offers, from a large stream of categorised transactions. We need the top few categories by count, not a full ranking. This is exactly top-k frequent, counting then selecting.

Problem 2 — There can be many distinct categories, so after counting we do not want to sort them all; we only want the top k, and we want selection cost to depend on k, not on the full number of categories. A size-k min-heap keyed by frequency gives exactly that.

In our mini-project we build a `CategoryAnalytics` service that returns the top k categories by transaction count using a frequency map plus a frequency-ordered PriorityQueue. The demo feeds a list of category codes and asks for the top two.

Input: the category codes grocery, fuel, grocery, dining, grocery, fuel, dining, grocery, fuel, travel, asking for the top two.

Step 1: We count in one pass. Grocery occurs four times, fuel three times, dining two times, travel once. The frequency map now holds these four counts.

Step 2: We build a min-heap keyed by count. We offer grocery with four. Heap holds grocery. We offer fuel with three. Heap holds fuel then grocery, with fuel smaller at the root.

Step 3: We offer dining with two. The heap size becomes three, exceeding k of two, so we poll the smallest count, which is dining with two, and evict it. The heap holds fuel three and grocery four.

Step 4: We offer travel with one. Size three again, poll the smallest, which is travel with one, and evict it. The heap holds fuel three and grocery four.

Step 5: All distinct categories processed. The heap holds the two most frequent, fuel and grocery, with fuel at the root because its count is smaller.

Step 6: We extract by polling and inserting at the front, so the final highest-first order is grocery with four then fuel with three. We never sorted all four categories fully; selection depended only on k.

  3.   for each entry: heap.offer; if size>k → poll
  4.   drain heap addFirst → return

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the top k frequent elements means returning the k values that appear most often, and I split it into two phases. First I count occurrences in a single linear pass using a hash map, where for each element I add one to its running count, creating the entry if it is new. After that pass the map holds every distinct value mapped to how many times it appeared.

Then I select the k highest counts with a size-k min-heap keyed by frequency. I offer each map entry into the heap, and whenever the heap grows beyond k I poll once, which removes the entry with the smallest count. Because it is a min-heap by frequency, the root is always the weakest of the current leaders, so evicting it is exactly right. After processing all distinct entries the heap holds the top k, and I drain it, reversing the order so the most frequent comes first. Counting is linear in n and selection is m log k over m distinct values, so the whole thing is n plus m log k, which beats fully sorting all distinct values whenever k is smaller than m.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to find the most common merchant categories customers transact in, to feed a targeted-offers engine. There can be many distinct categories, so I did not want to sort them all; the heap kept selection cost tied to k rather than to the full number of categories.

The senior-level point I make is that when counts are bounded, which they always are because any count is between one and n, there is a linear-time alternative called bucket sort by frequency. I create n-plus-one buckets indexed by count, drop each element into its count bucket, then walk the buckets from highest frequency down, collecting k elements. That is O(n) with no heap at all, trading a little extra memory for speed. So I present the heap solution as the clean general answer and name bucket sort as the linear optimisation when I want to squeeze out the log factor.

answers.question: Reverse the bits of a given 32-bit unsigned integer. For example, the binary representation read from the most significant bit becomes the least significant bit and vice versa.
answers.shortTitle: Reverse Bits — shift and OR bit by bit

s1_definition.profdef: Reversing bits mirrors the 32-bit word so bit position k moves to position 31 minus k. The standard approach shifts the result left by one to make room, ORs in the lowest bit of the input, then shifts the input right by one, repeating 32 times. Time O(32) which is constant, space O(1).
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, a device flag word must be read in the opposite endianness for a legacy terminal. Staff peel off the rightmost flag of the input and stack it onto the left of the output one at a time, so after 32 peels the flags are fully mirrored.
s1_definition.oneliner: For 32 rounds: `result = (result << 1) | (n & 1); n >>>= 1;` — peel input's lowest bit onto result's lowest end.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Reversing bits mirrors the 32-bit word so bit position k moves to position 31 minus k. The standard approach shifts the result left by one to make room, ORs in the lowest bit of the input, then shifts the input right by one, repeating 32 times. Time O(32) which is constant, space O(1).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, a device flag word must be read in the opposite endianness for a legacy terminal. Staff peel off the rightmost flag of the input and stack it onto the left of the output one at a time, so after 32 peels the flags are fully mirrored.

**One line to remember:** For 32 rounds: `result = (result << 1) | (n & 1); n >>>= 1;` — peel input's lowest bit onto result's lowest end.

sections.s2_technical:
Each round moves one bit from the input to the output in mirrored position. You make space in the result by shifting it left one bit, then you OR in the input's current lowest bit, then you discard that lowest bit of the input with an unsigned right shift. The example round is `result = (result << 1) | (n & 1); n >>>= 1;`.

Doing this exactly 32 times walks every bit of the input from least significant to most significant, and because each is appended to the growing low end of the result, the first input bit extracted ends up as the highest result bit, achieving the mirror.

The unsigned right shift operator with three angle brackets is essential in Java. The ordinary right shift with two angle brackets would copy the sign bit downward for negative numbers, corrupting the reversal, so you must use the zero-filling unsigned shift to treat the value as a true 32-bit pattern.

A senior nuance is performance. The bit-by-bit loop is clear and constant time, but for reversing many values you can precompute a lookup table for each byte and assemble four reversed bytes, or use a divide-and-conquer swap of bit groups. Java also offers `Integer.reverse(n)` as the production one-liner.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a legacy ATM terminal transmits its device status flags in reversed bit order compared to the core system, so each status word must be bit-reversed before processing. This is exactly how Reverse Bits works.

Problem 2 — The reversal must handle the full 32-bit pattern including the high bit without sign corruption. This is exactly why the unsigned right shift matters: it zero-fills instead of sign-extending.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is the status word forty-three million two hundred sixty-one thousand five hundred ninety-six, whose binary is a 32-bit pattern.

Step 1: The result starts at zero and the work copy holds the input.

Step 2: In round one the result shifts left making the low bit zero, then ORs the input's lowest bit into it, and the input is unsigned-shifted right to drop that bit.

Step 3: Each subsequent round repeats, so the second input bit lands just above the first in the result, steadily building the mirror image.

Step 4: After all 32 rounds, the input's most significant bit has become the result's least significant bit and vice versa, completing the full reversal.

Step 5: The reversed word nine hundred sixty-four million one hundred seventy-six thousand one hundred ninety-two is reported, matching the built-in Integer.reverse.

2026-10-27T07:20:00Z [INFO] builtin check         = 964176192
```

  n = ...0001111010011100 (32-bit)
  for 32 rounds:
    result <<= 1          (make room at low end)
    result |= (n & 1)     (append n's lowest bit)
    n >>>= 1              (drop n's lowest bit, zero-fill)
    ▼ MSB of input → LSB of result  ⇒ mirrored word
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reverse Bits mirrors a 32-bit word so that the bit at position k moves to position thirty-one minus k. The bit-by-bit approach is simple and constant time. In each of thirty-two rounds I shift the result left by one to open a slot at its low end, OR in the current lowest bit of the input, and then unsigned-shift the input right by one to discard that bit. Because the first input bit I peel off ends up pushed all the way to the top of the result as later bits stack beneath it, the final result is the mirror image.

The subtlety in Java that I always call out is the unsigned right shift with three angle brackets. An ordinary right shift copies the sign bit downward for negative numbers, which would corrupt the reversal, so I must use the zero-filling unsigned shift to treat the value as a genuine thirty-two-bit pattern.

For reversing many values, I would move beyond the per-bit loop to a precomputed byte lookup table that reverses eight bits at a time and assembles four reversed bytes, or a divide-and-conquer approach that swaps bit groups. In production Java there is also Integer.reverse as the one-liner.

In my project at National Bank of India, a legacy ATM terminal transmitted its device status flags in reversed bit order relative to the core system, so every status word had to be bit-reversed before the core engine could interpret it. The shift-and-OR reversal with the unsigned shift handled the full word including the high bit without any sign corruption, and I verified it against Integer.reverse.

answers.question: Implement a trie supporting inserting a word, searching for a complete word, and checking whether any word starts with a given prefix.
answers.shortTitle: Implement a Trie (Prefix Tree) with Insert, Search, and startsWith

s1_definition.profdef: A trie, or prefix tree, is a tree where each edge represents a character and each path from the root spells a prefix, so words that share a prefix share the same initial path. Each node holds child links and a boolean marking whether a complete word ends there. Insert, search, and prefix checks all run in time proportional to the length of the key, independent of how many words are stored.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India stores customer reference codes in a branching filing system where you follow one letter at a time. To file a code you walk letter by letter, creating a new drawer whenever one does not yet exist, and you put a little flag in the final drawer to say "a complete code ends here." To check a code you follow the same letters; if any drawer is missing the code was never filed, and even if the path exists, it only counts as a full code if the end flag is set. To check a prefix you just confirm the letter path exists, flag or no flag.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each edge is a character and each path is a prefix; a word-end flag distinguishes a full word from a mere prefix, and all operations are proportional to key length.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A trie, or prefix tree, is a tree where each edge represents a character and each path from the root spells a prefix, so words that share a prefix share the same initial path. Each node holds child links and a boolean marking whether a complete word ends there. Insert, search, and prefix checks all run in time proportional to the length of the key, independent of how many words are stored.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India stores customer reference codes in a branching filing system where you follow one letter at a time. To file a code you walk letter by letter, creating a new drawer whenever one does not yet exist, and you put a little flag in the final drawer to say "a complete code ends here." To check a code you follow the same letters; if any drawer is missing the code was never filed, and even if the path exists, it only counts as a full code if the end flag is set. To check a prefix you just confirm the letter path exists, flag or no flag.

**One line to remember:** Each edge is a character and each path is a prefix; a word-end flag distinguishes a full word from a mere prefix, and all operations are proportional to key length.

sections.s2_technical:
A trie node has two things: a way to reach child nodes by character and a boolean `isWord` that marks the end of a stored word. For lowercase letters you can use a fixed array of twenty-six child slots for speed, or a `HashMap<Character, TrieNode>` for flexibility with arbitrary characters. The map version is more general, so for banking reference codes with mixed characters I use `Map<Character, TrieNode> children`.

Insert walks the word character by character from the root. For each character you descend into the matching child, creating it if absent, for example `node = node.children.computeIfAbsent(c, x -> new TrieNode());`. After consuming the whole word you set `node.isWord = true` on the final node, which records that a complete word ends there. This is why two words sharing a prefix share nodes up to the point they diverge, which is where the space saving comes from.

Search also walks character by character, but if any character has no child you return false immediately, because the word is not present. If you consume the whole word, you return `node.isWord`, which is the crucial distinction: the path existing is not enough, the end flag must be set, otherwise you only stored a longer word that passes through here. The `startsWith` operation is the same walk but returns true as long as the path exists, ignoring the flag, because a prefix does not need a word to end exactly there.

A senior-level nuance is where tries beat hash sets. A hash set answers "is this exact word present" in constant time but cannot answer "does any word start with this prefix" without scanning everything. The trie answers prefix queries in key-length time, which is why it powers autocomplete, typeahead search, IP routing tables, and dictionary lookups. The cost is memory, since each node carries child pointers, and that is why compressed variants like radix trees collapse single-child chains to save space in production.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has an internal console where staff type account reference codes, and the console must offer prefix-based autocomplete so a teller typing the first few characters sees whether any codes match. A hash set cannot answer prefix queries, but a trie can in time proportional to the prefix length. This is exactly what a prefix tree is for.

Problem 2 — The console must distinguish a complete valid code from a mere prefix of some longer code, so entering a prefix that is not itself a registered code must not be treated as a match. The word-end flag on each node makes that distinction exact.

In our mini-project we build a `ReferenceCodeTrie` with insert, search, and startsWith. The demo inserts a few reference codes, searches for a full code and a prefix-only string, and checks a prefix, logging each result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: insert the codes "SAV", "SAV2001", and "CUR3001", then four queries.

Step 1: Insert "SAV". From the root we descend S, creating it, then A, then V. We set the end flag on the V node. The trie now has a path S-A-V with a word-end at V.

Step 2: Insert "SAV2001". We descend S, A, V, which already exist and are reused, then create 2, 0, 0, 1, and set the end flag on the final 1. The shared prefix "SAV" cost no new nodes.

Step 3: Insert "CUR3001". This shares nothing with the existing codes, so it creates a fresh path C-U-R-3-0-0-1 with the end flag on the last node.

Step 4: Search "SAV2001". We walk S, A, V, 2, 0, 0, 1, every child exists, and the final node has the end flag set, so we return true.

Step 5: Search "SAV2". We walk S, A, V, 2, every child exists, but the node at 2 does not have the end flag, because no code ends exactly at "SAV2"; it is only a prefix of "SAV2001", so we return false.

Step 6: startsWith "SAV" walks S, A, V, the path exists, so we return true regardless of the flag. startsWith "LOAN" fails at the very first character because the root has no L child, so we return false. All four operations touched only as many nodes as the query length.

```
[2026-10-26 23:28:01] INFO    search 'SAV2001' = true
[2026-10-26 23:28:01] INFO    search 'SAV2' = false
[2026-10-26 23:28:01] INFO    startsWith 'SAV' = true
[2026-10-26 23:28:01] INFO    startsWith 'LOAN' = false
```

  search  SAV2001 → path ✓, end flag ✓ → true
  search  SAV2    → path ✓, end flag ✗ → false
  starts  SAV     → path ✓ → true
  starts  LOAN    → no 'L' child → false
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A trie, or prefix tree, is a tree in which each edge represents a single character and each path from the root spells a prefix, so words that share a leading prefix share the same initial path through the tree. Every node holds links to its children and a boolean that marks whether a complete word ends at that node. The beauty is that insert, search, and prefix checks all run in time proportional to the length of the key, completely independent of how many words are stored.

Insert walks the word character by character, descending into the matching child and creating it when it does not exist, and at the end sets the word-end flag on the final node. Search does the same walk but returns false the moment a character has no child, and if it consumes the whole word it returns the word-end flag, because the path existing is not enough; the flag must be set, otherwise I only stored a longer word that happens to pass through. The startsWith check is the identical walk but returns true as long as the path exists, ignoring the flag, because a prefix does not need a word to end exactly there.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used a trie to power prefix autocomplete for account reference codes in an internal staff console. A hash set could confirm an exact code instantly but could not answer "does any code start with these characters," whereas the trie answers that in time proportional to the prefix length. The word-end flag was essential so that typing a prefix that is not itself a registered code was not wrongly treated as a match.

The senior-level point I make is that the trie's strength is prefix queries, which is why it underpins autocomplete, typeahead search, IP routing tables, and dictionary lookups, all places where a hash set falls short. The trade-off is memory, because every node carries child pointers, so in production I would consider a compressed variant like a radix tree that collapses single-child chains, or a fixed array of children when the alphabet is small and fixed, to reduce the per-node overhead.

answers.question: Given an array containing n distinct numbers taken from the range [0, n], find the missing number using the XOR technique. Compare it with the sum approach.
answers.shortTitle: Missing Number — XOR all indices with all values

s1_definition.profdef: XORing every index from 0 to n together with every array value cancels all present numbers, because each present value appears once as an index and once as a value, leaving only the missing number. Seeding the accumulator with n handles the top of the range. Time O(n), space O(1), and unlike the sum approach it cannot overflow.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, each expected slot number is matched against the actual value found there. Every present number cancels with its own slot, and the one slot whose expected number has no matching value reveals the missing number.
s1_definition.oneliner: Start accumulator at n, then XOR each index i and value nums[i]; the survivor is the missing number.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** XORing every index from 0 to n together with every array value cancels all present numbers, because each present value appears once as an index and once as a value, leaving only the missing number. Seeding the accumulator with n handles the top of the range. Time O(n), space O(1), and unlike the sum approach it cannot overflow.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, each expected slot number is matched against the actual value found there. Every present number cancels with its own slot, and the one slot whose expected number has no matching value reveals the missing number.

**One line to remember:** Start accumulator at n, then XOR each index i and value nums[i]; the survivor is the missing number.

sections.s2_technical:
The trick pairs each index with each value. If you XOR together all indices 0 through n and all values in the array, every number that is actually present contributes twice, once as an index and once as a value, so it cancels. The only number that appears solely as an index and never as a value is the missing one, so it survives.

A compact way to code this is to seed the accumulator with n and then fold index and value together in one loop: `int missing = nums.length; for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) missing ^= i ^ nums[i]; return missing;`. Seeding with n covers the top index n which the loop over array positions does not reach.

The cancellation is order-independent because XOR is commutative and associative, so you can interleave indices and values freely in a single pass, which is exactly what the one-loop form does.

A senior nuance is why XOR is preferable to the Gauss sum method. The sum approach computes n times n plus one over two minus the array sum, which is clean but can overflow a 32-bit integer for large n. XOR never overflows because it operates bitwise, so in production banking code where inputs can be large the XOR method is the safer, equally fast choice.

Problem 2 — The page range can be very large and the sum method risks integer overflow. This is exactly why the XOR technique matters: it is overflow-safe while remaining linear time and constant space.

The input is the page array three, zero, one with n equal to three.

Step 1: The accumulator is seeded with n, which is three.

Step 2: At index zero the value is three, so the accumulator XORs index zero and value three, cancelling the seeded three and leaving zero.

Step 3: At index one the value is zero, so the accumulator XORs index one and value zero, becoming one.

Step 4: At index two the value is one, so the accumulator XORs index two and value one, and the ones cancel while the index two contributes, leaving two.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Missing Number with the XOR technique finds the one absent value in an array of n distinct numbers drawn from zero to n. The idea is that if I XOR together all the indices from zero to n and all the array values, every number that is actually present appears exactly twice, once as an index and once as a value, so it cancels to zero. The only number that shows up as an index but never as a value is the missing one, so it survives the cancellation.

In code I seed the accumulator with n to cover the top index that the array loop does not reach, then in a single pass I fold each index and its value into the accumulator with XOR. Because XOR is commutative and associative the cancellation does not depend on order, so interleaving indices and values in one loop is correct.

I always compare this to the Gauss sum method, which subtracts the array sum from n times n plus one over two. The sum method is elegant but can overflow a thirty-two-bit integer for large n, whereas XOR operates bitwise and can never overflow, so in production I prefer XOR when inputs may be large.

In my project at National Bank of India, printed statement page numbers from zero to n were supposed to all be present in a batch, but one page went missing and had to be identified for reprinting, and the page ranges could be large enough that the sum method risked overflow. The XOR fold found the missing page in a single overflow-safe pass, which we routed to the reprint queue.
