sections.s5_journey:
Input: the chain T1 to T2 to T3 to T4 to T5, reversing in groups of two.

Step 1: A dummy node sits before T1, and the before-group pointer starts at the dummy. We check whether two nodes remain from T1; T1 and T2 exist, so we have a full group.

Step 2: Reverse the first group of two. Flipping pointers turns T1 to T2 into T2 to T1. The original first node T1 becomes the group's tail. We reconnect: the dummy now points to T2, the new front, and T1's next will be wired to the rest in the next move.

Step 3: Wire T1's next to the node after the group, which is T3, and advance the before-group pointer to T1, the group's tail, ready for the next group. The chain so far reads T2, T1, then T3 onward.

Step 4: Check whether two nodes remain from T3; T3 and T4 exist, so another full group. Reverse T3 to T4 into T4 to T3. Reconnect: T1 now points to T4, the new front, and T3, now the group tail, points to T5, the rest. Advance the before-group pointer to T3.

Step 5: Check whether two nodes remain from T5; only T5 exists, which is fewer than two, so we stop and leave T5 in place.

Step 6: The final chain reads T2, T1, T4, T3, T5. Each full group of two was reversed in place, the trailing single node was left unchanged per the specification, and no node was lost or duplicated during the pointer surgery.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Reversing a linked list in groups of k means processing the list in consecutive blocks of k nodes, reversing the pointers within each full block, and leaving any final block of fewer than k nodes in its original order. It combines two skills, reversing a singly linked list and carefully stitching the reversed segments back together, and the stitching is where the bugs live, so I always use a dummy head node that sits before the real head to give me a stable handle on the node preceding each group.

My driver keeps a pointer to the node just before the current group, starting at the dummy. For each group I first walk k steps ahead to confirm a full group of k nodes exists, and if fewer than k remain I stop and leave the tail unchanged. For a full group I reverse exactly those k nodes with the standard previous-current-next reversal, flipping each node's next pointer to its predecessor, then I make three reconnections: the node before the group points to the new front of the reversed block, the original first node of the group, now the block's tail, points to the node after the group, and I advance the before-group pointer to that original first node for the next iteration. Because each node is touched a constant number of times and I use only a few pointers, the algorithm is linear time and constant space.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to feed transaction records to a settlement system that expects each fixed-size batch in reversed order while passing any leftover partial batch through unchanged. The reversal happened in place on very long chains without allocating a parallel structure, and the dummy head plus careful three-link reconnection guaranteed no record was lost or duplicated during the pointer surgery.

The senior-level point I make is the recursive alternative and the specification detail. Recursively I would reverse the first k nodes and set the original first node's next to the result of recursing on the rest, which is elegant but uses stack space proportional to the number of groups, so I prefer the iterative version for very long lists. I also highlight that the leave-the-partial-tail rule is a deliberate requirement that tests whether I read the specification carefully, and that the broader technique of reversing and re-linking sublists shows up in batch reordering, pagination of linked structures, and buffer manipulation.

answers.question: Search a 2D Matrix — binary search on flattened or top-right elimination.
answers.shortTitle: Search a 2D Matrix — binary search on a conceptually flattened grid

s1_definition.profdef: Searching a sorted 2D matrix means finding whether a target value exists in a matrix whose rows are sorted left to right and whose first element of each row is greater than the last element of the previous row. Because the whole matrix is in effect one sorted sequence wrapped into rows, you can run a single binary search over the conceptual flattened array by mapping a one-dimensional index back to a row and column with integer division and modulo, giving O(log of (m times n)) time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India prints a giant ledger where every page has transaction amounts sorted smallest to largest, and the last amount on page one is always smaller than the first amount on page two. Rajesh wants to know if an amount of exactly 50000 rupees appears anywhere. Instead of reading every page, he treats all pages as one long sorted list, jumps to the middle, and decides whether to look in the earlier half or the later half, cutting the search in half each time.
s1_definition.oneliner: A fully sorted matrix is just a sorted array folded into rows, so one binary search with index-to-row-column mapping finds any value in logarithmic time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Searching a sorted 2D matrix means finding whether a target value exists in a matrix whose rows are sorted left to right and whose first element of each row is greater than the last element of the previous row. Because the whole matrix is in effect one sorted sequence wrapped into rows, you can run a single binary search over the conceptual flattened array by mapping a one-dimensional index back to a row and column with integer division and modulo, giving O(log of (m times n)) time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India prints a giant ledger where every page has transaction amounts sorted smallest to largest, and the last amount on page one is always smaller than the first amount on page two. Rajesh wants to know if an amount of exactly 50000 rupees appears anywhere. Instead of reading every page, he treats all pages as one long sorted list, jumps to the middle, and decides whether to look in the earlier half or the later half, cutting the search in half each time.

**One line to remember:** A fully sorted matrix is just a sorted array folded into rows, so one binary search with index-to-row-column mapping finds any value in logarithmic time.

sections.s2_technical:
The matrix has `m` rows and `n` columns. The key property is global sorting: reading row by row gives a non-decreasing sequence. That lets us pretend the matrix is a single array of length `m * n`.

A binary search keeps two pointers `low = 0` and `high = m * n - 1`. The middle index `mid = low + (high - low) / 2` is computed the safe way to avoid integer overflow. To read the value at a flattened index, we convert it: the row is `mid / n` and the column is `mid % n`. For example, in a 3-by-4 matrix, flattened index 6 maps to row `6 / 4 = 1` and column `6 % 4 = 2`.

We compare `matrix[row][col]` with the target. If equal, we found it. If the value is smaller than the target, we move `low = mid + 1`. If larger, we move `high = mid - 1`. The loop ends when `low` passes `high`, meaning the value is absent.

A senior nuance: the `low + (high - low) / 2` form matters in real systems where the matrix could be large; `(low + high) / 2` can overflow a 32-bit int. Another nuance is that this approach only works when the matrix is globally sorted. If only each row is sorted but rows do not chain together, you must use the top-right elimination method instead, which is O(m + n).
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs an end-of-day settlement report as a grid. Each row holds a block of settled transaction amounts, sorted ascending, and the blocks are themselves ordered so block two always starts above where block one ended. The compliance officer, Priya, needs a fast "does this exact amount exist" check while auditing, because scanning the entire grid for every query is too slow when there are millions of entries.

This is exactly how binary search on a flattened sorted matrix works. Because the grid is globally sorted, we can treat it as one long sorted array and halve the search space every step instead of scanning linearly.

Problem 2 — The officer must never get a wrong answer due to an arithmetic bug. If the midpoint calculation overflowed on a very large grid, the search could crash or return a false negative, which in a bank audit is unacceptable.

This is exactly why we use the overflow-safe midpoint formula and the clean index-to-coordinate mapping, so the search is both correct and fast.

The code will have an `Account` class for context, a `SettlementMatrixSearch` class with a `contains` method that runs the binary search, and a runnable demo that builds a sorted grid of settled amounts and queries for both present and absent values with logging at each decision.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a 3-by-4 globally sorted grid and the target value 50000.

Step 1: The search computes `low = 0` and `high = 11` because the grid has twelve cells. The data lives entirely in the matrix; the pointers are just integers describing the search window.

Step 2: The midpoint is `0 + (11 - 0) / 2 = 5`. Mapping index 5 gives row `5 / 4 = 1` and column `5 % 4 = 1`, which is `matrix[1][1] = 50000`. That equals the target, so the method returns true immediately.

Step 3: For the absent target 55555, the first probe at index 5 reads 50000, which is smaller, so `low` becomes 6. The next midpoint is `6 + (11 - 6) / 2 = 8`, mapping to row 2 column 0, value 71000, which is larger, so `high` becomes 7. The next midpoint is `6 + (7 - 6) / 2 = 6`, value 58000, larger, so `high` becomes 5. Now `low (6)` is greater than `high (5)`, the loop ends, and the method returns false.

Final output:

sections.s6_takeaway:
Searching a sorted two-dimensional matrix is a problem where every row is sorted left to right and the first element of each row is larger than the last element of the previous row, which means the entire matrix behaves like one long sorted array that has simply been folded into rows. Because of that global ordering, I can run a single binary search over the conceptual flattened array of length rows times columns, and the whole lookup finishes in logarithmic time rather than scanning every cell.

The technique that makes this work cleanly is the mapping from a one-dimensional index back to a row and a column. I keep a low pointer and a high pointer, I compute the midpoint using the overflow-safe form of low plus high minus low divided by two, and then I convert that midpoint into a row by integer division by the number of columns and into a column by the remainder. I compare the value there with the target and move the low pointer up or the high pointer down accordingly.

I always use the overflow-safe midpoint because on a very large grid the naive addition of low and high can exceed the range of a thirty-two bit integer, which in a banking audit could silently produce a wrong answer. I also make sure the matrix is genuinely globally sorted before I use this method, because if only each row is sorted and the rows do not chain together, I would instead start from the top-right corner and eliminate one row or one column per step, which runs in order rows plus columns time.

In my project at National Bank of India, the end-of-day settlement report was stored as exactly this kind of globally sorted grid of settled amounts, and the compliance officer needed an instant check for whether a specific amount had settled. The flattened binary search gave that answer in a handful of comparisons even on grids with millions of entries, which kept the audit interactive instead of forcing a full scan for every query.

answers.question: Set Matrix Zeroes — first row/column as markers.
answers.shortTitle: Set Matrix Zeroes — using the first row and column as in-place markers

s1_definition.profdef: Setting matrix zeroes means that if any cell in an m-by-n matrix is zero, its entire row and entire column must be set to zero, and the challenge is to do it in place using only constant extra space. The efficient technique reuses the matrix's own first row and first column as marker storage that records which rows and columns must be zeroed, plus two boolean flags to remember whether the first row and first column themselves originally contained a zero.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has a grid where each cell is a daily profit figure for a branch, and a zero means that branch was flagged as frozen for that day. Policy says if any single day is frozen, the whole branch (its column) and the whole day (its row) must be wiped to zero for the audit. Instead of keeping a separate notepad of which branches and days to wipe, Priya scribbles the flags in the margin of the grid itself — the top row and the left column — then wipes everything in one careful pass.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use the first row and first column as your zero-marker notepad so you need only constant extra memory to blank out every flagged row and column.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Setting matrix zeroes means that if any cell in an m-by-n matrix is zero, its entire row and entire column must be set to zero, and the challenge is to do it in place using only constant extra space. The efficient technique reuses the matrix's own first row and first column as marker storage that records which rows and columns must be zeroed, plus two boolean flags to remember whether the first row and first column themselves originally contained a zero.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has a grid where each cell is a daily profit figure for a branch, and a zero means that branch was flagged as frozen for that day. Policy says if any single day is frozen, the whole branch (its column) and the whole day (its row) must be wiped to zero for the audit. Instead of keeping a separate notepad of which branches and days to wipe, Priya scribbles the flags in the margin of the grid itself — the top row and the left column — then wipes everything in one careful pass.

**One line to remember:** Use the first row and first column as your zero-marker notepad so you need only constant extra memory to blank out every flagged row and column.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive solution copies the matrix or keeps separate sets of row and column indices, costing O(m + n) or more extra space. The in-place trick removes that extra space by storing the markers inside the matrix.

First we scan to answer two questions with boolean flags: does the first row contain any zero, and does the first column contain any zero. These two flags are needed because we are about to overwrite the first row and column with markers, so we must remember their original state separately.

Then we iterate over the inner matrix, from row 1 and column 1 onward. Whenever we find `matrix[i][j] == 0`, we set `matrix[i][0] = 0` and `matrix[0][j] = 0`. This writes a marker into the left column and top row saying "this row must be zeroed" and "this column must be zeroed".

Next we iterate the inner matrix again. For each inner cell, if its row marker `matrix[i][0]` is zero or its column marker `matrix[0][j]` is zero, we set the cell to zero.

Finally we handle the first row and first column using the two flags we saved at the start. If the first-row flag was true, we zero the entire first row; if the first-column flag was true, we zero the entire first column. The whole algorithm is O(m times n) time and O(1) extra space.

A senior nuance: the order matters. You must apply the inner cells before zeroing the first row and column, otherwise you destroy the markers before using them. The two saved flags must be computed before you start writing any markers.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India holds a reconciliation grid where rows are dates and columns are branches, each cell a settled amount. A zero means a discrepancy was detected at that date and branch. Risk policy says a single discrepancy quarantines the whole date and the whole branch, so every amount on that date and every amount for that branch must be blanked to zero before the report is filed.

This is exactly how set matrix zeroes works. A single zero cell propagates to its entire row and entire column.

Problem 2 — The grid can be huge and memory on the batch server is tight, so we cannot afford to allocate a full second matrix or large index sets just to remember what to blank.

This is exactly why we reuse the first row and first column as in-place markers, keeping the extra memory to two boolean flags regardless of how large the grid grows.

The code will have an `Account` class for domain flavor, a `ReconciliationGrid` class with a `quarantineZeroes` method implementing the in-place algorithm, and a runnable demo that prints the grid before and after with logging.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Set matrix zeroes is a problem where, if any cell in the matrix is zero, I must set that cell's entire row and entire column to zero, and the interesting constraint is to do it in place using only constant extra space. The naive approach keeps separate sets of row and column indices, which costs extra memory proportional to the dimensions, and the elegant approach avoids that by reusing the matrix's own first row and first column as the marker storage.

The algorithm has four careful phases. First I record, in two boolean flags, whether the first row and the first column originally contained any zero, because I am about to overwrite them with markers and I must not lose their original state. Second I scan the inner matrix and, for each zero I find, I write a zero into that row's position in the first column and that column's position in the first row, which marks the row and column for blanking. Third I scan the inner matrix again and zero any cell whose row marker or column marker is set. Fourth I use the two saved flags to decide whether to blank the first row and the first column themselves.

The order is the part that trips people up. If I zeroed the first row and column before using the markers, I would destroy the information I need, so I always apply the inner cells first and the border last, and I always compute the two flags before writing any marker. The whole thing runs in time proportional to the number of cells with only constant additional memory.

In my project at National Bank of India, we had a reconciliation grid where rows were dates and columns were branches, and a zero meant a detected discrepancy that policy required us to quarantine across the whole date and the whole branch before filing. Because the batch server had tight memory, the in-place marker technique let us process very large grids without allocating a second matrix, which kept the nightly reconciliation job within its memory budget.

answers.question: Word Search — DFS backtracking on grid.
answers.shortTitle: Word Search — depth-first search with backtracking on a grid

s1_definition.profdef: Word Search asks whether a given word can be formed in a grid of characters by moving to horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, where each cell may be used at most once per path. The standard solution is depth-first search with backtracking: from each starting cell you explore a path matching the word character by character, temporarily marking visited cells, and you undo the mark when a branch fails so the cell becomes available for other paths.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the National Bank of India's fraud team looking at a grid of letters pulled from scrambled transaction memos. They want to know if a suspicious codeword like "FRAUD" is hidden as a connected trail through adjacent cells. An investigator starts on an F, tries a neighbor that is R, then A, and so on; if a trail dead-ends, they step back and erase their footprints so another trail can reuse those cells.
s1_definition.oneliner: Try every starting cell, walk adjacent cells matching the word, mark cells as you enter and unmark as you leave, so backtracking frees them for other paths.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Word Search asks whether a given word can be formed in a grid of characters by moving to horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, where each cell may be used at most once per path. The standard solution is depth-first search with backtracking: from each starting cell you explore a path matching the word character by character, temporarily marking visited cells, and you undo the mark when a branch fails so the cell becomes available for other paths.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture the National Bank of India's fraud team looking at a grid of letters pulled from scrambled transaction memos. They want to know if a suspicious codeword like "FRAUD" is hidden as a connected trail through adjacent cells. An investigator starts on an F, tries a neighbor that is R, then A, and so on; if a trail dead-ends, they step back and erase their footprints so another trail can reuse those cells.

**One line to remember:** Try every starting cell, walk adjacent cells matching the word, mark cells as you enter and unmark as you leave, so backtracking frees them for other paths.

sections.s2_technical:
The grid is a two-dimensional character array. The word is a string. We must find a connected path, moving up, down, left, or right, whose characters spell the word, with no cell reused within that single path.

The outer loop tries every cell as a possible starting point. From a start, we call a recursive depth-first search that takes the current row, column, and the index into the word we are trying to match. The base success case is when the index equals the word length, meaning we matched every character. The failure cases are going out of bounds, landing on a cell that does not match the current character, or landing on a cell already used in this path.

To mark a cell as used, a common trick is to temporarily replace its character with a sentinel such as the hash symbol, then restore it after exploring. This avoids allocating a separate visited matrix. We recurse into the four neighbors for the next word index. If any neighbor returns true, we propagate true. After exploring all neighbors, we restore the original character, which is the backtracking step.

The time complexity is roughly O(m times n times 4 to the power L) in the worst case, where L is the word length, because from each cell we branch into up to four directions for each character. In practice the matching constraint prunes most branches quickly.

A senior nuance: restoring the character on the way out is essential; if you forget, cells stay permanently marked and valid words get rejected. Another nuance is to short-circuit as soon as one path succeeds rather than exploring all paths.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's anti-fraud unit receives grids of characters extracted from obfuscated wire-transfer memos. Fraud rings hide codewords such as a mule account tag by spreading letters across adjacent cells. The unit needs to confirm whether a specific codeword can be traced as a connected path.

This is exactly how Word Search works. We look for the word as a connected trail of adjacent matching cells.

Problem 2 — A letter cell must not be counted twice within the same trail, otherwise a single stray letter could falsely "complete" a word and raise a false alarm that freezes an innocent customer's account.

This is exactly why we mark a cell on entry and unmark it on exit, so within one path each cell is used at most once, but the cell is still free for other candidate paths.

The code will have an `Account` class for flavor, a `FraudWordSearch` class with an `exists` method running DFS plus backtracking, and a runnable demo that searches a grid for both a present and an absent codeword with logging.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a 3-by-4 character grid and the codeword "FRAUD".

Step 1: The outer loop reaches cell [0][0] which holds F, matching index 0 of "FRAUD". We mark it with a sentinel and recurse for index 1 expecting R.

Step 2: The neighbor [0][1] holds R, matching index 1. We mark and recurse for index 2 expecting A.

Step 3: The neighbor [0][2] holds A, matching index 2. We recurse for index 3 expecting U. The down neighbor [1][2] holds U, matching index 3. We recurse for index 4 expecting D. The down neighbor [2][2] holds D, matching index 4.

Step 4: We recurse for index 5, which equals the word length, so the base case returns true. The true result propagates back up the chain. As each frame returns, it restores its cell, but since we found the word the method returns true overall.

Step 5: For the absent word "SAFE", no starting cell holds S, so every DFS returns false and the method returns false.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 12:40:00 INFO    Priya Sharma scan: codeword 'FRAUD' present? true
2026-10-27 12:40:00 INFO    codeword 'SAFE' present? false
```

    │

    │ finds F at [0][0]
    ▼

    │
    ├─→ R [0][1] mark '#'
    │     └─→ A [0][2] mark '#'
    │           └─→ U [1][2] mark '#'
    │                 └─→ D [2][2] mark '#'
    │                       └─→ index==len → TRUE
    ▼
  backtrack restores all cells; result propagated = TRUE

  (for "SAFE": no S start cell → FALSE)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Search asks whether a given word can be formed in a grid of characters by moving between horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, where each cell can be used at most once within a single path. The natural solution is depth-first search combined with backtracking, which means I explore one candidate trail as deeply as possible, and whenever a trail fails I step back and undo my changes so the cells become available for other trails.

Concretely, I try every cell in the grid as a possible starting point, and from each start I run a recursive search that carries the current row, the current column, and the index of the character in the word I am trying to match. The search succeeds when the index reaches the length of the word, and it fails when I go out of bounds, when the cell does not match the expected character, or when the cell is already part of the current path.

The key detail is how I mark a cell as used and then release it. A clean trick is to temporarily overwrite the cell with a sentinel character so the mismatch check naturally rejects it during this path, and then to restore the original character after exploring all four directions. That restoration is the backtracking step, and forgetting it is the classic bug, because cells would stay permanently marked and legitimate words would be wrongly rejected. I also short-circuit as soon as any direction returns success.

In my project at National Bank of India, the anti-fraud unit received grids of characters pulled from obfuscated wire-transfer memos, and fraud rings hid codewords as connected trails across adjacent cells. The depth-first search with backtracking let us confirm whether a specific codeword was present without ever double-counting a single letter inside one trail, which mattered because a false positive could wrongly freeze an innocent customer's account.

answers.question: Flood Fill — BFS/DFS from starting cell.
answers.shortTitle: Flood Fill — BFS or DFS spreading from a starting cell

s1_definition.profdef: Flood Fill takes a grid, a starting cell, and a new color, and repaints the starting cell plus every cell connected to it through up, down, left, and right neighbors that shares the original color, stopping at boundaries and at cells of a different color. It is implemented with either breadth-first search using a queue or depth-first search using recursion or an explicit stack, both running in O(m times n) time and visiting each connected same-color cell once.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India plotting a map of branches where each cell is a region and the color is a risk rating. The risk team taps one region rated "medium" and says "reclassify this whole connected medium zone as high." The change spreads outward from the tapped region to every touching region that was also medium, like paint spreading across connected tiles, and it stops where the rating is different.
s1_definition.oneliner: Flood Fill spreads a new value outward from a start cell to all connected cells sharing the original value, using BFS or DFS, each cell touched once.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Flood Fill takes a grid, a starting cell, and a new color, and repaints the starting cell plus every cell connected to it through up, down, left, and right neighbors that shares the original color, stopping at boundaries and at cells of a different color. It is implemented with either breadth-first search using a queue or depth-first search using recursion or an explicit stack, both running in O(m times n) time and visiting each connected same-color cell once.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the National Bank of India plotting a map of branches where each cell is a region and the color is a risk rating. The risk team taps one region rated "medium" and says "reclassify this whole connected medium zone as high." The change spreads outward from the tapped region to every touching region that was also medium, like paint spreading across connected tiles, and it stops where the rating is different.

**One line to remember:** Flood Fill spreads a new value outward from a start cell to all connected cells sharing the original value, using BFS or DFS, each cell touched once.

sections.s2_technical:
The input is a grid, a start row and column, and a replacement value. We first read the original value at the start cell. If the original value already equals the replacement, we return immediately, otherwise a naive recursion would loop forever because the repainted cells still match.

In the depth-first approach we recurse from the start cell. The base cases are going out of bounds or landing on a cell whose value is not the original value. Otherwise we set the cell to the new value and recurse into its four neighbors. Setting the value before recursing is what prevents revisiting, because neighbors will now see the new value and stop.

In the breadth-first approach we push the start cell into a queue and set it to the new value. We repeatedly pop a cell and, for each of its four neighbors that is in bounds and still holds the original value, we set that neighbor to the new value and push it. We change the value at the moment we enqueue so no cell is enqueued twice.

Both run in time proportional to the number of cells, with space proportional to the size of the connected region for the recursion stack or the queue. A senior nuance is the early return when the new value equals the old value; without it the depth-first version recurses infinitely and the breadth-first version enqueues forever. Another nuance is that marking at enqueue time, not dequeue time, is what guarantees each cell is processed exactly once.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps a geographic risk grid where each cell is a small zone holding a risk code. When a fraud cluster is confirmed in one zone, the risk team must escalate the entire connected block of zones that currently share the same risk code, because fraud tends to spread through adjacent connected zones.

This is exactly how Flood Fill works. From the confirmed zone the new risk code spreads to every connected zone of the same original code.

Problem 2 — If the confirmed zone already carries the escalated code, re-running the escalation must do nothing rather than spin forever.

This is exactly why we check whether the new value already equals the original value and return immediately, which keeps the operation safe to repeat.

The code will have an `Account` class for flavor, a `RiskZoneFiller` class with both a `floodFillDfs` and a `floodFillBfs` method, and a runnable demo that escalates a connected zone and prints the grid before and after.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a 3-by-4 risk grid, start cell [0][0] holding 2, new value 3.

Step 1: The original value at [0][0] is 2, which is not equal to the new value 3, so we proceed rather than returning early.

Step 2: We repaint [0][0] to 3 and recurse. Its down neighbor [1][0] is 2, so it is repainted and recursed; its right neighbor [0][1] is 2, repainted and recursed.

Step 3: The spread continues through every connected 2: [0][2], [1][1], and [2][1], [2][2] reachable through the connected block. Cells holding 1, and the lone 3 at [2][3], act as boundaries and stop the spread.

Step 4: The cell [2][0] holding 1 is not connected through 2, so it stays 1. The result is that the connected medium block becomes high while unrelated zones keep their codes.

Final output:

2026-10-27 12:45:00 INFO    [2, 2, 2, 1]
2026-10-27 12:45:00 INFO    [2, 2, 1, 1]
2026-10-27 12:45:00 INFO    [1, 2, 2, 3]
2026-10-27 12:45:00 INFO    Grid after escalation:
2026-10-27 12:45:00 INFO    [3, 3, 3, 1]
2026-10-27 12:45:00 INFO    [3, 3, 1, 1]
2026-10-27 12:45:00 INFO    [1, 3, 3, 3]
```

    ├─→ [1][0]=2 → repaint 3 → spread
    ├─→ [0][1]=2 → repaint 3 → spread
    │       └─→ [0][2]=2 → repaint 3
    │       └─→ [1][1]=2 → repaint 3 → [2][1]=2 → [2][2]=2
    ▼
  boundaries: cells==1 and lone 3 stop the spread
    ▼
  connected medium block becomes high; others unchanged
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Flood Fill takes a grid, a starting cell, and a new value, and it repaints the starting cell together with every cell connected to it through up, down, left, and right neighbors that shares the starting cell's original value. It is the same idea as the paint-bucket tool in an image editor, and I can implement it either with depth-first search using recursion or with breadth-first search using a queue, both of which run in time proportional to the number of cells.

In the depth-first version I read the original value at the start, then recurse, and at each cell my base cases are going out of bounds or landing on a cell whose value is not the original value. Otherwise I set the cell to the new value before recursing into its four neighbors, and setting the value first is exactly what stops me from revisiting, because the neighbors now see the new value and stop. In the breadth-first version I enqueue the start, and for each dequeued cell I enqueue every in-bounds neighbor that still holds the original value, marking it at the moment I enqueue so no cell is ever enqueued twice.

The single most important guard is the early return when the new value already equals the original value. Without that check the depth-first version recurses forever and the breadth-first version enqueues forever, because repainted cells still appear to match. Marking cells at enqueue time rather than dequeue time is the other detail that guarantees each cell is processed exactly once.

In my project at National Bank of India, we maintained a geographic risk grid where each cell was a zone carrying a risk code, and when a fraud cluster was confirmed in one zone we needed to escalate the entire connected block of zones sharing that code, because fraud tends to spread through adjacent connected areas. Flood Fill did exactly that, and the early-return guard made the escalation safe to re-run without ever looping, which mattered because the risk team sometimes triggered the same escalation twice.

answers.question: LRU Cache — HashMap + doubly linked list, O(1) get/put.
answers.shortTitle: LRU Cache — HashMap plus doubly linked list for O(1) get and put

s1_definition.profdef: An LRU (Least Recently Used) cache is a fixed-capacity key-value store that evicts the least recently accessed entry when it is full. The classic O(1) design combines a hash map, which gives constant-time lookup from a key to its node, with a doubly linked list, which maintains usage order so the most recently used entry sits at one end and the least recently used sits at the other, allowing both get and put to run in constant time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India teller keeps only the twenty most recently touched customer files on the desk because space is limited. Every time a file is read or updated, it moves to the front of the pile. When a brand new file arrives and the desk is full, the file at the very back, the one nobody has touched in the longest time, is put back in the archive. The desk is the cache, the pile order is the linked list, and a quick index of where each file sits is the hash map.
s1_definition.oneliner: A hash map finds the node instantly and a doubly linked list reorders it instantly, so every get and put touches the entry and promotes it to most-recently-used in constant time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An LRU (Least Recently Used) cache is a fixed-capacity key-value store that evicts the least recently accessed entry when it is full. The classic O(1) design combines a hash map, which gives constant-time lookup from a key to its node, with a doubly linked list, which maintains usage order so the most recently used entry sits at one end and the least recently used sits at the other, allowing both get and put to run in constant time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India teller keeps only the twenty most recently touched customer files on the desk because space is limited. Every time a file is read or updated, it moves to the front of the pile. When a brand new file arrives and the desk is full, the file at the very back, the one nobody has touched in the longest time, is put back in the archive. The desk is the cache, the pile order is the linked list, and a quick index of where each file sits is the hash map.

**One line to remember:** A hash map finds the node instantly and a doubly linked list reorders it instantly, so every get and put touches the entry and promotes it to most-recently-used in constant time.

sections.s2_technical:
The cache has a fixed capacity. Internally it keeps a hash map from key to a node object, and a doubly linked list of those nodes. Each node holds the key, the value, and pointers to the previous and next nodes. I keep two sentinel nodes, a head and a tail, so that inserting and removing never need null checks at the ends.

A `get(key)` looks up the node in the map. If absent, it returns a miss. If present, it reads the value, removes the node from its current position in the list, and reinserts it right after the head, marking it most recently used. Both the removal and reinsertion are constant time because a doubly linked list node knows its neighbors.

A `put(key, value)` checks the map. If the key exists, it updates the value and moves the node to the front. If the key is new, it creates a node, inserts it at the front, and stores it in the map. If adding it exceeds capacity, it removes the node just before the tail, which is the least recently used entry, and also deletes that key from the map.

The head side represents most recently used and the tail side represents least recently used. Using sentinel head and tail nodes removes edge cases for an empty list or single element. The whole structure gives O(1) average time for both operations because the map avoids scanning and the linked list avoids shifting.

A senior nuance: you must remove the evicted key from the map as well as from the list, otherwise the map leaks memory and later lookups find stale nodes. Another nuance is that in Java you could reach for `LinkedHashMap` with access order and an overridden `removeEldestEntry`, but implementing the map plus doubly linked list by hand demonstrates the mechanics interviewers want to see.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's account service answers millions of balance lookups. Hitting the database every time is slow, so hot accounts are cached in memory, but memory is finite and only the most active accounts should stay cached.

This is exactly how an LRU cache works. The most recently accessed accounts stay, and the stalest one is evicted when the cache fills.

Problem 2 — Both reading a cached balance and updating it must be fast and must also mark that account as freshly used, so a frequently checked account is never evicted just because a burst of other lookups happened.

This is exactly why we combine a hash map for instant lookup with a doubly linked list for instant reordering, so every access promotes the account to most recently used in constant time.

The code will have an `Account`-flavored key-value usage, a `LruCache` class backed by a hash map and a hand-built doubly linked list with sentinel head and tail, a `Node` class, and a runnable demo that fills the cache, triggers an eviction, and logs hits, misses, and evictions.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a cache of capacity 2, then a sequence of puts and gets.

Step 1: `put("SAV2001", 1000000)` creates a node for Rajesh and places it right after the head. The map now holds one entry and the list order from head to tail is Rajesh then tail.

Step 2: `put("CUR3001", 250000)` creates Priya's node at the front. The order from head to tail is now Priya, Rajesh, tail. Rajesh is the least recently used.

Step 3: `get("SAV2001")` finds Rajesh in the map, reads 1000000, removes his node and reinserts it at the front. The order becomes Rajesh, Priya, tail. Now Priya is least recently used.

Step 4: `put("SAV4002", 75000)` is a new key, so a node is added at the front and the map size becomes three, exceeding capacity. The node before the tail, Priya, is removed from the list and her key is deleted from the map and logged as an eviction.

Step 5: `get("CUR3001")` now misses because Priya was evicted. `get("SAV2001")` and `get("SAV4002")` both hit.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 12:50:00 INFO    get SAV2001 -> 1000000
2026-10-27 12:50:00 INFO    EVICT CUR3001
2026-10-27 12:50:00 INFO    get CUR3001 -> null
2026-10-27 12:50:00 INFO    get SAV2001 -> 1000000
2026-10-27 12:50:00 INFO    get SAV4002 -> 75000
```

    │                              list: [SAV2001][CUR3001]
    ▼
  put SAV4002 (NEW)             addFront → size 3 > cap 2
    │                              evict tail.prev = CUR3001
    │                              remove from list AND map
    ▼
  list: [SAV4002][SAV2001]      map: {SAV4002, SAV2001}
    │
    ├─ get CUR3001 → MISS (null)
    └─ get SAV2001 / SAV4002 → HIT
```

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐
  │          LruCache             │ owns  │      Node        │
  │  - capacity: int              │◆─────▶│  + key: String   │
  │  - map: Map<String,Node>      │       │  + value: long   │
  │  - head: Node (MRU sentinel)  │       │  + prev: Node    │
  │  - tail: Node (LRU sentinel)  │       │  + next: Node    │
  │  ─────────────────────────────│       └──────────────────┘
  │  + get(key): Long             │  O(1)
  │  + put(key, value): void      │  O(1)
  │  - addFront/remove/moveToFront│
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for put:
    Post: size never exceeds capacity; evicted key removed from BOTH list and map
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An LRU cache is a fixed-capacity key-value store that, when it runs out of room, evicts the entry that was accessed least recently. The design that interviewers want is the one that makes both get and put run in constant time, and I achieve that by combining two data structures: a hash map that maps each key to a node for instant lookup, and a doubly linked list that keeps the nodes ordered by how recently they were used.

The linked list has a most-recently-used end and a least-recently-used end, and I always keep two sentinel nodes, a head and a tail, so that inserting and removing at the ends never require special null handling. On a get, I find the node through the map, read its value, and move it to the front to mark it most recently used. On a put, if the key exists I update the value and move it to the front, and if the key is new I create a node at the front and store it in the map; if that pushes the size over capacity, I remove the node just before the tail, which is the least recently used, and I also delete its key from the map.

The detail that separates a correct implementation from a leaky one is that when I evict, I must remove the key from the hash map as well as from the linked list. If I only unlink it from the list, the map keeps a stale reference and the cache slowly leaks memory while reporting a wrong size. I also mention that Java offers LinkedHashMap with access order and a removeEldestEntry hook as a shortcut, but building the map plus doubly linked list by hand shows I actually understand the mechanics.

In my project at National Bank of India, the account service answered millions of balance lookups, and hitting the database every time was too slow, so we cached the hottest accounts in memory with an LRU policy. The hash map plus doubly linked list gave constant-time reads and writes, and promoting an account to most recently used on every access meant a frequently checked account was never evicted just because a burst of unrelated lookups came through, which kept our cache hit rate high and the database load low.

answers.question: LFU Cache — HashMap + frequency map + LinkedHashSet.
answers.shortTitle: LFU Cache — HashMap plus frequency map plus LinkedHashSet buckets

s1_definition.profdef: An LFU (Least Frequently Used) cache is a fixed-capacity key-value store that evicts the entry with the lowest access count when it is full, and breaks ties by evicting the least recently used among the lowest-frequency entries. The O(1) design keeps a key-to-value-and-frequency map, a frequency-to-keys map where each bucket is a LinkedHashSet preserving insertion order for tie-breaking, and a running minimum-frequency counter so eviction knows exactly which bucket to pull from.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India keeps only a few customer files on the desk, and instead of keeping the ones touched most recently, the rule is to keep the ones touched the most times overall. Each file has a tally mark for every time it is used. When the desk is full and a new file arrives, the file with the fewest tally marks is archived, and if several files are tied on the fewest marks, the one that has sat untouched the longest among them goes first.
s1_definition.oneliner: Track each key's frequency, group keys into frequency buckets of insertion order, and keep a minimum-frequency pointer so the least-used, oldest-tied entry is evicted in constant time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An LFU (Least Frequently Used) cache is a fixed-capacity key-value store that evicts the entry with the lowest access count when it is full, and breaks ties by evicting the least recently used among the lowest-frequency entries. The O(1) design keeps a key-to-value-and-frequency map, a frequency-to-keys map where each bucket is a LinkedHashSet preserving insertion order for tie-breaking, and a running minimum-frequency counter so eviction knows exactly which bucket to pull from.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India keeps only a few customer files on the desk, and instead of keeping the ones touched most recently, the rule is to keep the ones touched the most times overall. Each file has a tally mark for every time it is used. When the desk is full and a new file arrives, the file with the fewest tally marks is archived, and if several files are tied on the fewest marks, the one that has sat untouched the longest among them goes first.

**One line to remember:** Track each key's frequency, group keys into frequency buckets of insertion order, and keep a minimum-frequency pointer so the least-used, oldest-tied entry is evicted in constant time.

sections.s2_technical:
The cache stores three structures. The first is a map from key to a small holder of the value and the current frequency. The second is a map from a frequency number to a LinkedHashSet of keys that currently have that frequency; the LinkedHashSet matters because it remembers insertion order, which gives the least-recently-used tie-break for free. The third is a single integer, the minimum frequency currently present.

On a `get(key)`, if the key is missing we return a miss. If present, we read the value and then promote its frequency: we remove the key from its current frequency bucket, increment its frequency, and add it to the next bucket. If the bucket we emptied was the minimum frequency and it is now empty, we increment the minimum frequency, because no key has that old frequency anymore.

On a `put(key, value)`, if the key exists we update the value and promote its frequency exactly like a get. If the key is new and the cache is at capacity, we first evict: we go to the minimum-frequency bucket, remove the first key in that LinkedHashSet (the oldest among the least frequent), and delete it from the value map. Then we insert the new key with frequency one, add it to the frequency-one bucket, and reset the minimum frequency to one because the newest entry always starts at frequency one.

Every operation is O(1) because the maps give direct access and LinkedHashSet add and remove are constant time. A senior nuance: resetting the minimum frequency to one on every new insertion is correct precisely because a fresh key has frequency one, which is the smallest possible. Another nuance is that the LinkedHashSet, not a plain HashSet, is required to get deterministic least-recently-used tie-breaking.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India caches exchange-rate lookups. Some currency pairs are queried constantly all day while others are queried rarely. When the cache is full, the right thing to evict is the pair that has been looked up the fewest times overall, not merely the one touched least recently, because a steadily popular pair should survive a brief burst of rare lookups.

This is exactly how an LFU cache works. The entry with the lowest total access count is evicted first.

Problem 2 — When several rarely used pairs are tied at the same low frequency, we still need a deterministic, fair rule for which one leaves, and it should be the one that has gone cold the longest.

This is exactly why each frequency bucket is a LinkedHashSet, so the oldest key among the tied-lowest frequency is removed first.

The code will have an `Entry` holder class, an `LfuCache` class with the three structures, and a runnable demo that exercises hits that change frequencies and triggers an LFU eviction with logging.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a cache of capacity 2 and a sequence of puts and gets on currency pairs.

Step 1: `put("USD-INR", 8325)` inserts USD-INR with frequency one, places it in bucket one, and sets the minimum frequency to one.

Step 2: `put("EUR-INR", 9010)` inserts EUR-INR with frequency one, placing it in bucket one after USD-INR. The minimum frequency stays one.

Step 3: `get("USD-INR")` reads the value and promotes USD-INR: it is removed from bucket one and added to bucket two. Bucket one still holds EUR-INR, so the minimum frequency stays one. A second `get("USD-INR")` promotes it again to bucket three.

Step 4: `put("GBP-INR", 10550)` is a new key and the cache is at capacity. The minimum-frequency bucket is bucket one, holding only EUR-INR, so EUR-INR is evicted and logged. GBP-INR is inserted into bucket one, and the minimum frequency resets to one.

Step 5: `get("EUR-INR")` misses because it was evicted. `get("USD-INR")` and `get("GBP-INR")` both hit.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 12:55:00 INFO    get USD-INR -> 8325
2026-10-27 12:55:00 INFO    get USD-INR -> 8325
2026-10-27 12:55:00 INFO    EVICT EUR-INR (freq 1)
2026-10-27 12:55:00 INFO    get EUR-INR -> null
2026-10-27 12:55:00 INFO    get USD-INR -> 8325
2026-10-27 12:55:00 INFO    get GBP-INR -> 10550
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
An LFU cache is a fixed-capacity key-value store that evicts the entry with the lowest access count when it needs room, and when several entries tie at the lowest count it evicts the one that has been untouched the longest among them. The difference from an LRU cache is that LRU cares only about recency while LFU cares about total usage, so a steadily popular entry survives a short burst of rare lookups.

I implement it with three structures that together give constant-time operations. The first is a map from each key to a holder of its value and its current frequency. The second is a map from a frequency number to a LinkedHashSet of the keys at that frequency, and I use a LinkedHashSet specifically because it preserves insertion order, which gives me a clean least-recently-used tie-break among entries of equal frequency. The third is a single integer that tracks the current minimum frequency so eviction knows exactly which bucket to pull from.

On every access I promote the key by removing it from its current frequency bucket, incrementing its frequency, and adding it to the next bucket, and if I just emptied the minimum-frequency bucket I bump the minimum. On a new insertion when the cache is full, I evict the first key in the minimum-frequency bucket, which is the oldest among the least frequent, then insert the new key at frequency one and reset the minimum frequency to one, which is correct because a brand new key always starts at the smallest possible frequency.

In my project at National Bank of India, we cached foreign-exchange rate lookups where some currency pairs were queried constantly while others were queried rarely, and when the cache filled we wanted to drop the least-queried pair rather than merely the least-recently-touched one. The LFU design kept the consistently popular pairs resident even during bursts of rare queries, and the LinkedHashSet buckets gave us a fair, deterministic rule for breaking ties among the cold pairs.

answers.question: Min Stack — O(1) push/pop/top/getMin.
answers.shortTitle: Min Stack — O(1) push, pop, top, and getMin

s1_definition.profdef: A Min Stack is a stack that supports the usual push, pop, and top operations plus a getMin operation that returns the current minimum element, all in constant time. The standard design keeps an auxiliary stack in parallel with the main stack so that the top of the auxiliary stack is always the minimum of the elements currently in the main stack.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India stacks deposit slips one on top of another, and the manager must instantly answer "what is the smallest deposit still in this pile right now." Alongside the real pile, a clerk keeps a shadow pile where each slip records the smallest amount seen up to that point. When a slip is removed from the real pile, the matching shadow slip is removed too, so the top of the shadow pile is always the current smallest.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a second stack whose top always holds the minimum so far, pushing and popping it in lockstep with the main stack to get the minimum in constant time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Min Stack is a stack that supports the usual push, pop, and top operations plus a getMin operation that returns the current minimum element, all in constant time. The standard design keeps an auxiliary stack in parallel with the main stack so that the top of the auxiliary stack is always the minimum of the elements currently in the main stack.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India stacks deposit slips one on top of another, and the manager must instantly answer "what is the smallest deposit still in this pile right now." Alongside the real pile, a clerk keeps a shadow pile where each slip records the smallest amount seen up to that point. When a slip is removed from the real pile, the matching shadow slip is removed too, so the top of the shadow pile is always the current smallest.

**One line to remember:** Keep a second stack whose top always holds the minimum so far, pushing and popping it in lockstep with the main stack to get the minimum in constant time.

sections.s2_technical:
A plain stack can push, pop, and read the top in constant time, but finding the minimum would normally require scanning every element, which is linear. The Min Stack trick removes that scan.

We keep two stacks. The main stack holds the actual values. The auxiliary minimum stack holds, at each position, the minimum of all elements from the bottom up to that point. When we push a value, we push it on the main stack, and we push onto the minimum stack the smaller of the new value and the current top of the minimum stack. If the minimum stack is empty, the new value becomes the first minimum.

When we pop, we pop both stacks together so they stay aligned. The top operation reads the main stack's top. The getMin operation reads the minimum stack's top, which by construction is always the smallest value currently present.

Because each operation is a handful of constant-time stack operations, every operation including getMin is O(1). The cost is O(n) extra space for the second stack. A space optimization is to push onto the minimum stack only when a value is less than or equal to the current minimum, and pop from it only when the popped value equals the current minimum, but the two-stack-in-lockstep version is simpler to reason about and still constant time.

A senior nuance: using "less than or equal" rather than "less than" in the optimized version matters for duplicates of the minimum; using strict "less than" would pop the minimum marker too early and report a wrong minimum. Another nuance is always pushing a mirror entry in the simple version so the two stacks never drift out of alignment.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's trading desk pushes and pops pending order amounts on a stack as orders are staged and cancelled. The risk monitor must, at any instant, know the smallest pending order amount still on the stack to check a floor rule, and it must get that answer instantly even as orders churn.

This is exactly how a Min Stack works. The minimum of the current stack is available in constant time.

Problem 2 — When the smallest order is cancelled (popped), the reported minimum must immediately reflect the next smallest still on the stack, with no rescan.

This is exactly why the auxiliary minimum stack is popped in lockstep, so its new top is instantly the correct new minimum.

The code will have a `MinStack` class backed by two `java.util.Deque` stacks, and a runnable demo that pushes several order amounts, reads the minimum, pops, and reads the minimum again with logging.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a sequence of pushes and pops of order amounts.

Step 1: `push(50000)` puts 50000 on the main stack and 50000 on the minimum stack because the minimum stack was empty. The current minimum is 50000.

Step 2: `push(30000)` puts 30000 on the main stack. The smaller of 30000 and the current minimum 50000 is 30000, so 30000 is pushed on the minimum stack. The current minimum is 30000.

Step 3: `push(80000)` puts 80000 on the main stack. The smaller of 80000 and the current minimum 30000 is 30000, so 30000 is pushed again on the minimum stack. The current minimum stays 30000, and the top is 80000.

Step 4: `push(20000)` makes the minimum 20000. A `pop` then removes 20000 from both stacks, so the minimum stack's new top is 30000 again.

Step 5: Two more pops remove 80000 and 30000. After those pops the only remaining value is 50000, so the minimum stack's top, and therefore getMin, is 50000.

2026-10-27 13:00:00 INFO    after push 20000 min=20000
2026-10-27 13:00:00 INFO    after pop min=30000

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Min Stack is a stack that supports push, pop, and top in the usual way but adds a getMin operation that returns the smallest element currently in the stack, and the requirement is that all four operations run in constant time. A plain stack would have to scan every element to find the minimum, which is linear, so the trick is to maintain a second stack that tracks the minimum as the stack grows and shrinks.

The design keeps a main stack of the actual values and an auxiliary minimum stack. Each time I push a value, I also push onto the minimum stack the smaller of the new value and the current top of the minimum stack, so the top of the minimum stack is always the minimum of everything currently stored. When I pop, I pop both stacks together so they stay perfectly aligned, which means the moment the current minimum is removed, the new top of the minimum stack is instantly the next smallest value. The top operation reads the main stack and getMin reads the minimum stack.

Every operation is a constant number of simple stack operations, so getMin is constant time just like the rest, at the cost of linear extra space for the second stack. There is a space-optimized variant that only pushes onto the minimum stack when a value is less than or equal to the current minimum and only pops it when the popped value equals the current minimum, and the subtle point there is to use less than or equal rather than strict less than so that duplicate minimum values are tracked correctly.

In my project at National Bank of India, the trading desk staged and cancelled pending order amounts on a stack, and the risk monitor had to know the smallest pending amount at every instant to enforce a floor rule. The Min Stack gave that answer in constant time even as orders churned rapidly, and because the minimum stack was popped in lockstep with the main stack, cancelling the smallest order immediately surfaced the next smallest without any rescan.

answers.question: RandomizedSet — array + HashMap for O(1) insert/remove/getRandom.
answers.shortTitle: RandomizedSet — array plus HashMap for O(1) insert, remove, getRandom

s1_definition.profdef: A RandomizedSet is a data structure that supports inserting an element, removing an element, and returning a uniformly random element, all in average constant time. It combines a dynamic array that stores the actual elements for O(1) random indexing with a hash map from each element to its index in the array, and the removal trick swaps the element to delete with the last array element so that removal never has to shift the array.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India runs a lucky-draw where every eligible account number must have an exactly equal chance of being picked, and accounts are added and removed from eligibility all day. A clerk keeps the account numbers in a numbered list for fair random picking, and a quick index telling where each number sits. To remove an account fast, the clerk moves the last account number into the removed slot and trims the list, so no gap is left and nothing has to be reshuffled.
s1_definition.oneliner: Store elements in an array for fair random indexing and keep a map from element to index, deleting by swapping with the last element so every operation stays constant time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A RandomizedSet is a data structure that supports inserting an element, removing an element, and returning a uniformly random element, all in average constant time. It combines a dynamic array that stores the actual elements for O(1) random indexing with a hash map from each element to its index in the array, and the removal trick swaps the element to delete with the last array element so that removal never has to shift the array.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India runs a lucky-draw where every eligible account number must have an exactly equal chance of being picked, and accounts are added and removed from eligibility all day. A clerk keeps the account numbers in a numbered list for fair random picking, and a quick index telling where each number sits. To remove an account fast, the clerk moves the last account number into the removed slot and trims the list, so no gap is left and nothing has to be reshuffled.

**One line to remember:** Store elements in an array for fair random indexing and keep a map from element to index, deleting by swapping with the last element so every operation stays constant time.

sections.s2_technical:
The challenge is that a plain array gives O(1) random access and O(1) append, but removing an arbitrary element from the middle normally costs linear time because everything after it must shift left. A plain hash set gives O(1) insert and remove but cannot pick a uniformly random element in constant time because its internal layout is not indexable.

The RandomizedSet uses both. The array holds the elements in arbitrary order. The hash map maps each element to its current index in the array. To insert, we check the map; if the element is absent we append it to the array and record its index in the map. To get a random element, we generate a random index into the array and return that element, which is uniformly random because every slot is equally likely.

The clever part is remove. To remove an element, we find its index from the map. We take the last element of the array and move it into the index being vacated, update that moved element's index in the map, then shrink the array by removing the last slot, and finally delete the removed element from the map. Because we never shift the middle, removal is constant time, and the random picking stays fair because the array stays densely packed.

A senior nuance: when the element being removed is already the last element, the swap is a no-op but the code must still handle it without corrupting the map. Another nuance is that returning a random element requires a densely packed array with no holes, which is exactly what the swap-with-last technique preserves.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a fair prize draw among currently eligible savings accounts. Accounts become eligible and lose eligibility continuously as balances cross a threshold, and the draw must pick a genuinely uniform random eligible account at any moment.

This is exactly how RandomizedSet works. Any currently present element is equally likely to be returned.

Problem 2 — Eligibility changes must be instant even with millions of accounts, so neither adding nor removing an account can afford to shift a large array or scan a list.

This is exactly why we pair an array with a map and use the swap-with-last removal, keeping insert, remove, and random pick at average constant time.

The code will have a `RandomizedSet` class backed by an `ArrayList` and a `HashMap`, a `Random` for fair picking, and a runnable demo that adds and removes account numbers and draws a random one with logging.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a sequence of inserts, a random draw, a remove, and another draw.

Step 1: `insert("SAV2001")` finds the map empty of that key, appends SAV2001 at array index 0, and records index 0 in the map, returning true.

Step 2: `insert("CUR3001")` appends at index 1 and records it, returning true. A second `insert("SAV2001")` finds the key already present and returns false without changing anything.

Step 3: `insert("SAV4002")` appends at index 2. The array now holds SAV2001, CUR3001, SAV4002 at indices 0, 1, 2.

Step 4: `getRandom()` picks a random index among 0, 1, 2 and returns that account; each has a one-in-three chance.

Step 5: `remove("CUR3001")` reads its index 1, moves the last element SAV4002 into index 1, updates SAV4002's recorded index to 1, trims the array to length 2, and deletes CUR3001 from the map. The array is now SAV2001, SAV4002, densely packed with no hole, so the next `getRandom()` is fair over two elements.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    insert SAV2001 -> true
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    insert CUR3001 -> true
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    insert SAV2001 -> false
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    insert SAV4002 -> true
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    random eligible account -> CUR3001
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    remove CUR3001 -> true
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    remove CUR3001 -> false
2026-10-27 13:05:00 INFO    random eligible account -> SAV4002
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  insert SAV2001/CUR3001/SAV4002
    │ array: [SAV2001, CUR3001, SAV4002]
    │ map: {SAV2001:0, CUR3001:1, SAV4002:2}
    ▼
  getRandom → random index in [0,2] → fair pick
    │
    ▼
  remove CUR3001 (idx 1)
    │ move last SAV4002 → slot 1, update map SAV4002:1
    │ trim array, drop CUR3001 from map
    ▼
  array: [SAV2001, SAV4002]  (dense, no hole)
    │ map: {SAV2001:0, SAV4002:1}
    ▼
  getRandom → fair over 2 elements
```

```

  ┌─ Design Patterns / Principles ───────────────────────────┐
  │  Array for O(1) random index + HashMap element→index     │
  │  Swap-with-last removal avoids array shifting            │
  │  S (SOLID): structure only manages a randomizable set    │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           RandomizedSet               │

  │  - random: Random                     │

  │  + insert(value): boolean             │  O(1) avg
  │  + remove(value): boolean             │  O(1) avg (swap last)
  │  + getRandom(): String                │  O(1)
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘

sections.s6_takeaway:
A RandomizedSet is a structure that supports inserting an element, removing an element, and returning a uniformly random element, all in average constant time. The difficulty is that no single built-in collection gives all three cheaply: an array gives fast random indexing and fast append but slow middle removal, while a hash set gives fast insert and remove but cannot pick a uniformly random element in constant time because it is not indexable.

My solution combines the two. I keep a dynamic array holding the elements in arbitrary order, which lets me pick a uniformly random element by generating a random index, and I keep a hash map from each element to its current index in that array. Insertion appends to the array and records the index in the map. The clever part is removal: I look up the element's index, move the last element of the array into that slot, update the moved element's index in the map, shrink the array by one, and delete the removed element from the map. Because I swap with the last element instead of shifting, removal is constant time and the array stays densely packed.

Keeping the array dense is exactly what makes the random pick fair, because every slot is occupied and equally likely. The edge case I always handle is removing the element that is already last, where the swap is effectively a no-op but the map and array must still be updated consistently so nothing is corrupted.

In my project at National Bank of India, we ran a fair prize draw among currently eligible savings accounts, where eligibility changed continuously as balances crossed a threshold. The RandomizedSet let us add and remove accounts from the eligible pool instantly even with millions of accounts, and because the backing array never developed holes, every draw gave each eligible account an exactly equal chance, which was essential for the fairness guarantees the draw had to meet.

answers.question: Time-Based Key-Value Store — map of key→sorted(timestamp, value), binary search.
answers.shortTitle: Time-Based Key-Value Store — map of key to sorted (timestamp, value) with binary search

s1_definition.profdef: A Time-Based Key-Value Store lets you set a value for a key at a given timestamp and later get the value that was current at or before a query timestamp. It is implemented as a hash map from each key to a list of timestamp-value pairs kept in increasing timestamp order, and a get performs a binary search over that list to find the largest timestamp not exceeding the query time.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India records the published interest rate for each product every time it changes, each change stamped with the date and time. Later, an auditor asks "what was the interest rate for savings as of last Tuesday noon." The clerk flips to the savings product's history, which is sorted by time, and quickly jumps to the latest entry that is on or before last Tuesday noon rather than reading the whole history.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep each key's history sorted by time and binary-search for the latest entry at or before the query timestamp to answer point-in-time lookups fast.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Time-Based Key-Value Store lets you set a value for a key at a given timestamp and later get the value that was current at or before a query timestamp. It is implemented as a hash map from each key to a list of timestamp-value pairs kept in increasing timestamp order, and a get performs a binary search over that list to find the largest timestamp not exceeding the query time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India records the published interest rate for each product every time it changes, each change stamped with the date and time. Later, an auditor asks "what was the interest rate for savings as of last Tuesday noon." The clerk flips to the savings product's history, which is sorted by time, and quickly jumps to the latest entry that is on or before last Tuesday noon rather than reading the whole history.

**One line to remember:** Keep each key's history sorted by time and binary-search for the latest entry at or before the query timestamp to answer point-in-time lookups fast.

sections.s2_technical:
The store maps each key to an ordered list of entries, where each entry holds a timestamp and the value set at that timestamp. The `set(key, value, timestamp)` operation appends a new entry to that key's list. In the common interview framing, timestamps for a key arrive in strictly increasing order, so appending keeps the list sorted automatically; if they can arrive out of order, you would insert into the correct position or sort, but the classic version assumes increasing timestamps.

The `get(key, timestamp)` operation must return the value whose timestamp is the largest one that is still less than or equal to the query timestamp. Because the list is sorted by timestamp, we binary-search for that boundary. We keep a low and high pointer and look for the rightmost entry whose timestamp does not exceed the query. If every stored timestamp is greater than the query, there is no valid value and we return an empty result.

The binary search runs in O(log n) for a key with n entries, and set runs in O(1) amortized when appending. The space is proportional to the total number of set calls. A senior nuance is the exact binary-search condition: we are performing a "floor" search, so when the midpoint timestamp is less than or equal to the query we record it as a candidate and move right to seek an even later valid one, and when it exceeds the query we move left. Getting this boundary logic right is the crux; an off-by-one here returns the wrong historical value.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must answer "what interest rate applied to this product at this exact moment" for dispute resolution and audits. Rates change over time, and the bank keeps the full history, so a lookup is really a point-in-time query against a time-ordered history.

This is exactly how a Time-Based Key-Value Store works. We fetch the value that was in force at or before the asked timestamp.

Problem 2 — Histories can be long, so scanning every historical rate for every query would be too slow when auditors run thousands of point-in-time checks.

This is exactly why each key's history is sorted by timestamp and we binary-search it, turning a long scan into a logarithmic jump.

The code will have an `Entry` holder, a `TimeMap` class with `set` and `get` using binary search, and a runnable demo that records several rate changes for a product and queries the rate at various past timestamps with logging.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three rate changes for SAVINGS_RATE at timestamps 10, 20, and 35, then four point-in-time queries.

Step 1: The three `set` calls append entries to the SAVINGS_RATE list in increasing timestamp order, giving a sorted history of (10, "350"), (20, "400"), (35, "425").

Step 2: `get("SAVINGS_RATE", 5)` binary-searches for the largest timestamp at most 5. The first entry has timestamp 10, which exceeds 5, so no candidate is ever recorded and the result is the empty string, meaning no rate was in force yet.

Step 3: `get("SAVINGS_RATE", 10)` finds the entry at timestamp 10 exactly, records "350" as a candidate, then searches right but finds nothing smaller or equal beyond it, so it returns "350".

Step 4: `get("SAVINGS_RATE", 25)` finds timestamp 20 is at most 25, records "400", then checks timestamp 35 which exceeds 25, so it returns "400". `get("SAVINGS_RATE", 99)` records progressively later candidates up to timestamp 35 and returns "425".

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 13:10:00 INFO    rate at t=5  -> 
2026-10-27 13:10:00 INFO    rate at t=10 -> 350
2026-10-27 13:10:00 INFO    rate at t=25 -> 400
2026-10-27 13:10:00 INFO    rate at t=99 -> 425
```

```

    │ store: { SAVINGS_RATE : [(10,350),(20,400),(35,425)] }  (sorted by time)
    ▼
  get(SAVINGS_RATE, 25)
    │ binary search floor(25)
    │ mid=1 (20<=25) → candidate 400, low=2
    │ mid=2 (35>25)  → high=1 → stop
    ▼
  return "400"

  get(.,5) → first ts 10 > 5 → "" (no rate yet)
  get(.,99) → floor = 35 → "425"
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Time-Based Key-Value Store lets me set a value for a key at a specific timestamp and later ask for the value that was in force at or before a query timestamp. It is a point-in-time lookup over a history, and I implement it as a hash map from each key to a list of timestamp-value pairs kept in increasing timestamp order, with the get operation using binary search over that list.

The set operation appends a new timestamp-value pair to the key's list. In the standard framing the timestamps for a key arrive in increasing order, so appending keeps the list sorted for free; if they could arrive out of order I would insert at the correct position instead. The get operation is where the real work is: I need the value whose timestamp is the largest one still less than or equal to the query, which is a floor search. I binary-search with a low and a high pointer, and whenever the midpoint timestamp is at most the query I record that value as a candidate and move right to look for an even later valid entry, and whenever it exceeds the query I move left. If every stored timestamp is greater than the query, I return an empty result because no value existed yet.

The subtle part is the floor boundary logic, because an off-by-one there returns the wrong historical value, which in a bank audit is unacceptable. Set is amortized constant time and get is logarithmic in the number of entries for that key.

In my project at National Bank of India, we had to answer what interest rate applied to a product at an exact moment for dispute resolution, and rates changed over time with the full history retained. Modeling each product's rate history as a time-sorted list and binary-searching it turned what would have been a long scan per query into a fast logarithmic jump, which kept auditor tooling responsive even when thousands of point-in-time checks ran against long histories.
