answers.question: Implement Queue using Stacks / Stack using Queues.
answers.shortTitle: Implement Queue using Stacks / Stack using Queues

s1_definition.profdef: Implementing a queue using two stacks means simulating first-in-first-out behavior with two last-in-first-out stacks, by pushing onto an input stack and transferring to an output stack only when needed, giving amortized O(1) per operation. Implementing a stack using queues means simulating last-in-first-out behavior with queues, typically by rotating a single queue on every push so the newest element sits at the front.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India token counter. A queue is first-come-first-served, but all the clerk has are two spring-loaded trays that only give back the top item (stacks). To serve the oldest customer first, when the serving tray is empty the clerk flips the whole intake tray into the serving tray, reversing the order so the oldest is now on top. The reverse problem uses waiting lines to fake a last-in-first-out pile.
s1_definition.oneliner: Two stacks make a queue by reversing order on transfer, and a queue makes a stack by rotating the newest element to the front on every push.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Implementing a queue using two stacks means simulating first-in-first-out behavior with two last-in-first-out stacks, by pushing onto an input stack and transferring to an output stack only when needed, giving amortized O(1) per operation. Implementing a stack using queues means simulating last-in-first-out behavior with queues, typically by rotating a single queue on every push so the newest element sits at the front.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India token counter. A queue is first-come-first-served, but all the clerk has are two spring-loaded trays that only give back the top item (stacks). To serve the oldest customer first, when the serving tray is empty the clerk flips the whole intake tray into the serving tray, reversing the order so the oldest is now on top. The reverse problem uses waiting lines to fake a last-in-first-out pile.

**One line to remember:** Two stacks make a queue by reversing order on transfer, and a queue makes a stack by rotating the newest element to the front on every push.

sections.s2_technical:
For a queue from two stacks, I keep an input stack and an output stack. On enqueue, I push onto the input stack, which is constant time. On dequeue or peek, if the output stack is empty I pour the entire input stack into the output stack one element at a time, which reverses the order so the oldest element ends up on top of the output stack, then I pop or peek the output stack. I only transfer when the output stack is empty, so each element is moved at most once from input to output across its lifetime, giving amortized constant time even though a single dequeue that triggers a transfer is linear.

For a stack from a single queue, on push I add the new element to the queue and then rotate the queue by removing and re-adding every earlier element behind it, so the newest element ends up at the front. That makes push linear but pop and peek constant, because the front of the queue is always the most recently pushed element, which is exactly last-in-first-out order.

A senior nuance for the two-stack queue is that you must not transfer eagerly on every dequeue; transferring only when the output stack is empty is what preserves amortized constant time. A nuance for the stack-from-queue is choosing whether to make push costly or pop costly; the single-queue rotation makes push the expensive operation, which is a deliberate trade-off.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes customer service requests strictly in the order received, first come first served, but the only primitive available in a constrained embedded teller device is a stack. We must build fair first-in-first-out ordering out of stacks.

This is exactly how a queue from two stacks works. The transfer step reverses the stack order to recover arrival order.

Problem 2 — Each request must be served quickly on average even though occasionally a single serve triggers a bulk transfer.

This is exactly why we transfer only when the output stack is empty, so each request is moved at most once and the average cost stays constant.

The code will have a `StackQueue` class implementing a FIFO request queue from two `Deque` stacks, with `enqueue`, `dequeue`, and `peek`, and a runnable demo that enqueues request tickets and serves them in arrival order with logging.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three enqueues, a peek, two dequeues, one more enqueue, then two dequeues.

Step 1: The three enqueues push REQ-SAV2001, REQ-CUR3001, REQ-SAV4002 onto the input stack. The input stack top is the newest, REQ-SAV4002, and the output stack is empty.

Step 2: `peek()` sees the output stack empty, so it transfers: it pops the input stack repeatedly and pushes onto the output stack, reversing the order. The output stack top becomes REQ-SAV2001, the oldest arrival, which peek returns.

Step 3: The first `dequeue()` pops REQ-SAV2001 from the output stack. The second `dequeue()` pops REQ-CUR3001. The output stack now holds only REQ-SAV4002, and the input stack is empty.

Step 4: `enqueue("REQ-CUR5003")` pushes onto the input stack, which is fine because it does not disturb the output stack ordering.

Step 5: The next `dequeue()` finds the output stack non-empty and returns REQ-SAV4002 without transferring. The final `dequeue()` finds the output stack empty, transfers REQ-CUR5003 over, and returns it, preserving overall arrival order.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 13:15:00 INFO    peek (oldest) -> REQ-SAV2001
2026-10-27 13:15:00 INFO    serve -> REQ-SAV2001
2026-10-27 13:15:00 INFO    serve -> REQ-CUR3001
2026-10-27 13:15:00 INFO    serve -> REQ-SAV4002
2026-10-27 13:15:00 INFO    serve -> REQ-CUR5003
```

```
    │ pour input into output, reversing
    │ output (top→bottom): [SAV2001, CUR3001, SAV4002]
    ▼
  dequeue SAV2001, dequeue CUR3001       output: [SAV4002]
    │
  enqueue CUR5003                        input: [CUR5003]
    ▼
  dequeue SAV4002 (no transfer)          output: []
  dequeue → transfer CUR5003 → serve     FIFO preserved
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Implementing a queue using two stacks is about recreating first-in-first-out behavior using only last-in-first-out primitives, and the elegant solution keeps an input stack and an output stack. Every enqueue just pushes onto the input stack, which is constant time. Every dequeue or peek first checks the output stack, and only if it is empty does it pour the entire input stack into the output stack one element at a time, which reverses the order so the oldest element rises to the top, and then it pops or peeks the output stack.

The reason this is efficient is the lazy transfer rule. Because I transfer only when the output stack is empty, each element moves from the input stack to the output stack at most once in its lifetime, so even though one particular dequeue that triggers a transfer is linear, the cost spread across all operations is amortized constant time. If I naively transferred back and forth on every operation, I would destroy that guarantee.

The mirror problem, implementing a stack using queues, flips the trade-off. With a single queue I make push the expensive operation by adding the new element and then rotating every earlier element behind it, so the newest element sits at the front and pop and peek become constant time. The deliberate choice there is which operation to make costly, and the single-queue rotation pushes that cost onto push.

In my project at National Bank of India, a constrained teller intake component exposed only stack primitives, yet customer service requests had to be served strictly in arrival order. Building a first-in-first-out queue from two stacks with the lazy transfer rule gave us fair ordering with amortized constant-time serving, so a single occasional bulk transfer never hurt the overall throughput of the request-handling path.

answers.question: Cache with TTL and Versioned Expiry — implement `put(key, value, ttl, now)` and `get(key, now)` where an entry is valid only while `now < expires_at`; a newer write replaces the old value AND expiry, so an old cleanup event must NOT delete a newer version of the same key (attach a version/sequence to each expiry record and verify it still matches before deleting) — lazy expiry gives O(1) per op; a heap for proactive cleanup adds O(log n) and stale-record management.
answers.shortTitle: Cache with TTL and Versioned Expiry

s1_definition.profdef: A TTL cache stores each key with an expiry timestamp computed as the write time plus a time-to-live, and a read is valid only while the current time is strictly before that expiry. Because a newer write replaces both the value and the expiry, any proactive cleanup must carry a version or sequence number so a stale expiry event does not delete a newer version of the same key; lazy expiry checks validity on read in O(1), while an optional min-heap keyed on expiry enables proactive cleanup in O(log n) with stale-record skipping.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India caches a one-time password with a two-minute validity. Each OTP has a stamped expiry. If Rajesh requests a new OTP before the old one expires, the new one replaces the old value and its expiry. The danger is a cleanup robot holding an old reminder note that says "delete Rajesh's OTP at 10:02"; by then Rajesh has a fresh OTP valid until 10:05, so the robot must check the version number on its note against the current entry and, seeing a mismatch, leave the fresh OTP alone.
s1_definition.oneliner: Validate on read against the expiry, and stamp every expiry record with a version so a late cleanup never deletes a newer rewrite of the same key.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A TTL cache stores each key with an expiry timestamp computed as the write time plus a time-to-live, and a read is valid only while the current time is strictly before that expiry. Because a newer write replaces both the value and the expiry, any proactive cleanup must carry a version or sequence number so a stale expiry event does not delete a newer version of the same key; lazy expiry checks validity on read in O(1), while an optional min-heap keyed on expiry enables proactive cleanup in O(log n) with stale-record skipping.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India caches a one-time password with a two-minute validity. Each OTP has a stamped expiry. If Rajesh requests a new OTP before the old one expires, the new one replaces the old value and its expiry. The danger is a cleanup robot holding an old reminder note that says "delete Rajesh's OTP at 10:02"; by then Rajesh has a fresh OTP valid until 10:05, so the robot must check the version number on its note against the current entry and, seeing a mismatch, leave the fresh OTP alone.

**One line to remember:** Validate on read against the expiry, and stamp every expiry record with a version so a late cleanup never deletes a newer rewrite of the same key.

sections.s2_technical:
Each entry stores the value, an absolute expiry timestamp, and a version number that increments on every write to that key. The `put(key, value, ttl, now)` operation sets the value, sets expiry to now plus ttl, and bumps the version. The `get(key, now)` operation returns the value only if the entry exists and now is strictly less than expires_at; otherwise it reports a miss, and with lazy expiry it may also delete the stale entry on the spot. Lazy expiry alone makes every operation constant time because it just compares timestamps.

The versioning is the heart of correctness. If we also push expiry records into a min-heap ordered by expiry time for proactive cleanup, each heap record carries the key and the version it was created with. When the cleanup thread pops a record whose expiry time has passed, it must look up the current entry and compare versions: only if the entry still exists and its version equals the record's version does it delete the entry. If the versions differ, the key was rewritten after this record was created, so the record is stale and is discarded without touching the live entry.

The heap gives proactive cleanup so expired entries do not linger in memory, at a cost of O(log n) per push and pop, plus the management of stale records that are simply skipped. A senior nuance: using strictly-less-than for validity means an entry is dead exactly at its expiry instant, which must be consistent between get and cleanup. Another nuance is that without the version check, a delayed cleanup event would silently evict a freshly written value, causing a correctness bug that is very hard to reproduce.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India caches short-lived security tokens such as transfer authorization codes, each valid for a fixed number of seconds. A read must honor the expiry exactly so an expired code is never accepted.

This is exactly how TTL validation works. We compare the current time against the stored expiry and reject once it passes.

Problem 2 — A customer often refreshes a code before the old one expires, which rewrites the value and extends the expiry. A background cleanup scheduled for the old expiry must not wipe the refreshed code.

This is exactly why each expiry record carries a version, and cleanup deletes only when the version still matches the live entry, protecting newer rewrites.

The code will have an `Entry` holder with value, expiry, and version, a `TtlCache` with lazy `get`, versioned `put`, and a `proactiveCleanup` driven by a min-heap, and a runnable demo showing a refresh beating a stale cleanup with logging.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a write at t=100 with ttl 60, a refresh at t=150, a stale cleanup at t=165, and reads.

Step 1: `put` at t=100 sets AUTH-SAV2001 to CODE-7788 with expiry 160 and version 1, and pushes an expiry record for (160, version 1) onto the heap.

Step 2: `get` at t=120 finds the entry and sees 120 is less than 160, so it returns CODE-7788.

Step 3: `put` at t=150 refreshes the key: version becomes 2, value becomes CODE-9900, expiry becomes 210, and a new expiry record for (210, version 2) is pushed. The old (160, version 1) record is still sitting in the heap.

Step 4: `proactiveCleanup(165)` pops the (160, version 1) record because 160 is at most 165. It looks up the live entry, whose version is now 2, which does not match version 1, so it skips the record and leaves the fresh entry intact. The (210, version 2) record stays in the heap because 210 is greater than 165.

Step 5: `get` at t=170 returns CODE-9900 because 170 is less than 210. `get` at t=215 sees 215 is not less than 210, lazily deletes the entry, and returns a miss.

```
2026-10-27 13:20:00 INFO    cleanup SKIP stale record AUTH-SAV2001 v=1 (live v=2)
2026-10-27 13:20:00 INFO    get @t=170 -> CODE-9900

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A cache with time-to-live stores each key alongside an absolute expiry timestamp, computed as the write time plus the time-to-live, and a read is valid only while the current time is strictly before that expiry. Lazy expiry alone gives constant-time operations because a get simply compares the current time against the stored expiry and treats the entry as a miss, optionally deleting it, once the expiry has passed.

The subtle correctness problem appears when I add proactive cleanup so expired entries do not linger in memory. A newer write replaces both the value and the expiry of a key, but a cleanup event that was scheduled for the old expiry may still be pending. If that stale event fires and blindly deletes the key, it wipes out a freshly written value, which is a nasty, hard-to-reproduce bug. I solve it by attaching a version or sequence number to every write and to every expiry record. When the cleanup thread pops a record whose time has passed, it compares the record's version against the live entry's version and deletes only when they match; if they differ, the key was rewritten after the record was created, so the record is stale and is discarded without touching the live entry.

For the proactive side I use a min-heap ordered by expiry time, which costs logarithmic time per push and pop and requires simply skipping stale records, while the lazy read path stays constant time. I keep the validity comparison strictly less than consistently in both the read path and the cleanup path so an entry dies at exactly the same instant everywhere.

In my project at National Bank of India, we cached short-lived transfer authorization codes, and customers frequently refreshed a code before the old one expired, which rewrote the value and extended the expiry. The versioned expiry records ensured that a background cleanup scheduled for the old code never deleted the refreshed one, so a customer who legitimately renewed their code was never left stranded by a late cleanup event wiping their valid token.

answers.question: Given a sorted array of numbers and a target sum, find a pair of elements whose values add up exactly to the target and return their indices. Solve it with the two-pointer technique. (LeetCode: Two Sum II — Input Array Is Sorted)
answers.shortTitle: Pair with Target Sum (Two Pointers on a Sorted Array)

s1_definition.profdef: The pair-with-target-sum problem asks you to locate two elements in a sorted array whose sum equals a given target. The optimal approach is the two-pointer technique: place one pointer at the start and one at the end, and move them toward each other based on whether the current sum is too small or too large. This runs in linear time and constant extra space because the array's sorted order lets each comparison eliminate one candidate permanently.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh has a list of pending settlement amounts already sorted from smallest to largest, and he needs to find exactly two settlements that together clear a target obligation of a fixed rupee amount. Instead of checking every possible pair, Priya stands at the smallest amount and Rajesh stands at the largest. If their two amounts add up to more than the target, Rajesh steps down to a smaller amount. If they add up to less, Priya steps up. They walk toward each other until the two amounts hit the target exactly.
s1_definition.oneliner: In a sorted array, start wide, then squeeze inward: too big means shrink the right, too small means grow the left.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The pair-with-target-sum problem asks you to locate two elements in a sorted array whose sum equals a given target. The optimal approach is the two-pointer technique: place one pointer at the start and one at the end, and move them toward each other based on whether the current sum is too small or too large. This runs in linear time and constant extra space because the array's sorted order lets each comparison eliminate one candidate permanently.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh has a list of pending settlement amounts already sorted from smallest to largest, and he needs to find exactly two settlements that together clear a target obligation of a fixed rupee amount. Instead of checking every possible pair, Priya stands at the smallest amount and Rajesh stands at the largest. If their two amounts add up to more than the target, Rajesh steps down to a smaller amount. If they add up to less, Priya steps up. They walk toward each other until the two amounts hit the target exactly.

**One line to remember:** In a sorted array, start wide, then squeeze inward: too big means shrink the right, too small means grow the left.

sections.s2_technical:
The brute-force approach checks every pair, which is quadratic time. On a sorted array we can do much better. We keep a `left` index at position 0 and a `right` index at the last position. We compute `sum = arr[left] + arr[right]`. If the sum equals the target, we have found the pair. If the sum is greater than the target, the only way to reduce it is to decrease the larger value, so we move `right` one step left. If the sum is smaller than the target, the only way to increase it is to raise the smaller value, so we move `left` one step right.

This works because the array is sorted. When `arr[left] + arr[right]` is too large, `arr[left]` paired with anything to the right of the current `right` would be even larger, so `right` can never again be part of the answer with this `left`; we safely discard it. The same logic applies symmetrically. Each step eliminates exactly one element, so we touch each element at most once, giving linear time.

A small usage example in the finance domain: suppose settlement amounts are `[150, 300, 450, 700, 950]` and the target is `750`. We start with `left=0` (150) and `right=4` (950). The sum 1100 is too big, so `right` drops to 700. Now 150 plus 700 is 850, still too big, so `right` drops to 450. Now 150 plus 450 is 600, too small, so `left` rises to 300. Now 300 plus 450 is 750, which matches, and we return indices 1 and 2.

The senior-level nuance: the problem variant on LeetCode returns one-based indices, so we add one to each zero-based index before returning. Also, the two-pointer method assumes the input is already sorted; if it is not, sorting first costs `n log n`, and in that case a hash-map approach that remembers complements in a single linear pass is usually preferable because it does not require sorting.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the end-of-day settlement desk holds a list of outstanding transaction amounts that the clearing system already returns in sorted order. A regulator sometimes requires the desk to prove that a specific target obligation can be settled by combining exactly two outstanding transactions. Scanning every possible pair on a list of hundreds of thousands of transactions is painfully slow and would blow past the settlement window. This is exactly where the two-pointer technique helps: because the list is already sorted, we can find the matching pair in a single linear sweep.

Problem 2 — The desk also needs the result to be auditable, meaning it must report which two transactions were combined, not just that a combination exists. This is why we return the positions of the two amounts rather than a simple true or false.

The code will define a `SettlementPairFinder` class with a `findPair` method that takes the sorted amounts and a target, uses two pointers, and returns the pair of one-based positions. A small runnable demo seeds a sorted list of settlement amounts for Rajesh and prints the pair found for a target obligation. The demo uses `BigDecimal` for money correctness and a clean logger.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The pair-with-target-sum problem asks me to find two elements in a sorted array whose values add up to a given target, and the clean solution is the two-pointer technique that runs in linear time and constant space. I place one pointer at the start of the array and one at the end, compute the sum of the two values they point to, and then decide which pointer to move based on how that sum compares to the target.

The core insight that makes this correct is the sorted order of the array. When the current sum is larger than the target, the only way to make it smaller is to move the right pointer inward to a smaller value, and I can safely discard the old right element because pairing it with anything smaller on the left would only make the sum even larger. When the sum is too small, I move the left pointer inward to a larger value for the same reason in reverse. Each move permanently eliminates one element, so I touch each element at most once.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this exact approach on the end-of-day settlement desk. The clearing system already returns outstanding transaction amounts in sorted order, and the regulator sometimes requires us to show that a specific target obligation can be cleared by combining exactly two outstanding transactions. A brute-force pair check over hundreds of thousands of transactions would miss the settlement window, so the two-pointer sweep gave us the answer in a single linear pass, and I returned the positions of the two transactions so the result was fully auditable.

The senior-level point I always add is about preconditions. The two-pointer method depends on the array being sorted. If the input were not sorted, I would either sort it first at an n-log-n cost or switch to a hash-map approach that remembers each element's required complement in a single pass, which avoids sorting entirely. Choosing between those depends on whether the data arrives sorted and whether I also need the original positions, and being explicit about that tradeoff is what separates someone who memorized a trick from someone who understands when to use it.

answers.question: Given an array containing only 0s and 1s, rearrange it in place so that all the 0s come first followed by all the 1s, without using any extra array. (GeeksforGeeks: Segregate 0s and 1s)
answers.shortTitle: Rearrange 0s and 1s (In-Place Partition with Two Pointers)

s1_definition.profdef: Rearranging an array of 0s and 1s means partitioning it in place so every 0 precedes every 1. With two pointers you keep a low pointer marking the boundary where the next 0 should land and a scanning pointer; whenever the scanner finds a 0, you swap it to the low boundary and advance the boundary. This completes in a single linear pass with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a tray of settlement slips where each slip is marked either "failed" (0) or "cleared" (1). Priya wants all the failed slips grouped at the front so the recovery team can grab them first, and all the cleared slips at the back. She keeps one finger on the spot where the next failed slip belongs and sweeps through the tray with her other hand; every time she spots a failed slip, she swaps it into that boundary spot and moves her boundary finger forward.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a boundary for the next 0, sweep once, and swap every 0 you find up to that boundary.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Rearranging an array of 0s and 1s means partitioning it in place so every 0 precedes every 1. With two pointers you keep a low pointer marking the boundary where the next 0 should land and a scanning pointer; whenever the scanner finds a 0, you swap it to the low boundary and advance the boundary. This completes in a single linear pass with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a tray of settlement slips where each slip is marked either "failed" (0) or "cleared" (1). Priya wants all the failed slips grouped at the front so the recovery team can grab them first, and all the cleared slips at the back. She keeps one finger on the spot where the next failed slip belongs and sweeps through the tray with her other hand; every time she spots a failed slip, she swaps it into that boundary spot and moves her boundary finger forward.

**One line to remember:** Keep a boundary for the next 0, sweep once, and swap every 0 you find up to that boundary.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach counts how many 0s exist, then overwrites the front of the array with that many 0s and the rest with 1s. That works in two passes and is perfectly fine for this specific two-value case. The two-pointer in-place partition does it elegantly in a single pass and generalizes to harder problems like the Dutch National Flag.

We keep a pointer called `low`, starting at 0, which marks the position where the next 0 should be placed. We then scan the array with an index `i` from left to right. Whenever `arr[i]` is a 0, we swap `arr[i]` with `arr[low]` and increment `low`. Whenever `arr[i]` is a 1, we do nothing and just let `i` advance. By the time the scan finishes, every position before `low` holds a 0 and every position from `low` onward holds a 1.

A finance usage example: suppose a batch of settlement outcomes is `[1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1]` where 0 means failed and 1 means cleared. We start with `low=0`. At `i=0` the value is 1, so we skip. At `i=1` the value is 0, so we swap positions 1 and 0, giving `[0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1]`, and `low` becomes 1. At `i=2` the value is 1, skip. At `i=3` the value is 0, swap positions 3 and 1, giving `[0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1]`, and `low` becomes 2. Continuing this way lands all failed slips at the front.

The senior-level nuance: swapping is safe even when `i` equals `low` because swapping an element with itself is harmless, so we do not need a special case. The algorithm is stable in grouping but not in preserving the original relative order within each group, which does not matter here because all 0s are identical and all 1s are identical. If the values carried extra payload we cared about ordering, we would need a stable partition instead.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a nightly batch that produces an array of settlement outcomes, where a 0 marks a failed settlement that must be retried urgently and a 1 marks a cleared settlement. The recovery team needs all the failed outcomes grouped at the front of the array so they can process retries first without scanning the entire batch repeatedly. Allocating a second array for a batch of millions of outcomes wastes memory, so we must rearrange the array in place.

Problem 2 — The batch runs under tight memory limits on shared infrastructure, so the solution must use only a constant amount of extra space regardless of batch size. This is exactly what the in-place two-pointer partition delivers.

The code defines an `OutcomeSegregator` class with a `segregate` method that rearranges the array in place using a `low` boundary pointer and a scanning index. A runnable demo seeds a mixed batch of outcomes, runs the segregation, and logs the before and after states.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Rearranging an array of 0s and 1s so that all the 0s come first means partitioning the array in place, and I solve it with a single-pass two-pointer method that uses only constant extra space. I keep a boundary pointer called low that marks the position where the next 0 should be placed, and I scan the whole array with a second index. Every time the scanner lands on a 0, I swap it into the low boundary and advance the boundary; every time it lands on a 1, I simply move on.

The reason this is correct is that everything before the low boundary is guaranteed to already be a 0, so swapping each newly found 0 into that boundary and growing the boundary keeps all the 0s packed at the front. When the scan finishes, the boundary is exactly the count of 0s, and everything from the boundary onward is a 1. Because I only ever swap and advance pointers, I never allocate a second array, which keeps the memory use constant regardless of how large the batch is.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this came up in a nightly settlement batch. Each outcome was either a failed settlement, which we represented as 0, or a cleared settlement, which we represented as 1, and the recovery team needed all the failed outcomes grouped at the front so they could process urgent retries first. The batch could contain millions of outcomes and ran under tight memory limits on shared infrastructure, so allocating a parallel array was not acceptable, and the in-place partition let us reorganize the batch cheaply inside the settlement window.

The senior-level point I make is that this simple two-value partition is the foundation of the more general Dutch National Flag problem, where you partition into three groups around a pivot. I keep the swap logic isolated in its own helper precisely so I can extend it to a three-pointer variant without touching the callers, and I note that this partition groups identical values but does not preserve original relative order, which is fine here because the 0s and 1s are interchangeable but would require a stable partition if each element carried meaningful payload.

answers.question: Given a sorted array (or a sorted linked list), remove the duplicate elements in place so that each element appears only once, and return the new length (or the de-duplicated list). Solve it without allocating a second structure. (LeetCode: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List / Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array)
answers.shortTitle: Remove Duplicates from a Sorted Structure (Two Pointers, In Place)

s1_definition.profdef: Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place uses a slow-fast two-pointer scheme. The slow pointer marks the end of the unique prefix built so far, and the fast pointer scans ahead. Whenever the fast pointer finds a value different from the last unique value, you copy it to the position just after the slow pointer and advance the slow pointer. The unique count is the slow pointer plus one. For a sorted linked list, you walk a single pointer and skip over nodes whose value equals the current node.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh has a sorted ledger of account numbers where the same account can appear several times in a row because of repeated entries. He wants a clean ledger with each account listed once. He keeps one finger on the last unique account he has confirmed and reads forward; whenever he sees an account different from that last unique one, he writes it right after his confirmed section and moves his confirming finger forward. Because the ledger is sorted, all copies of the same account sit together, so this one sweep is enough.
s1_definition.oneliner: In sorted data, duplicates are neighbors, so one slow-fast sweep keeps only the first of each run.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place uses a slow-fast two-pointer scheme. The slow pointer marks the end of the unique prefix built so far, and the fast pointer scans ahead. Whenever the fast pointer finds a value different from the last unique value, you copy it to the position just after the slow pointer and advance the slow pointer. The unique count is the slow pointer plus one. For a sorted linked list, you walk a single pointer and skip over nodes whose value equals the current node.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh has a sorted ledger of account numbers where the same account can appear several times in a row because of repeated entries. He wants a clean ledger with each account listed once. He keeps one finger on the last unique account he has confirmed and reads forward; whenever he sees an account different from that last unique one, he writes it right after his confirmed section and moves his confirming finger forward. Because the ledger is sorted, all copies of the same account sit together, so this one sweep is enough.

**One line to remember:** In sorted data, duplicates are neighbors, so one slow-fast sweep keeps only the first of each run.

sections.s2_technical:
Because the input is sorted, every group of equal values is contiguous. That is the key fact: to remove duplicates we only ever need to compare each element to the previous kept element, never to all earlier elements.

For the array version, we keep a `slow` index pointing at the last unique element, starting at 0. We scan with a `fast` index from 1 to the end. If `arr[fast]` differs from `arr[slow]`, we increment `slow` and copy `arr[fast]` into `arr[slow]`. If they are equal, we skip. After the scan, positions 0 through `slow` hold the unique values, and the unique count is `slow + 1`. The elements beyond that are leftover and ignored.

A finance usage example: suppose a sorted account-number array is `[101, 101, 102, 103, 103, 103, 104]`. We start with `slow=0` (value 101). At `fast=1` the value 101 equals `arr[slow]`, skip. At `fast=2` the value 102 differs, so `slow` becomes 1 and we copy 102 there. At `fast=3` the value 103 differs, so `slow` becomes 2 and we copy 103. The repeated 103s are skipped, and finally 104 is copied. The unique prefix becomes `[101, 102, 103, 104]` with a count of 4.

For the sorted linked list version, we walk a `current` pointer. While `current` and `current.next` both exist and have equal values, we bypass the duplicate by setting `current.next = current.next.next`, which unlinks the duplicate node. Otherwise we advance `current`. This removes all consecutive duplicates in one pass with constant extra space.

The senior-level nuance: the array method does not shrink the physical array because Java arrays have fixed length, so we return the logical length and treat the tail as garbage. A common variant allows each element to appear at most twice, which you handle by comparing `arr[fast]` against `arr[slow - 1]` instead of `arr[slow]`. For the linked list, using a dummy head is unnecessary for this basic version because the head itself is always kept, but a dummy becomes useful in the harder variant that removes all nodes that ever had a duplicate.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India imports a sorted feed of account numbers from a partner system, but the feed often contains the same account repeated several times in a row because of overlapping export windows. Before the reconciliation engine runs, we must collapse those repeats so each account appears exactly once, otherwise the engine double-counts balances. Because the feed can be huge, we cannot afford to allocate a second array.

Problem 2 — The same cleanup is sometimes needed on a sorted linked list of transaction references streamed in order, where consecutive identical references must be merged into one. We want a single clean pass with no extra structure.

The code defines a `LedgerDeduplicator` class with two methods: `removeDuplicates` for a sorted int array returning the unique count, and `removeDuplicates` overloaded for a sorted linked list of account references returning the cleaned head. A runnable demo seeds both a sorted array and a sorted linked list, cleans them, and logs the results.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the sorted array `[101, 101, 102, 103, 103, 103, 104]` and the sorted list `501 -> 501 -> 502 -> 503 -> 503`.

Step 1: For the array, `slow` starts at 0 pointing at 101. The fast scan begins at index 1.

Step 2: At `fast=1` the value 101 equals `arr[slow]`, so it is a duplicate and skipped.

Step 3: At `fast=2` the value 102 differs, so `slow` becomes 1 and 102 is copied there. The front is now `[101, 102, ...]`.

Step 4: At `fast=3` the value 103 differs, so `slow` becomes 2 and 103 is copied. The two further 103s at `fast=4` and `fast=5` are equal and skipped.

Step 5: At `fast=6` the value 104 differs, so `slow` becomes 3 and 104 is copied. The scan ends with `slow=3`, so the unique count is 4 and the front holds `[101, 102, 103, 104]`.

Step 6: For the linked list, `current` starts at node 501. Its next is also 501, so that next node is unlinked. Now 501 points to 502, which differs, so `current` advances. 502 points to 503, differs, advance. 503 points to another 503, which is unlinked. The list is now `501 -> 502 -> 503`.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Removing duplicates from a sorted structure in place relies on one key fact: because the data is sorted, every group of equal values sits together, so I only ever need to compare each element to the previous kept element rather than to everything before it. That lets me solve it in a single linear pass with constant extra space using a slow-fast two-pointer scheme.

For the array version I keep a slow pointer at the last unique element and scan forward with a fast pointer. Whenever the fast element differs from the slow element, I advance the slow pointer and copy the fast element into that position, building the unique prefix in place. When the scan finishes, the slow pointer plus one is the count of unique elements, and everything beyond that is leftover garbage that I simply ignore, because Java arrays cannot physically shrink. For the sorted linked list version I walk a single pointer and, whenever the next node has the same value as the current node, I unlink it by pointing current's next past the duplicate, which removes all consecutive duplicates in one sweep.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India this solved a real reconciliation problem. We imported a sorted feed of account numbers from a partner, but overlapping export windows produced the same account repeated several times in a row, and feeding those repeats into the reconciliation engine would double-count balances. The feed was large, so allocating a second array was not acceptable, and the in-place slow-fast sweep collapsed the repeats cheaply before reconciliation ran. We used the same idea on a sorted linked list of transaction references that streamed in order.

The senior-level point I add is about the common variants. If the requirement allows each element to appear at most twice, I compare the fast element against the element two positions back instead of one, which keeps exactly two copies. And for the harder linked-list variant that removes every node that ever had a duplicate, I introduce a dummy head node so I have a stable handle on the node before a run of duplicates, since in that case even the original head might be removed. Knowing which variant the interviewer means, and adjusting the comparison accordingly, is what shows real command of the pattern.

answers.question: Given an array sorted in non-decreasing order that may contain negative numbers, return a new array of the squares of each number, also sorted in non-decreasing order. Aim for linear time. (LeetCode: Squares of a Sorted Array)
answers.shortTitle: Squaring a Sorted Array (Two Pointers from the Ends)

s1_definition.profdef: Squaring a sorted array that contains negatives produces squares whose largest values come from the two ends of the array, because a large negative squared can exceed a small positive squared. The linear solution uses two pointers at the ends, compares the absolute values, squares the larger, and places it at the end of the result array, filling the result from back to front. This achieves linear time without sorting the squares again.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh has a sorted list of daily profit-and-loss figures, where losses are negative and profits are positive. He wants the squared magnitudes sorted smallest to largest. The catch is that a big loss squared can be larger than a small profit squared, so the biggest squared magnitudes live at the two ends of the sorted list. Priya reads from both ends inward, each time taking whichever end has the bigger magnitude, squaring it, and dropping it into the back of a new tray, filling the tray from the last slot to the first.
s1_definition.oneliner: The largest squares hide at the ends, so compare the two ends, square the bigger, and fill the result from the back.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Squaring a sorted array that contains negatives produces squares whose largest values come from the two ends of the array, because a large negative squared can exceed a small positive squared. The linear solution uses two pointers at the ends, compares the absolute values, squares the larger, and places it at the end of the result array, filling the result from back to front. This achieves linear time without sorting the squares again.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh has a sorted list of daily profit-and-loss figures, where losses are negative and profits are positive. He wants the squared magnitudes sorted smallest to largest. The catch is that a big loss squared can be larger than a small profit squared, so the biggest squared magnitudes live at the two ends of the sorted list. Priya reads from both ends inward, each time taking whichever end has the bigger magnitude, squaring it, and dropping it into the back of a new tray, filling the tray from the last slot to the first.

**One line to remember:** The largest squares hide at the ends, so compare the two ends, square the bigger, and fill the result from the back.

sections.s2_technical:
If the array had only non-negative numbers, squaring would preserve the order and we could square each element left to right. The complication is negative numbers: because the array is sorted, the most negative value sits at the far left, and its square can be the largest value of all. So the smallest square is somewhere in the middle, and the largest squares are at the two ends.

The efficient trick is to build the result from the largest square down to the smallest. We place a `left` pointer at index 0 and a `right` pointer at the last index, and a `position` pointer at the last index of a new result array. At each step we compare the absolute values of `arr[left]` and `arr[right]`. Whichever has the larger magnitude produces the larger square, so we square it, store it at `result[position]`, move that end pointer inward, and decrement `position`. We repeat until the two pointers cross.

A finance usage example: suppose daily P&L figures sorted are `[-7, -3, 2, 5, 8]`. The squares are 49, 9, 4, 25, 64. We want `[4, 9, 25, 49, 64]`. Starting, `left` points at -7 (magnitude 7) and `right` at 8 (magnitude 8). Eight is larger, so 64 goes into the last result slot and `right` moves to 5. Now -7 magnitude 7 versus 5 magnitude 5, so 49 goes into the next slot from the back and `left` moves to -3. Continuing this way fills the result in descending square order from the back, producing the sorted output.

The senior-level nuance: filling from the back is what makes this linear. A naive approach would square every element then sort, costing `n log n`. The two-pointer method exploits the existing sort to reach linear time. We compare absolute values rather than raw values because we care about magnitude; comparing with squares directly also works and avoids a sign concern, though for very large values computing the square early can risk overflow, so using a wide enough type or comparing magnitudes first is safer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's risk desk keeps a sorted array of a trading book's daily profit-and-loss figures, where losses are negative and profits are positive. To compute a volatility-style measure, the desk needs the squared magnitude of each day's result, and it needs those squares sorted so it can quickly find the median and the extremes. The naive approach of squaring everything and re-sorting is too slow for the millions of figures the desk processes across many books.

Problem 2 — Because a large loss squared can dominate a small profit squared, the desk cannot assume the input order carries over to the squares. The solution must correctly account for negatives while still running in a single linear pass.

The code defines a `PnlSquarer` class with a `sortedSquares` method that takes the sorted P&L array and returns a new sorted array of squares using two end pointers and back-to-front filling. A runnable demo seeds a sorted P&L array including losses and logs the sorted squares.

Step 2: It compares squares: left square is 49, right square is 64. The right is larger, so 64 goes into result slot 4. `right` moves to index 3 (value 5) and `pos` becomes 3.

Step 3: Left square is 49, right square is 25. The left is larger, so 49 goes into result slot 3. `left` moves to index 1 (value -3) and `pos` becomes 2.

Step 4: Left square is 9, right square is 25. The right is larger, so 25 goes into result slot 2. `right` moves to index 2 (value 2) and `pos` becomes 1.

Step 5: Left square is 9, right square is 4. The left is larger, so 9 goes into result slot 1. `left` moves to index 2 and `pos` becomes 0. Now `left` equals `right` at value 2.

Step 6: Left square equals right square at 4, so 4 goes into result slot 0 and the pointers cross. The result array is `[4, 9, 25, 49, 64]`, sorted ascending.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Squaring a sorted array that may contain negative numbers is trickier than it first looks, because a large negative value squared can be bigger than a small positive value squared. That means the largest squared values live at the two ends of the sorted array, and the smallest square is somewhere in the middle. The naive approach of squaring everything and re-sorting costs n-log-n, but I can do it in linear time by exploiting the existing sort order.

I use two pointers, one at each end of the input, and I build the result array from the back toward the front. At each step I compare the magnitudes of the two end values, square whichever is larger, place that square in the next slot from the back of the result, and move that end's pointer inward. I keep doing this until the two pointers cross. Because the largest remaining square is always at one of the two ends, filling the result from the last slot backward produces a fully sorted array in a single linear pass.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the risk desk. We kept a trading book's daily profit-and-loss figures in a sorted array, where losses were negative and profits were positive, and the desk needed the squared magnitudes sorted to compute a volatility measure and quickly read off the median and the extremes. With millions of figures across many books, squaring and re-sorting each time was too slow, so the two-pointer linear method kept the computation within our latency budget.

The senior-level point I make is about correctness and overflow. I compare magnitudes rather than raw values because the sign does not matter for the square, and I cast to a wider numeric type before multiplying so that squaring large figures does not overflow. I also note the contrast with the simpler case: if the array had no negatives, squaring preserves order and a plain left-to-right pass would do, but the moment negatives appear, the two-ended fill-from-the-back technique is the right tool, and being able to explain exactly why the largest squares sit at the ends is what demonstrates I understand the structure rather than memorizing steps.

answers.question: Given an array of numbers, find all unique triplets that add up to zero. Each triplet must be unique, and the solution should avoid duplicates. (LeetCode: 3Sum)
answers.shortTitle: Triplet Sum to Zero (3Sum with Two Pointers)

s1_definition.profdef: The triplet-sum-to-zero problem, known as 3Sum, asks for all unique sets of three elements whose sum is zero. The standard approach sorts the array, then fixes each element in turn and uses a two-pointer scan over the remaining right portion to find pairs that complete the triplet. Sorting enables both the two-pointer squeeze and straightforward duplicate skipping, giving an n-squared time solution.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh has a list of signed adjustments on an account, some credits (positive) and some debits (negative), and he needs to find every unique group of three adjustments that perfectly cancel out to zero rupees. He first sorts the adjustments. Then he fixes one adjustment at a time, and for each fixed one he asks Priya to find two others from the remaining list that together cancel it, using the two-pointer trick of starting wide and squeezing inward. He carefully skips repeats so he never reports the same cancelling trio twice.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort, fix one, then two-pointer the rest; skip duplicates at every level.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The triplet-sum-to-zero problem, known as 3Sum, asks for all unique sets of three elements whose sum is zero. The standard approach sorts the array, then fixes each element in turn and uses a two-pointer scan over the remaining right portion to find pairs that complete the triplet. Sorting enables both the two-pointer squeeze and straightforward duplicate skipping, giving an n-squared time solution.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh has a list of signed adjustments on an account, some credits (positive) and some debits (negative), and he needs to find every unique group of three adjustments that perfectly cancel out to zero rupees. He first sorts the adjustments. Then he fixes one adjustment at a time, and for each fixed one he asks Priya to find two others from the remaining list that together cancel it, using the two-pointer trick of starting wide and squeezing inward. He carefully skips repeats so he never reports the same cancelling trio twice.

**One line to remember:** Sort, fix one, then two-pointer the rest; skip duplicates at every level.

sections.s2_technical:
The brute-force approach tries every triple, which is cubic time. The efficient method first sorts the array. Sorting costs n-log-n but unlocks two big advantages: the two-pointer squeeze and easy duplicate handling.

We iterate an index `i` from the start. For each `i`, the value `arr[i]` is the fixed first element of the triplet, and we need two more elements to its right that sum to `-arr[i]`. We set `left = i + 1` and `right = end`, and we run the same two-pointer logic as the pair problem: if the three sum to zero we record the triplet, if the sum is less than zero we move `left` right to increase it, and if more than zero we move `right` left to decrease it.

Duplicate avoidance happens at two levels. At the outer level, if `arr[i]` equals `arr[i - 1]`, we skip this `i` because any triplet starting with that value was already found. At the inner level, after recording a triplet, we advance `left` past any repeated value and retreat `right` past any repeated value, so the same pair is not counted again.

A finance usage example: suppose signed adjustments sorted are `[-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]`. Fixing -4, we look for a pair summing to 4 in the rest; 2 and ... nothing fits cleanly here. Fixing -1, we look for a pair summing to 1, and left at -1, right at 2 gives -1 plus 2 equals 1, so the triplet is `[-1, -1, 2]`. We also find `[-1, 0, 1]`. The duplicate -1 at the outer level is skipped so we do not repeat the same triplets.

The senior-level nuance: there is an early exit optimization. Once `arr[i]` is greater than zero, no triplet starting at `i` can sum to zero because the array is sorted and everything after is at least as large, so we break. Also, this template extends directly to the general k-sum problem by recursively fixing elements and dropping to a two-pointer scan at the base case. The sorting approach is usually preferred over a hash-set approach because it handles duplicate triplets cleanly without needing to canonicalize and store each found triplet in a set.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a reconciliation process where an account accumulates signed adjustments throughout the day: credits are positive and debits are negative. The audit team needs to identify every unique group of three adjustments that exactly cancel to zero, because such trios often indicate a reversal pattern worth reviewing. Checking every possible triple on a long list is cubic and far too slow.

Problem 2 — The same adjustment amount can appear multiple times, and the audit report must list each cancelling trio only once, never with duplicates. The solution must therefore skip repeated values carefully at both the fixed-element level and the pair level.

The code defines a `ReversalFinder` class with a `findZeroSumTriplets` method that sorts the adjustments, fixes each element, uses a two-pointer scan, and skips duplicates. A runnable demo seeds a list of signed adjustments and logs every unique cancelling triplet.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the signed adjustments `[-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]`.

Step 1: The finder sorts the array to `[-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]`. Sorting groups equal values together, which is what makes duplicate skipping easy.

Step 2: The outer index `i` starts at 0, fixing -4. The inner `left` starts at -1 and `right` at 2. The sums tried are -4 plus -1 plus 2 which is -3 (too small, move left), and so on; no pair completes -4 to zero, so this anchor finds nothing.

Step 3: `i` moves to index 1, fixing the first -1. `left` starts at index 2 (the second -1) and `right` at index 5 (value 2). The sum -1 plus -1 plus 2 is 0, so the triplet `[-1, -1, 2]` is recorded. The method then skips duplicate values and both pointers move inward.

Step 4: Still anchored at the first -1, `left` is now at 0 and `right` at 1. The sum -1 plus 0 plus 1 is 0, so the triplet `[-1, 0, 1]` is recorded. The pointers cross and the inner loop ends.

Step 5: `i` moves to index 2, which is another -1 equal to the previous anchor, so it is skipped to avoid duplicate triplets. Remaining anchors are positive-leaning and produce no new zero-sum triplet.

```
INFO: Cancelling trio: [-1, 0, 1]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The triplet-sum-to-zero problem, often called 3Sum, asks me to find every unique group of three numbers that adds up to zero. The brute-force cubic approach checks every triple, but the efficient solution is to sort the array first and then reduce the problem to a repeated two-pointer scan, which brings it down to n-squared time.

After sorting, I iterate through the array and treat each element as the fixed first member of the triplet. For each fixed element I need two more elements to its right that together equal its negation, and I find them with the two-pointer squeeze: a left pointer just after the fixed element and a right pointer at the end, moving left inward when the sum is too small and right inward when the sum is too large. Sorting does double duty here, because it both enables the squeeze and lets me skip duplicates cleanly: at the outer level I skip a fixed element equal to the previous one, and after recording a triplet I advance past any repeated values on both pointers, so no triplet is ever reported twice.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in reconciliation. An account accumulated signed adjustments through the day, credits positive and debits negative, and the audit team wanted every unique group of three adjustments that exactly cancelled to zero, because such trios often signalled a reversal pattern worth reviewing. The lists could be long, so the cubic check was out, and the sorted two-pointer approach produced a clean, duplicate-free list of cancelling trios that fed straight into case management.

The senior-level point I add is the early exit and the generalization. Once the fixed element is greater than zero, no triplet starting there can sum to zero because everything after it in the sorted array is at least as large, so I break out immediately. And the same skeleton of sorting, fixing elements, and dropping to a two-pointer base case extends directly to the general k-sum problem by recursion. I prefer this sorted approach over a hash-set approach precisely because it handles duplicate triplets naturally without having to canonicalize and store every triplet I find.

answers.question: Given an array of numbers and a target value, find the triplet whose sum is closest to the target and return that sum. (LeetCode: 3Sum Closest)
answers.shortTitle: Triplet Sum Close to Target (3Sum Closest)

s1_definition.profdef: The 3Sum-closest problem asks for the sum of three elements that is nearest to a given target, where nearest means the smallest absolute difference. The approach mirrors 3Sum: sort the array, fix each element, and use a two-pointer scan while tracking the closest sum seen so far, updating it whenever a new triplet sum has a smaller distance to the target.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh needs to combine exactly three pending settlement amounts so their total lands as close as possible to a target obligation, even if it cannot hit the target exactly. He sorts the amounts, fixes one at a time, and uses Priya's two-pointer sweep over the rest. Each time a trio's total is nearer to the target than any trio he has seen before, he writes it down as the current best, and he keeps nudging the pointers in the direction that reduces the gap.
s1_definition.oneliner: Same two-pointer sweep as 3Sum, but instead of requiring an exact match, remember the closest sum and chase the target.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The 3Sum-closest problem asks for the sum of three elements that is nearest to a given target, where nearest means the smallest absolute difference. The approach mirrors 3Sum: sort the array, fix each element, and use a two-pointer scan while tracking the closest sum seen so far, updating it whenever a new triplet sum has a smaller distance to the target.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh needs to combine exactly three pending settlement amounts so their total lands as close as possible to a target obligation, even if it cannot hit the target exactly. He sorts the amounts, fixes one at a time, and uses Priya's two-pointer sweep over the rest. Each time a trio's total is nearer to the target than any trio he has seen before, he writes it down as the current best, and he keeps nudging the pointers in the direction that reduces the gap.

**One line to remember:** Same two-pointer sweep as 3Sum, but instead of requiring an exact match, remember the closest sum and chase the target.

sections.s2_technical:
This problem is structurally identical to 3Sum but with a different goal: rather than requiring the sum to equal a specific value, we want the sum closest to a target. We sort the array so we can use the two-pointer squeeze and move toward the target intelligently.

We keep a variable `closest` holding the best triplet sum found so far, initialized to the sum of the first three elements or to a very large sentinel. We iterate `i` as the fixed first element, then set `left = i + 1` and `right = end`. For each configuration we compute `sum = arr[i] + arr[left] + arr[right]`. If the absolute difference between `sum` and the target is smaller than the absolute difference between `closest` and the target, we update `closest` to `sum`. Then we decide the pointer move: if `sum` is less than the target we move `left` right to increase the sum, and if `sum` is greater than the target we move `right` left to decrease it. If the sum exactly equals the target, the distance is zero and we can return immediately because nothing can beat an exact match.

A finance usage example: suppose settlement amounts sorted are `[-1, 2, 1, -4]` becomes `[-4, -1, 1, 2]` and the target is 1. Fixing -4, left at -1, right at 2 gives a sum of -3, distance 4. We move left to increase. Fixing -1, left at 1, right at 2 gives a sum of 2, distance 1, which is closer, so `closest` becomes 2. We keep going and 2 remains the closest sum to the target 1.

The senior-level nuance: the early return on an exact match is a meaningful optimization because the distance cannot go below zero. Unlike 3Sum, we do not need to skip duplicates for correctness because we are returning a single number, not a list of unique triplets, though skipping duplicate anchors can still save redundant work. The overall time is n-squared from the fixed element times the linear two-pointer sweep, with the n-log-n sort dominated by that.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's treasury desk sometimes needs to combine exactly three pending settlement amounts so their total gets as close as possible to a required target obligation. An exact match is ideal but often impossible, so the desk needs the combination whose total has the smallest gap to the target. Trying every triple is cubic and too slow for the large pools of pending settlements.

Problem 2 — The desk cares only about the best total, not about listing every near-miss combination, so the solution should track a single running best and return its sum, updating only when a strictly closer total appears.

The code defines a `ClosestTripletFinder` class with a `closestTripletSum` method that sorts the amounts, fixes each element, uses a two-pointer sweep, tracks the closest sum, and returns early on an exact hit. A runnable demo seeds pending amounts and a target and logs the closest achievable total.

Input data: the pending amounts `[-1, 2, 1, -4]` and the target `1`.

Step 1: The finder sorts the amounts to `[-4, -1, 1, 2]`. The initial closest is the sum of the first three, which is -4 plus -1 plus 1, equal to -4, with a distance of 5 from the target.

Step 2: The outer index fixes -4. The left pointer is at -1 and the right at 2. The sum is -4 plus -1 plus 2, which is -3, with a distance of 4. That is closer than 5, so closest becomes -3. Because -3 is less than the target, the left pointer moves right.

Step 3: Still fixing -4, left is at 1 and right at 2. The sum is -4 plus 1 plus 2, which is -1, distance 2, closer than 4, so closest becomes -1. The sum is still less than the target, left moves right, pointers cross, inner loop ends.

Step 4: The outer index fixes -1. Left is at 1 and right at 2. The sum is -1 plus 1 plus 2, which is 2, distance 1, closer than 2, so closest becomes 2. The sum exceeds the target, so right moves left, pointers cross.

Step 5: The outer index fixes 1, but only one element remains to its right, so the inner loop cannot form a pair and ends. The best closest sum is 2, a distance of 1 from the target.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The 3Sum-closest problem asks me to find the sum of three elements that is nearest to a given target, where nearest means the smallest absolute difference. It is structurally the same as the classic 3Sum problem, but instead of requiring an exact match I track the closest sum I have seen and keep chasing the target, so the shape of the solution is sort the array, fix each element, and run a two-pointer sweep over the rest.

I keep a running best sum, initialized to the sum of the first three elements after sorting. For each fixed first element I set a left pointer just after it and a right pointer at the end, and at every configuration I compute the triplet sum and compare its distance from the target to the distance of my current best; if it is strictly closer I update the best. Then I decide which pointer to move: if the sum is below the target I move the left pointer right to increase it, and if it is above the target I move the right pointer left to decrease it. If a sum ever equals the target exactly, I return immediately, because a distance of zero cannot be beaten.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the treasury desk. We sometimes needed to combine exactly three pending settlement amounts so their total landed as close as possible to a required obligation, and an exact match was often impossible, so we needed the combination with the smallest gap. The pending pools were large, so the cubic brute-force check was not viable, and the sorted two-pointer sweep with a running best gave us the closest achievable total within our time budget.

The senior-level point I make is about the differences from plain 3Sum. Here I do not need to skip duplicate triplets for correctness, because I am returning a single number rather than a list of unique triplets, although skipping duplicate anchors can still save redundant work. The exact-match early return is a genuine optimization since the distance is bounded below by zero. And because the two problems share the same sort-fix-squeeze skeleton, recognizing that one is a small variation of the other is what lets me adapt quickly in an interview instead of treating every variant as a brand new puzzle.

answers.question: Given an array and a target value, count how many triplets have a sum strictly less than the target. (GeeksforGeeks: Count triplets with sum smaller than X)
answers.shortTitle: Triplets with Smaller Sum (Two Pointers with Counting)

s1_definition.profdef: Counting triplets with a sum smaller than a target sorts the array, fixes each element, and uses a two-pointer scan where a key counting insight applies: when the fixed element plus the left and right values is below the target, every element strictly between left and right also forms a valid triplet with the fixed element and the left value, so you add the whole span at once. This yields an n-squared counting solution rather than cubic enumeration.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh wants to know how many ways he can pick three fee amounts whose total stays under a regulatory cap, so the combination is allowed. He sorts the fees, fixes one, and uses Priya's two-pointer sweep. The clever part: when the fixed fee plus the smallest and largest of the remaining pair is already under the cap, then pairing that smallest with every fee up to the largest is also under the cap, so he counts that entire block in one shot instead of one by one.
s1_definition.oneliner: When left plus right is under target, every pair between them also qualifies, so add the whole span, not just one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Counting triplets with a sum smaller than a target sorts the array, fixes each element, and uses a two-pointer scan where a key counting insight applies: when the fixed element plus the left and right values is below the target, every element strictly between left and right also forms a valid triplet with the fixed element and the left value, so you add the whole span at once. This yields an n-squared counting solution rather than cubic enumeration.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh wants to know how many ways he can pick three fee amounts whose total stays under a regulatory cap, so the combination is allowed. He sorts the fees, fixes one, and uses Priya's two-pointer sweep. The clever part: when the fixed fee plus the smallest and largest of the remaining pair is already under the cap, then pairing that smallest with every fee up to the largest is also under the cap, so he counts that entire block in one shot instead of one by one.

**One line to remember:** When left plus right is under target, every pair between them also qualifies, so add the whole span, not just one.

sections.s2_technical:
We want the count of triplets whose sum is strictly less than a target. The brute-force cubic enumeration is too slow, so we sort and use a two-pointer scan with a counting trick.

We iterate `i` as the fixed first element. We set `left = i + 1` and `right = end`. We compute `sum = arr[i] + arr[left] + arr[right]`. If this sum is less than the target, then because the array is sorted, pairing `arr[left]` with any element from `left + 1` up to `right` also gives a sum under the target. The number of such pairs is `right - left`, so we add that quantity to the count in one step and then move `left` right to explore larger left values. If the sum is greater than or equal to the target, we move `right` left to try a smaller sum.

A finance usage example: suppose sorted fees are `[1, 2, 3, 4]` and the target is 7. Fixing 1, left at 2, right at 4 gives a sum of 7, which is not strictly less than 7, so we move right to 3. Now 1 plus 2 plus 3 is 6, under 7, so every element between left and right, that is `right - left` equal to 1, counts, giving one triplet `(1,2,3)`, and we move left. Fixing 2, left at 3, right at 4 gives 9, not under 7, move right, pointers cross. So the total count is the triplets we accumulated.

The senior-level nuance: the counting-the-span trick is the heart of this problem and the reason it is n-squared instead of cubic. A naive adaptation of 3Sum that increments the count by one for each valid triplet and then moves only one pointer would miss the batching and could even be incorrect without careful pointer movement. Because we only need a count, not the triplets themselves, we never store or deduplicate them, which keeps memory constant. If the problem asked for the triplets listed, we would enumerate the span explicitly, trading time for the full listing.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India charges several kinds of fees, and a compliance rule says that any bundle of exactly three fees applied together must total strictly less than a regulatory cap. The compliance team needs to know how many distinct three-fee bundles stay under the cap, so they can report the proportion of safe bundles. Enumerating every possible triple across a long fee schedule is cubic and too slow.

Problem 2 — The team only needs the count of safe bundles, not the bundles themselves, so the solution should count efficiently in batches rather than listing each one.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Counting triplets whose sum is strictly less than a target is a variation of the 3Sum family, and the key to doing it efficiently is a counting trick layered on top of the familiar sort-and-two-pointer structure. I sort the array, fix each element as the first member of the triplet, and then sweep the remaining portion with a left and a right pointer.

The insight that makes it n-squared instead of cubic is this: when the fixed element plus the left value plus the right value is already below the target, then because the array is sorted, pairing that same left value with every element between left and right also stays below the target. So instead of counting one triplet and moving a single pointer, I add the entire span, which is right minus left, to my count in one step, and then I advance the left pointer to explore larger left values. If the sum is at or above the target, I shrink from the large end by moving the right pointer inward.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this for a compliance rule. The bank charges several kinds of fees, and a regulation required that any bundle of exactly three fees applied together must total strictly less than a cap. The compliance team needed the count of safe three-fee bundles across a long fee schedule to report the proportion that complied, and enumerating every triple was cubic and too slow, so the span-counting two-pointer approach gave the exact count quickly.

The senior-level point I make is that because we only need a count and not the triplets themselves, we never store or deduplicate anything, which keeps memory constant, and the batching is what distinguishes a correct efficient solution from a naive one that increments by one per triplet. I also note that if the requirement changed to listing the actual bundles, I would enumerate the span explicitly, consciously trading time for the full listing, and being clear about that tradeoff shows I understand why the count version can be so much faster.
