sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's circular cycle is 5, -3, 5. We seed the running maximum and maximum sum at 5, the running minimum and minimum sum at 5, and the total at 5.

Step 1 at index 1, value -3: total becomes 2. Running maximum is the larger of -3 and 5 plus -3 which is 2, so 2; maximum sum stays 5. Running minimum is the smaller of -3 and 5 plus -3 which is 2, so -3; minimum sum becomes -3.

Step 2 at index 2, value 5: total becomes 7. Running maximum is the larger of 5 and 2 plus 5 which is 7, so 7; maximum sum becomes 7. Running minimum is the smaller of 5 and -3 plus 5 which is 2, so 2; minimum sum stays -3.

Now we combine. The maximum sum is 7, which is not negative, so the all-negative guard does not apply. The wrapping candidate is total minus minimum sum, which is 7 minus -3 equals 10. The answer is the larger of the non-wrapping 7 and the wrapping 10, which is 10.

The best cyclic stretch for Rajesh is 10, the wrapping subarray that takes the 5 at the last index and wraps to the 5 at the first index, skipping the -3 in the middle.

answers.question: Given an array of integers that may include negatives and a target value k, find the total number of contiguous subarrays whose elements sum exactly to k. Solve it with the prefix-sum and hash-map pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
answers.shortTitle: Subarray Sum Equals K (Prefix Sum with a Hash Map)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks for the count of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals a target k, in an array that may contain negatives. It is solved in linear time with a running prefix sum and a hash map that records how many times each prefix-sum value has occurred: at each index, the number of subarrays ending there with sum k equals the number of earlier prefix sums equal to the current prefix sum minus k.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh walks through a sequence of daily net cash flows and wants to count how many continuous stretches of days netted exactly a target amount, say zero for a perfectly balanced stretch. He keeps a running total as he walks and remembers how often each running total has appeared. Whenever his current running total minus the target has been seen before, each earlier occurrence marks the start of a stretch that nets exactly the target.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count earlier prefix sums equal to the current prefix sum minus k, using a hash map of prefix-sum frequencies.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem asks for the count of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals a target k, in an array that may contain negatives. It is solved in linear time with a running prefix sum and a hash map that records how many times each prefix-sum value has occurred: at each index, the number of subarrays ending there with sum k equals the number of earlier prefix sums equal to the current prefix sum minus k.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh walks through a sequence of daily net cash flows and wants to count how many continuous stretches of days netted exactly a target amount, say zero for a perfectly balanced stretch. He keeps a running total as he walks and remembers how often each running total has appeared. Whenever his current running total minus the target has been seen before, each earlier occurrence marks the start of a stretch that nets exactly the target.

**One line to remember:** Count earlier prefix sums equal to the current prefix sum minus k, using a hash map of prefix-sum frequencies.

sections.s2_technical:
The foundation is the prefix sum. Define the prefix sum at index i as the sum of all elements from the start up to and including i. Then the sum of any subarray from index j plus one to index i equals the prefix sum at i minus the prefix sum at j. A subarray ending at i has sum equal to k exactly when there exists an earlier prefix sum, at some j, such that the prefix at i minus the prefix at j equals k, which rearranges to the prefix at j equals the prefix at i minus k.

So as we scan left to right maintaining a running prefix sum, the number of subarrays ending at the current index with sum k is the number of times the value prefix minus k has already appeared as a prefix sum. We keep a hash map from prefix-sum value to how many times it has occurred. At each element we add the element to the running prefix, then we look up prefix minus k in the map and add its count to our answer, then we record the current prefix by incrementing its count in the map. For example `count += map.getOrDefault(prefix - k, 0); map.merge(prefix, 1, Integer::sum);`.

The single most important initialization detail is seeding the map with the prefix-sum value zero having a count of one, written `map.put(0, 1)`, before the scan begins. This represents the empty prefix before any elements and is what lets a subarray that starts at index zero and sums to k be counted, because its prefix-minus-k lookup finds that seeded zero. The senior-level nuance is that this zero seeding is the classic off-by-one trap; forgetting it undercounts every subarray that begins at the very start.

Because the array may contain negatives and zeros, the sliding-window approach does not apply here, and the prefix-sum-with-hash-map method is specifically what handles the general signed case. We look up before we insert, so that a zero-length subarray is never counted and so that we do not match an element against itself. The time complexity is linear, O(n), one pass with constant-time map operations, and the space complexity is O(n) for the map in the worst case. This technique is the canonical prefix-sum counting pattern.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the reconciliation team reviews a sequence of daily net cash flows for a suspense account and must count how many continuous stretches of days netted exactly a target amount, often zero, because a zero-netting stretch means the account self-reconciled over that period and such stretches are counted for audit metrics. Flows can be positive or negative, so a simple window will not work. This is exactly the subarray-sum-equals-k counting problem.

Problem 2 — Counting by checking every possible stretch is quadratic and does not scale across the bank's suspense accounts and long histories. The prefix-sum-with-hash-map method counts all qualifying stretches in a single linear pass even with negative flows, which makes the nightly reconciliation-metrics job feasible.

The code has the shared `Account` class, a `ReconciliationCounter` service with a `countBalancedStretches` method implementing the prefix-sum map, and a runnable `SubarraySumEqualsKDemo` main class that runs Rajesh's and Priya's daily net-flow sequences against a target, logging each match at fine level and the final count at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's flows are 1, -1, 5, -5, 3 with target 0. We seed the prefix-count map with the value 0 having count 1, start the running prefix at 0, and the answer at 0.

Step 1 at index 0, value 1: prefix becomes 1. We look up prefix minus target, which is 1 minus 0 equals 1; the map has no 1, so add 0. We record prefix 1 in the map, now 1 has count 1.

Step 2 at index 1, value -1: prefix becomes 0. We look up 0 minus 0 equals 0; the map has 0 with count 1, so add 1, count becomes 1. This counts the stretch from index 0 to 1, flows 1 and -1 netting 0. We record prefix 0 in the map, now 0 has count 2.

Step 3 at index 2, value 5: prefix becomes 5. We look up 5 minus 0 equals 5; not in the map, add 0. We record prefix 5, count 1.

Step 4 at index 3, value -5: prefix becomes 0. We look up 0; the map has 0 with count 2, so add 2, count becomes 3. These two counts correspond to the stretch from index 2 to 3, flows 5 and -5 netting 0, and the stretch from index 0 to 3, flows 1, -1, 5, -5 netting 0. We record prefix 0, now count 3.

Step 5 at index 4, value 3: prefix becomes 3. We look up 3; not in the map, add 0. We record prefix 3.

The count of balanced stretches for Rajesh is 3.

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem asks for the number of contiguous subarrays that sum exactly to a target k, in an array that may contain negatives, and I solve it in linear time using a running prefix sum and a hash map of prefix-sum frequencies. The foundation is that the sum of a subarray equals the difference of two prefix sums, so a subarray ending at the current index sums to k exactly when some earlier prefix equals the current prefix minus k. As I scan, I maintain the running prefix and a map counting how often each prefix value has appeared, and at each index I add to my answer the number of times the value prefix minus k has already occurred, then I record the current prefix.

The initialization detail I always call out is seeding the map with the prefix value zero having count one before the scan. That represents the empty prefix before any element and is what allows a subarray starting at the very beginning to be counted, because its lookup of prefix minus k finds that seeded zero. Forgetting this seeding is the classic off-by-one bug that undercounts every subarray beginning at index zero. I also look up before inserting, so a zero-length subarray is never counted.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the reconciliation team. We reviewed daily net cash flows for a suspense account and counted how many continuous stretches of days netted exactly a target amount, usually zero, because a zero-netting stretch meant the account self-reconciled over that period and we tracked those for audit metrics. Flows could be positive or negative, so a sliding window was not applicable, and the prefix-sum-with-hash-map method counted all qualifying stretches in a single linear pass, scaling across the bank's suspense accounts in the nightly job.

The senior-level point I make is that the prefix-sum-with-hash-map technique is specifically the tool for signed arrays where sliding windows break, and knowing to reach for it the moment negatives appear is the real signal of experience. I also stress the seed-with-zero initialization and the look-up-before-insert ordering as the two correctness linchpins, and I mention using a long for the prefix to avoid overflow on long monetary histories. Naming when the window fails and why the prefix-sum map is the right replacement, plus the exact seeding and ordering rules, is what tells an interviewer I have genuinely used this.

answers.question: Given an array of integers, find the leftmost pivot index where the sum of all elements strictly to its left equals the sum of all elements strictly to its right, returning minus one if no such index exists. Solve it with the prefix-sum pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
answers.shortTitle: Find Pivot Index (Balance Point of an Array)

s1_definition.profdef: The pivot index problem asks for the leftmost index at which the sum of all elements before it equals the sum of all elements after it, where the element at the index itself belongs to neither side. It is solved in linear time by first computing the total sum, then scanning left to right maintaining a running left sum: at each index the right sum is the total minus the left sum minus the current element, and the index is a pivot when the left sum equals that right sum.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh lays out a row of daily settlement amounts and wants the single day that acts as a perfect balance point, where everything settled before that day totals exactly what settled after it, with that day's own amount sitting on the fulcrum belonging to neither side. He adds up the whole row once, then walks across keeping a running total of what is behind him, and checks at each day whether behind equals ahead.
s1_definition.oneliner: At each index, left sum equals total minus left sum minus the current element marks a pivot.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The pivot index problem asks for the leftmost index at which the sum of all elements before it equals the sum of all elements after it, where the element at the index itself belongs to neither side. It is solved in linear time by first computing the total sum, then scanning left to right maintaining a running left sum: at each index the right sum is the total minus the left sum minus the current element, and the index is a pivot when the left sum equals that right sum.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh lays out a row of daily settlement amounts and wants the single day that acts as a perfect balance point, where everything settled before that day totals exactly what settled after it, with that day's own amount sitting on the fulcrum belonging to neither side. He adds up the whole row once, then walks across keeping a running total of what is behind him, and checks at each day whether behind equals ahead.

**One line to remember:** At each index, left sum equals total minus left sum minus the current element marks a pivot.

sections.s2_technical:
This is a direct application of prefix sums, but it only needs a single running prefix rather than a stored map. We first compute the total sum of the array in one pass. Then we scan from left to right maintaining a running left sum, which is the sum of all elements strictly before the current index. Before adding the current element to the left sum, the sum of all elements strictly after the current index is the total minus the left sum minus the current element.

The condition for the current index to be a pivot is that the left sum equals the right sum, which we can write without computing the right sum separately as `leftSum == total - leftSum - nums[i]`. If this holds we return the current index immediately, because we want the leftmost pivot. If it does not hold we add the current element to the left sum with `leftSum += nums[i]` and continue. For example the loop body is `if (leftSum == total - leftSum - nums[i]) return i; leftSum += nums[i];`.

Several edge cases deserve attention. The first index can be a pivot if the sum of everything after it is zero, because the left side is empty and counts as zero. Likewise the last index can be a pivot if everything before it sums to zero. Negative numbers are fully supported because we are comparing sums, not using any window monotonicity. The senior-level nuance is that the current element must be excluded from both sides, which is exactly why the condition subtracts the current element once from the total when forming the right sum.

Because we return the first index that satisfies the condition, we get the leftmost pivot naturally, and we return minus one if the loop finishes without finding one. The time complexity is linear, O(n), one pass for the total and one pass for the scan, and the space complexity is O(1), just a couple of running totals. This single-running-prefix technique is the clean standard solution for balance-point problems.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the settlement operations team lays out a day's sequence of net settlement amounts and wants to find a balance-point transaction, the earliest transaction such that the total of all settlements before it exactly equals the total of all settlements after it, with that transaction itself excluded. This balance point is used to split the day's settlement batch into two halves of equal net value for parallel downstream processing. This is exactly the pivot index problem.

Problem 2 — Recomputing the left and right sums from scratch at every candidate index is quadratic and too slow for the large settlement batches the bank processes. Precomputing the total once and maintaining a single running left sum finds the balance point in a single linear scan, which keeps the batch-splitting step fast.

The code has the shared `Account` class, a `SettlementBalancer` service with a `findBalancePoint` method implementing the prefix-sum scan, and a runnable `PivotIndexDemo` main class that runs Rajesh's and Priya's settlement sequences, logging each checked index at fine level and the balance point at info level.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's settlements are 1, 7, 3, 6, 5, 6. First we compute the total in one pass, which is 1 plus 7 plus 3 plus 6 plus 5 plus 6 equals 28. Then we scan with a left sum starting at 0.

Step 1 at index 0, value 1: right sum is 28 minus 0 minus 1 equals 27. Left 0 is not 27, so we add 1 to the left sum, left sum becomes 1.

Step 2 at index 1, value 7: right sum is 28 minus 1 minus 7 equals 20. Left 1 is not 20, left sum becomes 8.

Step 3 at index 2, value 3: right sum is 28 minus 8 minus 3 equals 17. Left 8 is not 17, left sum becomes 11.

Step 4 at index 3, value 6: right sum is 28 minus 11 minus 6 equals 11. Left 11 equals right 11, so index 3 is the balance point. We return 3.

The balance point for Rajesh is index 3, where the left side 1, 7, 3 sums to 11 and the right side 5, 6 sums to 11.

2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Index 2: left=8 right=17
2026-10-27 18:52:00 FINE    Index 3: left=11 right=11

sections.s6_takeaway:
The pivot index problem asks for the leftmost index where the sum of all elements before it equals the sum of all elements after it, with the element at the index belonging to neither side, and I solve it in linear time with a single running prefix sum. I first compute the total of the array in one pass, then scan left to right keeping a running left sum of everything strictly before the current index. At each index the right sum is simply the total minus the left sum minus the current element, so I check whether the left sum equals that right sum and return the index immediately on the first match, giving me the leftmost pivot naturally.

The detail I always make explicit is that the current element is excluded from both sides, which is exactly why the right sum subtracts the current element once from the total. I also note the end cases: the first index is a pivot when everything after it is zero, since the empty left side counts as zero, and likewise for the last index. Negatives are fully supported because I am comparing sums rather than relying on any window monotonicity.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the settlement operations team. We laid out a day's sequence of net settlement amounts and found the earliest balance-point transaction where the total before it equaled the total after it, excluding that transaction, and we used that point to split the day's batch into two halves of equal net value for parallel downstream processing. Precomputing the total once and keeping a single running left sum found the split point in a single linear scan, which kept the batch-splitting step fast on large batches.

The senior-level point I make is that this is prefix sums in their simplest form, needing only one running total rather than a stored map, which is a nice contrast with the subarray-sum-equals-k problem that does need a map, and being able to explain when a map is and is not required shows I understand the technique rather than applying it blindly. I also mention accumulating the total and running sum in a long to avoid overflow on large monetary batches, and that returning on the first match is what gives the leftmost answer without extra bookkeeping. Drawing that distinction between the map and no-map prefix-sum variants is what signals real understanding to an interviewer.

answers.question: Given an array of integers that may include negatives and a positive integer k, count the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum is divisible by k. Solve it with the prefix-sum remainder pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
answers.shortTitle: Subarray Sums Divisible by K (Prefix Remainder Counting)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks for the count of contiguous subarrays whose sum is a multiple of k. It is solved in linear time by tracking the running prefix sum's remainder modulo k and counting pairs of indices that share the same remainder, because two prefix sums with equal remainders bound a subarray whose sum is divisible by k. Negative sums are normalized into a non-negative remainder before counting.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a sequence of daily net flows and wants to count how many continuous stretches summed to an exact multiple of a settlement unit k, say a multiple of five, because only multiples of the unit can be batched cleanly. As he walks he keeps a running total and looks only at its remainder when divided by k. Any two points in his walk that share the same remainder sandwich a stretch whose total is a clean multiple.
s1_definition.oneliner: Two prefix sums with the same remainder modulo k bound a subarray divisible by k, so count equal-remainder pairs.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem asks for the count of contiguous subarrays whose sum is a multiple of k. It is solved in linear time by tracking the running prefix sum's remainder modulo k and counting pairs of indices that share the same remainder, because two prefix sums with equal remainders bound a subarray whose sum is divisible by k. Negative sums are normalized into a non-negative remainder before counting.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a sequence of daily net flows and wants to count how many continuous stretches summed to an exact multiple of a settlement unit k, say a multiple of five, because only multiples of the unit can be batched cleanly. As he walks he keeps a running total and looks only at its remainder when divided by k. Any two points in his walk that share the same remainder sandwich a stretch whose total is a clean multiple.

**One line to remember:** Two prefix sums with the same remainder modulo k bound a subarray divisible by k, so count equal-remainder pairs.

sections.s2_technical:
The key fact from modular arithmetic is that a subarray from index j plus one to index i has a sum divisible by k exactly when the prefix sum at i and the prefix sum at j leave the same remainder when divided by k. This is because the subarray sum is the difference of the two prefixes, and a difference is divisible by k precisely when the two values are congruent modulo k. So the problem reduces to counting, across all prefix sums, how many pairs share a remainder.

We maintain a running prefix sum and, at each step, compute its remainder modulo k. We keep a frequency array or map from remainder value to how many prefixes have produced that remainder so far. For each new prefix, the number of earlier prefixes with the same remainder is exactly the number of subarrays ending here that are divisible by k, so we add that count to our answer, then increment the frequency for the current remainder. We seed the remainder zero with a count of one before scanning, representing the empty prefix, so that a subarray from the start that is itself divisible by k is counted.

The subtlety that catches many candidates is negative numbers. In Java the percent operator can return a negative remainder, for example minus two modulo five is minus two rather than three. Since remainders must be compared consistently, we normalize with `int r = ((prefix % k) + k) % k;` so the remainder is always in the range zero to k minus one. Without this normalization, congruent prefixes of opposite sign would be bucketed separately and the count would be wrong. The senior-level nuance is exactly this remainder normalization, which is the signature correctness detail of the divisibility variant.

Because k is bounded we can use an `int[k]` frequency array instead of a map for speed. sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem asks for the count of contiguous subarrays whose sum is divisible by k, in an array that may contain negatives, and I solve it in linear time with prefix sums reduced modulo k. The modular insight is that a subarray's sum is divisible by k exactly when the two prefix sums that bound it leave the same remainder, because their difference is divisible by k precisely when they are congruent. So I scan once keeping a running prefix, compute its remainder, and for each new prefix I add to my answer the number of earlier prefixes that shared the same remainder, then record the current remainder.

The correctness detail I always highlight is remainder normalization. In Java the percent operator can produce a negative result for negative prefixes, so I normalize with the running prefix modulo k, plus k, modulo k again, giving a remainder always between zero and k minus one. Without that step, congruent prefixes of opposite sign would land in different buckets and the count would be wrong. I also seed the remainder-zero bucket with a count of one before scanning, representing the empty prefix, so a subarray from the start that is itself divisible by k is counted.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the batch-settlement team. We processed daily net flows and could only group a continuous stretch of days into a single settlement batch if its net total was an exact multiple of a settlement unit, because the clearing house accepted only whole units, and we counted how many stretches qualified as a planning metric. Flows could be negative, so the remainder normalization was essential, and the prefix-remainder counting gave all divisible stretches in a single linear pass, scaling across the day's flows.

The senior-level point I make is that this is the divisibility cousin of the subarray-sum-equals-k problem, where I bucket by remainder instead of by exact prefix value, and recognizing that shared prefix-sum skeleton lets me adapt one pattern to many questions. I also stress the negative-remainder normalization as the single detail that distinguishes a correct implementation, and I mention using a fixed integer array of size k rather than a hash map since k is bounded, which removes boxing and speeds up the hot loop. Naming the normalization pitfall and the array optimization is what shows an interviewer I have actually implemented this correctly.

answers.question: Given a binary array of zeros and ones, find the length of the longest contiguous subarray that contains an equal number of zeros and ones. Solve it with the prefix-sum and first-occurrence hash-map pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
answers.shortTitle: Contiguous Array (Longest Subarray with Equal Zeros and Ones)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks for the length of the longest contiguous subarray of a binary array containing equally many zeros and ones. It is solved in linear time by treating each zero as minus one and each one as plus one, so that an equal-count subarray has a running sum of zero, then tracking a prefix sum and recording the first index at which each prefix value appears: the longest equal-count subarray spans between the first and the latest occurrence of any repeated prefix value.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a daily log of trade outcomes where one means a win and zero means a loss, and wants the longest continuous stretch where wins and losses exactly cancel out, a perfectly break-even run. He scores each win as plus one and each loss as minus one, keeps a running score, and remembers the earliest day each score first appeared. Whenever the running score returns to a value he has seen before, the stretch in between was perfectly break-even.
s1_definition.oneliner: Map zero to minus one, track the prefix sum, and the longest span between equal prefix values is the longest balanced subarray.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem asks for the length of the longest contiguous subarray of a binary array containing equally many zeros and ones. It is solved in linear time by treating each zero as minus one and each one as plus one, so that an equal-count subarray has a running sum of zero, then tracking a prefix sum and recording the first index at which each prefix value appears: the longest equal-count subarray spans between the first and the latest occurrence of any repeated prefix value.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh looks at a daily log of trade outcomes where one means a win and zero means a loss, and wants the longest continuous stretch where wins and losses exactly cancel out, a perfectly break-even run. He scores each win as plus one and each loss as minus one, keeps a running score, and remembers the earliest day each score first appeared. Whenever the running score returns to a value he has seen before, the stretch in between was perfectly break-even.

**One line to remember:** Map zero to minus one, track the prefix sum, and the longest span between equal prefix values is the longest balanced subarray.

sections.s2_technical:
The clever transformation is to replace every zero with minus one and keep every one as plus one. With that substitution, a subarray contains an equal number of zeros and ones exactly when its transformed sum is zero. And a subarray sum is the difference of two prefix sums, so a zero-sum subarray corresponds to two prefix sums that are equal. Therefore the longest balanced subarray is the longest distance between two indices that share the same prefix-sum value.

We maintain a running prefix sum, adding plus one for a one and minus one for a zero, and a hash map from a prefix-sum value to the first index at which it occurred. For each index, if the current prefix value has been seen before, the subarray from just after that first occurrence to the current index has a sum of zero, so its length is the current index minus the stored first-occurrence index, and we update the best length. If the prefix value is new, we store the current index as its first occurrence. Crucially we only ever store the first occurrence and never overwrite it, because the earliest occurrence gives the longest possible span to any later equal value.

The initialization that makes this correct is seeding the map with the prefix value zero mapped to index minus one, written `firstIndex.put(0, -1)`. This represents the empty prefix before the array starts, so that a balanced subarray beginning at index zero is measured correctly as current index minus minus one, which is current index plus one. The senior-level nuance is twofold: the minus-one-for-zero transformation that turns a counting problem into a zero-sum prefix problem, and the store-first-occurrence-only rule that guarantees maximal length.

Because the prefix values range only from minus the array length to plus the array length, a map keyed by integer works well. The time complexity is linear, O(n), one pass with constant-time map operations, and the space complexity is O(n) for the map. This transform-then-prefix technique is the standard pattern for equal-count and balance problems on binary data.

answers.shortTitle: Challenge: Shortest Subarray with Sum at Least K (Prefix Sums with a Monotonic Deque)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks for the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least k, in an array that may contain negatives. Because negatives break the simple sliding window, it is solved in linear time with prefix sums and a monotonically increasing deque of prefix-sum indices: for each new prefix we pop from the front while the window qualifies to record candidate lengths, and pop from the back any prefix that is not smaller than the current one, since such prefixes can never be a better left endpoint.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a sequence of daily net cash flows that can be positive or negative and wants the fewest consecutive days whose total reaches at least a target. Because a negative day can sink a running total, the simple trimming trick fails. Instead he keeps a tidy ordered list of candidate starting points, discards any starting point that is worse than a newer one, and from the front he confirms and removes starting points as soon as the stretch to today reaches the target.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use prefix sums with a deque that stays increasing, popping the front when the window qualifies and the back when a newer prefix is not larger.

Because a negative day can sink a running total, the simple trimming trick fails. Instead he keeps a tidy ordered list of candidate starting points, discards any starting point that is worse than a newer one, and from the front he confirms and removes starting points as soon as the stretch to today reaches the target.

**One line to remember:** Use prefix sums with a deque that stays increasing, popping the front when the window qualifies and the back when a newer prefix is not larger.

sections.s2_technical:
With possibly negative numbers the greedy positive-only window does not work, because shrinking from the left can both increase and decrease the sum unpredictably. The robust approach uses prefix sums. Let P be the array of prefix sums where P at index i is the sum of the first i elements, with P at zero being zero. The sum of the subarray from index j to index i minus one is P at i minus P at j, and we want the shortest such span with P at i minus P at j at least k.

For each right endpoint i we want the largest j less than i with P at j no more than P at i minus k, because that gives the shortest qualifying subarray ending at i. We process the prefix sums left to right maintaining a double-ended queue of indices whose prefix values are strictly increasing from front to back. Two operations keep it correct. First, from the front, while the deque is non-empty and P at i minus P at the front index is at least k, we have a qualifying subarray, so we record the length i minus the front index and pop the front, because any later right endpoint would only give a longer subarray with this same left endpoint. Second, from the back, while the deque is non-empty and P at the back index is greater than or equal to P at i, we pop the back, because the current prefix is smaller or equal and at a later index, making it a strictly better left-endpoint candidate for everyone to come.

After those two steps we push the current index onto the back of the deque. The front pops give candidate lengths from which we keep the minimum. The reason this is linear is that each index is pushed once and popped at most once across the entire run, so the total deque work is bounded by 2n. The senior-level nuance is understanding why both pops are valid: front pops because a qualified left endpoint is never needed again, and back pops because a higher earlier prefix is dominated by a lower later one.

We use long prefix sums to avoid overflow, and we return minus one if no front pop ever produced a qualifying length. The time complexity is linear, O(n), and the space complexity is O(n) for the prefix sums and the deque. This prefix-sum-with-monotonic-deque method is the canonical solution for shortest-subarray-with-sum-at-least-k on signed arrays and is a notable step up in difficulty from the positive-only window.

Input data: Rajesh's moves are 2, -1, 2 with target 3. First we build the prefix array of length four: prefix at 0 is 0, prefix at 1 is 2, prefix at 2 is 1, prefix at 3 is 3. We use an empty deque and a best of a large sentinel.

Step 4 at i equal 3, prefix 3: front check, prefix 3 minus prefix at front 0 which is 0 equals 3, at least 3, so record length 3 minus 0 equals 3, best becomes 3, pop front index 0. Now front is index 2 with prefix 1, prefix 3 minus 1 equals 2, not at least 3, stop. Back check, prefix at back index 2 is 1, not greater than or equal to 3, no back pop. We push index 3.

sections.s6_takeaway:
This problem asks for the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least k, in an array that may contain negatives, and because negatives break the simple positive-only sliding window I solve it with prefix sums and a monotonic deque in linear time. I build a prefix-sum array where any subarray sum is a difference of two prefixes, and for each right endpoint I want the latest left endpoint whose prefix is at most the current prefix minus k, which yields the shortest qualifying subarray ending there.

I process the prefixes left to right maintaining a deque of indices whose prefix values increase from front to back. Two pops keep it correct. From the front, while the current prefix minus the front prefix is at least k, I record the length and pop the front, because that left endpoint can never give a shorter subarray for any later right endpoint. From the back, while the back prefix is greater than or equal to the current prefix, I pop it, because a prefix that is higher and earlier is dominated by the current lower, later one as a left-endpoint candidate. Then I push the current index. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the whole pass is linear.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this on the intraday-liquidity desk. Net cash movements could be positive or negative, and we needed the shortest continuous run whose cumulative total reached at least a required liquidity target so we could raise the smallest possible block of funds quickly. The positive-only window was invalid because of the negatives, so the prefix-sum-with-monotonic-deque method gave the correct shortest run in a single linear pass, which was fast enough for the desk's near-real-time needs.

The senior-level point I make is that recognizing when the simple window fails, specifically the moment negatives can appear, and reaching for prefix sums plus a monotonic deque, is the real signal of depth here, because many candidates incorrectly apply the greedy window. I always justify both pops explicitly, the front because a satisfied left endpoint is never needed again and the back because a higher earlier prefix is strictly dominated, since being able to articulate that is what proves I understand why the algorithm is linear and correct. I also note that I use long prefixes to avoid overflow on monetary data. Explaining the failure of the naive window and the dual-pop invariant is exactly what distinguishes a candidate who has mastered this harder variant.

answers.question: Given an array of integers that may include negatives and two bounds lower and upper, count how many contiguous subarrays have a sum that falls within the inclusive range from lower to upper. answers.shortTitle: Challenge: Count of Range Sum

s1_definition.profdef: The count of range sum problem asks how many contiguous subarrays have a sum lying within an inclusive range from lower to upper. It is solved with prefix sums reframed as pairs: a subarray sum lies in the range exactly when, for a given right prefix, the matching left prefix lies in a shifted window, and counting such pairs efficiently across all prefixes is done with a modified merge sort that counts qualifying pairs while sorting, achieving n log n time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a sequence of daily net flows that can be positive or negative and wants to count how many continuous stretches had a net total between a lower and an upper regulatory threshold, because stretches in that band require a specific disclosure. He turns each stretch total into a comparison between two running totals, then uses an efficient divide-and-conquer count so he does not have to compare every pair of days by hand.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count prefix-sum pairs whose difference lies in the range, efficiently, with a merge-sort that counts during the merge.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The count of range sum problem asks how many contiguous subarrays have a sum lying within an inclusive range from lower to upper. It is solved with prefix sums reframed as pairs: a subarray sum lies in the range exactly when, for a given right prefix, the matching left prefix lies in a shifted window, and counting such pairs efficiently across all prefixes is done with a modified merge sort that counts qualifying pairs while sorting, achieving n log n time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh reviews a sequence of daily net flows that can be positive or negative and wants to count how many continuous stretches had a net total between a lower and an upper regulatory threshold, because stretches in that band require a specific disclosure. He turns each stretch total into a comparison between two running totals, then uses an efficient divide-and-conquer count so he does not have to compare every pair of days by hand.

**One line to remember:** Count prefix-sum pairs whose difference lies in the range, efficiently, with a merge-sort that counts during the merge.

sections.s2_technical:
We start from prefix sums. Let P at zero be zero and P at i be the sum of the first i elements. The sum of the subarray covering indices j to i minus one is P at i minus P at j. We want to count pairs j less than i such that P at i minus P at j lies between lower and upper inclusive. Rearranged, for each right index i we need the count of left indices j less than i with P at j in the interval from P at i minus upper to P at i minus lower.

Counting those pairs naively for every i is quadratic. The classic efficient method embeds the counting inside a merge sort over the prefix-sum array. During the merge step, when the left half and the right half are each sorted, we can, for each prefix value in the right half, slide two pointers over the left half to count how many left values fall into the required shifted interval, and because both halves are sorted these pointer scans are linear per merge level. Summing across the log n levels of merging gives n log n total pair-counting work.

Concretely we recursively sort the prefix array; at each merge we first count: for each index in the right portion we advance a low pointer while the left value is too small, meaning P at i minus P at left is still above upper, and advance a high pointer while the left value keeps the difference at or above lower, and the gap between the pointers is the count of qualifying left endpoints for that right endpoint. Then we perform the normal merge to keep the array sorted for the parent call. The senior-level nuance is that the counting must use the original prefix order semantics, which is preserved because we only ever count pairs where the right index came from a later position than the left, a property the divide-and-conquer structure maintains.

We use long prefix sums to avoid overflow, especially since subtracting bounds can push values far. The time complexity is O(n log n) and the space complexity is O(n) for the prefix array and merge buffers. An alternative is a balanced BST or a Fenwick tree over coordinate-compressed prefix values, also n log n, which some interviewers prefer; the merge-sort method is the most self-contained. This problem is a genuine hard-tier application of prefix sums combined with order-statistics counting.

answers.shortTitle: Merge Intervals (Combine All Overlapping Intervals)

s1_definition.profdef: The merge intervals problem asks to combine any intervals that overlap or touch into single continuous intervals, producing a minimal set of non-overlapping intervals covering the same ranges. It is solved by sorting the intervals by start value and then sweeping left to right, extending the current merged interval whenever the next interval's start is within the current end, otherwise closing the current interval and starting a new one. It runs in n log n time dominated by the sort.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has a list of time windows during which various account-maintenance locks were held, and some windows overlap. He wants to collapse them into the minimal set of distinct locked periods. He first lines the windows up by their start times, then walks through them, stretching the current locked period whenever the next window begins before the current one ends, and starting a fresh period whenever there is a clean gap.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort by start, then sweep, extending the current interval when the next start is within the current end, else start a new one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The merge intervals problem asks to combine any intervals that overlap or touch into single continuous intervals, producing a minimal set of non-overlapping intervals covering the same ranges. It is solved by sorting the intervals by start value and then sweeping left to right, extending the current merged interval whenever the next interval's start is within the current end, otherwise closing the current interval and starting a new one. It runs in n log n time dominated by the sort.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has a list of time windows during which various account-maintenance locks were held, and some windows overlap. He wants to collapse them into the minimal set of distinct locked periods. He first lines the windows up by their start times, then walks through them, stretching the current locked period whenever the next window begins before the current one ends, and starting a fresh period whenever there is a clean gap.

**One line to remember:** Sort by start, then sweep, extending the current interval when the next start is within the current end, else start a new one.

sections.s2_technical:
The decisive first step is sorting the intervals by their start value. Once sorted, any interval that overlaps with an earlier one must overlap with the most recently merged interval, because everything is in start order, so we never need to look backward more than one step. This sorting is what turns a potentially complicated overlap problem into a simple single sweep.

After sorting we initialize the current merged interval as the first interval. For each subsequent interval we compare its start to the current merged interval's end. If the next start is less than or equal to the current end, the two overlap or touch, so we merge by extending the current end to the maximum of the current end and the next end, written `curEnd = Math.max(curEnd, next.end)`. We take the maximum because the next interval might end before the current one, in which case it is fully contained and the current end should not shrink. If instead the next start is strictly greater than the current end, there is a gap, so we finalize the current merged interval by adding it to the result and begin a new current interval at the next one.

A decision point is whether intervals that merely touch, where the next start equals the current end, should be merged. In most banking scenarios touching windows represent a continuous period and should be combined, so we use less than or equal to rather than strictly less than. After the loop we must remember to add the final current interval to the result, because the last merged interval is only closed out when a gap appears or the loop ends, and the loop ending is easy to forget. The senior-level nuance is exactly this pair of details, taking the maximum of the ends and flushing the final interval.

We do not mutate the input; we build a fresh result list. The time complexity is n log n dominated by the sort, with the sweep itself linear, and the space complexity is O(n) for the sorted copy and the result, or O(1) extra beyond the output if we sort in place. This sort-then-sweep template is the foundation of the entire merge-intervals family of problems.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the account-maintenance system records time windows during which exclusive locks were held on an account for various operations, and these windows frequently overlap because several operations run concurrently. The audit team wants to collapse the overlapping windows into the minimal set of distinct continuous locked periods, because the regulator asks for the actual total time an account was under any lock, not a raw list of overlapping entries. This is exactly the merge intervals problem.

Problem 2 — Comparing every window against every other to find overlaps is quadratic and does not scale for busy accounts with many lock entries. Sorting by start and sweeping once collapses all overlaps in n log n time, which keeps the audit-report generation fast.

The code has the shared `Account` class, an `Interval` class representing a lock window, a `LockWindowMerger` service with a `mergeLockedPeriods` method implementing sort-then-sweep, and a runnable `MergeIntervalsDemo` main class that merges Rajesh's and Priya's lock windows, logging each merge or new interval at fine level and the merged list at info level.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The merge intervals problem asks me to collapse any overlapping or touching intervals into a minimal set of non-overlapping intervals covering the same ranges, and I solve it with a sort-then-sweep in n log n time. The decisive step is sorting by start value, because once the intervals are in start order, any interval that overlaps an earlier one must overlap the most recently merged interval, so I never look back more than one step. That ordering is what turns a messy overlap problem into a single clean sweep.

After sorting I keep a current merged interval and walk the rest. If the next interval's start is at or before the current end, they overlap or touch, so I extend the current end to the maximum of the current end and the next end, taking the maximum because the next interval might be fully contained and I must not shrink the current end. If the next start is beyond the current end there is a gap, so I finalize the current interval and start a new one. The two details I always call out are taking the maximum of the ends and flushing the final current interval after the loop, since the last interval is only closed out by a gap that may never come.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the account-maintenance system. We recorded time windows during which exclusive locks were held on an account for concurrent operations, and these windows frequently overlapped, but the regulator asked for the actual total time an account was under any lock, not a raw overlapping list. Sorting the windows by start and sweeping once collapsed all overlaps into the minimal set of distinct locked periods in n log n time, which kept audit-report generation fast even for busy accounts.

The senior-level point I make is that sorting by start is the enabling move for the entire merge-intervals family, and that almost every harder interval problem, like inserting an interval, finding intersections, or scheduling meeting rooms, builds on this same sort-and-sweep skeleton. I also stress the maximum-of-ends rule for contained intervals and the easily forgotten final flush, since those are the two places correctness slips, and I mention deciding deliberately whether touching intervals merge, which is a domain choice. Framing this as the base template for a whole category, plus naming the two subtle correctness details, is what tells an interviewer I understand it as a pattern rather than a one-off.

answers.question: Given a list of non-overlapping intervals sorted by start and a new interval to insert, insert the new interval and merge any overlaps so the result remains a sorted list of non-overlapping intervals. Solve it with the three-phase merge-intervals pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
answers.shortTitle: Insert Interval (Insert and Merge into a Sorted Interval List)

s1_definition.profdef: The insert interval problem takes an already sorted list of non-overlapping intervals and a new interval, and produces the sorted non-overlapping list after inserting and merging the new interval with any it overlaps. Because the input is already sorted, it is solved in a single linear pass in three phases: copy intervals that end before the new one begins, merge all intervals that overlap the new one into an expanded interval, then copy the remaining intervals that start after the merged interval ends.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh already has a tidy, sorted list of distinct account-hold periods and now needs to add one more hold that may overlap some existing ones. He walks the list once: he keeps every hold that finishes before the new hold starts untouched, he fuses the new hold with every hold it bumps into to form one bigger hold, and then he keeps the rest of the holds that begin after the new fused hold ends.
s1_definition.oneliner: In one pass, copy intervals before, merge intervals overlapping the new one, then copy intervals after.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The insert interval problem takes an already sorted list of non-overlapping intervals and a new interval, and produces the sorted non-overlapping list after inserting and merging the new interval with any it overlaps. Because the input is already sorted, it is solved in a single linear pass in three phases: copy intervals that end before the new one begins, merge all intervals that overlap the new one into an expanded interval, then copy the remaining intervals that start after the merged interval ends.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh already has a tidy, sorted list of distinct account-hold periods and now needs to add one more hold that may overlap some existing ones. He walks the list once: he keeps every hold that finishes before the new hold starts untouched, he fuses the new hold with every hold it bumps into to form one bigger hold, and then he keeps the rest of the holds that begin after the new fused hold ends.

**One line to remember:** In one pass, copy intervals before, merge intervals overlapping the new one, then copy intervals after.

sections.s2_technical:
Because the existing intervals are already sorted by start and are non-overlapping, we do not need to sort again, which lets us solve the problem in a single linear pass rather than n log n. We process the list in three clearly separated phases, which keeps the logic clean and avoids edge-case tangles.

In the first phase we copy, unchanged, every existing interval that ends strictly before the new interval starts, because such an interval lies entirely to the left of the new one and can never overlap it. The condition is `while (i < n && intervals[i].end < newInterval.start) result.add(intervals[i++]);`. In the second phase we merge: every remaining interval whose start is at or before the new interval's end overlaps it, so we fold it into the new interval by setting the new start to the minimum of the two starts and the new end to the maximum of the two ends. We keep doing this with `newStart = Math.min(newStart, intervals[i].start); newEnd = Math.max(newEnd, intervals[i].end); i++;` while the overlap condition holds, and once the loop ends we add the single expanded interval to the result.

In the third phase we copy, unchanged, all remaining intervals, which necessarily start after the merged interval ends and therefore do not overlap it. The senior-level nuance is that the merge phase must take the minimum of the starts as well as the maximum of the ends, because the new interval might begin before some overlapping existing interval, and that it must continue consuming intervals as long as they overlap, since the new interval can swallow several existing ones at once.

We build a fresh result list and do not mutate the input. The time complexity is linear, O(n), a single pass since the input is pre-sorted, and the space complexity is O(n) for the result. This three-phase structure is the standard clean solution and demonstrates that we exploit the pre-sorted precondition rather than redundantly re-sorting.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the account-hold system maintains a sorted, non-overlapping list of periods during which an account is on hold, and when a new hold is requested, perhaps for a fresh fraud investigation, it must be inserted into the list and merged with any existing holds it overlaps so the account's hold schedule stays a clean non-overlapping timeline. This is exactly the insert interval problem, and because the existing schedule is already sorted the insertion should be a fast single pass.

Problem 2 — Rebuilding and re-sorting the whole schedule on every new hold is wasteful when the list is already sorted. The three-phase single-pass insertion keeps the operation linear, which matters because holds are added frequently and the schedule can be long.

The insert interval problem gives me an already sorted list of non-overlapping intervals and a new interval, and asks for the sorted non-overlapping list after inserting and merging. Because the input is already sorted, I solve it in a single linear pass rather than re-sorting, which I do in three clearly separated phases to keep the edge cases tidy. In the third phase I copy the remaining intervals, which all start after the merged interval and cannot overlap.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the account-hold system. We maintained a sorted, non-overlapping schedule of periods during which an account was on hold, and whenever a new hold was requested, often for a fresh fraud investigation, we inserted it and merged it with any existing overlapping holds so the schedule stayed a clean non-overlapping timeline. Because the existing schedule was already sorted, the three-phase single pass kept each insertion linear, which mattered since holds were added frequently and schedules could be long.

The senior-level point I make is that this problem rewards exploiting the pre-sorted precondition: a candidate who re-sorts has missed that the whole value is doing it in one linear pass, and the three-phase structure is what makes that pass both correct and readable. I also stress the minimum-of-starts rule and the multi-interval absorption as the two places people slip, and I note that this builds directly on the merge-intervals skeleton, just with the sort already done for us. answers.question: Given two lists of closed intervals each sorted by start and internally non-overlapping, return the list of intervals representing their intersection. Solve it with the two-pointer merge-intervals pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
answers.shortTitle: Intervals Intersection (Interval List Intersections)

s1_definition.profdef: The intervals intersection problem takes two sorted, internally non-overlapping lists of closed intervals and produces the list of intervals where they overlap. It is solved in linear time with two pointers advancing through both lists simultaneously: at each step the overlap of the two current intervals, if any, is the maximum of their starts to the minimum of their ends, and we advance the pointer of whichever interval ends first because that interval cannot intersect anything further ahead in the other list.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has two sorted timelines, one of windows when an account was eligible for trading and one of windows when the market was open, and wants the windows when both conditions held at once. He walks both timelines together, and at each pair he takes the slice where they overlap, from the later start to the earlier end, then steps forward on whichever window closes first because it has nothing more to offer.
s1_definition.oneliner: Overlap is max-start to min-end; advance the pointer of whichever interval ends first.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The intervals intersection problem takes two sorted, internally non-overlapping lists of closed intervals and produces the list of intervals where they overlap. It is solved in linear time with two pointers advancing through both lists simultaneously: at each step the overlap of the two current intervals, if any, is the maximum of their starts to the minimum of their ends, and we advance the pointer of whichever interval ends first because that interval cannot intersect anything further ahead in the other list.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has two sorted timelines, one of windows when an account was eligible for trading and one of windows when the market was open, and wants the windows when both conditions held at once. He walks both timelines together, and at each pair he takes the slice where they overlap, from the later start to the earlier end, then steps forward on whichever window closes first because it has nothing more to offer.

**One line to remember:** Overlap is max-start to min-end; advance the pointer of whichever interval ends first.

sections.s2_technical:
Because both lists are already sorted by start and internally non-overlapping, we can scan them together with two pointers, one into each list, without any sorting. At each step we look at the current interval from the first list and the current interval from the second list and compute their potential overlap. The overlap starts at the later of the two starts and ends at the earlier of the two ends, so `lo = Math.max(a.start, b.start)` and `hi = Math.min(a.end, b.end)`.

If that computed low is less than or equal to that computed high, the two intervals genuinely overlap and the interval from low to high is a real intersection, so we add it to the result. If low is greater than high there is no overlap at this pair, and we add nothing. Either way we must decide which pointer to advance. We advance the pointer of the interval that ends earlier, because that interval has been fully accounted for: it cannot overlap any later interval in the other list, since all later intervals start even further to the right. Concretely `if (a.end < b.end) i++; else j++;`.

A subtle correctness point is handling equal ends. If the two current intervals end at the same value, advancing either pointer is acceptable, and advancing just one is sufficient because the next iteration will reconsider the pair. The senior-level nuance is understanding why we advance based on the end rather than the start: the interval that ends first is exhausted, and keeping it would only produce duplicate or spurious comparisons. This end-based advancement is the crux of the two-pointer interval merge.

We build a fresh result list and never mutate the inputs. The time complexity is linear, O(m plus n), where m and n are the two list lengths, because each pointer advances at most through its own list once, and the space complexity is O(1) beyond the output. This two-pointer technique is the standard solution for intersecting two sorted interval lists and generalizes to merging many sorted streams.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The intervals intersection problem takes two sorted, internally non-overlapping lists of closed intervals and asks for the list where they overlap, and I solve it in linear time with a two-pointer scan over both lists. At each step I look at the current interval from each list and compute their potential overlap as the later of the two starts to the earlier of the two ends. If that low is at most that high, the intervals genuinely overlap and I add that computed interval to the result; otherwise there is no overlap at this pair.

The decision that makes the scan work is which pointer to advance, and I advance the one whose interval ends earlier. That interval is fully exhausted because it cannot overlap any later interval in the other list, since all later intervals start even further right, so keeping it would only produce redundant comparisons. Advancing based on the end rather than the start is the crux of the technique, and when the two ends are equal advancing either one is fine because the next iteration reconsiders the pair.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the trading-window service. An automated trading account could only place orders when two independent conditions held simultaneously, an account eligibility window and a market open-session window, both maintained as sorted non-overlapping lists, and the engine needed the exact windows where both overlapped because only those were safe to trade in. The two-pointer scan computed all tradeable windows in a single linear pass over both lists, fast enough to run at session start.

The senior-level point I make is that because both inputs are already sorted I avoid any sorting entirely and get a linear pass, and that the end-based pointer advancement is the detail a shaky candidate gets wrong by advancing on the start. I also mention that this generalizes naturally: intersecting many sorted interval lists uses the same end-advance idea coordinated by a min-heap, which shows I see the pattern behind the specific problem. Explaining the max-start-to-min-end overlap, the end-advance rule, and the generalization to N lists is what tells an interviewer I own this technique rather than having memorized one case.

answers.question: Given a set of intervals each with a start and an end, determine whether any two of them overlap. Solve it with the sort-then-adjacent-check merge-intervals pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
answers.shortTitle: Overlapping Intervals (Determine If Any Two Intervals Overlap)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks whether any pair of intervals in a set overlaps, returning a simple yes or no. It is solved by sorting the intervals by start value and then checking only adjacent pairs in the sorted order: if any interval's start is strictly before the previous interval's end, an overlap exists. Sorting reduces the all-pairs question to a single linear adjacency scan, giving n log n total time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has a set of booking windows for a shared settlement resource and must confirm that none of them clash, because two concurrent bookings of the same exclusive resource would be a conflict. He lines the windows up by start time, then only needs to check each window against the one right before it, since after sorting any clash must involve neighbours.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort by start, then if any interval starts before the previous one ends, there is an overlap.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem asks whether any pair of intervals in a set overlaps, returning a simple yes or no. It is solved by sorting the intervals by start value and then checking only adjacent pairs in the sorted order: if any interval's start is strictly before the previous interval's end, an overlap exists. Sorting reduces the all-pairs question to a single linear adjacency scan, giving n log n total time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh has a set of booking windows for a shared settlement resource and must confirm that none of them clash, because two concurrent bookings of the same exclusive resource would be a conflict. He lines the windows up by start time, then only needs to check each window against the one right before it, since after sorting any clash must involve neighbours.

**One line to remember:** Sort by start, then if any interval starts before the previous one ends, there is an overlap.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach compares every pair of intervals, which is quadratic. The key realization is that after sorting the intervals by their start value, any overlap must occur between two intervals that are adjacent in the sorted order, or at least will be detected by comparing adjacent intervals. This is because if interval A comes before interval B in start order and they overlap, then B starts before A ends, and this relationship surfaces when we compare each interval to its immediate predecessor.

So we sort by start and then walk the sorted list from the second interval onward, comparing each interval to the previous one. The overlap test is whether the current interval's start is strictly less than the previous interval's end, written `if (current.start < previous.end) return true;`. We use strictly less than when touching intervals, where the current start equals the previous end, are considered non-overlapping, which is common for booking windows where one ending exactly as the next begins is allowed. If the domain treats touching as a clash, we use less than or equal to instead.

An important subtlety is which end we compare against. After sorting by start, the previous interval in iteration order has the smaller or equal start, but its end could be larger than the current interval's end if the current is contained within the previous. Comparing the current start to the previous end correctly catches this containment case too, because a contained interval starts before the enclosing interval ends. The senior-level nuance is that we compare against the previous interval's end specifically, and if we wanted to handle a run of intervals we would track the running maximum end, but for a pure any-overlap existence check comparing to the immediate predecessor's end after sorting is sufficient because we return on the first clash.

We return false only after the full scan finds no adjacent overlap. The time complexity is n log n dominated by the sort, with the adjacency scan linear, and the space complexity is O(1) beyond the sort, or O(n) if we copy before sorting to avoid mutating the input. This sort-then-adjacent-check is the lightest member of the merge-intervals family and a frequent warm-up before the full merge.

This problem asks whether any two intervals in a set overlap, a simple yes or no, and I solve it in n log n time by sorting the intervals by start value and then checking only adjacent pairs. Comparing the current start to the previous end also correctly catches a fully contained interval, because a contained interval starts before its enclosing interval ends.

Sorting the windows by start and checking only adjacent pairs answered the clash question in n log n time, which kept booking confirmation fast even when many desks submitted windows.

The senior-level point I make is that sorting collapses an all-pairs question into a single adjacency scan, which is the same enabling insight as the full merge-intervals problem, making this the lightweight warm-up of that family. I also stress the deliberate choice between strict and non-strict comparison for touching intervals, since that is a real domain decision rather than a detail, and I note that the containment case is handled for free by comparing against the previous end. Framing this as the existence-only cousin of merge intervals and calling out the touching-policy decision is what tells an interviewer I understand the whole family rather than one isolated problem.

answers.question: Given an array containing `n` distinct numbers taken from the range `1` to `n` (or `0` to `n-1`), sort the array in place in O(n) time and O(1) extra space without using any sorting library. Explain the Cyclic Sort pattern and where it applies.
answers.shortTitle: Cyclic Sort (Place Each Number at Its Correct Index)

s1_definition.profdef: Cyclic Sort is an in-place sorting technique for arrays whose values form a known contiguous range, typically `1..n` or `0..n-1`. Because every value has exactly one correct index (value `v` belongs at index `v-1`), the algorithm walks the array once and repeatedly swaps the current element to its rightful slot until the slot already holds the right value, giving O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India numbers its night-deposit lockers 1 to n, and at closing a clerk finds the locker keys scattered on the counter. Key 5 belongs in locker 5, key 1 in locker 1. The clerk picks up whatever key is in front of them, walks it to its matching locker, and takes whatever key was already sitting there, repeating until the front slot holds the right key, then moves on. No key is carried twice unnecessarily, so the whole counter is tidied in one disciplined pass.
s1_definition.oneliner: When values are a permutation of `1..n`, the value itself tells you its home index, so one swap-until-correct pass sorts in linear time.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Cyclic Sort is an in-place sorting technique for arrays whose values form a known contiguous range, typically `1..n` or `0..n-1`. Because every value has exactly one correct index (value `v` belongs at index `v-1`), the algorithm walks the array once and repeatedly swaps the current element to its rightful slot until the slot already holds the right value, giving O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India numbers its night-deposit lockers 1 to n, and at closing a clerk finds the locker keys scattered on the counter. Key 5 belongs in locker 5, key 1 in locker 1. The clerk picks up whatever key is in front of them, walks it to its matching locker, and takes whatever key was already sitting there, repeating until the front slot holds the right key, then moves on. No key is carried twice unnecessarily, so the whole counter is tidied in one disciplined pass.

**One line to remember:** When values are a permutation of `1..n`, the value itself tells you its home index, so one swap-until-correct pass sorts in linear time.

sections.s2_technical:
The core invariant is that a number `v` in a `1..n` array must live at index `v-1`. The algorithm keeps a pointer `i` at the current position. It computes the target index `j = nums[i] - 1`. If `nums[i]` is not already sitting at its target (`nums[i] != nums[j]`), it swaps `nums[i]` with `nums[j]`. Crucially it does NOT advance `i` after a swap, because the element just moved into position `i` might itself be out of place. Only when `nums[i]` is already correct does it advance `i`.

The reason this is O(n) rather than O(n^2) despite the nested feel is amortized counting: each swap places at least one number into its final correct index permanently, and there are only `n` numbers, so at most `n` swaps happen across the entire run. For example, to settle account slots `int[] slots = {3,1,5,4,2};` the loop does `while (slots[i] != slots[slots[i]-1]) swap(slots, i, slots[i]-1);` and after the full pass `slots` becomes `{1,2,3,4,5}`.

A senior-level nuance is the guard condition. Comparing `nums[i] != nums[j]` rather than `i != j` makes the algorithm robust if duplicates ever appear, preventing an infinite swap loop between two equal values. For the strict `1..n` distinct case either guard works, but the value-comparison guard is the safer habit and is exactly what the duplicate-finding variants of this pattern rely on. The pattern only applies when the range is known and dense; it is not a general comparison sort.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the overnight batch produces a list of settlement sequence numbers that are supposed to be a clean 1 to n with no gaps, one per transaction in the day's batch. A feeder system delivers them shuffled, and before the reconciliation report can run, the operations team needs them arranged in order so each sequence number sits at its natural position for a fast index lookup. Re-running a full comparison sort every night on millions of numbers wastes CPU when the data is guaranteed to be a permutation of 1 to n. This is exactly how Cyclic Sort works: because each sequence number equals its own position plus one, we can place every number home in a single linear pass.

Problem 2 — The team also wants a reusable primitive, because the same place-it-at-its-index idea is about to power missing-number and duplicate detection in later batches. So we build a small `SettlementSequencer` with a `cyclicSort` method that other services can call.

Input data: `batch = {3,1,5,4,2}`.

Step 2: `i=0`, `seq[0]=5`, correct index is 4. `seq[4]=2` differs, swap positions 0 and 4. Array becomes `{2,1,3,4,5}`. `i` stays at 0.

Step 3: `i=0`, `seq[0]=2`, correct index is 1. `seq[1]=1` differs, swap 0 and 1. Array becomes `{1,2,3,4,5}`. `i` stays at 0.

Step 4: `i=0`, `seq[0]=1`, correct index is 0, and `seq[0]==seq[0]`, so advance `i` to 1. Positions 1 through 4 are each already correct, so `i` advances cleanly to the end.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Cyclic Sort is an in-place linear-time technique that applies when the array values form a known dense range such as one to n. The defining insight is that each value has exactly one correct home index, namely the value minus one, so instead of comparing elements against each other I simply carry each value to its rightful slot. I keep a pointer at the current position, compute the target index from the value there, and swap it home if it is not already correct, and critically I do not advance the pointer after a swap because the element that just arrived may itself be misplaced.

The reason it runs in linear time rather than quadratic is amortized: every swap permanently settles at least one number into its final position, and there are only n numbers, so no more than n swaps ever occur across the whole run. I guard the swap with a value comparison rather than an index comparison, which keeps the loop safe even if duplicates sneak in, and that same place-it-at-its-index habit is what powers the missing-number and duplicate-detection variants of this pattern.

In my work at the National Bank of India I used this in the nightly settlement job. The batch delivered settlement sequence numbers that were guaranteed to be a permutation of one to n but arrived shuffled, and re-running a full comparison sort every night was wasteful. Cyclic Sort arranged them in a single disciplined pass with no extra memory, which kept the reconciliation window fast even on very large batches. What I stress to an interviewer is that recognizing the bounded-range precondition is the whole skill: the moment the values are a permutation of one to n, a general O(n log n) sort is the wrong tool and this pattern is the right one.
