answers.question: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth, the number of nodes along the longest path from the root down to the farthest leaf.
answers.shortTitle: Maximum Depth of a Binary Tree (Count the Levels via BFS)

s1_definition.profdef: With Tree BFS, the maximum depth equals the number of levels processed. Run level-by-level BFS incrementing a counter once per level; when the queue empties, the counter holds the maximum depth. Unlike minimum depth, there is no early exit because every node must be visited to find the farthest leaf.
s1_definition.analogy: The maximum depth of the National Bank of India approval tree is the longest chain of sign-offs from the branch head down to the deepest end approver. You count every rank you process; the last rank number you reach is the longest chain length.
s1_definition.oneliner: BFS and count the levels; the number of levels is the maximum depth.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** With Tree BFS, the maximum depth equals the number of levels processed. Run level-by-level BFS incrementing a counter once per level; when the queue empties, the counter holds the maximum depth. Unlike minimum depth, there is no early exit because every node must be visited to find the farthest leaf.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The maximum depth of the National Bank of India approval tree is the longest chain of sign-offs from the branch head down to the deepest end approver. You count every rank you process; the last rank number you reach is the longest chain length.

**One line to remember:** BFS and count the levels; the number of levels is the maximum depth.

sections.s2_technical:
The queue-based BFS processes one full level per outer iteration using the level-size snapshot, incrementing `depth` each time a non-empty level begins. Because every node contributes to determining the farthest leaf, the whole tree is traversed, giving O(n) time and O(w) space for the widest level. When the queue drains, `depth` is the answer.

For example a tree with three levels returns 3. The BFS version counts levels directly, while the one-line recursive version `1 + max(maxDepth(left), maxDepth(right))` computes the same value through the call stack with O(h) space.

A senior-level nuance is the space comparison: recursive DFS uses stack proportional to height h, which is O(log n) for balanced trees but O(n) for degenerate ones, whereas BFS uses space proportional to the maximum width. For a bushy tree DFS can be far more memory-efficient, so unlike minimum depth, maximum depth does not favor BFS and the choice is driven by tree shape and recursion-depth safety.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India audits the longest approval chain in its hierarchy to ensure no request requires an excessive number of sign-offs, which would slow service. The system must measure the deepest path in the approval tree. This is exactly maximum depth: BFS counting every level, or equivalently a recursive depth computation.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the maximum depth of a binary tree with breadth first search simply means counting the levels. I run the level-by-level traversal, incrementing a depth counter once at the start of each non-empty level, and when the queue finally drains, that counter holds the number of levels, which is exactly the length of the longest path from the root to the farthest leaf. Unlike minimum depth, there is no early exit here, because determining the farthest leaf requires visiting every node.

I always contrast this with the recursive depth-first version, which computes one plus the maximum of the left and right subtree depths. Both are linear in time, but they differ in space: recursion uses stack proportional to the tree's height, which is logarithmic for a balanced tree but linear for a degenerate one, while BFS uses space proportional to the widest level. So for a bushy tree the recursive version can be far lighter, meaning maximum depth, unlike minimum depth, does not inherently favor BFS, and I choose based on tree shape and the risk of deep recursion.

In my work at the National Bank of India this audited the longest approval chain to ensure no request demanded an excessive number of sign-offs that would slow customer service. Measuring the deepest path in the approval tree by counting BFS levels gave that chain length directly, and being able to articulate the BFS-versus-DFS space trade-off is what signals to an interviewer that I understand the problem beyond just producing the number.

answers.question: Given the root of a binary tree and the value of a target node, find its level order successor, the node that appears immediately after the target in a breadth-first traversal. Return null if the target is the last node.
answers.shortTitle: Level Order Successor (Next Node in BFS Order)

s1_definition.profdef: Perform a plain Tree BFS without tracking level boundaries, enqueuing children as usual. When the dequeued node equals the target, the very next node still in the queue (the next to be dequeued) is its level order successor. Return that node, or null if the queue is then empty.
s1_definition.analogy: In the National Bank of India approval tree processed rank by rank left to right, the successor of a given approver is simply the next approver who would be called after them in that same sweep, even if that next approver is on the following rank.
s1_definition.oneliner: BFS without level tracking; once you dequeue the target, the next node waiting in the queue is the successor.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Perform a plain Tree BFS without tracking level boundaries, enqueuing children as usual. When the dequeued node equals the target, the very next node still in the queue (the next to be dequeued) is its level order successor. Return that node, or null if the queue is then empty.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** In the National Bank of India approval tree processed rank by rank left to right, the successor of a given approver is simply the next approver who would be called after them in that same sweep, even if that next approver is on the following rank.

**One line to remember:** BFS without level tracking; once you dequeue the target, the next node waiting in the queue is the successor.

sections.s2_technical:
Because the successor is defined across the entire BFS order (it may be the first node of the next level), you do not need the level-size snapshot here. Enqueue the root, then loop: dequeue a node, enqueue its children, and if the node you just dequeued is the target, break out; the next `queue.poll()` (or `queue.peek()`) is the successor. If the queue is empty after the target, there is no successor.

For example in a tree whose BFS order is 1,2,3,4,5, the successor of 3 is 4, and the successor of 5 is null. A clean way: after dequeuing and enqueuing children, check `if (node.id == target) break;` then return the queue's head.

A senior-level nuance is that children must be enqueued before the break check, so that when the target is the last node of its level, its children (the next level's start) are already in the queue and the successor is found correctly. Forgetting to enqueue first produces a wrong null at level boundaries, a subtle but common error.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes approvers in strict breadth-first order, and when one approver is unavailable the workflow must route the request to the next approver in that same processing order, which may be on the next rank. The system must find the level order successor of a given approver node. This is exactly level order successor: BFS and return the next queued node after the target.

The code contains a `RouteNode`, a `SuccessorRouter` with `levelOrderSuccessor(root, target)`, and a demo.

Step 2: Dequeue 2, enqueue children 4,5. Node 2 is not the target. Queue is [3,4,5].

Step 3: Dequeue 3, it has no children to enqueue. Node 3 equals the target, so break. Queue is [4,5].

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the level order successor is a lightweight Tree BFS variant because the successor is defined across the entire breadth-first order rather than within a single level, so I deliberately do not use the level-size snapshot. I enqueue the root and then repeatedly dequeue a node, enqueue its children, and check whether the node I just dequeued is the target. When it is, I stop, and the node now sitting at the head of the queue, the next one that would be dequeued, is the successor; if the queue is empty, the target was the last node and there is no successor.

The subtle but critical detail is that I enqueue a node's children before I check whether it was the target. That ordering guarantees that when the target happens to be the last node of its level, the first node of the next level is already waiting in the queue, so the successor is found correctly across the level boundary. Skipping that ordering produces a wrong null exactly at boundaries, which is the common trap in this problem.

In my work at the National Bank of India this drove approver fallback routing. Approvers were processed in strict breadth-first order, and when one approver was unavailable the request had to flow to the next approver in that same order, possibly on the following rank. Running the plain BFS, enqueuing children first, and returning the queue head after matching the target gave the correct next approver every time.

answers.question: Given a binary tree where each node has an extra `next` pointer, connect each node to its immediate right neighbor on the same level. The last node of each level should point to null.
answers.shortTitle: Connect Level Order Siblings (Populate Next Right Pointers per Level)

s1_definition.profdef: Run Tree BFS with the level-size snapshot. While draining a level, keep a reference to the previously dequeued node and set `previous.next = currentNode`; the first node of each level has no left neighbor, and the last node's `next` stays null by default. After processing, each level forms a left-to-right linked list via `next`.
s1_definition.analogy: In the National Bank of India approval tree, every approver on a rank should know who sits to their immediate right on the same rank, so a request can slide sideways along a rank. You walk each rank left to right and clip each approver to the next one on that rank.
s1_definition.oneliner: BFS per level; within a level, link each node's `next` to the node dequeued right after it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Run Tree BFS with the level-size snapshot. While draining a level, keep a reference to the previously dequeued node and set `previous.next = currentNode`; the first node of each level has no left neighbor, and the last node's `next` stays null by default. After processing, each level forms a left-to-right linked list via `next`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** In the National Bank of India approval tree, every approver on a rank should know who sits to their immediate right on the same rank, so a request can slide sideways along a rank. You walk each rank left to right and clip each approver to the next one on that rank.

**One line to remember:** BFS per level; within a level, link each node's `next` to the node dequeued right after it.

sections.s2_technical:
The level-size snapshot isolates each level. While draining, maintain a `previous` pointer initialized to null at the start of each level. For each dequeued node, if `previous` is not null set `previous.next = node`, then set `previous = node`. Enqueue children as usual. At the level's end, the last node's `next` remains null because nothing follows it. This wires each level into a singly linked chain through the `next` field.

For example a perfect tree level [4,5,6,7] ends with 4.next=5, 5.next=6, 6.next=7, 7.next=null. The connections are built purely from dequeue order, which is already left to right.

A senior-level nuance is that this BFS solution uses O(w) queue space, whereas the famous follow-up achieves O(1) extra space by using the `next` pointers already built on the current level to traverse and wire the next level without a queue. For a perfect binary tree that O(1) approach is expected at senior level; for a general tree the queue-based version is the robust, clearly correct choice.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants horizontal routing across each rank of its approval tree so a stalled request can be handed to the approver immediately to the right on the same rank without going back up to a parent. Each node needs a `next` pointer to its right sibling-level neighbor. This is exactly connect-level-order-siblings: BFS and link each node to the next within its level.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Connecting level order siblings means giving every node a next pointer to its immediate right neighbor on the same level, and I solve it with Tree BFS and the level-size snapshot. As I drain each level I keep a previous pointer, reset to null at the start of every level, and for each node I set the previous node's next to the current node before advancing previous. Because the dequeue order within a level is already left to right, this wires each level into a singly linked chain, and the last node of each level naturally keeps a null next because nothing follows it.

I always mention the famous follow-up: the queue-based solution uses space proportional to the widest level, but for a perfect binary tree there is an elegant constant-space version that reuses the next pointers already established on the current level to stitch the next level without any queue at all. At senior level the interviewer often expects that O(1) approach, while the queue version remains the robust, obviously correct choice for a general tree.

In my work at the National Bank of India this enabled horizontal routing across each rank of the approval tree, so a stalled request could be handed to the approver immediately to the right on the same rank instead of bubbling back up to a parent. Building the next pointers level by level with the previous-node linking gave exactly that sideways navigation.

answers.question: Given a binary tree with an extra `next` pointer on each node, connect all nodes so that `next` forms a single continuous chain in level order: the last node of each level points to the first node of the next level, not to null.
answers.shortTitle: Connect All Level Order Siblings (One Continuous Next Chain)

s1_definition.profdef: A variant of connect-level-order-siblings where level boundaries are not broken. Run Tree BFS without the level-size snapshot, maintaining a single `previous` pointer across the entire traversal, and for each dequeued node set `previous.next = node`. The result is one unbroken next chain spanning the whole tree in BFS order.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants one continuous routing path through every approver in breadth-first order, so a request can flow from the last approver on a rank straight to the first approver on the next rank without stopping. You clip every approver to the next one in the whole sweep.
s1_definition.oneliner: BFS without level breaks; link every node's `next` to the very next dequeued node across all levels.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A variant of connect-level-order-siblings where level boundaries are not broken. Run Tree BFS without the level-size snapshot, maintaining a single `previous` pointer across the entire traversal, and for each dequeued node set `previous.next = node`. The result is one unbroken next chain spanning the whole tree in BFS order.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants one continuous routing path through every approver in breadth-first order, so a request can flow from the last approver on a rank straight to the first approver on the next rank without stopping. You clip every approver to the next one in the whole sweep.

**One line to remember:** BFS without level breaks; link every node's `next` to the very next dequeued node across all levels.

sections.s2_technical:
Because the chain is continuous, there is no per-level reset; a single `previous` pointer persists for the whole traversal. Enqueue the root, then dequeue each node, set `previous.next = node` when `previous` is not null, advance `previous`, and enqueue children. The very last node of the whole tree ends with `next` null because nothing follows it.

For example a perfect tree yields the chain 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> 7 -> null, crossing level boundaries seamlessly. The only difference from the per-level version is dropping the level-size snapshot and not resetting `previous`.

A senior-level nuance is the distinction candidates often blur: connect-siblings terminates each level with null, while connect-all produces a single list. Both are the same BFS; the difference is purely whether `previous` resets per level. Articulating that single-pointer-persistence difference crisply is what separates a precise answer from a vague one.

Each node's `next` must point to the next approver in the whole BFS order. This is exactly connect-all-level-order-siblings: BFS with one persistent previous pointer.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Connecting all level order siblings produces one continuous next chain that threads every node in breadth-first order, crossing level boundaries instead of terminating each level with null. I solve it with the same Tree BFS, but with one crucial difference from the per-level version: I keep a single previous pointer that persists for the entire traversal and never resets at a level boundary. For each node I dequeue, I set the previous node's next to it and advance previous, and only the very last node of the whole tree ends with a null next.

The point I make crisply in an interview is the precise difference between this and connect-level-order-siblings. Both are the identical BFS traversal; the only distinction is whether the previous pointer resets at each level. Resetting per level terminates each level with null, which is connect-siblings, while keeping one persistent pointer produces a single unbroken list, which is connect-all. Being able to state that difference in one sentence demonstrates real understanding rather than memorized code.

In my work at the National Bank of India this built a continuous escalation thread that threaded every approver in breadth-first order, so an automated sweep could walk from the branch head through every approver without ever needing to reason about level boundaries. Running the BFS with a single persistent previous pointer wired that unbroken chain in one pass.

answers.question: Given the root of a binary tree, imagine standing on the right side of it; return the values of the nodes visible from the right, ordered top to bottom. This is the last node of each level in a level order traversal.
answers.shortTitle: Right View of a Binary Tree (Last Node of Each Level)

s1_definition.profdef: Run Tree BFS with the level-size snapshot and, for each level, record only the last node dequeued (when the index equals `levelSize - 1`). Those last nodes, top to bottom, are the right-side view. Time O(n), space O(w).
s1_definition.analogy: Looking at the National Bank of India approval tree from the right edge, you see only the rightmost approver on each rank, because they block the view of everyone to their left on that rank. Collecting the rightmost approver per rank top to bottom is the right view.
s1_definition.oneliner: BFS per level; capture the last node of each level into the result.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Run Tree BFS with the level-size snapshot and, for each level, record only the last node dequeued (when the index equals `levelSize - 1`). Those last nodes, top to bottom, are the right-side view. Time O(n), space O(w).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Looking at the National Bank of India approval tree from the right edge, you see only the rightmost approver on each rank, because they block the view of everyone to their left on that rank. Collecting the rightmost approver per rank top to bottom is the right view.

**One line to remember:** BFS per level; capture the last node of each level into the result.

sections.s2_technical:
The traversal is standard BFS with the level-size snapshot. Inside the drain loop, compare the loop index to `levelSize - 1`; when they match, that node is the last of its level, so add its value to the result. Enqueue children left then right as usual. The result ends up as the rightmost node per level in top-to-bottom order.

For example a tree with levels [1], [2,3], [4] yields right view [1,3,4], where level 3 has only the single node 4 even though it descends from the left side. That example shows the right view is not simply the right spine; it is the last node per level regardless of which parent it came from.

A senior-level nuance is exactly that subtlety: naive candidates follow only right children and get the wrong answer when the right subtree is shorter than the left. The level-based last-node rule is correct precisely because it is defined per level, not per branch. The symmetric left view just captures the first node of each level instead.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The right view of a binary tree is the set of nodes visible when standing on its right side, and the correct definition is the last node of each level, top to bottom. I compute it with Tree BFS and the level-size snapshot, and inside the drain loop I compare the loop index to the level size minus one; when they match, that node is the last of its level, so I add its value to the result. Children are enqueued left then right as usual.

The subtlety that I always highlight is that the right view is not simply the chain of right children. If the left subtree runs deeper than the right, the last node on a lower level can descend entirely from the left side, and a naive right-spine walk would miss it. Defining the answer per level rather than per branch is exactly what makes the level-based last-node rule correct, and the symmetric left view is the same algorithm capturing the first node of each level.

In my work at the National Bank of India this produced a right-edge approval summary showing the final approver on each rank, representing the most senior approver reachable at that depth on the right flank, and it had to stay correct even when the left side of the hierarchy ran deeper. Capturing the last node of each level with BFS gave that summary accurately, and being able to explain why it is not the right spine is what demonstrates genuine command of the problem.

answers.shortTitle: Left View of a Binary Tree (First Node of Each Level)

s1_definition.analogy: Looking at the National Bank of India approval tree from the left edge, you see only the leftmost approver on each rank, because they stand in front of everyone to their right on that rank. Collecting the leftmost approver per rank top to bottom is the left view.
s1_definition.oneliner: BFS per level; capture the first node of each level into the result.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The mirror of the right view. Run Tree BFS with the level-size snapshot and, for each level, record only the first node dequeued (when the index equals `0`). Those first nodes, top to bottom, are the left-side view. Time O(n), space O(w).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Looking at the National Bank of India approval tree from the left edge, you see only the leftmost approver on each rank, because they stand in front of everyone to their right on that rank. Collecting the leftmost approver per rank top to bottom is the left view.

**One line to remember:** BFS per level; capture the first node of each level into the result.

sections.s2_technical:
The traversal is the standard BFS with the level-size snapshot, enqueuing children left then right. Inside the drain loop, when the loop index is `0` the node is the first of its level, so add its value to the result. The result becomes the leftmost node per level in top-to-bottom order.

For example a tree with levels [1], [2,3], [4,5] gives left view [1,2,4]. As with the right view, the left view is defined per level, so the first node on a lower level can descend from a right subtree if the left side is shorter; the rule `i == 0` captures it correctly regardless of parentage.

A senior-level nuance is the symmetry with the right view and the common bug: following only left children fails when the right subtree runs deeper. The level-based first-node rule avoids that. An equally valid DFS variant visits left before right and records the first node seen at each new depth, using a depth-indexed result; both are O(n), and the BFS version is often clearer to reason about.

answers.question: Given a binary tree and a target sum, determine whether the tree has any root-to-leaf path such that adding up all the node values along the path equals the target sum. Return true or false, and explain why a depth-first traversal is the natural fit for this problem.
answers.shortTitle: Binary Tree Path Sum (Does a Root-to-Leaf Path Equal a Target?)

s1_definition.profdef: Binary Tree Path Sum is a Tree Depth First Search problem where we walk from the root down to each leaf, subtracting each node's value from the running target as we descend. The answer is true if and only if we reach a leaf node where the remaining target exactly equals that leaf's value. The traversal is recursive and visits every node once, so it runs in linear time in the number of nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height of the tree.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine at the National Bank of India there is an approval hierarchy. Rajesh submits a request and it flows down a chain of approvers, and each approver adds a fee. We want to know if there is any complete top-to-bottom chain whose total fee adds up to exactly the budget we set aside. We follow one chain all the way to the bottom, keep subtracting each fee from the budget, and when we reach the final approver we check if the budget landed exactly at zero.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk each root-to-leaf path depth first, subtract as you go, and declare success when a leaf makes the remainder exactly zero.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Binary Tree Path Sum is a Tree Depth First Search problem where we walk from the root down to each leaf, subtracting each node's value from the running target as we descend. The answer is true if and only if we reach a leaf node where the remaining target exactly equals that leaf's value. The traversal is recursive and visits every node once, so it runs in linear time in the number of nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height of the tree.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine at the National Bank of India there is an approval hierarchy. Rajesh submits a request and it flows down a chain of approvers, and each approver adds a fee. We want to know if there is any complete top-to-bottom chain whose total fee adds up to exactly the budget we set aside. We follow one chain all the way to the bottom, keep subtracting each fee from the budget, and when we reach the final approver we check if the budget landed exactly at zero.

**One line to remember:** Walk each root-to-leaf path depth first, subtract as you go, and declare success when a leaf makes the remainder exactly zero.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is that a root-to-leaf path is naturally explored by recursion. We define a helper method `hasPath(node, target)` that returns a boolean. At each node we subtract the node's value from the target. If the node is a leaf, meaning both children are null, we return whether the remaining target now equals zero. For example, `if (node.left == null && node.right == null) return remaining == 0;` captures the leaf test precisely.

If the node is not a leaf, we recurse into whichever children exist and combine the results with a logical OR, because a single successful path anywhere is enough. For example, `return hasPath(node.left, remaining) || hasPath(node.right, remaining);` short-circuits as soon as one branch succeeds, which is a small but real efficiency win.

A senior-level nuance is the leaf definition. We must only declare success at a true leaf, not at a null child, otherwise a path that happens to pass through a node whose value equals the remaining target would falsely succeed even though the path has not ended. Another nuance is that values can be negative in general trees, so we cannot prune a branch early just because the remaining target went negative; we must reach a leaf to decide. In a banking fee model where every fee is positive we could prune, but the general algorithm does not assume that.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, a transfer request from Rajesh travels through a tree of approval desks. Each desk charges a processing fee in rupees, and the bank's compliance team wants to confirm that at least one complete approval chain, from the top desk down to a final signing desk, carries a total fee that matches an agreed budget exactly. This matters because a chain that overshoots or undershoots the budget indicates a misconfigured desk. This is exactly how Binary Tree Path Sum works: the running budget is the target, each desk's fee is a node value, and a final signing desk is a leaf.

Problem 2 — The compliance team does not care which chain matches, only whether any chain matches. This is why the algorithm returns a plain boolean and stops early on the first match, because once a valid chain is found the configuration is proven acceptable.

The code will define an `ApprovalNode` class holding a desk name and a `BigDecimal` fee plus left and right child desks. A `PathSumService` will expose `hasApprovalChainMatching(root, budget)` that drives a recursive depth-first search. A small `Demo` main method will build a sample approval tree for Rajesh's transfer and check two budgets, one that matches and one that does not, logging each descent.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the approval tree with Branch(100) as root, Regional(250) and Audit(150) as children, SignA(50) and SignB(400) under Regional, and a budget of 400.

Step 1: We enter at Branch with budget 400. We subtract the fee 100, leaving a remaining budget of 300. Branch is not a leaf, so we recurse left into Regional carrying 300.

Step 2: At Regional we subtract 250 from 300, leaving 50. Regional is not a leaf, so we recurse left into SignA carrying 50.

Step 3: At SignA we subtract 50 from 50, leaving exactly 0. SignA is a leaf, and the remaining budget equals zero, so this branch returns true.

Step 4: The true result short-circuits back up through Regional and Branch, so we never explore Audit or SignB. The final answer is true.

```
  2.   → hasApprovalChainMatching(Regional, 300)  remaining 50
  3.     → hasApprovalChainMatching(SignA, 50)  remaining 0 → leaf → true
  4.   OR short-circuits; Audit/SignB skipped
  5. return true

  Contract for hasApprovalChainMatching(root, budget):
    Pre:  root may be null; budget is a BigDecimal
    Post: true iff some root-to-leaf fee sum equals budget
    Returns: boolean; stops on first match
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Binary Tree Path Sum asks whether any root-to-leaf path in a binary tree adds up to a given target, and it is a classic Tree Depth First Search problem. I solve it recursively: at each node I subtract the node's value from the running target, and when I reach a leaf I check whether the remaining target is exactly zero. For internal nodes I combine the results of the left and right recursions with a logical OR, so the search stops as soon as one valid path is found. The traversal visits each node once, giving linear time, and the recursion stack uses space proportional to the height of the tree.

The single most important correctness detail is the leaf test. I only declare success at a true leaf, where both children are null, never at a null child, because otherwise a path that merely passes through a node whose value equals the remaining target would falsely succeed before the path actually ends. I also keep in mind that node values can be negative in a general tree, so I cannot prune a branch just because the remaining target went below zero; I must descend to a leaf to decide.

In my work at the National Bank of India I used this exact pattern to validate approval-fee chains. A transfer request from Rajesh flowed through a tree of approval desks, each charging a processing fee, and compliance needed to confirm that at least one full top-to-bottom chain carried fees summing precisely to an agreed budget. I modelled each desk as a node with a BigDecimal fee, drove the depth-first search from the top desk, and returned true the moment a signing desk closed a chain at exactly zero remaining budget. Explaining the leaf-only success rule and the money-safe BigDecimal comparison is what shows an interviewer I understand both the algorithm and its real banking consequences.

answers.question: Given a binary tree and a target sum, find all root-to-leaf paths where the sum of the node values equals the target. Return the list of paths, and explain how backtracking lets you reuse one working list instead of copying at every node.
answers.shortTitle: All Paths for a Sum (Collect Every Root-to-Leaf Path Matching a Target)

s1_definition.profdef: All Paths for a Sum extends the single-boolean path-sum problem into a collection problem. We perform a depth-first traversal, pushing each node's value onto a running path list as we descend and popping it as we return, which is the backtracking step. Whenever we reach a leaf whose accumulated sum equals the target, we take a defensive copy of the running path and add it to the results. Time is linear to visit the tree plus the cost of copying each qualifying path, and space is proportional to the tree height plus the stored results.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, instead of asking "does any approval chain cost exactly the budget," compliance now wants the full list of every approval chain whose fees add up to the budget. We walk down each chain writing the desk names on a notepad, and whenever a complete chain hits the budget we photocopy the notepad into our report. Then we erase the last desk and try the next branch, reusing the same notepad.
s1_definition.oneliner: Depth-first with a running path, copy the path at every matching leaf, and backtrack by removing the node on the way back up.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** All Paths for a Sum extends the single-boolean path-sum problem into a collection problem. We perform a depth-first traversal, pushing each node's value onto a running path list as we descend and popping it as we return, which is the backtracking step. Whenever we reach a leaf whose accumulated sum equals the target, we take a defensive copy of the running path and add it to the results. Time is linear to visit the tree plus the cost of copying each qualifying path, and space is proportional to the tree height plus the stored results.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, instead of asking "does any approval chain cost exactly the budget," compliance now wants the full list of every approval chain whose fees add up to the budget. We walk down each chain writing the desk names on a notepad, and whenever a complete chain hits the budget we photocopy the notepad into our report. Then we erase the last desk and try the next branch, reusing the same notepad.

**One line to remember:** Depth-first with a running path, copy the path at every matching leaf, and backtrack by removing the node on the way back up.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep a single mutable list that represents the current path from the root to the node we are visiting. Before recursing into children we append the current node, for example `currentPath.add(node)`, and after both recursions return we remove it, for example `currentPath.remove(currentPath.size() - 1)`. This add-then-remove discipline is backtracking: the same list is reused for every path, which avoids allocating a fresh list at every node.

When we reach a leaf and the remaining target equals the leaf's value, we must store a snapshot, not the live list, for example `results.add(new ArrayList<>(currentPath))`. Forgetting the copy is the most common bug, because the live list keeps changing as backtracking continues, so all stored references would end up pointing at the same emptied list.

A senior-level nuance is that the total work is not simply linear when many paths qualify, because copying a path of length h costs O(h), and there can be up to O(n) leaves, giving O(n·h) in the worst case. That is inherent to returning the paths themselves rather than just a count. Another nuance is that we add the node to the path regardless of whether it is a leaf, and we only test the sum at a leaf, keeping the descent logic uniform.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India compliance team audits Rajesh's transfer approval tree and needs the complete list of every root-to-leaf approval chain whose processing fees sum to the agreed budget. A single yes-or-no answer is no longer enough because auditors must document each acceptable chain by desk name. This is exactly how All Paths for a Sum works: each full desk chain is one path, and we collect every chain that hits the budget.

Problem 2 — Building a brand-new list for every desk we touch would waste memory on a deep hierarchy. This is why we keep one running desk list and backtrack, removing the last desk as we climb back, so memory stays proportional to the current depth rather than to the whole tree.

The code defines an `ApprovalNode` with a desk name and `BigDecimal` fee. An `AllPathsService` exposes `findAllChainsMatching(root, budget)` returning a list of desk-name lists. A `Demo` builds a tree where two separate chains both sum to the budget, proving the collector returns both.

sections.s6_takeaway:
All Paths for a Sum is the collection version of the path-sum problem: instead of a single boolean, I return every root-to-leaf path whose node values add up to the target. I solve it with a depth-first traversal that carries one running path list. As I descend I append the current node to that list and subtract its value from the target, and when I reach a leaf whose remaining target is zero I store a defensive copy of the list in my results. After exploring both children I remove the current node, which is the backtracking step that lets me reuse the same list for every path.

The detail I always stress is that I store a copy, not the live list. If I added the live reference, continued backtracking would keep mutating it, and every stored path would end up pointing at the same emptied list. I also note that returning the paths themselves is not strictly linear work, because copying a path of height h across up to n leaves gives O(n times h), and that cost is inherent to producing the paths rather than merely counting them.

At the National Bank of India I applied this to audit Rajesh's approval hierarchy, where compliance needed the full documented list of every desk chain whose processing fees summed exactly to the agreed budget. I modelled each desk as a node with a BigDecimal fee, drove the backtracking traversal from the top desk, and emitted each matching chain by desk name into the audit report. Describing the reuse-and-backtrack discipline together with the defensive copy is what tells an interviewer I can implement backtracking correctly under real auditing requirements rather than just recite the idea.

answers.question: Given a binary tree where each node holds a single digit from 0 to 9, each root-to-leaf path represents a number formed by concatenating the digits along the path. Find the total sum of all such numbers, and explain the running-number technique.
answers.shortTitle: Sum of Path Numbers (Each Root-to-Leaf Path Is a Multi-Digit Number)

s1_definition.profdef: Sum of Path Numbers is a Tree Depth First Search problem where each root-to-leaf path encodes a decimal number built by treating node digits as place values. As we descend we maintain a running number computed as `running = running * 10 + node.digit`. At each leaf the running number is complete, and we add it to a total. The traversal is linear in the number of nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine a tree of routing codes where each desk holds one digit of an account-routing number. Every full path from the top desk to a bottom desk spells out one complete routing number. We want the sum of all those routing numbers. As we walk down we build the number digit by digit, shifting left and adding, and at the bottom we drop the finished number into a running total.
s1_definition.oneliner: Carry a running number down each path with `running * 10 + digit`, and add it to the total at every leaf.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sum of Path Numbers is a Tree Depth First Search problem where each root-to-leaf path encodes a decimal number built by treating node digits as place values. As we descend we maintain a running number computed as `running = running * 10 + node.digit`. At each leaf the running number is complete, and we add it to a total. The traversal is linear in the number of nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine a tree of routing codes where each desk holds one digit of an account-routing number. Every full path from the top desk to a bottom desk spells out one complete routing number. We want the sum of all those routing numbers. As we walk down we build the number digit by digit, shifting left and adding, and at the bottom we drop the finished number into a running total.

**One line to remember:** Carry a running number down each path with `running * 10 + digit`, and add it to the total at every leaf.

sections.s2_technical:
The place-value trick is the heart of the solution. Each time we move to a child we shift the accumulated number one decimal place to the left and add the child's digit, for example `int next = running * 10 + node.digit;`. This naturally builds the correct multi-digit value top to bottom, because the root contributes the most significant digit and the leaf the least significant.

At a leaf we return the completed number so the caller can add it, for example `if (node.isLeaf()) return next;`. For internal nodes we sum the results of both children, for example `return dfs(node.left, next) + dfs(node.right, next);`, where a null child contributes zero.

A senior-level nuance is overflow. With deep trees the concatenated number can exceed the range of a 32-bit int, so in a banking system that models long routing numbers we would carry the running value as a `long` or even a `BigInteger`. Another nuance is that we must handle a single-node tree correctly, where the root is itself a leaf and its digit is the whole number. Because routing-code sums are exact integers and not fractional money, an integral type is appropriate here rather than BigDecimal, but any genuine currency amount in the same system would still use BigDecimal.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores a routing tree where each desk node carries one digit. Every complete path from the head office down to a branch terminal spells a full routing number, and operations wants the arithmetic sum of all routing numbers to cross-check a reconciliation report. This is exactly how Sum of Path Numbers works: each leaf finishes one number, and we total them.

Problem 2 — Routing numbers can be long, so building them as plain 32-bit integers risks silent overflow and a wrong reconciliation total. This is why we carry the running value as a `long`, which comfortably holds realistic routing lengths.

The code defines a `RoutingNode` holding a single digit and children. A `PathNumberService` exposes `sumAllRoutingNumbers(root)` returning a `long`. A `Demo` builds a small routing tree and prints the total, logging each completed routing number at the leaves.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Sum of Path Numbers treats each root-to-leaf path as a multi-digit decimal number built from the single digit stored at each node, and asks for the total of all such numbers. I solve it with a depth-first traversal that carries a running number, and at every child I shift the running number one decimal place to the left and append the child's digit, which is the expression running times ten plus the digit. The root therefore contributes the most significant digit and the leaf the least significant, so the number is assembled correctly top to bottom. At each leaf I return the completed number, and internal nodes return the sum of their two children, with a null child contributing zero.

The nuance I always raise is overflow. On a deep tree the concatenated value can exceed a 32-bit integer, so I carry the running value as a long, or a BigInteger if the numbers can be very long, to keep the total exact. I also make sure a single-node tree is handled, because then the root is itself the leaf and its digit is the entire number.

At the National Bank of India I used this pattern over a routing tree where each desk node held one digit of an account-routing number, and operations needed the arithmetic sum of every complete routing number for a reconciliation cross-check. I carried the running value as a long to avoid silent overflow, logged each completed routing number at the leaves, and returned the exact total. Pointing out the place-value construction and the overflow-safe accumulator together shows an interviewer that I connect the clean recursive idea to a correct, production-safe implementation.

answers.question: Given a binary tree and an array of numbers representing a sequence, determine whether there exists a root-to-leaf path such that the node values along the path exactly match the sequence in order and length. Explain how an index into the sequence tracks progress during the depth-first search.
answers.shortTitle: Path With Given Sequence (Does a Root-to-Leaf Path Match an Exact Sequence?)

s1_definition.profdef: Path With Given Sequence is a Tree Depth First Search problem where we match node values against a fixed target sequence while descending. We carry an index into the sequence. At each node we check that the node's value equals the sequence element at the current index; if it does not, that branch fails immediately. The path succeeds only at a leaf where the index has consumed exactly the whole sequence. The traversal is linear in nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a payment must travel through an exact pre-approved sequence of desk codes, like a mandated handshake. We are given the required sequence and the desk tree, and we check whether any full top-to-bottom chain matches the sequence step for step, no more and no less. We walk down comparing each desk code to the next expected code, and if we ever mismatch we abandon that chain.
s1_definition.oneliner: Match node values against the sequence by index as you descend, and succeed only when a leaf lands exactly at the end of the sequence.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Path With Given Sequence is a Tree Depth First Search problem where we match node values against a fixed target sequence while descending. We carry an index into the sequence. At each node we check that the node's value equals the sequence element at the current index; if it does not, that branch fails immediately. The path succeeds only at a leaf where the index has consumed exactly the whole sequence. The traversal is linear in nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a payment must travel through an exact pre-approved sequence of desk codes, like a mandated handshake. We are given the required sequence and the desk tree, and we check whether any full top-to-bottom chain matches the sequence step for step, no more and no less. We walk down comparing each desk code to the next expected code, and if we ever mismatch we abandon that chain.

**One line to remember:** Match node values against the sequence by index as you descend, and succeed only when a leaf lands exactly at the end of the sequence.

sections.s2_technical:
We pass an integer `index` that tracks how far into the sequence we have matched. The first guard rejects impossible states: if the node is null, or the index has run past the sequence length, or the node's value does not equal `sequence[index]`, we return false. For example, `if (node == null || index >= seq.length || node.value != seq[index]) return false;` combines all three failure cases cleanly.

The success test happens at a leaf, where we must have matched the final element and have no sequence left over. For example, `if (node.isLeaf() && index == seq.length - 1) return true;`. For internal nodes we recurse into both children with `index + 1` and OR the results, because any single matching path is enough.

A senior-level nuance is the exact-length requirement. A path that matches the sequence as a prefix but continues past it is not a match, and a path that ends before consuming the sequence is not a match either. Both are handled: a too-long path fails the `index >= seq.length` guard at the extra node, and a too-short path fails because the leaf test requires `index == seq.length - 1`. Another nuance is short-circuit evaluation, so the first matching path stops the search.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A high-value payment from Rajesh at the National Bank of India must follow an exact mandated routing of desk codes for regulatory compliance, for instance the sequence must be head office, then regional, then a specific signing desk. Operations has the desk tree and the mandated sequence and must confirm that at least one real chain follows the sequence precisely. This is exactly how Path With Given Sequence works: the mandated codes are the sequence, and a matching leaf chain proves compliance.

Problem 2 — A chain that matches the first few codes but then continues to an extra desk is a violation, not a pass. This is why the leaf test demands that the sequence be fully and exactly consumed, rejecting both too-long and too-short chains.

The code defines a `DeskNode` with an integer desk code. A `SequencePathService` exposes `hasMandatedPath(root, sequence)` returning a boolean. A `Demo` builds a tree and checks one matching sequence and one that is a prefix only, proving the prefix is rejected.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Path With Given Sequence asks whether any root-to-leaf path in a binary tree matches a fixed target sequence exactly, both in order and in length. I solve it with a depth-first traversal that carries an index into the sequence. At each node I reject immediately if the node is null, if the index has run past the sequence, or if the node's value differs from the sequence element at the current index. I declare success only at a leaf where the index sits on the last element, and for internal nodes I recurse into both children with the index advanced by one and combine with a logical OR so a single matching chain is enough.

The subtlety I always highlight is that the match must be exact. A path that matches the sequence as a prefix but then continues to an extra node is not a match, and a path that ends before the sequence is consumed is not a match either. My guards handle both: an overrunning path trips the index-past-length check, and a short path never satisfies the leaf test that requires the index to equal the last position.

At the National Bank of India I used this to enforce mandated routing for high-value payments, where a payment from Rajesh had to travel through an exact regulator-approved sequence of desk codes. I modelled each desk as a node with an integer code, drove the depth-first search with an index into the mandated sequence, and returned true only when a real chain consumed the sequence exactly at a leaf. Explaining the exact-length rule and the index-driven matching, including why a prefix match is a compliance failure, is what demonstrates to an interviewer that I understand both the algorithm and the regulatory consequence of getting it wrong.

answers.question: Given a binary tree and a target sum, count all paths in the tree where the sum of the node values equals the target. The paths do not need to start at the root or end at a leaf, but they must go downward, from a node to one of its descendants. Explain the running-prefix-sum technique that makes this efficient.
answers.shortTitle: Count Paths for a Sum (Count All Downward Paths Summing to a Target)

s1_definition.profdef: Count Paths for a Sum counts every downward path, not only root-to-leaf paths, whose node values sum to a target. The efficient solution uses a running prefix sum from the root plus a hash map that records how many times each prefix-sum value has occurred along the current path. At each node, the number of valid paths ending at that node equals the count of the value `currentPrefix - target` already seen. The map is updated on the way down and rolled back on the way up, giving linear time and height-proportional space.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a stream of charges flows down a chain of desks, and auditors want to count every contiguous downward stretch of charges that adds up to a flagged amount. A stretch can start at any desk, not just the top, and end at any lower desk. We walk down keeping a running total of charges, and we remember how often each running total has appeared; whenever running-total minus the flagged amount has appeared before, each earlier appearance marks the start of a matching stretch.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a running prefix sum and a count map, and at each node add the number of earlier prefixes equal to current prefix minus the target.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Count Paths for a Sum counts every downward path, not only root-to-leaf paths, whose node values sum to a target. The efficient solution uses a running prefix sum from the root plus a hash map that records how many times each prefix-sum value has occurred along the current path. At each node, the number of valid paths ending at that node equals the count of the value `currentPrefix - target` already seen. The map is updated on the way down and rolled back on the way up, giving linear time and height-proportional space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a stream of charges flows down a chain of desks, and auditors want to count every contiguous downward stretch of charges that adds up to a flagged amount. A stretch can start at any desk, not just the top, and end at any lower desk. We walk down keeping a running total of charges, and we remember how often each running total has appeared; whenever running-total minus the flagged amount has appeared before, each earlier appearance marks the start of a matching stretch.

**One line to remember:** Keep a running prefix sum and a count map, and at each node add the number of earlier prefixes equal to current prefix minus the target.

sections.s2_technical:
The brute-force approach tries every node as a path start and re-walks downward, which is O(n²) on a skewed tree. The prefix-sum technique removes the repeated work. We maintain `currentSum`, the sum from the root to the current node, and a map `prefixCounts` from a prefix-sum value to how many ancestors produced it. A downward path ending at the current node sums to the target exactly when some ancestor prefix equals `currentSum - target`, so we add `prefixCounts.getOrDefault(currentSum - target, 0)` to the answer.

We seed the map with `prefixCounts.put(0L, 1)` so a path that starts at the root itself is counted, because then `currentSum - target` is zero. Before recursing we increment the count for `currentSum`, and after recursing into both children we decrement it, for example `prefixCounts.merge(currentSum, -1, Integer::sum);`. This rollback keeps the map scoped to the current root-to-node path, so sibling branches never see each other's prefixes.

A senior-level nuance is the rollback: without it, a prefix from a left branch would wrongly count paths in a right branch that are not actually connected. Another nuance is using a `long` running sum to avoid overflow, and recognizing that negative node values are allowed, which is exactly why the prefix-sum trick is needed rather than early pruning.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India logs charges down a desk chain, and fraud auditors want to count every contiguous downward run of charges that sums to a flagged suspicious amount. A suspicious run can begin at any desk in the middle of the chain, not only at the top, and can end at any desk below it. This is exactly how Count Paths for a Sum works: each downward run is a path, and we count all runs hitting the flagged amount.

Problem 2 — Recomputing every possible run from scratch would be far too slow on a deep desk chain. This is why we carry a running prefix sum and a map of how often each prefix appeared, so each node contributes its matching-run count in constant time, and we roll the map back as we climb so unrelated branches never interfere.

The code defines a `ChargeNode` holding a `BigDecimal` charge. A `CountPathsService` exposes `countFlaggedRuns(root, flagged)` returning an int. A `Demo` builds a charge tree with several matching downward runs and logs the count. Money is `BigDecimal`, and the prefix map keys on the scaled long-cents value to keep hashing exact.

Step 2: Go left into -50, currentSum 10000 + (-5000) = 5000. needed = 5000 - 10000 = -5000, not present, zero runs. Record prefix 5000.

Step 3: Go into 150, currentSum 5000 + 15000 = 20000. needed = 20000 - 10000 = 10000, present once (from the root prefix), so one run counted, the downward run -50 then 150. Record and then roll back 20000, then 5000 on return.

Step 4: Go right into 50, currentSum 10000 + 5000 = 15000. needed = 15000 - 10000 = 5000, not present after rollback, zero. Record 15000. Go into 50, currentSum 15000 + 5000 = 20000. needed = 10000, present once (root), one run, the downward run 50 then 50. Roll back.

Step 5: Total runs = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Count Paths for a Sum counts every downward path in a binary tree whose node values add up to a target, where a path may start and end at any node as long as it goes downward. The naive approach tries every node as a start and re-walks, which is quadratic on a skewed tree. I use the running-prefix-sum technique: I keep the sum from the root to the current node and a hash map of how many ancestors produced each prefix sum. At each node the number of valid paths ending there equals the number of earlier prefixes equal to the current sum minus the target, which I read from the map in constant time.

The two details I always call out are seeding and rollback. I seed the map with the value zero counted once so that a path starting right at the root is counted, and after visiting a node's children I decrement that node's prefix in the map so sibling branches never borrow each other's prefixes, which would otherwise count disconnected paths. I also carry the running sum as a long and allow negative node values, which is precisely why prefix sums are necessary instead of pruning.

At the National Bank of India I used this to scan charge chains for fraud, counting every contiguous downward run of desk charges that summed to a flagged amount, where a run could begin at any desk mid-chain. I stored charges as BigDecimal, converted them to exact long cents before hashing to avoid floating-point keys, seeded and rolled back the prefix map correctly, and reported the count to the fraud dashboard. Explaining why the prefix-sum map turns a quadratic scan into a linear one, and why the rollback keeps branches isolated, is what signals to an interviewer that I can optimise a tree traversal under real fraud-detection constraints.

answers.question: Given a binary tree, find its diameter, defined as the number of nodes on the longest path between any two nodes in the tree. The path may or may not pass through the root. Explain why a single post-order traversal that returns subtree heights while updating a global maximum is the efficient solution.
answers.shortTitle: Tree Diameter (Longest Path Between Any Two Nodes)

s1_definition.profdef: Tree Diameter is a Tree Depth First Search problem that finds the longest path between any two nodes, where the path need not pass through the root. The efficient solution is a single post-order traversal where each node returns its height to its parent while simultaneously updating a shared maximum with the candidate diameter that passes through that node, which equals the left height plus the right height plus one node. The traversal is linear in nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the approval hierarchy is a tree, and management wants the longest possible escalation path between any two desks, the two desks that are farthest apart in the chain of command. That longest stretch might not go through the head office at all; it could run up one branch and down another. We measure, at every desk, how deep its left reports and right reports go, and the widest span through that desk is a candidate for the longest stretch overall.
s1_definition.oneliner: Post-order return each subtree's height, and at every node update the best diameter as left height plus right height plus one.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Tree Diameter is a Tree Depth First Search problem that finds the longest path between any two nodes, where the path need not pass through the root. The efficient solution is a single post-order traversal where each node returns its height to its parent while simultaneously updating a shared maximum with the candidate diameter that passes through that node, which equals the left height plus the right height plus one node. The traversal is linear in nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the approval hierarchy is a tree, and management wants the longest possible escalation path between any two desks, the two desks that are farthest apart in the chain of command. That longest stretch might not go through the head office at all; it could run up one branch and down another. We measure, at every desk, how deep its left reports and right reports go, and the widest span through that desk is a candidate for the longest stretch overall.

**One line to remember:** Post-order return each subtree's height, and at every node update the best diameter as left height plus right height plus one.

sections.s2_technical:
The key realization is that the longest path through a particular node uses the deepest path going down its left child and the deepest path going down its right child, joined at the node. So if we know the height of the left subtree and the height of the right subtree, the candidate diameter centered at this node is `leftHeight + rightHeight + 1` counted in nodes. We keep a shared maximum and update it at every node, for example `maxDiameter = Math.max(maxDiameter, leftHeight + rightHeight + 1);`.

The same traversal must also return a height to the parent, so the recursion returns `Math.max(leftHeight, rightHeight) + 1`. A null child returns height zero. This dual role, updating a global while returning a local value, is what makes it a single linear pass rather than recomputing heights repeatedly.

A senior-level nuance is the counting convention. Some definitions count the diameter in edges rather than nodes; in nodes it is left height plus right height plus one, and in edges it is left height plus right height. I state the convention explicitly so the off-by-one is deliberate. Another nuance is that the naive approach of computing height independently at every node is O(n²); folding the height return into the same traversal removes the repeated work.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants to understand the longest escalation chain in its approval hierarchy, the greatest distance between any two desks, because a very long chain slows down approvals and signals an over-deep structure. The longest chain might run entirely within two sub-branches and never touch the head office. This is exactly how Tree Diameter works: the farthest two desks define the diameter, wherever they sit.

Problem 2 — Measuring each desk's depth over and over would be slow for a large hierarchy. This is why a single post-order pass returns each subtree's depth to its parent while updating the running longest-span, so every desk is measured once.

The code defines a `DeskNode`. A `TreeDiameterService` exposes `longestEscalationChain(root)` returning the diameter in nodes. A `Demo` builds a hierarchy whose longest chain does not pass through the root and logs the result.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Tree Diameter finds the longest path between any two nodes in a binary tree, and crucially that path need not pass through the root. The efficient solution is a single post-order traversal that does two jobs at once. For each node I recursively compute the height of its left and right subtrees, then I update a shared maximum with the candidate diameter that passes through that node, which is the left height plus the right height plus one node. The same call returns the node's own height to its parent, which is the deeper of the two child heights plus one.

The nuance I always state explicitly is the counting convention. Counting the diameter in nodes gives left height plus right height plus one; counting in edges gives left height plus right height. I announce which convention I am using so the plus-one is a deliberate decision rather than an accidental off-by-one. I also point out that computing height independently at every node would be quadratic, and folding the height return into the diameter pass is what keeps the algorithm linear.

At the National Bank of India I applied this to analyse the approval hierarchy, where management wanted the longest escalation chain between any two desks because an over-long chain slows approvals, and that chain often ran across two sub-branches without touching the head office. I ran one post-order pass that returned each subtree's depth while updating the longest span through each desk, and reported the diameter to the org-structure dashboard. Explaining the dual role of the single traversal, returning a height while updating a global maximum, is what shows an interviewer that I can turn a tempting quadratic solution into a clean linear one.

answers.question: Given a binary tree, find the path with the maximum sum, where a path is any sequence of connected nodes and need not pass through the root or start or end at a leaf. Node values may be negative. Return the maximum path sum, and explain the post-order traversal with a global maximum.
answers.shortTitle: Path with Maximum Sum (Maximum Sum of Any Path Between Two Nodes)

s1_definition.profdef: Path with Maximum Sum is a Tree Depth First Search problem that finds the maximum possible sum over any connected path in the tree. The solution is a post-order traversal where each node returns to its parent the best single downward branch sum, clamped at zero to discard harmful negative branches, while a shared maximum is updated with the best path that bends through the current node, which is the node's value plus both clamped child contributions. Time is linear in nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, each desk in a tree contributes a profit or a loss in rupees, and we want the single most profitable connected stretch of desks, which can run up one branch and down another through some middle desk. If a sub-branch would only drag the total down, we simply refuse to extend into it and treat its contribution as zero. We check, at every desk, the best profit we can gain by bending a path through it using its two best child branches.
s1_definition.oneliner: Return the best clamped downward branch to the parent, but update the global best with node value plus both clamped branches.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Path with Maximum Sum is a Tree Depth First Search problem that finds the maximum possible sum over any connected path in the tree. The solution is a post-order traversal where each node returns to its parent the best single downward branch sum, clamped at zero to discard harmful negative branches, while a shared maximum is updated with the best path that bends through the current node, which is the node's value plus both clamped child contributions. Time is linear in nodes with recursion-stack space proportional to the height.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, each desk in a tree contributes a profit or a loss in rupees, and we want the single most profitable connected stretch of desks, which can run up one branch and down another through some middle desk. If a sub-branch would only drag the total down, we simply refuse to extend into it and treat its contribution as zero. We check, at every desk, the best profit we can gain by bending a path through it using its two best child branches.

**One line to remember:** Return the best clamped downward branch to the parent, but update the global best with node value plus both clamped branches.

sections.s2_technical:
Each node plays two roles. To its parent it can only offer a straight downward extension, so it returns its own value plus the larger of its two child contributions, for example `node.value + Math.max(leftGain, rightGain)`. But within the node itself a path may bend, using both children, so the candidate best is `node.value + leftGain + rightGain`, which we feed into a shared maximum.

The clamping is essential. A child's contribution is `Math.max(0, childGain)`, because if extending into a child would lower the sum, the optimal path simply stops at the current node and ignores that child. This single `Math.max(0, ...)` is what lets negative values be handled gracefully without special cases.

A senior-level nuance is initializing the global maximum to the smallest possible value rather than zero, because a tree of all-negative nodes has a maximum path equal to the single least-negative node, and starting at zero would wrongly return zero. Another nuance is the asymmetry between what is returned upward, a single branch, and what updates the global, a bent path using both branches; conflating the two is the classic bug.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a tree of profit-and-loss desks, where each desk posts a signed rupee result. Strategy wants the single most profitable connected run of desks, which may bend through a middle desk, climbing one branch and descending another. This is exactly how Path with Maximum Sum works: a path can turn at a node and combine two downward branches.

Problem 2 — Some desks post losses, and extending a run into a loss-making sub-branch would only reduce the profit. This is why each child's contribution is clamped at zero, so the run refuses to extend into any branch that would hurt it, and a run of all loss-making desks still correctly reports the least bad single desk.

The code defines a `PnlNode` holding a `BigDecimal` result. A `MaxPathSumService` exposes `mostProfitableRun(root)` returning a `BigDecimal`. A `Demo` builds a tree where the best run bends through a middle desk and logs it, including a branch that is correctly ignored.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Path with Maximum Sum finds the maximum sum over any connected path in a binary tree, where the path can bend through a node and need not touch the root or a leaf, and node values may be negative. I solve it with a post-order traversal in which each node plays two roles. To its parent it can only offer a straight downward extension, so it returns its own value plus the larger of its two child gains. But within the node a path may bend using both children, so I update a shared maximum with the node's value plus both child gains.

The decisive detail is clamping each child's gain at zero. If extending into a child would lower the total, the optimal path simply stops at the current node, so I take the maximum of zero and the child gain, which handles all negative values without special cases. I also seed the global maximum with a very large negative value rather than zero, because a tree of all-negative nodes must return its least-negative single node, and seeding at zero would wrongly report zero.

At the National Bank of India I used this over a tree of profit-and-loss desks, where strategy wanted the single most profitable connected run, which often bent through a middle desk by climbing one branch and descending another while skipping loss-making sub-branches. I kept results as BigDecimal, clamped loss branches to zero so they were ignored, updated the global best with the bent two-branch path, and reported the most profitable run. Explaining the split between the single branch returned upward and the bent path that updates the global, together with the zero clamp for negatives, is exactly what convinces an interviewer I understand the trickiest tree-DFS problem.

answers.question: Design a data structure that accepts a continuous stream of numbers and can return the median of all numbers seen so far at any time. Insertion and median-query should both be efficient. Explain the two-heap technique.
answers.shortTitle: Find the Median of a Number Stream (Two Heaps)

s1_definition.profdef: Find the Median of a Number Stream is the canonical Two Heaps problem. We keep a max-heap holding the smaller half of the numbers and a min-heap holding the larger half, balanced so their sizes differ by at most one. The median is then either the top of the larger heap, or the average of the two tops when the counts are equal. Each insertion costs logarithmic time for the heap operations, and a median query costs constant time by peeking at the heap tops.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, transaction amounts arrive all day, and the risk team wants the running median amount at any moment to spot drift. We split the amounts into two buckets: a low bucket that always holds the smaller half with its largest value on top, and a high bucket that holds the larger half with its smallest value on top. The middle of all amounts sits right at the boundary between the two buckets, so we read it off the tops instantly.
s1_definition.oneliner: Smaller half in a max-heap, larger half in a min-heap, keep them balanced, and the median lives at the boundary.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Find the Median of a Number Stream is the canonical Two Heaps problem. We keep a max-heap holding the smaller half of the numbers and a min-heap holding the larger half, balanced so their sizes differ by at most one. The median is then either the top of the larger heap, or the average of the two tops when the counts are equal. Each insertion costs logarithmic time for the heap operations, and a median query costs constant time by peeking at the heap tops.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, transaction amounts arrive all day, and the risk team wants the running median amount at any moment to spot drift. We split the amounts into two buckets: a low bucket that always holds the smaller half with its largest value on top, and a high bucket that holds the larger half with its smallest value on top. The middle of all amounts sits right at the boundary between the two buckets, so we read it off the tops instantly.

**One line to remember:** Smaller half in a max-heap, larger half in a min-heap, keep them balanced, and the median lives at the boundary.

sections.s2_technical:
On each insertion we first decide which heap the number belongs in. A common rule is: if the max-heap (smaller half) is empty or the number is at most its top, push to the max-heap, otherwise push to the min-heap. For example, `if (maxHeap.isEmpty() || num <= maxHeap.peek()) maxHeap.offer(num); else minHeap.offer(num);`.

Then we rebalance so the heaps never differ by more than one element. If the max-heap has grown two larger than the min-heap, we move its top over, and vice versa. For example, `if (maxHeap.size() > minHeap.size() + 1) minHeap.offer(maxHeap.poll());`. This keeps the boundary exactly in the middle.

To read the median, if the heaps are equal in size the median is the average of the two tops, otherwise it is the top of the larger heap. A senior-level nuance in a banking context is that amounts are `BigDecimal`, so the max-heap uses `Comparator.reverseOrder()` and the average is computed with `BigDecimal` division at a controlled scale and rounding mode, never floating-point. Another nuance is that this streaming structure is far better than re-sorting on every query, which would be O(n log n) per query.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes a continuous stream of transaction amounts, and the risk team must see the running median amount at any instant to detect when typical transaction sizes drift. Sorting all amounts on every query would be far too slow for a live stream. This is exactly how the Two Heaps median structure works: it keeps the stream split so the median is always at the boundary.

Problem 2 — The stream never stops, so the structure must absorb each new amount cheaply and answer the median instantly. This is why insertion is a logarithmic heap operation and the query is a constant-time peek, rather than a full re-sort.

The code defines a `RunningMedian` class holding a max-heap and a min-heap of `BigDecimal`. It exposes `addAmount(BigDecimal)` and `median()`. A `Demo` feeds a stream of amounts for the National Bank of India and logs the running median after each insertion.
