sections.s5_journey:
Input stream: 500, 1500, 1000, 3000, 250.

Step 1: Add 500. Max-heap empty, so 500 goes to the max-heap. Sizes 1 and 0, odd, median is the max-heap top, 500.

Step 2: Add 1500. 1500 is greater than the top 500, so it goes to the min-heap. Sizes 1 and 1, even, median is the average of 500 and 1500, which is 750.00.

Step 3: Add 1000. 1000 is greater than 500, so it goes to the min-heap, making min-heap {1000, 1500}. Now min-heap is larger by one, so move its top 1000 back to the max-heap. Max-heap {500, 1000}, min-heap {1500}. Odd, median is the max-heap top, 1000.

Step 4: Add 3000. Greater than 1000, goes to the min-heap {1500, 3000}. Sizes 2 and 2, even, median is the average of tops 1000 and 1500, which is 1250.00.

Step 5: Add 250. At most 1000, goes to the max-heap {500, 1000, 250}. Max-heap now larger by two, move its top 1000 to the min-heap. Max-heap {500, 250}, min-heap {1000, 1500, 3000}. Odd, median is the min-heap... no: min-heap is larger so we already rebalanced to keep max-heap holding the extra only when it is bigger; here min-heap size 3 exceeds max-heap size 2, so move min-heap top 1000 to max-heap, making max-heap {500, 250, 1000} and min-heap {1500, 3000}. Median is max-heap top, 1000.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Find the Median of a Number Stream is the textbook Two Heaps problem. I keep a max-heap that holds the smaller half of all numbers and a min-heap that holds the larger half, and I keep their sizes within one of each other. The median then lives exactly at the boundary: when the counts are equal it is the average of the two heap tops, and when they differ it is the top of the larger heap. Each insertion is a logarithmic heap operation and each median query is a constant-time peek, which is vastly better than re-sorting the whole stream on every query.

The mechanics I describe are: on insertion I place the number in the correct heap based on the current max-heap top, then I rebalance by moving a top element across if one heap grew two larger than the other. In a banking context I stress that amounts are BigDecimal, so the max-heap uses a reverse-order comparator and the even-count median is computed with BigDecimal division at a fixed scale and rounding mode, never floating-point, because money must stay exact.

At the National Bank of India I used this to maintain the running median transaction amount over a live stream, so the risk team could watch for drift in typical transaction sizes in real time. I absorbed each amount with a logarithmic insertion and answered the median instantly from the heap tops, keeping the heaps balanced so the boundary stayed in the middle. Explaining the balance invariant and the money-safe averaging is what shows an interviewer that I can turn the Two Heaps idea into a correct streaming structure for real financial data.

answers.question: Given an array of numbers and a window size K, find the median of every contiguous window of size K as the window slides from left to right. Explain how two heaps with lazy deletion maintain the window median efficiently.
answers.shortTitle: Sliding Window Median (Two Heaps with Lazy Deletion)

s1_definition.profdef: Sliding Window Median extends the streaming-median Two Heaps structure to a fixed-size window. We maintain a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half of the current window. As the window advances we add the entering element and remove the leaving element. Because heaps do not support arbitrary removal cheaply, we use lazy deletion: we mark the leaving element and purge it from a heap top only when it surfaces. Each window move costs logarithmic amortized time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the risk team watches the median transaction amount over the last K transactions, a rolling window. As each new transaction arrives, the oldest one drops out. We keep the same two buckets as before, a low bucket and a high bucket, but now we must also evict the transaction that aged out. Rather than hunt for it inside a bucket, we note that it should be ignored and physically drop it only when it bubbles up to the top.
s1_definition.oneliner: Two heaps for the window, add the new element, lazily mark the old one, rebalance, and read the median at the boundary.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sliding Window Median extends the streaming-median Two Heaps structure to a fixed-size window. We maintain a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half of the current window. As the window advances we add the entering element and remove the leaving element. Because heaps do not support arbitrary removal cheaply, we use lazy deletion: we mark the leaving element and purge it from a heap top only when it surfaces. Each window move costs logarithmic amortized time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the risk team watches the median transaction amount over the last K transactions, a rolling window. As each new transaction arrives, the oldest one drops out. We keep the same two buckets as before, a low bucket and a high bucket, but now we must also evict the transaction that aged out. Rather than hunt for it inside a bucket, we note that it should be ignored and physically drop it only when it bubbles up to the top.

**One line to remember:** Two heaps for the window, add the new element, lazily mark the old one, rebalance, and read the median at the boundary.

sections.s2_technical:
The window median logic is the same as the streaming case: equal heaps average the tops, otherwise the larger heap top is the median. The new challenge is removing the element that leaves the window. A `PriorityQueue` only removes its minimum or maximum efficiently, so deleting an arbitrary value is O(n). Lazy deletion fixes this: we keep a map of values scheduled for removal, for example `Map<BigDecimal,Integer> toRemove`, and before reading a heap top we repeatedly purge the top while it is marked.

After adding the entering value to the correct heap and scheduling the leaving value for removal, we must also account for balance, since a lazily removed element still counts against a heap's logical size. We track the logical balance separately and rebalance based on it, then prune the tops of both heaps so the actual tops are valid before we read the median. For example a helper `prune(heap)` loops `while (!heap.isEmpty() && toRemove.getOrDefault(heap.peek(),0) > 0) { toRemove.merge(heap.peek(), -1, Integer::sum); heap.poll(); }`.

A senior-level nuance is that lazy deletion keeps each window step at amortized logarithmic cost even though a marked element may sit in the heap for a while, because each element is physically removed at most once. Another nuance is handling duplicate amounts, which is why the removal structure is a count map keyed by value rather than a simple set.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India risk team monitors the median of the last K transaction amounts as a rolling indicator. Each new transaction pushes the oldest one out of the window, and the team needs the fresh median immediately. This is exactly how Sliding Window Median works: a fixed window whose median is recomputed cheaply as it slides.

Problem 2 — Removing the transaction that aged out from inside a heap is expensive if done directly. This is why we use lazy deletion, marking the departed amount and dropping it only when it reaches a heap top, which keeps each slide fast even with repeated amounts.

The code defines a `WindowMedian` class with two `BigDecimal` heaps and a removal count map. It exposes `medians(amounts, k)` returning a list of window medians. A `Demo` runs it over a National Bank of India amount series and logs each window median.

  2. remove(leaving)→ schedule lazy deletion + rebalance
  3. prune tops     → currentMedian(k)

  Contract for medians(amounts, k):
    Pre:  1 <= k <= amounts.size()
    Post: list of medians, one per size-k window
    Note: duplicates handled by count map
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Sliding Window Median extends the streaming-median Two Heaps structure to a fixed window of size K. I keep a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half of the current window, and the median sits at the boundary exactly as in the streaming case. The new difficulty is that as the window slides I must remove the element that aged out, and a priority queue cannot delete an arbitrary value cheaply. I solve that with lazy deletion: I record the departed value in a count map and physically drop it from a heap only when it reaches the top, so each element is removed at most once and every slide stays at amortized logarithmic cost.

Because a lazily marked element still occupies space in a heap, I track the logical balance between the two halves with a separate counter rather than trusting the raw heap sizes, and I prune both heap tops before reading the median so no stale value corrupts the answer. I also key the removal structure by value with a count, not a set, so repeated amounts are handled correctly.

At the National Bank of India I used this to maintain the median of the last K transaction amounts as a rolling risk indicator, where each new transaction evicts the oldest one. I kept amounts as BigDecimal, averaged the two tops with a fixed scale and rounding for even windows, and used lazy deletion so each slide stayed fast even with duplicate amounts. Explaining lazy deletion and the logical balance counter is what shows an interviewer I understand why a naive arbitrary-removal approach is too slow and how the Two Heaps structure is adapted for a moving window.

answers.question: You are given an initial capital and a list of projects, each with a capital requirement and a profit. You can complete at most K projects, and completing a project adds its profit to your capital, which can then fund later projects. Choose projects to maximize final capital. Explain the two-heap greedy approach.
answers.shortTitle: Maximize Capital (Two Heaps — Greedy Project Selection)

s1_definition.profdef: Maximize Capital is a Two Heaps problem combining a min-heap keyed by capital requirement with a max-heap keyed by profit. In each of the K rounds, we move every project now affordable with the current capital from the min-heap into the max-heap, then pick the single most profitable affordable project. Adding its profit raises our capital, unlocking more projects next round. The algorithm runs in roughly K log N time plus the cost of the initial heap setup.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the investment desk has a budget and a list of deals, each needing a minimum capital to enter and returning a profit. We can do only K deals. Each deal we close increases our budget, letting us afford bigger deals next. So each round we unlock every deal we can now afford and greedily pick the most profitable one, because taking the biggest profit first grows the budget fastest.
s1_definition.oneliner: Unlock all affordable projects into a profit max-heap, grab the most profitable, bank the profit, and repeat K times.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Maximize Capital is a Two Heaps problem combining a min-heap keyed by capital requirement with a max-heap keyed by profit. In each of the K rounds, we move every project now affordable with the current capital from the min-heap into the max-heap, then pick the single most profitable affordable project. Adding its profit raises our capital, unlocking more projects next round. The algorithm runs in roughly K log N time plus the cost of the initial heap setup.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the investment desk has a budget and a list of deals, each needing a minimum capital to enter and returning a profit. We can do only K deals. Each deal we close increases our budget, letting us afford bigger deals next. So each round we unlock every deal we can now afford and greedily pick the most profitable one, because taking the biggest profit first grows the budget fastest.

**One line to remember:** Unlock all affordable projects into a profit max-heap, grab the most profitable, bank the profit, and repeat K times.

sections.s2_technical:
We sort projects by capital requirement implicitly using a min-heap keyed on required capital, so the cheapest-to-enter projects surface first. Each round, we drain from the min-heap every project whose requirement is at most our current capital and push it into a max-heap keyed on profit. For example, `while (!minCapital.isEmpty() && minCapital.peek().required <= capital) maxProfit.offer(minCapital.poll());`.

Then we take the top of the profit max-heap, which is the most profitable affordable project, and add its profit to our capital. For example, `capital = capital.add(maxProfit.poll().profit);`. If the profit heap is empty at the start of a round, no affordable project remains and we stop early.

A senior-level nuance is why greedy is correct here: once a project is affordable it stays affordable because capital only grows, so deferring it never makes it unavailable, and taking the maximum profit each round provably maximizes capital under the K-project limit. Another nuance is that capital and profit are money, so they are `BigDecimal`, and the max-heap comparator compares profits with `compareTo` in reverse order.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India investment desk starts with a budget and faces a set of deals, each with a minimum capital to enter and a profit on completion. The desk may close at most K deals, and each closed deal grows the budget for the next. The desk wants to end with the largest possible budget. This is exactly how Maximize Capital works: a budget-gated greedy selection.

Problem 2 — Some deals are unaffordable at the start but become affordable after earlier profits land. This is why we keep a min-heap of deals by required capital and move newly affordable deals into a profit max-heap each round, so the choice set grows as the budget grows.

The code defines a `Project` with `BigDecimal` required capital and profit. A `CapitalMaximizer` exposes `maximizeCapital(initial, k, projects)` returning the final `BigDecimal` capital. A `Demo` runs the National Bank of India investment desk through a few rounds and logs each pick.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Maximize Capital is a Two Heaps greedy problem where I start with some capital and can complete at most K projects, each of which requires a minimum capital to begin and returns a profit that increases my capital. I use a min-heap keyed on the required capital so the cheapest-to-enter projects surface first, and a max-heap keyed on profit so the most profitable affordable project is always on top. In each of the K rounds I move every project now affordable with my current capital from the min-heap into the max-heap, then take the single most profitable one and add its profit to my capital, which unlocks more projects next round.

The reason greedy is correct here is that capital only ever increases, so once a project becomes affordable it stays affordable, and taking the maximum profit each round provably maximizes the final capital under the K-project limit. I also stop early if a round begins with no affordable project, since nothing more can be done.

At the National Bank of India I applied this to the investment desk, which started with a budget, faced deals each gated by a minimum capital and offering a profit, and could close at most K deals, with every closed deal enlarging the budget for the next. I kept all money as BigDecimal, unlocked newly affordable deals into a profit max-heap each round, and greedily closed the most profitable one. Explaining why the two heaps cooperate, one gating by affordability and one ranking by profit, and why the greedy choice is optimal, is what shows an interviewer that I can reason about correctness, not just code a heap.

answers.question: Given an array of intervals, for each interval find the index of the next interval, meaning the interval with the smallest start that is greater than or equal to the current interval's end. If no such interval exists, record -1. Explain how two heaps keyed on start and end solve this efficiently.
answers.shortTitle: Next Interval (Two Heaps — Find the Next Starting Interval)

s1_definition.profdef: Next Interval is a Two Heaps problem. We build a max-heap keyed on interval start and a max-heap keyed on interval end, both carrying the original index. We repeatedly take the interval with the largest end, then pop starts greater than or equal to that end to find the smallest qualifying start among them; the last one popped before the start drops below the end is the answer for that interval. The approach runs in roughly N log N time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, each loan has a disbursement window with a start date and an end date. For every loan we want the next loan whose window starts on or after the current loan's window ends, so repayments can be chained back to back. We sort by end and by start cleverly with two heaps, and for the loan that ends latest we scan the starts to find the earliest one that begins on or after it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Max-heap by end and max-heap by start, process the latest-ending interval first, and pop starts to find the earliest start that is at least that end.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Next Interval is a Two Heaps problem. We build a max-heap keyed on interval start and a max-heap keyed on interval end, both carrying the original index. We repeatedly take the interval with the largest end, then pop starts greater than or equal to that end to find the smallest qualifying start among them; the last one popped before the start drops below the end is the answer for that interval. The approach runs in roughly N log N time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, each loan has a disbursement window with a start date and an end date. For every loan we want the next loan whose window starts on or after the current loan's window ends, so repayments can be chained back to back. We sort by end and by start cleverly with two heaps, and for the loan that ends latest we scan the starts to find the earliest one that begins on or after it.

**One line to remember:** Max-heap by end and max-heap by start, process the latest-ending interval first, and pop starts to find the earliest start that is at least that end.

sections.s2_technical:
We create two max-heaps, each entry pairing a value with the interval's original index: one ordered by start descending and one ordered by end descending. We pop the interval with the greatest end first. Then we pop from the start heap every interval whose start is greater than or equal to that end, keeping track of the last such index popped, because popping in descending start order means the last valid pop is the smallest qualifying start. For example, `while (!startHeap.isEmpty() && startHeap.peek().start >= end) { topIndex = startHeap.poll().index; }`.

If at least one start qualified, that last popped index is the next interval for the current end's interval; otherwise the answer is -1. Crucially, any start we popped and did not use for this end would still qualify for an interval with a smaller end, which is exactly why we process ends in descending order, so popped starts remain valid for subsequent, smaller ends. We must not discard them; we push the candidate back if needed, or more simply retain the running `topIndex` logic where unused larger starts are re-pushed.

A senior-level nuance is the monotonic argument: because ends are processed from largest to smallest, a start that was too small for a large end may become valid for a smaller end, so we re-offer unused starts. Another nuance is correct index bookkeeping, since the answer is an array of original indices, not sorted positions.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India schedules loan disbursement windows, each with a start and end date represented as integers. For each loan the operations team wants the next loan whose window begins on or after the current loan's window ends, so facilities can be chained without overlap. This is exactly how Next Interval works: for each interval find the earliest-starting interval that begins at or after its end.

Problem 2 — Comparing every loan against every other loan is quadratic and slow for a large book. This is why two heaps, one ordered by start and one by end, let us resolve each loan's successor in logarithmic steps by processing the latest-ending loan first.

The code defines an `Interval` with integer start and end. A `NextIntervalService` exposes `findNextIntervals(intervals)` returning an int array of successor indices. A `Demo` runs a small loan schedule and logs the resulting successor map.

Input: loans 0 is [2,3], 1 is [3,4], 2 is [5,6].

Step 1: Build a start max-heap holding starts 5, 3, 2 with indices 2, 1, 0, and an end max-heap holding ends 6, 4, 3 with indices 2, 1, 0. Initialize all answers to -1.

Step 2: Pop the largest end, 6 for loan 2. Look for a start greater than or equal to 6. The largest start is 5, which is less than 6, so no qualifying start; loan 2's answer stays -1.

Step 3: Pop the next end, 4 for loan 1. Look for a start at least 4. The largest start is 5 for loan 2, which qualifies; pop it, no smaller qualifying start remains, so loan 1's next is loan 2. Re-offer start 5 for later ends.

Step 4: Pop the next end, 3 for loan 0. Look for a start at least 3. Starts 5 (loan 2) and 3 (loan 1) both qualify; we pop down to the smallest qualifying start, which is 3 for loan 1, so loan 0's next is loan 1.

Step 5: Final successor map is loan 0 to loan 1, loan 1 to loan 2, loan 2 to -1, which is the array [1, 2, -1].

sections.s6_takeaway:
Next Interval asks, for each interval, for the index of the interval with the smallest start that is greater than or equal to the current interval's end, or minus one if none exists. I solve it with Two Heaps: a max-heap keyed on start and a max-heap keyed on end, both carrying each interval's original index. I pop the interval with the largest end first, then pop from the start heap every start that is at least that end, and because starts are ordered descending the last one popped before the starts drop below the end is the smallest qualifying start, which is the answer for that interval.

The insight that makes this correct is processing ends from largest to smallest. A start that was too small to serve a large end may still serve a smaller end later, so I re-offer the chosen start back into the start heap rather than discarding it. I also keep each interval's original index inside the heap entries, because the result is a mapping of original positions, not of sorted order.

At the National Bank of India I used this to chain loan disbursement windows, finding for each loan the next loan whose window begins on or after the current one ends, so facilities could be scheduled back to back without overlap. The dates were integer day indices, so plain integers were correct there, while any rupee amount in the same service still used BigDecimal. Explaining the largest-end-first ordering and why unused starts are re-offered is what shows an interviewer that I understand the subtle correctness argument behind the two-heap interval matching, not just the mechanics.

answers.question: Given a set of distinct numbers, generate all possible subsets, including the empty set and the full set. Explain the iterative doubling technique that builds subsets one element at a time.
answers.shortTitle: Subsets (Generate All Subsets of a Distinct Set)

s1_definition.profdef: Subsets is the foundational Subsets-pattern problem. For a set of n distinct elements there are exactly two to the power n subsets. The iterative technique starts with a list containing only the empty subset and, for each new element, duplicates every existing subset and adds the element to each duplicate. This doubles the collection with each element, naturally producing all subsets in O(2^n) total work, which is optimal because that many subsets must be output.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a customer like Rajesh can opt into any combination of add-on services, say overdraft, insurance, and a rewards card. We want every possible service bundle he could choose, from choosing nothing to choosing all three. We start with one empty bundle, and for each new service we copy every bundle we have so far and add the service to each copy, so the number of bundles doubles each time.
s1_definition.oneliner: Start with the empty subset and, for each element, duplicate all existing subsets and add the element to each copy.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Subsets is the foundational Subsets-pattern problem. For a set of n distinct elements there are exactly two to the power n subsets. The iterative technique starts with a list containing only the empty subset and, for each new element, duplicates every existing subset and adds the element to each duplicate. This doubles the collection with each element, naturally producing all subsets in O(2^n) total work, which is optimal because that many subsets must be output.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a customer like Rajesh can opt into any combination of add-on services, say overdraft, insurance, and a rewards card. We want every possible service bundle he could choose, from choosing nothing to choosing all three. We start with one empty bundle, and for each new service we copy every bundle we have so far and add the service to each copy, so the number of bundles doubles each time.

**One line to remember:** Start with the empty subset and, for each element, duplicate all existing subsets and add the element to each copy.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep a list of subsets, seeded with one empty list. For each incoming number we record the current size, then iterate over exactly that many existing subsets, copying each and appending the new number. For example, `int size = subsets.size(); for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) { List<Integer> copy = new ArrayList<>(subsets.get(i)); copy.add(num); subsets.add(copy); }`. Capturing the size first is essential so we iterate only over the pre-existing subsets and not the ones we are adding in this round.

This produces all subsets without recursion, which avoids stack depth concerns for larger inputs. Each subset is a fresh list, so later rounds that extend subsets never mutate earlier results.

A senior-level nuance is that the elements are assumed distinct; duplicates require a different approach that skips over-counting. Another nuance is that the output size is inherently exponential, so the algorithm is optimal in the sense that it spends time proportional to the size of what it must produce, and one should warn that enumerating subsets of a large set is infeasible by nature, not by implementation.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India offers Rajesh a set of distinct add-on services, and the product team wants to enumerate every possible bundle he could select, including the empty bundle, to price and present options. This is exactly how Subsets works: each bundle is a subset of the available services.

Problem 2 — Building bundles by hand is error-prone and misses combinations. This is why we generate them systematically by doubling: each new service copies every existing bundle and adds itself, guaranteeing completeness.

  │     : List<List<String>>              │
  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── State: collection size per round ──────────────────────
  [1] → [2] → [4] → [8]   (doubles each element)

  Contract for allBundles(services):
    Pre:  services are distinct
    Post: returns all 2^n subsets, each an independent list
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Subsets is the foundational problem of the Subsets pattern: given a set of distinct elements I generate all two-to-the-n subsets, including the empty set and the full set. I use the iterative doubling technique. I start with a collection containing only the empty subset, and for each new element I take a snapshot of the current collection size, then copy every existing subset and add the new element to each copy. Each element therefore doubles the collection, and after processing all elements I have exactly every subset.

The one detail that trips people up is capturing the size before the round begins. If I iterated over the live collection while adding to it, I would process subsets I just created and over-generate, so I snapshot the size first and extend only the pre-existing subsets. I also make each subset a fresh copy so extending subsets in a later round never mutates an earlier result.

At the National Bank of India I used this to enumerate every add-on service bundle a customer like Rajesh could choose, from the empty bundle to the full bundle, so the product team could price and present all options. I generated the bundles by doubling as each service was considered, which guaranteed completeness without recursion. Explaining the snapshot-the-size subtlety and acknowledging that the output is inherently exponential, so the method is optimal for what it must produce, is what shows an interviewer I understand both the technique and its limits.

answers.question: Given a set of numbers that may contain duplicates, generate all possible unique subsets, with no two subsets identical. Explain how sorting plus a controlled expansion of only the newly added subsets prevents duplicate subsets.
answers.shortTitle: Subsets With Duplicates (Generate Unique Subsets When Elements Repeat)

s1_definition.profdef: Subsets With Duplicates generates every distinct subset when the input contains repeated elements. We first sort the input so equal elements are adjacent. We then use iterative doubling, but when the current element equals the previous element, we only extend the subsets created in the previous round, not all subsets, which prevents producing the same subset twice. The work is proportional to the number of distinct subsets produced.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh's available cashback coupons may include duplicates, like two identical five-percent coupons. When we enumerate every distinct coupon bundle, choosing the first five-percent coupon or the second must not count as two different bundles. We sort the coupons so identical ones sit together, and when we process a repeat we only grow the bundles that received the previous identical coupon, which stops us from generating the same bundle twice.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort first, and for a repeated element extend only the subsets added in the previous round to avoid duplicate subsets.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Subsets With Duplicates generates every distinct subset when the input contains repeated elements. We first sort the input so equal elements are adjacent. We then use iterative doubling, but when the current element equals the previous element, we only extend the subsets created in the previous round, not all subsets, which prevents producing the same subset twice. The work is proportional to the number of distinct subsets produced.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, Rajesh's available cashback coupons may include duplicates, like two identical five-percent coupons. When we enumerate every distinct coupon bundle, choosing the first five-percent coupon or the second must not count as two different bundles. We sort the coupons so identical ones sit together, and when we process a repeat we only grow the bundles that received the previous identical coupon, which stops us from generating the same bundle twice.

**One line to remember:** Sort first, and for a repeated element extend only the subsets added in the previous round to avoid duplicate subsets.

sections.s2_technical:
Sorting places equal values next to each other, which is the precondition for the duplicate-skip rule. We track the start index into the subsets list where the previous round began. For a fresh, non-duplicate element we extend all existing subsets, as in the plain subsets problem. For an element equal to the previous one we extend only the subsets from `startIndex` to the end of the list, which are exactly the ones that gained the previous identical element.

For example, we compute `int start = (num == previous) ? previousRoundStart : 0;` and then iterate `for (int i = start; i < size; i++)` copying and extending. We update `previousRoundStart` to the size before this round each time. This surgical restriction is what avoids over-counting.

A senior-level nuance is why extending only the previous round is correct: a new copy of a duplicate value must attach to subsets that already contain the earlier copy, otherwise we would create a subset with one copy that is indistinguishable from one produced earlier. Another nuance is that without sorting the adjacency assumption breaks, so sorting is not optional here.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India issues Rajesh a basket of cashback coupons that can include identical duplicates, and marketing wants every distinct coupon bundle for display. Treating two identical coupons as distinct would flood the list with duplicate bundles. This is exactly how Subsets With Duplicates works: it enumerates only distinct subsets.

Problem 2 — The naive doubling approach would generate the same bundle multiple times when coupons repeat. This is why we sort the coupons and, on a repeated coupon, extend only the bundles from the previous round, producing each distinct bundle exactly once.

The code defines a `DupSubsetsService` exposing `distinctBundles(coupons)` returning distinct coupon-value lists. A `Demo` runs it over coupons that include a duplicate and logs the distinct bundles.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Subsets With Duplicates generates every distinct subset when the input may contain repeated elements, and the challenge is to avoid producing the same subset twice. I first sort the input so that equal elements sit next to each other, which is a hard precondition for the technique. Then I use iterative doubling, but with one rule: when the current element equals the previous element, I extend only the subsets created in the previous round rather than all existing subsets. For a brand-new element I extend everything as usual.

The reason this works is that a second copy of a duplicate value must attach only to subsets that already contain the first copy. If I extended all subsets, I would attach the second copy to subsets that have no copy, producing a subset indistinguishable from one I already made with the first copy. Restricting the expansion to the previous round's subsets produces each distinct subset exactly once.

At the National Bank of India I used this to enumerate distinct cashback-coupon bundles for a customer like Rajesh, whose basket could contain identical coupons, so marketing needed each real bundle listed once rather than duplicated by which identical coupon was chosen. I sorted the coupons, extended only the previous round on repeats, and produced clean distinct bundles. Explaining the sort precondition and the previous-round-only expansion is what tells an interviewer that I understand precisely how the Subsets pattern is adapted to handle duplicates.

answers.question: Given a set of distinct numbers, generate all possible permutations, meaning every possible ordering. Explain the backtracking technique that fixes one position at a time.
answers.shortTitle: Permutations (Generate All Orderings of a Distinct Set)

s1_definition.profdef: Permutations is a Subsets-pattern problem that generates all n factorial orderings of n distinct elements. The backtracking technique builds a permutation position by position: at each position we try every element not yet used, mark it used, recurse to fill the next position, and then unmark it to try the next choice. When the current permutation reaches full length we record a copy. The work is proportional to the number of permutations times their length.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a batch of payments from Rajesh must be tried in every possible processing order to stress-test the settlement engine. We build an order one slot at a time: for the first slot we try each payment, for the next slot each remaining payment, and so on, undoing each choice to explore the next. When all slots are filled we have one complete ordering to test.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fill positions one at a time, try each unused element, recurse, then undo the choice to explore the rest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Permutations is a Subsets-pattern problem that generates all n factorial orderings of n distinct elements. The backtracking technique builds a permutation position by position: at each position we try every element not yet used, mark it used, recurse to fill the next position, and then unmark it to try the next choice. When the current permutation reaches full length we record a copy. The work is proportional to the number of permutations times their length.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a batch of payments from Rajesh must be tried in every possible processing order to stress-test the settlement engine. We build an order one slot at a time: for the first slot we try each payment, for the next slot each remaining payment, and so on, undoing each choice to explore the next. When all slots are filled we have one complete ordering to test.

**One line to remember:** Fill positions one at a time, try each unused element, recurse, then undo the choice to explore the rest.

sections.s2_technical:
We maintain a current partial permutation and a way to know which elements are still available. A clean approach uses a boolean `used` array parallel to the input. At each recursion level we loop over all elements and skip used ones, for example `if (used[i]) continue;`. We choose element i by adding it to the current list and setting `used[i] = true`, recurse to fill the next position, then backtrack with `used[i] = false` and remove it from the list.

When the current list size equals the input length we have a complete permutation, so we store a defensive copy, for example `result.add(new ArrayList<>(current));`. The base case and the choose-recurse-unchoose discipline are the whole algorithm.

A senior-level nuance is that the elements are distinct, so no duplicate-skipping is needed; with duplicates we would sort and skip equal siblings at the same level. Another nuance is that permutation count grows factorially, so this is only feasible for small n, and we should state that limit explicitly rather than let a caller request permutations of a large batch.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India settlement team must verify that a batch of distinct payments settles correctly regardless of processing order, so they need every possible ordering of the batch to replay through the engine. This is exactly how Permutations works: each ordering is one permutation of the batch.

Problem 2 — Enumerating orderings by hand misses cases and cannot scale even to a handful of payments. This is why we generate them with backtracking, which systematically fixes one position at a time and guarantees all orderings appear.

The code defines a `PermutationService` exposing `allOrderings(payments)` returning a list of orderings. A `Demo` runs it over three distinct payment ids and logs the six orderings.

Input: payments PAY1, PAY2, PAY3.

Step 3: Backtrack to the second slot and try PAY3 instead, leaving PAY2 for the third slot, giving PAY1, PAY3, PAY2. Store it.

Step 4: Backtrack to the first slot and try PAY2, then PAY3, generating the remaining four orderings similarly.

Step 5: The result holds all six orderings, which is three factorial.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Permutations generates every ordering of a set of distinct elements, and there are n factorial of them. I use backtracking that fills the permutation one position at a time. I keep a current partial ordering and a boolean used-array that marks which elements are already placed. At each level I loop over all elements, skip the used ones, and for each available element I choose it by adding it and marking it used, recurse to fill the next position, then un-choose by removing it and clearing the used flag so the next sibling choice can be explored. When the current ordering reaches full length I store a defensive copy.

The discipline I emphasise is choose, explore, un-choose, with the state restored exactly after every branch so sibling branches start clean. Because the elements are distinct, I do not need any duplicate skipping; if there were duplicates I would sort and skip equal siblings at the same level. I also state plainly that the number of permutations grows factorially, so this is only practical for small inputs, and I would guard against a caller requesting permutations of a large batch.

At the National Bank of India I used this to stress-test the settlement engine, which had to settle a batch of distinct payments correctly regardless of processing order, so we replayed every ordering of the batch through the engine. I generated the orderings with backtracking and a used-array, storing each full ordering as a fresh copy. Explaining the choose-explore-un-choose pattern and the factorial feasibility limit is what shows an interviewer that I understand backtracking as a general tool, not just this one problem.

answers.question: Given a string with letters and digits, generate all strings that can be formed by changing the case of the letters, leaving digits unchanged. Explain the doubling technique that forks only on letters.
answers.shortTitle: String Permutations by Changing Case (Letter Case Permutation)

s1_definition.profdef: Letter Case Permutation is a Subsets-pattern problem. Starting from the original string we process each character; for a digit we leave every existing string unchanged, but for a letter we duplicate every existing string and flip the case of that one letter in the copy. The number of results is two to the power of the number of letters, and the work is proportional to that output size.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a reference code like a2b may be typed by customers in mixed case, and support wants every case variant to match against records while leaving the digits alone. We start with the original code and, for each letter, make a copy of every variant so far with that letter's case flipped, so the number of variants doubles at each letter but stays the same at each digit.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each letter, duplicate all current strings with that letter's case flipped; for each digit, do nothing.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Letter Case Permutation is a Subsets-pattern problem. Starting from the original string we process each character; for a digit we leave every existing string unchanged, but for a letter we duplicate every existing string and flip the case of that one letter in the copy. The number of results is two to the power of the number of letters, and the work is proportional to that output size.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a reference code like a2b may be typed by customers in mixed case, and support wants every case variant to match against records while leaving the digits alone. We start with the original code and, for each letter, make a copy of every variant so far with that letter's case flipped, so the number of variants doubles at each letter but stays the same at each digit.

**One line to remember:** For each letter, duplicate all current strings with that letter's case flipped; for each digit, do nothing.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep a list seeded with the original string as a character array or `StringBuilder`. For each index, we check whether the character is a letter. If it is a digit we skip, leaving the list unchanged. If it is a letter we snapshot the current size, then for each existing string we create a copy and flip the case at that index, for example `char flipped = Character.isUpperCase(c) ? Character.toLowerCase(c) : Character.toUpperCase(c);`.

Snapshotting the size before the round, exactly as in the plain subsets problem, ensures we only fork the strings that existed before this letter. Case flipping uses `Character.toLowerCase` and `Character.toUpperCase`, and `Character.isLetter` distinguishes letters from digits.

A senior-level nuance is that only alphabetic characters fork the result, so a code with many digits and few letters has a small result even if it is long. Another nuance is to avoid mutating shared backing arrays; each forked variant must be an independent copy so flipping one does not change another.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores reference codes mixing letters and digits, and customers type them in arbitrary case. Support wants to generate every case variant of a code to match it against stored records, while digits stay fixed. This is exactly how Letter Case Permutation works: letters fork into two cases, digits do not.

Problem 2 — Flipping cases by hand misses variants and cannot cover long codes. This is why we generate variants by doubling on letters only, guaranteeing all case combinations appear.

The code defines a `CaseVariantService` exposing `allCaseVariants(code)` returning a list of variant strings. A `Demo` runs it over a code with two letters and one digit and logs the four variants.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Letter Case Permutation generates every string obtainable by changing the case of the letters in an input while leaving its digits untouched. I process the string character by character over a growing list of variants seeded with the original. For a digit I do nothing, leaving the list unchanged. For a letter I snapshot the current size, then for each existing variant I make an independent copy and flip the case of that one letter, which doubles the list on every letter. The result count is two to the power of the number of letters.

The two details I stress are that only letters fork the result, so a mostly-digit code stays small even if it is long, and that each forked variant must be an independent copy of the backing array, because flipping a character in a shared array would corrupt other variants. Snapshotting the size before each letter round, just like in the plain subsets problem, keeps me from forking variants I created in the same round.

At the National Bank of India I used this in support tooling to match customer-typed reference codes against stored records, generating every case variant of a code while keeping digits fixed so the match was robust to how the customer typed it. I forked only on letters using Character.isLetter and copied the backing array before flipping. Explaining that digits do not branch and that copies must be independent is what shows an interviewer I understand the Subsets doubling pattern applied to strings rather than numeric sets.

answers.question: For a given number N, generate all combinations of N pairs of balanced parentheses. Explain the backtracking technique that tracks open and close counts to keep every prefix valid.
answers.shortTitle: Balanced Parentheses (Generate All Valid Combinations)

s1_definition.profdef: Balanced Parentheses generates all valid strings of N open and N close parentheses using backtracking. We build the string character by character, tracking how many open and close parentheses have been placed. We may place an open parenthesis while fewer than N opens have been used, and a close parenthesis only while closes are fewer than opens, which guarantees every prefix stays valid. The number of results is the Nth Catalan number.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, nested approval brackets must open and close in balance, like opening a sub-approval only inside an open parent approval and closing children before parents. For N levels we want every valid bracketing. We build left to right: we can open a new bracket as long as we have brackets left to open, and we can close one only if there is an unclosed bracket waiting, which keeps the structure valid at every step.
s1_definition.oneliner: Backtrack placing an open while opens are below N, and a close only while closes trail opens.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Balanced Parentheses generates all valid strings of N open and N close parentheses using backtracking. We build the string character by character, tracking how many open and close parentheses have been placed. We may place an open parenthesis while fewer than N opens have been used, and a close parenthesis only while closes are fewer than opens, which guarantees every prefix stays valid. The number of results is the Nth Catalan number.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, nested approval brackets must open and close in balance, like opening a sub-approval only inside an open parent approval and closing children before parents. For N levels we want every valid bracketing. We build left to right: we can open a new bracket as long as we have brackets left to open, and we can close one only if there is an unclosed bracket waiting, which keeps the structure valid at every step.

**One line to remember:** Backtrack placing an open while opens are below N, and a close only while closes trail opens.

sections.s2_technical:
We recurse with two counters, `openCount` and `closeCount`, and a builder for the current string. If `openCount < n` we may append an open parenthesis and recurse with `openCount + 1`. If `closeCount < openCount` we may append a close parenthesis and recurse with `closeCount + 1`. When the string length reaches two times N it is a complete valid combination and we record it.

The close rule, `closeCount < openCount`, is the key invariant: a close is only legal when there is an unmatched open before it, so no prefix ever has more closes than opens. Backtracking undoes the last character after each recursive branch, for example by trimming the builder back to its previous length.

A senior-level nuance is that this generate-and-prune avoids ever building an invalid prefix, so unlike filtering all two-to-the-two-N strings it does no wasted work on invalid candidates. Another nuance is that the count of valid combinations is the Catalan number, which grows fast, so N must be modest.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India models nested approval structures where a sub-approval can only exist inside an open parent approval, and all children must close before their parent. For N approval levels the governance team wants every valid nesting to review possible workflows. This is exactly how Balanced Parentheses works: an open is a parent approval opening and a close is one closing.

Problem 2 — Enumerating structures and then checking validity wastes effort on invalid ones. This is why we backtrack with open and close counts so every string we build is valid by construction, never producing a broken nesting.

The code defines a `ParenthesesService` exposing `allBalanced(n)` returning the valid strings. A `Demo` runs it for N equal to two and logs the two valid combinations.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: N equal to two.

Step 1: Start empty with zero opens and zero closes. Opens are below two, so append an open. The string is "(" with one open.

Step 2: Opens are below two, so append another open. The string is "((" with two opens. Opens are no longer below two, so we cannot open more; closes are below opens, so append a close, giving "(()".

Step 3: Closes are still below opens, so append another close, giving "(())". The length is four, which is two times N, so store "(())". Backtrack.

Step 4: Return to the state "(" with one open, and this time append a close, giving "()". Then opens are below two, append an open, giving "()(", then a close, giving "()()" of length four, so store "()()".

Step 5: The result is "(())" and "()()", the two valid combinations for N equal to two.

```
Oct 27, 2026 8:41:55 PM com.bank.governance.service.ParenthesesService backtrack
FINE: Completed bracketing (())
FINE: Completed bracketing ()()
INFO: Generated 2 valid bracketings for n=2
INFO: NBI valid approval nestings for n=2: [(()), ()()]
```

  └──────────────────────────────────────┘

  may open  iff openCount < n
  may close iff closeCount < openCount
  complete  iff length == 2n

  Contract for allBalanced(n):
    Pre:  n >= 0
    Post: all Catalan(n) valid parenthesis strings
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Balanced Parentheses generates all valid combinations of N pairs of parentheses using backtracking. I build the string one character at a time while tracking how many opens and closes I have placed. I may append an open parenthesis whenever the open count is still below N, and I may append a close parenthesis only when the close count is strictly less than the open count. That close rule is the essential invariant, because it guarantees that no prefix ever has more closes than opens, so every string I build is valid without any after-the-fact checking. When the length reaches two times N I record a complete combination.

The reason I prefer this generate-and-prune approach over generating all possible strings and filtering is that it never builds an invalid prefix, so it does no wasted work. I also note that the number of valid combinations is the Catalan number, which grows quickly, so N must stay modest.

At the National Bank of India I used this to enumerate valid nested approval structures, where a sub-approval can only open inside an open parent and every child must close before its parent, so for a given number of levels governance could review all valid workflow shapes. I backtracked with open and close counters so every generated structure was valid by construction. Explaining the two placement rules and why they keep every prefix valid is what shows an interviewer that I understand backtracking with invariants, not just brute-force enumeration.

answers.question: Given a word, generate all of its unique generalized abbreviations, where any contiguous run of characters can be replaced by its count. Explain the backtracking choice at each character of keeping it or abbreviating it.
answers.shortTitle: Unique Generalized Abbreviations (All Abbreviations of a Word)

s1_definition.profdef: Unique Generalized Abbreviations enumerates every abbreviation of a word, where each contiguous group of characters may be replaced by the number of characters it covers. The backtracking solution makes a binary choice at every character: keep the character as a literal, or abbreviate it by extending a running count of skipped characters. There are two to the power of the word length abbreviations, and each is emitted once.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, long product names like "loan" can be abbreviated in system messages by replacing runs of letters with a count, so "loan" could appear as "l3", "4", "lo2", and so on. We want every such abbreviation. We walk the word deciding for each letter whether to spell it out or to fold it into a running skip count, and when a skip run ends we write the count.
s1_definition.oneliner: At each character choose to keep it or to count it, flushing the running count whenever you keep a character or reach the end.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Unique Generalized Abbreviations enumerates every abbreviation of a word, where each contiguous group of characters may be replaced by the number of characters it covers. The backtracking solution makes a binary choice at every character: keep the character as a literal, or abbreviate it by extending a running count of skipped characters. There are two to the power of the word length abbreviations, and each is emitted once.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, long product names like "loan" can be abbreviated in system messages by replacing runs of letters with a count, so "loan" could appear as "l3", "4", "lo2", and so on. We want every such abbreviation. We walk the word deciding for each letter whether to spell it out or to fold it into a running skip count, and when a skip run ends we write the count.

**One line to remember:** At each character choose to keep it or to count it, flushing the running count whenever you keep a character or reach the end.

sections.s2_technical:
We recurse with the current index, a `StringBuilder` for the abbreviation so far, and a `count` of consecutive characters currently being abbreviated. At each index we branch two ways. The first branch abbreviates the current character by recursing with `count + 1` and the index advanced, not yet writing anything. The second branch keeps the current character: if there is a pending count we first append it, then we append the literal character and recurse with `count` reset to zero.

At the base case, when the index reaches the word length, we append any remaining count and record the abbreviation. For example, `if (count > 0) current.append(count); result.add(current.toString());`. Careful length bookkeeping is needed to backtrack the builder to its previous state after each branch.

A senior-level nuance is that the two choices at every character, keep or abbreviate, map directly onto the subsets pattern: each abbreviation corresponds to a subset of positions chosen to be kept. Another nuance is that because every position independently is kept or counted, all abbreviations are automatically unique, so no deduplication is needed.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India shortens product names in constrained displays like SMS and receipts, replacing runs of letters by counts. The content team wants every possible abbreviation of a product name to pick a readable one. This is exactly how Unique Generalized Abbreviations works: each abbreviation is one way of counting runs.

Problem 2 — Listing abbreviations by hand is incomplete and error-prone. This is why we backtrack with a keep-or-count choice at each character, which produces all two-to-the-length abbreviations, each exactly once.

The code defines an `AbbreviationService` exposing `allAbbreviations(word)` returning the abbreviation strings. A `Demo` runs it over a short product word and logs all abbreviations.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: word fd.

Step 1: At index 0 with count zero, first branch abbreviates f, recursing to index 1 with count one. Second branch keeps f, appending "f" and recursing to index 1 with count zero.

Step 2: Down the abbreviate-f branch at index 1 with count one, first sub-branch abbreviates d, recursing to index 2 with count two; at the end we flush count two, giving "2". The second sub-branch keeps d, flushing the pending count one to "1" then appending "d", giving "1d".

Step 3: Down the keep-f branch at index 1 with count zero, first sub-branch abbreviates d, recursing to index 2 with count one; at the end we flush, giving "f1". The second sub-branch keeps d, giving "fd".

Step 4: The four abbreviations are "2", "1d", "f1", and "fd".

```
Oct 27, 2026 8:46:18 PM com.bank.content.service.AbbreviationService backtrack
FINE: Completed abbreviation 2
FINE: Completed abbreviation 1d
FINE: Completed abbreviation f1
FINE: Completed abbreviation fd
INFO: Generated 4 abbreviations for 'fd'
INFO: NBI abbreviations for 'fd': [2, 1d, f1, fd]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  word: f d   (keep or count at each index)
    │
    ▼
  index0
    ├ abbreviate f (count=1)
    │    ├ abbreviate d (count=2) → end flush → "2"
    │    └ keep d → flush 1 → "1d"
    └ keep f ("f", count=0)
         ├ abbreviate d (count=1) → end flush → "f1"
         └ keep d → "fd"
    │
    ▼
  result: [2, 1d, f1, fd]   (2^2)
```

  abbreviate → count++
  keep       → flush count, append char, count=0
  end        → flush trailing count

  Contract for allAbbreviations(word):
    Pre:  word may be empty
    Post: all 2^len abbreviations, each unique
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Unique Generalized Abbreviations generates every abbreviation of a word, where any contiguous run of characters can be replaced by the number of characters it covers. I solve it with backtracking that makes a binary choice at each character: either abbreviate it by extending a running count of skipped characters, or keep it as a literal. When I keep a character I first flush any pending count, then append the literal and reset the count to zero, and at the end of the word I flush any remaining count before recording the abbreviation.

The insight I highlight is that this keep-or-count decision at every position maps directly onto the subsets pattern, where each abbreviation corresponds to a subset of positions chosen to be kept. Because each position is decided independently, every abbreviation is distinct automatically, so I need no deduplication step. I am careful with builder length bookkeeping, saving and restoring it around each branch so backtracking leaves no leftover characters.

At the National Bank of India I used this to shorten product names for constrained displays like SMS and receipts, where runs of letters are replaced by counts, so the content team could review every abbreviation of a name and pick a readable one. I backtracked with a keep-or-count choice and flushed the running count correctly before literals and at the end. Explaining the mapping to subsets and why the abbreviations are inherently unique is what shows an interviewer that I can recognise a subsets-style decision inside a problem that does not obviously look like one.

answers.question: Given a string expression of numbers and the operators plus, minus, and multiply, compute all possible results from different ways of grouping the numbers and operators with parentheses. Explain the divide-and-conquer recursion that splits at each operator.
answers.shortTitle: Evaluate Expression (Different Ways to Group Numbers and Operators)

s1_definition.profdef: Evaluate Expression, also called Different Ways to Add Parentheses, is a Subsets-pattern divide-and-conquer problem. At each operator we split the expression into a left part and a right part, recursively compute all results of each part, then combine every left result with every right result using that operator. A pure number returns itself as a single result. Memoizing by substring removes repeated recomputation, giving Catalan-number-many results produced efficiently.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a fee formula like a times b plus c can be computed in different groupings, and different groupings can give different totals. The finance team wants every possible total so they can see the range a formula could produce. We split the formula at each operator, work out all totals of the left side and all totals of the right side, and combine them with the operator to get all totals through that split.
s1_definition.oneliner: Split at every operator, recurse on both sides, and combine all left results with all right results.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Evaluate Expression, also called Different Ways to Add Parentheses, is a Subsets-pattern divide-and-conquer problem. At each operator we split the expression into a left part and a right part, recursively compute all results of each part, then combine every left result with every right result using that operator. A pure number returns itself as a single result. Memoizing by substring removes repeated recomputation, giving Catalan-number-many results produced efficiently.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a fee formula like a times b plus c can be computed in different groupings, and different groupings can give different totals. The finance team wants every possible total so they can see the range a formula could produce. We split the formula at each operator, work out all totals of the left side and all totals of the right side, and combine them with the operator to get all totals through that split.

**One line to remember:** Split at every operator, recurse on both sides, and combine all left results with all right results.

sections.s2_technical:
We scan the expression, and whenever we see an operator we treat it as the top-level operation of one grouping. We recursively evaluate the substring to its left and the substring to its right, obtaining lists of all possible results for each. Then we combine: for each left value and each right value we apply the operator, for example for a plus we add, and collect every combined result.

The base case is a substring with no operator, which is a plain number returning a single-element list. For example, `if (!containsOperator(expr)) return List.of(new BigDecimal(expr));`. Memoization caches results keyed by substring, so overlapping subproblems are solved once.

A senior-level nuance is that the number of groupings is the Catalan number, so memoization matters for larger expressions. Another nuance is money safety: although this is integer-like arithmetic on fees, we use `BigDecimal` and its `add`, `subtract`, and `multiply` methods so the results stay exact, and we never use floating-point.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India computes fees from small formulas combining base amounts with plus, minus, and multiply, and because grouping changes the result, finance wants every possible total a formula could yield to understand its range. This is exactly how Evaluate Expression works: each grouping is one parenthesization.

Problem 2 — Recomputing the same sub-formula repeatedly is wasteful for longer formulas. This is why we memoize results by substring, so each sub-formula's set of totals is computed once and reused.

The code defines an `ExpressionService` exposing `allResults(expr)` returning a list of `BigDecimal` totals. A `Demo` runs it over a small fee formula and logs all possible totals.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: formula 2*3-4.

Step 1: Scan for operators. The first operator is the multiply at index 1. Split into left "2" and right "3-4".

Step 2: The left "2" has no operator, so it returns the single value 2. The right "3-4" has a minus; split into "3" and "4", each a plain number, combine to 3 minus 4 equal to minus 1. So "3-4" returns minus 1.

Step 3: Combine the multiply split: 2 times minus 1 equals minus 2. So one possible total is minus 2.

Step 4: The second operator is the minus at index 3. Split into left "2*3" and right "4". The left "2*3" combines 2 times 3 equal to 6. Combine the minus split: 6 minus 4 equals 2. So another possible total is 2.

Step 5: The possible totals are minus 2 and 2, from the two groupings 2 times the quantity 3 minus 4, and the quantity 2 times 3, minus 4.

```

FINE: Sub-formula '2' yields [2]
FINE: Sub-formula '3' yields [3]
FINE: Sub-formula '4' yields [4]
FINE: Sub-formula '3-4' yields [-1]
FINE: Sub-formula '2*3' yields [6]
FINE: Sub-formula '2*3-4' yields [-2, 2]
INFO: NBI possible fee totals for '2*3-4': [-2, 2]
```

    │     "2"=[2] , "3-4"=[3-4=-1]  → 2*-1 = -2
    └ split at '-' : left "2*3" , right "4"
          "2*3"=[2*3=6] , "4"=[4]  → 6-4 = 2
    │
    ▼
  results: [-2, 2]   (memo reused for shared sub-formulas)
```

  │  Memoization by substring (overlapping subproblems)      │
  │     WHY: Catalan-many groupings; reuse sub-results        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ──────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: service only evaluates groupings                     │
  │  O: new operators extend apply(), not the recursion      │
  │  D: depends only on String/BigDecimal                    │

  2.   split '*' → allResults("2"), allResults("3-4")
  3.   split '-' → allResults("2*3"), allResults("4")
  4.   combine → [-2, 2]

  Contract for allResults(expr):
    Pre:  expr uses numbers and + - *
    Post: every result over all groupings
    Note: BigDecimal keeps totals exact; memo keyed by substring
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Evaluate Expression, also known as Different Ways to Add Parentheses, asks for every possible result of an arithmetic expression over all ways of grouping the numbers and operators. I solve it with divide and conquer: at every operator I split the expression into a left part and a right part, recursively compute all results of each part, and then combine every left result with every right result using that operator. A substring with no operator is a plain number that returns itself as a single result. I memoize results by substring so that overlapping sub-expressions are computed only once.

The two points I stress are that the number of groupings is the Catalan number, so memoization is what keeps larger expressions tractable, and that in a banking context the arithmetic must be exact, so I use BigDecimal with its add, subtract, and multiply methods rather than any floating-point type.

At the National Bank of India I used this to explore the range of totals a fee formula could produce, because grouping changes the result and finance needed to see every possible total for a formula combining base amounts with plus, minus, and multiply. I split at each operator, combined all left and right results, kept the money as BigDecimal, and cached sub-formula results in a memo. Explaining the split-and-combine recursion and why memoization and BigDecimal both matter is what shows an interviewer that I can apply the subsets-style divide and conquer to a real, precision-sensitive financial calculation.

answers.question: Given a number N, generate all structurally unique binary search trees that store values 1 through N. Explain how choosing each value as the root and recursively building left and right subtrees enumerates every shape.
answers.shortTitle: Structurally Unique Binary Search Trees (Generate All Shapes)

s1_definition.profdef: Structurally Unique Binary Search Trees is a Subsets-pattern divide-and-conquer problem. For values in a range, we pick each value in turn as the root; all smaller values form the left subtree and all larger values form the right subtree. We recursively generate every left-subtree shape and every right-subtree shape, then pair each left shape with each right shape under the chosen root. The count of trees is the Catalan number, and each is a distinct BST.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, an interest-tier lookup can be organized as a search tree over tier numbers one to N, and different tree shapes give different lookup performance. The analytics team wants every valid tree shape to benchmark. We pick each tier as the root, put the lower tiers on the left and the higher tiers on the right, build every shape of each side, and combine them.
s1_definition.oneliner: Make each value the root, recurse to build all left and all right subtree shapes, and pair them under the root.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Structurally Unique Binary Search Trees is a Subsets-pattern divide-and-conquer problem. For values in a range, we pick each value in turn as the root; all smaller values form the left subtree and all larger values form the right subtree. We recursively generate every left-subtree shape and every right-subtree shape, then pair each left shape with each right shape under the chosen root. The count of trees is the Catalan number, and each is a distinct BST.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, an interest-tier lookup can be organized as a search tree over tier numbers one to N, and different tree shapes give different lookup performance. The analytics team wants every valid tree shape to benchmark. We pick each tier as the root, put the lower tiers on the left and the higher tiers on the right, build every shape of each side, and combine them.

**One line to remember:** Make each value the root, recurse to build all left and all right subtree shapes, and pair them under the root.

sections.s2_technical:
We define a recursion over an inclusive range, `generate(start, end)`, returning a list of all tree roots for that range. If `start > end` the range is empty and we return a single-element list containing `null`, which represents a missing subtree and is essential for pairing. For each value i from start to end we recursively generate `leftTrees = generate(start, i - 1)` and `rightTrees = generate(i + 1, end)`.

Then we pair: for each left-subtree root and each right-subtree root we create a new node with value i, attach the two subtrees, and add it to the result. For example, `TreeNode root = new TreeNode(i); root.left = l; root.right = r; result.add(root);`. Memoizing by range can avoid recomputation when only counting, though generating distinct node objects typically rebuilds them.

A senior-level nuance is the empty-range sentinel: returning a list with one null lets the pairing loops run once even when a subtree is absent, which is what correctly produces trees where the root has only one child. Another nuance is that the number of shapes is the Catalan number, so N must be small for generation.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Structurally Unique Binary Search Trees asks me to generate every distinct BST that stores the values one through N. I use divide and conquer driven by the BST ordering property. I pick each value in turn as the root; everything smaller must form the left subtree and everything larger the right subtree. I recursively generate every possible left-subtree shape and every possible right-subtree shape over those ranges, then pair each left shape with each right shape under the chosen root to form complete trees.

The detail that makes the recursion clean is the empty-range sentinel. When the range is empty I return a list containing a single null, which represents a missing subtree, so the pairing loops still execute once and correctly produce trees whose root has only one child. I also note that the number of shapes is the Catalan number, which grows quickly, so generation is only practical for small N.

At the National Bank of India I used this to benchmark interest-tier lookup trees, where tiers one to N were stored in a BST and the tree shape affected lookup depth, so analytics wanted every valid shape to measure. I generated the shapes by choosing each tier as root and combining all left and right sub-shapes, and rendered each tree in a parenthesized form for the benchmark report. Explaining how the BST ordering splits the range and why the empty-range sentinel is needed is what shows an interviewer that I can turn a structural property into a correct generative recursion.

answers.question: Given a number N, count how many structurally unique binary search trees can store values 1 through N, without generating them. Explain the dynamic-programming recurrence derived from choosing each root.
answers.shortTitle: Count of Structurally Unique BSTs (How Many Shapes Exist)

s1_definition.profdef: Count of Structurally Unique BSTs returns only the number of distinct BSTs over N values. It follows from the same root-choice argument as generation, but because we only count, we multiply the number of left-subtree shapes by the number of right-subtree shapes for each root and sum over all roots. This is the Catalan-number recurrence, computed bottom up in O(N squared) time with O(N) space, far cheaper than enumerating the trees.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, before benchmarking interest-tier trees, analytics first wants to know how many distinct tree shapes even exist for N tiers, so they can decide whether to enumerate them. We do not build the trees; we just count. For each tier chosen as the root, the number of whole trees is the count of left shapes times the count of right shapes, and we add that across all roots.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count of trees over N equals the sum over each root of left-count times right-count, which is the Catalan recurrence.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Count of Structurally Unique BSTs returns only the number of distinct BSTs over N values. It follows from the same root-choice argument as generation, but because we only count, we multiply the number of left-subtree shapes by the number of right-subtree shapes for each root and sum over all roots. This is the Catalan-number recurrence, computed bottom up in O(N squared) time with O(N) space, far cheaper than enumerating the trees.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, before benchmarking interest-tier trees, analytics first wants to know how many distinct tree shapes even exist for N tiers, so they can decide whether to enumerate them. We do not build the trees; we just count. For each tier chosen as the root, the number of whole trees is the count of left shapes times the count of right shapes, and we add that across all roots.

**One line to remember:** Count of trees over N equals the sum over each root of left-count times right-count, which is the Catalan recurrence.

sections.s2_technical:
Let `count[k]` be the number of unique BSTs that store k values. There is exactly one way to arrange zero values, the empty tree, and one way to arrange a single value, so `count[0] = 1` and `count[1] = 1`. For a tree of k values, choosing the j-th smallest value as the root leaves j minus one values on the left and k minus j values on the right, contributing `count[j-1] * count[k-j]` trees. Summing over all j gives `count[k]`.

In code this is two nested loops: the outer builds counts from two up to N, and the inner sums the products. For example, `for (int root = 1; root <= k; root++) count[k] += count[root - 1] * count[k - root];`. The result `count[N]` is the answer.

A senior-level nuance is that this is the closed-form Catalan number, but the DP recurrence is the clearer derivation and avoids large factorials and overflow surprises if one is careful; for large N the counts grow beyond a 64-bit range, so a production version would use `BigInteger`. Another nuance is that counting is O(N squared), whereas generating is exponential, so when only the count is needed, generation must be avoided.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — Before the National Bank of India analytics team enumerates interest-tier tree shapes, they need the count of shapes for N tiers to judge whether enumeration is even feasible, because the count explodes with N. This is exactly how Count of Structurally Unique BSTs works: it answers the how-many question cheaply.

Problem 2 — Generating all trees just to count them would be exponential and wasteful. This is why we use the dynamic-programming recurrence, computing the count in quadratic time without building a single tree.

The code defines a `BstCountService` exposing `countShapes(n)` returning a `long` (with a note about BigInteger for large N). A `Demo` prints the count for a few values of N and logs them.

Input: counting for N up to five.
