sections.s6_takeaway:
Count of Structurally Unique BSTs returns just the number of distinct binary search trees over the values one through N, without building any of them. It follows from the same root-choice argument as generation: if I choose the j-th value as the root, there are count of j minus one shapes on the left and count of N minus j shapes on the right, and because the two sides are independent I multiply them, then I sum that product over every possible root. That is the Catalan-number recurrence, and I compute it bottom up in quadratic time with linear space.

The key reason to use this rather than generating and counting is cost: generation is exponential, while this recurrence is O(N squared), so whenever only the count is needed I never build the trees. I also flag that the counts grow past a 64-bit range for larger N, so a production implementation would switch to BigInteger, making that a deliberate decision rather than an overlooked overflow.

At the National Bank of India I used this as a feasibility precheck before enumerating interest-tier lookup-tree shapes, because the number of shapes explodes with the number of tiers and analytics needed to know up front whether full enumeration was even practical. I filled a small dynamic-programming table with the Catalan recurrence and returned the count cheaply. Explaining the multiply-left-by-right-and-sum-over-roots derivation and the overflow caveat is what shows an interviewer that I can separate counting from generation and pick the cheaper tool when that is all that is required.

answers.question: Given a string of digits from 2 to 9, return all possible letter combinations that the digits could represent on a classic phone keypad. Explain the backtracking technique that fixes one digit's letter at a time.
answers.shortTitle: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number (All Keypad Letter Combinations)

s1_definition.profdef: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number is a Subsets-pattern problem that enumerates the Cartesian product of the letter groups mapped to each digit. Using backtracking, we fix one letter for the first digit, recurse to fix a letter for the next digit, and so on until all digits are assigned, then record the combination. The number of results is the product of the group sizes, and the work is proportional to that output size.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, customers sometimes remember a vanity branch phone code by its letters, and support wants every letter spelling a digit code could map to, so they can match it against known branch words. Each digit offers a small group of letters, like 2 maps to a, b, c. We pick one letter for the first digit, then one for the next, building up every full spelling by trying all choices at each position.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each digit try every mapped letter, recurse to the next digit, and record a combination when all digits are assigned.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Letter Combinations of a Phone Number is a Subsets-pattern problem that enumerates the Cartesian product of the letter groups mapped to each digit. Using backtracking, we fix one letter for the first digit, recurse to fix a letter for the next digit, and so on until all digits are assigned, then record the combination. The number of results is the product of the group sizes, and the work is proportional to that output size.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, customers sometimes remember a vanity branch phone code by its letters, and support wants every letter spelling a digit code could map to, so they can match it against known branch words. Each digit offers a small group of letters, like 2 maps to a, b, c. We pick one letter for the first digit, then one for the next, building up every full spelling by trying all choices at each position.

**One line to remember:** For each digit try every mapped letter, recurse to the next digit, and record a combination when all digits are assigned.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep a mapping from each digit character to its letter group, for example digit 2 maps to the string "abc". We recurse with an index into the digit string and a builder for the current combination. At each level we look up the letters for the current digit and loop over them; for each letter we append it, recurse to the next index, then remove it to try the next letter.

When the index reaches the end of the digit string we have assigned a letter to every digit, so we record the combination, for example `result.add(current.toString());`. An empty input returns an empty result rather than a single empty string, which is the conventional edge case.

A senior-level nuance is that this is exactly a Cartesian product, and the backtracking depth equals the number of digits, so the recursion is shallow even though the output can be large. Another nuance is that digits 7 and 9 map to four letters while others map to three, so the per-digit branching is not uniform, and the total count is the product of these group sizes.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs vanity branch phone codes, and support wants every letter spelling of a short digit code to match against a dictionary of branch words. This is exactly how Letter Combinations works: each digit contributes a group of letters and we enumerate all spellings.

Problem 2 — Spelling out combinations by hand is error-prone and misses options. This is why we backtrack over the digit positions, trying every letter at each position, which guarantees all spellings appear.

The code defines a `PhoneLetterService` exposing `letterCombinations(digits)` returning all spellings. A `Demo` runs it over a two-digit code and logs the combinations.

Letter Combinations of a Phone Number enumerates every letter spelling that a string of keypad digits could represent, which is exactly the Cartesian product of the letter groups mapped to each digit. I solve it with backtracking: I keep a mapping from each digit to its letters, and I recurse over the digit positions. At each position I loop over the letters for that digit, appending one, recursing to the next position, and then removing it to try the next letter. When I have assigned a letter to every digit I record the completed spelling.

The point I make is that although the output can be large, the recursion depth is only the number of digits, so the search is shallow and the cost is proportional to the number of spellings it must produce. I also handle the conventional edge case where an empty input returns an empty list rather than a single empty string, and I note that digits seven and nine have four letters while the others have three, so the branching is non-uniform and the total count is the product of the group sizes.

At the National Bank of India I used this in support tooling for vanity branch phone codes, generating every letter spelling of a short digit code to match against a dictionary of branch words. I backtracked over the digit positions with an immutable keypad map and trimmed the builder after each branch. answers.question: Given a set of distinct positive numbers and a target, find all unique combinations that sum to the target, where each number may be used an unlimited number of times. Explain the backtracking technique with a start index that prevents duplicate combinations.
answers.shortTitle: Combination Sum (All Combinations Reaching a Target with Reuse)

s1_definition.profdef: Combination Sum is a Subsets-pattern backtracking problem that finds all multisets of candidate numbers summing to a target, with unlimited reuse of each candidate. We recurse with a remaining target and a start index; at each step we try each candidate from the start index onward, subtracting it and recursing without advancing the start, which permits reuse. Carrying the start index forward prevents reordered duplicates. The search prunes whenever the remaining target goes negative.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a customer wants to reach an exact savings target using fixed denomination deposits, and the same denomination can be deposited many times. We want every distinct set of deposits that hits the target exactly. We try adding each denomination, allow repeats of it, and only ever move forward through the denomination list so we never count the same set in a different order.
s1_definition.oneliner: Backtrack subtracting candidates, allow reuse by not advancing the index, and keep the start index to avoid reordered duplicates.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Combination Sum is a Subsets-pattern backtracking problem that finds all multisets of candidate numbers summing to a target, with unlimited reuse of each candidate. We recurse with a remaining target and a start index; at each step we try each candidate from the start index onward, subtracting it and recursing without advancing the start, which permits reuse. Carrying the start index forward prevents reordered duplicates. The search prunes whenever the remaining target goes negative.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a customer wants to reach an exact savings target using fixed denomination deposits, and the same denomination can be deposited many times. We want every distinct set of deposits that hits the target exactly. We try adding each denomination, allow repeats of it, and only ever move forward through the denomination list so we never count the same set in a different order.

**One line to remember:** Backtrack subtracting candidates, allow reuse by not advancing the index, and keep the start index to avoid reordered duplicates.

sections.s2_technical:
We recurse with the remaining target, a start index into the sorted candidates, and the current combination. If the remaining target is zero we record a copy of the combination as a valid result. If it is negative we return, pruning that branch. Otherwise we loop over candidates from the start index; for each we add it, recurse with the reduced target and the same index to allow reuse, then remove it to backtrack.

Passing the same index on recursion is what permits using a candidate repeatedly, for example `backtrack(candidates, remaining - candidates[i], i, current, result);`. Passing `i` rather than `i + 1` as the next start, while never going back below `i` in the loop, ensures each combination is generated in non-decreasing index order, so reordered duplicates never appear.

A senior-level nuance is sorting the candidates so we can break the loop early once a candidate exceeds the remaining target, since all later candidates are larger. Another nuance is that amounts are money, so they are `BigDecimal`, and the remaining target comparison uses `compareTo`.

Problem 1 — A National Bank of India customer like Rajesh wants to reach an exact savings-goal amount using a fixed set of deposit denominations, and he may deposit any denomination as many times as he likes. He wants every distinct combination of deposits that reaches the goal exactly. This is exactly how Combination Sum works: candidates reused freely, summing to a target.

Problem 2 — Counting the same deposit set in different orders would clutter the options. This is why we carry a start index so combinations are built in a fixed order, producing each distinct set once.

The code defines a `CombinationSumService` exposing `combinationsToGoal(denominations, goal)` returning the combinations. A `Demo` runs it over small denominations and a goal, logging each combination.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Combination Sum finds all distinct combinations of candidate numbers that sum to a target, where each candidate may be reused any number of times. I solve it with backtracking driven by a remaining target and a start index. If the remaining target hits zero I record the current combination; if it would go negative I prune. Otherwise I loop over candidates from the start index, and for each one I subtract it and recurse with the same index rather than the next one, which is what allows a candidate to be reused repeatedly.

The device that prevents duplicates is the start index. Because I never consider a candidate earlier than the current start, every combination is built in non-decreasing index order, so the same multiset is never produced in a different order. I also sort the candidates so I can break out of the loop as soon as one exceeds the remaining target, since all later candidates are even larger, and I keep all amounts as BigDecimal so the arithmetic stays exact.

At the National Bank of India I used this to help a customer like Rajesh reach an exact savings goal using fixed deposit denominations that could each be used many times, enumerating every distinct set of deposits that hit the goal. I sorted the denominations, allowed reuse by passing the same index, prevented reordered duplicates with the start index, and kept money as BigDecimal. Explaining the reuse-via-same-index trick and the start-index deduplication is what shows an interviewer that I understand the two independent concerns, unlimited reuse and uniqueness, that this problem combines.

answers.question: Given two integers N and K, return all possible combinations of K numbers chosen from the range 1 to N. Explain the backtracking technique with a start index and how to prune when not enough numbers remain.
answers.shortTitle: Combinations (All Ways to Choose K Items from N)

s1_definition.profdef: Combinations is a Subsets-pattern backtracking problem that enumerates every size-K subset of the numbers 1 through N, where order does not matter. We recurse with a start value and a current partial combination; at each step we try each number from the start onward, add it, recurse with the next start, and backtrack. A combination is complete when it holds K numbers. Pruning stops branches that cannot possibly be completed to size K. The result count is N choose K.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a review committee must pick exactly K auditors from a pool of N, and HR wants every possible committee. Order does not matter, so picking auditors one and two is the same committee as two and one. We build committees by always choosing auditors in increasing number, so each committee is formed exactly once, and we stop a branch early if too few auditors remain to fill the committee.
s1_definition.oneliner: Backtrack choosing numbers in increasing order up to size K, and prune branches that cannot reach K.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Combinations is a Subsets-pattern backtracking problem that enumerates every size-K subset of the numbers 1 through N, where order does not matter. We recurse with a start value and a current partial combination; at each step we try each number from the start onward, add it, recurse with the next start, and backtrack. A combination is complete when it holds K numbers. Pruning stops branches that cannot possibly be completed to size K. The result count is N choose K.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a review committee must pick exactly K auditors from a pool of N, and HR wants every possible committee. Order does not matter, so picking auditors one and two is the same committee as two and one. We build committees by always choosing auditors in increasing number, so each committee is formed exactly once, and we stop a branch early if too few auditors remain to fill the committee.

**One line to remember:** Backtrack choosing numbers in increasing order up to size K, and prune branches that cannot reach K.

sections.s2_technical:
We recurse with the next candidate `start`, the target size `k`, and the current combination. When the combination size equals k we record a copy and return. Otherwise we loop from `start` to N, add the number, recurse with `start` advanced by one so numbers strictly increase, then backtrack by removing the number.

The important optimization is pruning: if the numbers still available, which is N minus the current number plus one, are fewer than the slots still needed, which is k minus the current size, this branch cannot succeed and we can stop looping. A common form is bounding the loop end, for example `for (int i = start; i <= n - (k - current.size()) + 1; i++)`, so we never start a number too large to leave enough remaining.

A senior-level nuance is that choosing in strictly increasing order is exactly what makes combinations rather than permutations, since it fixes one canonical order per subset. Another nuance is that this is a special case of subset generation restricted to a fixed size, so it shares the backtracking skeleton with the broader subsets problem.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India forms an audit committee by choosing exactly K auditors from a numbered pool of N, and HR wants every possible committee for conflict-of-interest review. Order does not matter, so the same set of auditors must count once. This is exactly how Combinations works: size-K subsets chosen in a fixed order.

Problem 2 — Exploring branches that cannot be filled wastes time on a large pool. This is why we prune: if too few auditors remain to complete a committee, we abandon that branch early.

The code defines a `CommitteeService` exposing `allCommittees(n, k)` returning committees as lists of auditor numbers. A `Demo` runs it for N equal to four and K equal to two and logs the six committees.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Combinations enumerates every way to choose K numbers from the range one to N, where order does not matter. I solve it with backtracking using a start value and a current partial combination. When the combination reaches size K I record a copy; otherwise I loop over numbers from the start onward, add one, recurse with the start advanced by one so my picks strictly increase, and backtrack. Choosing in strictly increasing order is exactly what distinguishes a combination from a permutation, because it fixes one canonical ordering per subset so no subset is produced twice.

The optimization I always add is pruning. If the numbers still available are fewer than the slots I still need to fill, the branch cannot succeed, so I bound the loop end at N minus the remaining need plus one and never start a number that is too large to leave enough behind. This avoids exploring doomed branches on a large pool.

At the National Bank of India I used this to enumerate audit committees, choosing exactly K auditors from a numbered pool of N so HR could run a conflict-of-interest review over every possible committee, where the same set of auditors must count once regardless of order. I chose auditors in increasing order and pruned branches that could not be completed. Explaining why increasing-order selection yields combinations rather than permutations, and how the prune bound avoids wasted work, is what shows an interviewer that I understand this as the fixed-size specialisation of subset generation.

answers.question: Given a string, partition it so that every substring of the partition is a palindrome, and return all possible palindrome partitionings. Explain the backtracking technique that cuts the string at each position and only recurses when the prefix is a palindrome.
answers.shortTitle: Palindrome Partitioning (All Ways to Split a String into Palindromes)

s1_definition.profdef: Palindrome Partitioning is a Subsets-pattern backtracking problem that enumerates every way to cut a string into pieces where each piece reads the same forwards and backwards. We recurse from a start index, try every end position to form a prefix, and only when that prefix is a palindrome do we add it to the current partition and recurse on the remainder. A partition is complete when the start index reaches the end of the string. The search is exponential in the worst case, bounded by the number of palindromic partitionings.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a reference token must be split into symmetric segments for a legacy validator, where every segment must read the same both ways. We want every valid way to split the token into such segments. We try cutting after the first character, after the second, and so on; whenever the piece we cut off is symmetric we accept it and recursively split what remains, otherwise we skip that cut.
s1_definition.oneliner: From each start, try every prefix, recurse only on palindromic prefixes, and record a partition when the whole string is consumed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Palindrome Partitioning is a Subsets-pattern backtracking problem that enumerates every way to cut a string into pieces where each piece reads the same forwards and backwards. We recurse from a start index, try every end position to form a prefix, and only when that prefix is a palindrome do we add it to the current partition and recurse on the remainder. A partition is complete when the start index reaches the end of the string. The search is exponential in the worst case, bounded by the number of palindromic partitionings.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a reference token must be split into symmetric segments for a legacy validator, where every segment must read the same both ways. We want every valid way to split the token into such segments. We try cutting after the first character, after the second, and so on; whenever the piece we cut off is symmetric we accept it and recursively split what remains, otherwise we skip that cut.

**One line to remember:** From each start, try every prefix, recurse only on palindromic prefixes, and record a partition when the whole string is consumed.

sections.s2_technical:
We recurse with a start index, a current list of pieces, and the results. If the start index equals the string length, the current list is a complete valid partition and we record a copy. Otherwise we loop the end index from start to the last character, forming the substring from start to end inclusive; if that substring is a palindrome we add it, recurse with the next start being end plus one, then remove it to backtrack.

Checking a palindrome is a simple two-pointer comparison from both ends. For example, a helper `isPalindrome(s, lo, hi)` walks inward while characters match. Only palindromic prefixes trigger recursion, which prunes the vast majority of invalid cuts early.

A senior-level nuance is that the palindrome checks can be precomputed with a dynamic-programming table so each check is constant time, turning repeated inner checks into a lookup; without it the checks add a linear factor. Another nuance is that this is subset-style exploration over cut positions, where each partitioning corresponds to a choice of where to cut.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India feeds a legacy validator that requires a reference token be broken into symmetric segments, each reading the same both ways, and operations wants every valid segmentation to test the validator. This is exactly how Palindrome Partitioning works: each segmentation is a partition into palindromic pieces.

Problem 2 — Trying every possible cut blindly would explore many invalid segmentations. This is why we only recurse when the prefix is a palindrome, pruning invalid cuts immediately and exploring only promising partitions.

The code defines a `PartitionService` exposing `palindromePartitions(token)` returning all partitionings. A `Demo` runs it over a short token and logs each partition.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Palindrome Partitioning enumerates every way to cut a string into pieces where each piece is a palindrome. I solve it with backtracking driven by a start index. From the current start I try every end position to form a prefix, and only when that prefix is a palindrome do I accept it into the current partition and recurse on the remainder beginning just after it. When the start index reaches the end of the string the current list of pieces is a complete valid partition and I record a copy.

The key to efficiency is that I recurse only on palindromic prefixes, which prunes the enormous number of invalid cuts immediately rather than building them and rejecting them later. I check a palindrome with a simple two-pointer inward comparison, and I mention that these checks can be precomputed into a dynamic-programming table so each check becomes constant time, which matters for longer strings since the same substrings are tested repeatedly.

At the National Bank of India I used this to feed a legacy validator that required a reference token to be split into symmetric segments, generating every valid segmentation so operations could test the validator thoroughly. I backtracked over cut positions, recursed only when a prefix was a palindrome, and stored each full partition as a fresh copy. Explaining the palindrome-only recursion as the pruning mechanism, and recognising that the choice of cut positions is a subset-style exploration, is what shows an interviewer that I can apply backtracking with a correctness-driven prune to a real string-processing task.

answers.question: Given a sorted array of numbers whose sort direction (ascending or descending) is not known in advance, find the index of a target key using binary search. Explain how you detect the order and adjust the comparisons.
answers.shortTitle: Order-agnostic Binary Search (Search a Sorted Array When the Order Is Unknown)

s1_definition.profdef: Order-agnostic Binary Search is the first Modified Binary Search problem. The array is sorted, but we do not know whether it is ascending or descending. We first compare the two ends to detect the direction, then run standard binary search while flipping the comparison logic according to that direction. The search stays O(log n) because detecting the order is a single comparison done once.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India we store a sorted ledger of daily closing balances, but one feed sends them oldest-to-newest and another newest-to-oldest. When Rajesh asks on which row a specific balance sits, we first peek at the top and bottom rows to learn which way the list runs, then we binary-search, halving the rows each step, adjusting whether we go up or down based on that direction.
s1_definition.oneliner: Detect ascending or descending once by comparing the ends, then binary-search with the comparison flipped to match.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Order-agnostic Binary Search is the first Modified Binary Search problem. The array is sorted, but we do not know whether it is ascending or descending. We first compare the two ends to detect the direction, then run standard binary search while flipping the comparison logic according to that direction. The search stays O(log n) because detecting the order is a single comparison done once.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India we store a sorted ledger of daily closing balances, but one feed sends them oldest-to-newest and another newest-to-oldest. When Rajesh asks on which row a specific balance sits, we first peek at the top and bottom rows to learn which way the list runs, then we binary-search, halving the rows each step, adjusting whether we go up or down based on that direction.

**One line to remember:** Detect ascending or descending once by comparing the ends, then binary-search with the comparison flipped to match.

sections.s2_technical:
We set `start = 0` and `end = n - 1` and compute whether the array is ascending by a single check: `boolean asc = arr[start] < arr[end]`. Then in the loop we compute `mid = start + (end - start) / 2` using that safe form to avoid integer overflow. If `arr[mid] == key` we return `mid`. Otherwise for an ascending array we move `start = mid + 1` when `key > arr[mid]` and `end = mid - 1` when `key < arr[mid]`; for a descending array we do the opposite. For example, `if (asc) { if (key < arr[mid]) end = mid - 1; else start = mid + 1; } else { if (key > arr[mid]) end = mid - 1; else start = mid + 1; }`.

The loop continues while `start <= end`. If it exits without a match we return -1. Using `start + (end - start) / 2` rather than `(start + end) / 2` matters because the naive sum can overflow for very large indices, a classic senior-level correctness detail.

A senior nuance is that detecting order from only the two ends assumes at least two distinct values; if all values are equal, direction is irrelevant and either branch finds the key. This single-check detection keeps the overall complexity at O(log n) time and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India ingests a sorted array of daily closing balances, but depending on the upstream system the array arrives ascending or descending, and operations cannot hardcode the direction. This is exactly how Order-agnostic Binary Search works: we detect direction at runtime from the endpoints.

Problem 2 — A linear scan to find a specific balance is too slow for very large ledgers. This is why we binary-search, halving the search space each step, while flipping the comparison to match the detected order.

The code defines a `LedgerSearchService` exposing `search(balances, key)` that returns the index of the balance or minus one. A `Demo` searches both an ascending and a descending ledger for one of Rajesh's balances and logs the result.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Order-agnostic Binary Search is the opening problem of the Modified Binary Search pattern. The array is sorted but I do not know whether it ascends or descends, so I first detect the direction with a single comparison of the two endpoints, then run a normal binary search while flipping the comparison logic to match that direction. Because the detection is just one comparison, the whole search stays logarithmic.

The important details are computing the midpoint as start plus end minus start over two to avoid integer overflow on very large indices, and branching the comparison on the detected direction so that in an ascending array I move right when the key is larger and in a descending array I move right when the key is smaller. I continue while start is less than or equal to end and return minus one if the window closes without a match.

At the National Bank of India I used this to search a sorted ledger of daily closing balances that could arrive either oldest-to-newest or newest-to-oldest depending on the upstream feed. I detected the direction from the endpoints and then halved the search space each step, so operations could locate a specific balance in a huge ledger instantly regardless of the feed's order. Explaining the one-time direction detection and the overflow-safe midpoint is what shows an interviewer that I understand both the pattern and the correctness pitfalls.

answers.question: Given an array of numbers sorted in ascending order, find the ceiling of a given key, defined as the smallest element greater than or equal to the key. If no such element exists, return minus one. Explain how binary search converges to the ceiling.
answers.shortTitle: Ceiling of a Number (Smallest Element Greater Than or Equal to the Key)

s1_definition.profdef: Ceiling of a Number is a Modified Binary Search variant. The ceiling of a key is the smallest array element that is greater than or equal to the key. We binary-search, and when the middle element is smaller than the key we move right, otherwise we move left while remembering the position. When the window closes, the start pointer lands on the ceiling index, or past the end if the key is larger than every element.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, loan interest slabs are stored in an ascending array, and when Priya requests a loan amount that is not exactly a slab boundary, we must charge the next slab at or above her amount. We binary-search the slab list, and the first slab that is at least her amount is the ceiling we apply.
s1_definition.oneliner: Binary-search; when the key is above mid go right, otherwise go left, and the start pointer finally points at the smallest value greater than or equal to the key.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Ceiling of a Number is a Modified Binary Search variant. The ceiling of a key is the smallest array element that is greater than or equal to the key. We binary-search, and when the middle element is smaller than the key we move right, otherwise we move left while remembering the position. When the window closes, the start pointer lands on the ceiling index, or past the end if the key is larger than every element.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, loan interest slabs are stored in an ascending array, and when Priya requests a loan amount that is not exactly a slab boundary, we must charge the next slab at or above her amount. We binary-search the slab list, and the first slab that is at least her amount is the ceiling we apply.

**One line to remember:** Binary-search; when the key is above mid go right, otherwise go left, and the start pointer finally points at the smallest value greater than or equal to the key.

sections.s2_technical:
We handle the easy edge case first: if the key is greater than the last element there is no ceiling, so we return minus one. Otherwise we binary-search with `start = 0` and `end = n - 1`. In the loop, `mid = start + (end - start) / 2`; if `key < arr[mid]` we set `end = mid - 1`, if `key > arr[mid]` we set `start = mid + 1`, and if equal we return `mid`. When the loop ends with `start > end`, the `start` index points to the smallest element greater than or equal to the key, so we return `arr[start]` (or its index, depending on the required output).

The reason `start` lands on the ceiling is that every time we move `end` left we keep the window of candidates that are at least the key, and every time we move `start` right we discard elements smaller than the key. For example, in array 1, 3, 8, 10, 15 with key 5, the search narrows until `start` points at 8, the ceiling.

A senior nuance is that the symmetric problem, the floor, which is the largest element less than or equal to the key, is solved identically except that `end` lands on the floor index. Recognising the start-ends-on-ceiling and end-ends-on-floor invariant is the key insight. Complexity is O(log n) time and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores interest-rate slab thresholds in an ascending array, and when Priya requests a loan amount that falls between two slabs, policy requires charging the next slab at or above her amount. This is exactly how the ceiling works: we need the smallest threshold greater than or equal to her amount.

Problem 2 — Scanning the slabs linearly is wasteful when there are many slabs. This is why we binary-search so the ceiling is found in logarithmic time, and we return minus one when the amount exceeds every slab, signalling a special-case escalation.

The code defines a `SlabService` exposing `ceilingSlab(slabs, amount)` returning the ceiling threshold or minus one. A `Demo` finds the slab applied to Priya's requested amount and logs it.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Ceiling of a Number is a Modified Binary Search variant where I find the smallest array element that is greater than or equal to the key. I first short-circuit the case where the key is larger than the last element, since then no ceiling exists and I return minus one. Otherwise I binary-search: when the key is below the middle element I move the end pointer left, when it is above I move the start pointer right, and on an exact match I return immediately.

The elegant part is the invariant that when the loop finishes with start past end, the start pointer is sitting exactly on the ceiling. That is because moving end left always preserves candidates at or above the key while moving start right discards everything smaller. The mirror problem, the floor, is identical except the end pointer lands on the answer, and knowing both invariants together is what demonstrates real command of the pattern.

At the National Bank of India I used this to apply interest-rate slabs: when Priya requested a loan amount sitting between two slab thresholds, policy required charging the next slab at or above her amount, which is precisely the ceiling. I binary-searched the ascending slab table so the correct slab was found in logarithmic time, and returned minus one to trigger an escalation when the amount exceeded every slab. Explaining the start-lands-on-ceiling invariant and the symmetric floor case is what shows an interviewer I truly understand the convergence.

answers.question: Given an array of lowercase letters sorted in ascending order and a target letter, find the smallest letter in the array that is strictly greater than the target. The letters wrap around, so if the target is greater than or equal to the last letter, return the first letter. Explain the binary-search approach.
answers.shortTitle: Next Letter (Smallest Letter Strictly Greater Than the Key, Wrapping Around)

s1_definition.profdef: Next Letter is a Modified Binary Search variant very close to the ceiling, but it requires the smallest element strictly greater than the key and it wraps around the array. We binary-search, and whenever the middle letter is less than or equal to the key we move right, otherwise we move left. When the window closes, the start pointer, taken modulo the array length, points at the answer, which naturally handles the wrap-around.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, cheque batches are labelled with cyclic letter codes a through z, and the next batch to process must carry the next code strictly after the current one. If we are at z we wrap back to a. We binary-search the sorted codes to find the next code after the current one.
s1_definition.oneliner: Binary-search for the smallest letter strictly greater than the key, and take the start pointer modulo the length to wrap around.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Next Letter is a Modified Binary Search variant very close to the ceiling, but it requires the smallest element strictly greater than the key and it wraps around the array. We binary-search, and whenever the middle letter is less than or equal to the key we move right, otherwise we move left. When the window closes, the start pointer, taken modulo the array length, points at the answer, which naturally handles the wrap-around.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, cheque batches are labelled with cyclic letter codes a through z, and the next batch to process must carry the next code strictly after the current one. If we are at z we wrap back to a. We binary-search the sorted codes to find the next code after the current one.

**One line to remember:** Binary-search for the smallest letter strictly greater than the key, and take the start pointer modulo the length to wrap around.

sections.s2_technical:
We binary-search with `start = 0` and `end = n - 1`. In the loop `mid = start + (end - start) / 2`. The crucial rule, because we want strictly greater, is: if `key >= letters[mid]` we move `start = mid + 1`, otherwise we move `end = mid - 1`. Notice the comparison uses greater-than-or-equal so that a letter equal to the key is skipped. For example, `if (key >= letters[mid]) start = mid + 1; else end = mid - 1;`.

When the loop ends, `start` may equal `n`, which means the key is greater than or equal to every letter, so we wrap by returning `letters[start % n]`, which is the first letter. In all other cases `start` already points at the smallest strictly-greater letter. For instance, in letters a, c, f, h with key f, the search lands start on the index of h.

A senior nuance is the subtle difference from the ceiling: the ceiling uses greater-than-or-equal on the answer and keeps equal elements, while Next Letter needs strictly greater, so the mid comparison includes equality on the move-right branch. The wrap-around via the modulo is what makes this a cyclic search. Complexity is O(log n) time and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India labels nightly cheque-clearing batches with cyclic single-letter codes, and the scheduler must pick the next code strictly after the current batch's code, wrapping from z back to a. This is exactly how Next Letter works: smallest code strictly greater than the current, with wrap-around.

Problem 2 — A linear scan of all codes each night is wasteful, and a naive approach forgets the wrap-around. This is why we binary-search for the strictly-greater code and use a modulo to wrap cleanly.

The code defines a `BatchCodeService` exposing `nextCode(codes, current)` returning the next cyclic code. A `Demo` finds the code after a given batch and demonstrates the wrap-around and logs both.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Next Letter is a Modified Binary Search variant that is deliberately close to the ceiling but with two twists: I need the smallest element strictly greater than the key, not greater-than-or-equal, and the letters wrap around so that if the key is at or past the last letter I return the first. I binary-search and whenever the middle letter is less than or equal to the key I move the start pointer right, which skips any letter equal to the key, otherwise I move the end pointer left.

The clean part is that when the loop finishes, the start pointer indexes the answer, and if it has run off the end of the array I simply take it modulo the length, which wraps me back to the first letter. That single modulo is what makes the search cyclic without any special-case branching. The subtle contrast with the ceiling, where equal elements are kept rather than skipped, is the detail that separates someone who memorised the pattern from someone who understands it.

At the National Bank of India I used this for scheduling nightly cheque-clearing batches labelled with cyclic single-letter codes, where the scheduler must pick the next code strictly after the current one and wrap from z back to a. I binary-searched the sorted codes for the strictly-greater code and wrapped with a modulo, so the scheduler always picked the correct next batch in logarithmic time. Explaining the strictly-greater comparison and the modulo wrap is what shows an interviewer I handle the cyclic boundary correctly.

answers.question: Given an array of numbers sorted in ascending order, find the range, meaning the first and last index, of a given key. If the key is not present, return minus one for both. Explain how two biased binary searches find the two ends.
answers.shortTitle: Number Range (First and Last Position of a Key in a Sorted Array)

s1_definition.profdef: Number Range is a Modified Binary Search problem solved with two biased binary searches. One search is biased toward the left to find the first occurrence of the key, and the other is biased toward the right to find the last occurrence. Each search, after finding the key, does not stop but continues shrinking the window toward the desired side, giving an overall O(log n) solution.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, transaction records are sorted by amount, and when the audit team asks for every record of a particular amount, we need the first and last row of that block of equal amounts. We binary-search once leaning left to find where the block starts and once leaning right to find where it ends.
s1_definition.oneliner: Run binary search twice, once biased left for the first index and once biased right for the last index of the key.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Number Range is a Modified Binary Search problem solved with two biased binary searches. One search is biased toward the left to find the first occurrence of the key, and the other is biased toward the right to find the last occurrence. Each search, after finding the key, does not stop but continues shrinking the window toward the desired side, giving an overall O(log n) solution.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, transaction records are sorted by amount, and when the audit team asks for every record of a particular amount, we need the first and last row of that block of equal amounts. We binary-search once leaning left to find where the block starts and once leaning right to find where it ends.

**One line to remember:** Run binary search twice, once biased left for the first index and once biased right for the last index of the key.

sections.s2_technical:
We write a helper `search(arr, key, findFirst)`. It binary-searches normally, but when `arr[mid] == key` it records `mid` as a candidate and, instead of returning, it keeps searching: if `findFirst` is true it sets `end = mid - 1` to look further left, otherwise it sets `start = mid + 1` to look further right. The other comparisons are standard: `key < arr[mid]` moves end left, `key > arr[mid]` moves start right. For example, when finding the first index, `if (arr[mid] == key) { result = mid; end = mid - 1; }`.

We call this helper twice: once with `findFirst = true` for the left end and once with `findFirst = false` for the right end. If the first search returns minus one the key is absent and we return the pair minus one and minus one; otherwise we return the two recorded indices. For the array 1, 3, 3, 3, 5 and key 3, the first search returns index 1 and the second returns index 3.

A senior nuance is that this is strictly O(log n) because each of the two searches is logarithmic, which is better than finding one occurrence and then linearly expanding outward, which could be O(n) when the key fills most of the array. The bias is the whole trick. Complexity is O(log n) time and O(1) space.

Problem 2 — Finding one match and then scanning outward can be linear when many transactions share the amount, which is too slow during large audits. This is why we run two biased binary searches, each logarithmic, to pin both ends directly.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Number Range asks for the first and last index of a key in a sorted array, and I solve it with two biased binary searches rather than one search plus a linear expansion. I write a single helper that takes a boolean saying whether I want the first or the last occurrence. The helper binary-searches normally, but when it lands on the key it does not stop; it records that index as a candidate and keeps shrinking the window toward the side I care about, left for the first occurrence and right for the last.

The reason this matters is performance. If I found one occurrence and then walked outward to find the block's edges, that walk could be linear when the key fills most of the array, which defeats the purpose of binary search. By biasing each search I keep both searches logarithmic, so the whole operation is logarithmic. If the first search returns minus one the key is absent and I return a pair of minus ones.

At the National Bank of India I used this during audits of transaction records sorted by amount, where the team needed the exact first and last position of every transaction of a specific amount so they could extract that contiguous block. I ran one left-biased and one right-biased binary search to pin both ends directly, which stayed fast even when thousands of transactions shared the amount. Explaining the recording-and-continuing bias, and why it beats linear expansion, is what shows an interviewer I understand the efficiency argument behind the pattern.

answers.question: Given an infinite sorted array, or one whose length is unknown and can only be probed through an accessor that returns a large sentinel for out-of-bounds indices, find the index of a given key. Explain how you first find a bounding window and then binary-search within it.
answers.shortTitle: Search in a Sorted Infinite Array (Find a Key Without Knowing the Length)

s1_definition.profdef: Search in a Sorted Infinite Array is a Modified Binary Search problem where the array length is unknown. We cannot start binary search because we have no end index. So we first find a bounding window by exponentially expanding a small window, doubling its size, until the key is guaranteed to lie inside it, then we binary-search that window. The expansion is O(log position) and the final search is also logarithmic.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a streaming market-data feed exposes an endlessly growing sorted array of tick prices through a reader that returns a huge sentinel past the end. To find a specific price, we first jump in doubling strides to bracket where the price must be, then binary-search inside that bracket.
s1_definition.oneliner: Exponentially double a window until it brackets the key, then binary-search within that bracket.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Search in a Sorted Infinite Array is a Modified Binary Search problem where the array length is unknown. We cannot start binary search because we have no end index. So we first find a bounding window by exponentially expanding a small window, doubling its size, until the key is guaranteed to lie inside it, then we binary-search that window. The expansion is O(log position) and the final search is also logarithmic.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a streaming market-data feed exposes an endlessly growing sorted array of tick prices through a reader that returns a huge sentinel past the end. To find a specific price, we first jump in doubling strides to bracket where the price must be, then binary-search inside that bracket.

**One line to remember:** Exponentially double a window until it brackets the key, then binary-search within that bracket.

sections.s2_technical:
We access elements through a reader `get(index)` that returns a very large sentinel, effectively positive infinity, for out-of-bounds indices, so the array still reads as sorted. We begin with `start = 0` and `end = 1`. While `reader.get(end) < key` we advance the window: `start = end` and `end = end + (end - start + 1) * 2`, doubling the window size each time. For example, `int newEnd = end + (end - start + 1) * 2; start = end; end = newEnd;`.

Once `reader.get(end)` is greater than or equal to the key, the key, if present, lies in the window `start..end`, so we run a standard binary search in that window, treating any sentinel as a value larger than the key, which naturally pushes the search left. We return the found index or minus one.

A senior nuance is why we double rather than step linearly: doubling reaches position p in about log p probes, so the whole algorithm is logarithmic in the key's position rather than linear. Another nuance is that the sentinel for out-of-bounds must be larger than any real value so the sorted property and the comparisons hold at the boundary. Complexity is O(log p) time where p is the key's position, and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India consumes a continuously growing sorted array of market tick prices whose total length is not known, exposed through a reader that returns a huge sentinel beyond the current end. To locate a specific price, we cannot binary-search directly because there is no end index. This is exactly how the infinite-array search works: we first bracket the key.

Problem 2 — Probing every index from the start is linear and far too slow for a fast-moving feed. This is why we expand the window exponentially to bracket the key in logarithmic probes, then binary-search the small bracket.

The code defines an `InfiniteReader` that wraps a backing array and returns a sentinel past the end, and a `TickSearchService` exposing `search(reader, key)`. A `Demo` searches a simulated infinite feed for a tick price and logs the index.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Search in a Sorted Infinite Array is a Modified Binary Search problem where I cannot start a normal binary search because the array's length is unknown; I only have a reader that returns a huge sentinel for indices past the end. So I split the work into two phases. First I bracket the key by starting with a tiny window and doubling its size each step until the value at the window's end is at least the key. Then, knowing the key must lie inside that window, I run a standard binary search over it.

The reason I double the window rather than step through it is efficiency: doubling reaches the key's position in about a logarithm of that position's worth of probes, so the bracketing phase is logarithmic rather than linear. During the inner binary search I treat the out-of-bounds sentinel as larger than any real value, which keeps the array sorted at the boundary and naturally pushes the search leftward when I probe past the end.

At the National Bank of India I used this against a continuously growing sorted feed of market tick prices exposed through a reader that returned a sentinel beyond the current end. To locate a specific price I expanded a doubling window to bracket it and then binary-searched the bracket, which stayed fast even as the feed grew without bound. Explaining the two phases, the doubling rationale, and the sentinel-as-infinity trick is what shows an interviewer I can adapt binary search when the usual end index is missing.

answers.question: Given an array of numbers sorted in ascending order, find the element whose absolute difference from a given key is smallest. If two elements are equally close, return the smaller one. Explain how binary search plus a comparison of the two neighbours around the closing window finds it.
answers.shortTitle: Minimum Difference Element (Closest Element to a Key in a Sorted Array)

s1_definition.profdef: Minimum Difference Element is a Modified Binary Search problem. We binary-search for the key, and if we find it exactly the difference is zero. If we do not find it, the closing window leaves the start pointer just above the key and the end pointer just below it, so the closest element is whichever of those two neighbours has the smaller absolute difference, with ties broken toward the smaller value.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, foreign-exchange desk quotes are stored as a sorted array, and when Rajesh wants to convert at a target rate that may not be quoted exactly, we must offer the nearest available quote. We binary-search the quotes, and if the exact rate is missing we compare the two quotes bracketing it and offer the closer one.
s1_definition.oneliner: Binary-search; if the key is absent the start and end pointers straddle it, so return whichever neighbour is closer, preferring the smaller on a tie.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Minimum Difference Element is a Modified Binary Search problem. We binary-search for the key, and if we find it exactly the difference is zero. If we do not find it, the closing window leaves the start pointer just above the key and the end pointer just below it, so the closest element is whichever of those two neighbours has the smaller absolute difference, with ties broken toward the smaller value.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, foreign-exchange desk quotes are stored as a sorted array, and when Rajesh wants to convert at a target rate that may not be quoted exactly, we must offer the nearest available quote. We binary-search the quotes, and if the exact rate is missing we compare the two quotes bracketing it and offer the closer one.

**One line to remember:** Binary-search; if the key is absent the start and end pointers straddle it, so return whichever neighbour is closer, preferring the smaller on a tie.

sections.s2_technical:
We binary-search with `start = 0` and `end = n - 1`. If `arr[mid] == key` we return `arr[mid]` immediately, difference zero. The standard moves apply otherwise: `key < arr[mid]` sets `end = mid - 1`, `key > arr[mid]` sets `start = mid + 1`. When the loop ends with `start > end`, the key lies between `arr[end]` and `arr[start]`, so we compare `arr[start] - key` against `key - arr[end]` and return the element with the smaller difference. For example, `if (arr[start] - key < key - arr[end]) return arr[start]; else return arr[end];`.

The reason this works is that binary search, when it fails to find the key, always leaves `start` pointing at the smallest element greater than the key and `end` pointing at the largest element smaller than the key, which are exactly the two candidates for the closest element. Using the less-than comparison in that final check means a tie returns `arr[end]`, the smaller value, satisfying the tie-break rule.

A senior nuance is guarding the edges: if the key is smaller than every element, `end` becomes minus one and we return `arr[0]`; if the key is larger than every element, `start` becomes `n` and we return the last element. Those edge guards are easy to forget. Complexity is O(log n) time and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores foreign-exchange quotes in a sorted array, and when Rajesh requests conversion at a target rate that may not be quoted, the desk must offer the nearest available quote. This is exactly how Minimum Difference Element works: find the element closest to the key.

Problem 2 — Scanning all quotes to find the closest is wasteful when there are many quotes. This is why we binary-search and, on a miss, compare only the two quotes straddling the target, preferring the smaller rate on a tie so the customer is never over-charged by rounding.

The code defines a `FxQuoteService` exposing `closestQuote(quotes, target)` returning the nearest quote. A `Demo` finds the nearest quote for a target rate and logs it.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Minimum Difference Element is a Modified Binary Search problem where I find the array element whose absolute difference from the key is smallest. I binary-search for the key, and if I hit it exactly the difference is zero and I am done. The real insight is what happens when the search fails: the loop always finishes with the start pointer sitting on the smallest element greater than the key and the end pointer on the largest element smaller than the key, so those two neighbours straddle the key and one of them must be the closest.

So on a miss I simply compare the difference between the upper neighbour and the key against the difference between the key and the lower neighbour, and return whichever is smaller. I write that comparison with a strict less-than so that a tie returns the lower neighbour, which satisfies the rule of preferring the smaller value. I also guard the two edges first: if the key is below everything I return the first element, and if it is above everything I return the last.

At the National Bank of India I used this on the foreign-exchange desk, where quotes are stored sorted and a customer like Rajesh may ask to convert at a target rate that is not quoted exactly. I binary-searched the quotes and, when the exact rate was missing, compared only the two quotes straddling the target and offered the closer one, preferring the smaller rate on a tie so rounding never worked against the customer. Explaining the straddle invariant and the tie-break is what shows an interviewer I understand why only two candidates ever need checking.

answers.question: A bitonic array strictly increases to a single maximum and then strictly decreases. Find the maximum value using binary search. Explain how comparing the middle element with its right neighbour tells you which side the peak is on.
answers.shortTitle: Bitonic Array Maximum (Find the Peak of an Array That Rises Then Falls)

s1_definition.profdef: Bitonic Array Maximum is a Modified Binary Search problem. A bitonic array rises to one peak and then falls. We binary-search, and at each step we compare the middle element with its right neighbour: if the middle is smaller than its right neighbour we are on the rising side and move right, otherwise we are on the falling side and move left. The pointers converge exactly on the peak.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a single trading day's intraday price of Rajesh's stock rises to a daily high and then falls. Stored as a bitonic array, we find the daily high by binary search: if the current price is still climbing we look right, if it is already falling we look left, until we land on the high.
s1_definition.oneliner: Compare mid with its right neighbour; climbing means go right, falling means go left, and the pointers meet at the peak.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Bitonic Array Maximum is a Modified Binary Search problem. A bitonic array rises to one peak and then falls. We binary-search, and at each step we compare the middle element with its right neighbour: if the middle is smaller than its right neighbour we are on the rising side and move right, otherwise we are on the falling side and move left. The pointers converge exactly on the peak.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a single trading day's intraday price of Rajesh's stock rises to a daily high and then falls. Stored as a bitonic array, we find the daily high by binary search: if the current price is still climbing we look right, if it is already falling we look left, until we land on the high.

**One line to remember:** Compare mid with its right neighbour; climbing means go right, falling means go left, and the pointers meet at the peak.

sections.s2_technical:
We set `start = 0` and `end = n - 1`. In the loop `mid = start + (end - start) / 2`. We compare `arr[mid]` with `arr[mid + 1]`: if `arr[mid] > arr[mid + 1]` we are on the descending side so the peak is at `mid` or to its left, so `end = mid`; otherwise we are ascending so the peak is to the right, so `start = mid + 1`. For example, `if (arr[mid] > arr[mid + 1]) end = mid; else start = mid + 1;`. The loop condition is `start < end`, and when it ends `start == end` points at the peak, so we return `arr[start]`.

Note we do not use `start <= end` here; we use `start < end` because we are converging two pointers to a single index rather than looking for an exact value, and we never let `mid + 1` run out of bounds because `mid` is always strictly less than `end` when `start < end`.

A senior nuance is that this finds the index of the peak, which is the pivot for the related Search Bitonic Array problem, so solving this cleanly is a building block. The strictly-increasing-then-strictly-decreasing assumption guarantees a single peak and no plateaus, which is what makes the neighbour comparison decisive. Complexity is O(log n) time and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India records a single trading day's intraday prices for Rajesh's stock as a bitonic array that rises to the day's high and then falls, and the analytics team needs the daily high quickly. This is exactly how Bitonic Array Maximum works: find the single peak.

Problem 2 — Scanning the whole day's ticks is wasteful when there can be thousands of them. This is why we binary-search by comparing each middle tick with its right neighbour to decide which side the high is on.

The code defines a `PeakPriceService` exposing `dailyHigh(prices)` returning the peak price. A `Demo` finds the daily high of a bitonic price series and logs it.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Bitonic Array Maximum finds the single peak of an array that strictly rises and then strictly falls. I binary-search, but instead of comparing against a target I compare the middle element with its right neighbour. If the middle is larger than its right neighbour I am standing on the falling side, so the peak is at the middle or to its left and I move the end pointer to the middle. If the middle is smaller than its right neighbour I am on the rising side, so the peak is further right and I move the start pointer past the middle.

I use a start-less-than-end loop because I am converging two pointers onto one index rather than hunting for an exact value, and because the middle is always strictly below the end in that condition, reading the right neighbour never goes out of bounds. When the pointers meet, that single index is the peak.

At the National Bank of India I used this to compute the daily high of Rajesh's stock from a day's intraday prices stored as a bitonic series that climbs to the high and then declines. Rather than scanning thousands of ticks, I binary-searched on the slope by comparing each middle tick with its neighbour, landing on the high in logarithmic time, and this peak index also became the pivot for the related problem of searching a bitonic array. Explaining the slope comparison and the strict single-peak assumption is what shows an interviewer I understand why the neighbour test is decisive.

answers.question: Given a bitonic array, strictly increasing then strictly decreasing, find the index of a given key. If the key appears on both sides, return the smaller index. Explain how you first find the peak and then binary-search each side with the correct order.
answers.shortTitle: Search Bitonic Array (Find a Key in a Rise-Then-Fall Array)

s1_definition.profdef: Search Bitonic Array combines two Modified Binary Search ideas. First we find the peak index of the bitonic array. That peak splits the array into an ascending part on the left and a descending part on the right. We binary-search the ascending part normally, and if the key is not there we binary-search the descending part with reversed comparisons. Returning the first match gives the smaller index when the key appears twice.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, the intraday price series of Rajesh's stock rises to a high then falls, and the compliance team asks at which point in the day the price first hit a specific value. We find the daily high, then search the rising half, and if not found there, search the falling half.
s1_definition.oneliner: Find the peak, binary-search the ascending left half, then if needed binary-search the descending right half, returning the earlier match.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Search Bitonic Array combines two Modified Binary Search ideas. First we find the peak index of the bitonic array. That peak splits the array into an ascending part on the left and a descending part on the right. We binary-search the ascending part normally, and if the key is not there we binary-search the descending part with reversed comparisons. Returning the first match gives the smaller index when the key appears twice.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, the intraday price series of Rajesh's stock rises to a high then falls, and the compliance team asks at which point in the day the price first hit a specific value. We find the daily high, then search the rising half, and if not found there, search the falling half.

**One line to remember:** Find the peak, binary-search the ascending left half, then if needed binary-search the descending right half, returning the earlier match.

sections.s2_technical:
We first find the peak index with the Bitonic Maximum technique, comparing each middle with its right neighbour. Once we have `peak`, we run a standard ascending binary search over indices `0..peak`. If it returns a valid index we return it, because the left side holds the smaller indices. Otherwise we run a descending binary search over indices `peak + 1..n - 1`, where the comparisons are reversed: `key < arr[mid]` moves `start = mid + 1` and `key > arr[mid]` moves `end = mid - 1`. For example, the descending search uses `if (key == arr[mid]) return mid; else if (key < arr[mid]) start = mid + 1; else end = mid - 1;`.

Returning the left-side match first naturally yields the smaller index when the key exists on both the rising and falling sides. Each of the three phases, finding the peak and the two searches, is logarithmic, so the whole algorithm is logarithmic.

A senior nuance is that the descending search is just an ordinary binary search with the inequality signs flipped, so reusing a single order-aware search routine keeps the code clean. Another nuance is correctly partitioning at the peak so neither search overlaps the other. Complexity is O(log n) time and O(1) space.

Search Bitonic Array is a composite Modified Binary Search problem. Because the array first rises and then falls, it is not globally monotonic, so a single binary search fails. My first move is to find the peak index using the slope comparison, where I compare each middle element with its right neighbour. That peak splits the array into a clean ascending half on the left and a clean descending half on the right.

Then I binary-search the ascending half with the usual comparisons, and if the key is not there I binary-search the descending half with the inequality signs reversed. I search the rising half first on purpose, because when the key appears on both sides the rising half holds the smaller index, so returning its match first gives the earliest occurrence. I keep both searches in one order-aware routine driven by a boolean so I am not duplicating logic.

At the National Bank of India I used this against the intraday price series of Rajesh's stock, stored as a bitonic series, when compliance asked at which earliest point in the day the price reached a specific value. I found the daily high to split the series, searched the rising half, and only searched the falling half if needed, returning the earlier index, all in logarithmic time. Explaining the peak split, the reversed comparisons on the descending side, and the left-first rule for the smaller index is what shows an interviewer I can compose two binary-search variants correctly.

answers.question: Given an ascending sorted array that has been rotated at some unknown pivot, find the index of a given key in O(log n). Explain how, at each step, one half of the array is always sorted and how that lets you decide which half to keep.
answers.shortTitle: Search in Rotated Array (Find a Key in a Sorted Array Rotated at an Unknown Pivot)

s1_definition.profdef: Search in Rotated Array is a Modified Binary Search problem. A sorted array rotated at an unknown pivot is no longer globally sorted, but at every step at least one half, either left of the middle or right of it, is still sorted. We detect which half is sorted, check whether the key lies within that sorted half's range, and discard the other half accordingly. This keeps the search logarithmic.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a sorted list of settlement sequence numbers was rotated when the day rolled over at midnight, so it starts in the middle of the range, climbs, wraps, and climbs again. To find a specific sequence number, at each step we spot the half that is still cleanly sorted and decide whether our number falls inside it.
s1_definition.oneliner: One half is always sorted; check if the key lies in that sorted half's range, and keep that half or discard it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Search in Rotated Array is a Modified Binary Search problem. A sorted array rotated at an unknown pivot is no longer globally sorted, but at every step at least one half, either left of the middle or right of it, is still sorted. We detect which half is sorted, check whether the key lies within that sorted half's range, and discard the other half accordingly. This keeps the search logarithmic.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a sorted list of settlement sequence numbers was rotated when the day rolled over at midnight, so it starts in the middle of the range, climbs, wraps, and climbs again. To find a specific sequence number, at each step we spot the half that is still cleanly sorted and decide whether our number falls inside it.

**One line to remember:** One half is always sorted; check if the key lies in that sorted half's range, and keep that half or discard it.

sections.s2_technical:
We binary-search with `start` and `end`. At each step `mid = start + (end - start) / 2`; if `arr[mid] == key` we return `mid`. To decide which half is sorted, we compare `arr[start]` with `arr[mid]`: if `arr[start] <= arr[mid]` the left half is sorted, otherwise the right half is sorted. If the left half is sorted and the key lies between `arr[start]` and `arr[mid]` we move `end = mid - 1`, else `start = mid + 1`. Symmetrically, if the right half is sorted and the key lies between `arr[mid]` and `arr[end]` we move `start = mid + 1`, else `end = mid - 1`. For example, `if (arr[start] <= arr[mid]) { if (key >= arr[start] && key < arr[mid]) end = mid - 1; else start = mid + 1; }`.

The key realisation is that a rotation creates exactly one break point, so any middle index always has at least one side without a break, which is the sorted side. Checking the key against that sorted side's clean range is an exact decision with no ambiguity.

A senior nuance is handling duplicates: if `arr[start]`, `arr[mid]`, and `arr[end]` are all equal we cannot tell which side is sorted, so we shrink both ends by one, degrading to O(n) in the worst case for arrays with heavy duplication; for the distinct-values version the comparisons are decisive and the search stays logarithmic. Complexity is O(log n) time with distinct values and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps settlement sequence numbers in a sorted array that gets rotated at the midnight roll-over, so the array is sorted but starts partway through its range. To find a specific sequence number we cannot use a plain binary search. This is exactly how Search in Rotated Array works.

Problem 2 — A linear scan is too slow for large settlement batches. This is why we detect, at each step, which half is cleanly sorted and use its range to decide where the key must be, staying logarithmic.

The code defines a `SettlementSearchService` exposing `indexOf(seqNumbers, key)` returning the index or minus one. A `Demo` searches a rotated array of sequence numbers and logs the index.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Search in Rotated Array is a Modified Binary Search problem on a sorted array that was rotated at an unknown pivot, so it is no longer globally sorted. The crucial observation is that a single rotation introduces exactly one break point, which means that for any middle index at least one of the two halves is still perfectly sorted. My job each step is to detect which half is sorted and use its clean range to decide where the key can be.

I detect the sorted half by comparing the start element with the middle element: if the start is less than or equal to the middle, the left half is sorted, otherwise the right half is. Once I know the sorted half, I check whether the key falls inside that half's inclusive range, and if it does I keep that half, otherwise I discard it and search the other side. Because every decision is an exact range check, the search stays logarithmic for distinct values.

At the National Bank of India I used this on settlement sequence numbers stored sorted but rotated at the midnight roll-over, where a plain binary search would fail. I detected the sorted half at each step and used its range to locate a specific sequence number in logarithmic time even on large settlement batches. I would also mention the duplicate-values caveat, where equal endpoints force me to shrink both ends and the worst case degrades to linear, which shows an interviewer I know the boundary of the pattern.

answers.question: Given an ascending sorted array that has been rotated an unknown number of times, count how many times it was rotated, which equals the index of its smallest element. Explain how binary search locates the minimum.
answers.shortTitle: Rotation Count (How Many Times a Sorted Array Was Rotated)

s1_definition.profdef: Rotation Count is a Modified Binary Search problem equivalent to finding the index of the smallest element in a rotated sorted array, because the number of rotations equals that index. We binary-search comparing the middle element with its neighbours to locate the single point where an element is smaller than its predecessor, which is the minimum, and its index is the rotation count.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a sorted list of cheque serial numbers was rotated some unknown number of times when batches were re-queued, and we need to know how many rotations happened. That count is exactly where the smallest serial sits, so we binary-search for the minimum and report its index.
s1_definition.oneliner: The rotation count equals the index of the minimum, so binary-search for the smallest element and return its index.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Rotation Count is a Modified Binary Search problem equivalent to finding the index of the smallest element in a rotated sorted array, because the number of rotations equals that index. We binary-search comparing the middle element with its neighbours to locate the single point where an element is smaller than its predecessor, which is the minimum, and its index is the rotation count.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a sorted list of cheque serial numbers was rotated some unknown number of times when batches were re-queued, and we need to know how many rotations happened. That count is exactly where the smallest serial sits, so we binary-search for the minimum and report its index.

**One line to remember:** The rotation count equals the index of the minimum, so binary-search for the smallest element and return its index.

sections.s2_technical:
We binary-search with `start = 0` and `end = n - 1`. At each step `mid = start + (end - start) / 2`. We compare `arr[mid]` with `arr[end]`: if `arr[mid] > arr[end]` the minimum must be to the right of the middle, so `start = mid + 1`; otherwise the minimum is at the middle or to its left, so `end = mid`. For example, `if (arr[mid] > arr[end]) start = mid + 1; else end = mid;`. The loop runs while `start < end`, and when it ends `start` points at the minimum, so `start` is the rotation count.

Comparing with the right end rather than the left end is the robust choice because it correctly handles the case where the array is not rotated at all, in which case the minimum is at index zero and the comparison keeps moving end left until start equals zero. If the array is fully sorted and un-rotated, the answer is zero rotations.

A senior nuance is that with duplicate values the `arr[mid] > arr[end]` test can be inconclusive when they are equal, in which case we decrement `end` by one, which can degrade to O(n); with distinct values the search is strictly logarithmic. Returning `start` directly gives both the minimum's index and the rotation count in one value. Complexity is O(log n) time with distinct values and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India re-queues cheque batches, which rotates a sorted array of serial numbers an unknown number of times, and reconciliation needs to know exactly how many rotations occurred. This is exactly how Rotation Count works: the count equals the index of the smallest serial.

Problem 2 — Scanning the whole array to find the minimum is wasteful for large batches. This is why we binary-search by comparing the middle serial with the last serial to converge on the minimum, staying logarithmic.

The code defines a `RotationCountService` exposing `countRotations(serials)` returning the rotation count. A `Demo` counts rotations of a rotated serial array and logs the result.
