sections.s6_takeaway:
Rotation Count asks how many times a sorted array was rotated, and the elegant reframing is that the answer equals the index of the smallest element, because rotating a sorted array moves the minimum to the position equal to the number of rotations. So I binary-search for the minimum. At each step I compare the middle element with the element at the right end: if the middle is larger than the right end, the break point and therefore the minimum must lie to the right, so I move the start pointer past the middle; otherwise the minimum is at the middle or to its left, so I move the end pointer to the middle.

I deliberately compare against the right end rather than the left, because that handles the un-rotated case cleanly: when the array was never rotated the comparison keeps pulling the end leftward and the pointers converge on index zero, correctly reporting zero rotations. When the loop finishes, the start pointer sits on the minimum, and that index is my answer.

At the National Bank of India I used this during reconciliation of cheque batches that were re-queued, which rotated a sorted array of serial numbers an unknown number of times. By binary-searching for the minimum serial I recovered the exact rotation count in logarithmic time even for large batches. I would also note the duplicate-values caveat, where equal middle and end values force me to step the end inward and the worst case becomes linear, which shows an interviewer I understand both the clean case and its boundary.

answers.question: In an array where every number appears exactly twice except for one number that appears once, find that single number using constant extra space. Explain why XOR of all elements gives the answer.
answers.shortTitle: Single Number (Find the One Element That Appears Once)

s1_definition.profdef: Single Number is the foundational Bitwise XOR problem. Because XOR of a number with itself is zero and XOR with zero leaves the number unchanged, XOR-ing every element together cancels each pair and leaves only the unpaired number. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) space, beating a hash-set approach on memory.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, every reconciliation entry should appear twice, once as a debit leg and once as a matching credit leg, except for one orphan entry that was posted only once. If we XOR all the entry codes together, every matched pair cancels out and the lone orphan code remains.
s1_definition.oneliner: XOR all numbers together; pairs cancel to zero and the single unpaired number survives.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Single Number is the foundational Bitwise XOR problem. Because XOR of a number with itself is zero and XOR with zero leaves the number unchanged, XOR-ing every element together cancels each pair and leaves only the unpaired number. This runs in O(n) time and O(1) space, beating a hash-set approach on memory.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, every reconciliation entry should appear twice, once as a debit leg and once as a matching credit leg, except for one orphan entry that was posted only once. If we XOR all the entry codes together, every matched pair cancels out and the lone orphan code remains.

**One line to remember:** XOR all numbers together; pairs cancel to zero and the single unpaired number survives.

sections.s2_technical:
XOR has three properties we rely on: a number XOR itself is zero, a number XOR zero is itself, and XOR is commutative and associative so order does not matter. We start a running result at zero and XOR every element into it: `int result = 0; for (int n : nums) result ^= n;`. Because each paired value appears an even number of times, those values XOR to zero, and only the odd-one-out remains in `result`.

This is strictly better than the obvious approaches. Sorting then scanning is O(n log n); a hash set counting occurrences is O(n) time but O(n) space. The XOR method is O(n) time and O(1) space, which is the senior-level answer the interviewer is looking for.

A senior nuance is that XOR works here precisely because every other element is perfectly paired; if elements could appear three times or some other odd count, this simple XOR would not isolate the single number and we would need bit-counting across positions instead. Complexity is O(n) time and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India posts reconciliation entries in matched debit and credit pairs, but a glitch left exactly one entry unmatched, and operations must find that orphan code without allocating a big lookup structure on a memory-constrained batch node. This is exactly how Single Number works.

Problem 2 — Building a hash set of all codes would work but wastes memory on huge batches. This is why we XOR all codes together so matched pairs cancel and the orphan survives, using only one integer of extra space.

The code defines a `ReconService` exposing `findOrphan(codes)` returning the unmatched code. A `Demo` runs it over a batch with one orphan and logs the orphan code.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Single Number is the foundational Bitwise XOR problem. Every element appears twice except one, and I exploit three properties of XOR: a number XOR-ed with itself is zero, a number XOR-ed with zero is unchanged, and XOR is order-independent. So if I fold every element into a running accumulator with XOR, each perfectly paired value cancels itself to zero, and the only value left standing is the one that appeared once.

This beats the alternatives on the metric interviewers care about. Sorting and scanning is n log n, and a hash set is linear time but linear space. The XOR fold is linear time and constant space, which is the senior answer. I would be clear that this trick depends on every other element being exactly paired; if elements repeated an odd number of times I would instead count set bits across each bit position.

At the National Bank of India I used this when reconciliation entries, which should always come in matched debit and credit pairs, left exactly one orphan after a glitch, and the batch node was memory-constrained. I XOR-ed all the entry codes together so every matched pair cancelled and the orphan code remained, using just a single integer of extra space. Explaining the self-inverse property of XOR and why it gives constant space is what shows an interviewer I understand the bit-level reasoning rather than just the trick.

answers.question: In an array where every number appears twice except two numbers that each appear once, find both single numbers using constant extra space. Explain how a distinguishing set bit splits the array into two groups.
answers.shortTitle: Two Single Numbers (Find the Two Elements That Each Appear Once)

s1_definition.profdef: Two Single Numbers extends the XOR trick. XOR-ing the whole array gives the XOR of the two unpaired numbers, call it x. Because the two numbers differ, x has at least one set bit; we isolate its rightmost set bit and use it to partition the array into two groups, one where that bit is set and one where it is not. Each group contains exactly one of the singles, so XOR-ing within each group isolates them separately.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, two orphan reconciliation entries slipped through unmatched while everything else is paired. XOR-ing all codes gives the combined fingerprint of the two orphans. We pick one bit where they differ and sort every code into two buckets by that bit, so each orphan falls alone into its own bucket, and XOR-ing each bucket reveals it.
s1_definition.oneliner: XOR everything to combine the two singles, isolate a differing bit, split into two groups by that bit, and XOR each group to recover each single.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Two Single Numbers extends the XOR trick. XOR-ing the whole array gives the XOR of the two unpaired numbers, call it x. Because the two numbers differ, x has at least one set bit; we isolate its rightmost set bit and use it to partition the array into two groups, one where that bit is set and one where it is not. Each group contains exactly one of the singles, so XOR-ing within each group isolates them separately.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, two orphan reconciliation entries slipped through unmatched while everything else is paired. XOR-ing all codes gives the combined fingerprint of the two orphans. We pick one bit where they differ and sort every code into two buckets by that bit, so each orphan falls alone into its own bucket, and XOR-ing each bucket reveals it.

**One line to remember:** XOR everything to combine the two singles, isolate a differing bit, split into two groups by that bit, and XOR each group to recover each single.

sections.s2_technical:
First we XOR the whole array into `x`, which equals the two singles XOR-ed together because all pairs cancel. Since the two singles are distinct, `x` is non-zero and has at least one set bit. We isolate the rightmost set bit with `int rightmostBit = x & -x;`, a classic two's-complement idiom. This bit is set in exactly one of the two singles, so it cleanly separates them.

Then we scan the array again, and for each number we test whether that bit is set: if `(num & rightmostBit) != 0` we XOR it into `num1`, otherwise into `num2`. For example, `if ((num & rightmostBit) != 0) num1 ^= num; else num2 ^= num;`. Within each group the paired values still cancel, leaving one single in `num1` and the other in `num2`.

A senior nuance is why `x & -x` isolates the rightmost set bit: negating in two's complement flips all bits and adds one, so ANDing the original with its negation keeps only the lowest set bit. Any set bit of `x` would work as the splitter; the rightmost is just the cheapest to compute. Complexity is O(n) time and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India found that two reconciliation entries, not one, were left unmatched while every other entry is paired, and operations must recover both orphan codes with constant extra space. This is exactly how Two Single Numbers works.

Problem 2 — A single XOR fold would only give the combined fingerprint of both orphans, not each one. This is why we isolate a bit where the two orphans differ and use it to split all codes into two buckets so each orphan is isolated in its own bucket.

The code defines a `DualOrphanService` exposing `findTwoOrphans(codes)` returning an int array of the two orphan codes. A `Demo` runs it over a batch with two orphans and logs both.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Two Single Numbers extends the basic XOR trick to the case where two elements each appear once. If I XOR the whole array, every pair cancels and I am left with the XOR of the two singles combined into one value. That combined value is not an answer by itself, but because the two singles are different numbers it must have at least one bit set, and any set bit is a bit where the two singles differ.

So I isolate one such bit, conventionally the rightmost set bit using the x-and-negative-x idiom from two's complement, and I use it as a splitter. I pass over the array a second time and route each number into one of two groups depending on whether that bit is set in it. The two singles are guaranteed to fall into different groups, while every paired value still cancels within whichever group it lands in, so XOR-ing each group independently hands me the two singles.

At the National Bank of India I used this when two reconciliation entries, rather than one, were left unmatched while everything else was paired, and the node had to recover both orphans with constant extra space. I XOR-ed all codes to get their combined fingerprint, isolated a differing bit, and partitioned the codes into two buckets so each orphan was isolated and revealed by XOR. Explaining the distinguishing-bit split and the rightmost-set-bit idiom is what shows an interviewer I can reason at the bit level under a space constraint.

answers.question: Given a positive base-ten integer, find its complement, which is the number formed by flipping every bit in its binary representation, considering only the bits up to and including its highest set bit. Explain how a mask of all ones of the right width makes this a single XOR.
answers.shortTitle: Complement of Base 10 Number (Flip Every Bit Within the Number's Width)

s1_definition.profdef: Complement of Base 10 Number is a Bitwise XOR problem. The complement flips every bit of the number but only within its own bit width, not the full thirty-two bits of an int. We build a mask of all ones that is exactly as wide as the number's highest set bit, then XOR the number with that mask, which flips precisely the relevant bits and leaves the result in range.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a legacy device encodes an account flag as a small binary number, and an inverted mirror flag must be produced by flipping each of its bits, but only the bits the number actually uses. We make a stamp of all ones the same width as the flag and press it with XOR to flip exactly those bits.
s1_definition.oneliner: Make an all-ones mask as wide as the number, then XOR to flip only the bits the number uses.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Complement of Base 10 Number is a Bitwise XOR problem. The complement flips every bit of the number but only within its own bit width, not the full thirty-two bits of an int. We build a mask of all ones that is exactly as wide as the number's highest set bit, then XOR the number with that mask, which flips precisely the relevant bits and leaves the result in range.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a legacy device encodes an account flag as a small binary number, and an inverted mirror flag must be produced by flipping each of its bits, but only the bits the number actually uses. We make a stamp of all ones the same width as the flag and press it with XOR to flip exactly those bits.

**One line to remember:** Make an all-ones mask as wide as the number, then XOR to flip only the bits the number uses.

sections.s2_technical:
We first find the bit width of the number by right-shifting a copy until it becomes zero, counting the shifts: `int bitCount = 0; int n = num; while (n > 0) { bitCount++; n >>= 1; }`. For a number like 8, whose binary is 1000, the bit count is 4. Then we build a mask of that many ones with `int mask = (1 << bitCount) - 1;`, which for four bits gives 1111 in binary, or 15. Finally the complement is `num ^ mask`, flipping each used bit.

For example, 8 is 1000, the mask is 1111, and 8 XOR 15 is 0111 which is 7, the complement. The XOR with an all-ones mask flips every bit under the mask, which is exactly the definition of complement within the number's width.

A senior nuance is why we restrict the mask to the number's width rather than flipping all thirty-two bits: flipping the leading zero bits would produce a huge or negative number, which is not the intended complement. The edge case of zero is worth mentioning: its complement is conventionally one, which a careful implementation handles explicitly. Complexity is O(number of bits) time and O(1) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India integrates a legacy device that stores a small account flag as a compact binary number, and a downstream system needs the mirror flag, which is every bit flipped but only across the bits the flag actually occupies. This is exactly how the complement works.

Problem 2 — Naively flipping all thirty-two bits of the integer would corrupt the value with leading ones. This is why we measure the flag's width, build an all-ones mask of exactly that width, and XOR once to flip only the used bits.

The code defines a `FlagComplementService` exposing `complement(flag)` returning the mirror flag. A `Demo` computes the complement of a sample flag and logs it.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Complement of Base 10 Number asks me to flip every bit of a number, but only across the width the number actually uses, not the full thirty-two bits of an integer. The clean way to flip a set of bits is to XOR them with ones, so the whole problem reduces to building an all-ones mask that is exactly as wide as the number and XOR-ing once.

I measure the width by right-shifting a copy of the number until it reaches zero, counting the shifts, which gives me the position of the highest set bit. Then I build the mask as two raised to that width minus one, which is a run of ones of the right length, and I XOR the number with it. The reason I limit the mask to the number's width is important: if I flipped all thirty-two bits I would turn the leading zeros into ones and get a huge or negative number, which is not the intended complement. I also handle zero explicitly, whose complement is conventionally one.

At the National Bank of India I used this to bridge a legacy device that stored an account flag as a compact binary number, where a downstream system needed the mirror flag with every used bit inverted. I measured the flag's width, built an all-ones mask of that width, and XOR-ed once to produce the mirror. Explaining why the mask must match the number's width, and the mask-is-two-to-the-width-minus-one construction, is what shows an interviewer I understand bit widths rather than blindly inverting.

answers.question: Given a binary matrix, produce a new matrix where each row is first reversed horizontally and then each bit is inverted. Explain how XOR with one performs the inversion and how reversing and inverting can be fused in a single pass.
answers.shortTitle: Flip and Invert an Image (Flip Each Row Horizontally Then Invert with XOR)

s1_definition.profdef: Flip and Invert an Image is a Bitwise XOR problem on a binary matrix. Flipping a row horizontally reverses its order, and inverting replaces each zero with one and each one with zero, which is exactly XOR with one. The two operations can be fused: walking a row from both ends inward, we XOR each end value with one and swap them, so one pass per row does both the flip and the invert.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a cheque-scanning module stores each scanned line as a row of zeros and ones, and a legacy reader needs each line mirrored left-to-right and with its ink bits inverted. We walk each line from both ends toward the middle, flipping each bit by XOR-ing with one and swapping the two ends as we go.
s1_definition.oneliner: XOR with one inverts a bit, so reverse each row from both ends while XOR-ing each value with one in a single pass.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Flip and Invert an Image is a Bitwise XOR problem on a binary matrix. Flipping a row horizontally reverses its order, and inverting replaces each zero with one and each one with zero, which is exactly XOR with one. The two operations can be fused: walking a row from both ends inward, we XOR each end value with one and swap them, so one pass per row does both the flip and the invert.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a cheque-scanning module stores each scanned line as a row of zeros and ones, and a legacy reader needs each line mirrored left-to-right and with its ink bits inverted. We walk each line from both ends toward the middle, flipping each bit by XOR-ing with one and swapping the two ends as we go.

**One line to remember:** XOR with one inverts a bit, so reverse each row from both ends while XOR-ing each value with one in a single pass.

sections.s2_technical:
Inverting a single bit is `bit ^ 1`, because zero XOR one is one and one XOR one is zero. To flip a row horizontally we reverse it, and we can fuse the invert into the reversal with two pointers, `lo` starting at the left and `hi` at the right. At each step we set the new left value to `row[hi] ^ 1` and the new right value to `row[lo] ^ 1`, then move the pointers inward. For example, `int left = row[lo] ^ 1; row[lo] = row[hi] ^ 1; row[hi] = left; lo++; hi--;`.

When `lo` meets `hi` at the exact middle of an odd-length row, that single element is only inverted, not swapped, with `row[lo] ^= 1`. Doing it this way touches each cell once and uses no extra matrix, modifying in place.

A senior nuance is recognising that two logically separate operations, reverse and invert, commute cell-wise and can be fused to halve the passes and avoid a temporary matrix, which is the kind of micro-optimisation an interviewer appreciates. Another nuance is handling the odd-length middle element so it is inverted but not double-processed. Complexity is O(rows times columns) time and O(1) extra space beyond the output.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a cheque-scanning module that records each scanned line as a binary row, and a legacy reader expects every line mirrored left-to-right and with its bits inverted. This is exactly how Flip and Invert works.

Problem 2 — Doing a separate reverse pass and then a separate invert pass, or allocating a second matrix, wastes time and memory on large scan batches. This is why we fuse the two operations into one two-pointer pass per row that modifies the row in place.

The code defines an `ImageService` exposing `flipAndInvert(image)` returning the transformed matrix. A `Demo` transforms a small binary image and logs each resulting row.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Flip and Invert an Image combines two row operations on a binary matrix: flip each row horizontally, which just reverses its order, and invert each bit, which turns zeros into ones and ones into zeros. The bit-level insight is that inverting a single bit is exactly XOR with one, because zero XOR one is one and one XOR one is zero, so the inversion needs no conditional at all.

The optimisation I reach for is fusing the two operations. Instead of reversing the row and then inverting it in a second pass, or allocating a second matrix, I walk each row from both ends toward the middle with two pointers and, at each step, place the inverted right value on the left and the inverted left value on the right, swapping as I go. When the two pointers meet at the middle of an odd-length row, that single element is inverted once without a swap. This touches every cell exactly once and works in place.

At the National Bank of India I used this in a cheque-scanning module where each scanned line was stored as a binary row and a legacy reader expected every line mirrored and inverted. I fused the reverse and the invert into one two-pointer pass per row, which avoided a second matrix and halved the work on large scan batches. Explaining that invert is simply XOR with one, and that reverse and invert commute cell-wise so they can be fused, is what shows an interviewer I look for the clean single-pass solution.

answers.question: Given an unsorted array of numbers and a value K, find the K largest numbers. Explain why a min-heap of size K is the efficient structure and how it maintains the K largest seen so far.
answers.shortTitle: Top K Numbers (Find the K Largest Numbers with a Min-Heap)

s1_definition.profdef: Top K Numbers is the foundational Top K Elements problem. We maintain a min-heap limited to size K. We push the first K numbers, then for each remaining number, if it is larger than the heap's smallest element, which is the root, we pop the root and push the new number. The heap always holds the K largest numbers seen so far, giving O(n log K) time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, we want the K biggest transactions of the day from a long stream. We keep a small bucket that holds only the K biggest so far, where the smallest of those K sits at the top for quick checking. Each new transaction only enters the bucket if it beats the smallest one currently in it, pushing that smallest one out.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a min-heap of size K; a new number replaces the heap root only if it is bigger, so the heap always holds the K largest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Top K Numbers is the foundational Top K Elements problem. We maintain a min-heap limited to size K. We push the first K numbers, then for each remaining number, if it is larger than the heap's smallest element, which is the root, we pop the root and push the new number. The heap always holds the K largest numbers seen so far, giving O(n log K) time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, we want the K biggest transactions of the day from a long stream. We keep a small bucket that holds only the K biggest so far, where the smallest of those K sits at the top for quick checking. Each new transaction only enters the bucket if it beats the smallest one currently in it, pushing that smallest one out.

**One line to remember:** Keep a min-heap of size K; a new number replaces the heap root only if it is bigger, so the heap always holds the K largest.

sections.s2_technical:
We use a `PriorityQueue<Integer>` as a min-heap, the default ordering in Java. We first offer the initial K elements so the heap fills to size K. Then for each remaining element we compare it with `minHeap.peek()`, the smallest of the current K: if the new element is larger we `poll()` the root and `offer()` the new element. For example, `if (num > minHeap.peek()) { minHeap.poll(); minHeap.offer(num); }`. At the end the heap contains exactly the K largest numbers.

The reason a min-heap of size K beats sorting is cost. Sorting the whole array is O(n log n); the min-heap approach is O(n log K), which is much smaller when K is small relative to n, and it uses only O(K) extra space. The smallest-at-the-root arrangement is what makes the keep-or-discard decision a single constant-time peek.

A senior nuance is that we want the K largest, so counter-intuitively we use a min-heap, not a max-heap, because the root being the smallest of the kept set lets us cheaply evict the weakest candidate. If we wanted the K smallest we would use a max-heap by symmetry. Complexity is O(n log K) time and O(K) space.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes a long stream of daily transaction amounts and the risk team wants only the K largest for a priority review, without sorting the entire stream. This is exactly how Top K Numbers works.

Problem 2 — Sorting every transaction to take the top K is wasteful when K is small. This is why we keep a min-heap of size K, where each new amount only displaces the smallest kept amount if it is larger, costing a cheap peek and an occasional heap operation.

Top K Numbers is the foundational Top K Elements problem, and the key counter-intuitive choice is that to find the K largest numbers I use a min-heap, not a max-heap. I keep the heap bounded to size K. I seed it with the first K numbers, and then for every remaining number I compare it against the heap's root, which is the smallest of the K numbers I am currently keeping. If the new number is larger I evict the root and insert the new number; if not I discard it.

I kept a size-K min-heap where each new amount only displaced the smallest kept amount if it was larger. Explaining why a min-heap rather than a max-heap gives the K largest, and the n log K versus n log n argument, is what shows an interviewer I understand the structure choice, not just the result.

answers.question: Given an unsorted array of numbers and a value K, find the Kth smallest number. Explain how a max-heap of size K keeps the K smallest seen so far, with its root being the answer.
answers.shortTitle: Kth Smallest Number (Find the Kth Smallest with a Max-Heap)

s1_definition.profdef: Kth Smallest Number is a Top K Elements problem solved with a max-heap of size K. We keep the K smallest numbers seen so far in a max-heap, whose root is the largest of those K, which is exactly the Kth smallest overall once all numbers are processed. Each new number replaces the root only if it is smaller, giving O(n log K) time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, to find the Kth cheapest fee among many charged, we keep a small bucket of only the K smallest fees seen, where the biggest of those K sits on top. A new fee enters only if it is smaller than that top one, and after all fees are seen, the top of the bucket is the Kth smallest fee.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a max-heap of size K of the smallest numbers; its root is the Kth smallest.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kth Smallest Number is a Top K Elements problem solved with a max-heap of size K. We keep the K smallest numbers seen so far in a max-heap, whose root is the largest of those K, which is exactly the Kth smallest overall once all numbers are processed. Each new number replaces the root only if it is smaller, giving O(n log K) time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, to find the Kth cheapest fee among many charged, we keep a small bucket of only the K smallest fees seen, where the biggest of those K sits on top. A new fee enters only if it is smaller than that top one, and after all fees are seen, the top of the bucket is the Kth smallest fee.

**One line to remember:** Keep a max-heap of size K of the smallest numbers; its root is the Kth smallest.

sections.s2_technical:
We use a max-heap, which in Java is `new PriorityQueue<>(Collections.reverseOrder())`. We offer the first K numbers, then for each remaining number, if it is smaller than the root, which is the largest of the kept K, we poll the root and offer the new number. For example, `if (num < maxHeap.peek()) { maxHeap.poll(); maxHeap.offer(num); }`. After processing all numbers, `maxHeap.peek()` is the Kth smallest, because exactly the K smallest numbers remain and the root is the largest of them.

This mirrors Top K Numbers but inverted: there we used a min-heap to keep the K largest; here we use a max-heap to keep the K smallest. The root always being the largest of the kept K is why it equals the Kth smallest at the end.

A senior nuance is that this general heap method handles streaming data where we cannot sort, and it extends to the Kth largest by flipping to a min-heap. For a one-shot in-memory array, quickselect gives average O(n), which is worth mentioning as the alternative when a single query on a static array is all that is needed. Complexity is O(n log K) time and O(K) space.

answers.question: Given a list of points on a plane and a value K, find the K points closest to the origin. Explain how a max-heap keyed on squared distance keeps the K nearest and why squared distance avoids the square root.
answers.shortTitle: K Closest Points to the Origin (Nearest K Points by Distance)

s1_definition.profdef: K Closest Points to the Origin is a Top K Elements problem. We keep a max-heap of size K ordered by distance from the origin, where the root is the farthest of the kept points. Each new point replaces the root only if it is closer. We compare by squared distance to avoid the cost and precision loss of the square root, since ordering is preserved. This gives O(n log K) time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, each branch is a point on a map and we want the K branches nearest to head office at the origin. We keep a small bucket of the K nearest branches, with the farthest of them on top. A new branch enters only if it is nearer than that farthest one. We rank by distance-squared because taking actual distances with a square root is unnecessary for ordering.
s1_definition.oneliner: Max-heap of size K by squared distance; a closer point evicts the farthest kept point.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** K Closest Points to the Origin is a Top K Elements problem. We keep a max-heap of size K ordered by distance from the origin, where the root is the farthest of the kept points. Each new point replaces the root only if it is closer. We compare by squared distance to avoid the cost and precision loss of the square root, since ordering is preserved. This gives O(n log K) time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, each branch is a point on a map and we want the K branches nearest to head office at the origin. We keep a small bucket of the K nearest branches, with the farthest of them on top. A new branch enters only if it is nearer than that farthest one. We rank by distance-squared because taking actual distances with a square root is unnecessary for ordering.

**One line to remember:** Max-heap of size K by squared distance; a closer point evicts the farthest kept point.

sections.s2_technical:
For a point with coordinates x and y, the squared distance from the origin is x times x plus y times y. We never need the actual Euclidean distance because comparing squared distances gives the same ordering, and it avoids a floating-point square root. We build a max-heap keyed on that squared distance: `PriorityQueue<int[]> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> (b[0]*b[0] + b[1]*b[1]) - (a[0]*a[0] + a[1]*a[1]));`.

We push the first K points, then for each remaining point we compare its squared distance with the root's squared distance, which is the farthest kept; if the new point is closer we poll and offer. At the end the heap holds the K closest points. Keeping the farthest at the root makes the keep-or-discard decision a single comparison.

A senior nuance is the squared-distance optimisation, which both saves the square-root computation and avoids floating-point rounding issues by staying in integer arithmetic when coordinates are integers. Another nuance is that for a static array quickselect on squared distance gives average linear time, but the heap shines for streaming points. Complexity is O(n log K) time and O(K) space.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India plots branches as coordinates and wants the K branches nearest to head office at the origin, for a cash-logistics route, without sorting all branches. This is exactly how K Closest Points works.

Problem 2 — Computing exact distances with square roots for every branch and sorting them is wasteful and imprecise. This is why we keep a max-heap of size K keyed on squared distance, evicting the farthest kept branch when a nearer one appears.

answers.question: Given ropes of different lengths, connecting two ropes costs the sum of their lengths, and the combined rope can be connected again. Find the minimum total cost to connect all ropes into one. Explain why always joining the two shortest ropes is optimal and how a min-heap implements it.
answers.shortTitle: Connect Ropes (Minimum Cost to Connect All Ropes)

s1_definition.profdef: Connect Ropes is a Top K Elements problem with a greedy min-heap. Because every join costs the sum of the two joined lengths and that sum is then re-joined later, shorter ropes should be combined first so their lengths are counted in fewer future sums. We repeatedly extract the two smallest lengths from a min-heap, add them, accumulate that cost, and push the combined length back, until one rope remains.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, we merge many small daily settlement batches into one, and merging two batches costs effort equal to their combined size, which then gets merged again. To minimise total effort we always merge the two smallest batches first, because their sizes will otherwise be re-counted in every later merge.
s1_definition.oneliner: Always join the two shortest ropes using a min-heap, add each join's cost, and push the result back until one rope remains.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Connect Ropes is a Top K Elements problem with a greedy min-heap. Because every join costs the sum of the two joined lengths and that sum is then re-joined later, shorter ropes should be combined first so their lengths are counted in fewer future sums. We repeatedly extract the two smallest lengths from a min-heap, add them, accumulate that cost, and push the combined length back, until one rope remains.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, we merge many small daily settlement batches into one, and merging two batches costs effort equal to their combined size, which then gets merged again. To minimise total effort we always merge the two smallest batches first, because their sizes will otherwise be re-counted in every later merge.

**One line to remember:** Always join the two shortest ropes using a min-heap, add each join's cost, and push the result back until one rope remains.

sections.s2_technical:
We load all rope lengths into a min-heap so the two smallest are always at hand. While the heap has more than one rope, we poll the two smallest, add them into `cost`, accumulate `cost` into a running total, and offer `cost` back as a new combined rope. For example, `int first = minHeap.poll(); int second = minHeap.poll(); int cost = first + second; total += cost; minHeap.offer(cost);`. When one rope remains, `total` is the minimum cost.

The greedy choice of always joining the two smallest is optimal because of a Huffman-coding argument: a rope joined early participates in more subsequent sums, so the shortest ropes, which contribute the least, should be joined earliest to be re-summed the most, and the longest ropes should be joined last to be re-summed the fewest times. This minimises the weighted total.

A senior nuance is that this is structurally identical to building a Huffman tree, where the total cost equals the sum over all leaves of length times depth, and the min-heap is the standard way to always pick the two lightest nodes. Loading the heap is O(n), and each of the n minus one joins is O(log n). Complexity is O(n log n) time and O(n) space.

Problem 2 — Merging in an arbitrary order wastes effort because large early merges get re-counted. This is why we always merge the two smallest batches first using a min-heap, which is provably optimal.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Connect Ropes is a greedy Top K Elements problem. Joining two ropes costs the sum of their lengths, and because the combined rope is joined again later, every length gets re-counted in all the merges it participates in. The optimal strategy is therefore to always join the two shortest ropes first, so that the smallest lengths, which cost the least, are the ones re-summed the most times, while the largest lengths are joined last and re-summed the fewest times.

I implement this with a min-heap of all the lengths. While more than one rope remains, I poll the two smallest, add them to get the cost of that join, accumulate that cost into a running total, and push the combined length back into the heap so it can be joined again. When a single rope is left, the accumulated total is the minimum cost. This is structurally the same as building a Huffman tree, where the total equals the sum of each leaf's length times its depth.

At the National Bank of India I used this when merging many small settlement batches into one final batch, where each merge costs effort proportional to the combined size and the merged batch is merged again. I always merged the two smallest batches first using a min-heap, which minimised total effort, running in n log n time. Explaining the greedy exchange argument, that the shortest ropes should be re-summed the most, and the Huffman connection is what shows an interviewer I understand why the greedy choice is provably optimal.

answers.question: Given an unsorted array of numbers, find the K numbers that appear most frequently. Explain how a frequency map plus a min-heap keyed on frequency finds them efficiently.
answers.shortTitle: Top K Frequent Numbers (Find the K Most Frequently Occurring Numbers)

s1_definition.profdef: Top K Frequent Numbers is a Top K Elements problem combined with frequency counting. We first count occurrences of each number into a hash map, then keep a min-heap of size K ordered by frequency. Each distinct number is offered to the heap; when the heap exceeds K we evict the least frequent. The heap ends with the K most frequent numbers, giving O(n plus d log K) time where d is the number of distinct values.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, we want the K merchant categories that Rajesh spends on most often. We first tally how many times each category appears, then keep a small bucket of the K most frequent categories, where the least frequent kept category sits on top so a more frequent one can push it out.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count frequencies in a map, then keep a size-K min-heap keyed on frequency, evicting the least frequent when the heap overflows.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Top K Frequent Numbers is a Top K Elements problem combined with frequency counting. We first count occurrences of each number into a hash map, then keep a min-heap of size K ordered by frequency. Each distinct number is offered to the heap; when the heap exceeds K we evict the least frequent. The heap ends with the K most frequent numbers, giving O(n plus d log K) time where d is the number of distinct values.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, we want the K merchant categories that Rajesh spends on most often. We first tally how many times each category appears, then keep a small bucket of the K most frequent categories, where the least frequent kept category sits on top so a more frequent one can push it out.

**One line to remember:** Count frequencies in a map, then keep a size-K min-heap keyed on frequency, evicting the least frequent when the heap overflows.

sections.s2_technical:
We build a frequency map with `map.merge(num, 1, Integer::sum)` for each number, counting occurrences in O(n). Then we create a min-heap ordered by the map's frequency values: `PriorityQueue<Integer> minHeap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> map.get(a) - map.get(b));`. We iterate over the distinct keys, offering each; whenever the heap size exceeds K we poll, which removes the least frequent kept number. For example, `minHeap.offer(key); if (minHeap.size() > K) minHeap.poll();`.

After processing all distinct keys, the heap holds the K numbers with the highest frequencies. Ordering the heap by frequency with the root being the least frequent is what lets the overflow eviction drop exactly the weakest candidate each time.

A senior nuance is that when K approaches the number of distinct values, a bucket sort by frequency, placing numbers into buckets indexed by their count and reading from the high end, gives O(n) time, which beats the heap's O(n plus d log K); mentioning both shows range. Another nuance is that ties in frequency are broken arbitrarily unless the problem specifies otherwise. Complexity is O(n plus d log K) time and O(n) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants the K merchant categories that a customer like Rajesh transacts in most frequently, for a rewards recommendation, from a long transaction history. This is exactly how Top K Frequent Numbers works.

Problem 2 — Sorting all categories by frequency is more work than needed when only K are wanted. This is why we count frequencies once and keep a size-K min-heap keyed on frequency, evicting the least frequent kept category whenever a more frequent one arrives.

The code defines a `SpendPatternService` exposing `topKFrequent(categoryIds, k)` returning the K most frequent category ids. A `Demo` finds the top two categories and logs them.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Top K Frequent Numbers blends frequency counting with the Top K Elements pattern. I first pass over the array once and count how many times each number occurs into a hash map. Then I keep a min-heap of size K, but crucially the heap is ordered by frequency rather than by the numbers themselves, so its root is the least frequent of the numbers I am currently keeping.

I iterate over the distinct numbers, offering each into the heap, and whenever the heap grows beyond K I poll the root, which removes the least frequent kept number. That overflow-then-evict step guarantees I always discard the weakest candidate, so when I have processed every distinct number the heap holds exactly the K most frequent ones. The counting is linear, and the heap work is the number of distinct values times the logarithm of K.

At the National Bank of India I used this to find the K merchant categories a customer like Rajesh transacts in most often, powering a rewards recommendation from a long transaction history. I counted category frequencies once and kept a size-K min-heap keyed on frequency, evicting the least frequent kept category whenever a more frequent one arrived. I would also mention that when K is close to the number of distinct values, a bucket sort by frequency achieves linear time, which shows an interviewer I know when to switch tools.

answers.question: Given a string, sort its characters in decreasing order of how often they appear. Explain how a frequency map plus a max-heap keyed on frequency builds the result.
answers.shortTitle: Frequency Sort (Sort Characters by Decreasing Frequency)

s1_definition.profdef: Frequency Sort is a Top K Elements problem using a max-heap. We count how often each character appears, push all distinct characters into a max-heap ordered by frequency, then repeatedly extract the most frequent character and append it to the output as many times as it occurs. This produces a string sorted by decreasing frequency in O(n plus d log d) time where d is the number of distinct characters.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a transaction reference string mixes many status codes, and a report must list codes most-frequent first. We tally each code, keep a bucket with the most frequent code on top, and pour out each code repeated by its count, starting with the one that occurred most.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count frequencies, push characters into a max-heap by frequency, then pop and repeat each character by its count.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Frequency Sort is a Top K Elements problem using a max-heap. We count how often each character appears, push all distinct characters into a max-heap ordered by frequency, then repeatedly extract the most frequent character and append it to the output as many times as it occurs. This produces a string sorted by decreasing frequency in O(n plus d log d) time where d is the number of distinct characters.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a transaction reference string mixes many status codes, and a report must list codes most-frequent first. We tally each code, keep a bucket with the most frequent code on top, and pour out each code repeated by its count, starting with the one that occurred most.

**One line to remember:** Count frequencies, push characters into a max-heap by frequency, then pop and repeat each character by its count.

sections.s2_technical:
We count characters into a frequency map with `freq.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum)`. We create a max-heap ordered by frequency, `PriorityQueue<Character> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> freq.get(b) - freq.get(a));`, and offer every distinct character. Then while the heap is non-empty we poll the most frequent character and append it to a `StringBuilder` that many times: `char c = maxHeap.poll(); for (int i = 0; i < freq.get(c); i++) sb.append(c);`.

The max-heap ordered by frequency makes each poll return the next most frequent character, so the output is naturally built in decreasing-frequency order. Using a StringBuilder avoids the quadratic cost of repeated string concatenation.

A senior nuance is that characters with equal frequency can appear in any relative order unless the problem fixes a tie-break, and if a specific tie-break is required we add it as a secondary comparator. Another nuance is that for a fixed small alphabet a counting-array approach can replace the heap for linear time. Complexity is O(n plus d log d) time and O(n) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India produces a status report from a reference string of transaction status codes, and the report must list codes most-frequent first so operations focus on the dominant statuses. This is exactly how Frequency Sort works.

Problem 2 — Sorting the raw characters alphabetically does not reflect importance by frequency. This is why we count each code and use a max-heap keyed on frequency to emit codes in decreasing frequency order.

The code defines a `StatusReportService` exposing `sortByFrequency(codes)` returning the frequency-sorted string. A `Demo` sorts a status-code string and logs the result.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Frequency Sort arranges a string's characters in decreasing order of how often they appear, and it is a clean application of the Top K Elements pattern with a max-heap. I first count every character into a frequency map in one pass. Then I push all the distinct characters into a max-heap that is ordered by their frequency, so the character that appears most often sits at the root.

I then drain the heap: each time I poll the most frequent remaining character and append it to a StringBuilder exactly as many times as its count. Because the heap always surfaces the next most frequent character, the output is assembled in decreasing-frequency order without any extra sorting, and the StringBuilder keeps the appends linear rather than quadratic.

At the National Bank of India I used this to build a status report from a reference string of transaction status codes, where operations wanted the dominant statuses listed first. I counted each code and used a max-heap keyed on frequency to emit codes most-frequent first. I would note that equal-frequency characters may come out in any order unless a tie-break is specified, and that a fixed small alphabet could use a counting array for linear time, which shows an interviewer I understand both the heap approach and its alternatives.

answers.question: Design a class that, given a value K and an initial list of numbers, returns the Kth largest number each time a new number is added to the stream. Explain how a min-heap of size K supports this efficiently.
answers.shortTitle: Kth Largest Number in a Stream (Maintain the Kth Largest as Numbers Arrive)

s1_definition.profdef: Kth Largest Number in a Stream is a Top K Elements design problem. We maintain a min-heap bounded to size K containing the K largest numbers seen so far. The root of this heap is always the Kth largest. When a new number arrives we offer it and, if the heap exceeds K, poll the root, so the root remains the Kth largest and each add is O(log K).
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, we continuously watch incoming transaction amounts and must always report the Kth largest so far, for a live threshold alert. We keep a small bucket of the K largest amounts with the smallest of those K on top; that top value is the Kth largest, and each new amount updates it cheaply.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep a min-heap of size K of the largest numbers; its root is always the Kth largest as the stream grows.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kth Largest Number in a Stream is a Top K Elements design problem. We maintain a min-heap bounded to size K containing the K largest numbers seen so far. The root of this heap is always the Kth largest. When a new number arrives we offer it and, if the heap exceeds K, poll the root, so the root remains the Kth largest and each add is O(log K).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, we continuously watch incoming transaction amounts and must always report the Kth largest so far, for a live threshold alert. We keep a small bucket of the K largest amounts with the smallest of those K on top; that top value is the Kth largest, and each new amount updates it cheaply.

**One line to remember:** Keep a min-heap of size K of the largest numbers; its root is always the Kth largest as the stream grows.

sections.s2_technical:
The class holds a min-heap and the value K. In the constructor we add all initial numbers via the same add routine so the heap self-limits to K. The `add(num)` method offers the number and, if `minHeap.size() > k`, polls the root: `minHeap.offer(num); if (minHeap.size() > k) minHeap.poll(); return minHeap.peek();`. The peek returns the current Kth largest.

Keeping the heap at exactly K elements means the smallest of the K largest, the root, is by definition the Kth largest overall. Adding a number that is too small to be in the top K will be immediately polled back out, so it never disturbs the answer; adding a number large enough pushes the old Kth largest out and the new root becomes the updated Kth largest.

A senior nuance is that this is a stateful streaming design, so correctness depends on always re-trimming to K after each insert, and on seeding the heap through the same add path to avoid duplicated logic. Each add is O(log K) and the structure uses O(K) space regardless of how long the stream runs, which is the key scalability property. Complexity is O(log K) per add and O(K) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a live threshold alert that must always know the Kth largest transaction amount seen so far on a never-ending stream, to flag unusually large activity. This is exactly how Kth Largest in a Stream works.

Problem 2 — Storing and re-sorting the whole stream is impossible as it grows without bound. This is why we keep only a size-K min-heap whose root is the Kth largest, using fixed memory no matter how long the stream runs.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kth Largest Number in a Stream is a stateful design problem from the Top K Elements family. The structure I maintain is a min-heap bounded to size K that always contains the K largest numbers seen so far. Because it is a min-heap, its root is the smallest of those K, which is exactly the Kth largest overall, so answering a query is just reading the root.

When a new number arrives I offer it into the heap and then, if the heap now holds more than K elements, I poll the root to trim it back to K. A number too small to belong in the top K gets polled straight back out and never affects the answer, while a large enough number pushes the old Kth largest out and the new root becomes the updated Kth largest. I also seed the initial numbers through the very same add routine so there is only one place that enforces the size limit.

At the National Bank of India I used this for a live threshold alert that had to always know the Kth largest transaction amount on a never-ending stream, flagging unusually large activity. Keeping only a size-K min-heap meant fixed memory no matter how long the stream ran, with each update costing just the logarithm of K. Explaining why the root of a size-K min-heap is the Kth largest, and why the memory stays constant for an unbounded stream, is what shows an interviewer I can design for streaming, not just batch.

answers.question: Given a sorted array, a target value X, and a count K, find the K numbers closest to X. If two numbers are equally close, prefer the smaller. Explain how binary search locates X and a two-pointer window then selects the K closest.
answers.shortTitle: K Closest Numbers (Find the K Elements Nearest a Target in a Sorted Array)

s1_definition.profdef: K Closest Numbers is a Top K Elements problem that exploits the array being sorted. We binary-search to find the position of the target, then run two pointers outward from that position, repeatedly taking whichever neighbour is closer to the target until we have K numbers. Because the array is sorted, the K closest always form a contiguous window, giving O(log n plus K) time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, interest-rate quotes are stored sorted, and when Rajesh targets a particular rate we want the K quotes nearest to it. We jump near the target with binary search, then step left and right, each time grabbing the side whose quote is closer, until we have K quotes.
s1_definition.oneliner: Binary-search to the target, then expand two pointers outward taking the closer side each time until K numbers are chosen.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** K Closest Numbers is a Top K Elements problem that exploits the array being sorted. We binary-search to find the position of the target, then run two pointers outward from that position, repeatedly taking whichever neighbour is closer to the target until we have K numbers. Because the array is sorted, the K closest always form a contiguous window, giving O(log n plus K) time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, interest-rate quotes are stored sorted, and when Rajesh targets a particular rate we want the K quotes nearest to it. We jump near the target with binary search, then step left and right, each time grabbing the side whose quote is closer, until we have K quotes.

**One line to remember:** Binary-search to the target, then expand two pointers outward taking the closer side each time until K numbers are chosen.

sections.s2_technical:
We first binary-search for the index of the target or its insertion point, giving a starting boundary. We set `low = index - 1` and `high = index`, two pointers straddling the target. We take K numbers: at each step, if `low >= 0` and either `high >= n` or the target minus `arr[low]` is less than or equal to `arr[high]` minus the target, we take the left number and decrement `low`; otherwise we take the right number and increment `high`. For example, `if (low >= 0 && (high >= n || X - arr[low] <= arr[high] - X)) { result.addFirst(arr[low--]); } else { result.addLast(arr[high++]); }`.

The less-than-or-equal comparison on the left side implements the tie-break that prefers the smaller number when distances are equal. Because the array is sorted, the closest numbers are always adjacent, so this outward expansion collects exactly the K closest in sorted order.

A senior nuance is that adding to the front of the result keeps it sorted, for which an ArrayDeque or inserting at index zero works; using a linked structure avoids shifting. Another nuance is that an alternative pure-binary-search finds the left boundary of the K-window directly in O(log n log K)-style bounds, but the two-pointer expansion after one binary search is simpler and O(log n plus K). Complexity is O(log n plus K) time and O(K) space for the output.

answers.question: Given an array of numbers and a value K, you may remove up to K elements. Maximize the number of distinct elements remaining. Explain how a frequency count and a min-heap of the duplicate counts guide which removals help most.
answers.shortTitle: Maximum Distinct Elements (Maximize Distinct Values After K Removals)

s1_definition.profdef: Maximum Distinct Elements is a Top K Elements problem. Numbers that already appear once are distinct and cost nothing. For numbers appearing more than once, we need to remove all but one copy to make them distinct. We put the surplus counts into a min-heap and spend our K removals on the smallest surpluses first, because each small surplus cleared turns a number distinct for the fewest removals.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a report lists merchant category codes with duplicates, and we may delete up to K entries to maximise how many categories appear exactly once. Categories already appearing once are free wins; for the rest we clear the ones needing the fewest deletions first, because they convert to distinct most cheaply.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep single-occurrence numbers free, then spend K removals clearing the smallest surplus counts first to turn the most numbers distinct.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Maximum Distinct Elements is a Top K Elements problem. Numbers that already appear once are distinct and cost nothing. For numbers appearing more than once, we need to remove all but one copy to make them distinct. We put the surplus counts into a min-heap and spend our K removals on the smallest surpluses first, because each small surplus cleared turns a number distinct for the fewest removals.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a report lists merchant category codes with duplicates, and we may delete up to K entries to maximise how many categories appear exactly once. Categories already appearing once are free wins; for the rest we clear the ones needing the fewest deletions first, because they convert to distinct most cheaply.

**One line to remember:** Keep single-occurrence numbers free, then spend K removals clearing the smallest surplus counts first to turn the most numbers distinct.

sections.s2_technical:
We count frequencies. Every number with frequency exactly one is already distinct and contributes to the answer without spending removals. For numbers with frequency greater than one, we push their counts into a min-heap, because the surplus we must remove to make such a number distinct is its count minus one, and smaller counts need fewer removals. We also start a distinct counter at the number of already-unique values.

Then while we have removals left and the heap is non-empty, we poll the smallest count, compute how many removals are needed to reduce it to one, namely count minus one, and if we can afford that, we spend them and increment the distinct counter. For example, `int count = minHeap.poll(); int needed = count - 1; if (k >= needed) { k -= needed; distinct++; }`. If we cannot fully afford a count we stop, because partial removals on the smallest remaining count cannot make any further number distinct.

A senior nuance is the greedy justification: spending removals on the smallest surplus first maximises how many numbers we can fully reduce to a single copy, since larger surpluses would consume our budget while converting the same one number. Starting the distinct count with the already-unique values avoids double counting. Complexity is O(n plus d log d) time and O(d) space where d is the number of distinct values.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has a category report with duplicate codes and may delete up to K entries to maximise how many categories appear exactly once, improving the report's clarity. This is exactly how Maximum Distinct Elements works.

Problem 2 — Deleting entries arbitrarily wastes the budget. This is why we treat already-unique codes as free, and spend deletions on the smallest surplus counts first using a min-heap, turning the most codes distinct per deletion.

The code defines a `DistinctService` exposing `maxDistinct(codes, k)` returning the maximum distinct count achievable. A `Demo` runs it over a sample report and logs the result.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Maximum Distinct Elements asks me to maximise how many values appear exactly once after removing up to K elements, and it is a greedy Top K Elements problem. I start by counting frequencies. Every value that already appears exactly once is distinct for free and goes straight into my distinct count without spending any of my removal budget. The interesting values are the ones appearing more than once.

For each repeated value, the cost to make it distinct is its count minus one, because I must delete every copy but one. I put those counts into a min-heap and spend my budget on the smallest surpluses first, since clearing a small surplus converts a value to distinct for the fewest removals, letting me convert the most values overall. I keep polling the smallest count and, if I can afford its count-minus-one removals, I spend them and increment the distinct count; the moment the next conversion is unaffordable I stop, because no further value can then be made distinct.

At the National Bank of India I used this to clean a category report riddled with duplicate codes, where we could delete up to K entries to maximise how many categories appeared exactly once. I treated already-unique codes as free and spent deletions on the cheapest conversions first via a min-heap. Explaining the greedy argument, that the smallest surpluses should be cleared first, and starting the count with the already-unique values is what shows an interviewer I reason about the budget optimally.

answers.question: Given an array and two values K1 and K2, find the sum of all elements that are strictly greater than the K1-th smallest and strictly smaller than the K2-th smallest. Explain how two heaps, or finding the two order statistics, let you sum the band in between.
answers.shortTitle: Sum of Elements Between K1 and K2 Smallest (Sum Strictly Between Two Order Statistics)

s1_definition.profdef: Sum of Elements Between K1 and K2 Smallest is a Top K Elements problem. The elements strictly between the K1-th and K2-th smallest are exactly the ones whose rank is from K1 plus one up to K2 minus one. Using a max-heap of size K2, we can pop the K2-th through just-after-K1-th smallest, summing the ones we want, so we obtain the band without fully sorting.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, we rank account balances and want the total of the balances that sit strictly between the K1-th smallest and the K2-th smallest, excluding both endpoints, for a mid-tier analysis. We use a heap to peel off balances by rank and add up only those falling in the middle band.
s1_definition.oneliner: The target elements have ranks K1 plus one through K2 minus one; use a size-K2 max-heap to peel them off and sum them.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Sum of Elements Between K1 and K2 Smallest is a Top K Elements problem. The elements strictly between the K1-th and K2-th smallest are exactly the ones whose rank is from K1 plus one up to K2 minus one. Using a max-heap of size K2, we can pop the K2-th through just-after-K1-th smallest, summing the ones we want, so we obtain the band without fully sorting.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, we rank account balances and want the total of the balances that sit strictly between the K1-th smallest and the K2-th smallest, excluding both endpoints, for a mid-tier analysis. We use a heap to peel off balances by rank and add up only those falling in the middle band.

**One line to remember:** The target elements have ranks K1 plus one through K2 minus one; use a size-K2 max-heap to peel them off and sum them.

sections.s2_technical:
One clean method uses a max-heap of size K2. We push numbers, keeping only the K2 smallest, so after processing the heap holds the K2 smallest numbers with the largest, the K2-th smallest, at the root. We then pop the root once to discard the K2-th smallest itself, since the band is strictly below it, and then pop and sum the next elements until only K1 remain in the heap, which correspond to ranks one through K1 that we must exclude. For example, after building the size-K2 max-heap, `maxHeap.poll(); while (maxHeap.size() > k1) sum += maxHeap.poll();`.

The remaining K1 elements in the heap are the K1 smallest, which are excluded, and the one we popped first was the K2-th smallest, also excluded, so what we summed is exactly ranks K1 plus one through K2 minus one. Building the heap is O(n log K2) and the final pops are O(K2 log K2).

A senior nuance is that an even simpler approach, when a full sort is acceptable, sorts once and sums the slice from index K1 to K2 minus two, which is O(n log n); the heap method is preferable when K2 is much smaller than n. Being careful with the strict exclusions at both ends, discarding the K2-th smallest and leaving the K1 smallest, is the correctness crux. Complexity is O(n log K2) time and O(K2) space.

Problem 2 — Fully sorting all balances is more than needed when K2 is small. This is why we keep a size-K2 max-heap of the K2 smallest balances and peel off exactly the middle band to sum.

Sum of Elements Between K1 and K2 Smallest asks for the total of the elements whose rank falls strictly between the K1-th smallest and the K2-th smallest, excluding both endpoints, so the target ranks are K1 plus one through K2 minus one. I solve it with a single size-K2 max-heap. I push every number but keep the heap trimmed to K2, so it ends holding exactly the K2 smallest numbers with the K2-th smallest sitting at the root.

Then I peel off the band precisely. I first pop the root once to discard the K2-th smallest, because the upper endpoint is excluded. After that I keep popping and summing until only K1 elements remain in the heap; those remaining K1 are the K1 smallest, which are also excluded. Everything I summed in between is exactly ranks K1 plus one through K2 minus one, so the two strict exclusions are handled by one discard at the top and by stopping when K1 elements are left at the bottom.

answers.question: You are given K sorted linked lists. Merge them into a single sorted linked list and return its head. Explain the K-way Merge pattern, the heap-based technique, the time and space complexity, and how it maps to a real banking scenario.
answers.shortTitle: Merge K Sorted Lists (Combine K Sorted Linked Lists into One)

s1_definition.profdef: Merge K Sorted Lists is the foundational problem of the K-way Merge pattern. We maintain a min-heap that holds one node from each list, always the smallest unmerged node across all lists. We pop the global minimum, append it to the result, and push the popped node's successor. The heap never grows beyond K entries, so each of the N total nodes is inserted and removed once, giving N log K time and K space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has K branch ledgers, each already sorted by transaction time. Rajesh asks for one combined statement in time order. Instead of dumping everything and re-sorting, a clerk keeps the earliest unread line from each branch on a small desk of size K, always picks the globally earliest, writes it down, and replaces it with the next line from that same branch. The desk never holds more than K lines.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep one candidate per list in a size-K min-heap and always take the global minimum.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Merge K Sorted Lists is the foundational problem of the K-way Merge pattern. We maintain a min-heap that holds one node from each list, always the smallest unmerged node across all lists. We pop the global minimum, append it to the result, and push the popped node's successor. The heap never grows beyond K entries, so each of the N total nodes is inserted and removed once, giving N log K time and K space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has K branch ledgers, each already sorted by transaction time. Rajesh asks for one combined statement in time order. Instead of dumping everything and re-sorting, a clerk keeps the earliest unread line from each branch on a small desk of size K, always picks the globally earliest, writes it down, and replaces it with the next line from that same branch. The desk never holds more than K lines.

**One line to remember:** Keep one candidate per list in a size-K min-heap and always take the global minimum.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach concatenates all N nodes and sorts them, which costs N log N and ignores the fact that each list is already sorted. The K-way Merge pattern exploits the existing order so we only ever compare K current heads at a time.

The engine is a `PriorityQueue` ordered by node value. We seed it with the head of every non-empty list: `pq.add(head)` for each list. Then we loop while the heap is not empty. Each iteration calls `pq.poll()` to get the smallest node, links it to the tail of the result, and if that node has a `next`, we call `pq.add(node.next)` to bring the next candidate from the same list into contention. For example, if the heap holds nodes valued 100, 250, and 400 and we poll 100 from Rajesh's list, we immediately push 100's successor so that list stays represented.

The heap comparator must be explicit: `new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a.val, b.val))`. Senior nuance: using a dummy head node for the result list removes special-casing the first append, and the heap size is bounded by K because we only ever add a successor after removing its predecessor, so memory stays at K regardless of how many millions of nodes flow through.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Merge K Sorted Lists is the foundational problem of the K-way Merge pattern. Given K lists that are each already sorted, I merge them into one sorted list using a min-heap that holds exactly one candidate from every list. I seed the heap with each list's head, then repeatedly poll the global minimum, append it to the result, and push the successor of whatever I just polled so that list stays represented. The heap never exceeds K entries, so I touch each of the N total nodes once and the whole merge costs N log K time and K space.

The key insight I explain to an interviewer is why this beats collecting everything and sorting. Concatenating and sorting ignores the existing order and costs N log N. The heap approach uses the fact that the next global minimum can only be one of the K current heads, so I never compare more than K items at a time. A dummy head node keeps the append logic clean, and pushing a node's successor only after removing the node itself is what bounds the heap at K.

At the National Bank of India I used this to produce a single time-ordered audit statement from many per-account transaction lists that were each already sorted, without the cost of pulling everything into memory and re-sorting. I kept a size-K min-heap of the earliest unmerged amount per account and drained it into one stream. Explaining the N log K complexity, the size-K heap invariant, and the dummy-head trick is what signals to an interviewer that I understand the K-way Merge pattern rather than just reciting a merge.

answers.question: Given M sorted lists of numbers, find the Kth smallest number among all of them. Explain the K-way Merge technique, the heap contents, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Kth Smallest Number in M Sorted Lists (Find the Kth Smallest Across Sorted Lists)

s1_definition.profdef: Kth Smallest Number in M Sorted Lists applies the K-way Merge pattern to produce only the first K numbers of the virtual merge rather than the full merge. We seed a min-heap with the first element of each list along with which list it came from and its index, then pop K times, each time pushing the next element from the same list. The Kth popped value is the answer. Time is K log M and space is M.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has M branch lists of fee amounts, each sorted. Priya wants the Kth cheapest fee overall. A clerk keeps the current cheapest unseen fee from each branch on a desk of size M, pops the cheapest, and replaces it with the next fee from that same branch. After K pops, the last fee removed is the Kth cheapest.
s1_definition.oneliner: Pop the global minimum K times from a size-M min-heap; the Kth pop is the answer.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kth Smallest Number in M Sorted Lists applies the K-way Merge pattern to produce only the first K numbers of the virtual merge rather than the full merge. We seed a min-heap with the first element of each list along with which list it came from and its index, then pop K times, each time pushing the next element from the same list. The Kth popped value is the answer. Time is K log M and space is M.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has M branch lists of fee amounts, each sorted. Priya wants the Kth cheapest fee overall. A clerk keeps the current cheapest unseen fee from each branch on a desk of size M, pops the cheapest, and replaces it with the next fee from that same branch. After K pops, the last fee removed is the Kth cheapest.

**One line to remember:** Pop the global minimum K times from a size-M min-heap; the Kth pop is the answer.

sections.s2_technical:
We do not merge everything. We only advance the merge K steps, because the Kth smallest is revealed exactly when we have removed K elements in sorted order. The heap entry must remember three things: the value, the index of the list it came from, and the position within that list, so we can fetch the successor.

In Java we can model the entry as an int array `{value, listIndex, elementIndex}` and order the heap by the first slot: `new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]))`. We seed it with `pq.add(new int[]{lists.get(i).get(0), i, 0})` for each list. Then we pop K times; on each pop we read the entry, and if the element index plus one is still within that list, we push `new int[]{lists.get(li).get(ei + 1), li, ei + 1}`.

Senior nuance: guard K against the total count so we never pop more than exists, and note that the heap size is bounded by M, not by K or N, because each list contributes at most one live candidate. This is the same engine as Merge K Sorted Lists, simply stopped early at the Kth removal.
