answers.question: Given K sorted integer lists, find the smallest range that includes at least one number from each of the K lists. If several ranges are equally small, return the one with the smaller start. Explain the K-way Merge technique and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Smallest Number Range Covering K Lists (Find the Tightest Range Including One Element from Each List)

s1_definition.profdef: Smallest Number Range Covering K Lists is a K-way Merge problem. We keep a min-heap of one current element per list and separately track the maximum of those current elements. The current window spans from the heap minimum to the tracked maximum and already covers every list. We repeatedly record the window, pop the minimum, and push its successor, updating the maximum; the smallest window ever seen is the answer. Time is N log K and space is K.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has K sorted lists of interest rates from K lenders. We want the narrowest rate band that still contains at least one rate from every lender. A clerk keeps the current lowest unused rate per lender, notes the highest of those, and the band from lowest to highest covers everyone. The clerk nudges the lowest rate forward, trying to shrink the band, and remembers the tightest band seen.
s1_definition.oneliner: The window from heap-min to running-max always covers all lists; shrink it by advancing the minimum.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Smallest Number Range Covering K Lists is a K-way Merge problem. We keep a min-heap of one current element per list and separately track the maximum of those current elements. The current window spans from the heap minimum to the tracked maximum and already covers every list. We repeatedly record the window, pop the minimum, and push its successor, updating the maximum; the smallest window ever seen is the answer. Time is N log K and space is K.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has K sorted lists of interest rates from K lenders. We want the narrowest rate band that still contains at least one rate from every lender. A clerk keeps the current lowest unused rate per lender, notes the highest of those, and the band from lowest to highest covers everyone. The clerk nudges the lowest rate forward, trying to shrink the band, and remembers the tightest band seen.

**One line to remember:** The window from heap-min to running-max always covers all lists; shrink it by advancing the minimum.

sections.s2_technical:
The crucial invariant is that if the heap holds exactly one element from each list, then the span from the smallest of them to the largest of them necessarily contains at least one element from every list. So that span is a valid covering range at all times.

We seed the heap with each list's first element and compute the maximum of those seeds. Each iteration: read the heap minimum, compare the span `max - min` against the best so far and update if tighter, then pop the minimum and push its successor while updating the running maximum with the pushed value. The moment any list runs out, no further window can cover all lists, so we stop.

In code the heap entry is `{value, listIndex, elementIndex}` ordered by value, and we hold a separate `int currentMax`. On each push we do `currentMax = Math.max(currentMax, nextValue)`. Senior nuance: the stop condition is reached exactly when the popped element has no successor, because advancing is the only way to keep all lists represented, and ties on window width are resolved by keeping the first (smaller-start) window since we only replace when strictly tighter.

Step 4 — We pop 5 from lender three, push 18, maximum becomes 18. Band [9, 18], width nine, not tighter. We continue popping and the windows widen.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Smallest Number Range Covering K Lists is a K-way Merge problem built on one clean invariant. If my min-heap holds exactly one element from each list, then the span from the smallest of those elements to the largest of them must contain at least one number from every list, so that span is always a valid covering range. I keep the heap minimum and separately track the running maximum of whatever is currently in the heap.

To shrink the range I repeatedly record the current span, pop the minimum, and push its successor from the same list while updating the running maximum. Advancing the minimum is the only lever that can tighten the window, and the maximum can only stay or rise. The instant any list runs out, no further window can cover all lists, so I stop. Ties on width are resolved toward the smaller start because I only replace the best when a new window is strictly tighter.

At the National Bank of India I used this to advertise the tightest home-loan rate band that still included at least one genuine quote from every lender, so the advertisement was honest for all of them. I kept one live rate per lender in a heap, tracked the running maximum, and remembered the narrowest covering band. Explaining the heap-min-to-running-max invariant, why advancing the minimum is what shrinks the window, and the exhaustion stop condition is what shows an interviewer that I understand this subtle K-way Merge variant.

answers.question: Given K sorted arrays, merge them into a single sorted array. Explain the K-way Merge technique with a heap, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Merge K Sorted Arrays (Combine K Sorted Arrays into One Sorted Array)

s1_definition.profdef: Merge K Sorted Arrays is the array form of the K-way Merge pattern. We keep a min-heap of one candidate per array, each entry remembering the array index and position, pop the global minimum into the output, and push the successor from the same array. With N total elements across K arrays the merge runs in N log K time and K space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has K sorted arrays of daily settlement amounts, one per desk. To build one chronological settlement sheet, a clerk keeps the earliest unused amount from each desk, writes the smallest, and pulls the next amount from that same desk. The desk tray never holds more than K slips.
s1_definition.oneliner: Same engine as merging K lists, but over arrays with index-and-position heap entries.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Merge K Sorted Arrays is the array form of the K-way Merge pattern. We keep a min-heap of one candidate per array, each entry remembering the array index and position, pop the global minimum into the output, and push the successor from the same array. With N total elements across K arrays the merge runs in N log K time and K space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has K sorted arrays of daily settlement amounts, one per desk. To build one chronological settlement sheet, a clerk keeps the earliest unused amount from each desk, writes the smallest, and pulls the next amount from that same desk. The desk tray never holds more than K slips.

**One line to remember:** Same engine as merging K lists, but over arrays with index-and-position heap entries.

sections.s2_technical:
With arrays we cannot follow a `next` pointer, so each heap entry carries the value, the array index, and the element index: `{value, arrayIndex, elementIndex}`. We seed the heap with the first element of each non-empty array, then pop repeatedly. On each pop we append the value to the result and, if the element index plus one is still within that array, push the next element.

A concrete seed looks like `pq.add(new int[]{arrays[i][0], i, 0})`. On pop of `{v, ai, ei}` we do `result.add(v)` and, if `ei + 1 < arrays[ai].length`, `pq.add(new int[]{arrays[ai][ei+1], ai, ei+1})`. Senior nuance: pre-sizing the output to the known total avoids repeated growth, and because each element is pushed and popped exactly once the comparisons total N log K, strictly better than N log N re-sorting when K is small relative to N.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India collects daily settlement amounts from K processing desks, each desk's array already sorted. The operations team needs one combined sorted array for the end-of-day reconciliation, and re-sorting the combined pile wastes the existing order. sections.s6_takeaway:
Merge K Sorted Arrays is the array form of the K-way Merge pattern. Because arrays have no next pointer, each heap entry carries the value together with the array index and the element index, so after I pop a value I can fetch its successor in the same array. I seed the min-heap with the first element of every array, then pop the global minimum into the output and push the next element from whichever array I just drew from.

The efficiency argument is the same as for lists. The heap holds at most K candidates, one per array, so each of the N total elements is pushed and popped once at log K cost, giving N log K overall rather than the N log N of collecting everything and re-sorting. I usually pre-size the output array to the known total so there is no repeated resizing, which matters when the combined set is large.

At the National Bank of India I used this to build one end-of-day settlement sheet from several processing desks, each of which already produced its amounts in sorted order. I kept one earliest amount per desk in a heap and drained them into a single sorted array for reconciliation. Explaining that the heap entry must carry array and element indices, that the heap stays bounded by K, and that this beats re-sorting when K is small is what shows an interviewer that I apply the K-way Merge pattern correctly to arrays.

answers.question: Given an N by N matrix where each row and each column is sorted in ascending order, find the Kth smallest element in the matrix. Explain the K-way Merge heap technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix (Row and Column Sorted Matrix)

s1_definition.profdef: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix treats each row as a sorted list and applies early-stopped K-way Merge. We seed a min-heap with the first element of each row, pop K times, and after each pop push the next element in that same row. The Kth popped value is the answer, costing K log N time and N space for an N by N matrix.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India keeps a grid of fees where each row and column rises. To find the Kth cheapest fee, a clerk starts with the leftmost fee of every row on a small tray, pops the cheapest, and slides one step right in that same row to replace it. After K pops the last fee removed is the Kth cheapest.
s1_definition.oneliner: Rows are sorted lists; run K-way Merge across rows and stop at the Kth pop.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix treats each row as a sorted list and applies early-stopped K-way Merge. We seed a min-heap with the first element of each row, pop K times, and after each pop push the next element in that same row. The Kth popped value is the answer, costing K log N time and N space for an N by N matrix.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India keeps a grid of fees where each row and column rises. To find the Kth cheapest fee, a clerk starts with the leftmost fee of every row on a small tray, pops the cheapest, and slides one step right in that same row to replace it. After K pops the last fee removed is the Kth cheapest.

**One line to remember:** Rows are sorted lists; run K-way Merge across rows and stop at the Kth pop.

sections.s2_technical:
Each row is already ascending, so the matrix is really N sorted rows. The heap entry stores the value, the row, and the column: `{value, row, col}`. We seed with column zero of each row, then pop K times. After popping `{v, r, c}` we push `{matrix[r][c+1], r, c+1}` if the column plus one is still in range.

A seed looks like `pq.add(new int[]{matrix[r][0], r, 0})` for each row r. Senior nuance: we only need to seed as many rows as K at most, but seeding all N rows is simple and still N space; the heap size stays bounded by N because each row contributes one live candidate. The column-sorted property is not needed for correctness here, only the row-sorted property, which is a point interviewers like to probe.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores a fee matrix where moving right along a row or down a column only increases the fee, and the product team needs the Kth smallest fee to set a tier boundary. Scanning and sorting every cell wastes the built-in ordering. This is exactly how Kth Smallest in a Sorted Matrix works: it advances a row-wise K-way merge only K steps.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix is a K-way Merge problem once I notice that each row is already a sorted list. I seed a min-heap with the first element of each row, carrying the value along with its row and column so I can fetch the next element in that row, then I pop K times and after every pop I push the next cell to the right in the same row. The value of the Kth pop is the Kth smallest in the whole matrix.

What I highlight to an interviewer is that only the row-sorted property is required for this approach to be correct; the column-sorted property is a nice bonus the problem gives but my heap merge does not depend on it. The heap holds at most N candidates, one per row, so K pops cost K log N and the space is N. I also seed only up to K rows because no element below row K can be among the first K smallest.

At the National Bank of India I used this on a fee grid where moving right or down only increased the fee, and the product team needed the Kth smallest fee to set a pricing tier boundary. Rather than flattening and sorting every cell, I ran a row-wise K-way merge and stopped at the Kth removal. Explaining that rows are sorted lists, that the column order is not needed for this method, and that the cost is K log N is what shows an interviewer I see the K-way Merge pattern hidden inside a matrix question.

answers.question: Given two sorted arrays, find the median of the combined sorted order. Explain how the K-way Merge pattern locates the middle without fully merging, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Median of Two Sorted Arrays (K-way Merge View of the Middle Element)

s1_definition.profdef: Median of Two Sorted Arrays, viewed through the K-way Merge pattern, advances a two-way merge only up to the middle position rather than merging everything. We keep the two array heads as candidates, repeatedly take the smaller, and stop once we have passed the middle index or indices. For a combined length that is odd the single middle value is the median; for even we average the two middle values. This merge-to-the-middle runs in linear time in the total length.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has two sorted lists of account balances and wants the middle balance of the combined set. A clerk walks both lists together, always taking the smaller next balance, counting steps, and stops at the middle. There is no need to write out the whole combined list.
s1_definition.oneliner: Two-way merge, but stop at the middle position to read off the median.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Median of Two Sorted Arrays, viewed through the K-way Merge pattern, advances a two-way merge only up to the middle position rather than merging everything. We keep the two array heads as candidates, repeatedly take the smaller, and stop once we have passed the middle index or indices. For a combined length that is odd the single middle value is the median; for even we average the two middle values. This merge-to-the-middle runs in linear time in the total length.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has two sorted lists of account balances and wants the middle balance of the combined set. A clerk walks both lists together, always taking the smaller next balance, counting steps, and stops at the middle. There is no need to write out the whole combined list.

**One line to remember:** Two-way merge, but stop at the middle position to read off the median.

sections.s2_technical:
We treat the two arrays as two sorted lists in a K-way merge with K equal to two. We keep an index into each array and compare the current heads, advancing whichever is smaller. We count how many elements we have consumed and keep the last one or two values needed for the median.

For combined length `n`, if `n` is odd the median is the value at consumed position `n/2` (zero-based), and if `n` is even it is the average of the values at positions `n/2 - 1` and `n/2`. We therefore only need to merge up to `n/2` steps and remember the previous value. A concrete comparison is `if (j >= b.length || (i < a.length && a[i] <= b[j])) take a[i++]; else take b[j++];`. Senior nuance: for money we average with BigDecimal to avoid precision loss, and although a full binary-search solution reaches log time, the merge-to-the-middle view is the clear K-way Merge framing and is linear, which is perfectly acceptable to explain in an interview as the pattern-based answer.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps two sorted lists of customer balances from two regions and the analytics team needs the median balance of the two regions combined to report a typical customer. sections.s6_takeaway:
Median of Two Sorted Arrays, framed through the K-way Merge pattern, is a two-way merge that I stop at the middle instead of running to completion. I keep an index into each array, repeatedly take the smaller of the two current heads, and count how many elements I have consumed. Because both arrays are already sorted, walking them together produces the combined order element by element, and I only need to reach the middle position.

For the combined length I decide the median rule up front. If the total is odd, the median is the single value sitting at the middle consumed position. If the total is even, it is the average of the two middle values, so I remember both the previous and the current value as I merge. For balances I average using BigDecimal so I never lose a paisa to floating-point error. This merge-to-the-middle view is linear in the total length, which is a clean and correct pattern answer even though a binary-search version can reach logarithmic time.

At the National Bank of India I used this to report a typical customer balance across two regions whose balance lists were each already sorted. I merged the two lists only as far as the middle and read off the median, averaging with BigDecimal when the combined count was even. Explaining that this is a K-way Merge with K equal to two, that I stop at the middle rather than merging everything, and that I handle odd and even lengths separately is what shows an interviewer I can map a classic median question onto the merge pattern.

answers.question: Given weights and profits of N items, put a subset of these items into a knapsack of capacity C so that the total profit is maximized, where each item can be used at most once. Explain the 0/1 Knapsack dynamic programming pattern, the table, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: 0/1 Knapsack (Maximize Value Within a Weight Capacity, Each Item Once)

s1_definition.profdef: 0/1 Knapsack is the foundational problem of the 0/1 Knapsack dynamic programming pattern. For each item we make a binary choice, include it or skip it, subject to a capacity constraint, and we maximize total value. The standard solution is a two-dimensional table over items and capacities, or a space-optimized one-dimensional array iterated from high capacity down to low so each item is counted once. Time is N times C and optimized space is C.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India gives Rajesh a fixed investment budget. Each investment has a cost and an expected return and he can either buy it once or not at all. He wants the highest total return without exceeding the budget. 0/1 Knapsack decides, for every budget level, the best return achievable, by asking item by item whether including it beats leaving it out.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each item choose include or skip; a table over items and capacity stores the best value.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** 0/1 Knapsack is the foundational problem of the 0/1 Knapsack dynamic programming pattern. For each item we make a binary choice, include it or skip it, subject to a capacity constraint, and we maximize total value. The standard solution is a two-dimensional table over items and capacities, or a space-optimized one-dimensional array iterated from high capacity down to low so each item is counted once. Time is N times C and optimized space is C.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India gives Rajesh a fixed investment budget. Each investment has a cost and an expected return and he can either buy it once or not at all. He wants the highest total return without exceeding the budget. 0/1 Knapsack decides, for every budget level, the best return achievable, by asking item by item whether including it beats leaving it out.

**One line to remember:** For each item choose include or skip; a table over items and capacity stores the best value.

sections.s2_technical:
The recurrence is the heart of the pattern. For item `i` and capacity `c`, the best value is the larger of two options: skip item `i`, giving the best value using earlier items at the same capacity, or include item `i` if it fits, giving its profit plus the best value using earlier items at capacity `c minus weight[i]`. Formally `dp[i][c] = max(dp[i-1][c], profit[i] + dp[i-1][c - weight[i]])` when `weight[i] <= c`.

The space-optimized version keeps a single array `dp[c]` and iterates capacity from high down to low for each item: `for (int c = C; c >= weight[i]; c--) dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], profit[i] + dp[c - weight[i]])`. Iterating downward is essential because it ensures each item is used at most once; iterating upward would allow reusing the same item, which is the unbounded variant. Senior nuance: the answer sits at `dp[C]`, and reconstructing which items were chosen requires either the full two-dimensional table or a parallel record of decisions.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India offers Rajesh a set of one-time investment products, each with a rupee cost and an expected return, and a fixed investment budget. He may buy each product at most once. The advisory engine must pick the subset that maximizes expected return without exceeding the budget. This is exactly how 0/1 Knapsack works: each product is an include-or-skip decision under a capacity limit.

The code defines a `PortfolioKnapsackService` exposing `maxReturn(costs, returns, budget)` that returns the best achievable return. A `Demo` runs it over a small product set and logs the maximum return within budget.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four products with costs 2, 3, 4, 5 and returns 3, 4, 5, 6, and a budget of five. The dp array has indices zero through five, all starting at zero.

Step 1 — Process product zero, cost two, return three. For capacities five down to two we set dp[c] to the better of its current value and three plus dp[c minus two]. Now dp is 0, 0, 3, 3, 3, 3.

Step 2 — Process product one, cost three, return four. Iterating five down to three, dp[5] becomes max of 3 and 4 plus dp[2] which is 4 plus 3 equals 7; dp[4] becomes max of 3 and 4 plus dp[1] equals 4; dp[3] becomes 4. Now dp is 0, 0, 3, 4, 4, 7.

Step 3 — Process product two, cost four, return five. dp[5] becomes max of 7 and 5 plus dp[1] equals 5, stays 7; dp[4] becomes max of 4 and 5 plus dp[0] equals 5. Now dp is 0, 0, 3, 4, 5, 7.

Step 4 — Process product three, cost five, return six. dp[5] becomes max of 7 and 6 plus dp[0] equals 6, stays 7. The array settles.

Step 5 — The best return within budget five is dp[5], which is seven, achieved by buying products zero and one, costing five and returning seven. The output is below.

```
Oct 27, 2026 8:54:10 PM com.bank.portfolio.service.PortfolioKnapsackService maxReturn
INFO: Max return within budget = 7
Oct 27, 2026 8:54:10 PM com.bank.portfolio.PortfolioKnapsackApplication main
INFO: Best expected return within budget 5 lakh: 7 lakh
```

    │ product2 (c4,r5): dp = 0 0 3 4 5 7
    │ product3 (c5,r6): dp = 0 0 3 4 5 7

  Output: best return = 7 lakh

sections.s6_takeaway:
0/1 Knapsack is the foundational problem of the 0/1 Knapsack dynamic programming pattern. Every item presents a binary choice, include it or skip it, under a shared capacity limit, and I maximize total value. The recurrence says the best value for the current item at a given capacity is the larger of skipping it, which keeps the best value from earlier items at that capacity, or including it when it fits, which adds its profit to the best value from earlier items at the reduced capacity.

The detail that proves I understand the pattern is the space optimization. I collapse the table to a single array indexed by capacity and, for each item, I sweep capacity from high down to low. The downward sweep guarantees each item is counted at most once, because when I update a higher capacity I am reading values that have not yet been touched by the current item. Sweeping upward instead would let the same item be reused, which is the unbounded knapsack variant, so the direction of the loop is a deliberate correctness decision, not a style choice.

At the National Bank of India I used this in an advisory engine that picked one-time investment products for a customer like Rajesh, each product having a cost and an expected return, to maximize total return within his budget. I used the one-dimensional array with the downward capacity sweep and read the answer at the full budget. Explaining the include-or-skip recurrence, the N times C cost, and why the high-to-low sweep enforces the use-each-item-once rule is what shows an interviewer that I truly understand 0/1 Knapsack rather than having memorized a loop.

answers.question: Given a set of positive numbers, determine if it can be partitioned into two subsets whose sums are equal. Explain how this reduces to 0/1 Knapsack, the DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Equal Subset Sum Partition (Split an Array into Two Equal-Sum Halves)

s1_definition.profdef: Equal Subset Sum Partition reduces to a 0/1 Knapsack subset-sum feasibility check. If the total sum is odd no equal split exists; otherwise we ask whether some subset sums to exactly half the total. We solve this with a boolean dynamic programming array where each entry says whether that target is reachable. Time is N times sum-over-two and space is sum-over-two.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to divide a pile of equal-priority payouts into two trays of exactly equal rupee value for two tellers. If the total is odd it is impossible. Otherwise the question becomes: can we pick some payouts that add up to exactly half? That picking question is a 0/1 Knapsack subset-sum check.
s1_definition.oneliner: If total is even, ask whether a subset sums to half using a boolean reachability array.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Equal Subset Sum Partition reduces to a 0/1 Knapsack subset-sum feasibility check. If the total sum is odd no equal split exists; otherwise we ask whether some subset sums to exactly half the total. We solve this with a boolean dynamic programming array where each entry says whether that target is reachable. Time is N times sum-over-two and space is sum-over-two.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to divide a pile of equal-priority payouts into two trays of exactly equal rupee value for two tellers. If the total is odd it is impossible. Otherwise the question becomes: can we pick some payouts that add up to exactly half? That picking question is a 0/1 Knapsack subset-sum check.

**One line to remember:** If total is even, ask whether a subset sums to half using a boolean reachability array.

sections.s2_technical:
First compute the total. If it is odd, return false immediately, because two equal integer subsets cannot sum to an odd total. Otherwise the target is total divided by two, and the problem is: does any subset sum to exactly the target?

We use a boolean array `dp[t]` meaning target `t` is achievable using some subset. We start with `dp[0] = true` because the empty subset sums to zero. For each number we sweep targets from high down to low and set `dp[t] = dp[t] || dp[t - num]`. The downward sweep again ensures each number is used at most once, identical to 0/1 Knapsack. A concrete update is `for (int t = target; t >= num; t--) dp[t] = dp[t] || dp[t - num];`. Senior nuance: we can early-exit as soon as `dp[target]` becomes true, and because sums are bounded by the total, the array length is target plus one, which keeps memory modest.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India needs to split a batch of equal-priority payout amounts between two settlement tellers so that each teller handles exactly the same total rupee value, keeping their workloads perfectly balanced. If the total is odd this is impossible, and if it is even we must find a subset that sums to half. This is exactly how Equal Subset Sum Partition works: it is a 0/1 Knapsack subset-sum feasibility test.

The code defines a `PayoutSplitService` exposing `canSplitEqually(amounts)` returning a boolean. A `Demo` runs it over a payout batch and logs whether an equal split is possible.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four payouts 15, 5, 10, 20. The total is fifty, which is even, so the target is twenty-five.

Step 1 — We create a boolean array of length twenty-six, all false except dp[0] which is true. Only the sum zero is reachable with nothing chosen.

Step 2 — Process 15. Sweeping targets twenty-five down to fifteen, dp[15] becomes true because dp[0] is true. Now reachable sums are zero and fifteen.

Step 3 — Process 5. Sweeping down, dp[20] becomes true from dp[15], and dp[5] becomes true from dp[0]. Reachable sums are zero, five, fifteen, twenty.

Step 4 — Process 10. dp[25] becomes true from dp[15], dp[10] from dp[0], and others fill in. As soon as dp[25] turns true we can stop early.

Step 5 — dp[25] is true, meaning a subset sums to exactly twenty-five, for example fifteen plus ten. An equal split between two tellers is possible, shown below.

```

```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Equal Subset Sum Partition is a 0/1 Knapsack problem in disguise. I first compute the total, and if it is odd I return false immediately because two equal integer subsets can never sum to an odd number. If the total is even, the whole question collapses to a single subset-sum feasibility check: can some subset of the numbers add up to exactly half the total?

I answer that with a boolean dynamic programming array where each slot records whether that sum is reachable. I begin with the sum zero reachable via the empty subset, then for each number I sweep the targets from high down to low, marking a target reachable if it was already reachable or if the target minus the current number was reachable. The downward sweep is the same device as in 0/1 Knapsack and guarantees each number is used at most once. I also exit early the moment the half-total becomes reachable.

At the National Bank of India I used this to split a batch of equal-priority payout amounts between two settlement tellers so each handled exactly the same rupee total, keeping their workloads balanced. I checked the total for oddness first, then ran the boolean subset-sum DP toward half the total. Explaining the reduction from partition to subset-sum, the odd-total short-circuit, and the high-to-low sweep that enforces using each payout once is what shows an interviewer that I recognise the 0/1 Knapsack pattern behind a partition question.

answers.question: Given a set of positive numbers, determine if there is a subset whose sum equals a given target S. Explain the 0/1 Knapsack boolean DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Subset Sum (Decide if a Subset Reaches an Exact Target)

s1_definition.profdef: Subset Sum is the pure feasibility core of the 0/1 Knapsack pattern. We ask whether any subset of the numbers adds up to an exact target S. A boolean dynamic programming array marks which sums are reachable, filled by considering each number once. Time is N times S and space is S.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a list of individual transaction amounts and wants to know whether some combination of them exactly matches a disputed figure. Subset Sum checks, without trying every combination by brute force, whether any subset reaches that exact amount.
s1_definition.oneliner: A boolean array over target sums, filled once per number, answers can-we-hit-exactly-S.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Subset Sum is the pure feasibility core of the 0/1 Knapsack pattern. We ask whether any subset of the numbers adds up to an exact target S. A boolean dynamic programming array marks which sums are reachable, filled by considering each number once. Time is N times S and space is S.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a list of individual transaction amounts and wants to know whether some combination of them exactly matches a disputed figure. Subset Sum checks, without trying every combination by brute force, whether any subset reaches that exact amount.

**One line to remember:** A boolean array over target sums, filled once per number, answers can-we-hit-exactly-S.

sections.s2_technical:
We maintain a boolean array `dp[t]` where `t` ranges from zero to the target S, and `dp[t]` is true when some subset sums to `t`. The base case is `dp[0] = true` because choosing nothing sums to zero.

For each number we sweep `t` from S down to the number and set `dp[t] = dp[t] || dp[t - num]`. If `t` was already reachable we keep it, otherwise it becomes reachable when `t - num` was reachable, meaning we add the current number to an existing subset. A concrete update is `for (int t = S; t >= num; t--) dp[t] = dp[t] || dp[t - num];`. The final answer is `dp[S]`.

Senior nuance: the high-to-low sweep is what makes this 0/1 rather than unbounded, because it prevents a single number from being added to itself within the same pass. We can stop early once `dp[S]` is true, and if the target exceeds the total of all numbers we can answer false without any DP.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India investigates a disputed statement where a customer claims a specific total was charged, and the fraud team needs to know whether some subset of the actual individual charges adds up exactly to the disputed figure. Trying every combination explicitly would be far too slow for a long charge list. This is exactly how Subset Sum works: it decides exact reachability with a boolean DP.

The code defines a `DisputeCheckService` exposing `hasSubsetSum(charges, target)` returning a boolean. A `Demo` runs it over a charge list and a disputed target and logs whether the target is reachable.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is four charges 120, 75, 200, 45 with a disputed target of 165.

Step 1 — We build a boolean array of length 166, all false except dp[0] which is true. Only the sum zero is reachable at the start.

Step 2 — Process 120. Sweeping 165 down to 120, dp[120] becomes true from dp[0]. Reachable sums are zero and 120.

Step 3 — Process 75. dp[195] is out of range; within range dp[120 plus 75 equals 195] is skipped, but dp[75] becomes true from dp[0]. Reachable sums are zero, 75, 120.

Step 4 — Process 200. Two hundred exceeds the target range, so the inner loop does nothing because the loop condition t at least 200 never holds within a target of 165. Reachable sums are unchanged.

Step 5 — Process 45. dp[165] becomes true from dp[120], because 120 plus 45 equals 165. We stop early. The disputed figure is exactly reachable as 120 plus 45, shown below.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Subset Sum is the pure feasibility core of the 0/1 Knapsack pattern. The question is simply whether any subset of the given numbers adds up to an exact target, and I answer it with a boolean dynamic programming array where each slot records whether that sum is reachable. I seed the array with the sum zero reachable through the empty subset, then for every number I mark new sums reachable by extending sums that were already reachable with that number added.

The correctness hinge is the sweep direction. I iterate the target from high down to the current number so that, within a single number's pass, I never add that number to a sum it just created, which is what keeps each number usable at most once. This is the identical device that distinguishes 0/1 Knapsack from the unbounded variant. I also exit as soon as the target becomes reachable and I can reject instantly if the target exceeds the total of all numbers.

At the National Bank of India I used this in dispute reconciliation, where a customer claimed a specific total was charged and the fraud team needed to know whether some subset of the real individual charges summed exactly to that disputed figure. I ran the boolean subset-sum DP over the charge list toward the disputed target. Explaining that the answer is reachability rather than value, that the high-to-low sweep enforces using each charge once, and that the cost is N times the target is what shows an interviewer I understand the 0/1 Knapsack feasibility pattern.

answers.question: Given a set of positive numbers, partition them into two subsets so that the absolute difference of their sums is minimized. Return that minimum difference. Explain the 0/1 Knapsack DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Minimum Subset Sum Difference (Split into Two Subsets with the Smallest Difference)

s1_definition.profdef: Minimum Subset Sum Difference is a 0/1 Knapsack optimization. We find the subset sum closest to half the total that does not exceed half, call it `s1`; the other subset then sums to total minus `s1`, and the minimum difference is total minus two times `s1`. We compute all reachable sums up to half the total with a boolean DP and take the largest reachable one. Time is N times sum-over-two and space is sum-over-two.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to divide a pile of payouts between two tellers as evenly as possible, even if a perfectly equal split is impossible. The best we can do is make one tray as close to half the total as we can without going over; the gap between the two trays is then as small as possible.
s1_definition.oneliner: Find the largest reachable subset sum not exceeding half the total; the difference is total minus twice that sum.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Minimum Subset Sum Difference is a 0/1 Knapsack optimization. We find the subset sum closest to half the total that does not exceed half, call it `s1`; the other subset then sums to total minus `s1`, and the minimum difference is total minus two times `s1`. We compute all reachable sums up to half the total with a boolean DP and take the largest reachable one. Time is N times sum-over-two and space is sum-over-two.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to divide a pile of payouts between two tellers as evenly as possible, even if a perfectly equal split is impossible. The best we can do is make one tray as close to half the total as we can without going over; the gap between the two trays is then as small as possible.

**One line to remember:** Find the largest reachable subset sum not exceeding half the total; the difference is total minus twice that sum.

sections.s2_technical:
We compute the total and set the target to total divided by two using integer division. We then find every reachable subset sum from zero up to that target using the same boolean DP as subset sum: `dp[0] = true`, and for each number sweep targets from the target down to the number setting `dp[t] = dp[t] || dp[t - num]`.

After filling the array we scan downward from the target to find the largest `s1` with `dp[s1]` true. The first subset sums to `s1`, the second sums to total minus `s1`, and since `s1` is at most half the total the difference is `total - 2 * s1`, which is non-negative. A concrete scan is `for (int s = target; s >= 0; s--) if (dp[s]) { best = s; break; }`. Senior nuance: picking the largest reachable sum at or below half is what minimizes the difference, and the whole method relies on the fact that every number is positive so sums are monotone and bounded by the total.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must divide a batch of payout amounts between two settlement tellers as evenly as possible to balance their workloads, but a perfectly equal split is often impossible. The operations team needs the split that minimizes the rupee difference between the two tellers. This is exactly how Minimum Subset Sum Difference works: it finds the closest-to-half subset and reports the smallest achievable gap.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Minimum Subset Sum Difference is a 0/1 Knapsack optimization built on the same subset-sum reachability I use for feasibility. I compute the total and aim for half of it, then I find every reachable subset sum from zero up to that half using a boolean dynamic programming array, sweeping each number from high down to low so each number is used once. After filling the array I scan downward from half the total to find the largest reachable sum.

That largest reachable sum at or below half, which I call the first subset's sum, is the key. The second subset must then sum to the total minus that value, and because my chosen sum is at most half, the difference between the two subsets is the total minus twice my chosen sum, which is guaranteed non-negative and as small as possible. Choosing the largest reachable sum not exceeding half is precisely what minimizes the gap, and the whole approach depends on all numbers being positive so sums stay bounded by the total.

At the National Bank of India I used this to divide a batch of payouts between two settlement tellers as evenly as possible, even when a perfectly equal split was impossible, to balance their workloads. I computed all reachable sums up to half the total and picked the closest one, reporting the minimal rupee gap. Explaining that the difference equals the total minus twice the best half-bounded sum, and that this reuses the 0/1 Knapsack reachability DP, is what shows an interviewer I can turn a balancing problem into a knapsack optimization.

answers.question: Given a set of positive numbers, count the number of subsets whose sum equals a given target S. Explain the 0/1 Knapsack counting DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Count of Subset Sum (Count How Many Subsets Reach an Exact Target)

s1_definition.profdef: Count of Subset Sum is the counting variant of the 0/1 Knapsack pattern. Instead of a boolean reachability array we keep an integer count array where each slot holds how many subsets reach that sum. We add counts rather than OR-ing booleans, processing each number once. Time is N times S and space is S.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to know not just whether some combination of charges hits a disputed figure, but how many distinct combinations do. Count of Subset Sum tallies every distinct subset that sums exactly to the target.
s1_definition.oneliner: Replace the boolean OR with integer addition to count subsets that reach the target.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Count of Subset Sum is the counting variant of the 0/1 Knapsack pattern. Instead of a boolean reachability array we keep an integer count array where each slot holds how many subsets reach that sum. We add counts rather than OR-ing booleans, processing each number once. Time is N times S and space is S.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to know not just whether some combination of charges hits a disputed figure, but how many distinct combinations do. Count of Subset Sum tallies every distinct subset that sums exactly to the target.

**One line to remember:** Replace the boolean OR with integer addition to count subsets that reach the target.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep an integer array `dp[t]` meaning the number of subsets that sum to exactly `t`. The base case is `dp[0] = 1` because there is exactly one subset that sums to zero, the empty subset.

For each number we sweep targets from S down to the number and accumulate: `dp[t] += dp[t - num]`. This says every subset that previously summed to `t - num` becomes a subset summing to `t` once we add the current number, so those counts carry over. A concrete update is `for (int t = S; t >= num; t--) dp[t] += dp[t - num];`. The final count sits at `dp[S]`.

Senior nuance: the high-to-low sweep again ensures each number is used at most once, so we count subsets rather than multisets. If counts can be large we use long to avoid overflow, and the same base case `dp[0] = 1` is what seeds the whole count correctly, a detail interviewers often test.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India investigates a disputed figure and the fraud team wants to know how many distinct combinations of the real charges could produce that exact figure, because many combinations means the dispute is ambiguous while a single combination points to one likely set of charges. This is exactly how Count of Subset Sum works: it counts the distinct subsets reaching the target.

The code defines a `CombinationCountService` exposing `countSubsets(charges, target)` returning the number of subsets. A `Demo` runs it over a charge list and a target and logs the count.

The input is charges 1, 1, 2, 3 with a target of four.

Step 1 — We build a long array of length five, with dp[0] equal to one and the rest zero. There is one way to make sum zero, the empty subset.

Step 2 — Process the first 1. Sweeping four down to one, dp[1] gets plus dp[0] becoming one. Counts are dp[0] one, dp[1] one.

Step 3 — Process the second 1. dp[2] gets plus dp[1] becoming one, dp[1] gets plus dp[0] becoming two. Counts are dp[0] one, dp[1] two, dp[2] one.

Step 4 — Process 2. dp[4] gets plus dp[2] becoming one, dp[3] gets plus dp[1] becoming two, dp[2] gets plus dp[0] becoming two. Counts now dp[2] two, dp[3] two, dp[4] one.

Step 5 — Process 3. dp[4] gets plus dp[1] which is two, becoming three, dp[3] gets plus dp[0] becoming three. The final dp[4] is three, meaning three distinct subsets sum to four: the two ones plus the two, the first one plus the three, and the second one plus the three. The output is below.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Count of Subset Sum is the counting variant of the 0/1 Knapsack pattern. Instead of asking whether a target is reachable, I ask how many distinct subsets reach it, so I replace the boolean reachability array with an integer count array. Each slot holds the number of subsets that sum to that value, and the crucial base case is that there is exactly one subset summing to zero, namely the empty subset.

The update changes from a boolean OR to an addition. For each number I sweep the target from high down to the number and add the count at target minus number into the count at target, because every subset that summed to the smaller value becomes a new subset at the larger value once I include the current number. The high-to-low sweep still enforces using each number at most once, so I count genuine subsets rather than multisets, and I use long for the counts to stay safe against overflow when the input is large.

At the National Bank of India I used this in dispute analysis, where it was not enough to know that some combination of charges hit a disputed figure; the fraud team needed to know how many distinct combinations did, because a single combination points to one likely explanation while many combinations mean the dispute is ambiguous. I ran the counting DP toward the disputed target. Explaining that the only changes from feasibility are the integer counts, the addition instead of OR, and the base count of one for the empty subset is what shows an interviewer I understand the counting flavour of 0/1 Knapsack.

answers.question: Given a set of positive numbers and a target T, assign a plus or minus sign to each number so that the signed total equals T, and count the number of ways to do so. Explain how this reduces to Count of Subset Sum, the DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Target Sum (Assign Plus and Minus Signs to Reach a Target)

s1_definition.profdef: Target Sum reduces to the counting variant of 0/1 Knapsack. Splitting the numbers into a positive group P and a negative group N, we have P minus N equal to T and P plus N equal to the total, so P equals the total plus T over two. We then count the subsets summing to that derived target with a counting DP. Time is N times the derived target and space is the derived target.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a set of adjustments, each of which can be applied as a credit or a debit, and wants to count how many sign assignments produce a required net effect. By algebra this becomes counting how many subsets form the positive group, which is a 0/1 Knapsack counting problem.
s1_definition.oneliner: Signs turn into a subset: count subsets summing to (total plus target) over two.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Target Sum reduces to the counting variant of 0/1 Knapsack. Splitting the numbers into a positive group P and a negative group N, we have P minus N equal to T and P plus N equal to the total, so P equals the total plus T over two. We then count the subsets summing to that derived target with a counting DP. Time is N times the derived target and space is the derived target.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a set of adjustments, each of which can be applied as a credit or a debit, and wants to count how many sign assignments produce a required net effect. By algebra this becomes counting how many subsets form the positive group, which is a 0/1 Knapsack counting problem.

**One line to remember:** Signs turn into a subset: count subsets summing to (total plus target) over two.

sections.s2_technical:
The algebra is the whole trick. Let P be the sum of numbers we mark positive and N the sum we mark negative. We need P minus N equal to T, and we know P plus N equals the total S. Adding the two equations gives two P equal to S plus T, so P equals S plus T over two. Counting sign assignments that reach T is therefore counting subsets whose sum is exactly P.

Two guards are required. If S plus T is odd, P is not an integer and the answer is zero. If the absolute value of T exceeds S, no assignment can reach T and the answer is zero. Otherwise we run Count of Subset Sum toward the derived target P: `dp[0] = 1`, and for each number sweep high to low with `dp[t] += dp[t - num]`. Senior nuance: handling zeros carefully matters because a zero can be signed either way yet maps to the same subset, but for strictly positive inputs the clean reduction holds and the derived-target counting DP gives the answer directly.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India applies a set of fixed adjustment amounts to an account, and each adjustment can be posted as a credit or a debit. The reconciliation team wants to count how many ways the signs can be chosen so that the net effect equals a required target. This is exactly how Target Sum works: by algebra it becomes counting subsets that form the positive group.

The code defines a `SignAssignmentService` exposing `countWays(amounts, target)` returning the number of valid sign assignments. A `Demo` runs it over a set of adjustments and a target and logs the count.

Target Sum looks like a sign-assignment problem but reduces cleanly to the counting variant of 0/1 Knapsack. I split the numbers into a positive group and a negative group. Their difference must equal the target and their sum must equal the total, so by adding those two equations the positive group's sum is the total plus the target, all divided by two. When the guards pass I run the same counting DP as Count of Subset Sum toward the derived target, seeding one subset for the sum zero and sweeping each number high to low so each is used once.

At the National Bank of India I used this during reconciliation, where each fixed adjustment could be posted as a credit or a debit and the team needed to count how many sign choices produced a required net effect on the account. I derived the positive-group target by algebra and counted the subsets reaching it. answers.question: Given weights and profits of N items and a knapsack capacity C, maximize total profit where each item can be used any number of times. Explain the Unbounded Knapsack dynamic programming pattern, how it differs from 0/1, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Unbounded Knapsack (Maximize Value with Unlimited Copies of Each Item)

s1_definition.profdef: Unbounded Knapsack is the foundational problem of the Unbounded Knapsack pattern, where each item may be chosen unlimited times. It uses the same capacity-indexed DP as 0/1 Knapsack but sweeps capacity from low to high, which deliberately permits reusing an item within the same pass. Time is N times C and space is C.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India offers investment instruments that Rajesh can buy repeatedly, as many units of each as he likes, up to his budget. He wants the highest total return. Unbounded Knapsack decides the best return for each budget level while allowing the same instrument to be bought over and over.
s1_definition.oneliner: Same table as 0/1 Knapsack, but sweep capacity low to high so items can repeat.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Unbounded Knapsack is the foundational problem of the Unbounded Knapsack pattern, where each item may be chosen unlimited times. It uses the same capacity-indexed DP as 0/1 Knapsack but sweeps capacity from low to high, which deliberately permits reusing an item within the same pass. Time is N times C and space is C.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India offers investment instruments that Rajesh can buy repeatedly, as many units of each as he likes, up to his budget. He wants the highest total return. Unbounded Knapsack decides the best return for each budget level while allowing the same instrument to be bought over and over.

**One line to remember:** Same table as 0/1 Knapsack, but sweep capacity low to high so items can repeat.

sections.s2_technical:
The recurrence allows reuse. For capacity `c`, the best value is the larger of not adding the current item, keeping the best from processing earlier items at `c`, or adding one more copy of the current item if it fits, giving its profit plus the best value at `c minus weight[i]` where that inner value may already include the same item.

The one-dimensional form is `for (int c = weight[i]; c <= C; c++) dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], profit[i] + dp[c - weight[i]])`. The direction is the only difference from 0/1 Knapsack: here we sweep capacity upward so that when we read `dp[c - weight[i]]` it may already have counted the current item, which is exactly what enables unlimited copies. A concrete step: if a product costs two and we are at capacity six, `dp[6]` can build on `dp[4]` that already used that same product. Senior nuance: looping items on the outside and capacity on the inside, upward, is one clean formulation; an alternative loops capacity outside and items inside, both correct, and interviewers appreciate knowing why the sweep direction flips relative to 0/1.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India offers Rajesh investment instruments he can buy in unlimited units, each with a unit cost and a unit return, up to a fixed budget. The advisory engine must maximize total return while allowing repeated purchases of the best instruments. This is exactly how Unbounded Knapsack works: each instrument is an unlimited-use item under a capacity limit.

The code defines an `UnboundedPortfolioService` exposing `maxReturn(costs, returns, budget)` returning the best achievable return with repetition. A `Demo` runs it over a small instrument set and logs the maximum return.

The input is three instruments with costs 1, 3, 4 and unit returns 15, 50, 60 and a budget of eight. The dp array spans indices zero through eight, all zero to start.

Step 4 — After all instruments, dp[8] holds the best achievable return for budget eight, mixing repeated units optimally.

Step 5 — The best return within budget eight is dp[8], which comes out to 125, achieved by buying instruments that repeat the strong fifty-return item. The output is below.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Unbounded Knapsack is the foundational problem of the Unbounded Knapsack pattern, where I may choose each item as many times as I like. The surprising part for many candidates is how little the code changes from 0/1 Knapsack. I still keep a capacity-indexed array and ask, for each item, whether adding one more copy beats leaving it. The single meaningful difference is the direction of the capacity sweep.

In 0/1 Knapsack I sweep capacity from high down to low so an item cannot be reused within its pass. In Unbounded Knapsack I sweep from low up to high precisely so that when I read the best value at the reduced capacity, that value may already include a copy of the same item, which is what lets the item repeat. So the loop direction is not cosmetic; it is the exact lever that switches between use-once and use-unlimited, and being able to explain that flip is what signals real understanding.

At the National Bank of India I used this in an advisory engine for instruments that a customer like Rajesh could buy in unlimited units, each with a unit cost and unit return, to maximize total return within a budget. I ran the capacity-indexed DP with the upward sweep and read the answer at the full budget. Explaining the shared recurrence with 0/1 Knapsack and why reversing the sweep direction enables repetition is what shows an interviewer I understand the Unbounded Knapsack pattern deeply rather than memorizing two separate loops.

answers.question: Given a rod of length N and a list of prices for each length, cut the rod into pieces to maximize total revenue, where each length can be used any number of times. Explain how this is an Unbounded Knapsack, the DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Rod Cutting (Maximize Revenue by Cutting a Rod into Pieces)

s1_definition.profdef: Rod Cutting is an Unbounded Knapsack problem where the capacity is the rod length, each cut length is an item with its length as weight and its price as value, and lengths may be reused. We fill a length-indexed DP sweeping low to high and the answer is the best revenue for the full length. Time is N squared in the common formulation and space is N.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India holds a fixed-term deposit of a certain duration and can break it into sub-terms, each sub-term paying a known rate. The bank wants to split the term to maximize total interest, reusing profitable sub-terms as often as they fit. Rod Cutting maximizes that total.
s1_definition.oneliner: Lengths are unlimited-use items; maximize revenue for the full length with an upward DP sweep.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Rod Cutting is an Unbounded Knapsack problem where the capacity is the rod length, each cut length is an item with its length as weight and its price as value, and lengths may be reused. We fill a length-indexed DP sweeping low to high and the answer is the best revenue for the full length. Time is N squared in the common formulation and space is N.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India holds a fixed-term deposit of a certain duration and can break it into sub-terms, each sub-term paying a known rate. The bank wants to split the term to maximize total interest, reusing profitable sub-terms as often as they fit. Rod Cutting maximizes that total.

**One line to remember:** Lengths are unlimited-use items; maximize revenue for the full length with an upward DP sweep.

sections.s2_technical:
We model each available length `len` with price `price[len]` as an item whose weight is `len` and whose value is `price[len]`. Because any length can be cut repeatedly, this is Unbounded Knapsack with capacity equal to the rod length N.

The one-dimensional DP is `dp[0] = 0`, and for each length `len` we sweep capacity from `len` up to N with `dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], price[len] + dp[c - len])`. The upward sweep lets us reuse the same length many times, so a rod can be cut into several identical profitable pieces. A concrete step: if length three sells for nine and we are at total length six, `dp[6]` can build on `dp[3]` that already used a length-three piece, giving two such pieces. Senior nuance: the answer is `dp[N]`, and reconstructing the actual cuts needs a parallel record of which length improved each capacity, which is useful when the business wants the cut plan, not just the revenue.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India holds a fixed-term deposit of a whole-number duration and can split it into sub-terms, each sub-term paying a published interest amount for that length. The treasury team wants to split the full term to maximize total interest, and the same profitable sub-term length can be reused as many times as it fits. This is exactly how Rod Cutting works: it is Unbounded Knapsack over lengths.

The code defines a `TermSplitService` exposing `maxRevenue(prices, length)` where `prices[i]` is the interest for a sub-term of length `i`, returning the best total interest. A `Demo` runs it over a price list and a term length and logs the maximum interest.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Rod Cutting is an Unbounded Knapsack problem once I map each available length to an item whose weight is that length and whose value is its price, with the rod length playing the role of capacity. Because any length can be cut as many times as it fits, the item is reusable, which is the defining feature of the unbounded pattern.

I fill a length-indexed array where each entry is the best revenue achievable for that total length. For each available length I sweep the capacity from that length up to the full length, taking the better of the current best or the price of this length plus the best revenue for the remaining length. The upward sweep is what lets the same profitable length appear several times in one rod, so the rod can be cut into multiple identical pieces when that maximizes revenue. The answer sits at the full length, and if the business needs the actual cut plan I keep a parallel record of which length improved each capacity.

At the National Bank of India I used this to split a fixed-term deposit into sub-terms, each paying a published interest for its length, to maximize total interest, reusing the most profitable sub-term length as often as it fit. I ran the length-indexed unbounded DP and read the answer at the full term. Explaining the mapping from lengths to reusable items, the upward sweep that enables repetition, and how to reconstruct the cuts is what shows an interviewer that I recognise Rod Cutting as a direct instance of Unbounded Knapsack.

answers.question: Given coin denominations and a total amount, count the number of distinct combinations that make up that amount, where each denomination can be used unlimited times. Explain the Unbounded Knapsack counting DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Coin Change — Number of Ways (Count Combinations to Make an Amount)

s1_definition.profdef: Coin Change number of ways is the counting variant of the Unbounded Knapsack pattern. We count combinations, not permutations, by looping denominations on the outside and amounts on the inside so each coin type is considered once as a layer. The count array accumulates the number of ways to form each amount. Time is denominations times amount and space is amount.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to know how many distinct ways a cash dispenser can make a requested amount using available note denominations, where each note type is unlimited. Coin Change counts those distinct combinations.
s1_definition.oneliner: Loop coins outside, amounts inside, and add counts to count combinations with unlimited coins.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Coin Change number of ways is the counting variant of the Unbounded Knapsack pattern. We count combinations, not permutations, by looping denominations on the outside and amounts on the inside so each coin type is considered once as a layer. The count array accumulates the number of ways to form each amount. Time is denominations times amount and space is amount.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to know how many distinct ways a cash dispenser can make a requested amount using available note denominations, where each note type is unlimited. Coin Change counts those distinct combinations.

**One line to remember:** Loop coins outside, amounts inside, and add counts to count combinations with unlimited coins.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep an integer array `dp[a]` meaning the number of distinct combinations that form amount `a`. The base case is `dp[0] = 1` because there is exactly one way to make zero, using no coins.

The loop order is the critical detail. We put the coins in the outer loop and the amounts in the inner loop, sweeping amounts from the coin value up to the target: `for (int coin : coins) for (int a = coin; a <= amount; a++) dp[a] += dp[a - coin];`. Processing one coin type fully before moving to the next is what counts combinations rather than permutations, because we never revisit an earlier coin type after moving on, so order of coins does not create duplicate counts. Senior nuance: if we instead put amounts outside and coins inside we would count ordered sequences, which is a different question; this loop-order distinction is one of the most commonly tested points in interviews, and we use long if counts can be large.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India operates cash dispensers and the operations team wants to know how many distinct combinations of available note denominations can make up a requested withdrawal amount, which helps them understand flexibility and plan note stocking. Each note denomination is effectively unlimited in stock. This is exactly how Coin Change number of ways works: it counts combinations under an unbounded supply.

The code defines a `DispenserCombinationService` exposing `countWays(denominations, amount)` returning the number of combinations. A `Demo` runs it over note denominations and a withdrawal amount and logs the count.

The input is note denominations 1, 2, 5 and a requested amount of five.

Step 1 — We build a long array of length six with dp[0] equal to one and the rest zero. There is one way to make zero.

Step 2 — Process note one. Sweeping one up to five, each dp[a] gets plus dp[a minus one], so every amount becomes reachable in exactly one way using only ones. Now dp is 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1.

Step 3 — Process note two. Sweeping two up to five, dp[2] gets plus dp[0] becoming two, dp[3] gets plus dp[1] becoming two, dp[4] gets plus dp[2] becoming three, dp[5] gets plus dp[3] becoming three. Now dp is 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3.

Step 4 — Process note five. Sweeping five up to five, dp[5] gets plus dp[0] becoming four. Now dp[5] is four.

Step 5 — There are four distinct combinations to make five: five ones, one two plus three ones, two twos plus one one, and one five. The output is below.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Coin Change number of ways is the counting variant of the Unbounded Knapsack pattern, and the subtle point an interviewer always looks for is the loop order. I keep an integer array where each slot counts the distinct combinations that form that amount, seeded with one way to make zero using no coins. Then I put the coin denominations in the outer loop and the amounts in the inner loop.

Processing one coin type completely before moving to the next is exactly what makes me count combinations rather than permutations. Because I never return to an earlier coin type once I advance, two combinations that use the same coins in a different order are never counted twice. If I reversed the loops, placing amounts outside and coins inside, I would count ordered sequences, which answers a different question entirely. The amounts sweep upward from the coin value, which also reflects the unbounded supply of each denomination.

At the National Bank of India I used this for cash dispensers, where the operations team wanted to know how many distinct combinations of available note denominations could make a requested withdrawal, to understand dispensing flexibility and plan note stocking. I ran the counting DP with coins outside and amounts inside. Explaining the base case of one way to make zero, the coins-outer loop order that counts combinations, and why reversing the loops would count permutations is what shows an interviewer I understand this classic Unbounded Knapsack counting problem precisely.

answers.question: Given coin denominations and a total amount, find the minimum number of coins needed to make that amount, where each denomination can be used unlimited times. Return minus one if it cannot be made. Explain the Unbounded Knapsack minimization DP technique, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Minimum Coin Change (Fewest Coins to Make an Amount)

s1_definition.profdef: Minimum Coin Change is the minimization variant of the Unbounded Knapsack pattern. We fill an array where each slot holds the fewest coins to form that amount, initialized to an impossible-high sentinel, and for each amount we try every coin and take the best. If the final slot is still the sentinel the amount is unreachable. Time is amount times denominations and space is amount.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants its cash dispenser to hand out a requested amount using as few notes as possible, which keeps the dispenser efficient and the customer's wallet tidy. Minimum Coin Change computes that fewest-note count.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fill each amount with the fewest coins by trying every denomination and taking one plus the best remainder.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Minimum Coin Change is the minimization variant of the Unbounded Knapsack pattern. We fill an array where each slot holds the fewest coins to form that amount, initialized to an impossible-high sentinel, and for each amount we try every coin and take the best. If the final slot is still the sentinel the amount is unreachable. Time is amount times denominations and space is amount.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants its cash dispenser to hand out a requested amount using as few notes as possible, which keeps the dispenser efficient and the customer's wallet tidy. Minimum Coin Change computes that fewest-note count.

**One line to remember:** Fill each amount with the fewest coins by trying every denomination and taking one plus the best remainder.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep an array `dp[a]` meaning the fewest coins to form amount `a`. We initialize every slot to a sentinel larger than any real answer, such as amount plus one, and set `dp[0] = 0` because zero needs no coins.

For each amount from one to the target we try each coin that fits and take `dp[a] = Math.min(dp[a], 1 + dp[a - coin])`, meaning one coin of that denomination plus the best way to make the remainder. A concrete step: to make amount six with a coin of value four, consider one coin plus the fewest coins for amount two. After filling, if `dp[amount]` still holds the sentinel the amount cannot be formed and we return minus one. Senior nuance: this is a minimization over an unbounded supply, so the amount loop can be outer and the coin loop inner without worrying about combination versus permutation, because we are taking a minimum rather than counting; the greedy largest-coin-first approach can fail for arbitrary denominations, which is why the DP is necessary.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants its cash dispensers to use the fewest notes possible when dispensing a requested amount, which reduces mechanical wear and gives the customer fewer notes to handle. A naive largest-note-first greedy can fail for some denomination sets, dispensing more notes than necessary or getting stuck. This is exactly how Minimum Coin Change works: a DP that always finds the true minimum.

The code defines a `MinNotesService` exposing `minCoins(denominations, amount)` returning the fewest notes, or minus one if impossible. A `Demo` runs it over note denominations and an amount and logs the fewest-note count.

The input is note denominations 1, 3, 5 and an amount of seven.

Step 1 — We create an array of length eight filled with the sentinel eight, then set dp[0] to zero. Only amount zero has a known fewest-note count.

Step 2 — For amount one, only note one fits, so dp[1] becomes one plus dp[0] equals one. For amount two, dp[2] becomes one plus dp[1] equals two.

Step 3 — For amount three, note one gives one plus dp[2] equals three, and note three gives one plus dp[0] equals one, so dp[3] is one. For amount four, note one gives one plus dp[3] equals two, note three gives one plus dp[1] equals two, so dp[4] is two.

Step 4 — For amount five, note five gives one plus dp[0] equals one, so dp[5] is one. For amount six, note three gives one plus dp[3] equals two, so dp[6] is two.

Recomputing: dp[7] is the minimum over note one giving one plus dp[6] equals three, note three giving one plus dp[4] equals three, note five giving one plus dp[2] equals three. So the fewest notes for seven is three, for example five plus one plus one, or three plus three plus one. The output is below.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Minimum Coin Change is the minimization flavour of the Unbounded Knapsack pattern. I keep an array where each slot stores the fewest coins needed to form that amount, and I initialize every slot to a sentinel larger than any possible real answer, except the amount zero which needs zero coins. This sentinel lets me distinguish an amount that genuinely cannot be formed from one that simply needs many coins.

For each amount I try every denomination that fits and take the minimum of the current value and one plus the fewest coins for the remaining amount after using that denomination. Because the supply is unlimited and I am taking a minimum rather than counting, I do not have to worry about the combination-versus-permutation loop-order subtlety that the counting version has. After filling the table, if the target slot still holds the sentinel I return minus one. I always reach for the DP rather than a greedy largest-coin-first rule, because greedy can fail for arbitrary denomination sets.

At the National Bank of India I used this so cash dispensers handed out a requested amount using the fewest notes, reducing mechanical wear and giving customers fewer notes to carry. I ran the minimization DP with a sentinel initialization and returned minus one when an amount could not be formed from the available denominations. Explaining the sentinel, the one-plus-best-remainder recurrence, and why greedy is unsafe for general denominations is what shows an interviewer I understand the minimization form of Unbounded Knapsack.
