answers.question: Given two strings, find the length of the longest substring that appears in both, where a substring must be contiguous. Explain the Longest Common Substring DP pattern, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Longest Common Substring (Longest Contiguous Run Shared by Two Strings)

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Common Substring is the foundational problem of the Longest Common Substring pattern. We fill a two dimensional table where an entry holds the length of the common contiguous run ending at a given pair of positions: when the current characters match the entry is one plus the diagonal neighbour, and when they differ the entry resets to zero because contiguity is broken. We track the maximum entry. This runs in quadratic time and space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India compares two transaction narration strings to find the longest identical unbroken phrase they share, because a long shared phrase suggests the two narrations came from the same automated source. Rajesh and Priya each have a narration, and the bank measures their longest shared run.
s1_definition.oneliner: On a match the run extends from the diagonal by one, and on a mismatch it resets to zero.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Common Substring is the foundational problem of the Longest Common Substring pattern. We fill a two dimensional table where an entry holds the length of the common contiguous run ending at a given pair of positions: when the current characters match the entry is one plus the diagonal neighbour, and when they differ the entry resets to zero because contiguity is broken. We track the maximum entry. This runs in quadratic time and space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India compares two transaction narration strings to find the longest identical unbroken phrase they share, because a long shared phrase suggests the two narrations came from the same automated source. Rajesh and Priya each have a narration, and the bank measures their longest shared run.

**One line to remember:** On a match the run extends from the diagonal by one, and on a mismatch it resets to zero.

sections.s2_technical:
We define the table entry for positions i and j as the length of the longest common substring that ends exactly at character i of the first string and character j of the second string. When those two characters are equal, the run is one longer than the run ending at the previous pair, which is the diagonal cell, so the entry is one plus that diagonal value. When they differ, no common run can end here because a substring must be contiguous, so the entry resets to zero. The answer is the largest value anywhere in the table.

Bottom-up: `for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) { if (a.charAt(i-1) == b.charAt(j-1)) { dp[i][j] = 1 + dp[i-1][j-1]; best = Math.max(best, dp[i][j]); } else dp[i][j] = 0; }`. A concrete check: comparing SALARYPAY and MYSALARY, the longest shared run SALARY has length six. Senior nuance: this is quadratic in time and space, it differs sharply from the subsequence version because a mismatch resets rather than carrying forward, and a rolling two-row array reduces space to linear.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India compares two transaction narration strings to find the longest identical unbroken phrase they share, because a long shared contiguous phrase is a strong signal that both narrations were produced by the same automated upstream system during a reconciliation check. Comparing all substrings directly is cubic or worse. This is exactly how the Longest Common Substring works: it finds the longest shared contiguous run in quadratic time with the extend-on-match, reset-on-mismatch recurrence.

The inputs are SALARYPAY and MYSALARY. We want the longest contiguous run they share.

```
  ── State: dp[i][j] run ending at pair, best tracked ──────
  mismatch resets, match extends diagonal

  Contract for longestSharedRun(a, b):
    Pre:  a and b not null
    Post: length of longest shared contiguous run
    Quadratic time, linear space with rolling rows
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Longest Common Substring is the foundational problem of the Longest Common Substring pattern, and the mental model I use is a two dimensional grid where I align one string down the rows and the other across the columns. Each cell holds the length of the common contiguous run that ends exactly at that pair of characters. When the two characters match, the run is one longer than the diagonally previous run, so the cell is one plus the diagonal value. When they differ, contiguity is broken and the cell resets to zero.

Because a common substring can end anywhere, the answer is not in a corner but is the maximum value found anywhere in the table, which I track as I fill it. This runs in quadratic time and space, and I can drop the space to linear with two rolling rows. The point I always stress is that the reset on mismatch is what distinguishes the substring version from the subsequence version, where a mismatch carries the better neighbour forward instead of resetting.

At the National Bank of India I used this during reconciliation to compare two transaction narration strings and find the longest identical unbroken phrase, because a long shared contiguous phrase strongly suggested both narrations came from the same automated upstream system. I filled the run table and tracked the maximum. Explaining the extend-on-match, reset-on-mismatch recurrence, the fact that the answer is the table maximum rather than a corner, and the contrast with the subsequence version is what shows an interviewer I understand the Longest Common Substring pattern.

answers.shortTitle: Longest Common Subsequence (Longest Ordered Sequence Shared by Two Strings)

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Common Subsequence is the subsequence form of the Longest Common Substring pattern. We fill a two dimensional table where an entry is the length of the longest common subsequence of the two prefixes: on a character match it is one plus the diagonal, and on a mismatch it carries forward the better of the cell above or the cell to the left. The answer sits in the far corner. This runs in quadratic time and space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India compares a customer's historical spending category sequence against a reference lifestyle pattern to see how closely they align in order, allowing gaps. The longest in-order overlap, even with skipped items, measures the similarity.
s1_definition.oneliner: On a match add one to the diagonal, on a mismatch keep the larger of the top or left neighbour.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Common Subsequence is the subsequence form of the Longest Common Substring pattern. We fill a two dimensional table where an entry is the length of the longest common subsequence of the two prefixes: on a character match it is one plus the diagonal, and on a mismatch it carries forward the better of the cell above or the cell to the left. The answer sits in the far corner. This runs in quadratic time and space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India compares a customer's historical spending category sequence against a reference lifestyle pattern to see how closely they align in order, allowing gaps. The longest in-order overlap, even with skipped items, measures the similarity.

**One line to remember:** On a match add one to the diagonal, on a mismatch keep the larger of the top or left neighbour.

sections.s2_technical:
We define the table entry for prefixes of length i and j as the length of the longest common subsequence of those prefixes. When the current characters match, that shared character extends the best subsequence of the shorter prefixes, so the entry is one plus the diagonal cell. When they differ, the last character of one prefix cannot help, so we take the better of dropping it, which is the cell above, or dropping the other, which is the cell to the left. Unlike the substring version, a mismatch never resets, it carries the best result forward.

Bottom-up: `for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i-1) == b.charAt(j-1) ? 1 + dp[i-1][j-1] : Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);` and the answer is `dp[m][n]`. A concrete check: comparing GROCERY and GAMERY the longest common subsequence is GRY or GEY of length three. Senior nuance: this is quadratic in time and space, the answer is in the corner because a subsequence can span the whole prefixes, and you reconstruct the actual subsequence by walking back from the corner following matches and the larger neighbour.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India compares a customer's historical spending category sequence against a reference lifestyle pattern to measure how closely the customer's ordering of categories aligns with the pattern, allowing skipped categories, because a strong ordered overlap feeds a lifestyle segmentation model. Checking every subsequence is exponential. This is exactly how the Longest Common Subsequence works: it finds the longest in-order overlap in quadratic time with the match-extends-diagonal, mismatch-keeps-best recurrence.

The inputs are GROCERY and GAMERY. We want the longest in-order overlap allowing gaps.

Step 1 — We align GROCERY down the rows and GAMERY across the columns, with the border cells all zero.

Step 2 — The leading G matches G, so that cell becomes one plus its zero diagonal, giving one. This one propagates rightward and downward as a carried best.

Step 3 — Later the R in GROCERY meets the R in GAMERY and matches, extending a diagonal to two where the preceding G overlap was one.

Step 4 — The E meets E and the Y meets Y, each matching and extending the carried best. Mismatched cells in between simply keep the larger of their top or left neighbour, never resetting.

Step 5 — The corner cell ends at three, the length of an overlap such as G, then R or E, then Y. The answer is three. The output is below.

answers.question: Given two strings, find the minimum number of deletions and insertions needed to transform the first string into the second, using only deletions and insertions. Explain how the Longest Common Substring pattern solves it through the longest common subsequence, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Minimum Deletions and Insertions to Transform One String into Another

s1_definition.profdef: Minimum Deletions and Insertions to Transform One String into Another is solved with the Longest Common Substring pattern through the longest common subsequence. The shared subsequence is kept, every character of the first string outside it is deleted, and every character of the second string outside it is inserted. So deletions equal the first length minus the common subsequence, and insertions equal the second length minus the common subsequence. This runs in quadratic time and space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India migrates an old account label into a new standard label and wants to know the fewest removals and additions to convert one into the other. Whatever the two labels share in order is kept, the rest of the old label is deleted, and the missing parts of the new label are inserted.
s1_definition.oneliner: Deletions equal first length minus common subsequence, insertions equal second length minus common subsequence.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Minimum Deletions and Insertions to Transform One String into Another is solved with the Longest Common Substring pattern through the longest common subsequence. The shared subsequence is kept, every character of the first string outside it is deleted, and every character of the second string outside it is inserted. So deletions equal the first length minus the common subsequence, and insertions equal the second length minus the common subsequence. This runs in quadratic time and space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India migrates an old account label into a new standard label and wants to know the fewest removals and additions to convert one into the other. Whatever the two labels share in order is kept, the rest of the old label is deleted, and the missing parts of the new label are inserted.

**One line to remember:** Deletions equal first length minus common subsequence, insertions equal second length minus common subsequence.

sections.s2_technical:
The key realisation is that any character belonging to the longest common subsequence can stay in place during the transformation, because it appears in both strings in the same relative order. Every character of the first string that is not part of that shared subsequence must be deleted, and every character of the second string that is not part of it must be inserted. So the number of deletions is the length of the first string minus the common subsequence length, and the number of insertions is the length of the second string minus the common subsequence length.

We compute the longest common subsequence with the standard prefix table: `for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i-1) == b.charAt(j-1) ? 1 + dp[i-1][j-1] : Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);` then deletions are `m - dp[m][n]` and insertions are `n - dp[m][n]`. A concrete check: turning a six-character label into a five-character label with a four-character shared subsequence needs two deletions and one insertion. Senior nuance: this is quadratic in time and space, it uses only deletions and insertions so it is simpler than full edit distance that also allows substitution, and both answers come from the single common subsequence value.
sections.s3_banking:

Trying all edit sequences is exponential. This is exactly how Minimum Deletions and Insertions works: it computes the longest common subsequence with the Longest Common Substring pattern and derives both counts from it.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Minimum Deletions and Insertions to Transform One String into Another is a neat application of the Longest Common Substring pattern through its subsequence form. The insight is that any character belonging to the longest common subsequence of the two strings can remain untouched during the transformation, because it already appears in both strings in the same relative order. Everything else in the first string has to be deleted, and everything missing from the second string has to be inserted.

So I compute the longest common subsequence once with the standard prefix table, and then the number of deletions is the first string's length minus that shared length, while the number of insertions is the second string's length minus the same shared length. Both answers fall out of a single quadratic time and space computation. I usually point out that because this problem allows only deletions and insertions, not substitutions, it is simpler than the full edit distance and maps directly onto the common subsequence.

At the National Bank of India I used this while migrating old account labels into a new standard scheme, where the team needed the fewest removals and additions to convert each old label into its new form. I computed the longest common subsequence and derived both counts from it. Explaining that the shared subsequence stays, the extra old characters are deleted, the missing new characters are inserted, and that both numbers come from one common subsequence value is what shows an interviewer I understand this use of the Longest Common Substring pattern.

answers.question: Given an array of numbers, find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence, where a subsequence keeps relative order but need not be contiguous. Explain the Longest Common Substring pattern connection, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Longest Increasing Subsequence (Longest Strictly Rising Ordered Subsequence)

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Increasing Subsequence belongs to the Longest Common Substring family of subsequence dynamic programs. We define, for each index, the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends at that index, built from the best earlier index holding a smaller value. The answer is the maximum over all indices. The simple recurrence is quadratic, and a patience-sorting variant reaches order n log n.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India looks at a customer's monthly closing balances and finds the longest stretch of months, not necessarily consecutive, where the balance kept strictly rising, because a long rising streak signals steady financial health. Rajesh's balances are scanned to find that longest rising subsequence.
s1_definition.oneliner: The best increasing run ending at an index is one plus the best run ending at any earlier smaller value.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Increasing Subsequence belongs to the Longest Common Substring family of subsequence dynamic programs. We define, for each index, the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends at that index, built from the best earlier index holding a smaller value. The answer is the maximum over all indices. The simple recurrence is quadratic, and a patience-sorting variant reaches order n log n.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India looks at a customer's monthly closing balances and finds the longest stretch of months, not necessarily consecutive, where the balance kept strictly rising, because a long rising streak signals steady financial health. Rajesh's balances are scanned to find that longest rising subsequence.

**One line to remember:** The best increasing run ending at an index is one plus the best run ending at any earlier smaller value.

sections.s2_technical:
We define a length array where the entry at index i is the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence that ends with the element at i. Every element alone is a subsequence of length one, so we seed each entry with one. For each i we look back at every earlier index j: if the value at j is strictly less than the value at i, the subsequence ending at j can be extended by the element at i, so the entry at i becomes the larger of itself and one plus the entry at j. The answer is the maximum entry overall, since an increasing subsequence can end anywhere.

Bottom-up: `int[] len = new int[n]; Arrays.fill(len, 1); int best = n == 0 ? 0 : 1; for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) if (a[j] < a[i]) { len[i] = Math.max(len[i], len[j] + 1); best = Math.max(best, len[i]); }`. A concrete check: for balances two, nine, three, six, five, eight, the longest increasing subsequence is two, three, six, eight of length four. Senior nuance: the naive form is quadratic in time, the patience-sorting method with binary search over a tails array is order n log n, and this is a subsequence pattern cousin of longest common subsequence.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India reviews a customer's monthly closing balances and wants the longest stretch of months, not necessarily consecutive, where the balance kept strictly rising, because a long rising streak is a positive signal in a financial health score. Enumerating every subsequence is exponential. This is exactly how the Longest Increasing Subsequence works: it finds that longest rising run with the best-earlier-smaller recurrence.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Longest Increasing Subsequence is a subsequence dynamic program in the same family as longest common subsequence, and the way I frame it is per ending index. For each index I compute the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence that ends exactly at that element. Every element alone is a subsequence of length one, and to extend I look back at every earlier index holding a strictly smaller value, because the rising run that ends there can be continued by the current element.

So the length ending at an index is one plus the best length ending at any earlier smaller value, and since an increasing subsequence can finish anywhere, the final answer is the maximum length over all indices rather than the last one. The straightforward version is quadratic in time. I always mention the faster patience-sorting approach that keeps a tails array and uses binary search to place each element, which brings it down to order n log n.

At the National Bank of India I used this to examine a customer's monthly closing balances and find the longest stretch of months, not necessarily consecutive, where the balance kept strictly rising, because a long rising streak was a positive signal in a financial health score. I computed the best rising run ending at each month and took the maximum. Explaining the extend-the-best-earlier-smaller recurrence, why the answer is the overall maximum, and the n log n optimisation is what shows an interviewer I understand this member of the subsequence pattern family.

answers.shortTitle: Maximum Sum Increasing Subsequence (Rising Subsequence with the Largest Total)

s1_definition.profdef: The Maximum Sum Increasing Subsequence adapts the Longest Increasing Subsequence dynamic program to optimise total value rather than count. We define, for each index, the maximum sum of a strictly increasing subsequence that ends at that index, seeded with the element's own value. The answer is the maximum over all indices. This runs in quadratic time.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India looks at a customer's series of deposit amounts and finds the rising subsequence of deposits, not necessarily consecutive, whose amounts add up to the most money, because the bank rewards growing deposit discipline. The goal is the largest total among strictly rising deposit picks.
s1_definition.oneliner: The best sum ending at an index is its own value plus the best sum ending at any earlier smaller value.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Maximum Sum Increasing Subsequence adapts the Longest Increasing Subsequence dynamic program to optimise total value rather than count. We define, for each index, the maximum sum of a strictly increasing subsequence that ends at that index, seeded with the element's own value. The answer is the maximum over all indices. This runs in quadratic time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India looks at a customer's series of deposit amounts and finds the rising subsequence of deposits, not necessarily consecutive, whose amounts add up to the most money, because the bank rewards growing deposit discipline. The goal is the largest total among strictly rising deposit picks.

**One line to remember:** The best sum ending at an index is its own value plus the best sum ending at any earlier smaller value.

sections.s2_technical:
We define a sum array where the entry at index i is the maximum sum of a strictly increasing subsequence that ends with the element at i. We seed each entry with the element's own value, because the element by itself is a valid rising subsequence. For each i we look back at every earlier index j with a strictly smaller value, because such a subsequence can be extended by the element at i, and we take the best extension, which is the element at i plus the best sum ending at j. The answer is the maximum entry overall, since the best rising subsequence may end anywhere.

Bottom-up: `int[] sum = a.clone(); int best = a.length == 0 ? 0 : a[0]; for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) { for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) if (a[j] < a[i]) sum[i] = Math.max(sum[i], sum[j] + a[i]); best = Math.max(best, sum[i]); }`. A concrete check: for deposits four, one, three, seven the best sum is four plus seven equals eleven or three plus seven equals ten, so eleven wins. Senior nuance: this mirrors the longest increasing subsequence structure but swaps count for value, so it maximises sum not length, and it stays quadratic because the value objective breaks the tails-array trick that speeds up the length version.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India examines a customer's series of deposit amounts and wants the strictly rising subsequence of deposits, not necessarily consecutive, whose amounts add up to the largest total, because the bank rewards customers whose deposits show growing discipline. Enumerating subsequences is exponential. This is exactly how the Maximum Sum Increasing Subsequence works: it finds the largest rising total with the best-earlier-smaller sum recurrence.

The input is the deposit array four, one, three, seven. We want the largest sum of a strictly rising subsequence.

Step 4 — The best sum ending at seven is therefore eleven, from the rising subsequence four then seven.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Maximum Sum Increasing Subsequence is the Longest Increasing Subsequence dynamic program with the objective swapped from counting elements to summing values. For each index I compute the maximum sum of a strictly increasing subsequence that ends at that element, and I seed each index with the element's own value because the single element is a valid rising subsequence on its own.

This stays quadratic in time, and I note that the value objective prevents the tails-array speedup that works for the length version.

At the National Bank of India I used this to examine a customer's series of deposit amounts and find the strictly rising subsequence whose amounts summed to the most, because the bank rewarded customers whose deposits showed growing discipline. answers.question: Given two strings, find the length of the shortest string that has both of them as subsequences. Explain how the Longest Common Substring pattern through the longest common subsequence solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Shortest Common Supersequence (Shortest String Containing Both as Subsequences)

s1_definition.profdef: The Shortest Common Supersequence is solved with the Longest Common Substring pattern through the longest common subsequence. The shared subsequence is written only once, and the characters unique to each string are added around it, so the shortest length is the sum of the two lengths minus the longest common subsequence length. This runs in quadratic time and space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India merges two partial transaction logs into one combined log that preserves the order of both, writing the shared events only once. The shortest combined log length is the two lengths added together minus their longest shared ordered overlap.
s1_definition.oneliner: Shortest supersequence length equals the two lengths added minus the longest common subsequence.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Shortest Common Supersequence is solved with the Longest Common Substring pattern through the longest common subsequence. The shared subsequence is written only once, and the characters unique to each string are added around it, so the shortest length is the sum of the two lengths minus the longest common subsequence length. This runs in quadratic time and space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India merges two partial transaction logs into one combined log that preserves the order of both, writing the shared events only once. The shortest combined log length is the two lengths added together minus their longest shared ordered overlap.

**One line to remember:** Shortest supersequence length equals the two lengths added minus the longest common subsequence.

sections.s2_technical:
A common supersequence must contain both strings as subsequences, which means it must include every character of both while preserving each string's order. The only characters that can be shared between the two strings and written a single time are those in a common subsequence, and to be as short as possible we share the longest common subsequence. Every other character is unique to one string and must appear separately. So the shortest length is the first length plus the second length minus the longest common subsequence length, because that shared part would otherwise be double counted.

We compute the longest common subsequence with the prefix table: `for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i-1) == b.charAt(j-1) ? 1 + dp[i-1][j-1] : Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);` then return `m + n - dp[m][n]`. A concrete check: for ABAC and BAB the longest common subsequence BA has length two, so the shortest supersequence has length four plus three minus two equals five. Senior nuance: this is quadratic in time and space, you can reconstruct the actual supersequence by walking the table and emitting shared characters once, and it is a direct complement of the longest common subsequence.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India merges two partial transaction logs captured on different nodes into one combined log that preserves the order of events from both, writing any shared event only once to keep the log compact. Naively concatenating duplicates shared events and loses the minimal length. This is exactly how the Shortest Common Supersequence works: it uses the longest common subsequence from the Longest Common Substring pattern to compute the shortest merged length.

The code defines a `LogMergeService` exposing `shortestMergedLength(a, b)` returning the shortest common supersequence length. A `Demo` runs it over two sample log strings and logs the length.

Step 4 — The shortest supersequence writes BA once and adds the leftover characters of each string around it, so its length is four plus three minus two.

Step 5 — That gives five, matching a merged log such as ABABC that contains both ABAC and BAB in order. The answer is five. The output is below.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Shortest Common Supersequence is the natural complement of the longest common subsequence, so it lives squarely in the Longest Common Substring pattern. A supersequence has to contain both strings as subsequences, which means it must include every character of both while respecting each string's order. The only characters I can write once and share between the two strings are those that form a common subsequence, and to make the result as short as possible I share the longest common subsequence.

Everything outside that shared subsequence is unique to one string and has to appear on its own, so the shortest length is the first length plus the second length minus the longest common subsequence, because that overlap would otherwise be counted twice. I compute the longest common subsequence with the usual prefix table and apply that formula, which keeps the whole thing in quadratic time and space. I can also reconstruct the actual supersequence by walking the table and emitting each shared character only once.

At the National Bank of India I used this to merge two partial transaction logs captured on different nodes into one compact combined log that preserved the order of both while writing shared events only once. I computed the longest common subsequence and applied the sum-minus-overlap formula. Explaining that the shared subsequence is written once, the unique characters are added around it, and that the length is the two lengths minus the common subsequence is what shows an interviewer I understand this complement within the Longest Common Substring pattern.

answers.question: Given two strings, find the minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions, and substitutions needed to transform the first into the second. Explain the Edit Distance dynamic program within the Longest Common Substring pattern family, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Edit Distance (Minimum Insertions, Deletions, and Substitutions Between Two Strings)

s1_definition.profdef: Edit Distance, also called Levenshtein distance, belongs to the Longest Common Substring family of two-string dynamic programs. We fill a table where an entry is the minimum edits to turn the first prefix into the second prefix: on a character match we copy the diagonal, and on a mismatch we take one plus the minimum of substitute, delete, or insert. The answer is the far corner. This runs in quadratic time and space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India compares a typed beneficiary name against the registered name on the account to decide how different they are, because a small edit distance suggests a harmless typo while a large one suggests a wrong beneficiary. Rajesh types a name and the bank measures the edits to reach the registered name.
s1_definition.oneliner: On a match copy the diagonal, on a mismatch add one to the smallest of substitute, delete, or insert.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Edit Distance, also called Levenshtein distance, belongs to the Longest Common Substring family of two-string dynamic programs. We fill a table where an entry is the minimum edits to turn the first prefix into the second prefix: on a character match we copy the diagonal, and on a mismatch we take one plus the minimum of substitute, delete, or insert. The answer is the far corner. This runs in quadratic time and space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India compares a typed beneficiary name against the registered name on the account to decide how different they are, because a small edit distance suggests a harmless typo while a large one suggests a wrong beneficiary. Rajesh types a name and the bank measures the edits to reach the registered name.

**One line to remember:** On a match copy the diagonal, on a mismatch add one to the smallest of substitute, delete, or insert.

sections.s2_technical:
We define the table entry for prefixes of length i and j as the minimum number of edits to transform the first i characters into the first j characters. The borders are the base cases: turning a prefix into an empty string needs that many deletions, and building a prefix from empty needs that many insertions. When the current characters are equal, no edit is needed for them, so the entry copies the diagonal cell. When they differ, we consider three moves and take the cheapest: substitute, which is one plus the diagonal, delete the first character, which is one plus the cell above, or insert a character, which is one plus the cell to the left.

Bottom-up: `for (int i = 0; i <= m; i++) dp[i][0] = i; for (int j = 0; j <= n; j++) dp[0][j] = j; for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i-1) == b.charAt(j-1) ? dp[i-1][j-1] : 1 + Math.min(dp[i-1][j-1], Math.min(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]));` and the answer is `dp[m][n]`. A concrete check: transforming KITTEN into SITTING has edit distance three. Senior nuance: this is quadratic in time and space, it generalises the deletions-and-insertions-only problem by adding substitution, and a rolling two-row array reduces space to linear.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India compares a typed beneficiary name against the registered name on the destination account during a transfer, because a small number of edits suggests a harmless typo that can be accepted with a warning while a large number suggests a genuinely wrong beneficiary that must be blocked. Checking all edit sequences is exponential. This is exactly how Edit Distance works: it computes the minimum edits in quadratic time with the match-copies-diagonal, mismatch-adds-one recurrence.

The code defines a `BeneficiaryMatchService` exposing `editDistance(typed, registered)` returning the minimum number of edits. A `Demo` runs it over a typed and registered name and logs the distance.

The inputs are the typed name RAJESH and the registered name RAJES. We want the minimum edits to turn the first into the second.

Step 1 — We set the borders. Turning RAJESH into an empty string needs six deletions, and building RAJES from empty needs five insertions, so the first row and column count up from zero.

Step 2 — The characters R, A, J, E, S all match in order, so each matching cell copies its diagonal, carrying a running distance of zero through the shared prefix RAJES.

Step 3 — At the final H of RAJESH there is no matching character left in RAJES, so we take one plus the minimum of the three moves at that cell.

Step 4 — The cheapest move is a deletion of the trailing H, which is one plus the zero accumulated through RAJES, giving one.

Step 5 — The corner cell holds one, meaning a single deletion turns RAJESH into RAJES. The answer is one. The output is below.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Edit Distance, the Levenshtein distance, is a two-string dynamic program in the same family as the longest common subsequence, but it allows three operations rather than two. I fill a table where each cell is the minimum number of edits needed to turn one prefix into the other prefix. The borders are the base cases, because turning a prefix into empty is pure deletion and building a prefix from empty is pure insertion.

Inside the table, when the two current characters are equal there is nothing to fix for them, so the cell simply copies the diagonal. When they differ, I consider the three single-character moves and take the cheapest: substitute, which is one plus the diagonal, delete, which is one plus the cell above, or insert, which is one plus the cell to the left. The final answer is the far corner, the computation is quadratic in time and space, and it reduces to linear space with two rolling rows. I note that this generalises the deletions-and-insertions-only problem by adding substitution.

At the National Bank of India I used this to compare a typed beneficiary name against the registered name on the destination account during a transfer, where a small edit distance meant a harmless typo that could be accepted with a warning while a large distance meant a wrong beneficiary that had to be blocked. I filled the edit distance table and read the corner. Explaining the match-copies-diagonal rule, the three-move minimum on a mismatch, and the deletion and insertion base cases is what shows an interviewer I understand Edit Distance within the Longest Common Substring pattern family.

answers.shortTitle: Topological Sort (Linear Ordering of a Directed Acyclic Graph)

s1_definition.profdef: Topological Sort is the foundational problem of the Topological Sort pattern. Using Kahn's algorithm we compute the in-degree of every node, start a queue with all zero in-degree nodes, and repeatedly remove a node and decrement its neighbours' in-degrees, enqueuing any that reach zero. The order of removal is a valid topological order. This runs in linear time in the number of nodes and edges.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a set of end-of-day batch jobs where some jobs must finish before others can start, and it needs a safe run order so no job starts before its prerequisites. Topological Sort finds that order by always running the jobs that currently have no pending prerequisites.
s1_definition.oneliner: Repeatedly take any node with no remaining prerequisites, output it, and relax its outgoing edges.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Topological Sort is the foundational problem of the Topological Sort pattern. Using Kahn's algorithm we compute the in-degree of every node, start a queue with all zero in-degree nodes, and repeatedly remove a node and decrement its neighbours' in-degrees, enqueuing any that reach zero. The order of removal is a valid topological order. This runs in linear time in the number of nodes and edges.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a set of end-of-day batch jobs where some jobs must finish before others can start, and it needs a safe run order so no job starts before its prerequisites. Topological Sort finds that order by always running the jobs that currently have no pending prerequisites.

**One line to remember:** Repeatedly take any node with no remaining prerequisites, output it, and relax its outgoing edges.

sections.s2_technical:
Kahn's algorithm models prerequisites as directed edges from a prerequisite to its dependent. The in-degree of a node is how many prerequisites still point at it. We build the adjacency list and the in-degree array, then enqueue every node with in-degree zero, because those have no prerequisites and can go first. We repeatedly remove a node from the queue, append it to the order, and for each neighbour reduce its in-degree by one, enqueuing the neighbour when its in-degree falls to zero because all its prerequisites are now placed.

The core loop is `while (!queue.isEmpty()) { int node = queue.poll(); order.add(node); for (int next : adj.get(node)) if (--indeg[next] == 0) queue.add(next); }`. If the final order contains fewer nodes than exist, the graph has a cycle and no topological order is possible. A concrete check: with job A before B and B before C, the order is A, B, C. Senior nuance: this is linear time in nodes plus edges, a depth-first variant pushes nodes onto a stack in post-order, and a shortfall in the output count is the standard cycle detector.

The input is three jobs with dependencies that job zero precedes job one and job one precedes job two. We want a safe run order.

Step 4 — We remove job one, append it, and relax its edge to job two, dropping job two's in-degree to zero, so job two enters the queue.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Topological Sort is the foundational problem of the Topological Sort pattern, and I solve it with Kahn's algorithm, which is a breadth-first approach driven by in-degrees. I model each prerequisite as a directed edge from the prerequisite to its dependent, and the in-degree of a node counts how many prerequisites still point at it. I build the adjacency list and the in-degree array, then start a queue with every node whose in-degree is zero, because those have no unmet prerequisites and can safely go first.

I then repeatedly remove a node, append it to the order, and relax each of its outgoing edges by decrementing the neighbour's in-degree, enqueuing a neighbour the moment its in-degree hits zero because all its prerequisites are now placed. The removal order is a valid topological order. The whole algorithm is linear in the number of nodes plus edges. A built-in benefit is cycle detection, because if the final order has fewer nodes than the graph, a cycle prevented some nodes from ever reaching in-degree zero.

At the National Bank of India I used this to order end-of-day batch jobs where interest posting had to precede statement generation and statement generation had to precede archival, so operations needed a run order that never started a job before its prerequisites. I ran Kahn's algorithm over the dependency graph. Explaining the in-degree queue, the relax-on-removal step, and the shortfall-means-cycle check is what shows an interviewer I understand the Topological Sort pattern.

answers.question: Given a number of tasks and a list of prerequisite pairs, determine whether it is possible to finish all tasks. Explain how the Topological Sort pattern decides feasibility, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Tasks Scheduling (Can All Tasks Be Finished Given Prerequisites)

s1_definition.profdef: Tasks Scheduling is a feasibility variant of the Topological Sort pattern. We run Kahn's algorithm and count how many tasks we manage to place. If that count equals the number of tasks, a valid order exists and all tasks can finish, otherwise a cycle blocks some tasks and completion is impossible. This runs in linear time in tasks plus prerequisites.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to know whether a set of compliance tasks can all be completed given their dependencies, or whether two tasks mutually block each other in a loop. Tasks Scheduling answers yes or no by checking whether a safe order covering every task exists.
s1_definition.oneliner: All tasks finish exactly when topological sort places every task, meaning the graph has no cycle.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Tasks Scheduling is a feasibility variant of the Topological Sort pattern. We run Kahn's algorithm and count how many tasks we manage to place. If that count equals the number of tasks, a valid order exists and all tasks can finish, otherwise a cycle blocks some tasks and completion is impossible. This runs in linear time in tasks plus prerequisites.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to know whether a set of compliance tasks can all be completed given their dependencies, or whether two tasks mutually block each other in a loop. Tasks Scheduling answers yes or no by checking whether a safe order covering every task exists.

**One line to remember:** All tasks finish exactly when topological sort places every task, meaning the graph has no cycle.

sections.s2_technical:
We treat each prerequisite pair as a directed edge from the prerequisite task to the dependent task, and we build the adjacency list and in-degree array. We enqueue every task with in-degree zero and process the queue exactly as in Kahn's algorithm, counting each task as we place it. Each time we remove a task we relax its outgoing edges, enqueuing any neighbour whose in-degree reaches zero.

The key decision is the final count: `return placed == taskCount;` where placed is how many tasks left the queue. If a cycle exists, the tasks inside the cycle never reach in-degree zero, so placed stays below the task count and we return false. The core loop is `while (!queue.isEmpty()) { int t = queue.poll(); placed++; for (int next : adj.get(t)) if (--indeg[next] == 0) queue.add(next); }`. A concrete check: two tasks that each require the other form a cycle, so completion is impossible. Senior nuance: this is linear time in tasks plus edges, it is the pure cycle-detection use of topological sort, and it returns a boolean rather than the order itself.

Tasks Scheduling is the feasibility variant of the Topological Sort pattern, where the question is simply whether every task can be completed rather than producing an order. I run Kahn's algorithm exactly as for a normal topological sort: I model each prerequisite as a directed edge from the prerequisite to its dependent, build the in-degree array, and start a queue with every task that has in-degree zero.

As I process the queue I count how many tasks I manage to place, relaxing each removed task's outgoing edges and enqueuing neighbours that reach in-degree zero. If the final order is missing any task, a cycle existed, so I return an empty list to signal that no valid order is possible. The algorithm is linear in tasks plus prerequisites.

At the National Bank of India I used this to generate a corporate onboarding playbook where document verification had to precede account opening and account opening had to precede card issuance, and operations needed the actual ordered steps, not just a feasibility answer. I ran Kahn's algorithm and returned the removal order. Explaining that the removal order respects every prerequisite, that any valid order is acceptable, and that an empty return signals a cycle is what shows an interviewer I understand this order-producing use of the Topological Sort pattern.

s1_definition.profdef: All Tasks Scheduling Orders extends the Topological Sort pattern with backtracking to list every valid topological order rather than just one. At each step we try every task currently with in-degree zero, recurse after placing it, and then undo the choice to explore alternatives. The number of orders can be large, so this is exponential in the worst case.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to see all the different legal sequences for running a small set of dependent audit steps, so reviewers can choose the one that fits their staffing. All Tasks Scheduling Orders lists every sequence that respects the prerequisites.
s1_definition.oneliner: At each step branch on every zero in-degree task, recurse, then undo to find all orders.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** All Tasks Scheduling Orders extends the Topological Sort pattern with backtracking to list every valid topological order rather than just one. At each step we try every task currently with in-degree zero, recurse after placing it, and then undo the choice to explore alternatives. The number of orders can be large, so this is exponential in the worst case.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to see all the different legal sequences for running a small set of dependent audit steps, so reviewers can choose the one that fits their staffing. All Tasks Scheduling Orders lists every sequence that respects the prerequisites.

**One line to remember:** At each step branch on every zero in-degree task, recurse, then undo to find all orders.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep the adjacency list and a mutable in-degree array. The recursion maintains the partial order built so far. At each level we scan for every task that currently has in-degree zero and is not yet used, and for each such task we add it to the partial order, decrement its neighbours' in-degrees, and recurse. After the recursion returns we undo those changes by removing the task and restoring the neighbours' in-degrees, which lets us try a different task at this level. When the partial order contains all tasks we record a complete order.

The recursion is `void build(partial, indeg, adj, used, results) { if (partial.size() == n) { results.add(copy(partial)); return; } for each task t with indeg[t]==0 and not used: { use t; for next in adj[t] indeg[next]--; partial.add(t); build(...); partial.removeLast(); for next in adj[t] indeg[next]++; unuse t; } }`. A concrete check: tasks zero before two and one before two give two orders, zero one two and one zero two. Senior nuance: this is exponential because the count of topological orders can be factorial, so it is only practical for small graphs, and it combines the in-degree idea from Kahn's algorithm with classic backtracking.

The input is three audit steps with prerequisites that step zero precedes step two and step one precedes step two. We want every valid order.

Step 4 — We undo back to the top and take step one first, which by the same reasoning yields the order one zero two.

answers.question: Given a list of words sorted according to an unknown alphabet, derive a valid ordering of the characters in that alphabet. Explain how the Topological Sort pattern solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Alien Dictionary (Derive Character Order from a Sorted Word List)

s1_definition.profdef: The Alien Dictionary is a graph-construction application of the Topological Sort pattern. From each adjacent pair of sorted words we find the first differing character, which gives a directed edge showing that one character precedes another. We then topologically sort the characters with Kahn's algorithm to produce a valid alphabet, detecting contradictions as cycles. This runs in linear time in the total input size.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India receives a list of product tier codes already sorted by an internal ranking whose rule is unknown, and it wants to recover the ranking of the individual tier symbols. The Alien Dictionary derives that symbol order from the sorted list.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each adjacent word pair's first difference gives one ordering edge, then topologically sort the characters.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Alien Dictionary is a graph-construction application of the Topological Sort pattern. From each adjacent pair of sorted words we find the first differing character, which gives a directed edge showing that one character precedes another. We then topologically sort the characters with Kahn's algorithm to produce a valid alphabet, detecting contradictions as cycles. This runs in linear time in the total input size.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India receives a list of product tier codes already sorted by an internal ranking whose rule is unknown, and it wants to recover the ranking of the individual tier symbols. The Alien Dictionary derives that symbol order from the sorted list.

**One line to remember:** Each adjacent word pair's first difference gives one ordering edge, then topologically sort the characters.

sections.s2_technical:
We first collect every distinct character so each becomes a node. Then for each adjacent pair of words we compare them character by character until we find the first position where they differ: that tells us the character in the earlier word comes before the character in the later word, so we add a directed edge and increment the in-degree of the later character. An important edge case is that if the earlier word is a prefix of the later word everything is fine, but if the later word is a strict prefix of the earlier word the input is invalid.

After building the graph we run Kahn's algorithm over the characters, enqueuing zero in-degree characters and appending them as we remove them, relaxing edges along the way. The core edge extraction is `for the first index where a.charAt(k) != b.charAt(k): adj.get(a.charAt(k)).add(b.charAt(k)); indeg.merge(b.charAt(k), 1, Integer::sum); break;`. If the final order omits any character a cycle made the ordering contradictory. A concrete check: words that sort as the list implies B before A yields an alphabet with B before A. Senior nuance: this is linear in the total number of characters across all words, the prefix check prevents an invalid dictionary from slipping through, and only the first differing character gives information.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India receives product tier codes sorted by an internal ranking whose ordering rule over the individual symbols is unknown, and it needs to recover the rank order of the symbols so it can apply the same ranking elsewhere. Guessing the order is unreliable. This is exactly how the Alien Dictionary works: it extracts ordering edges from adjacent sorted codes and topologically sorts the symbols with the Topological Sort pattern.

Step 4 — Comparing ac and cab, the first difference is at position zero where a comes before c, an edge we already have, so c's in-degree stays consistent. Now b has in-degree zero, a has in-degree one, and c has in-degree one.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Alien Dictionary is a graph-construction application of the Topological Sort pattern, where the real work is turning sorted words into ordering edges before I sort anything. I first register every distinct character as a node, then I walk through each adjacent pair of words and compare them character by character until the first position where they differ. That first difference is the only informative one, and it tells me the character from the earlier word precedes the character from the later word, so I add a directed edge and raise the in-degree of the later character.

I watch for the invalid case where the later word is a strict prefix of the earlier word, because a correctly sorted dictionary can never do that. Once the graph is built I run Kahn's algorithm over the characters, enqueuing zero in-degree characters and appending them as I remove them. If the final order omits any character, a cycle made the ordering contradictory and I return empty. The whole thing is linear in the total number of characters across the words.

At the National Bank of India I used this to recover the rank order of product tier symbols from a list of tier codes that were sorted by an internal ranking whose rule over the symbols was unknown. I extracted the ordering edges from adjacent codes and topologically sorted the symbols. Explaining that only the first differing character gives an edge, that a later-word-prefix case is invalid, and that a cycle means contradiction is what shows an interviewer I understand this construction-plus-sort use of the Topological Sort pattern.

answers.question: Given a number of courses and prerequisite pairs, determine whether the dependency graph contains a cycle, using a depth-first colouring approach. Explain this depth-first variant of the Topological Sort pattern, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Course Schedule Cycle Check (Detect a Dependency Cycle with DFS Colouring)

s1_definition.profdef: The Course Schedule Cycle Check is the depth-first colouring variant of the Topological Sort pattern. We colour each node white when unvisited, grey while it is on the current recursion stack, and black when fully explored. If a depth-first traversal reaches a grey node we have found a back edge, which means a cycle, so no valid order exists. This runs in linear time in nodes plus edges.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to confirm that a set of dependent approval steps does not contain a circular dependency, where step A waits on step B which waits back on step A. The depth-first colouring check reports whether any such loop exists.
s1_definition.oneliner: If depth-first search meets a node currently on its recursion stack, a cycle exists.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Course Schedule Cycle Check is the depth-first colouring variant of the Topological Sort pattern. We colour each node white when unvisited, grey while it is on the current recursion stack, and black when fully explored. If a depth-first traversal reaches a grey node we have found a back edge, which means a cycle, so no valid order exists. This runs in linear time in nodes plus edges.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to confirm that a set of dependent approval steps does not contain a circular dependency, where step A waits on step B which waits back on step A. The depth-first colouring check reports whether any such loop exists.

**One line to remember:** If depth-first search meets a node currently on its recursion stack, a cycle exists.

sections.s2_technical:
We build the adjacency list from the prerequisite pairs. Each node has a colour: white meaning not yet visited, grey meaning it is currently in the active recursion path, and black meaning it and all its descendants are fully processed. We start a depth-first search from every white node. When we enter a node we mark it grey, recurse into each neighbour, and only after all neighbours finish do we mark it black. The cycle test is simple: if during recursion we reach a neighbour that is already grey, that neighbour is an ancestor on the current path, so the edge back to it closes a cycle.

The recursion is `boolean hasCycle(node) { color[node] = GREY; for (next : adj.get(node)) { if (color[next] == GREY) return true; if (color[next] == WHITE && hasCycle(next)) return true; } color[node] = BLACK; return false; }`. Reaching a black neighbour is safe because it was fully explored on an earlier path and led to no cycle. A concrete check: steps zero before one, one before two, and two before zero form a loop that colouring detects. Senior nuance: this is linear time in nodes plus edges, it is the depth-first counterpart to Kahn's in-degree method, and the grey colour is exactly the recursion stack membership that distinguishes a back edge from a harmless cross or forward edge.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Course Schedule Cycle Check is the depth-first colouring variant of the Topological Sort pattern, and the whole idea rests on three colours that track each node's state. White means I have not visited the node, grey means the node is currently on my active recursion path, and black means I have finished the node and everything reachable from it. I start a depth-first search from every white node, colour a node grey when I enter it, recurse into its neighbours, and colour it black only after all its neighbours are done.

The cycle test is reaching a grey neighbour during recursion, because grey means that neighbour is an ancestor still sitting on my current path, so the edge back to it closes a loop. Reaching a black neighbour is perfectly safe, because that subtree was fully explored on an earlier path and produced no cycle. The grey colour is literally recursion-stack membership, which is what lets me tell a dangerous back edge apart from a harmless cross or forward edge. The traversal is linear in nodes plus edges.

At the National Bank of India I used this to confirm that a set of dependent approval steps had no circular dependency, because a loop where one approval waited on another that waited back on the first would deadlock the whole workflow. I ran the three-colour depth-first search over the dependency graph. Explaining the white, grey, and black states, that a grey neighbour signals a back edge and therefore a cycle, and that this is the depth-first counterpart to Kahn's in-degree method is what shows an interviewer I understand this variant of the Topological Sort pattern.

answers.question: Implement a trie, also called a prefix tree, supporting inserting a word, searching for a complete word, and checking whether any word starts with a given prefix. Explain the Trie pattern, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Implement a Trie (Prefix Tree with Insert, Search, and StartsWith)

s1_definition.profdef: A trie is the core data structure of the Trie pattern, a tree where each edge represents one character and each path from the root spells a prefix. Each node holds child links and a flag marking whether a complete word ends there. Insert, search, and prefix checks all walk the tree one character at a time, so each runs in time proportional to the key length, independent of how many keys are stored.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India stores a large set of registered merchant names and wants to look up names and check prefixes quickly as a teller types. A trie stores shared prefixes once, so RELIANCE and RELIABLE share the same early branch, making lookups fast and memory efficient.
s1_definition.oneliner: A trie stores characters along edges so every key operation costs only the length of the key.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A trie is the core data structure of the Trie pattern, a tree where each edge represents one character and each path from the root spells a prefix. Each node holds child links and a flag marking whether a complete word ends there. Insert, search, and prefix checks all walk the tree one character at a time, so each runs in time proportional to the key length, independent of how many keys are stored.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India stores a large set of registered merchant names and wants to look up names and check prefixes quickly as a teller types. A trie stores shared prefixes once, so RELIANCE and RELIABLE share the same early branch, making lookups fast and memory efficient.

**One line to remember:** A trie stores characters along edges so every key operation costs only the length of the key.

sections.s2_technical:
Each trie node has an array or map of child links, one slot per possible character, and a boolean marking the end of a complete word. To insert a word we start at the root and for each character follow the matching child, creating it if it does not exist, and after the last character we set the end flag. To search for a complete word we walk the same path and succeed only if every character has a link and the final node has its end flag set. To check a prefix we walk the path and succeed as long as every character has a link, regardless of the end flag.

The insert core is `TrieNode node = root; for (char c : word.toCharArray()) { node = node.children.computeIfAbsent(c, k -> new TrieNode()); } node.isWord = true;`. Search and prefix share a traversal helper that returns the node reached, then search checks the end flag while prefix just checks the node exists. A concrete check: after inserting RELIANCE, searching RELIANCE succeeds, searching RELI fails as a word but succeeds as a prefix. Senior nuance: operations are order of the key length, memory can be reduced with a compressed radix tree, and a character map scales better than a fixed array for large alphabets.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores a large set of registered merchant names and a teller needs to look up whether a typed name is registered and whether any registered name starts with what has been typed so far, with instant response. Scanning a flat list on every keystroke is slow. This is exactly how a trie works: it stores shared prefixes once and answers each lookup in time proportional only to the typed length.

The code defines a `MerchantTrie` with `insert(name)`, `search(name)`, and `startsWith(prefix)`, plus a supporting `TrieNode`. A `Demo` inserts a few merchant names and logs the results of searches and prefix checks.

The input is inserting RELIANCE and RELIABLE, then searching RELIANCE, searching RELI, and checking the prefix RELI.

Step 1 — Inserting RELIANCE walks from the root creating nodes for R, E, L, I, A, N, C, E, and marks the final E node as the end of a word.

Step 2 — Inserting RELIABLE reuses the shared branch R, E, L, I, then creates A, B, L, E, marking the final E as the end of a word. The shared prefix RELI is stored only once.

Step 3 — Searching RELIANCE walks the full path and finds the end flag set on the last node, so it returns true.

Step 4 — Searching RELI walks to the I node, which exists but has no end flag because no complete name ends there, so it returns false.

Step 5 — Checking the prefix RELI walks to the same I node, which exists, so the prefix check returns true. The output is below.

sections.s6_takeaway:
A trie, or prefix tree, is the core data structure of the Trie pattern, and I describe it as a tree where each edge carries one character so that the path from the root to any node spells a prefix. Every node keeps links to its children and a boolean marking whether a complete word ends at that node. The beauty is that shared prefixes are stored exactly once, so two names that begin the same way share their early branch.

To insert a word I walk from the root following or creating a child for each character and set the end flag on the final node. To search for a complete word I walk the same path and succeed only if every character has a link and the final node has its end flag set. To check a prefix I walk the path and succeed as long as every character has a link, ignoring the end flag. Because each operation follows one link per character, they all cost time proportional to the key length, independent of how many keys are stored, which is the trie's defining advantage.

At the National Bank of India I used a trie to store registered merchant names so a teller could instantly check whether a typed name was registered and whether any registered name started with the typed prefix. I warmed the trie from the database at startup and served every keystroke from memory. Explaining that characters live on edges, that the end-of-word flag separates a complete name from a mere prefix, and that each operation costs only the key length is what shows an interviewer I understand the Trie pattern.

answers.question: Given a grid of characters and a set of dictionary words, find all dictionary words that can be formed by a path of adjacent cells without reusing a cell. Explain how the Trie pattern accelerates the search, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Word Search with a Trie (Find Which Dictionary Words Appear in a Character Grid)

s1_definition.profdef: Word Search with a Trie combines a backtracking grid traversal with the Trie pattern. We load all dictionary words into a trie, then run a depth-first search from every cell, descending the trie by the current character. When we land on a trie node marked as a word we record it. The trie lets us explore all words simultaneously and prune the moment no word shares the current prefix.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India scans a grid of characters pulled from a scanned cheque region to spot any known keyword like SALARY or RENT appearing along connected cells. A trie of the keywords lets the scan follow all keywords at once and stop early on dead ends.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk the grid and the trie together, pruning any path whose prefix matches no word.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Word Search with a Trie combines a backtracking grid traversal with the Trie pattern. We load all dictionary words into a trie, then run a depth-first search from every cell, descending the trie by the current character. When we land on a trie node marked as a word we record it. The trie lets us explore all words simultaneously and prune the moment no word shares the current prefix.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India scans a grid of characters pulled from a scanned cheque region to spot any known keyword like SALARY or RENT appearing along connected cells. A trie of the keywords lets the scan follow all keywords at once and stop early on dead ends.

**One line to remember:** Walk the grid and the trie together, pruning any path whose prefix matches no word.

sections.s2_technical:
We build a trie from all target words so that every prefix is represented. Then from each grid cell we start a depth-first search that carries the current trie node. At a cell we first check that the trie node has a child for the cell's character, and if not we prune immediately because no word continues with this prefix. If it does, we descend to that child, and if that child is marked as a word we record the word. We mark the cell visited, recurse into the four adjacent cells, then unmark the cell on the way back so other paths can reuse it.

The search core is `void dfs(r, c, node) { char ch = grid[r][c]; TrieNode child = node.children.get(ch); if (child == null) return; if (child.word != null) found.add(child.word); char save = grid[r][c]; grid[r][c] = '#'; for each neighbour dfs(nr, nc, child); grid[r][c] = save; }`. Storing the full word on the terminal node avoids rebuilding it. A concrete check: a grid containing S, A, L, A, R, Y along a connected path reports SALARY. Senior nuance: the trie turns many separate word searches into one shared traversal, pruning dead prefixes early, and marking the cell during recursion enforces the no-reuse rule.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India scans a small grid of characters extracted from a cheque region and wants to detect any known keyword such as SALARY or RENT formed along connected cells, because spotting such keywords helps classify the cheque. Searching each keyword separately across the grid is wasteful. This is exactly how Word Search with a Trie works: it loads the keywords into a trie and runs one shared backtracking search that prunes dead prefixes.

The code defines a `GridKeywordService` with `findKeywords(grid, words)`, plus a `TrieNode`. A `Demo` builds a small grid and keyword set and logs the keywords found.

The input is a three by three grid and the keyword set SAL, RENT, RAT. We want every keyword formed along connected cells.

Step 1 — We build the trie from the keywords, so the root branches into S for SAL and R for RENT and RAT, sharing the R branch.

Step 2 — Starting the search at the top-left S, the trie has a child for S, so we descend, then the neighbour A has a child, then the neighbour L has a child marked as the word SAL, so we record SAL.

Step 3 — Starting at the centre R, the trie descends, then A to the right has a child, then T below A has a child marked as the word RAT, so we record RAT.

Step 4 — Still from the R branch, following R then E then N then T along connected cells reaches the node marked as the word RENT, so we record RENT.

Step 5 — Any path whose prefix matches no keyword is pruned immediately, so the found list is SAL, RAT, RENT in discovery order. The output is below.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Search with a Trie marries a backtracking grid traversal with the Trie pattern, and the reason the trie matters is that it lets me search for every dictionary word at the same time instead of once per word. I first load all the words into a trie so that every prefix is represented, then I launch a depth-first search from each grid cell, and crucially each search frame carries the current trie node alongside the grid position.

At every cell I check whether the current trie node has a child for the cell's character. If it does not, I prune that path immediately because no word continues with this prefix, which is exactly where the trie saves work. If it does, I descend into that child, and if the child is marked as a complete word I record it. I mark the cell visited so the path cannot reuse it, recurse into the four neighbours, and then restore the cell on the way back so other paths are free to use it.

At the National Bank of India I used this to scan a small grid of characters extracted from a cheque region for known keywords like SALARY and RENT formed along connected cells, which helped classify the cheque. I loaded the keywords into a trie and ran one shared backtracking search. Explaining that the trie drives the traversal, that a missing child prunes the path early, and that marking and restoring the cell enforces the no-reuse rule is what shows an interviewer I understand this combined application of the Trie pattern.

answers.question: Given a list of words, find the longest word that can be built one character at a time, where every prefix of that word is also present in the list; break ties by taking the smallest word in dictionary order. Explain how the Trie pattern solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Longest Word in Dictionary (Longest Word Buildable One Character at a Time)

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Word in Dictionary is a traversal application of the Trie pattern. We insert every word into a trie, then run a depth-first search that only descends through nodes marked as complete words, because such a path means every prefix along it is itself a valid word. We keep the longest such reachable word, breaking ties by dictionary order. This runs in time proportional to the total characters.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India builds product feature codes incrementally, where each longer code must extend a code that already exists at every step. The bank wants the longest code reachable by adding one character at a time, which this finds with a trie.
s1_definition.oneliner: Only descend through nodes that are themselves words, and keep the longest reachable such path.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Word in Dictionary is a traversal application of the Trie pattern. We insert every word into a trie, then run a depth-first search that only descends through nodes marked as complete words, because such a path means every prefix along it is itself a valid word. We keep the longest such reachable word, breaking ties by dictionary order. This runs in time proportional to the total characters.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India builds product feature codes incrementally, where each longer code must extend a code that already exists at every step. The bank wants the longest code reachable by adding one character at a time, which this finds with a trie.

**One line to remember:** Only descend through nodes that are themselves words, and keep the longest reachable such path.

sections.s2_technical:
We insert all words into a trie, marking the end of each word. The key rule is that a word is buildable one character at a time only if every one of its prefixes is also a word in the list. In the trie that means a path is valid only if every node along it, below the root, is marked as a complete word. So we run a depth-first search from the root and only step into a child if that child is marked as a word, stopping a branch the moment a node is not a word.

As we descend we track the current string, and whenever we reach a node that is a word and the path is longer than the best so far, or equal in length but smaller in dictionary order, we update the best. We can get the dictionary-order tie-break for free by visiting children in sorted character order and preferring the first longest found. A concrete check: with words A, AP, APP, APPL, APPLE the answer is APPLE because each prefix exists. Senior nuance: this is linear in the total characters, the word-only descent rule is what encodes the buildable constraint, and sorted child traversal handles the tie-break cleanly.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India builds product feature codes incrementally, and a longer code is only valid if every shorter prefix of it is also a registered code, so the product team wants the longest buildable code, preferring the dictionary-smallest on ties. Checking every code's prefixes separately is wasteful. This is exactly how the Longest Word in Dictionary works: it uses the Trie pattern and a word-only descent to find the longest reachable code.

The code defines a `FeatureCodeService` with `longestBuildable(codes)`, plus a `TrieNode`. A `Demo` inserts a small code set and logs the longest buildable code.

The input is the code set A, AP, APP, APPL, APPLE, B. We want the longest code whose every prefix is also present.

Step 1 — We build the trie, marking A, AP, APP, APPL, APPLE as words along one branch and B as a word on another branch.

Step 2 — The depth-first search starts at the root and, visiting children in sorted order, steps into A first because A is a word, recording A as the best so far of length one.

Step 3 — From A it steps into AP because AP is a word, updating the best to AP of length two, then into APP, then APPL, each a word, extending the best each time.

Step 4 — From APPL it steps into APPLE because APPLE is a word, updating the best to APPLE of length five. There is no further word child, so this branch stops.

Step 5 — The search then considers B, which is a word of length one, but one is shorter than five so the best stays APPLE. The answer is APPLE. The output is below.
