    Linear in total characters
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Longest Word in Dictionary is a traversal application of the Trie pattern, and the insight that makes it clean is that a word can be built one character at a time exactly when every one of its prefixes is also a word in the list. Once all words are inserted into a trie and each word end is marked, that condition becomes a simple structural rule: a path from the root is valid only if every node along it is marked as a complete word.

So I run a depth-first search from the root and only step into a child if that child is marked as a word, which stops a branch the instant a node is not a word. As I descend I track the current string, and I update my best answer whenever I reach a word node that is longer than my current best. I get the dictionary-order tie-break for free by storing children in sorted order and visiting them in that order, so among equal-length candidates the smallest is found first. The whole search is linear in the total number of characters.

At the National Bank of India I used this to find the longest incrementally buildable product feature code, where a longer code was only valid if every shorter prefix of it was also a registered code, preferring the dictionary-smallest on ties. I inserted the codes into a trie and ran the word-only descent. Explaining that the path-of-words rule encodes the buildable constraint, and that sorted children handle the tie-break, is what shows an interviewer I understand this traversal use of the Trie pattern.

answers.question: Given a set of root words and a sentence, replace every word in the sentence with the shortest root that is a prefix of it, leaving words with no matching root unchanged. Explain how the Trie pattern solves it, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Replace Words with Root (Shorten Words to Their Shortest Registered Root)

s1_definition.profdef: Replace Words with Root is a prefix-matching application of the Trie pattern. We insert all root words into a trie, then for each sentence word we walk the trie character by character and stop at the first node marked as a root, which is the shortest matching root. We replace the word with that root, or keep the word if no root prefixes it. Each word costs time proportional to its length.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India normalises long transaction descriptor words down to their shortest registered root code, so SALARYCREDIT collapses to the root SAL. A trie of root codes lets each descriptor be shortened to its earliest matching root.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk each word through the trie and cut it at the first node marked as a root.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Replace Words with Root is a prefix-matching application of the Trie pattern. We insert all root words into a trie, then for each sentence word we walk the trie character by character and stop at the first node marked as a root, which is the shortest matching root. We replace the word with that root, or keep the word if no root prefixes it. Each word costs time proportional to its length.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India normalises long transaction descriptor words down to their shortest registered root code, so SALARYCREDIT collapses to the root SAL. A trie of root codes lets each descriptor be shortened to its earliest matching root.

**One line to remember:** Walk each word through the trie and cut it at the first node marked as a root.

sections.s2_technical:
We insert every root word into a trie and mark the end of each root. To process a sentence word we walk the trie from the root following the word's characters. The moment we reach a node marked as a root, we stop, because that is the shortest root that is a prefix of the word, and we use the characters consumed so far as the replacement. If at some character there is no matching child, no root prefixes the word, so we keep the original word. If we finish the word without ever hitting a root node, we also keep the original.

The per-word core is `StringBuilder prefix = new StringBuilder(); TrieNode node = root; for (char c : word) { if (node.isRoot || !node.children.containsKey(c)) break; node = node.children.get(c); prefix.append(c); } return node.isRoot ? prefix.toString() : word;`. A concrete check: with roots SAL and REN, SALARY becomes SAL and RENTPAID becomes REN. Senior nuance: this is linear in the total sentence length plus root size, stopping at the first root node gives the shortest root automatically, and it is a classic prefix-replacement use of the trie.

The input is the root set SAL and REN and the sentence SALARYCREDIT RENTPAID FEES. We want each word shortened to its shortest matching root.

Step 4 — For FEES we try to walk F, but the root node has no child F, so no root prefixes this word and we keep FEES unchanged.

answers.question: Given a set of words and a typed prefix, return all words that start with that prefix, optionally limited to the top few. Explain how the Trie pattern provides autocomplete, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Autocomplete Suggestions (Return Words Matching a Typed Prefix)

s1_definition.profdef: Autocomplete Suggestions is a prefix-collection application of the Trie pattern. We insert all words into a trie, walk down to the node at the end of the typed prefix, then run a depth-first search from that node to gather every completed word beneath it. Reaching the prefix node costs the prefix length, and gathering suggestions costs time proportional to the matching subtree.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India offers a search box where a teller types the start of a payee name and the system instantly suggests all registered payees beginning with those letters. A trie walks straight to the typed prefix and collects every name underneath it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk to the prefix node, then collect every word in the subtree below it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Autocomplete Suggestions is a prefix-collection application of the Trie pattern. We insert all words into a trie, walk down to the node at the end of the typed prefix, then run a depth-first search from that node to gather every completed word beneath it. Reaching the prefix node costs the prefix length, and gathering suggestions costs time proportional to the matching subtree.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India offers a search box where a teller types the start of a payee name and the system instantly suggests all registered payees beginning with those letters. A trie walks straight to the typed prefix and collects every name underneath it.

**One line to remember:** Walk to the prefix node, then collect every word in the subtree below it.

sections.s2_technical:
We build a trie of all words, marking each word end. To autocomplete a prefix we first walk from the root following the prefix characters. If any character has no matching child, no word starts with the prefix and we return an empty list. Otherwise we arrive at the prefix node, and every complete word stored in the subtree rooted there is a valid suggestion. We run a depth-first search from that node, building up the suffix as we descend and recording a full word each time we pass a node marked as a word end.

The collection core is `void collect(TrieNode node, StringBuilder cur, List<String> out, int limit) { if (out.size() >= limit) return; if (node.isWord) out.add(cur.toString()); for (var e : node.children.entrySet()) { cur.append(e.getKey()); collect(e.getValue(), cur, out, limit); cur.deleteCharAt(cur.length() - 1); } }`. Visiting children in sorted order yields alphabetical suggestions, and an early return enforces a top-few limit. A concrete check: with payees RAJESH, RAJIV, PRIYA and prefix RAJ, the suggestions are RAJESH and RAJIV. Senior nuance: reaching the prefix node is order of the prefix length, gathering is proportional to the matched subtree, and for very large tries each node can cache its top suggestions to answer instantly.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India provides a payee search box where a teller types the first few letters of a registered payee name and expects an instant list of all matching payees, limited to a handful of top suggestions. Scanning the full payee list on every keystroke does not scale. This is exactly how Autocomplete Suggestions works: it walks a trie to the typed prefix and collects the matching payee names beneath it.

The code defines a `PayeeAutocompleteService` with `suggest(prefix, limit)` and `insert(name)`, plus a `TrieNode`. A `Demo` inserts a few payee names and logs the suggestions for a prefix.

Step 3 — From the J node we run a depth-first collection, descending in alphabetical order. The E branch completes RAJESH, which we record first.

Step 4 — Back at the J node we take the I branch, which completes RAJIV, which we record second. The PRIYA name is on a different branch and is never reached from the RAJ prefix node.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Autocomplete Suggestions is a prefix-collection application of the Trie pattern, and I describe it in two clean phases. First I insert all the words into a trie and mark each word end, then to autocomplete a typed prefix I walk from the root following the prefix characters. If any character has no matching child, nothing starts with that prefix and I return an empty list. Otherwise I arrive at the prefix node, and every complete word stored in the subtree beneath that node is a valid suggestion.

The second phase is a depth-first search from the prefix node, building up the suffix as I descend and recording a full word each time I pass a node marked as a word end. If I store the children in sorted order the suggestions come out alphabetically, and an early return once I have gathered enough enforces a top-few limit. Reaching the prefix node costs time proportional to the prefix length, and gathering the suggestions costs time proportional to the matched subtree, which is exactly why a trie powers fast autocomplete.

At the National Bank of India I used this behind a payee search box where a teller typed the first few letters of a registered payee name and expected an instant list of matching payees. I warmed the trie from the database, served keystrokes from memory, and cached hot prefixes in Redis. Explaining the walk-to-prefix-then-collect-subtree structure, the alphabetical ordering from sorted children, and the limit through an early return is what shows an interviewer I understand this prefix-collection use of the Trie pattern.

answers.question: Given n cities, a list of flights as (from, to, price), a source, a destination, and a maximum number of stops K, find the cheapest price to reach the destination using at most K stops. Explain the Bellman-Ford style relaxation, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops (Shortest Path with a Limit on Hops)

s1_definition.profdef: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops is a bounded-hop shortest path problem solved with a Bellman-Ford style relaxation. We relax every edge exactly K+1 times, each round allowing one more hop, and we read the relaxed distances from a snapshot of the previous round so a single round never chains multiple hops together. The answer is the cheapest cost to the destination after at most K+1 edges.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India routes an international wire through correspondent banks, and each hop charges a fee. The bank will tolerate at most K intermediate banks, so we want the cheapest route that uses no more than K hops.
s1_definition.oneliner: Relax all edges K+1 times from a frozen previous-round snapshot so each round adds exactly one hop.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Cheapest Flights Within K Stops is a bounded-hop shortest path problem solved with a Bellman-Ford style relaxation. We relax every edge exactly K+1 times, each round allowing one more hop, and we read the relaxed distances from a snapshot of the previous round so a single round never chains multiple hops together. The answer is the cheapest cost to the destination after at most K+1 edges.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India routes an international wire through correspondent banks, and each hop charges a fee. The bank will tolerate at most K intermediate banks, so we want the cheapest route that uses no more than K hops.

**One line to remember:** Relax all edges K+1 times from a frozen previous-round snapshot so each round adds exactly one hop.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep an array `cost` where `cost[c]` is the cheapest known price to reach city `c`, starting with the source at zero and everyone else at infinity. We then repeat K+1 rounds. In each round we copy the current costs into a snapshot, and for every flight from `u` to `v` with price `p` we check `snapshot[u] + p` and keep it in `cost[v]` if it is cheaper. Copying into a snapshot is the crucial detail: it guarantees that within one round a path cannot gain two hops, because all relaxations read the frozen values from the end of the previous round.

The core relaxation is `for (int[] f : flights) { int u = f[0], v = f[1], p = f[2]; if (snap[u] != INF && snap[u] + p < cost[v]) cost[v] = snap[u] + p; }`. A concrete check: with flights SRC to A costing 100, A to DST costing 100, and SRC to DST costing 500, with K equal to one stop, after round one A is 100 and DST is 500, after round two DST becomes 200, so the two-hop route wins. Senior nuance: the complexity is order of K times the number of edges, and the snapshot prevents the classic mistake of letting one round telescope an unbounded number of hops.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India sends an international wire that must pass through correspondent banks, each charging a fee, and regulation allows at most K intermediate banks. Taking the fewest hops is not always cheapest, and the cheapest route without a hop limit may use too many banks. This is exactly how Cheapest Flights Within K Stops works: it finds the cheapest route under a hard limit on the number of hops.

The code defines a `WireRoutingService` with `cheapestWithin(n, flights, src, dst, k)` that runs the bounded relaxation. A `Demo` builds a small correspondent-bank graph and logs the cheapest fee under the hop limit.

The input is three correspondent-bank fees and a hop limit of one stop. Step 1: we initialise the cost of the source bank to zero and every other bank to infinity. The two-hop route is cheaper than the direct route and still respects the one-stop limit, so we return two hundred.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Cheapest Flights Within K Stops is a bounded-hop shortest path problem, and I solve it with a Bellman-Ford style relaxation rather than plain Dijkstra, because Dijkstra has no natural way to respect a hard limit on the number of hops. I keep an array of the cheapest known cost to each city, starting the source at zero and everyone else at infinity, and I run exactly K plus one rounds, because allowing K stops means allowing K plus one edges.

The detail that makes it correct is that each round reads from a frozen snapshot of the previous round's costs. If I relaxed in place I could accidentally chain several hops together inside a single round and violate the hop limit. By copying the costs into a snapshot and relaxing every edge against that snapshot, I guarantee that each round extends every path by at most one hop, so after the loop the destination cost reflects the cheapest route using no more than the allowed number of stops.

At the National Bank of India I used exactly this for international wire routing through correspondent banks, where each hop charges a fee and regulation caps the number of intermediate banks. I loaded the fee graph from the database, cached it in Redis, and ran the bounded relaxation to pick the cheapest compliant route. Explaining the snapshot trick, the K plus one rounds, and why it beats Dijkstra under a hop limit is what shows an interviewer I understand this bounded shortest path technique.

answers.question: Given a connected weighted undirected graph, find the minimum spanning tree — the subset of edges that connects every vertex with the smallest total weight. Explain Prim's algorithm with a priority queue, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Prim's Minimum Spanning Tree (Cheapest Way to Connect Every Node)

s1_definition.profdef: Prim's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree by growing one tree outward from a starting vertex. At every step it adds the cheapest edge that connects a vertex already inside the tree to a vertex still outside it, using a min-heap of candidate edges keyed by weight. It stops once every vertex is inside the tree, and the sum of the chosen edges is the minimum total connection cost.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to lay a secure leased-line network connecting all its branches at the least total cost. Prim's starts at one branch and keeps attaching the cheapest cable to a branch not yet connected, until every branch is on the network.
s1_definition.oneliner: Grow one tree by always pulling in the cheapest edge that reaches a new vertex.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Prim's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree by growing one tree outward from a starting vertex. At every step it adds the cheapest edge that connects a vertex already inside the tree to a vertex still outside it, using a min-heap of candidate edges keyed by weight. It stops once every vertex is inside the tree, and the sum of the chosen edges is the minimum total connection cost.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to lay a secure leased-line network connecting all its branches at the least total cost. Prim's starts at one branch and keeps attaching the cheapest cable to a branch not yet connected, until every branch is on the network.

**One line to remember:** Grow one tree by always pulling in the cheapest edge that reaches a new vertex.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep a boolean `inTree` for each vertex and a min-heap of candidate edges stored as weight with destination vertex. We start by pushing the starting vertex with weight zero. We then repeatedly pop the cheapest edge from the heap; if its destination is already in the tree we discard it, otherwise we add that vertex to the tree, add the weight to our total, and push all edges from the new vertex that lead to vertices still outside the tree. The heap always surfaces the globally cheapest frontier edge, which is why the greedy choice is safe.

The core loop is `while (!pq.isEmpty()) { int[] top = pq.poll(); int w = top[0], v = top[1]; if (inTree[v]) continue; inTree[v] = true; total += w; for (int[] e : adj.get(v)) if (!inTree[e[0]]) pq.offer(new int[]{e[1], e[0]}); }`. A concrete check: with branches forming a triangle of edge weights 1, 2, and 3, Prim's picks weights 1 and 2 for a total of three and skips the heaviest edge. Senior nuance: with a binary heap the complexity is order of E log V, and the lazy variant that skips already-in-tree pops is simpler than decrease-key while staying efficient enough for most real graphs.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must connect all its branches with secure leased lines, and each possible cable between two branches has a monthly cost. Connecting every branch to every other branch is wasteful; the bank only needs enough cables so that every branch is reachable, at the lowest total cost. This is exactly how Prim's minimum spanning tree works: it selects the cheapest set of cables that keeps all branches connected.

The code defines a `BranchNetworkService` with `minimumCableCost(n, edges)` that runs Prim's with a priority queue. A `Demo` builds a small branch graph and logs the minimum total cable cost.

The input is a triangle of three branches with edge costs one, two, and three. Step 1: we build an undirected adjacency list and push branch zero with weight zero into the heap. Step 4: the heap now holds branch two at cost two and branch two at cost three; we pop cost two first, add branch two, and the total becomes three. Step 5: every branch is connected, so we stop and return a minimum cable cost of three, skipping the heaviest edge of cost three.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Prim's algorithm finds a minimum spanning tree by growing a single tree outward from any starting vertex, and at every step it greedily adds the cheapest edge that connects a vertex already in the tree to one still outside it. I drive this with a min-heap of frontier edges keyed by weight, so the cheapest safe edge is always at the top, and I keep going until every vertex has joined the tree.

The reason the greedy choice is correct is the cut property: for any way of splitting the vertices into those inside the tree and those outside, the cheapest edge crossing that cut must belong to some minimum spanning tree. Prim's always picks exactly that crossing edge, so each step is provably safe. In the lazy version I use a plain heap and simply discard any popped edge whose destination has already joined the tree, which avoids the complexity of a decrease-key operation while keeping the running time at E log V with a binary heap.

At the National Bank of India I used this to plan the leased-line network connecting all branches at the lowest total monthly cost, where each potential cable between two branches had a price. I loaded the link-cost graph from the database, cached it in Redis, and ran Prim's to choose the minimum set of cables that still kept every branch reachable. Explaining the growing tree, the cut property that justifies the greedy step, and the lazy-heap implementation is what shows an interviewer I genuinely understand minimum spanning trees.

answers.question: Given a begin word, an end word, and a dictionary of equal-length words, find the length of the shortest transformation sequence that changes one letter at a time, where every intermediate word must be in the dictionary. Explain the breadth-first search solution, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Word Ladder (Shortest Transformation Chain One Letter at a Time)

s1_definition.profdef: Word Ladder is a shortest path problem on an implicit graph where each word is a node and an edge connects two words that differ by exactly one letter. Because every edge has the same unit cost, breadth-first search from the begin word finds the fewest transformations to reach the end word. We generate neighbours on the fly by trying every single-letter change and keeping only those present in the dictionary.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India migrates an old product code to a new one, but compliance forces every intermediate code to be a valid registered code in the catalogue, changing one character at a time. We want the shortest valid chain of codes from the old to the new.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each word is a node, one-letter changes are edges, so BFS gives the shortest valid chain.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Word Ladder is a shortest path problem on an implicit graph where each word is a node and an edge connects two words that differ by exactly one letter. Because every edge has the same unit cost, breadth-first search from the begin word finds the fewest transformations to reach the end word. We generate neighbours on the fly by trying every single-letter change and keeping only those present in the dictionary.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India migrates an old product code to a new one, but compliance forces every intermediate code to be a valid registered code in the catalogue, changing one character at a time. We want the shortest valid chain of codes from the old to the new.

**One line to remember:** Each word is a node, one-letter changes are edges, so BFS gives the shortest valid chain.

sections.s2_technical:
We put all dictionary words into a hash set for constant-time membership checks, then run breadth-first search starting from the begin word at distance one. For the word at the front of the queue we generate every neighbour by replacing each position with each letter from a to z, and if the generated word is in the set we add it to the queue with distance plus one and remove it from the set so we never revisit it. The first time we generate the end word, its distance is the shortest chain length. Removing visited words from the set is how we mark them visited without a separate structure.

The neighbour generation is `for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) { char old = arr[i]; for (char c = 'a'; c <= 'z'; c++) { arr[i] = c; String next = new String(arr); if (dict.remove(next)) queue.add(next); } arr[i] = old; }`. A concrete check: from HIT to COG with dictionary HOT, DOT, DOG, LOT, LOG, COG, BFS finds HIT, HOT, DOT, DOG, COG, a length of five. Senior nuance: the complexity is order of N times L times 26 where N is the dictionary size and L is the word length, and a bidirectional BFS from both ends can dramatically cut the explored frontier.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India is retiring an old product code and must transform it into a new product code, but a compliance rule says every intermediate code must already exist in the official catalogue and only one character may change at each step. We want the shortest valid sequence of code changes so the migration touches as few intermediate codes as possible. This is exactly how Word Ladder works: it finds the fewest one-character steps through a dictionary of valid codes.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Ladder is a shortest path problem hiding behind a string puzzle. I treat each word as a node in an implicit graph, with an edge between any two words that differ by exactly one letter, and because every such edge costs the same single step, breadth-first search from the begin word finds the fewest transformations to reach the end word. I never build the graph explicitly; instead I generate each word's neighbours on the fly by trying every single-letter substitution and keeping only the results that exist in the dictionary.

The two details that make this efficient are a hash set for the dictionary, which gives constant-time membership checks, and removing each word from that set the moment I enqueue it, which doubles as a visited marker so I never process the same word twice. I process the queue level by level, incrementing the step count after each level, so the first time I dequeue the end word its distance is exactly the shortest chain length. For large dictionaries I would reach for bidirectional BFS, searching from both ends and meeting in the middle, which shrinks the explored frontier dramatically.

At the National Bank of India I used this shape for a product-code migration where compliance required every intermediate code to be a valid catalogue code and only one character could change per step. I loaded the catalogue into a set cached in Redis and ran the level-by-level search to find the shortest compliant chain from the old code to the new one. Explaining the implicit graph, the on-the-fly neighbour generation, and the set-as-visited trick is what shows an interviewer I can recognise a shortest path problem even when it is dressed up as string manipulation.

answers.question: Compute the nth Fibonacci number, where each number is the sum of the two before it. Explain the naive recursion, why it is slow, how memoization and the bottom-up rolling approach fix it, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Fibonacci Number (Introduction to Dynamic Programming with Memoization)

s1_definition.profdef: The Fibonacci sequence defines each term as the sum of the previous two terms, with base cases of zero and one. The naive recursion recomputes the same subproblems exponentially, so dynamic programming caches each result once. Memoization stores computed values top-down, while the bottom-up form keeps only the last two values in rolling variables for constant space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India projects a reward-points balance that each month equals the sum of the two previous months. Instead of recomputing the whole history every time, we remember the last two months and roll forward.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each term is the sum of the previous two, so cache results and roll two values forward.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Fibonacci sequence defines each term as the sum of the previous two terms, with base cases of zero and one. The naive recursion recomputes the same subproblems exponentially, so dynamic programming caches each result once. Memoization stores computed values top-down, while the bottom-up form keeps only the last two values in rolling variables for constant space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India projects a reward-points balance that each month equals the sum of the two previous months. Instead of recomputing the whole history every time, we remember the last two months and roll forward.

**One line to remember:** Each term is the sum of the previous two, so cache results and roll two values forward.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive recursion `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)` is correct but recomputes the same calls an exponential number of times, giving order of two-to-the-n work. The first dynamic programming fix is memoization: we keep an array or map, and before computing `fib(n)` we check if it is already stored, returning the cached value if so. This turns the exponential tree into a linear number of distinct computations. The second fix is bottom-up tabulation, where we compute from the base cases upward.

The bottom-up rolling core is `int prev2 = 0, prev1 = 1; for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) { int cur = prev1 + prev2; prev2 = prev1; prev1 = cur; } return n == 0 ? 0 : prev1;`. A concrete check: for n equal to six the sequence is 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, so the answer is eight. Senior nuance: memoization uses order-n time and order-n space, while the rolling bottom-up uses order-n time and constant space, which is the version to prefer when only the final value is needed and overflow is handled with long or BigInteger.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a loyalty programme where the projected reward-points target for a month equals the sum of the two previous months' targets, and analysts frequently ask for the target many months ahead. Recomputing the full chain each time is wasteful when the same intermediate months are requested repeatedly. This is exactly how the Fibonacci number works under dynamic programming: we cache each month's value once and roll forward.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Fibonacci number is the classic introduction to dynamic programming, and I use it to show that I understand the difference between a correct solution and an efficient one. The naive recursion, where each term calls itself for the previous two terms, is perfectly correct but does an exponential amount of work because it recomputes the same subproblems over and over. The entire point of dynamic programming is to compute each distinct subproblem exactly once.

There are two standard fixes, and I explain both. Memoization keeps the recursion but caches each result in an array or map, so the second time a term is needed it is returned instantly, turning the exponential call tree into a linear number of real computations. Tabulation flips this to bottom-up: I start from the base cases and build upward, and since each term only depends on the previous two, I keep just two rolling variables and discard everything older, which gives linear time and constant space.

At the National Bank of India I applied this shape to a loyalty projection where each month's reward target was the sum of the two previous months, and analysts queried targets far into the future. I computed the value with the rolling two-variable approach and cached results in Redis so repeated queries were instant. Explaining why the naive version is exponential, how memoization and tabulation each fix it, and why the rolling form reaches constant space is exactly how I demonstrate that I understand the foundation of dynamic programming.

answers.question: You climb a staircase of n steps, and at each move you take either one step or two steps. Count the number of distinct ways to reach the top. Explain the dynamic programming recurrence, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Climbing Stairs (Count Distinct Ways with Steps of One or Two)

s1_definition.profdef: Climbing Stairs counts the distinct ways to reach step n when each move advances one or two steps. The number of ways to reach step i equals the ways to reach step i minus one plus the ways to reach step i minus two, because the final move is either a single or a double step. This is the Fibonacci recurrence, solved bottom-up with two rolling variables in constant space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India lets a customer clear an instalment plan of n units by paying either one or two units per transaction, and we count how many distinct payment sequences finish the plan.
s1_definition.oneliner: Ways to reach a step equal the ways to the two steps below it, so it is Fibonacci.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Climbing Stairs counts the distinct ways to reach step n when each move advances one or two steps. The number of ways to reach step i equals the ways to reach step i minus one plus the ways to reach step i minus two, because the final move is either a single or a double step. This is the Fibonacci recurrence, solved bottom-up with two rolling variables in constant space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India lets a customer clear an instalment plan of n units by paying either one or two units per transaction, and we count how many distinct payment sequences finish the plan.

**One line to remember:** Ways to reach a step equal the ways to the two steps below it, so it is Fibonacci.

sections.s2_technical:
The key insight is that the very last move onto step i was either a one-step from step i minus one or a two-step from step i minus two, and those two groups of sequences are completely distinct. So the count at step i is the sum of the counts at the two steps below it. The base cases are one way to stand at step zero (do nothing) and one way to reach step one (a single step). From there we build upward.

The rolling core is `int oneBelow = 1, twoBelow = 1; for (int i = 2; i <= n; i++) { int cur = oneBelow + twoBelow; twoBelow = oneBelow; oneBelow = cur; } return oneBelow;`. A concrete check: for n equal to four the counts go 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, so there are five distinct ways. Senior nuance: it is the Fibonacci recurrence with shifted base cases, running in linear time and constant space; if the allowed step sizes were a general set, the recurrence would sum over each allowed step and become the coin-change style count.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India offers an instalment plan of n units where the customer may pay one or two units per transaction, and the product team wants to know how many distinct payment sequences complete the plan, for modelling customer behaviour. Counting by hand explodes quickly as n grows. This is exactly how Climbing Stairs works: the number of sequences to finish equals the sum of the sequences for the two smaller remaining amounts.

The code defines an `InstalmentPlanService` with `countPaymentSequences(units)` using the rolling recurrence. A `Demo` requests a plan size and logs the count.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Climbing Stairs is a counting problem that reduces to the Fibonacci recurrence once you see the key insight. To reach step n, the final move was either a single step from step n minus one or a double step from step n minus two, and those two sets of ways are completely separate. Therefore the number of ways to reach step n is simply the sum of the ways to reach the two steps below it, with base cases of one way to stand at the bottom and one way to reach the first step.

Because each count depends only on the two counts immediately below it, I do not need a full array. I keep two rolling variables, compute each step as their sum, and slide the window forward, which gives linear time and constant space. This is the same recurrence as Fibonacci but with shifted base cases, and I always mention that if the allowed step sizes were a general set rather than just one or two, the recurrence would sum over every allowed step size and turn into the coin-change style counting problem.

At the National Bank of India I used this to model an instalment plan where a customer could pay one or two units per transaction, and the product team wanted the number of distinct payment sequences that complete a plan of a given size. I computed it with the two-variable rolling recurrence and cached the results in Redis. Explaining why the last move splits the count into two independent groups, and why that makes it Fibonacci with constant space, is what shows an interviewer I can translate a word problem into a clean dynamic programming recurrence.

answers.question: Given an array of non-negative values, pick a subset with the maximum total such that no two picked elements are adjacent. Explain the dynamic programming recurrence, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: House Robber (Maximum Sum of Non-Adjacent Elements)

s1_definition.profdef: House Robber selects a maximum-value subset of an array with the constraint that no two chosen elements are adjacent. At each index the best total is the larger of skipping the element, keeping the previous best, or taking the element plus the best from two indices earlier. It is a linear dynamic programming scan solvable with two rolling variables in constant space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India runs promotional cash-back on a row of consecutive days but a rule forbids claiming cash-back on two back-to-back days. We pick the days that maximise total cash-back without ever choosing two in a row.
s1_definition.oneliner: At each element choose the better of skipping it or taking it plus the best from two back.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** House Robber selects a maximum-value subset of an array with the constraint that no two chosen elements are adjacent. At each index the best total is the larger of skipping the element, keeping the previous best, or taking the element plus the best from two indices earlier. It is a linear dynamic programming scan solvable with two rolling variables in constant space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India runs promotional cash-back on a row of consecutive days but a rule forbids claiming cash-back on two back-to-back days. We pick the days that maximise total cash-back without ever choosing two in a row.

**One line to remember:** At each element choose the better of skipping it or taking it plus the best from two back.

sections.s2_technical:
For each index we face a binary choice: either we skip the current value, in which case the best total is whatever it was at the previous index, or we take the current value, in which case we must add it to the best total from two indices back because the immediately previous index is now forbidden. We keep the maximum of these two options. Because the decision only looks one and two positions behind, two rolling variables suffice.

The rolling core is `int twoBack = 0, oneBack = 0; for (int v : values) { int take = twoBack + v; int best = Math.max(oneBack, take); twoBack = oneBack; oneBack = best; } return oneBack;`. A concrete check: with values 2, 7, 9, 3, 1, the best is taking 2, 9, and 1 for a total of twelve, which the scan produces. Senior nuance: the complexity is linear time and constant space; a circular variant where the first and last elements are also adjacent is solved by running the linear scan twice, once excluding the first element and once excluding the last.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India offers daily cash-back on a sequence of consecutive days, but a fraud-prevention rule forbids claiming cash-back on two adjacent days. The analytics team wants to know the maximum total cash-back a customer could legitimately claim across the promotion. Trying every combination is exponential. This is exactly how House Robber works: it finds the maximum non-adjacent sum in a single linear pass.

The code defines a `CashbackOptimizerService` with `maxNonAdjacentCashback(amounts)` using the rolling recurrence. A `Demo` provides daily cash-back values and logs the best total.

sections.s6_takeaway:
House Robber is the canonical maximum non-adjacent sum problem, and the insight is to frame each element as a binary decision. At every position I can either skip the current value, in which case my best running total is unchanged from the previous position, or I can take the current value, in which case I must add it to the best total from two positions back, because taking the immediately previous element is forbidden by the adjacency rule. The answer at each position is simply the larger of those two options.

Since every decision looks only one and two positions behind, I do not keep a full table. I carry two rolling variables, the best total ending one position back and the best ending two positions back, update them as I scan left to right, and the final value of the one-back variable is the answer. This runs in linear time and constant space, which I always contrast with the exponential cost of trying every subset.

At the National Bank of India I used this for a cash-back promotion where a fraud rule forbade claiming cash-back on two consecutive days, and the analytics team wanted the maximum total a customer could legitimately claim. I ran the linear scan over the daily values, and for a wrap-around promotion where the first and last days also counted as adjacent I ran the scan twice, once excluding the first day and once excluding the last, taking the better result. Explaining the skip-versus-take decision, the two-back dependency, and the circular variant is what shows an interviewer I understand this family of linear dynamic programming problems.

answers.question: Given items each with a weight and a value, and a knapsack capacity, choose a subset to maximise total value without exceeding the capacity, where each item is taken at most once. Explain the top-down memoized recursion, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: 0/1 Knapsack (Maximum Value Within a Weight Budget, Memoized)

s1_definition.profdef: The 0/1 Knapsack problem chooses a subset of items, each used at most once, to maximise total value subject to a weight capacity. The recursion at each item decides to include it, if it fits, or exclude it, and takes the better outcome. Overlapping subproblems indexed by item position and remaining capacity are cached, turning exponential recursion into a pseudo-polynomial solution.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a fixed capital budget and a shortlist of loan applications, each needing a certain amount of capital and promising a certain profit. We pick the subset of loans that maximises total profit without exceeding the capital budget.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each item take the better of including it (if it fits) or excluding it, and cache by index and capacity.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The 0/1 Knapsack problem chooses a subset of items, each used at most once, to maximise total value subject to a weight capacity. The recursion at each item decides to include it, if it fits, or exclude it, and takes the better outcome. Overlapping subproblems indexed by item position and remaining capacity are cached, turning exponential recursion into a pseudo-polynomial solution.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a fixed capital budget and a shortlist of loan applications, each needing a certain amount of capital and promising a certain profit. We pick the subset of loans that maximises total profit without exceeding the capital budget.

**One line to remember:** For each item take the better of including it (if it fits) or excluding it, and cache by index and capacity.

sections.s2_technical:
We define the subproblem as the best value achievable considering items from a given index onward with a given remaining capacity. At each item we always have the option to exclude it and move to the next item with the same capacity. If the item's weight fits in the remaining capacity, we also have the option to include it, adding its value and reducing the capacity by its weight. The answer for the subproblem is the maximum of these options. Because the same index-and-capacity pair recurs through different decision paths, we memoize results in a two-dimensional cache.

The recursion core is `int best(int i, int cap) { if (i == n) return 0; if (memo[i][cap] != -1) return memo[i][cap]; int exclude = best(i+1, cap); int include = weight[i] <= cap ? value[i] + best(i+1, cap - weight[i]) : 0; return memo[i][cap] = Math.max(exclude, include); }`. A concrete check: with weights 1, 3, 4, 5 and values 1, 4, 5, 7 and capacity 7, the best is items of weight 3 and 4 for value nine. Senior nuance: the complexity is order of items times capacity in both time and space, which is pseudo-polynomial because it depends on the numeric capacity, not just the item count.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has a fixed capital budget for the quarter and a shortlist of loan applications, each consuming a specific amount of capital and projected to return a specific profit. Each loan is either fully funded or not funded at all; there is no partial funding. The bank wants the subset of loans that maximises total projected profit without exceeding the capital budget. This is exactly how 0/1 Knapsack works: include or exclude each item to maximise value under a budget.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The 0/1 Knapsack problem is the archetype of include-or-exclude dynamic programming. Each item is taken at most once, so at every item I face a clean binary decision. I can always exclude the item and move to the next one with the same remaining capacity, and if the item fits I can also include it, adding its value and reducing the remaining capacity by its weight. The best value for that subproblem is the maximum of those two choices.

The reason plain recursion is slow is that the same subproblem, defined by which item I am considering and how much capacity remains, is reached through many different decision paths. I eliminate that waste by memoizing on a two-dimensional cache indexed by item position and remaining capacity, so each distinct subproblem is solved exactly once. This brings the running time down to the number of items times the capacity, which I am careful to describe as pseudo-polynomial because it scales with the numeric value of the capacity, not just the count of items.

At the National Bank of India I used this to pick loan applications under a fixed quarterly capital budget, where each loan needed a certain amount of capital and promised a certain profit, and each loan was either fully funded or not at all. I ran the memoized recursion over the shortlist to choose the subset that maximised projected profit without breaching the budget. Explaining the include-versus-exclude decision, the index-and-capacity subproblem, and why memoization makes it pseudo-polynomial is what shows an interviewer I understand knapsack-style dynamic programming.

answers.question: Explain the concept of tabulation in dynamic programming — how it differs from memoization, how you fill a table from base cases upward, the trade-offs, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Tabulation Introduction (Bottom-Up Dynamic Programming Explained)

s1_definition.profdef: Tabulation is the bottom-up form of dynamic programming. Instead of recursing from the goal down to base cases and caching on the way back, we fill a table starting from the base cases and iterate in an order where every subproblem's dependencies are already solved before we reach it. It eliminates recursion, avoids stack overflow, and often enables space optimisation by keeping only the most recent rows.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India builds a running end-of-day balance ledger starting from the opening balance and adding each day's transactions in order. Every day's figure relies only on days already posted, so we never have to look ahead or recurse.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fill the table from the base cases upward in dependency order, no recursion needed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Tabulation is the bottom-up form of dynamic programming. Instead of recursing from the goal down to base cases and caching on the way back, we fill a table starting from the base cases and iterate in an order where every subproblem's dependencies are already solved before we reach it. It eliminates recursion, avoids stack overflow, and often enables space optimisation by keeping only the most recent rows.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India builds a running end-of-day balance ledger starting from the opening balance and adding each day's transactions in order. Every day's figure relies only on days already posted, so we never have to look ahead or recurse.

**One line to remember:** Fill the table from the base cases upward in dependency order, no recursion needed.

sections.s2_technical:
Memoization is top-down: we write the natural recursion from the goal, and a cache remembers results so repeated subproblems are not recomputed. Tabulation is bottom-up: we identify the base cases, then choose an iteration order so that when we compute a cell, every cell it depends on is already filled. We never recurse, so there is no call-stack risk for large inputs. The hardest part is getting the iteration order right so dependencies are satisfied.

A representative skeleton is `dp[0] = base; for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) dp[i] = combine(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]); return dp[n];`, and when each cell depends only on a few recent cells we can replace the full array with rolling variables for constant space. A concrete check: tabulating Fibonacci fills dp as 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8 left to right, each cell reading its two predecessors. Senior nuance: tabulation and memoization have the same asymptotic complexity, but tabulation avoids recursion overhead and stack limits and makes space optimisation obvious, while memoization can be faster when only a small fraction of the state space is actually reachable.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India computes a daily running balance for an account where each day's closing balance depends on the previous day's closing balance plus that day's net transactions. Because each day strictly depends on earlier days, there is a natural bottom-up order. This is exactly how tabulation works: we fill the ledger from the opening balance forward, and each day reads only already-computed days.

The code defines a `RunningBalanceService` with `closingBalances(opening, dailyNet)` that fills a table bottom-up. A `Demo` provides daily net amounts and logs the closing balances.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Tabulation is the bottom-up way of doing dynamic programming, and I contrast it directly with memoization to show I understand both. Memoization is top-down: I write the natural recursion from the goal toward the base cases and let a cache remember each result so repeated subproblems are not recomputed. Tabulation flips the direction: I start from the base cases and fill a table outward, choosing an iteration order such that by the time I compute any cell, every cell it depends on is already filled.

The practical advantages of tabulation are that it uses no recursion, so there is no risk of a stack overflow on large inputs, and it makes space optimisation obvious, because once I see that each cell depends only on a couple of recent cells, I can throw away the rest of the table and keep rolling variables. The main discipline it demands is working out the correct iteration order up front so that dependencies are always satisfied. Asymptotically it matches memoization, but memoization can win when only a small fraction of the possible states is ever actually reached.

At the National Bank of India I used tabulation to compute daily running balances, where each day's closing balance depends only on the previous day's closing balance plus that day's net transactions. Filling the ledger left to right from the opening balance satisfied every dependency naturally and needed no recursion, and I could reduce it to a single rolling value when only the final balance mattered. Explaining the top-down versus bottom-up distinction, the need for a correct fill order, and the space optimisation that tabulation unlocks is what shows an interviewer I understand the foundations of dynamic programming.

answers.question: Solve the 0/1 Knapsack problem bottom-up with a table instead of recursion, then reduce the table to a single row. Explain the recurrence, the reverse-capacity iteration, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: 0/1 Knapsack Tabulation (Bottom-Up Table with Space Optimisation)

s1_definition.profdef: The tabulated 0/1 Knapsack fills a table where each cell holds the best value using the first i items within a capacity c. Each cell chooses the better of excluding item i, copying the value from the row above, or including item i, adding its value to the cell for the reduced capacity in the row above. The table reduces to one row iterated in reverse capacity order so each item is used at most once.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India allocates a fixed capital budget across one-time loan deals, each either fully funded or skipped. We build a table of best profit for every budget level as we consider each deal, then collapse it to a single running row.
s1_definition.oneliner: Fill best-value cells bottom-up, and with one row iterate capacity downward so each item is used once.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The tabulated 0/1 Knapsack fills a table where each cell holds the best value using the first i items within a capacity c. Each cell chooses the better of excluding item i, copying the value from the row above, or including item i, adding its value to the cell for the reduced capacity in the row above. The table reduces to one row iterated in reverse capacity order so each item is used at most once.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India allocates a fixed capital budget across one-time loan deals, each either fully funded or skipped. We build a table of best profit for every budget level as we consider each deal, then collapse it to a single running row.

**One line to remember:** Fill best-value cells bottom-up, and with one row iterate capacity downward so each item is used once.

sections.s2_technical:
The two-dimensional recurrence says the best value using the first i items at capacity c is the maximum of two options. Excluding item i copies the value from the cell directly above, meaning the best using the first i minus one items at the same capacity. Including item i, allowed only if its weight is at most c, adds its value to the cell above at capacity c minus its weight. We fill the table row by row, and the bottom-right cell is the answer.

The one-row optimisation is `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) for (int c = cap; c >= weight[i]; c--) dp[c] = Math.max(dp[c], value[i] + dp[c - weight[i]]);`. The capacity loop must run downward so that `dp[c - weight[i]]` still refers to the previous item's value, which enforces using each item at most once; iterating upward would allow reusing the same item and silently solve the unbounded knapsack instead. A concrete check: with weights 1, 3, 4, 5 and values 1, 4, 5, 7 and capacity 7, the final `dp[7]` is nine. Senior nuance: the time is items times capacity and the space drops from items times capacity down to just capacity with the single-row trick.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must allocate a fixed capital budget across a set of one-time loan deals, where each deal is either fully funded or skipped and promises a fixed profit for a fixed capital cost. The bank wants the maximum total profit within the budget, computed without deep recursion so it is safe for large deal lists. This is exactly how the tabulated 0/1 Knapsack works: build the best-profit table bottom-up and collapse it to one row.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The tabulated 0/1 Knapsack turns the recursive include-or-exclude logic into a bottom-up table, and the recurrence is exactly the same choice expressed over a grid. The best value using the first i items at capacity c is the larger of excluding item i, which copies the value from the row above at the same capacity, or including item i when it fits, which adds its value to the row above at the capacity reduced by its weight. I fill the grid row by row and read the answer from the bottom-right cell.

The part interviewers really want to hear is the space optimisation and why the loop direction matters. Because each row depends only on the row immediately above, I can collapse the whole grid into a single row. The catch is that when I update a cell I must read an older value that belongs to the previous item, so I iterate the capacity from high down to low. If I iterated upward I would read a value that was already updated for the current item, which would let me use the same item multiple times and silently turn it into the unbounded knapsack.

At the National Bank of India I used this to allocate a fixed capital budget across one-time loan deals, each either fully funded or skipped, computing the maximum total profit without any recursion so it stayed safe for large deal lists. I kept a single profit row sized to the budget and walked the capacity downward for each deal. Explaining the grid recurrence, the collapse to one row, and the crucial downward capacity loop that keeps it a 0/1 problem is what shows an interviewer I truly understand bottom-up knapsack.

answers.question: Given an array of non-negative integers and a target, determine whether any subset sums exactly to the target. Explain the dynamic programming boolean table, the reverse-iteration single-row optimisation, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Subset Sum (Can a Subset Reach an Exact Target)

s1_definition.profdef: Subset Sum decides whether some subset of the given numbers adds up exactly to a target. It is a boolean variant of 0/1 Knapsack: a reachable-sum flag is true if we can form that sum either without the current item or by taking the current item and reaching the remaining amount. A single boolean row iterated in reverse target order solves it in capacity space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India must settle an exact outstanding amount by combining whole invoice payments, each used at most once. We check whether any combination of invoices sums precisely to the amount due.
s1_definition.oneliner: A sum is reachable if it was reachable before, or reachable after subtracting the current number.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Subset Sum decides whether some subset of the given numbers adds up exactly to a target. It is a boolean variant of 0/1 Knapsack: a reachable-sum flag is true if we can form that sum either without the current item or by taking the current item and reaching the remaining amount. A single boolean row iterated in reverse target order solves it in capacity space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India must settle an exact outstanding amount by combining whole invoice payments, each used at most once. We check whether any combination of invoices sums precisely to the amount due.

**One line to remember:** A sum is reachable if it was reachable before, or reachable after subtracting the current number.

sections.s2_technical:
We keep a boolean array where entry s is true if some subset sums to s. We start with entry zero true, because the empty subset sums to zero. For each number we try to extend existing reachable sums: if sum s minus the current number was reachable, then s is now reachable too. To ensure each number is used at most once, we iterate the target from high down to low, so we read the state from before the current number was processed.

The single-row core is `boolean[] dp = new boolean[target + 1]; dp[0] = true; for (int num : nums) for (int s = target; s >= num; s--) if (dp[s - num]) dp[s] = true;`. A concrete check: with numbers 3, 34, 4, 12, 5, 2 and target 9, the subset 4 and 5 reaches nine, so the answer is true. Senior nuance: the complexity is numbers times target in time and target in space; the downward loop is the same correctness guard as in 0/1 Knapsack, preventing a single number from being counted multiple times.

This is exactly how Subset Sum works: it tests whether a subset reaches an exact target.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Subset Sum asks whether some subset of a set of numbers adds up exactly to a target, and I recognise it immediately as the boolean cousin of the 0/1 Knapsack. Instead of tracking the best value, I track a simple truth: for each possible sum, can I form it with some subset? I seed the sum of zero as reachable, because the empty subset always sums to zero, and then each number lets me extend any already-reachable sum by that number.

The implementation is a single boolean row sized to the target plus one. For each number I ask, for every sum from the target downward, whether the sum minus that number was already reachable, and if so I mark the sum reachable. The downward iteration is the same correctness guard as in 0/1 Knapsack: it ensures I am reading the reachability state from before the current number was introduced, so a single number is never counted more than once. I can also exit early the moment the target slot becomes reachable.

At the National Bank of India I used this in invoice settlement, where we needed to pay a vendor an exact outstanding amount by combining whole invoices, each paid in full or skipped. I ran the boolean subset-sum table over the invoice amounts to confirm whether an exact combination existed before attempting settlement, avoiding any over- or under-payment. Explaining the reachable-sum flag, the empty-subset seed, and the downward loop that keeps each number single-use is what shows an interviewer I understand this boolean dynamic programming pattern.

answers.question: Given an array of non-negative integers and a target, count the number of ways to assign a plus or minus sign to each number so the signed sum equals the target. Explain the reduction to a subset-count problem, the dynamic programming, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Target Sum (Count Ways to Assign Plus and Minus Signs)

s1_definition.profdef: Target Sum counts sign assignments, each number getting a plus or minus, whose total equals the target. By letting P be the sum of plus numbers and N the sum of minus numbers, P minus N equals the target and P plus N equals the total, so P equals the total plus the target divided by two. This reduces the problem to counting subsets that sum to that value, a counting variant of Subset Sum.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India reconciles a net position where each pending entry can be a credit or a debit, and it wants to count how many credit-debit labellings produce an exact target net balance.
s1_definition.oneliner: Reduce signed sums to counting subsets that total (sum plus target) over two.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Target Sum counts sign assignments, each number getting a plus or minus, whose total equals the target. By letting P be the sum of plus numbers and N the sum of minus numbers, P minus N equals the target and P plus N equals the total, so P equals the total plus the target divided by two. This reduces the problem to counting subsets that sum to that value, a counting variant of Subset Sum.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India reconciles a net position where each pending entry can be a credit or a debit, and it wants to count how many credit-debit labellings produce an exact target net balance.

**One line to remember:** Reduce signed sums to counting subsets that total (sum plus target) over two.

sections.s2_technical:
Split the numbers into a positive group P and a negative group N. We need P minus N equal to the target, and we know P plus N equals the total of all numbers. Adding these two equations gives two times P equals total plus target, so P equals total plus target divided by two. If total plus target is negative or odd, no assignment works and the answer is zero. Otherwise we count the subsets whose sum equals that P, which is the counting form of subset sum.

The counting core is `int[] dp = new int[subset + 1]; dp[0] = 1; for (int num : nums) for (int s = subset; s >= num; s--) dp[s] += dp[s - num]; return dp[subset];`. A concrete check: with numbers 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 and target 3, total is five, so P is four, and the number of subsets summing to four is five, matching the known answer. Senior nuance: the dp entries count ways rather than feasibility, the base case dp of zero is one empty way, and the time is numbers times the derived subset value with space equal to that value.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India reconciles a set of pending ledger entries where each entry may post as a credit or a debit, and the reconciliation team wants to count how many credit-debit labellings produce an exact target net position. Enumerating all two-to-the-n labellings is infeasible for many entries. This is exactly how Target Sum works: it reduces the signed-sum count to counting subsets that reach a derived value.

The code defines a `ReconciliationService` with `countLabellings(entries, target)` using the subset-count table. A `Demo` provides entries and logs the number of labellings.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Target Sum looks like a brute-force sign-assignment problem, but the key move is an algebraic reduction that turns it into a clean counting problem. I split the numbers into those that get a plus sign and those that get a minus sign. The plus group minus the minus group must equal the target, and the plus group plus the minus group equals the total of all numbers. Adding those two facts tells me the plus group must sum to the total plus the target, divided by two.

Once I have that derived value, the whole problem becomes counting how many subsets sum to it, which is the counting form of subset sum. I guard the edge cases first: if the total plus the target is negative or odd, no valid assignment exists and the answer is zero. Otherwise I use a single integer row seeded with one way to make zero, and for each number I accumulate ways by adding the count from the slot one number lower, iterating the sum downward so each number is used at most once.

At the National Bank of India I used this during reconciliation, where each pending ledger entry could post as a credit or a debit and we wanted to count how many credit-debit labellings produced an exact target net position. Rather than enumerate an exponential number of labellings, I applied the reduction and counted subsets with the dynamic programming row. Explaining the algebra that converts signs into a subset target, the feasibility guards, and the counting recurrence is what shows an interviewer I can simplify a hard-looking problem into a known pattern.

answers.question: Given an array of numbers, find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence, where the chosen elements keep their original order but need not be contiguous. Explain the quadratic dynamic programming and the optimal patience-sorting approach, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Longest Increasing Subsequence (Longest Strictly Rising Pick)

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Increasing Subsequence finds the longest subsequence whose values strictly increase while preserving the original order. The quadratic dynamic programming defines the best length ending at each index as one plus the best among all earlier smaller elements. The optimal approach maintains the smallest possible tail for each achievable length using binary search, giving n log n time.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India reviews a customer's monthly closing balances and wants the longest run of months, not necessarily consecutive, where the balance kept strictly rising, as a signal of improving financial health.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep the smallest tail for each length and binary-search each element into place for n log n.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Increasing Subsequence finds the longest subsequence whose values strictly increase while preserving the original order. The quadratic dynamic programming defines the best length ending at each index as one plus the best among all earlier smaller elements. The optimal approach maintains the smallest possible tail for each achievable length using binary search, giving n log n time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India reviews a customer's monthly closing balances and wants the longest run of months, not necessarily consecutive, where the balance kept strictly rising, as a signal of improving financial health.

**One line to remember:** Keep the smallest tail for each length and binary-search each element into place for n log n.

sections.s2_technical:
The quadratic version keeps an array where the entry at index i is the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending exactly at i. For each i we look back at every earlier index j, and if the value at j is smaller than the value at i we can extend that subsequence, so we take one plus the best such length. The answer is the maximum entry. This is simple but costs order n squared.

The optimal version maintains a list of tails, where tails at position k is the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k plus one: `for (int x : nums) { int pos = lowerBound(tails, x); if (pos == tails.size()) tails.add(x); else tails.set(pos, x); } return tails.size();`. A concrete check: with balances 10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18 the longest increasing run has length four, for example 2, 3, 7, 18. Senior nuance: the tails list is not itself a valid subsequence, only its length is meaningful; reconstructing the actual subsequence needs predecessor pointers, and the binary search gives n log n time with linear space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India analyses a customer's sequence of monthly closing balances and wants the longest stretch of months, not necessarily back to back, during which the balance strictly increased, as a measure of improving financial health for a credit decision. Checking every possible stretch is exponential. This is exactly how Longest Increasing Subsequence works: it finds the longest strictly rising pick in order.

The code defines a `FinancialHealthService` with `longestRisingRun(balances)` using the patience-sorting binary search. A `Demo` provides monthly balances and logs the longest rising run length.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Longest Increasing Subsequence asks for the longest strictly rising pick of elements while keeping their original order, and I always present two solutions to show depth. The straightforward dynamic programming keeps, for each index, the length of the best increasing subsequence ending there, computed by looking back at every earlier smaller element and extending it, which is clear but costs quadratic time.

The optimal approach is patience sorting with binary search. I maintain a list of tails where the entry at each position holds the smallest possible ending value of an increasing subsequence of that length. For each new element I binary-search for the first tail that is greater than or equal to it; if none exists the element extends the longest run and I append it, otherwise I overwrite that tail because this element gives a smaller, more extendable ending for that length. The length of the tails list is the answer, and I am careful to note that the tails list itself is not a valid subsequence, only its length is meaningful, so reconstructing the actual sequence needs predecessor pointers.

At the National Bank of India I used this on a customer's monthly closing balances to find the longest stretch of strictly rising balances as a credit-health signal. I ran the n log n version so it stayed fast even over long balance histories pulled from the warehouse. Explaining the quadratic dynamic programming, the smallest-tail insight behind the n log n method, and the subtlety that the tails array encodes only the length are exactly what convince an interviewer I understand this problem beyond a memorised template.

answers.question: Explain the classic quadratic bottom-up tabulation for the Longest Increasing Subsequence, how each cell is built from earlier cells, how to reconstruct the actual subsequence with predecessor pointers, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: LIS Tabulation (Quadratic Bottom-Up and Reconstructing the Sequence)

s1_definition.profdef: The quadratic tabulation for Longest Increasing Subsequence fills an array where each cell holds the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at that index. Each cell is one plus the maximum length among all earlier indices with a smaller value, defaulting to one. Predecessor pointers recorded during the fill let us walk back and reconstruct the actual elements, not just the length.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India not only wants the longest run of strictly rising monthly balances but also wants to list exactly which months formed that run, so analysts can point to the specific improving months in a credit report.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each cell is one plus the best smaller-earlier cell, and predecessor links rebuild the actual run.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The quadratic tabulation for Longest Increasing Subsequence fills an array where each cell holds the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at that index. Each cell is one plus the maximum length among all earlier indices with a smaller value, defaulting to one. Predecessor pointers recorded during the fill let us walk back and reconstruct the actual elements, not just the length.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India not only wants the longest run of strictly rising monthly balances but also wants to list exactly which months formed that run, so analysts can point to the specific improving months in a credit report.

**One line to remember:** Each cell is one plus the best smaller-earlier cell, and predecessor links rebuild the actual run.

sections.s2_technical:
We create a length array where every entry starts at one, because any single element is an increasing subsequence of length one. For each index i we scan all earlier indices j, and whenever the value at j is smaller than the value at i and the length at j plus one beats the current length at i, we update the length at i and record j as the predecessor of i. We track the overall best length and the index where it ends. To reconstruct, we follow predecessor links from that ending index back to the start, collecting values, then reverse them.

The fill core is `for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { len[i] = 1; prev[i] = -1; for (int j = 0; j < i; j++) if (nums[j] < nums[i] && len[j] + 1 > len[i]) { len[i] = len[j] + 1; prev[i] = j; } }`. A concrete check: with balances 3, 4, 1, 5 the length array becomes 1, 2, 1, 3 and following predecessors from the last index yields 3, 4, 5. Senior nuance: this is order n squared time and linear space, slower than the n log n patience method, but it reconstructs the actual subsequence very naturally, which the binary-search method does not do without extra bookkeeping.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants not just the length of the longest strictly rising run of monthly balances but the exact months that formed it, so a credit report can cite the specific improving months. The length alone is not enough; analysts need the actual sequence. This is exactly how the quadratic tabulation with predecessor pointers works: it builds lengths bottom-up and reconstructs the real run.

  ── State: len[i], prev[i], bestLen, bestEnd ──────────────
  prev links form a chain from bestEnd back to start

  Contract for longestRisingSequence(balances):
    Pre:  balances not null
    Post: the actual longest strictly increasing subsequence
    Time O(n^2), Space O(n)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The quadratic tabulation for the Longest Increasing Subsequence is the version I reach for when I need the actual elements, not merely the length. I keep a length array where each entry holds the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends exactly at that index, and I start every entry at one because a single element is itself an increasing subsequence. For each index I scan all earlier indices, and whenever an earlier value is smaller and extending its run would beat my current best, I update my length and record that earlier index as my predecessor.

The predecessor array is what makes reconstruction clean. After the fill I know the best overall length and the index where it ends, so I follow the predecessor links backward from that ending index, collecting each value, and then reverse the collected list to put it in forward order. This is order n squared time and linear space, which is slower than the n log n patience-sorting method, but it reconstructs the real subsequence naturally, whereas the binary-search method only gives the length without extra bookkeeping.

At the National Bank of India I used this when a credit report needed to cite the exact months during which a customer's balance strictly rose, not just how many such months there were. I ran the quadratic fill over the monthly balances and followed the predecessor chain to produce the actual list of improving months. Explaining the length-ending-here definition, the predecessor links, and the trade-off against the faster method that cannot easily reconstruct is what shows an interviewer I understand both the computation and the recovery of the answer.
