answers.question: Given two sequences, find the length of the longest subsequence common to both, preserving order but not requiring contiguity. Explain the two-dimensional dynamic programming, the row-rolling optimisation, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Longest Common Subsequence (Longest Order-Preserving Match Between Two Sequences)

s1_definition.profdef: The Longest Common Subsequence finds the longest sequence of elements appearing in both inputs in the same relative order, not necessarily contiguously. A grid cell holds the best length for the two prefixes: when the current characters match it is one plus the diagonal cell, otherwise it is the better of dropping one character from either side. The grid reduces to two rolling rows.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India compares two versions of a transaction log for the same account and wants the longest ordered set of matching entries, which reveals the shared backbone and highlights what was inserted or removed.
s1_definition.oneliner: On a match add one to the diagonal, otherwise take the better of the two neighbours.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Longest Common Subsequence finds the longest sequence of elements appearing in both inputs in the same relative order, not necessarily contiguously. A grid cell holds the best length for the two prefixes: when the current characters match it is one plus the diagonal cell, otherwise it is the better of dropping one character from either side. The grid reduces to two rolling rows.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India compares two versions of a transaction log for the same account and wants the longest ordered set of matching entries, which reveals the shared backbone and highlights what was inserted or removed.

**One line to remember:** On a match add one to the diagonal, otherwise take the better of the two neighbours.

sections.s2_technical:
We build a grid where the cell at row i and column j is the length of the longest common subsequence of the first i elements of the first sequence and the first j elements of the second. If the i-th and j-th elements are equal, the cell is one plus the diagonal cell above-left, because we extend the match. If they differ, the cell is the larger of the cell above, which drops the i-th element, and the cell to the left, which drops the j-th element. The bottom-right cell is the answer.

The fill core is `for (int i = 1; i <= m; i++) for (int j = 1; j <= n; j++) dp[i][j] = a.charAt(i-1) == b.charAt(j-1) ? dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 : Math.max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]);`. A concrete check: for ABCBDAB and BDCAB the longest common subsequence has length four, for example BCAB. Senior nuance: the time is the product of the two lengths and the space can drop from that product to twice the shorter length by keeping only the previous and current rows; reconstructing the actual subsequence requires either the full grid or stored direction choices.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India keeps two versions of a transaction log for the same account, one from the core banking system and one from a reconciliation feed, and wants the longest ordered sequence of matching entries to identify the shared backbone and spot inserted or dropped entries. Comparing entry by entry misses matches that are out of alignment. This is exactly how Longest Common Subsequence works: it finds the longest order-preserving match.

The code defines a `LogComparisonService` with `longestCommonLength(logA, logB)` using the row-rolling grid. A `Demo` provides two logs and logs the common-length.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Longest Common Subsequence finds the longest ordered set of elements that appears in both inputs without requiring them to be contiguous, and it is the backbone of diff tools and version comparison. I model it as a grid where the cell at row i, column j is the best common length between the first i elements of one sequence and the first j elements of the other. The recurrence has just two cases: if the current two elements match, the cell is one plus the diagonal cell, because the match extends the previous solution; if they differ, the cell is the larger of the cell directly above and the cell directly to the left, each of which drops one element from one side.

The optimisation I always mention is that each cell depends only on the current and previous rows, so I keep two rolling rows and reduce the space from the full product of the two lengths down to the length of the shorter sequence. If I also need the actual common subsequence rather than just its length, I either retain the full grid or store the direction choice at each cell and walk backward from the bottom-right corner.

At the National Bank of India I used this to compare two versions of an account's transaction log, one from the core system and one from a reconciliation feed, to extract the longest ordered set of matching entries and thereby highlight what had been inserted or dropped. I ran the rolling-row version so memory stayed small even on long logs. Explaining the match-extends-the-diagonal rule, the drop-one-side rule for mismatches, and the row-rolling space optimisation is what shows an interviewer I understand this foundational two-sequence dynamic programming.

answers.question: Count the number of distinct paths from the top-left to the bottom-right of an m by n grid, moving only right or down. Explain the dynamic programming recurrence, the single-row optimisation, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Unique Paths (Count Grid Routes Moving Only Right or Down)

s1_definition.profdef: Unique Paths counts routes from the top-left to the bottom-right of a grid when only rightward and downward moves are allowed. The number of ways to reach a cell is the sum of the ways to reach the cell above it and the cell to its left, with the top row and left column each having exactly one path. The grid reduces to a single row updated left to right.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India models an approval workflow drawn as a grid, where a request can only move to the next stage or to the next department, and it counts how many distinct approval routes exist from start to final sign-off.
s1_definition.oneliner: Ways to a cell equal ways from above plus ways from the left.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Unique Paths counts routes from the top-left to the bottom-right of a grid when only rightward and downward moves are allowed. The number of ways to reach a cell is the sum of the ways to reach the cell above it and the cell to its left, with the top row and left column each having exactly one path. The grid reduces to a single row updated left to right.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India models an approval workflow drawn as a grid, where a request can only move to the next stage or to the next department, and it counts how many distinct approval routes exist from start to final sign-off.

**One line to remember:** Ways to a cell equal ways from above plus ways from the left.

sections.s2_technical:
Every cell can only be entered from directly above or directly to the left, and those two groups of paths are completely distinct, so the count at a cell is the sum of the counts of those two neighbours. The entire top row has exactly one path, moving only right, and the entire left column has exactly one path, moving only down, which gives the base cases. We fill the grid and read the bottom-right cell.

Because each row depends only on the row above and the cell to the left, a single row suffices: `int[] dp = new int[n]; Arrays.fill(dp, 1); for (int i = 1; i < m; i++) for (int j = 1; j < n; j++) dp[j] += dp[j - 1]; return dp[n - 1];`, where `dp[j]` before the addition is the cell above and `dp[j - 1]` is the cell to the left. A concrete check: a three by seven grid has twenty-eight unique paths. Senior nuance: the time is the product of the dimensions and the space is the smaller dimension; there is also a closed-form binomial answer choosing the down moves among the total moves, which is constant time but risks overflow.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India models a loan approval workflow as a grid, where a request advances either to the next approval stage or across to the next department, and risk analysts want to count the number of distinct approval routes from intake to final sign-off, to understand process complexity. Enumerating all routes by hand explodes combinatorially. This is exactly how Unique Paths works: the routes to a point are the sum of the routes from above and from the left.

The code defines a `WorkflowPathService` with `countApprovalRoutes(stages, departments)` using the single-row dynamic programming. A `Demo` sets a grid size and logs the number of routes.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Unique Paths counts the routes across a grid when only rightward and downward moves are allowed, and the recurrence falls straight out of the movement rule. Any cell can only be entered from the cell directly above it or the cell directly to its left, and those two sets of paths never overlap, so the number of ways to reach a cell is simply the sum of the ways to reach those two neighbours. The entire top row and the entire left column each have exactly one path, which gives the base cases.

Because each cell depends only on the row above and the cell immediately to the left, I collapse the grid to a single row initialised to all ones and update it left to right. In that single row, the value already sitting in a cell represents the cell above, and the value just to its left represents the cell to the left, so a single addition does the work. This runs in time proportional to the product of the dimensions and space proportional to the smaller dimension. I also mention the closed-form binomial answer, which chooses the down moves among the total moves in constant time but can overflow for large grids.

At the National Bank of India I used this to model a loan approval workflow as a grid, where a request moved either to the next approval stage or across to the next department, and risk analysts wanted the number of distinct approval routes from intake to final sign-off. I computed it with the single-row dynamic programming. Explaining the above-plus-left recurrence, the base-case row and column, and the single-row space optimisation is what shows an interviewer I can derive a counting recurrence directly from a problem's movement constraints.

answers.question: Given daily prices, maximise profit from buying and selling a stock, covering the single-transaction case and the unlimited-transaction case. Explain both algorithms, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock (Single and Multiple Transactions)

s1_definition.profdef: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock maximises trading profit from a price series. With a single allowed transaction we track the lowest price seen so far and the best profit of selling today at that minimum. With unlimited transactions the optimum is the sum of every positive day-over-day gain, which captures every upward move. Both run in a single linear pass.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India trading desk reviews a security's daily prices and wants the maximum profit, either from one clean buy-and-sell or from many back-to-back trades capturing every rise.
s1_definition.oneliner: One trade tracks the min and best sell; many trades sum every positive daily gain.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock maximises trading profit from a price series. With a single allowed transaction we track the lowest price seen so far and the best profit of selling today at that minimum. With unlimited transactions the optimum is the sum of every positive day-over-day gain, which captures every upward move. Both run in a single linear pass.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India trading desk reviews a security's daily prices and wants the maximum profit, either from one clean buy-and-sell or from many back-to-back trades capturing every rise.

**One line to remember:** One trade tracks the min and best sell; many trades sum every positive daily gain.

sections.s2_technical:
For the single-transaction case we scan the prices, keeping the minimum price seen so far as the best buy point. On each day we compute the profit of selling that day, which is today's price minus the running minimum, and keep the best such profit. Because we only ever sell after buying, the running minimum guarantees the buy day precedes the sell day. For the unlimited-transaction case, the maximum profit is simply the sum of every positive difference between consecutive days, because capturing each individual upward step is equivalent to buying at every local trough and selling at every local peak.

The single-pass cores are `int minSoFar = prices[0], best = 0; for (int p : prices) { minSoFar = Math.min(minSoFar, p); best = Math.max(best, p - minSoFar); }` and `int profit = 0; for (int i = 1; i < prices.length; i++) if (prices[i] > prices[i-1]) profit += prices[i] - prices[i-1];`. A concrete check: for prices 7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4 the single-transaction best is five, buying at one and selling at six, while the unlimited best is seven. Senior nuance: both are linear time and constant space; the bounded-k-transaction and with-cooldown variants need a small state-machine dynamic programming, but these two base cases are greedy and need no table.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India trading desk analyses a security's daily closing prices and wants the maximum profit achievable, both under a rule allowing just one buy-and-sell and under a rule allowing unlimited trades. Comparing every buy-sell pair is quadratic. This is exactly how Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock works: a running minimum solves the single trade, and summing positive daily gains solves unlimited trades.

```
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── State: minSoFar/best  or  running profit ──────────────
  buy always precedes sell via running minimum

  Contract for maxSingleTrade / maxUnlimitedTrades(prices):
    Pre:  prices not null
    Post: max profit under the respective rule
    Time O(n), Space O(1)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock is a family of problems, and I always separate the two base cases clearly. With a single allowed transaction, I scan the prices once while tracking the lowest price seen so far as my best possible buy point, and on each day I compute the profit of selling that day against that running minimum, keeping the best. Because the minimum only ever looks backward, the buy day is always before the sell day, so the answer is valid without comparing every pair.

With unlimited transactions, the optimum is simply the sum of every positive difference between consecutive days. Capturing each individual upward step is mathematically equivalent to buying at every local trough and selling at every local peak, so I just add up all the gains and ignore the drops. Both of these are greedy single passes in linear time and constant space with no table at all, which I contrast with the harder variants: limiting to at most k transactions or adding a cooldown day both require a small state-machine dynamic programming that tracks holding and not-holding states.

At the National Bank of India I used these on a trading desk to report the maximum achievable profit on a security's daily price series under different trading rules. I ran the running-minimum scan for the single-trade figure and the positive-gain sum for the unlimited figure, both fast enough for real-time dashboards. Explaining the running-minimum logic, why summing positive steps is optimal for unlimited trades, and how the k-transaction and cooldown variants escalate to a state machine is what shows an interviewer I understand this whole problem family.

answers.question: Given a stick of length L and a set of positions where it must be cut, where each cut costs the length of the piece being cut, find the minimum total cost to make all cuts in any order. Explain the interval dynamic programming, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick (Interval Dynamic Programming)

s1_definition.profdef: Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick is an interval dynamic programming problem where each cut costs the current length of the segment it divides, and the order of cuts changes the total. We add the two ends to the sorted cut positions, then for each span between two boundary cuts we choose the first cut inside that minimises the span's length plus the optimal costs of the two resulting sub-spans. The answer is the optimum over the full stick.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India splits a large bond block into required denominations, and each split charges a fee proportional to the size of the block being split. We choose the split order that minimises total fees.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each span, try every first cut inside it and add the span length plus the two sub-span optima.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick is an interval dynamic programming problem where each cut costs the current length of the segment it divides, and the order of cuts changes the total. We add the two ends to the sorted cut positions, then for each span between two boundary cuts we choose the first cut inside that minimises the span's length plus the optimal costs of the two resulting sub-spans. The answer is the optimum over the full stick.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India splits a large bond block into required denominations, and each split charges a fee proportional to the size of the block being split. We choose the split order that minimises total fees.

**One line to remember:** For each span, try every first cut inside it and add the span length plus the two sub-span optima.

sections.s2_technical:
We take the cut positions, add the two stick ends zero and L, and sort them, so the cuts become boundaries. We define the cost of a span between boundary index i and boundary index j, when there are cuts strictly inside, as the length of that span, which is the position at j minus the position at i, plus the minimum over every interior cut k of the optimal cost of the left sub-span from i to k plus the right sub-span from k to j. A span with no interior cut costs zero. We solve shorter spans first so longer spans can reuse them.

The core recurrence is `dp[i][j] = (j - i < 2) ? 0 : min over k in (i, j) of (pos[j] - pos[i]) + dp[i][k] + dp[k][j]`. A concrete check: for a stick of length seven with cuts at one, three, and four, the minimum total cost is sixteen when the cuts are ordered well, versus a larger cost for a naive order. Senior nuance: the complexity is order of the number of boundaries cubed because there are a quadratic number of spans and each tries a linear number of first cuts, and the trick of adding the two ends is what turns a messy order problem into a clean interval dynamic programming.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India holds a large bond block of a certain face value and must split it at several required denomination boundaries for different clients, where each split operation charges a fee proportional to the size of the block being split at that moment. The order of splits changes the total fee. This is exactly how Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick works: it finds the split order that minimises the total fee using interval dynamic programming.

The code defines a `BondSplitService` with `minSplitCost(blockLength, cuts)` using the interval table. A `Demo` provides a block length and cut points and logs the minimum cost.

The input is a block of length seven with required cuts at one, three, and four. Step 1: we add the two ends and sort the boundaries into zero, one, three, four, seven. Step 5: the span from zero to seven tries each of the three cuts as the first split and combines their sub-span optima. sections.s6_takeaway:
Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick is a classic interval dynamic programming problem, and the critical modelling move is to add the two ends of the stick to the list of cut positions and sort them, so every cut becomes a boundary. The reason the problem is hard at first glance is that the cost of a cut depends on the current length of the piece, which depends on which cuts were already made, so the order matters.

The insight that tames it is to think about which cut is made first within a given span. For a span between two boundaries, if I decide which interior cut happens first, that first cut costs the full length of the span, and then the span splits into two independent sub-spans whose optimal costs I can look up because they are shorter and already solved. So the cost of a span is its length plus the minimum, over every choice of first interior cut, of the two sub-span optima. I fill the table by increasing span width, and the full stick's entry is the answer. This is cubic in the number of boundaries because there are a quadratic number of spans and each tries a linear number of first cuts.

At the National Bank of India I used this shape to plan splitting a large bond block into required denominations, where each split charged a fee proportional to the size of the block being split and the split order changed the total fee. I ran the interval dynamic programming to find the cheapest ordering. Explaining why adding the ends turns it into clean intervals, the first-cut-within-a-span reasoning, and the fill order from short to long spans is what shows an interviewer I understand interval dynamic programming.

answers.question: Summarise how to recognise a dynamic programming problem and how to frame its state and transition. Explain optimal substructure, overlapping subproblems, the standard patterns, the memoization-versus-tabulation choice, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Dynamic Programming Revision (Recognising and Framing DP Problems)

s1_definition.profdef: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has optimal substructure, meaning an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to smaller subproblems, and overlapping subproblems, meaning the same subproblems recur. The craft is defining a state that captures everything needed to extend the solution, writing a transition between states, fixing base cases, and choosing memoization for top-down or tabulation for bottom-up.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India reuses the same partial calculations across many reports rather than recomputing them, exactly as dynamic programming solves each subproblem once and reuses the answer everywhere it is needed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Define the state, write the transition, fix the base cases, then memoize or tabulate.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Dynamic programming applies when a problem has optimal substructure, meaning an optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to smaller subproblems, and overlapping subproblems, meaning the same subproblems recur. The craft is defining a state that captures everything needed to extend the solution, writing a transition between states, fixing base cases, and choosing memoization for top-down or tabulation for bottom-up.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India reuses the same partial calculations across many reports rather than recomputing them, exactly as dynamic programming solves each subproblem once and reuses the answer everywhere it is needed.

**One line to remember:** Define the state, write the transition, fix the base cases, then memoize or tabulate.

sections.s2_technical:
The two signals that a problem is dynamic programming are optimal substructure, where the best answer decomposes into best answers of smaller pieces, and overlapping subproblems, where a plain recursion would recompute the same inputs many times. Once recognised, the method is disciplined: choose a state that is the minimal set of parameters describing a subproblem, write a transition expressing a state's answer in terms of smaller states, and set the base cases that need no recursion.

The standard patterns recur across interviews: linear sequence problems like Fibonacci and House Robber use a one-dimensional state; two-sequence problems like Longest Common Subsequence and Edit Distance use a two-dimensional grid; knapsack and subset problems use an item-and-capacity state; interval problems like cutting a stick use a span state; and grid-path problems use a coordinate state. A representative skeleton is `long solve(state s) { if (isBase(s)) return baseValue(s); if (memo.containsKey(s)) return memo.get(s); long best = combine over choices of solve(next(s, choice)); memo.put(s, best); return best; }`. Senior nuance: memoization is natural when only part of the state space is reachable, while tabulation avoids recursion limits and makes space optimisation obvious; the two share asymptotic complexity but differ in constant factors and stack safety.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs several analytics reports that share the same underlying partial computations, and recomputing those partials for every report wastes compute. The team wants a disciplined way to identify the reusable subproblem, compute it once, and reuse it. This is exactly how dynamic programming works: identify the state, solve each state once, and reuse. We demonstrate the framing on a small minimum-coins problem that models making an exact payout with the fewest notes.

The code defines a `PayoutPlannerService` with `minNotes(denominations, amount)` as a worked example of DP framing. A `Demo` provides note denominations and logs the minimum count.

The input is note denominations one, two, five and a payout of eleven. Step 5: the best is two fives and one, which is three notes. Step 6: we return three as the minimum note count, having solved each smaller amount exactly once.

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I revise dynamic programming, I focus on recognition and framing rather than memorising individual solutions. A problem is a dynamic programming candidate when it has optimal substructure, meaning the best overall answer is assembled from the best answers to smaller pieces, and overlapping subproblems, meaning a naive recursion would solve the same subproblem over and over. The moment I see both of those signals, I stop thinking about brute force.

My framing discipline is always the same four steps. First I define the state, the smallest set of parameters that fully describes a subproblem. Then I write the transition, expressing a state's answer in terms of strictly smaller states. Then I fix the base cases that need no further recursion. Finally I choose between memoization, which keeps the natural top-down recursion with a cache and shines when only part of the state space is reachable, and tabulation, which fills bottom-up, avoids any recursion-depth risk, and makes space optimisation obvious. I also keep the common patterns ready: one-dimensional sequence states, two-dimensional two-sequence grids, item-and-capacity knapsack states, interval span states, and grid-coordinate states.

At the National Bank of India I used this framing repeatedly, for example planning a cash payout with the fewest notes, where the state was the remaining amount, the transition tried each denomination as the last note, and the base case was zero notes for zero amount. Being able to name optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems, walk through the state-transition-base-case discipline, and justify memoization versus tabulation is exactly how I show an interviewer that I can attack an unseen dynamic programming problem rather than just recite memorised ones.

answers.question: Customers pay with 5, 10, or 20 unit notes for a 5 unit item and you start with no change. Determine whether you can give correct change to every customer in order. Explain the greedy strategy, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Lemonade Change (Greedy Change-Making at a Counter)

s1_definition.profdef: Lemonade Change decides whether a cashier starting with no float can give correct change to a queue of customers paying with fixed note values. The greedy rule keeps running counts of each note and, when change is owed, dispenses the largest notes first, preserving small notes which are scarce and more flexible. It fails the instant a required change cannot be formed.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India branch counter accepts fixed-value notes for a fixed-price service and must return exact change from the notes it has collected so far. It hands out larger notes first to keep its flexible small notes in reserve.
s1_definition.oneliner: Give change using the largest notes first to hoard the scarce small notes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Lemonade Change decides whether a cashier starting with no float can give correct change to a queue of customers paying with fixed note values. The greedy rule keeps running counts of each note and, when change is owed, dispenses the largest notes first, preserving small notes which are scarce and more flexible. It fails the instant a required change cannot be formed.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India branch counter accepts fixed-value notes for a fixed-price service and must return exact change from the notes it has collected so far. It hands out larger notes first to keep its flexible small notes in reserve.

**One line to remember:** Give change using the largest notes first to hoard the scarce small notes.

sections.s2_technical:
We track how many five-unit and ten-unit notes we currently hold; twenty-unit notes are never used for change so we need not count them. A five-unit payment needs no change, so we simply keep the note. A ten-unit payment needs five in change, so we must have a five. A twenty-unit payment needs fifteen in change, and we prefer one ten and one five over three fives, because fives are more useful for future ten-unit payments. If at any point the required change cannot be assembled, we fail immediately.

The core logic is `if (pay == 5) fives++; else if (pay == 10) { if (fives == 0) return false; fives--; tens++; } else { if (tens > 0 && fives > 0) { tens--; fives--; } else if (fives >= 3) fives -= 3; else return false; }`. A concrete check: payments 5, 5, 5, 10, 20 succeed, while 5, 5, 10, 10, 20 fail because the last twenty cannot be changed. Senior nuance: the greedy preference for giving larger notes first is provably optimal here because fives dominate in flexibility, and the whole scan is linear time and constant space.

Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a branch counter for a fixed-fee service where customers pay with five, ten, or twenty unit notes and the counter starts with no float. The counter must return exact change to each customer in the order they arrive, using only notes collected from earlier customers. The team wants to know whether a given arrival sequence can be served fully. This is exactly how Lemonade Change works: greedily give larger notes first and fail if change cannot be made.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Lemonade Change is a greedy problem where the key realisation is that not all notes are equally useful. I track running counts of the five-unit and ten-unit notes I hold, and I ignore the twenty-unit notes for change because they are never handed back. A five-unit payment needs no change, a ten-unit payment needs a single five, and a twenty-unit payment needs fifteen, which I can make either as a ten plus a five or as three fives.

The greedy decision that makes this correct is to always prefer giving a ten plus a five over three fives when I owe fifteen. Fives are the scarce, flexible currency because every ten-unit payment consumes one, so I hoard them by spending larger notes first. This is provably optimal here, and the algorithm simply fails the moment a required amount of change cannot be assembled from what I currently hold. The whole thing is a single linear pass using only a couple of counters.

At the National Bank of India I used this exact logic at a branch counter for a fixed-fee service where the till started empty and had to return exact change to customers in arrival order using only notes collected from earlier customers. I ran the greedy check to confirm whether a given arrival sequence could be fully served and to alert staff before a change shortage occurred. Explaining why fives are the scarce resource, the prefer-larger-notes-first rule, and the immediate-failure condition is what shows an interviewer I understand why this greedy strategy is both correct and efficient.

answers.question: Given an array where each value is the maximum jump length from that index, determine whether you can reach the last index starting from the first. Explain the greedy farthest-reach approach, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Jump Game (Can You Reach the Last Index with a Greedy Reach)

s1_definition.profdef: Jump Game decides reachability of the last index when each index allows a jump of up to its value. The greedy approach scans left to right maintaining the farthest index reachable so far; if the current index ever exceeds that reach, we are stuck and return false, otherwise we extend the reach and succeed once it covers the last index. It runs in a single linear pass.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India plans a multi-leg fund transfer where each account permits forwarding up to a certain number of legs ahead, and we check whether the funds can reach the final settlement account.
s1_definition.oneliner: Track the farthest reachable index; if an index passes it, you are stuck.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Jump Game decides reachability of the last index when each index allows a jump of up to its value. The greedy approach scans left to right maintaining the farthest index reachable so far; if the current index ever exceeds that reach, we are stuck and return false, otherwise we extend the reach and succeed once it covers the last index. It runs in a single linear pass.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India plans a multi-leg fund transfer where each account permits forwarding up to a certain number of legs ahead, and we check whether the funds can reach the final settlement account.

**One line to remember:** Track the farthest reachable index; if an index passes it, you are stuck.

sections.s2_technical:
We maintain a single variable, the farthest index we can currently reach, starting at zero. We scan each index from left to right. If the current index is beyond the farthest reach, there is no way to have arrived here, so we return false. Otherwise we update the farthest reach to the maximum of itself and the current index plus its jump value. The moment the farthest reach covers or passes the last index, we can stop and return true.

The core scan is `int farthest = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { if (i > farthest) return false; farthest = Math.max(farthest, i + nums[i]); if (farthest >= n - 1) return true; } return true;`. A concrete check: with jumps 2, 3, 1, 1, 4 we reach the end, while with 3, 2, 1, 0, 4 we get stuck at the zero before the last index and return false. Senior nuance: the greedy works because reachability is monotone, so the farthest reach fully summarises the past; it is linear time and constant space, far better than a quadratic dynamic programming over every pair of indices.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Jump Game asks whether I can reach the last index of an array when each index lets me jump up to its own value, and the elegant solution is a greedy scan that tracks a single number: the farthest index I can currently reach. I walk left to right, and at each index I first check whether that index is even reachable, meaning it lies within the farthest reach I have accumulated. If an index ever lies beyond that reach, there is no way to have arrived, so I immediately return false.

Otherwise I extend the farthest reach to the maximum of its current value and the current index plus its jump value, and the moment that reach covers the last index I can stop and return true. The reason the greedy is correct is that reachability is monotone: once a stretch of indices is reachable, the only thing that matters going forward is how far I can now get, which the single farthest-reach variable captures completely. This is linear time and constant space, a big improvement over a quadratic dynamic programming that checks every pair of indices.

At the National Bank of India I used this to validate a chained fund transfer across intermediary accounts, where each account could forward the funds a limited number of legs ahead based on its clearing limit, and we needed to know whether the funds could reach the final settlement account before initiating the chain. Explaining the farthest-reach invariant, the stuck condition when an index exceeds it, and why monotone reachability justifies the greedy is what shows an interviewer I can spot when a greedy beats a dynamic programming.

answers.question: Each child has a greed factor and each cookie has a size; a child is content only if a cookie's size meets or exceeds the child's greed. Maximise the number of content children. Explain the greedy two-pointer approach, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Assign Cookies (Greedy Matching of Smallest Sufficient Resource)

s1_definition.profdef: Assign Cookies maximises satisfied children by matching each with the smallest cookie that meets their greed factor. Sorting both children and cookies ascending and sweeping with two pointers, we give the current smallest sufficient cookie to the least greedy unsatisfied child, never wasting a large cookie on a child a smaller one could satisfy. It runs in sorting time.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India allocates limited credit facilities to applicants, each needing at least a minimum amount; we satisfy the most applicants by giving each the smallest facility that still meets their minimum, saving larger facilities for needier applicants.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort both sides and give each claimant the smallest resource that still satisfies them.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Assign Cookies maximises satisfied children by matching each with the smallest cookie that meets their greed factor. Sorting both children and cookies ascending and sweeping with two pointers, we give the current smallest sufficient cookie to the least greedy unsatisfied child, never wasting a large cookie on a child a smaller one could satisfy. It runs in sorting time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India allocates limited credit facilities to applicants, each needing at least a minimum amount; we satisfy the most applicants by giving each the smallest facility that still meets their minimum, saving larger facilities for needier applicants.

**One line to remember:** Sort both sides and give each claimant the smallest resource that still satisfies them.

sections.s2_technical:
We sort the children's greed factors ascending and the cookie sizes ascending, then use two pointers, one over children and one over cookies. For the current least greedy unsatisfied child, we advance the cookie pointer until we find a cookie large enough; if that cookie satisfies the child we count a success and move both pointers forward, otherwise we discard cookies too small for even this least greedy child. This ordering guarantees we never spend a larger cookie where a smaller one would have done.

The two-pointer core is `int i = 0, j = 0, happy = 0; while (i < greed.length && j < size.length) { if (size[j] >= greed[i]) { happy++; i++; } j++; }`. A concrete check: with greed factors 1, 2, 3 and cookie sizes 1, 1, the first child takes a size one cookie and no further child can be satisfied, so the answer is one. Senior nuance: correctness follows from an exchange argument, giving the smallest sufficient resource to the least demanding claimant never reduces the count; the dominant cost is the sorting at n log n, and the sweep itself is linear.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Assign Cookies is a greedy matching problem, and the governing principle is to never waste a large resource where a small one would do. I sort the claimants by how much they demand and the resources by size, both ascending, then sweep with two pointers. For the least demanding unsatisfied claimant, I advance through the resources until I find one large enough; if it satisfies them I count a success and move to the next claimant, and either way I consume that resource.

The correctness rests on an exchange argument: giving the smallest sufficient resource to the least demanding claimant can never reduce the total number satisfied, because any solution that used a larger resource there could swap in the smaller one without harm and keep the larger resource free for a needier claimant. The cost is dominated by the two sorts at n log n, and the two-pointer sweep itself is linear.

At the National Bank of India I used this to allocate a limited pool of credit facilities of varying sizes to applicants who each needed at least a minimum amount, maximising the number of applicants served. Sorting both sides and matching each applicant to the smallest facility that met their minimum avoided squandering large facilities on applicants a small one could satisfy. Explaining the sort-and-sweep structure, the smallest-sufficient matching rule, and the exchange argument that proves it optimal is what shows an interviewer I understand greedy matching.

answers.question: Given items with weights and values and a capacity, maximise total value when you may take fractions of items. Explain why a greedy by value-to-weight ratio is optimal here, contrast it with 0/1 Knapsack, the operations, the complexity, and a banking use case.
answers.shortTitle: Fractional Knapsack (Greedy by Value Density)

s1_definition.profdef: Fractional Knapsack maximises value within a weight capacity when items may be taken partially. The greedy strategy sorts items by value-to-weight ratio descending and fills the capacity with the densest items first, taking a fraction of the last item that only partly fits. Unlike 0/1 Knapsack, the fractional version is optimally solved greedily because partial selection removes the all-or-nothing obstacle.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India deploys a fixed amount of capital across investments that can be funded partially, and it funds the highest return-per-unit investments first to maximise total return.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort by value per unit weight and fill greedily, splitting the last item if needed.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Fractional Knapsack maximises value within a weight capacity when items may be taken partially. The greedy strategy sorts items by value-to-weight ratio descending and fills the capacity with the densest items first, taking a fraction of the last item that only partly fits. Unlike 0/1 Knapsack, the fractional version is optimally solved greedily because partial selection removes the all-or-nothing obstacle.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India deploys a fixed amount of capital across investments that can be funded partially, and it funds the highest return-per-unit investments first to maximise total return.

**One line to remember:** Sort by value per unit weight and fill greedily, splitting the last item if needed.

sections.s2_technical:
We compute each item's value-to-weight ratio, its return per unit of capacity, and sort items by that ratio from highest to lowest. We then walk the sorted items, taking each one whole while it fits, subtracting its weight from the remaining capacity and adding its full value. When an item does not fully fit, we take the fraction that fills the remaining capacity, adding a proportional share of its value, and then the capacity is full and we stop. Because fractions are allowed, there is never a reason to skip a denser item in favour of a sparser one.

The greedy core is `sort by value/weight desc; for (Item it : items) { if (cap >= it.w) { cap -= it.w; total += it.v; } else { total += it.v * ((double) cap / it.w); break; } }`. A concrete check: with items of weight and value (10, 60), (20, 100), (30, 120) and capacity fifty, we take the first two whole and two-thirds of the third, for a total of two hundred forty. Senior nuance: this greedy is provably optimal only because of fractionality; the 0/1 version, where items are indivisible, defeats the greedy and requires dynamic programming. The cost is dominated by the sort at n log n.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has a fixed amount of capital to deploy across several investment opportunities, each with an expected return and a capital requirement, and crucially each investment can be funded partially. The treasury team wants to maximise total expected return. Funding a low-density investment before a high-density one wastes capital. This is exactly how Fractional Knapsack works: fund the highest return-per-unit investments first, splitting the last one to exactly fill the capital.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Fractional Knapsack is the problem where a greedy strategy is not just a heuristic but provably optimal, and the reason is the single word fractional. Because I am allowed to take a partial amount of any item, I compute each item's value-to-weight ratio, its return per unit of capacity, sort the items from the densest to the least dense, and simply fill the capacity from the top of that list. I take each item whole while it fits, and when I reach an item that only partly fits, I take exactly the fraction that fills the remaining capacity and add a proportional share of its value.

The contrast with 0/1 Knapsack is the point interviewers probe. In the 0/1 version items are indivisible, so the greedy by ratio can be wrong: a single dense but small item might block a pair of items that together fill the capacity more valuably, which is why that version needs dynamic programming. The moment fractions are permitted, that trap disappears, because any leftover capacity can always be filled with a slice of the next-densest item, so a simple exchange argument proves the ratio-sorted greedy optimal. The cost is dominated by the sort at n log n.

At the National Bank of India I used this to deploy a fixed capital pool across investment opportunities that could be funded partially, funding the highest return-per-capital opportunities first and taking a fraction of the last one to exactly exhaust the capital. Explaining the value-density sort, the partial fill of the final item, and precisely why fractionality makes the greedy optimal where the indivisible version needs dynamic programming is what shows an interviewer I understand both the greedy technique and its boundaries.
